title: The Celebrity Traitors review – Ross Kemp really needs to get a grip | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: The most hotly anticipated TV show of the year is here! And a number of the stars – ahem Grant Mitchell – are struggling already …
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The most hotly anticipated TV show of the year is here! And a number of the stars – ahem Grant Mitchell – are struggling already …
Content: Clothes and attitude … Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAView image in fullscreenClothes and attitude … Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PATV reviewThe TraitorsReviewThe Celebrity Traitors review – Ross Kemp really needs to get a gripThe most hotly anticipated TV show of the year is here! And a number of the stars – ahem Grant Mitchell – are struggling already …Lucy ManganThu 1 Oct 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWarning: this article contains spoilers for episode one of The Celebrity Traitors.So – have they managed to capture lightning in a franchised bottle again? The new series of The Celebrity Traitors, more hotly anticipated than Nigella entering the Bake Off tent, is here. Twenty-one contestants of varying levels of fame, but never dipping below C-list, have signed up to endure Claudia Winkleman’s tyranny in Ardross Castle, in the hope of winning up to £100,000 for their chosen charity and a place in the nation’s consciousness and possible heart for between one week and a lifetime, depending how things work out.We get our first glimpse of the gang as they file into a church replete with masked guards and floral tributes spelling out RIP and VIP at the altar. Actors, broadcasters, comedians, musicians and some miscellanea start to fill up the pews. Young Sebastian Croft pauses to genuflect before continuing down the aisle, and such is the power of the format that you immediately wonder if this is a tactic to make himself seem trustworthy. Will it work? Or is anyone with a religious belief marked as a weirdo for whom anything is possible these days?If you think that’s sensitivity gone mad, may I introduce you to Ross Kemp? Before the episode is out, he is turning bewildered circles in the castle, convinced that anyone who touches him is trying to murder him in plain sight. Get it together, Kemp. We’ve a long way to go yet.View image in fullscreen‘Already iconic’ … Richard E Grant.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/BBC Creative/PABut this is what we came for, of course. To see behind famous faces to the reality beneath. The hard man who is actually a soft target will do nicely. If mathematician Hannah Fry proves incapable of putting stats to work in her service, it will be noted. If Julie Hesmondhalgh (“I get hungry for friendship with people I see on the telly!”) turns out to be a Machiavellian genius, we will be over the moon. How long can they last in a game that is all about personalities before they have to reveal the true nature of theirs?It’s about 30 seconds for Richard E Grant. Most people – apart from Hannah Fry (“I am dripping with prefect energy”) – want to be chosen as traitors. But Reg publicly longs to be chosen as a traitor (“It would be the jackpot!”). He is chosen as a traitor. He is asked by Joe Lycett whether he is a traitor. “I am a traitor!” he gleefully replies. A drama queen without guile. An actor’s actor. “Already iconic,” says Claudia.View image in fullscreenRed alert … Jerry Hall.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/BBC Creative/PASome choose to ignore this revelation – unprecedented in the history of either Celebrity or peon Traitors. “He’s just acting out because he hasn’t been chosen,” says Jerry Hall, who has known him for 30 years – and you can well imagine him doing so. But in this case, he has just exuberantly shared the truth. Much of his time in the extended opening episode is spent trying to walk it back.From shocking cruelty to the reason Claudia hid in a bush: 10 things you need to know about The Celebrity TraitorsRead moreHis partner in treacherous crime is Love Island presenter Maya Jama (“My villain era has begun!”). Together, in one of the twists that any iteration of the series must serve up to keep participants and audience engaged, they must choose the third traitor from two people they haul in to plead their cases. The loser will be murdered (or, if you are one of the three people who do not know how the game works yet, “murdered”). They agree that they must choose two contestants who have taken Reg at his word and believe him (“I’m a traitor!”) to be a traitor. It’s between journalist Amol Rajan and comedian James Acaster. They wait in coffins – I am not a huge fan of this recurring motif, to be honest – to hear their fates, and we hear one of the lids bang shut as the credits roll.So, the lightning – is it bottled? Not quite as successfully as last time. The law of diminishing returns is brutal in television. The cast feels slightly more muted – the energy is not quite there yet. But Claudia and her clothes and attitude are, and the opening episode of any Traitors outing is always the weakest. It is relationships and alliances that make the show, and they of course take time to build. Seeds have been sown (is Jerry Hall bossy? Is former army captain James Blunt about to reinvent himself as a national hero? Will Romesh Ranganathan and Rob Beckett’s real-life friendship be an asset or a liability?) and will flourish in due course. But it feels as if they are at work in ever so slightly less fertile soil this time round.The Celebrity Traitors aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now. title: Welcome to the new Reform roadshow. Same as the last but more desperate | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Nige is not rattled that the UK likes its new PM. Or that Reform is second in the polls. Oh no. Because Nige believes in Nige
Author: John Crace
Headline: Nige is not rattled that the UK likes its new PM. Or that Reform is second in the polls. Oh no. Because Nige believes in Nige
Content: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage at a party rally in Doncaster.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersView image in fullscreenReform UK leader Nigel Farage at a party rally in Doncaster.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersThe politics sketchReform UKWelcome to the new Reform roadshow. Same as the last but more desperateJohn CraceNige is not rattled that the UK likes its new PM. Or that Reform is second in the polls. Oh no. Because Nige believes in NigeThu 1 Oct 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTShareNearly 10 years ago,Nigel Faragetold LBC he would leave the country if Brexit were not a stunning success. For reasons that no one can quite fathom, he is still here. Could it be that he is a man who can’t be trusted to keep his word? Surely not.Nige wants you to know he’s very much still around. He might have been a bit quiet over the past few weeks, as Reform had to deal with one or two unfortunate investigations into their funding, but now he’s very much back. And he’s definitely not rattled that Labour has a prime minister the country likes. Nor is he at all rattled that Reform has tumbled into second placein the polls. Oh, no. Because Nige believes in Nige. Now more than ever. The last creepy-crawly after the apocalypse. Lying on its back, gasping for air. But still breathing. The dream still alive.Welcome to the new Reform roadshow. Much the same as the last Reform roadshow, only with added desperation. You can almost sense the jeopardy. A dream receding into the distance. Supporters clinging just that bit tighter to each other in the echo chamber. The cheers just a bit too forced. The performance ever more contrived. Just a rehash of all the old lines with a flashing light show thrown in. We are promised one a week from now until the next general election. It’s going to be a long three years. Even Nige might be sick of Nige by then.Do parents make the politician? Find out on the Today programme’s psychotherapy couch | John CraceRead moreFor the first outing of The Rolling Grievance Tour, Reform had taken over a room at Doncaster racecourse. But we were made to wait for Nige. The Reform leader goes nowhere these days without a couple of charisma-free fluffers as his warm-up acts. Men whose sole job is to make Nige look good. Men who are guaranteed to have the audience begging to be let out within minutes. First up was Matt Goodwin, the candidate who failed to get elected in Gorton and Denton. Someone who everyone seems to dislike on sight. Because it saves time that way. His sole function appears to be to make Nige look a little less unpleasant.Then we had Richard Tice. Dicky would travel the length of the country if he was told there was going to be an audience of two. He is the very definition of needy. He is also spectacularly dim in the way that only posh boys can be. On the self-awareness scale he drops below zero. He has no idea people are laughing at him, not with him.His attempts to be down with the little people were met with collective despair. “My first job was digging trenches,” he said, desperate to ingratiate himself with an audience he openly despises. Mate, you became director of that multimillion-pound property empire because your grandfather owned it. In a fairer world, you would still be a complete nobody. At best, you would be a low-achieving middle manager somewhere. Instead, Dicky thinks he is eyeing up a cabinet post in the next government. “If I fail to deliver in 100 days, I will resign,” he promised. Why not just call it quits now?Then a video of Nige saying he couldn’t be bought. Except he can. With a £70 cameo video or what looked like a £5m inducement from a Thai crypto-billionaire to lure him out of retirement. Then the man himself. Looking tired. Struggling to find his usual energy as he went through his familiar numbers. All this hate must be exhausting. But it was worth it, when he was a novelty. No one asked too many questions. He could pretend to be an insurgent. The anti-establishment choice. Except he will never be anything but the establishment.He began by insulting his audience. First by claiming the St Leger was the first classic of the season when it is the last – if you’re going to try to ingratiate yourself, you should at least get some basic facts right – then by rubbishing Doncaster itself. It was a shithole. He couldn’t imagine why anyone still lived there. If what the residents did could actually be called living. Still, he was doing them a favour by granting them an hour in his presence. So they did have that.“Ed Miliband is never seen in Doncaster,” he declared. Yup. And you’re never seenin Clacton. So that evens things up. At least he’s in the cabinet. Time to talk about foreigners coming over in small boats. They were all a security risk. As the incident at Fairford proved (not). I’m sure the police will be thrilled to have Nige commenting on a live investigation. He had earlier even suggested that the men had deliberately got themselves arrested so they could time the police response. Even Matt the Twat isn’t that half-witted.On and on Nige went. Same old lines. Same old grievances. Nothing positive to say other than that he would miraculously cure the entire country in 100 days. A task that may take other politicians decades. It goes without saying he didn’t say how. Just believe. A man of his brilliance can do anything. Moral decline, he said sadly. We are a Judeo-Christian country. Foreigners had been put on warning. Yawn.Inevitably, we got to Andy Burnham’s promise to reset the country’s relationship with the EU. Nige was certain it would be a disaster. Because Brexit had been a tremendous success and Burnham was seeking division. The irony meter had ramped up several notches. No one does division quite like Nige. It’s his USP. Though weirdly he has achieved some consensus. Thanks to him, most of the country now thinks Brexit was an idiotic idea. Quite the achievement. He also went on to accuse Andy of smashing the pensioners by removing the triple lock. He may want to tell Thick Dick that. Dicky is on record as saying thetriple lockhad to go.“I am different,” he said in conclusion. He wasn’t in politics for rank or status. He had enough money to do what he liked. He was getting on a bit. In fact, he wasn’t sure why he was doing this. Other than the fact he is a raging narcissist who craves constant attention and affirmation. As if to prove the point he insisted that people kept begging him to save them. In his mind, he is the Messiah. The second coming. He didn’t want to change the electoral system, he wanted to abolish it. After him, there would be no need for elections. The thousand year Reich. Nirvana.All he wanted was just a normal far-right country. A place where England was for the English. Once we had deported all foreign criminals there would be no need for prisons because white people would stop breaking the law. Foreigners were dragging us down. Spiritually, financially, morally. We had lost our way like lost sheep. All we had to do was believe in Nige. An act of faith. Only not even Nige believes in Nige any more.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchNigel FaragecommentShareReuse this content

title: Hay Fever review – Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski host Coward’s country house shenanigans | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Grant brings shock-haired vigour as a vain novelist forced to welcome his boho children’s surprise guests in comedy of clipped social embarrassment
Author: Emma John
Headline: Grant brings shock-haired vigour as a vain novelist forced to welcome his boho children’s surprise guests in comedy of clipped social embarrassment
Content: Brew haha … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski in Hay Fever at Wyndham’s theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenBrew haha … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski in Hay Fever at Wyndham’s theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewHay Fever review – Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski host Coward’s country house shenanigansWyndham’s theatre, LondonGrant brings shock-haired vigour as a vain novelist forced to welcome his boho children’s surprise guests in comedy of clipped social embarrassmentEmma JohnThu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHay Fever, now one of Noël Coward’s best-known and most-performed works, hasn’t always been a smash hit. British critics who found itsWest Enddebut in 1925 amusing enough nevertheless noted its lack of plot, and the first Broadway production was a flop. A critic for Vogue called it “funny in places”, which sounds like the kind of stinging putdown you’d expect from the playwright’s own hand.A century of performances have proved the play’s lasting power, but its comic effect has always lain less in the words as written than their delivery – it is, after all, about a family that is “artificial to the point of lunacy”. At their centre is diva Judith Bliss, who has retired from the stage to take up the role of country hostess. When she, her husband and their self-consciously bohemian children Sorel and Simon all invite surprise guests for the weekend, the unfortunate attendees find themselves embroiled in a self-serving drama of exquisite embarrassment.View image in fullscreenRadiating charm … Ophelia Lovibond in Hay Fever.Photograph: Marc BrennerThe action takes place on Frankie Bradshaw’s sumptuous set, with corniced ceilings and French windows at the Blisses’ Berkshire pile that are almost an extension of the Wyndham’s ornate interior. The stage is populated with effusions of flowers and a fine cast, not leastRichard E Grantwho seems to be having a heyday of robe-and-slipper roles. He brings his trademark shock-haired vigour to the narcissist-novelist David, bounding down a grand staircase to read his latest work to his family.Will Close’s Simon swings from pretentious artiste – in paint-stained plus-fours and buttoned boots – to Tiggerish lover at the arrival of the experienced Myra (a statuesque Nancy Carroll). And even the seen-it-all-seductress is less in command than she thought as the games progress from after-dinner entertainments to more overtly saucy ones. Charles Edwards, meanwhile, maintains an endless gallantry as the visiting diplomat whose social skills are strained to the limit as he falls beneath Judith’s spell.Judith was inspired by real-life American actor Laurette Taylor – excuse enough, should Christine Baranski have chosen, to play the part in her own accent. Instead, a technically sound RP oddly constrains her. Judith’s combination of pretend languor and genuine vagueness mean that jokes go begging and some lines land too earnestly, as when she tells her daughter: “I’m very glad you’re pretty.” The squabbles and blow-ups are comically theatrical enough, but there’s not enough of Judith’s much-vaunted “vitality” to entirely make sense of them when they come.‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatreRead moreInstead it’s Ophelia Lovibond’s Sorel who emerges as the most vital character. She’s the only one of the bunch with any self-awareness, a smile half-playing on her lips, radiating charm that makes even her own selfishness seem forgivable. Director Emily Burns’s CV majors in farce and she stages some lovely bits of business, including a scene when a servant silently lays a breakfast table to a swellingly romantic soundtrack and a Gone With the Wind-crimson backdrop. On the first of multiple press nights, some of the comic timing isn’t quite up and running – but a stronger second half suggests that when the production beds in, there will be plenty of classic Coward to enjoy.AtWyndham’s theatre, London, until 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreNoel CowardWest EndRichard E GrantComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham is right that ‘hope comes from honesty’. That’s why Labour must make the case for rejoining the EU | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: Brexit was a disastrous act of national self-harm. Britain needs EU membership to bring growth and security in an increasingly volatile world, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: Brexit was a disastrous act of national self-harm. Britain needs EU membership to bring growth and security in an increasingly volatile world, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: Andy Burnham meets with European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, at the UN general assembly, in New York, 22 September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham meets with European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, at the UN general assembly, in New York, 22 September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersOpinionBrexitBurnham is right that ‘hope comes from honesty’. That’s why Labour must make the case for rejoining the EUSadiq KhanBrexit was a disastrous act of national self-harm. Britain needs EU membership to bring growth and security in an increasingly volatile worldThu 1 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTShareHope again. That was theprime minister’s messageto the country this week. Anational social care system, greater public control of water and energy, help for first-time buyers and a crackdown on rogue landlords and empty homes. With clarity and conviction, Andy Burnham set out a bold plan to put Britain on a new path, steeped in Labour values.It felt like a conference speech that would be remembered for years to come, marking a decisive break with a broken political model that has let British people down for decades. And perhaps most encouraging of all was the prime minister’s promise torethink Britain’s relationship with the EU.Burnham’s words were simple but stark: “Brexit has done more harm than good.” He is right – and the reality of the vote’s impact on the UK is sobering. Researchcommissioned by City Hall in 2024showed that London’s economy was £30bn smaller than it would have been without Brexit and that there were nearly 2m fewer jobs overall in the UK as a result of us leaving. Earlier this year, weset out new analysisshowing that our country has grown more slowly than our comparable European counterparts since 2016. If that trend continues, our economy could be £250bn smaller than similar EU countries’ by 2030.Ten years after the referendum, the sunlit uplands promised by the Brexiters have proven to be a total fiction. Instead, Britain finds itself battling an economic and geopolitical storm.Earlier this year,I warned thatDonald Trump’s bombing of Iran could have catastrophic consequences for Londoners, and it gives me no pleasure to be proved right. The folly of this reckless war of choice is now clear for all to see. The conflict is sending shock waves through the global economy, hiking up mortgage costs and pushing up fuel prices. The price of diesel hashit an all-time highat nearly £2 per litre, while energy bills are forecastto rise 25% this winter, piling unbearable pressure on many households across the UK already grappling with a cost-of-living crisis.I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen JonesRead moreAt the same time, Trump’s fondness for unilateralism has shaken the foundations of the transatlantic alliance on which our national security depends. As Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, persists with his illegal and unconscionable full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Trump’s unpredictable actions and unsettling ambivalence towards European security can no longer be ignored.In this geopolitical storm, Europe offers us not just a safe harbour, but a huge opportunity for growth. The EU is our biggest trading partner and our most reliable ally. That’s why, at the UK-EU summit in November, I will call on the government to lay the groundwork for Britain’s swift return to both the customs union and the single market – a move that should happen within this parliament.Rejoining the customs union and the single market would deliver an immediate boost to economic growth, improving living standards for communities across the country and helping to grant Londoners some respite from the most acute cost of living pressures. In the long term, however, we must raise our ambitions higher still. Our party must immediately start making the case for rejoining the EU, so we can fight and win a general election with EU membership effectively on the ballot paper in 2029.The brutal truth is that leaving the EU was the biggest act of economic and geopolitical self-harm in our country’s history. Rejoining is the only viable path to long-term prosperity and security. Anything less will fail to undo the severe damage that’s been done.For far too long, theLabourparty’s debate about Europe has been constrained by “red lines” that make rebuilding our relationship with the EU impossible. But Burnham has now recognised that these lines were drawn up for a different world.In Canada,Mark Carney has set out his planto partner much more closely with the EU on defence, critical minerals and energy security, with the country now on the path to becoming the bloc’s first associate member. In this multipolar world, middle powers such as Canada, the UK and our European neighbours must come together, both to safeguard our own security and economies and to stand up for free trade and our liberal democratic values.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDeeper integration can – and will – unlock a new age of growth and productivity, but it will also provide us with a louder voice on the world stage. From bolstering our military defences to safely developing AI and combating the climate crisis, if we are to make ourselves heard, we must speak as one. And in a world whose superpowers appear ever more comfortable with throwing their weight around, the EU is the only organisation with the economic and geopolitical heft to hold its own.For me, the most memorable line inBurnham’s speechcame a couple of minutes in: “Hope comes from honesty.” They were the words of a leader unafraid to change the terms of Britain’s dysfunctional political debate by taking on the seemingly intractable problems that too many would be inclined to avoid.Today, Brexit is foremost among those problems. If we are to bring back hope, we must be honest about the disastrous costs of our decision to leave the EU. And we must be honest about the fact that reversing it is the best chance we have to get Britain back on track – and get the country firing on all cylinders again.Sadiq Khan is mayor of LondonExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionLabourEuropeForeign policyLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Esther Rantzen: one of the UK’s boldest, bravest ever campaigners – right to the very end | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: The TV host, who died this week aged 86, was in recent years one of the most vociferous proponents of assisted dying, but her activism dates back decades to her time on That’s Life!
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The TV host, who died this week aged 86, was in recent years one of the most vociferous proponents of assisted dying, but her activism dates back decades to her time on That’s Life!
Content: Esther Rantzen, after revealing her lung cancer diagnosis in January 2023.Photograph: Esther Rantzen/PAView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen, after revealing her lung cancer diagnosis in January 2023.Photograph: Esther Rantzen/PAEsther RantzenEsther Rantzen: one of the UK’s boldest, bravest ever campaigners – right to the very endWhen she got serious, she got very serious. The TV host boosted organ donations, closed down a school for abuse, founded two revolutionary helplines – and put assisted dying on the agenda for years to comeFrom Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeEsther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in picturesStuart HeritageThu 1 Oct 2026 07.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy no means should That’s Life! have ever worked as a television programme. For more than 20 years it functioned as an absurd grab bag of features that at times seemed specifically designed to induce tonal whiplash in its viewers.To demonstrate this point, That’s Life! was the show that introduced the nation to Prince, a talking dog who could say the word“sausages”, but it was also the show that put pressure on the government to introduce mandatory seatbelt use for children. This was the show that invented a new animal as an April fool’s joke, only for coachloads of tourists to arrive at London Zoo to try to spot it. It was also the show that embarked on a vigorous three-month investigation into allegations of widespread sexual abuse by teachers at a boys’ boarding school, resulting in the school’s closure less than two weeks after the feature aired.All of which makes That’s Life! sound like The One Show on human growth hormones. Yet the show was one of the most popular of its time, regularly pulling in close to 20 million viewers. Key to its success was its producer and presenter,Esther Rantzen.Starting her career as a BBC Radio trainee sound effects assistant, Rantzen rose up the ranks as a researcher on shows such as Ned Sherrin’s BBC-3 before being given her first shot at presenting on Braden’s Week, a magazine show that came to sticky end when its host, Bernard Braden, was fired for advertising margarine on ITV. Nevertheless, that was all the grounding Rantzen needed to start a show of her own.View image in fullscreenRantzen with other members of the That’s Life! cast in 1989.Photograph: Bill Lovelace/Daily Mail/REX/ShutterstockAlong with producer John Lloyd, Rantzen devised That’s Life!, a series that would encompass every issue and indignity known to man. Fronted by Rantzen, with an ever-changing swirl of co-presenters around her, That’s Life would take on everything from dubious advertising to theover-proliferation of crisp flavours. There would be vox pops about theshare of domestic tasks undertaken by menand genuinely nightmarish features where people would pose as waxworks thenburst into songin a bid to inspire more singing in Britain.And Rantzen was the perfect host. This was down to her ability to maintain a sense of ease between all these tonal extremes. It paid off in spades, since when That’s Life! got serious, it got extremely serious. In 1984 it used a story about Ben Hardwick, a two-year-old boy who needed a liver transplant, to push for more widespread organ donation. And it worked – MPs noted in parliament in 1988 that it had directly led to a boom in the number of transplants.Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86Read moreIt also revealed the story of Nicholas Winton, dubbed the British Schindler, a man who assisted in the rescue of 669 children from what was then Czechoslovakia on the eve of the second world war. Winton’s acts went unacknowledged for half a century, until a 1988 episode of That’s Life! sat him in the studio audience, revealing that he was surrounded by dozens of the children he saved, along with their children and grandchildren. It was a profoundly emotional piece of television, and one that Rantzen was rightly proud of; this year she wrote the Guardian a letter of complaint when its list of theBBC’s 100 greatest moments omitted the episode.That’s Life! also focused heavily on child abuse, which resulted in Rantzen setting up Childline, the first national helpline for children in danger or distress. According to the NSPCC, Childline has helped six million children since it was established in 1986.When That’s Life! ended in 1994, Rantzen continued to embody the spirit of the series in all her ventures. She hosted her own talkshow, named Esther, which ran for eight years. And Hearts of Gold, which was inspired by Winton, shone a light on members of the public who had done good deeds, seeking out numerous unsung heroes. She continued to champion consumer rights with the shows Old Dogs New Tricks and Esther Rantzen’s House Trap. She also had stints on Strictly, I’m a Celebrity and Celebrity First Dates.Following the death of her husband, Desmond Wilcox, in 2000, Rantzen increasingly turned her focus towards end of life care. BBC Two’s How to Have a Good Death was a landmark programme about palliative care, and she built on this further after her cancer diagnosis in 2023. When she found out her cancer had reached stage four, she publicly announced that she had joined Dignitas, and used her final stretch of time to campaign heavily for assisted dying. Three weeks ago,MPs voted against an attempt to legalise it in England and Wales.But Rantzen’s relentless campaigning means that the conversation is unlikely to go away. Even in death, she may yet prove to be one of this country’s greatest campaigners.Share your tributes and memoriesYou can share your tributes and memories of Esther Rantzen using this form.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceit | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: No spoilers here – TV’s grand illusionist meets his match when he moves in with Theranos founder and her family
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: No spoilers here – TV’s grand illusionist meets his match when he moves in with Theranos founder and her family
Content: Elizabeth Holmes is quizzed by Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes is quizzed by Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24First look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewYou Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitNew York film festival:No spoilers here – TV’s grand illusionist meets his match when he moves in with Theranos founder and her familyAdrian HortonThu 1 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 20.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor anyone remotely near the worlds of documentary, comedy or medical fraud, there has been one thing on the mind for weeks now: a single-minute clip ofNathan Fielder, the absurdist comedian whose boundary-pushing HBO seriesThe Rehearsalcemented his status as docu-reality’s premier auteur, staring into the deep blue eyes ofElizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of the blood-testing startup Theranos. Unblinking, faces inches apart, the famously dry purveyor of harebrained business schemes and the convicted fraudster appeared locked in a battle of wills. “Are you being real right now?” Fielder asked her, in a classically meta bit – could Fielderreallyhave spent years filming a secret documentary with one of Silicon Valley’s most notorious pariahs?The prospect ofTV’s grand illusionistversusemblematic girl-boss scammerseemed potentially too good to be true; buzz for You Can See Everything, Fielder’s furtive documentary co-directed with wunderkind du jour Lance Oppenheim (whose narrative feature debut, the Robert Pattinson-starringPrimetime, premiered last month) was such that access to the film’s New York film festival premiere on Wednesday became this fall’shottest ticket.Those who were there can confirm: the hype is deserved. You Can See Everything is, somehow, more shocking, twistier, thornier and revealing than billed – a stupefying and gloriously destabilizing hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject. You know from the minute Billy Evans, Holmes’s shifty husband-cum-business partner who entered the picture post-Theranos, claims that “the best way for people to see who she is … is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”, while lying with Holmes on a playroom floor, that you’re in for a wild ride. My mouth was agape for, conservatively, one half of the film’s unusually deserved three-hour run time.Godzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise’s winning streakRead moreLet me say now, if you’ve made it this far: I will not spoil major shifts – and if you are at all familiar with the Fielder canon, you know they’re coming – for a singular movie whose enjoyment depends, in part, on an element of surprise, both for viewers and for film-makers who genuinely seem to not know what they signed up for when they walked into the Holmes-Evans household rental in 2023. Arguably the less you know about anything that is to come, the better.What I can tell you is that You Can See Everything is a masterpiece of who’s playing who, the fragility and absurdities of trust, seemingly begotten by chance. Back in 2023, convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy and awaiting the start of her 11-year sentence in prison, Holmes, along with Evans – who appears to be her match made in heaven, as neither ever blink and are maybe always lying – sought out a film crew to document their life with their two young children, in an attempt to protest her innocence and, perhaps, rebrand for Theranos 2.0. For some reason, they chose Oppenheim, adocumentarianwhose distinctive style – hyper-saturation, tight frames, creeping zooms – exposes the eerie in the mundane, and Fielder, whose precise style of spectrum-y, extreme cringe means that no question will be off the table. As Fielder points out on camera, in one of several exquisitely blunt confrontations, itisan odd choice to allow a comedian famous for his business scams to make a documentary that will supposedly clear your name of arguably the most famous fraud scandal of the 2010s.View image in fullscreenFielder and Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24The result is a three-hour documentary filmed like a thriller and scored like a drama that plays like an unraveling of certainty in real time. Oppenheim’s house style, shots tightly hugging then boring into a face with laser-like curiosity, perfectly suits the material; scenes that could be an unlikely tableau instead become a fascinating parade of inscrutable motivations, isolated actors bristling against the others. There is something extremely satisfying in watching Fielder’s sharp angles – arched eyebrows, needling questions, dispensation of social buffers – tangle with Holmes’s disposition (or performance? or genuine personality?) of guileless warmth, a strange and compelling chemistry building within a reality distortion field. If Fielder’s earlier work felt at times like it was punching down, trading on the naivety of regular people, well, he has finally met his match.Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand?Read moreI am, admittedly, writing around a film that must be seen to be discussed, and will surely engender much chatter as to what, exactly, we just witnessed. But trust that things devolve in a very Fielderian spiral, into a dissection of the form unlike anything I have ever seen or, as things get going and participants’ either lose their filters or sharpen their game, anything I have ever hoped to see when it comes to the figure known asElizabeth Holmes. Trust, too, that if there was a question you were hoping to ask Holmes or, moreover, her husband – did hereallyhave no reservations when he met the disgraced founder at a party in 2017, at the height of her scandal? – it gets asked, and then some (I did not need to know about conjugal visits, or lack thereof, in the Texas prison where Holmes continues to reside).Trust, ultimately, that you can see more than you ever imagined you’d see about Elizabeth Holmes and maybe get no closer to discerning the truth – and yet it will all be worth it.You Can See Everything screened at the New York film festival and will be released in the US on 16 October with UK and Australian release dates to be announcedExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewNathan FielderElizabeth HolmesDocumentary filmsA24reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes | Welfare | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment
Content: The plans are part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16- to 24-year-olds not in work, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe plans are part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16- to 24-year-olds not in work, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWelfareKey disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changesExclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employmentRowena Mason,Pippa CrerarandPatrick ButlerThu 1 Oct 2026 14.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned.Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work.The move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion byLabourMPs. But ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade them the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned.The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviewsby Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, andthe Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs.However, a central option under consideration for young people is removing the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month, and offering intensive support for people to get into work. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is being looked at.The extra support will include subsidised jobs for younger people, more targeted “back to work” schemesand support with mental health, as part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.As part of the same package, officials are looking at a new system to replace the Pip, which is claimed by four million people, after attempts to change existing eligibility criteria were rejected by MPs last year.One possible plan is for a separate regime to apply to the under-25 agegroup, with reduced or withdrawn entitlements – although those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities would not lose any money.View image in fullscreenProtests were held last summer outside parliament against proposals to change the personal independence payment (Pip). Officials are looking at a new system for Pip, which could involve a separate regime for under-25s.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianMore broadly, officials are working up plans under the replacement system for a new set of eligibility criteria and assessments for the extra costs of disability, and looking at whether this would apply to all claimants of working age, or those below a cut-off point such as 50 or 60. Again, those with the most severe conditions would not lose money or be reassessed.Officials have also been returning to the idea of cuts to the Motability scheme at a future budget, after axing tax breaks worth £300m. The scheme allows disabled people to use their Pip benefit to lease new cars for three years.One Whitehall source said removing or further cutting the health element of universal credit for those older than 25 had been considered, but government sources said this was not on the table.Officials have looked at systems in other countries, such as Denmark, which restricts access to its “disability pension” for under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they have no ability permanently to work.A government source said: “We will be bringing forward a comprehensive package of support and reform to tackle the scandal of a million young people not in education, employment or training. The details are yet to be decided, but we are committed to enabling work and opportunity, while always protecting those unable to work.”The significant changes would need legislation, with ministers and officials looking at a bill encompassing the replacement for Pip and changes to the under-25 system to be presented in the next session of parliament next year.Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, used his conference speech this week to describe changing the welfare system asa “moral crusade”, saying too many younger people were stuck claiming benefits for too long.However, the scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the impact on the cost of living for disabled people, particularly when Pip is a non-means-tested benefit that is unrelated to a person’s employment status.Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has gone further by saying she would ban young people from signing straight on to the benefits system if her party won the next election, aspart of a planto cut £23bn from the welfare bill. Under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment would no longer be able to claim universal credit and would instead have to undergo intensive job coaching.Reform UK plans to cut the overall welfare bill by £50bn, with Pip replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”, while “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by local authorities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the cost of living for disabled people.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianPolling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe thattackling the root causesof joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts”, and used hisparty conference speechto signal an overhaul of the welfare system to pay for an expansion of youth jobs and training support.UK welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people including Neets – but not children – about 2.5%. Milburn said it was “shameful” the government spent 25 times as much on benefits for them than it did on supporting them into work.More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities warned ministers earlier this year against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.The disability charity Scope has estimated about half of households with an under-22 receiving the universal credit health element are already in poverty, which it said could rise to more than nine in 10 if support was removed.Campaigners warned that any move to cut benefits or increase conditionality rules was likely to drive many youngsters further away from the jobs market.Lucy Schonegevel, the director of impact at Action for Children, said: “We are deeply concerned by reports that disability benefits for under-25s could be cut. If confirmed, that would be at odds with the prime minister’s recent warning against ‘crude cuts’ … Serious investment in high quality, tailored employment support is vital, but employment support alone cannot overcome a lack of jobs.”A DWP spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews, due in the autumn, will lay the foundation for sustainable reform, and we will not pre-empt their findings.“We are already changing the system through the youth guarantee, narrowing the gap between universal credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing a record £3.5bn in employment support for disabled people and those with long-term conditions. We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.”Milburn has said that too few young people who moved on to disability benefits received help into work. Many became “trapped” on benefits, with evidence showing half were not in work 15 years later, an outcome he called a “catastrophic failure”.He appeared to hint at the potential political risks of cuts to benefits at a Labour party conference fringe meeting on youth employment on Monday, saying “when it comes to benefit cuts it will be tricky” – but added that not acting would be financially unsustainable and worse for young people.About 184,000 young people in the UK aged 16-24 receive the universal credit health element. The government has already cut this benefit, having previously announced a 50% reduction to £217 a month for most new claimants from next April.Explore more on these topicsWelfareBenefitsUniversal creditDisabilityYoung peopleYouth unemploymentState benefitsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK-Iran national arrested under Terrorism Act over RAF Fairford incident | UK news | The Guardian
description: Counter-terrorism police arrest 25-year-old in Westminster and search two properties in central London
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Counter-terrorism police arrest 25-year-old in Westminster and search two properties in central London
Content: A police roadblock near RAF Fairford airbase on 29 September.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenA police roadblock near RAF Fairford airbase on 29 September.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersUK newsUK-Iran national arrested under Terrorism Act over RAF Fairford incidentCounter-terrorism police arrest 25-year-old in Westminster and search two properties in central LondonJamie GriersonThu 1 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDetectives have arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of an investigation into a suspected plot near RAF Fairford.Counter-terrorism police said the 25-year-old man was arrested on Thursday in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.Five men in their 20s were arrested in the village of Whelford, Gloucestershire, outside the RAF base in the early hours of Sunday after police were alerted to suspicious vans in the area. They were released on police bail.Announcing the most recent arrest, Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism police, said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”Counter-terrorism police said two properties had been searched in Westminster, London.Evans added: “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry.”An Iranian link to the events in the Gloucestershire countryside over the weekend is considered increasingly likely, as the police and security services’ investigation continues. Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.It was revealed on Sunday that a farmer driving home from a party at about 1am on Sunday had spotted the men and vans and called 999.But on Tuesday it emerged that one of the five men arrested near the base called the police to report the incident.The mounting view among investigators that Iran was likely involved was a key reason for Andy Burnham’s decision to call a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, which was attended by senior police and security officials.Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days.Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.The suspects were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. The decision on Monday to bail the men came after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London, all of which found no evidence of a viable device.Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation, which is trying to establish why the five men, all British nationals from London, were in the Gloucestershire countryside, close to a sensitive site in the middle of the night.The vans were marked with the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles.People detained for terrorism offences can be detained under two legal schedules that dictate how long they can be held without charge.Under the terrorism schedule, a suspect can be held for up to 14 days but cannot be bailed.The 25-year-old man arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace), a spokesperson for CTP said.That means he could be released on bail under investigation, but detectives have much less time to hold him.The five men arrested early on Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside were held under Pace before being bailed the next day.The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on Whelford.Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester, and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting | France | The Guardian
description: About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
Content: Students take part in a blockade outside Voltaire high school in Paris's 11th arrondissement.Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStudents take part in a blockade outside Voltaire high school in Paris's 11th arrondissement.Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/ShutterstockFranceFrance school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meetingAbout 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the countryJon Henleyin ParisThu 1 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfast-growing protestby high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.View image in fullscreenThe pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves.Photograph: CLPress/Abaca/ShutterstockNearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured.The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils.Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.View image in fullscreenRiot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”.Studentswere protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.View image in fullscreenInjuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesWhile many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”The government has accused the radical left LaFranceInsoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestSchoolsEuropeStudentsYoung peopleHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier League | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister
Content: Andy Burnham accused the Premier League of ‘abuse of process’ when it punished Everton in 2023.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham accused the Premier League of ‘abuse of process’ when it punished Everton in 2023.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAManchester CityAndy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier LeagueGovernment said to be unhappy at lack of warningTreasury committee chair wants HMRC involved in City caseMatt HughesThu 1 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s intervention in theManchester Citydebate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister.Government officials are ­understood to be unhappy they were not given notice that the ­independent commission’s damning judgment of £900m offinancial manipulation and “sham contracts”would be published shortly after Burnham’s address at the Labour party ­conference on Tuesday, and his response has not gone down well with several ­Premier League clubs concerned by his ­relationship with City’s owners.Manchester City fans are right to feel angry – now they need to direct it at the owners | Will UnwinRead moreIn a series of interviews on Wednesday Burnham saidhe would be “really concerned”if City’s owners were forced to sell after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.Such was the reaction that ­Downing Street felt compelled to ­clarify ­Burnham’s position on ­Thursday, with a No 10 ­spokesperson saying the prime minister had made clear that “the initial judgment is ­serious” and “there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules”.With City appealing against the verdict, the spokesperson noted the process had to be allowed to run its course but said: “If wrongdoing is established those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.” That phrase raised eyebrows given City have been found guilty by an independent commission after a 42-day hearing that produced 7,000 pages of witness evidence, eight years after thePremier Leaguebegan investigating the club.Burnham’s apparent sympathy for City, with a warning about ­jumping to conclusions and praise for the ­owners’ investment in ­Manchester, has alarmed some clubs but the ­Premier League declined to respond.HMRC is facing calls to get involved, with Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury committee, asking for its response to the commission’s judgment. In a letter to John-Paul Marks, the permanent secretary of HMRC, Hillier sought assurances that the tax authority was “seized of the importance” of the case and asked whether it had requested an unredacted copy of the commission’s verdict.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe Times and Daily Mail have reported that City’s appeal will be based on evidence the club claim proves their sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club. Thecommission rejected that argumentas “untrue”.Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and ­conceal the realities of the Disguised ­Funding Scheme.”Burnham has history with the ­Premier League, which he ­mentioned in Wednesday’s ­interviews by ­referencing his criticisms of its ­prosecution of his club, Everton, for financial rule breaches afterthey were docked 10 points–reduced to six on appeal – by an independent commission three years ago.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with the Manchester City chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at Vincent Kompany’s testimonial in 2019.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Live NewsIn November 2023, Burnham, when mayor of Greater Manchester, wrote to the Premier League chair, Alison Brittain, accusing the league of an “abuse of process” and claimedEvertonwere being used as a pawn in efforts to show an independent ­regulator was not required in football.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham made similar ­complaints on Wednesday despite ­Everton ­having admitted ­breaching ­profitability and sustainability rules, with the club contesting only the extent of the breach and sanction. “I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,” he said. “I still hold the view very firmly that they weren’t fairly treated in that process.”The Premier League was unhappy with Burnham’s behaviour in 2023, particularly as his office posted on X two letters of complaint he sent to the league, but did not publicise replies sent by Brittain that explained the competition’s financial regulations governance process.The Independent Football Regulator chief executive, David Kogan, has made clear he will not tolerate political interference in his role, telling the Times last year that he would resign if he sensed ­government pressure.The City case has the potential to present an early test of his ­mettle and the IFR’s powers, given ­Burnham’s previous working relationship with the club’s owner, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), and the £25bn annual UK-Abu Dhabi ­trading ­relationship. One of Burnham’s first calls after he succeeded Sir Keir Starmer in July was with Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, ­president of the United Arab ­Emirates and the ultimate owner of ADUG.Kogan confirmed the IFR was monitoring the case and has powers “to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives” to protect “honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals”.City’s owners are unlikely to fall foul of the licensing system that will be introduced next season, because that is an assessment of financial sustainability and separate from the new owners, directors and senior executives test, which the IFR uses to examine honesty and integrity.The Premier League and IFR declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityAndy BurnhamPremier LeagueEvertonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage  | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’
Content: Nigel Farage addressed hundreds of Reform supporters at an event space in Doncaster racecourse.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersView image in fullscreenNigel Farage addressed hundreds of Reform supporters at an event space in Doncaster racecourse.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersNigel FarageBurnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says FarageReform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’UK politics live – latest updatesBen QuinnPolitical correspondentThu 1 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” byreviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party.The prime minister’s pledges to theLabourconference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said.Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum.Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro.“Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.”Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.While theReform UKleader said he believed Burnham had calculated that new language on the EU might help win back voters from the Greens in big cities, Farage added: “Here in Doncaster and across the ‘red wall’ in the north and Midlands, I think he’s opened up a huge flank to us.”To cheers from hundreds of Reform supporters who gathered inside an event space at Doncaster racecourse, Farage said: “Today I’m back on the road and today is when our general election campaign starts.”There were even bigger cheers when Farage said he would relish – “Bring it on, I say” – the prospect of fighting Burnham in red wall areas such as Doncaster on the issue of rejoining the EU.“He might just have given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy, if you’re watching.”The focus of the rally – “100 days to save Britain” – had been planned before Burnham’s announcement about UK-EU relations. However, Reform sources claim that the prime minister’s intervention has energised them and that specific donors are already discussing how they can fund a rerun of the 2016 campaign.Meanwhile, Farage strongly hinted that Reform’s internal inquiry into the donations controversy that has overshadowed the party this year would absolve two key aides and that legal action would be launched against journalists involved.Indicating that he had already seen the report and knew its conclusions, Farage said its release was “imminent”.“It’s been done. It’ll be out in public very soon and I think some of your co-conspirators might find themselves with one or two legal challenges,” he told a Channel 4 journalist among reporters who questioned him.Reform was rocked on the eve of its party conference after some of Farage’s team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.In Channel 4 News’s investigation, footage showed that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.Jukes has denied “any wrongdoing” while Orr has said he would cooperate with the party’s internal investigation “fully”.The Metropolitan police are carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform over allegations it broke foreign funding laws.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageBrexitEuropean UnionAndy BurnhamLabourForeign policyReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’
Content: The change would require airlines to seat passengers under 14 next to their parents.Photograph: Viacheslav Iakobchuk/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe change would require airlines to seat passengers under 14 next to their parents.Photograph: Viacheslav Iakobchuk/AlamyAirline industryUK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with childrenPlanned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’Nadeem BadshahThu 1 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans.The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake.It is understood that ministers will try to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister,Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays.MPs are in the process of debating a new set of rules for travel companies, as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament. The proposed law will give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports.Burnham dodges questions on Heathrow third runway as project faces four-year delayRead moreBurnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”An arrangement to sit together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey, according to the Department forTransport.Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights. The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children aged between two and 11 to pay to reserve what was referred to as a mandatory family seat.Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge. The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority watchdog found.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRyanair will dispute passenger’s claim he was sucked out of windowRead moreUnder the new policy, parents will still have the option of paying to reserve a seat of their choosing and have their children alongside them free of charge.The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the government, airlines and trade unions working on a new system for sharing information about disruptive passengers.Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.Using the new system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryAndy BurnhamBooking feesAir transportTransportConsumer affairsChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: Co-pilot in flight stabbing had ‘Islamic radical indoctrination’, says Netanyahu | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
Author: William Christou
Headline: Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
Content: Yaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers who intervened on the flydubai plane, is welcomed at Ben Gurion airport.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APView image in fullscreenYaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers who intervened on the flydubai plane, is welcomed at Ben Gurion airport.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APFlydubai plane incidentCo-pilot in flight stabbing had ‘Islamic radical indoctrination’, says NetanyahuAlleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opensWilliam ChristouandJonathan YerushalmyThu 1 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, has claimed.Israeli passengers intervened tostop the attackon Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia.The plane had more than 170 people onboard and Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened, announcing that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a “heroism” award for preventing a potential disaster.A ‘hero’ pilot, plumber and dentist among those who saved flydubai flight to IsraelRead moreNetanyahu told Fox News: “We know that he underwent Islamic radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information.”The co-pilot, whose identity is still not known, was being interrogated by Saudi security services, which arrested him on the plane’s arrival in Tabuk, in the north-west of the country.Saudi investigators were cooperating with theUnited Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker’s motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” they told the Associated Press.GraphicTwo Israeli security officials said that Israel’s initial assessment was that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, Reuters reported.Netanyahu said that the co-pilot was probably suicidal, citing preliminary “indications”.“It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue,” he said, emphasising that final conclusions had yet to be made.Netanyahu had previously said it was “too early to say” if there was any state backing – namely Iranian – of the attack. Two Israeli security sources told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.The attack came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election. The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat and the opposition leader Yair Lapid said that a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat.Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a “terror attack”, with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE.Map of flight pathDonald Trump suggested the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, and told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length.Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel’s involvement in the investigation.Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.3:28How the stabbing incident unfolded on Israel-bound flydubai plane | DeconstructedThe UAE announced on Thursday that it would conduct its own investigation into the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai.
