It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker’s motive and if he had any links to any “terrorist purpose”.Passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – putting the captain of the plane on the floor, after which the plane began to plummet. The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane’s descent.A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard had played out.Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India’s ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain’s family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said.Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk,but was in good health and recovering well, according to the Indian embassy in the UAE, which said the ambassador had visited the pilot.“Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,” Modi said, in a post on social media. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentIsraelUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuAir transportSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: How success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in power | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: PM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformation
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: PM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformation
Content: Andy Burnham, then the mayor of Greater Manchester, speaks to a reporter after watching a match at the Etihad Stadium in May 2021.Photograph: Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham, then the mayor of Greater Manchester, speaks to a reporter after watching a match at the Etihad Stadium in May 2021.Photograph: Alamy Live NewsAndy BurnhamHow success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in powerPM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformationJosh HallidayNorth of England editorThu 1 Oct 2026 14.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn July 2016, theManchester Cityplayer Yaya Touré ambled into a small bar near Beijing’s Workers’ Stadium and offered a bemused smile as dozens of Chinese fans rushed towards him.Manchester City had just won their sixth trophy under the big-spending ownership of Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group and the blues were international megastars. They were also magnets for investment.On a trade mission led by Sir Howard Bernstein, the architect of modernManchester, civic leaders rolled out club legends such as Mike Summerbee and Sun Jihai in a charm offensive to football-mad Chinese businessmen who saw that the club and the city were on the rise.A decade on, Manchester istransformed. Estate agents advertise £15,000-a-month penthouses in a city-region growing faster economically than any other in Britain, while the success of “Manchesterism” has powered its mayor, Andy Burnham, to Downing Street.Yet the city’s close ties with Abu Dhabi United Group are now facing fresh scrutiny, after Manchester City’s owners were found guilty ofmore than 100 breachesof Premier League financial rules.Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier LeagueRead moreIn a surprising intervention on Wednesday, Burnham praised Abu Dhabi United Group as “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” and said he would be “really concerned” to lose them as the club’s owners.View image in fullscreenSheikh Mansour.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAThe prime minister went on to say that he would not get involved in the Premier League’s disciplinary process, but appeared to express some sympathy for City’s plight by referring to a similar investigation into Everton, the club he supports.“I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,” he said.Burnham’s comments raised eyebrows given the continuing disciplinary process – the Premier League is considering a range of sanctions – and because it turned the spotlight on to Abu Dhabi United Group’s wider investments inGreater Manchester, where he was mayor from 2017 until June this year.One Burnham ally said it was “absolutely mad” for the prime minister to comment and risk being seen to be influencing a disciplinary process, describing it as his “biggest mistake so far”.In an attempt to clarify the prime minister’s remarks on Thursday, a No 10 spokesperson said: “As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process.“It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.”When Mansour’s Abu Dhabi group took over Manchester City in 2008, the grounds for success had already been laid.The club had a gleaming new stadium, built with taxpayers’ money for the Commonwealth games just four years earlier, and council bosses were eager for a reliable long-term investor in a city battling the financial crash.View image in fullscreenManchester City's Etihad stadium.Photograph: Jon Super/APIn 2014, Manchester city council announced a “£1bn deal” with Mansour, one of the world’s richest men, to transform a large stretch of land between the stadium and the edge of the city centre. Richard Leese, then the council leader, promised it to be “a world-class exemplar of regeneration”.The partnership between the council and Manchester City’s owner, which was called Manchester Life, included more than 1,000 private rented apartments and 395 built-for-sale homes – but not one social or affordable home.In a sharply critical assessment of the Manchester Life partnershippublished in 2024, researchers at the University of Sheffield said it appeared that the council had leased the land to Abu Dhabi at a much cheaper rate than many comparable developments – they had “sold the family silver too cheaply”, the academics said – and did not appear to be receiving any rental income or revenue from the property sales.All of the property, with an estimated worth of £350m, is controlled by Jersey-domiciled subsidiaries and ultimately owned by Abu Dhabi interests, the researchers found.They described it as a “transfer of public wealth to private hands that is difficult to justify as prudent”.Dr Richard Goulding, who co-authored the University of Sheffield research, said on Thursday that the Manchester Life development raised “questions about what type of Britain we’re trying to build and who the type of Manchester that we’ve built works for”.He added: “On the one hand, [the Abu Dhabi deal] was bringing money in. On the other hand, a lot of that money was flowing into flats whose rents, according to our research, are being taken offshore.”In July, Manchester city councilpublished a reviewof its deals with private developers. It found that while these agreements had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals.A Manchester city council spokesperson said: “We do not recognise the criticisms linked to the disposal of public land and the idea that there is no financial benefit to the council through this partnership.View image in fullscreenSkyscrapers have transformed Manchester’s skyline over the past decade as the city’s population has grown to nearly 100,000 people.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“The tired claim that working in partnership with Manchester City FC’s owners has not been a good deal for the council or the city has been debunked repeatedly. It is a one-sided perspective that fails to take into account the positive impact of investment in Ancoats and New Islington as well as the wider east Manchester area.”The council added: “Claims that some land was sold too cheaply to Manchester Life ignore the fact that there was zero market interest at the time of the sale, that the land is worth more now precisely because of Manchester Life’s investment and the significant financial return the council is receiving through profit-sharing arrangements.”Gleaming skyscrapers have transformed Manchester’s skyline over the past decade, as the city’s population has grown bynearly 100,000 peopleand become one of Europe’s most attractive destinations for foreign money.Yet born-and-bred Mancunians have felt increasingly pushed out. A report publishedearlier this yearby Greater Manchester combined authority, which Burnham led until June, revealed that of the 10,974 homes built across the region in the nine years to 2024, only 679 (6%) were classed as affordable.Hayley Flynn, an anti-gentrification campaigner who leads tours of Manchester, said development of luxury flats in Ancoats, the home of the Manchester Life project, had not benefited the area’s existing community.“What provisions have we got for them? They’re not going to spend £7 on a loaf of bread in Pollen [a trendy bakery], but that’s their nearest bakery,” she said. “All these apartments for influencers – it’s quite a forceful erosion that’s just pushing the community out.”Tim Heatley, a co-founder of the Manchester developer Capital & Centric, said the city had benefited from Abu Dhabi’s riches and that the success of City had “put Manchester on the map internationally”.Under the ownership of Mansour, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and one Champions League, becoming one of the world’s elite clubs.The club, whichcontinues to denyany wrongdoing, won eight trophies, including three Premier League titles between 2009 and 2018, the period under investigation.Heatley said Abu Dhabi had had “a major impact on that particular area of the city” between the Etihad Stadium and Manchester city centre, but that he believed the region’s economic upturn would have happened without the football investment.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamManchester CityGentrificationGreater ManchesterSheikh MansourLocal politicsCity mayorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Falling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plants  | Edinburgh | The Guardian
description: After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done
Content: The £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburghFalling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plantsAfter five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be donePatrick GreenfieldThu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early autumn sunlight, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh’s extensive plant collection appears safe in their glass enclosures. But danger lurks from above for the tropical ferns, cycads and rare alpine heathers.Soon the September sunshine will give way to the storms and gales of the Scottish winter, which can bring hundreds of glass panels crashing to the greenhouse floor on the windiest days. Nobody is allowed inside when the wind is above 30mph.“We’ve had plants that have essentially been decapitated by falling bits of glass,” says Sadie Barber, the glasshouse curator at RBGE. “You go into one of these tropical spaces in winter and there’s icy air coming in. It’s traumatic for those of us who put decades into caring for these plants. A storm can literally just wipe them out.”View image in fullscreenProf Julia Knights, regius keeper and CEO of RBGE, officially opening the doors.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBut this week, change is in the air for the creaking infrastructure at the 356-year-old botanic garden, the second oldest in Britain after Oxford. On Friday, the palm houses are reopening after five years of painstaking restoration work, complete with 5,750 panels of toughened glass to keep out the elements.Before they closed for renovation works, the horticultural team had installed a net in case panels fell from the weathered structure. The new ones are not bulletproof – but they are strong enough to resist a bird strike.View image in fullscreenDamage to one of the glasshouses after a storm.Photograph: Helen Pugh PhotographyPart-Georgian, part-Victorian, the £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell. Inside, more than 600 temperate plants have returned to the building. The air is clean and crisp, purified by ferns that naturally remove toxins from the air. Its temperature and humidity is still controlled by the original pulleys and winches.“We have made it one vast cathedral-like space for temperate plants,” says Prof Julia Knights, the garden’s regius Keeper and the royally appointed chief executive. She points out her favourite tree fern, which comes from Tasmania and has a Scottish liverwort growing on its woody stem. “They can grow outside in our botanic garden in Logan on the west coast ofScotlandbecause of the oceanic climate,” she says.View image in fullscreenExtensive work has been done to replace and strengthen panels at the greenhouse.Photograph: Helen Pugh PhotographyFounded by two physicians in 1670 to teach doctors about medicinal plants, RBGE has morphed into one of the most important collections of plant biodiversity in the world. Its research glasshouses are stuffed with rare ginger species, bananas, blueberries and dozens of begonias.It is a global authority on rhododendrons and ferns, houses rare plant species that have gone extinct in the wild, and its scientists have helped pioneer new technology, such as DNA barcoding which is used to identify plant species. Arthur Conan Doyle studied here, infusing Sherlock Holmes novels with his botanical knowledge. Today, conservation is its primary focus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Our conservation collections are so important to have. The threats are extreme in the wild,” said Prof Pete Hollingsworth, RBGE’s director of science. “The driver[s] for environmental damage are so strong, so having these ex situ safe sites is really important,” he said.View image in fullscreenNew display benches in the restored building.Photograph: RBGEBut the restored palm houses aside, many of the glasshouses used to care for the plants are decades past their originally intended lifespan and are waiting for upgrades. Leaks from Scottish rain rot the rootstock of plants, sometimes killing them. Last year, horticulturalists were not allowed inside the greenhouses for 20 days due to high winds. In 2026, they have been shut out 15 times. When they return, they have often worn hard hats and safety gear to pick out the broken glass.“The glasshouses are the one thing we don’t want to break. It’s the plants inside that suffer,” said Barber. “I was looking at one of our records the other day of a plant we lost in the lowland tropical house. It just had ‘storm’ written next to it. It had either suffered from the cold, or even been cut by falling glass.”Explore more on these topicsEdinburghScotlandPlantsGardensConservationBiodiversitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped? | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems
Content: A British Border Force vessel arrives at Ramsgate after picking up people trying to cross the Channel in a small boat.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreenA British Border Force vessel arrives at Ramsgate after picking up people trying to cross the Channel in a small boat.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersImmigration and asylumExplainerWhy is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problemsUK politics live – latest updatesDiane TaylorThu 1 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government’s “one in, one out” deal withFrance, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said.What was one in, one out?The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026.Why didn’t it work out?The UK’s official explanation was thatit had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scoresreturnedto the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to havevanishedafter being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey.How many people were sent back under it and how many returned to the UK?Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total whoarrived in small boatsover seven days in the second half of last month. More than 40,000 have arrived in Britain in small boats during the period the deal has been in place.What do the French say about the scheme?It is understood France wanted to end the deal because it did not want to carry the weight of accepting small boat arrivals back from the UK alone and instead wanted the rest of Europe to also get involved. Other European countries have so far not agreed to join the scheme. “Why do we have to manage this border on our own?” the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said at a parliamentary hearing this year. “We believe that France should not have to bear the burden alone, and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”What do the British say?The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said at a recent session of the Commons home affairs committee that it was difficult to pinpoint exactly why there had been a reduction of more than 40% in the number of people crossing the Channel so far this year compared with the same period last year. Others say that lower levels of irregular migration into the UK from France in the first five months of this year compared with the same period last year are likely at least partially to be due to a drop in arrivals of irregular migrants to Europe overall. The Home Office said it would continue to remove as many small boat arrivals as possible. But it is not possible to forcibly remove people to unsafe countries such as Iran, Eritrea, Sudan and others, where many on small boats come from.What do critics of the scheme say?NGOs such as Medical Justice havecondemnedthe trauma they have documented due to the detention of this group, many of whom are survivors of trafficking or torture. Force was used against one in 10 of 224 asylum seekers during their removal to France in the first three months of this year, according to Home Office freedom of information data. Both the NGO Médecins Sans Frontières and the French health organisationSamusocial, which provides treatment for returnees to France, documented physical and psychological injuries. At the home affairs committee the home secretary suggested these injuries may have been self-inflicted. The Labour MP and committee member Bell Ribeiro-Addy accused the home secretary of “victim blaming” and said there was independent evidence of injuries sustained as a result of use of force.What could the UK government do now?Successive prime ministers and home secretaries have vowed to stop small boats crossing the Channel. So far none have succeeded. For as long as people flee war and conflict a percentage of them are likely to turn up in the UK by one means or another. The use of return hubs in third countries is under discussion by some European countries although no details have been confirmed.How do asylum seekers feel about the end of one in, one out?In a word, overjoyed. “Thank God. You gave me the best news,” said one asylum seeker forcibly returned to France, after hearing the news. He is now considering returning to the UK. Another who is also hoping to return said: “That’s good news. We just hope the UK doesn’t make a worse agreement with a new country.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumRefugeesFranceEuropeexplainersShareReuse this content

title: School gate to checkmate: British chess prodigy, 11, is youngest ever woman grandmaster | Chess | The Guardian
description: Bodhana Sivanandan’s father taught her to play age five and soon she was beating ex-champions. Now she is lighting up the Chess Olympiad
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Bodhana Sivanandan’s father taught her to play age five and soon she was beating ex-champions. Now she is lighting up the Chess Olympiad
Content: Bodhana Sivanandan at Harrow chess club. She has said she wants to become an outright grandmaster ‘as soon as possible’.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersView image in fullscreenBodhana Sivanandan at Harrow chess club. She has said she wants to become an outright grandmaster ‘as soon as possible’.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersChessSchool gate to checkmate: British chess prodigy, 11, is youngest ever woman grandmasterBodhana Sivanandan’s father taught her to play age five and soon she was beating ex-champions. Now she is lighting up the Chess OlympiadMatthew WeaverThu 1 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the weekend, 11-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan became theyoungest everholder of the title of woman grandmaster at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board. By Tuesday morning she was back at school in north London for a design and technology lesson.Bodhana has to juggle the competing pressures of being an international chess sensation with the more ordinary challenges of childhood and her first term at secondary school.She takes it all in her stride. “I’m used to going to tournaments and then coming back to school the next day,” she told the Guardian in her first interview since returning to the family home in Harrow. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework, but I should be able to manage.”She has won three smartphones at various tournaments but she is still too young to be allowed to use them. “One day I’d like a phone, but I’m fine without,” she said. Sitting beside her, her father, Sivanandan Velayutham, who works in IT, added: “I don’t think it is the right time for her to have a phone.”Bodhana’s meteoric rise up the chess rankings suggests she is thriving without the distraction of social media, even if it means missing congratulatory posts from her growing fanbase includingRachel Reeves,Rishi Sunakand the children’s commissioner,Rachel de Souza.View image in fullscreenRishi Sunak hosting Bodhana at No 10 in 2023.Photograph: Simon Walker/No 10 Downing StreetCompeting in Uzbekistan meant the family had to secure an authorised absence from her new school and she will have to catch up on a fortnight of missed classes. But Bodhana is a fast learner; her father taught her to play chess when she was five, and within a year, and with the help of YouTube videos, she was beating him.When she was seven, Bodhana won 5-1 playing simultaneously against six members of her local Harrow chess club. At eight she managed tobeat the former British champion Peter Lee. In July she became theyoungest girl to beat a grandmaster with a rating of over 2,600, and she was the youngest person ever to be selected for an England team in any sport.Bodhana’s latest victories in Samarkand give her a rating of 2,382, surpassing the required 2,300 points to become a woman grandmaster. She is just a few points away from the 2,400 required for international master status and needs 2,500 points to be an outright grandmaster. If she achieves that in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever grandmaster.Bodhana is not aware of that deadline. “I want to become a grandmaster as soon as possible, but I’m doing it because I like it, not to just chase records,” she said.Her ambition is simply to be the best player in the world.Nigel Short, one of Britain’s best ever chess players, was roundly criticised in 2015 for claimingmen’s brains were hardwired to be better at chessthan women. Bodhana has other ideas. She said: “By rating, yes men are better than women, but a woman could also achieve the same thing if they work hard enough, so I don’t agree fully.”View image in fullscreenBodhana Sivanandan: ‘I just try to focus on the game and forget about everything else.’Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersShe took on the current world No 1, Magnus Carlsen, in a game of speed chess earlier this year. “It was a blitz game, and I lasted about 10 minutes. No one likes losing, but losing is kind of necessary to learn.”Bodhana has a fearless approach to chess. “I don’t get nervous, but even when I do, I just try to focus on the game and forget about everything else,” she said.Jonathan Eckert, 67, a keen tournament player, could only manage to draw against Bodhana when she was six. “I was fairly confident of winning, but she played the endgame extremely well, which is the sign of a classical player. A lot of these youngsters are incredibly good at tactics, because they’re playing against computers all the time. I was quite surprised she was battling with me on strategy.”Bodhana is used to being praised on her classical play and positional sense. “Lots of people say that about me. It means you don’t play very sharp tactics, but I can also do that if I need to.”The booster seat can help unnerve opponents. “Sometimes it distracts them, but I don’t know if it freaks them out,” she said.Her favourite player is José Raúl Capablanca, a Cuban world champion from the 1920s whose books and games she has studied. “I like the way he plays in his endgames,” she said.Away from chess, Bodhana enjoys playing the piano and violin, and reading. She does not watch television because she does not have time; she has eight hours of chess tuition a week paid for by EnglishChessFederation and the Chess Trust.Her father is keen to add that the family is also grateful for sponsorship from the Turkish investor Evren Üçok, Tangram Therapeutics and the John Robinson Youth Chess Trust.Bodhana’s next nine-day tournament could be theLondonChess Classic at the end of November, but only if it fits in with school and the schedules of her parents and younger twin sisters. “If good tournaments come up we try to work it around,” said her father.“We’re not pushy, we just work on our goals and keep going. Opportunities are scarce in this world. You have to understand your kids and know what they like and allow them to shine.”Explore more on these topicsChessLondonChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: Sex, drugs and amoebic dysentery: the 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, we rate cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenes
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, we rate cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenes
Content: Impossibly ambitious … Romy Schneider in Henri-Georges Clouzot's Inferno.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenImpossibly ambitious … Romy Schneider in Henri-Georges Clouzot's Inferno.Photograph: Publicity imageRankedMoviesSex, drugs and amoebic dysentery: the 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked!From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, we rate cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenesRyan GilbeyThu 1 Oct 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Document of the Dead (1985)Behind-the-scenes footage from Dawn of the Dead is the highlight of this aficionados-only affair, which follows the 1979 satirical zombie horror all the way through to distribution. Director George A Romero, makeup maestro Tom Savini and the occasional zombie actor shoot the breeze in the deserted shopping mall that provides the movie with its incongruous central location.19. The Death of “Superman Lives”: What Happened? (2015)Imagining what might have been if Tim Burton’s Superman Lives had got off the ground, documentary maker Jon Schnepp cosies up on screen with his interviewees and insinuates himself unforgivably into the story. The material is almost good enough to transcend his vanity: there is test footage of lead actor Nicolas Cage in his Man of Steel duds, plus interviews with Burton, original screenwriter Kevin Smith and producer Jon Peters, who was adamant that Superman should fight polar bears and a giant spider.18. Becoming Bulletproof (2014)A group of actors with disabilities form the bulk of the cast of the short western Bulletproof, shot in the California desert courtesy of the inclusive arts project Zeno Mountain Farm. Crucially, Bulletproof itself isn’t about disability, but rather an attempt to highlight the lack of on-screen representation – and plug the gap. This affectionate documentary tracks the film from preproduction to premiere.17. They’ll Love Me When I’m Dead (2018)Orson Welles spent five years shooting what became his final film, The Other Side of the Wind, with three years elapsing before its star – director and sometime actor John Huston – even stepped in front of the camera. After all that, the footage ended up impounded by the Iranian revolutionary government. A version eventually premiered in 2018 and is now on Netflix, along with this scattershot documentary, presented by Alan Cumming, which strings together archive footage, new interviews and typically Wellesian stories of on-set bluffs, tomfoolery and procrastination.16. Filmmaker: A Diary by George Lucas (1968)A half-hour snapshot by Lucas of his new buddy Francis Ford Coppola, who is hard at work on his fourth film, The Rain People, and not too shy to argue with his lead actor, Shirley Knight. Contains one choice detail: in preparation for driving across the country shooting this road movie, all the men on the crew, Coppola included, shave off their beards to look more presentable for any hippy-hating officials they might encounter along the way.15.Boorman and the Devil(2025)In declining The Exorcist but taking on Exorcist II: The Heretic, John Boorman perhaps displayed a preference for poisoned chalices over champagne flutes. He is candid and good-humoured, if still a little shell-shocked, as he recounts the experience of filming the sequel once derided as “the stupidest major movie ever made”, and the despair that led him to contemplate self-immolation on Hollywood Boulevard. Sand-related illness, a sozzled Richard Burton, locusts and tap-dancing: this has it all.14. Doomed! The Untold Story of Roger Corman’s The Fantastic Four (2015)Filmed in a rat-infested studio on sets recycled from the Jurassic Park rip-off Carnosaur, with special effects entrusted to a local outfit called Mr Film, this cheapo superhero adventure was made in a rush to prevent the rights to The Fantastic Four reverting from producer Bernd Eichinger to Marvel. (“That movie was never supposed to be shown to anybody,” said Stan Lee.) This heartening documentary, which shows the crestfallen cast refusing to let their film die, feels even more pertinent after Warner Bros recently shelved some movies as tax write-offs, including Batgirl and Coyote Vs Acme, the latter rescued only by the skin of its teeth.13. Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013)In trying to adapt Frank Herbert’s Dune in the mid-1970s, cinematic shaman Alejandro Jodorowsky (Santa Sangre, El Topo) bit off more than he could chew, just as David Lynch would when his version came to painful fruition in 1984. But Frank Pavich’s documentary proves that Jodorowsky’s intention to make “a film that gives LSD hallucinations without taking LSD” was not too fanciful. Among those in his corner were the artist HR Giger, who went on to design the monsters in Alien, and a cast including Salvador Dalí, Mick Jagger and Orson Welles, with the latter being bribed to take part with the promise of having his favourite chef on set.View image in fullscreenHallucinatory … concept artwork from Jodorowsky’s Dune.Photograph: Sony classics/Sony Classics12. Lost Soul: The Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley’s Island of Dr Moreau (2014)When the studio New Line tried to ditch South African director Richard Stanley from his own HG Wells adaptation, he asked a warlock called Skip to pull some cosmic strings. That did the trick for a while, helping Stanley to charm the film’s star, Marlon Brando. But black magic was no match for cast member Val Kilmer, who demanded a 40% reduction in his own shooting days, then spent his time on set playing power games. There was nature to contend with, too, in the form of wild animals (a puma pisses on Stanley’s tailored suit) and a hurricane that ravages the location in Cairns, Queensland. Finally replaced by curmudgeonly veteran John Frankenheimer, Stanley refuses to leave Australia, which is when things go from mad to worse.11. No Frank in Lumberton (1988) / Blue Velvet Revisited (2016)Two behind-the-scenes Blue Velvet documentaries from one director. Peter Braatz was still a film student when David Lynch, with whom he had been corresponding for several years, invited him to Wilmington, North Carolina in 1985 to chart the making of what would become his twisted masterpiece. Braatz marshalled just under an hour of the resulting Super-8 material into his 1988 documentary, which straddled the line between orthodox and experimental. He then reshaped it into a full-on ambient head-trip for the 86-minute 2016 version, which mixes flickering footage and crisp black-and-white photographs with a woozy score and the voices of Lynch, Dennis Hopper and others to form an ethereal audiovisual collage.10. The Sweatbox (2002)Disney had high hopes for Kingdom of the Sun, a Prince and the Pauper-style animated musical drama set in the Inca empire. The studio sent Lion King co-director Roger Allers on a research trip to Peru and commissioned a suite of new songs by Sting. But it was back to the drawing board after a calamitous screening of an early rough cut; Allers and Sting were given the heave-ho, and the movie was retooled as the larky comedy The Emperor’s New Groove. Sting’s wife, Trudie Styler, charts every disastrous step in a documentary that Disney hasdone its darnedest to suppress.9. From Darkness to Light (2024)A 10-a-penny title for an account of a once-in-a-lifetime film-making folly: Jerry Lewis’s abandoned, incomplete 1972 Holocaust dramaThe Day The Clown Cried. Directing himself as a former clown who entertains children in a concentration camp, Lewis made a misguided bid to be taken seriously. “It was bad work,” he admits here. It wasn’t only the dubious material that defeated the former Nutty Professor: unbeknown to him, the option on the script had expired, rendering the entire project illegal. It was his decision, though, to hire a repentant former concentration camp guard as part of the crew. “He was a human being!” Lewis protests.View image in fullscreen‘Bad work’ … Jerry Lewis on the set of The Day the Clown Cried.Photograph: Venice Film Festival8. Poultry in Motion: Truth Is Stranger Than Chicken (2008)Seventy-odd fans of horror exploitation studio Troma worked unpaid on Poultrygeist: Night of the Chicken Dead while living in a deserted church in a rundown corner of Buffalo, New York, with one cold shower between them. Meanwhile, the chicken-themed zombie flick was shot at a nearby abandoned McDonald’s. This documentary captures all the on-set horror, from the sexually disinhibited auditions to the hourly cast-and-crew bust-ups. Actors walk off, burst into tears and throw punches; a zombie extra accidentally sets himself on fire; and bilious co-director and Troma boss Lloyd Kaufman proves both lackadaisical and tyrannical.7. Shirkers (2018)When budding film-maker Sandi Tan met the enigmatic Georges Cardona, he cited Fitzcarraldo as his inspiration and claimed to know crew members from Apocalypse Now. Those pictures – famously troubled productions that spawned their own jaw-dropping documentaries – look like red flags considering what came next: Cardona directed Tan’s indie road movie Shirkers, swallowing up $10,000 of her savings when he ran out of money, then vanished with the resulting 70 reels of unprocessed film. She didn’t see the footage until decades later, when those reels were returned to her by Cardona’s widow. Tan’s sobering 2018 documentary attempts to make sense of the betrayal.6. The Peddler (2010)“Good film directors will notice many mistakes,” says prolific camcorder auteur and 67-year-old Santa Claus lookalike Daniel Burmeister. “But I like what I do: making hand-crafted films.” In exchange for a month’s food and accommodation, Burmeister sets up shop in a remote Argentinian village to bring the community together by shooting a movie from one of his own scripts. His budget may be nonexistent but his resourcefulness is boundless: in place of a dolly shot, for instance, he sits on a blanket, camera on his shoulder, while being dragged across the floor. This delightful, deeply humanistic portrait of grassroots DIY cinema has all the charm and idiosyncrasies of a Jared Hess comedy.5.Lost in La Mancha(2002)View image in fullscreen‘We’re fucked!’ … Jean Rochefort and Terry Gilliam in Lost in La Mancha.Photograph: Blue Finch Film ReleasingTerry Gilliam was happy to have documentary makers Keith Fulton and Louis Pepe on set for The Man Who Killed Don Quixote after being impressed by The Hamster Factor, their behind-the-scenes film on the making of his earlier 12 Monkeys. The anguished result shows exactlywhy Quixote was abandonedafter six days’ shooting in Spain in September 2000. Takes were rendered unusable by the roar of F16s from a nearby Nato base; Jean Rochefort, co-lead opposite Johnny Depp, fell seriously ill; and the equipment was destroyed by a merciless storm. Gilliam’s on-set catchphrase sums it up: “We’re fucked!” (When Quixote was eventually made in 2018, Fulton and Pepe documented that shoot, too, inHe Dreams of Giants.)4. Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno (2009)The subgenre of documentaries about unfinished films stretches back to the BBC’s 1965 The Epic That Never Was, which investigated Josef von Sternberg’s planned version of I, Claudius starring Charles Laughton and Merle Oberon. But it reached its apotheosis with Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno, Ruxandra Medrea and Serge Bromberg’s ravishing reflection on an early-1960s Proustian psychological drama from the director of Les Diaboliques. Lavishly funded by Columbia, Clouzot’s vision was impossibly ambitious, with three crews and a trippy array of complicated in-camera special effects. The director, who could not be dissuaded from shooting time-consuming test footage, suffered a heart attack three weeks into the 18-week shoot. The fragments of his vision, cherrypicked here from 15 hours of unseen footage, are intoxicating: where else can you see Romy Schneider covered in glitter, cellophane and olive oil?3.Burden of Dreams (1982)Deep in the rainforests of South America, Werner Herzog battles mud and misery, along with his leading man Klaus Kinski, to make Fitzcarraldo, about one man’s dream of building an opera house in the Amazon. Les Blank’s documentary, which is arguably more compelling than the movie it’s about, enables us to watch in disbelief as a film about a lunatic mission turns into one itself. Herzog’s initial footage has to be abandoned when the lead actor, Jason Robards, falls ill with amoebic dysentery and co-star Mick Jagger is needed on a world tour. Up and running again, the production is forced to relocate more than 1,000 miles away due to a border war, while Herzog’s plans to move a steamship up a hillside provide a textbook example of madness eclipsing method.2.American Movie(1999)Mark Borchardt, a Milwaukee junkyard poet with a mullet and plateglass specs, may be best suited to factory work or serial killing, according to his brother, but he positively glows with a passion for cinema. Lacking the funds to finish his feature debut, he instead tries to complete a short horror film, Coven, undaunted by his inability to pronounce the title. MoreWiseauthan Welles, he has optimism and indefatigability to burn. Not to mention a crew of colourful collaborators, including his mother, whom he enlists as an extra despite her protestations that she needs to go shopping; his bleary, poodle-haired pal and former acid-head Mike; and the gnarled, trailer-dwelling Uncle Bill, who needs 30 takes to deliver four lines. Director Chris Smith (who later made the pricelessFyre festival documentary) rightly portrays Mark as one of cinema’s most inspiring heroes – even if he still hasn’t finished his first feature.1.Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse(1991)View image in fullscreen‘I’m thinking of shooting myself’ … Francis Ford Coppola directing Apocalypse Now, from Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMegadoc, the forthcoming behind-the-scenes film about Francis Ford Coppola’s $120mpassion project Megalopolis, is directed by Mike Figgis, though earlier Coppola-related documentaries tended to be family affairs. The director’s late wife, Eleanor, was responsible for Making Marie Antoinette, released later this month, about their daughter Sofia’s 2006 historical fantasia. And it was Eleanor, too, who co-directed the extraordinary Hearts of Darkness, which draws on her 60 hours of footage and 40 hours of audio recordings, as well as her own diaries, all from the turbulent 238-day shooting of Apocalypse Now. The film reveals her husband arguing on set with Dennis Hopper, frantically typing new scenes just moments before the cameras roll, and negotiating with Marlon Brando, who has piled on the pounds but neglected to learn his lines. “I’m thinking of shooting myself,” the director confides. “This is one crisis I can’t pull myself out of.”Boorman and the Devil is in cinemas in the UK and Ireland now. Making Marie Antoinette is in cinemas in the UK, Ireland and US from 23 October and streaming on Mubi from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmRankedDocumentary filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Enter Shikari announce indefinite hiatus from 2027: ‘We don’t think we’re splitting up’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next 12 months, but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next 12 months, but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’
Content: Rou Reynolds on stage with Enter Shikari in Leeds in 2024. The rock band have announced they are taking a break.Photograph: Georgina HarrisonView image in fullscreenRou Reynolds on stage with Enter Shikari in Leeds in 2024. The rock band have announced they are taking a break.Photograph: Georgina HarrisonMusicEnter Shikari announce indefinite hiatus from 2027: ‘We don’t think we’re splitting up’Rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next year but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’Press AssociationThu 1 Oct 2026 19.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British rock band Enter Shikari have announced they will go on hiatus at the end of 2027, a decision that may result in the band’s “extinction”.The St Albans band, who formed in 1999 as Hybryd, are due to tour the UK in November, Europe and the US next year, and said they hoped to play some of their favourite places “one last time”.A statement from band reads: “As of December 31, 2027, Enter Shikari will fall dormant as a recording and performing entity. This dormancy may eventually end with an eruption back into activity, or may end with extinction, we have no idea which.“As everyone keeps reminding us, 2027 will be 20 years since the release of our debut album. We’ve been playing music together since we were 15, and friends longer still, but there’s no doubt this is a huge milestone.Enter Shikari review – sensory overload by a British band hitting the big leaguesRead more“For the past two decades, we’ve run amok in a cultural landscape that elevates easily-pigeonholed art, so being an Enter Shikari hasn’t always been easy, professionally or personally, with obvious negative impact on one’s mental health when tasked with coming up with the goods.“But we do this because we love it, and we are lucky enough to have built an audience who understand that the less-trodden path is sometimes the more interesting journey. However, it gets to the point where the often difficult terrain of that path starts to frazzle and drain the humble traveller.“We are far from being the same kids who recorded that debut album, and as much as we love what we do, and still love being in each other’s company, as humans our priorities and capacities have changed.”The band said their lead singer, Rou Reynolds, had suffered “recent illness” but they had already had “difficult conversations” about their future before that.“To then see a friend in trouble made those conversations more pertinent,” the statement reads. “While we don’t think we’re splitting up, we do not have a diary that extends beyond 2027 … Maybe we’ll be like Fugazi and just get together to rehearse for fun, without feeling the need to make anyone else listen to it.“All we really know is after two decades of being a professional band, not having plans three years in advance is liberating.”The band also said they were working on new music, which fans “should get to hear sooner rather than later, along with another thing we’ve just finished filming”.Enter Shikari added that they would not be announcing a “farewell world tour”.The statement concludes: “It’s not the sort of statement we thought we’d be making if you’d asked us a year ago, but we felt it was time to let you know our headspace.“We really hope we’ll be seeing you over the next 14 months or so, somehow. But if not, all that remains to be said is thank-you for your support, your sweat, your passion, your energy.”Since forming in 1999, the band have released six UK top 10 albums, including a No 1 with A Kiss for the Whole World in 2023.They have also scored a handful of hit singles including Anything Can Happen in the Next Half, Juggernauts and Sssnakepit.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Smashing glass ceilings, Strictly and a courageous final sign-off: Esther Rantzen’s 10 best TV moments  | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: Rantzen was one of the most powerful women in British television. From making vegetable innuendos to changing lives and bestowing her own medals on brilliant people – here are her finest small-screen moments
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Rantzen was one of the most powerful women in British television. From making vegetable innuendos to changing lives and bestowing her own medals on brilliant people – here are her finest small-screen moments
Content: Esther Rantzen filming That's Life! in March 1983.Photograph: Radio Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen filming That's Life! in March 1983.Photograph: Radio Times/Getty ImagesEsther RantzenSmashing glass ceilings, Strictly and a courageous final sign-off: Esther Rantzen’s 10 best TV momentsRantzen was one of the most powerful women in British television. From making vegetable innuendos to changing lives and bestowing her own medals on brilliant people – here are her finest small-screen momentsDame Esther Rantzen obituaryEsther Rantzen: one of the UK’s boldest, bravest ever campaigners – right to the very endMark LawsonThu 1 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEsther Rantzen,who has died aged 86, revolutionised three areas of TV: consumer journalism, the visibility of presenters and viewer participation. Hers was a remarkable career full of landmarks – and here are some of the highlights.Braden’s Week (BBC One, 1968-72)This early customer advice programme, fronted by Canadian émigré Bernard Braden, created Rantzen’s TV persona: bashfully ambitious and passionately championing public causes but also, as a very rare frontline female presenter at the time, making some male colleagues resentful. She was hired as a researcher but had a sliding office doors moment after a decision was made to put the off-screen team in the studio to make the scams and complaints more dramatic. In an acknowledgment of her break, Rantzen made backroom staff a feature of the show that soon made her career.That’s Life! (BBC One, 1973-94)View image in fullscreenRantzen, centre right, filming That’s Life! in October 1980.Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesWhen Braden returned to Canada, Rantzen, in her early 30s, took the helm of the BBC’s prime-time replacement. As de facto editor, she became one of the most powerful women on British television then or since. Braden’s Week had made shopper support into light entertainment and Rantzen, in a paradox that always confused her critics, made it both lighter – puns, poems, ditties, vegetable-based innuendo – and heavier: exposing institutional and domestic child abuse, campaigning successfully for rear seatbelts and safer playgrounds and, after taking on the case of one viewer’s child, improving the NHS organ transplant system. The lurches in tone – signalled by Rantzen smoothing her toothy grin into a grave face – were controversial but, with the show reaching more than 20 million viewers at its peak, among the thousands of lives changed by the programme was Rantzen’s own.The Big Time (BBC One, 1976-80)Rantzen has been given insufficient credit (or, for some, blame) as a pioneer of the now engulfing genre of reality TV. Her consumer work was viewer-driven – often incorporating high-street vox pops – and, in The Big Time, she enabled citizens to live out their dreams: a keen home cook cheffing at the Dorchester, a gymnast performing as a circus trapeze artist or, most prophetically, becoming a TV star for a day.Hearts of Gold (BBC One, 1988-96)View image in fullscreenRantzen, centre, on Hearts of Gold.Photograph: handoutThe queen of TV went on to set up her own honours system, bestowing medals on members of the public secretly commended for feats of kindness, courage and caring. The show’s prank and ambush element – recipients were lured to the presentation by a ruse and surprised by Rantzen and team, often in disguise – confirmed Rantzen’s theory that viewers preferred their TV with a cheesy garnish.Esther (BBC Two, 1994-2002)Claudia Winkleman’srecent doomed attempt at the formatillustrated the extent to which the celebrity chatshow is a male-dominated field. Some early coverage had even suggested that Winkleman may be breaking the glass ceiling. Characteristically, though, Rantzen had smashed it long ago with 532 episodes over eight years of her biggest show after That’s Life!. For some, its standing as the UK’s most successful solo female-fronted talkshow was reduced by it not airing at prime time, but Rantzen also flourished as one of the most able substitutes for fellow chatshow host Terry Wogan.From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeRead moreThe British Schindler (ITV, 2003)She started her career at the BBC and met her husband and mentor, Desmond Wilcox, at the corporation, so Rantzen was something of a Beeb loyalist. However, she participated in two ITV documentaries about Nicholas Winton, a British stockbroker who organised rescues of mainly Jewish refugee children from Nazi Germany. His story was first told by Rantzen on That’s Life! in 1988 and Rantzen’s six-decade connection with him culminated in the 2023 movie One Life, in which she is played by Samantha Spiro.Strictly Come Dancing (BBC One, 2004)Having pioneered, in The Big Time, the type of reality TV that makes celebrities of ordinary citizens, Rantzen got in early on the genre that forces already famous facesout of their comfort zones when she took part in the second series of Strictly, in 2004. She was paired with Anton Du Beke and was the third contestant to be eliminated.I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! (ITV, 2008)View image in fullscreenLeaving the I’m a Celebrity … jungle after being the fifth contestant to be voted out in the show’s eighth series, in 2008.Photograph: ShutterstockWhether doing a waltz or chewing marsupial genitalia, reality TV is a circular industry: participation in one show makes you more likely to be offered another. Rantzen completed the big two with the eighth series of I’m a Celeb in 2008. The audience’s relatively benevolent attitude to her was evidenced by her always ranking low in the public vote-off and being fifth to be eliminated, before Joe Swash eventually won.Esther Rantzen: Living With Grief (Channel 5, 2021)Widowed young, Rantzen, in the last phase of her campaigning TV career, focused on bereavement and the potential loneliness of older age, issues she also tried to tackle through numerous charities and trusteeships. In this thoughtful documentary, she benefited from 5’s policy of forefronting former BBC presenters.Good Morning Britain (ITV, 2026)A commendable and courageous recent tradition on Good Morning Britain has been inviting terminally ill TV personalities – such as Bill TurnbullandDermot Murnaghan– on as guests to promote research and encourage at-risk viewers to attend medical screenings and seek early diagnosis. In her final broadcast, Rantzen advocated for assisted dying, a topic that she had discussed in numerous TV appearances even as her health precipitously declined. Unusually for her, in what had been a career marked by successful campaigning, heraim was thwarted by parliament last month.Explore more on these topicsEsther RantzenTelevisionBBCStrictly Come DancingI'm a Celebrity ...BereavementAssisted dyingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fixer, financier, spymaster: how the UAE’s Sheikh Tahnoon is setting his sights on AI dominance |  | The Guardian
description: The long read: The Emirati royal is increasingly influential on the world stage. Some see him as a visionary. Others compare him to a Bond villain. Who is he?
Author: Jack Shenker
Headline: The long read: The Emirati royal is increasingly influential on the world stage. Some see him as a visionary. Others compare him to a Bond villain. Who is he?
Content: Sheikh Tahnoon.Composite: Guardian Design/AP/Getty Images/Photoshot/PA/AFP/EPA/AlamyView image in fullscreenSheikh Tahnoon.Composite: Guardian Design/AP/Getty Images/Photoshot/PA/AFP/EPA/AlamyThe long readFixer, financier, spymaster: how the UAE’s Sheikh Tahnoon is setting his sights on AI dominanceThe Emirati royal is increasingly influential on the world stage. Some see him as a visionary. Others compare him to a Bond villain. Who is he?Jack ShenkerThu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShareOn the night of 12 November 1993, a slim, young Brazilian named Royce Gracie stepped into an octagonal cage in Denver, Colorado, and found himself staring up into the eyes of a giant. Gerard Gordeau, a Dutch kickboxer, stood five inches taller, weighed almost three stone more than him, and had an extra decade of fighting experience under his belt. Now the pair were about to engage in bare-knuckle combat: no judges, no separation of opponents by size, no respite until someone either got knocked out cold or begged for mercy.Thefight lastedbarely 100 seconds. In that time, Gracie calmly tripped Gordeau up, jumped on his back, and clutched at his throat, forcing the big man to hammer the floor in submission.About 80,000 pay-per-view spectators watched Gracie’s legendary victory – the finale of the first ever Ultimate Fighting Championship – live on television. Among them was an unassuming business studies student living in San Diego, California. Mesmerised by what he had seen, the student presented himself at a local martial arts academy that specialised in Brazilian jiu-jitsu – the discipline employed by Gracie to humble Gordeau in the cage – and asked to begin lessons. His classmates found it hard to take the newcomer seriously. “I was there the day he showed up,” said Kid Peligro, who went on to become one of the biggest jiu-jitsu stars in the world. “He was wearing shorts, flip-flops and a tank-top; he sat in the corner and barely spoke to anybody.”The student, who introduced himself as Ben, was in his mid-20s and hailed from the Middle East, but revealed little else about his background. Peligro assumed that he served as the butler or bodyguard to the rich Englishman who sometimes accompanied him to lessons. “Ben was quiet, and he was dedicated,” Peligro told me. “He would often stay behind after class to sweep the mats.” Ben also took physical pain in his stride, even when it involved fractured bones. “If you trained in jiu-jitsu in the 1990s, you were going to get hurt,” said Bobby Razak, a film producer and martial arts enthusiast. “It wasn’t like it is now: very clean, very professional. Back then, it was raw.”After more than a year of training, Ben made a startling announcement: he was about to return home to Abu Dhabi, capital of the United Arab Emirates, and would be taking the academy’s founder, Nelson Monteiro, along with him. Other invitations soon followed. Rumours spread that Ben was trying to establish his own martial arts centre on the shores of the Persian Gulf. One day, Peligro and his wife were sent a pair of first-class flight tickets to the UAE, worth $24,000 each. When they stepped off the plane, they were astonished to see pictures of a familiar-looking man – clearly Ben’s father – everywhere they turned, from billboards to banknotes. “Ben’s training centre turned out to be one of his family’s palaces,” Peligro said, still marvelling at the memory. “It’s like a fairytale.”For those trying to uncover the truth behind His Highness Sheikh Tahnoon bin (or “Ben”) Zayed Al Nahyan – royal fixer, reclusive spymaster, financial behemoth – fairytales are nearly all we have to go on. Tahnoon, who really did enrol in Nelson Monteiro’s class under a pseudonym and eventually went on to become a jiu-jitsu black belt in his own right, now sits atop an economic fortune larger than the GDP of several major countries, and isclosely entwinedboth personally and financially with the Trump White House. The global holdings overseen by Tahnoon span windfarms in Scotland and spaceships in Texas, Rihanna’s lingerie line and Richard Caring’s Ivy restaurants. From hospitals to housing blocks, solar farms to ski resorts, there is almost no place on Earth untouched by his financial firepower.But despite his ever-growing influence on the world stage, Tahnoon prefers to remain in the shadows. He has never given a substantive interview to the press. Those who have worked closely with him are almost always made to sign non-disclosure agreements. Very few people outside the UAE even know his name. “He’s quiet,” says one former US national security official, “and he’s always everywhere.” Sheikh Tahnoon did not respond to an interview request for this article. The UAE foreign ministry did not offer any other senior government figure for interview, and declined to provide any comment.Tahnoon’s power is soon going to extend over more human lives than ever before. As one of the most important AI financiers on the planet, he is rapidly embedding himself within the infrastructure that will underpin our digital future: its information pipelines and its microchip foundries, its datacentres and the enormous energy plants needed to power and cool them. Some see him as a technological prophet and saviour. Others compare him to a Bond villain. So who is the real “Ben”, and what are his plans for the rest of us?Anyone trying to find Sheikh Tahnoon must first navigate concentric circles of gatekeepers. These include his closest business associates, as well as a cast of morecolourful characters: the former Lebanese prime minister Saad Hariri, for example, or Melissa Moncada, one-time winner of the Miss Globe Colombia beauty pageant, and now a fitness entrepreneur. Even if you get this far, it may not be enough to be granted an audience, and supplicants go to extraordinary lengths to stand out from the crowd.About a decade ago, Tom Barrack, an American private-equity tycoon who now serves as Donald Trump’s ambassador to Turkey, was seeking funds for his investment firm, Colony Capital, when he decided to approach Tahnoon. Barrack’s extended courtship involved sending the sheikh a rare, first-edition book from the 1950s about the breeding of Arabian horses (one of Tahnoon’s passions), offering him the chance to meet Barrack’s friend, the West Wing actor Rob Lowe (Tahnoon declined), and joining a gruelling bike ride across the Moroccan desert that Tahnoon had arranged with a group of professional cyclists. (Tahnoon rode twice as fast as Barrack, leaving him for dust.)Eventually, Barrack was granted a conference with Tahnoon on the prince’s $250m superyacht, which boasts a nightclub, spa, cinema and sushi bar, as well as 27 guest bedrooms serviced by 60 permanent crew. “Why was I excited to see Sheikh Tahnoon?” explained Barrack, during his federal trial in 2022 concerning alleged illegal lobbying for the UAE. (Barrack was ultimatelyacquitted of all charges.) “He’s one of the biggest businessmen in the world. One of the wealthiest Middle Easterners of any country. One of the most powerful.”Mapping the extent of Tahnoon’s power is almost as challenging as tracking down the man himself. But if you turn left off the 12-lane Sheikh Zayed highway that connects the UAE’s capital, Abu Dhabi, with Dubai, and drive out across the desert before striking north along the Taweelah coastline, you can glimpse some of its building blocks. First come chimneys, tankers and low-rise workers’ compounds. These form the onshore conduit of the UAE’s colossal oil reserves, most of which lie far below the seabed beyond. Continue and you’ll pass the high, windowless walls and forbidding gun towers of al-Sadr, the UAE’s most notorious prison. Eventually you’ll reach Khalifa port and its flat, grey industrial zone. Somewhere ahead, at an undisclosed location deep within a warren of container stacks, chemical drums and chain-link fences, one of thelargest AI datacentresin the world is currently rising from the sand.View image in fullscreenSheikh Tahnoon with Donald Trump at the White House, Washington, 18 March 2025.Photograph: Abu Dhabi Media Office (ADMO)These scattered landmarks form the backstage of the modern Emirates. Together, they also tell the story of the six brothers who have come to dominate the country – a story that began more than half a century ago, with their father,Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the UAE’s first leader following independence from Britain in 1971. During his 33-year reign, a loose network of Bedouin tribespeople living among mud-brick forts and palm-frond houses was transformed into an oil-rich regional superpower, home to some of the tallest buildings on Earth.Zayed married seven times and is believed to have fathered at least 30 children. But it was the offspring of his third and favourite wife, Fatima Al Ketbi, who – under her tutelage – emerged as their nation’s powerbrokers. Tahnoon was one of them. Today, he and his siblings – known as thebani Fatima, or “sons of Fatima” – sit at the apex of arguably the wealthiest dynasty in the world.Tahnoon and his brothers grew up steeped in a worldview that placed their family at the centre of the universe. Any form of dissent was seenas an existential threat, not just to their own power but also to the small and fragile state they were responsible for protecting. “The family is the first school of values, the authentic guardian of identity, and the truest source of trust and belonging,” their mother, Fatima, once said, reflecting both the paternalistic ethics that prevail among the Emirati elite, and the Al Nahyans’ visceral hostility towards alternative ideologies such as socialism or political Islam. By the time Tahnoon returned from the US in 1995, a state-sponsored crackdown on Islamist civil society groups was under way, alongside reprisals against smaller emirates that resisted it.During this period, the UAE’s leadership became increasingly conscious that money alone could not buy them international clout. Despite oil finds in the Gulf, it was the big Arab republics such as Egypt and Syria that still dominated the Middle East, both diplomatically and culturally. Military strength and strategic influence were needed to propel the Emirates into the big time. In the final years of his reign, Sheikh Zayed ensured that the bani Fatima were favourably positioned to drive this project forward.As a younger brother, Tahnoon knew that the Abu Dhabi throne – and consequently the presidency of the UAE, which always accompanies it – was not destined for him. Instead, he was given the task of running his father’s private department, which oversaw Sheikh Zayed’s extensive personal assets, including palaces, farms and overseas landholdings such as London’s Berkeley Square. The role demanded a blend of charm and coercion, and the deployment of hard cash. By the late 1990s Tahnoon was making the latter his speciality, founding a company called the Royal Group that became the primary investment vehicle for his family’s many business interests. The group’s assets are currently worth $300bn.Following Sheikh Zayed’s death in 2004, Tahnoon’s reputation as the UAE’s top money man grew. As comfortable in the boardrooms of Wall Street as he was in the Emiratimajlis(the traditional court of the tribal ruler), Tahnoon melded the rhetoric of Bedouin values – duty, loyalty and humility – with a new vocabulary of technocratic managerialism. Today, the country’s largest sovereign wealth vehicle is run by Tahnoon; so is First Abu Dhabi Bank, its largest lender, and Alterra, the biggest climate investment fund in the world. In the UK alone, Tahnoon oversees healthcare providers and property giants, and controls investments in public utilities such as Thames Water. The economic empire he oversees is estimated to be worth about $1.5tr, as large as the entire economic output of Indonesia or Turkey.But the line between Tahnoon’s personal fortune, the wider wealth of the Abu Dhabi royal family, and collective assets held – at least in theory – by the citizenry of the UAE, is blurry. According to the bani Fatima, that division is moot, as the wellbeing of the Al Nahyans is indistinguishable from the wellbeing of the nation at large. Not everyone agrees. “A lot of merchants in the UAE complain constantly – very quietly, very privately – about how Tahnoon crowds them out of the market,” Mira Al Hussein, an Emirati sociologist based at the University of Edinburgh, told me. In healthcare, for example, sovereign wealth funds and Tahnoon’s own corporate vehicles dominate the local industry; the private sector “cannot compete”, one senior executive recentlytold the Financial Times. “The general perception is that the country is a ship,” said Al Hussein, “and if that ship ever begins to sink, then the ruling family will jump off and take all of the wealth funds and investments and portfolios with them.”Tahnoon is obsessed with winning. In the late 1990s, the sheikh became so determined to beat his brothers at the newly released video game Age of Empires – in which players attempt to transform pre-modern societies into monumental civilisations by hoarding resources and overpowering opponents – that he hired one of the game’s software developers tocoach him. By the early 2000s, his attention had switched to chess. He personally financed the development of a refrigerator-sized supercomputer called Hydra, which soon became the most powerful chess player in the world, beating several grandmasters along the way. Hydra could only ever be used by a single person at a time. For hours at a stretch, day and night, that person was Tahnoon. In 2005, Hydra’s chief architect claimed in an online chess forum that Tahnoon was the greatest computer-chess freak alive.Tahnoon has brought all these skills – fierce competitiveness, the careful accumulation of positional advantage, and an abiding fascination with melding human ingenuity and computing intelligence – to the financial realm. They have also proved vital in his other main role: as the man in charge of national security in the Emirates, and his country’s spymaster-in-chief.Many of the individuals targeted by Tahnoon’s security apparatus can’t share their testimony. The UAE has a long history of enforced disappearances, secret detention sites and vicious reprisals against the family members of exiled dissidents – all extensively documented by international human rights organisations. But some survive to tell their tale.In April 2018, Matthew Hedges, a young British academic, travelled to the UAE to conduct research for his PhD exploring the country’s national security strategy, a subject that touches directly on Tahnoon’s domain. By the end of his two-week visit, Hedges had started to feel uneasy. “I knew I was being followed,” he told me recently.Entering Dubai airport on his way back to the UK, Hedges got no further than passport control. There he says he found a large group of masked men waiting for him, all dressed in black and carrying guns. He alleges that he was blindfolded, handcuffed and thrown in the back of an SUV. He was accused of working as a British spy and over the months of solitary confinement that followed, he says he was subjected to interrogations lasting up to 15 hours a day and made to swallow a cocktail of medications against his will. His captors allegedly threatened him with rendition to an overseas military base, and warned that they could harm his relatives. Following seven months of maltreatment, Hedges attempted to take his own life. “I knew their threats to be meaningful, because I knew the country,” he told me.View image in fullscreenThe British academic Matthew Hedges after he was released from prison in the UAE, December 2018.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianIn the room where he was questioned by officials, Hedges says he saw bloodstains on the carpet and bloody footprints on the walls. “They were above my head height, and facing down,” he told me. “I’m over 6ft tall, so that means someone had been lifted up there.” When I asked Hedges who was ultimately responsible for his ordeal, he ran carefully up the chain of command within the Emirati security services, reciting names and job titles, before sitting quietly for a moment and taking a breath. “Then you get above the clouds,” he replied, eventually. “Then there is Tahnoon.” (In a government statement issued in 2023, the UAE insisted that Hedges “received entirely proper care … He was never subjected to, or threatened with, either torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of any sort.”)Hedges ultimately confessed to a series of crimes, but insists that he did so under duress. In November 2018, following a hearing that lasted only five minutes, at which there was no defence lawyer present, he wassentenced to lifein jail by an Emirati court. Following a diplomatic row with the British government, he was later granted aroyal pardon. After his release, the UAE government mounted asmear campaignagainst him that included the release of a 19-page dossier of personal information including a psychiatric report. Compared with many others who pass through the country’s interrogation cells, he got off lightly. “Hedges’ experience is unfortunately common in the UAE, and abuses against Emirati civil society are even more repressive,” said Joey Shea, a senior Gulf researcher for Human Rights Watch.Supporters of the Emirati regime bridle at this sort of criticism. They insist that it is grounded in western resentment at the UAE’s rise, and overlooks the unique security threats the nation faces from hostile neighbours and ideological insurgents. “The UAE has become a success story, and that’s led to you guys thinking, ‘Wait, these were the little ducklings that we used to run and now look at what they’re doing,’” said Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, an Emirati professor of political science who is well connected to ruling officials in the UAE. “I resent the claim that the UAE must ‘level up’ to international standards [on human rights]. You have your standard, we have ours.”The Al Nahyan dynasty has good reason to feel insecure. Located on the tip of a landmass roiled by conflict to the north and south, and staring out across the Gulf at its far larger rival Iran, the UAE’s petro-riches make it an obvious target. Tahnoon and his brothers also know that their brand of autocratic monarchy is despised by political Islamists and pro-democracy Arab revolutionaries alike. Some 20 years ago, Christopher Davidson, an expert in Gulf politics at Durham University, spoke to one of the bani Fatima about the Emirates’ rising prestige. “He said to me, ‘You need to understand the mindset of this region. Others will try to take that away from us, or destroy us’,” Davidson recalled. “‘Whether it’s Iran, Yemen, the Muslim Brotherhood, Al-Qaeda … they’ll all be coming, one after another.’”For the UAE’s leaders, the 9/11 attacks – perpetrated by a group of extremists that included two Emiratis – were a realisation of their darkest fears about violent enemies lurking within, and helped fuel an obsession with Islamism that persists to this day. (The UAE has beenlinkedto covert funding and political support forfar-right political partiesin Europe who are seen to share Abu Dhabi’s perspective on this issue.) The US war on terror was also a moment of opportunity, enabling the Al Nahyans to present themselves to Washington as an island of stability within an otherwise forbidding region.Throughout the 2000s, the Emirati regime ramped up its intelligence activities and increasingly focused on espionage technologies. The aim was to mitigate the country’s most obvious vulnerability: its tiny native population of 1.4 million people, which comprises only 11% of the UAE’s total residents, and makes it hard for the country to raise a significant army or to function in the absence of foreigners. By the end of the decade, it had struck a landmark security deal with the former US counterterrorism czar Richard Clarke, who was instrumental in lobbying Congress for more intrusive surveillance programmes both at home and abroad. Clarke moved out to Abu Dhabi and set up a secretive UAE spying unit, which was given the codenameProject Raven.Initially billed as a vital cog in the “war on terror”, Project Raven morphed into a vast and pervasive digital wiretap operation targeting not only Emiratis accused of terrorism, but many others merely suspected of being unfriendly to the UAE’s dictatorship. Although technically an Emirati initiative, much of theteam running Project Ravenwere former US National Security Agency spies, Washington contractors and senior White House veterans. “The incentive was to help in the fight against terrorism,” Clarke later insisted. “The UAE is a very good counterterrorism partner.”By 2011, when anti-government uprisings erupted across the Arab world, the focus of Project Raven’s energies had become clear. After a group of prominent Emirati judges, lawyers and journalists put their names to a petition calling for mild democratic reforms, the state’s response was uncompromising; over the next two years the majority of themwere arrested, and dozens of signatories remain in jail today. More paranoid than ever, and harbouring fears that Emirati soldiers might refuse to turn their guns on fellow Muslims in the event of widespread street protests, the bani Fatima mobilised an 800-strong paramilitary force of Colombian and South African mercenaries to tighten their grip on power, and even greater resources were funnelled into digital hacking operations. To the Al Nahyans, mass politics was a threat: in their eyes, grateful subjects could only ever petition their leaders for concessions, never make demands of them as citizens. “The UAE’s internal security structure increasingly prioritised regime protection above all else,” said Mira Al Hussein.It was against this backdrop that Tahnoon – alongside his role as the UAE’s money man – began rising up the ranks of the Emirati security establishment. In 2014, he became the country’s deputy national security adviser; two years later, he assumed the top job. As security chief, his new brief included some of the UAE’s most sensitive diplomatic missions, among them the breaking of a decades-long taboo in the Arab world bynormalising relations with Israel. As the Middle East’s other leader in the field of cyber-espionage, Israeli intelligence had much to offer the Emiratis: not least access toPegasus, the most advanced spyware ever built.
