With Pegasus, operatives were able to infiltrate almost any Apple or Android device without the user’s knowledge, and transform it into a permanent, pocket-sized spy.View image in fullscreenSheikh Tahnoon’s $250m superyacht anchored off Antibes in the Mediterranean.Photograph: Ed Holt/AlamyUnder Tahnoon’s stewardship, Project Raven – control of which had now passed into the hands of a private, state-linked Emirati company named DarkMatter – scaled up its hacking and surveillance activities. Local dissidents and suspicious foreigners on Emirati soil were targeted. But so, too, were human rights activists, journalists and politicians all over the world. Fiona Shackleton, a high-profile British divorce lawyer representing an estranged wife of the ruler of Dubai – whose other clients have included Prince Charles and Paul McCartney – wasone such victim. Then UK prime ministerBoris Johnsonis believed to have been another. It seemed that no matter who you were, if you were deemed to threaten the interests of the Al Nahyan family and their friends, even tangentially, then you were a potential target.In early 2019, aReuters investigation– building on work by the Canadian research group The Citizen Lab – exposed much of Project Raven’s operations, and multiple legal proceedings were launched in the US against the initiative’s American contractors. Over the next year, Tahnoon officially shut down DarkMatter and broke apart its various entities. By that time, it appears he was nursing more ambitious plans.A powerful new frontier in computing power – artificial intelligence – was just beginning to open up. To be genuinely transformative, this technology was going to require fantastical amounts of cash and data. By fusing together elements of his business and security empires, Tahnoon would be in a unique position to supply both. A company like no other was about to be born.In Douglas Adams’s The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, a superintelligent computer programme named Deep Thought is asked “the great Question of Life, the Universe and Everything’”. After seven and a half million years, it finally delivers its famous answer: 42. Deep Thought goes on to say that, in order to explain its answer, it needs to design another giant computer programme. This one will be called “Earth”, and one of its core operational components will be human beings.In this vision, the number 42 represents more than the meaning of life. It speaks to a world in which every facet of reality can ultimately be reduced to lines of code, and where ordinary people unwittingly live out their days in the service of computers rather than the other way around. In the late 2010s, when Tahnoon refashioned the ruins of DarkMatter into a new AI-focused company, he decided to honour Adams by calling it Group 42, or G42 for short.G42 isthe culmination of Tahnoon’s dual identity as a financier and spymaster, and the scale of its aspirations is staggering. Like many other tech giants, it aims to reconceptualise AI as a foundational form of infrastructure like water or electricity – a concept known as the “intelligence grid”. Unlike its Silicon Valley peers, however, G42’s intelligence grid has grown out of an actual nation state’s intelligence apparatus. The company’s marketing heavily emphasises its security capabilities, promising “real-time threat defence” for governments and businesses, and predictive tools that encompass “suspect profiling”, “relationship mapping” and “behavioural analysis”.The tech industry is not short on exaggeration and bombast. Compared with many of his Silicon Valley peers, however, Tahnoon – a true AI believer who claims to have designed the entirety of one of his homes via ChatGPT – is in a unique position to deliver. G42 built on the espionage talents behind Project Raven and DarkMatter: Peng Xiao, who was the head of a key DarkMatter unit, is now G42’s CEO; Karim Sabbagh, DarkMatter’s former boss, currently runs one of G42’s main subsidiaries. One of G42’s first public products was a popular messaging app called ToTok, which was later revealed by the New York Times to be apiece of spyware, designed to “track every conversation, movement, relationship, appointment, sound and image of those who install it on their phones”.In a statement to the Guardian, G42 denied that the company’s origins lay in cyber-espionage operations, or that it conducts or enables unlawful surveillance. “G42 was established as an AI and technology company focused on cloud and AI infrastructure,” the firm said. “Our businesses operate under applicable laws, contractual data protections, and rigorous security and compliance frameworks.”If US tech giants are wary of G42’s links to cyberhacking, they are doing a good job of hiding it. Microsoft has invested $1.5bn in the company and its vice-chair, Brad Smith, now has a seat on G42’s board of directors. G42 and its specialist AI investment fund – also chaired by Tahnoon – are either direct investors in or major partners of Anthropic, xAI and OpenAI. Sam Altman, the latter’s CEO, calls Tahnoon “a dear personal friend”. Microsoft and OpenAI were approached for comment on this article, but neither company provided a response. In its statement to the Guardian, G42 noted that its partnership with Microsoft “is governed by a binding agreement developed in consultation with the US and UAE governments, covering cybersecurity, data protection, responsible AI, export controls and business integrity”.Tahnoon’s appeal to Silicon Valley is obvious. After all, if you’re going to go into business with a cash-laden Gulf autocrat, then picking one who presides over a heavily digitised state-security empire – and who boasts a proven track record of hoovering up humongous amounts of personal data, the raw ingredient upon which your technology depends – feels like a logical choice. Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elon Musk may all be hugely influential AI leaders, but none of them simultaneously runs the CIA.Another powerful figure to have clutched Tahnoon and G42 close to his bosom is Donald Trump, who has hosted lavish state banquets for the sheikh at the White House andposed for photoswith him in the Oval Office. The American security services have long harboured fears about Emirati influence on US politics: in 2022 the National Intelligence Council produced a confidential report for Washington policymakers warning of Abu Dhabi’s “illegal and legal attempts to steer US foreign policy”. Joe Biden’s administration restricted the export of AI chips to the UAE because of concerns over the country’s close ties to China. But last year Trump reversed that decision, authorising the transfer of hundreds of thousands of Silicon Valley’s most advanced chips to the Al Nahyan regime. Many of them will go straight to G42.View image in fullscreenSheikh Tahnoon with Mark Zuckerberg in Washington in March 2025.Photograph: Abu Dhabi Media Office (ADMO)The deal was announced only two weeks after one of Tahnoon’s investment vehicles acquired $2bn-worth of cryptocurrency issued by World Liberty, a company owned by the Trump family, who earn interest on all its reserves. Tahnoon is also a direct investor in World Liberty, having purchased 49% of the firm less than a month before Trump’s second inauguration. Both the White House and World Liberty have denied any connection between Tahnoon’s investments and the chip transfer. A spokesperson for G42 told the New York Times that the company was “grounded in integrity”.“Corruption, plain and simple,” is how the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren describes the murky entanglement of Tahnoon’s money and the US White House. But the rapid ascent of Tahnoon and G42 within the AI industry reflects a sincerely held conviction on the part of both the Trump administration and the bani Fatima that AI is set to replace oil as the elemental global commodity – and ultimate determinant of global power – and that now is the time to master it.The result is that G42, under Tahnoon’s control, has successfully positioned itself at the heart of global AI infrastructure for decades to come. The “AI campus” currently being constructed on the UAE’s coastline is projected to have a 5GW power capacity, up to 250 times the size of the largest hyperscale datacentres today. G42 is helping to finance a $500bn rollout of new datacentres within the US, and has now acquired several of the construction companies involved. Last year, Microsoft and G42 officially co-launched the Responsible AI Future Foundation, designed to shape “ethical development and deployment of AI systems”. It is headquartered – of course – in Abu Dhabi.Does it matter if significant chunks of our AI infrastructure sit in the hands of a man with the entire arsenal of a police state at his disposal? One person who might be able to answer that is Ahmed Mansoor, a mild-mannered Emirati electrical engineer and aspiring poet. In the early 2010s, Mansoor was among that group of public intellectuals who signed a petition calling for the creation of an elected parliament in the UAE; he also ran a website on which content critical of the Al Nahyan regime was sometimes posted. In April 2011, he was arrested on multiple charges, including the defamation of the bani Fatima, but initially released thanks to a presidential pardon.In the years that followed, though, Mansoor was relentlessly targeted by the Emirati security services, who spent millions of dollars attempting to gain access to his electronic devices, and those of his wife. Eventually, Mansoor succumbed to a malicious email attachment, which sent all of his private data to a computer server registered to PO box 5151 in Abu Dhabi: the postal address of Sheikh Tahnoon’s personal office. He later found out that his baby monitor had also been hacked, turning it into a camera and microphone that captured every moment of his family life. He was arrested again in 2017, subjected to a secret trial, and convicted of insulting the “status and prestige of the UAE and its symbols, including its leaders”. Sentenced to 10 years in jail, he has remained in solitary confinement in al-Sadr, the maximum-security jail located about 10 miles south-west of G42’s AI mega-campus, ever since.We don’t know if Tahnoon will use his commanding position at the heart of the AI industry to directly hack, surveil and intimidate critics, as his security services did with Mansoor. But the character of those controlling this new technology matters. Today, we don’t just use major tech platforms to store files and send messages: more and more people use AI to be their therapist, friend or even lover. Tech executives assure us that our data is safe from prying eyes but ordinary citizens have very few ways of verifying this. In its pomp, the early smartphone manufacturer BlackBerry insisted that “privacy and security form the crux of everything we do”. It failed to mention that BlackBerry was secretly working with the cybersecurity unit of a foreign government at the time, and helping it to carry out digital surveillance of mobile users. That cybersecurity unit was the UAE’s DarkMatter group, the precursor to G42.The potential risks of untrustworthy actors controlling AI may be more insidious than direct hacking and surveillance. A group of researchersrecently revealedthat AI tools – including products from Meta, Google and SpaceX – are regularly altering the meaning of texts on sensitive political topics, in ways that could reshape public opinion. “I’m very worried about Tahnoon’s perception of the world,” says Al Hussein. “He’s the video-game prince who wants to press a button and eliminate all threats.”View image in fullscreenSheikh Tahnoon with Palantir cofounder Alex Karp in Washington in March 2025.Photograph: Abu Dhabi Media Office (ADMO)For a glimpse of what a world reshaped in Tahnoon’s image might look like, consider the UAE. Here, political parties are nonexistent, trade unions and labour strikes prohibited, and protests and lèse-majesté met with rapid punishment. Migrant workers, who make up the vast majority of the country’s residents, are kept in a state of legalised insecurity and suffer from thousands of officially unexplained deaths each year, which human rights organisations attribute to heat stress, construction accidents and other poor working conditions. Businesses, by contrast, can pick and choose the regulations that govern them from a patchwork quilt of 40-odd “freezones”, all competing to lure investors with bespoke tax regimes and legal frameworks.Beyond the UAE’s borders, Abu Dhabi’s dominion encompasses a vast network of ports, security partners, client regimes and financial flows spanning the Red Sea and huge swathes of north, eastern and central Africa. Often presented as a neutralentrepot, torn between rival global power blocs to the east and the west, the reality is that the UAE has always served faithfully as capital’s emirate: shielding the wealth of international elites, opening up inhospitable markets, paving the way for western investors, and – as Colin Powers, a political economist specialising in the Middle East,puts it– “energetically extending the circuitry of global wealth accumulation”.Under the bani Fatima, this function has included the brutal suppression of any democratic experiment within the Emirati field of influence that might threaten the material interests of the Al Nahyans or their allies. In Egypt, the UAE has helped sustain the military dictatorship of Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, which has turned its guns upon thousands of protesters. In Yemen, Libya and Ethiopia, it has armed paramilitaries and fuelled shocking levels of state violence against civilians. In Sudan, it is accused ofcomplicity in genocide. In response, Abu Dhabi hasdeployed AI toolsas part of a sophisticated disinformation campaign designed to discredit the United Nations. Several dissidents wanted by other dictatorships – from Iran to Saudi Arabia and Rwanda – have also been kidnapped while transiting through Dubai airport, before being “delivered” by the Emiratis to their home country’s security forces. Not all of Abu Dhabi’s foreign adventures have been successful; many have led to military quagmires and reputational damage on the world stage. But for those on the receiving end of Emirati intervention, the consequences have been dire.The imperial ambitions of Tahnoon and his brothers do not seem to rest on direct occupation of land, but rather on controlling key “nodes” outside their borders: the sites at which the movement of money, arms, trade, technology and ideas intersect. AI, the functioning of which is distributed across territories around the world, is the ideal asset for a nodal empire. Tahnoon’s goal of making the UAE an AI superpower is framed domestically as part of his family’s historic mission to improve the lot of the Emirati people. But the UAE’s accumulation of power in recent decades has been delivered on the bani Fatima’s own terms. Central to the Al Nahyan family’s worldview is the notion that, amid a planet riven by the chaos and humiliation of democracy, their nation is a demonstration that things can and should work differently. According to Tahnoon’s brother, President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, “The UAE is a tangible model for the world.”With his array of spy tools, superyachts and supercomputers, his preference for remaining far from public view, his habit of always wearing dark glasses in public (even indoors), and – of course – his obsession with personal longevity (he aims to live to 150), it would be easy to characterise Tahnoon as a cartoon villain. But in truth, this is not a story about a malevolent prince plotting vile deeds from his palace in the Persian Gulf. It is a far more prosaic tale about how power and money function in the world today.In Washington, just as in Abu Dhabi, politics is increasingly governed by personal relationships and transactional gains rather than popular demands. In the UK, as in the UAE, firms such as Palantir that offer AI-enabled surveillance and data crunching are being integrated with the basic functions of the state. All over the planet, business-friendly strongmen are the order of the day. “For the last 20 years, democracy has been in decline,” said Ronald Deibert, the founder and director of The Citizen Lab. “That happens to coincide with an enormous expansion of digital surveillance capabilities for both commercial and national security purposes. The epicentre of a lot of this is the UAE. And where do all roads lead in the UAE? They lead to Sheikh Tahnoon.”On 27 February, Tahnoon chaired a board meeting at G42’s AI investment fund. That night, the sky above Abu Dhabi’s seafront lit up with the flashes of US and Israeli missiles raining down across the Persian Gulf, marking the start of the Iran war. One of Tehran’s first acts of retaliation was to directly bomb two AI datacentres in the UAE. The Iranian government soon published an official list of what they considered“legitimate” military targetswhich included the Emirati offices of US technology companies such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Western journalists speculated that this could spell the end of Tahnoon’s AI dreams. “Why did we ever think datacentres in the Gulf were a good idea?”ran one headlinein the Financial Times.The go-between: how Qatar became the global capital of diplomacyRead moreOver the following months, Tahnoon shuttled around the Middle East, conducting covert diplomacy. According to Reuters, senior officials from Iran’s revolutionary guards were hosted by Tahnoon in his Abu Dhabi guesthouse. By mid-June, he had reportedly struck an agreement that provided billions of dollars for the Iranian government, and brought Iran’s strikes on the UAE to a halt. A few weeks later, on the same day that Trump announced that the US’s ceasefire with Iran was “over”, the US commerce department quietly confirmed that it was removing the last remaining export controls restricting the sale of advanced AI chips to Abu Dhabi.As life in Abu Dhabi gradually returned to something resembling normality, Tahnoon’s family members began reappearing in public. A company founded by his daughter, Sheikha Fatima bint Tahnoon, signed a memorandum of understanding with G42 last month, suggesting that she is being primed to follow in his footsteps and eventually assume a commanding role within the UAE’s tech-security empire. Tahnoon’s son, Sheikh Zayed bin Tahnoon, was the guest of honour at several major jiu-jitsu events this summer. Tahnoon himself, meanwhile, stayed far from the public eye. Judging when to retreat, and knowing when to strike: “Ben” had outmanoeuvred his doubters once again.Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: Borrowing can be good, there is no such thing as the ‘nation’s credit card’, and, yes, you can buck the markets – as previous governments have shown, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: Borrowing can be good, there is no such thing as the ‘nation’s credit card’, and, yes, you can buck the markets – as previous governments have shown, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: Photograph: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianOpinionEconomic policyRightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to KeynesLarry ElliottBorrowing can be good, there is no such thing as the ‘nation’s credit card’, and, yes, you can buck the markets – as previous governments have shownThu 1 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTShareAndy Burnham does a nice line in nostalgia. Hisfirst party conference speechas prime minister was full of fond memories for the Britain of the 1950s and 1960s, when working-class families could sense their lives steadily getting better. The underlying message of his address was that, given time, he could rekindle that optimism and return the country to how it was before Margaret Thatcher wrecked everything.Much of what Burnham says is true. The 1980s was a decade of deindustrialisation, asset-stripping and financial deregulation that has shaped modern Britain – and not in a good way.But listen a bit more closely to the speech and it becomes clear that Burnham is struggling to find a way to turn back the clock. For a start, he might not be given time. Energy bills are forecastto rise sharply this winter. John Healey’s first budget, in less than a month’s time, is expected to raise taxes or cut spending – taking money out of an economy that is already struggling.There’s no question that Burnham and Healey would prefer not to be taking these actions but feel they have no choice. Burnham may well rail against 40 years of neoliberalism. He may think neoliberalism was a dud. But his government is constrained by neoliberal ideas and the language used to express them. Burnham and Healey would never use this language themselves, but that’s irrelevant. To make a real difference, they need to tackle head-on the nostrums of the past four decades. Otherwise they will be for ever in thrall to them.Top of the list is the idea that the UK government is no different from a household. That means it should match its spending to its income as closely as possible, borrowing prudently and within tightly defined limits. Otherwise it will“max out the nation’s credit card”and risk spiralling into unsustainable debt.This analogy has the benefit of sounding like a statement of the obvious to many voters, but is actually entirely false. There is no such thing as the nation’s credit card, and a country that prints its own currency can never “max out” or face bankruptcy in the way an individual can.The notion that the government is living well beyond its means is convenient for those on the political right who have an aversion to public spending. The reality is that, as John Maynard Keynesonce said: “Anything we can actually do we can afford.” It was that mentality that allowed the Attlee government to create the welfare state when debt was running at more than250% of national income– more than double today’s level. I don’t know whether Burnham has seen thenew play about Keynesin London’s West End, but it seems as if he ought to.View image in fullscreenRory Kinnear (right) as John Maynard Keynes alongside Luke Cinque White in The Standard of Living.Photograph: Manuel HarlanBy the same token, it makes no sense to talk about “black holes” in the public finances every time the government looks on course to miss its targets for borrowing as set out in its fiscal rules. These rules are treated as totemic when in reality they can be changed at any time – and are ditched altogether when there is a crisis.Again, the idea of a black hole is a convenient fiction for those with an interest in shrinking the size of the state. As with “maxing out the credit card”, it forms part of the inquisition every time a minister goes on the TV or radio with a new spending measure: “That’s all very well but how are you going to pay for it?”Burnham is committed to re-industrialising Britain, but to do so he will have to break with the neoliberal convention that it is not the job of the government to pick winners. As the prime minister should point out, China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea have all built up their manufacturing strength by picking winners, and Britain could do the same. Indeed, the one sector that Thatcher picked out for special care and attention – financial services – has gone from strength to strength. Breaking the taboo on picking winners is central to a successful industrial strategy.Last but not least, Burnham has to address Thatcher’s famous dictum: you can’t buck the market. A cursory glance back at recent economic history shows that governments buck the market all the time. In 2009, the Bank of England responded to the risk of a second Great Depression posed by the global financial crisis by buying government bonds. This provided money to the banking system while cutting the interest rate – or yield – on bonds. This was bucking the market. In 2020, the then Conservative government spent hundreds of billions on a furlough scheme thatpaid up to 80% of the wagesof workers at risk of losing their jobs during the pandemic. This, too, was bucking the market.So when Burnham, in his conference speech, harked back to the Britain in the immediate decades after the second world war, he missed out a key part of the reason working people felt things were getting better. Rather than being constrained by fiscal rules, governments were committed to full employment. Capital controls meant that financial markets were tightly controlled.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBefore we get too nostalgic, it’s worth remembering that things were far from perfect in the so-called postwar golden age. By today’s standards, growth rates were spectacular, but they lagged well behind those of Germany and France. Even so, managed capitalism certainly delivered more for working people than has been the case in the unmanaged capitalism that has followed.The postwar status quo has been turned on its head. Then, financial markets were caged to ensure that governments could pursue domestic economic goals. Now, governments are caged and the markets are free. It is a classic case of the tail wagging the dog.Shifting back to a world where finance is fettered is not going to be easy – but until it happens, governments will remain boxed in. Burnham and Healey will be forced to do things they know will harm the economy because they know any deviation from what is acceptable to the received wisdom risks a backlash from the financial markets.Some new economic thinking is required, and if ever there were a time for an iconoclast like Keynes, it is surely now. He would certainly have no truck with the wrong-headed economic policies of the past half-century and the seemingly commonsense phrases – such as maxing out the credit card – that have been used to disguise just how nonsensical they are.All credit to Burnham. His analysis of what has gone wrong has clearly rattled his political enemies. Even so, he risks becoming the nearly man of British politics: the prime minister who asked the right questions but failed to come up with the right answers.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEconomic policyOpinionAndy BurnhamJohn Maynard KeynesEconomicsLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Flipping public opinion on the triple lock was Burnham magic – he’ll need more of it to see his social care plans through | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Rebuilding a complex and broken system into one that’s fair for all, and in the face of steely opposition: that will be the PM’s real challenge, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Rebuilding a complex and broken system into one that’s fair for all, and in the face of steely opposition: that will be the PM’s real challenge, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andy Burnham speaks to residents, care workers and volunteers during visit to a care home in London, 29 July 2026.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/Pool AP/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaks to residents, care workers and volunteers during visit to a care home in London, 29 July 2026.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/Pool AP/APOpinionSocial careFlipping public opinion on the triple lock was Burnham magic – he’ll need more of it to see his social care plans throughPolly ToynbeeRebuilding a complex and broken system into one that’s fair for all, and in the face of steely opposition: that will be the PM’s real challengeThu 1 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTShareHere is rare clearcut proof of the power of political persuasion. Party conference speeches, the lifeblood of political obsessives, rarely reach the public beyond a brief news clip. But this time was different.Andy Burnham’s speechspun the dial on public opinion on several political hot potatoes, defining who he is.The pensions triple lock, which guarantees that pensions rise faster than average incomes, has been a no-go electoral minefield despite a groundswell of economists (and even aTimes leader) calling for reform to prevent pensions skyrocketing. Touching this live rail was an act of bravery – or recklessness.Polls over the years strongly supported the lock: a Persuasion UK poll this week found65% in favourof keeping it, more among over-65s. A Times YouGov poll this month went as high as93% of pension-age peopledefending it. So the sudden change in public opinion after the speech has been astonishing. YouGovnow reportsthat 48% support the Burnham plan, with just 28% against. Survation finds64% backing itwith only 15% against. The magic was linking reform of the lock with creating a national care service. Never mind that it barely begins to cover the cost, it makes an emotional link between the two policies.I can’t think of any other conference speech that reversed public opinion on such a sensitive policy. Kemi Badenoch’s Tories protested that it was just “robbing Peter to pay Paul”, whileNigel Farage’s party vowed, “Reform UK will always protect our pensioners and maintain the triple lock.” Both are out of touch with the public (at least, for now).But this is only week one on a long and winding journey to 2030, when plans for the triple lock and a national care service have appeared in the nextLabourmanifesto – and fickle voters have reelected a Labour government. When the world so often turns upside down in the blink of an eye (Burnham keeps reminding himself he is the seventh PM in a decade), 2030 can feel light years away.We don’t yet know what a national care service is. But the most moving and easiest to implement promise in Burnham’s speech is to improve the lives and status of care workers like those he watched looking after his father: “Caring for other people’s parents on poverty pay, but doing it with huge skill, humour and humanity.” He pledged, “I promise you, I won’t leave this job without doing everything I can to change things for you.” Starmer’s fair-pay agreement for care workers is already on its way, to be agreed between trade unions and employers. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary,this week announcedthe first national pension scheme for care workers. Next, they need training, pay and career ladders the same as NHS healthcare assistants, merging the two together.But the rest of Burnham’s “landmark policy as significant as the creation of the NHS itself” looks perplexingly difficult. He promised “care that is about people, not profit”, but Margaret Thatcher privatised care, breaking it into fragments by denying central funds to any council keeping its own service. There are now about19,000 organisationsproviding adult care in England, some big, most small, some good, some pretty terrible, some voluntary, many understaffed. In theory, they are inspected by the regulator, but the Care Quality Commission, knowing the shortage of beds and services, sets alow bar in standards. Could that be in-sourced?But here’s the biggest conundrum of all. Who pays for social care goes right to the heart of social justice and fair taxation. Currently, most people in England already have their care paid for by the state, because they have less than £23,250 in savings and no property that is not lived in by a partner. But23% of peoplein England who get at-home careand 37% of thosein residential careare self-funders. Between them, they pay £14bn a year. Burnham seemed to imply they would be relieved of that burden, NHS style – but if so, that would be a whopping £14bn given to better-off elderly people, paid for by taxpayers. That’s unthinkably expensive and unfair to younger working people, a generation with less income and less property. So it won’t and shouldn’t happen.Instead, as hastily explained afterwards, self-payers will only get their care paid for, but they will stillpay for their bed and boardin care homes – as in Scotland, where standard weekly costs of about £1,000 are mitigated by the statecontributing £260 for care. Burnham said that people should no longer lose their homes to pay care costs; they still do in Scotland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritons are not ageing healthily – we need to learn from countries that have made it a priority | Devi SridharRead moreAnd rightly. Only 21% of people think the state should pay for it all, regardless of the recipient’s wealth, according to aKing’s Fund survey. Keeping an empty home to pass on as inheritance is not something the state should subsidise, when every spare penny is needed to pay for better social care. More than 400,000 are on officialcare waiting listsin England, while Age UK says2 million older peoplehave unmet care needs, putting a huge burden on families. Burnham himself talked of the miserably inadequate 15-minute homecare visits. Meanwhile, the NHS desperately needs a better care service to save the13,000 beds a dayfilled with those waiting for a care package.At any one time, few people use social care, so few understand the system, according to the King’s Fund. Simon Bottery, who leads its work on adult social care, says, “Frailty and dementia in later life are issues that most people just don’t want to think about until they really need to.” But it’s about to become a hot political battleground, with its fiendish complexities and its difficult moral and political choices.When problems look insoluble, the last five prime ministers have summoned the great troubleshooterLouise Casey. She reports next year on what should be done. With the political right preparing for war, her job is to find answers acceptable enough to most. But that’s unlikely to include a carbon copy of the free NHS, nor should that be on the table.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSocial careOpinionOlder peopleNHSLabourHealthAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: As the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking point
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: As the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking point
Content: ‘The Trump administration seems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe.’Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The Trump administration seems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe.’Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea?Arwa MahdawiAs the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking pointThu 1 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.27 EDTShareDonald Trump seems to spend an unusual amount of time thinking about toilets.Back in 2019, he bizarrelyclaimed: “People are flushing toilets 10 times, 15 times as opposed to once.” He repeated this claim at a Michigan rally the followingyear. “Ten times, right, 10 times,” Trump complained. “Not me, of course not me, but you,” he added while pointing at an unfortunate audience member.A couple of years later, he was back to the toilet talk: angrilydisputing claimsby the New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman that he’d once clogged a White House toilet by attempting to dispose of documents in it.I regret to inform you that the president is once again responsible for a national conversation about toilets. In a fitting encapsulation of Trumpism, explosive diarrhea has become a midtermtalking point. Food recalls and stomach-churning parasites have been a mainstay of the news this year and Democrats are milking the issue.Food-borne illnesses, funding cuts and layoffs: Maha movement’s glaring limitations are now showingRead moreIn August, for example, the Democratic party’s official Twitter/X accounthighlightedthe number of foods that have been recalled in 2026 and demanded that RFK Jr resign from his role as health secretary. Last month (which happened to be Food Safety Month – who knew?), the Rhode Island congressman Gabe Amoarguedthat Trump’s cuts to the federal workforce had contributed to decreased food safety. Senator Elizabeth Warrensimilarly accused“slashed food safety agencies” of contributing to the “cyclospora outbreak” and demanded Trump be held accountable in November.To be fair, the number offood recallsduring Trump’s second term is not remarkably different than it was under Joe Biden. What is different, however, is the scale of the problem. The US only recently declared the end of thelargest ever recordedcyclosporiasis outbreak, which was linked to contaminated lettuce. That resulted in 570 hospitalizations and two ⁠deaths.Also different is the fact that, as Warren noted, theTrump administrationseems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe. Ever since 1995, there has been a federal-state partnership called the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet) which tracks infections caused by various pathogens, including Cyclospora.Starting on 1 July, however, the CDCdowngradedthis program so that mandatory surveillance for the 10 state health departments that participate in the program was limited to salmonella andEcoli. This downgrading of pathogen surveillance didn’t cause the cyclospora outbreak, but it might have made it harder for health authorities torespond to it.And it’s not just food that the current administration is making less safe: the air we breathe and the water we drink are all getting more dangerous in the name of maximizing corporate profits.On Monday, for example, the Trump administrationannouncedit was relaxing rules that govern how fuel-efficient auto companies have to make their new gasoline-powered cars and light trucks. The rationale given by Sean Duffy, the reality show star turned transportation secretary, is that removing stringent pollution-control requirements will reduce the average costs of new vehicles by $1,300.We’ll see if that actually happens (corporations are not keen on passing on cost savings), but even if it does reduce car prices, it’s going to cost consumers and the environment in other ways. Reduced efficiency will increase fuel spending, for one thing. And the change is poised to create more air pollution and worsen climate change.Donald Trump’s Maga cult is finally crumbling | Arwa MahdawiRead moreThe Trump administration is also working toroll back regulationof toxic air pollutants. Earlier this year the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed weakening air pollution limits on ethylene oxide (EtO), a knowncarcinogenthat is used to clean medical devices. A Biden-era rule finalized in 2024 required stringent testing for hazardous emissions and required emitters to cut the amount of EtO they were producing.If the EPA is successful in overturning these rules, then tons of the carcinogenic gas will continue to be released into the community. And it’s obviously not people in the vicinity of Mar-a-Lago breathing in the brunt of this poisonous air, is it? It’s people in largely low-income neighborhoods.Then there’s our water supply. A Biden-era rule set drinking-water limits for several Pfas (commonly known as “forever chemicals”). You know what happened next, don’t you? The Trump administration is trying to roll backthose limits, arguing that the standards are expensive and legally flawed.They’ve also terminated a regulatory review of Pfas-contaminatedsewage sludgefertilizer that is used on farmland. What does that mean? Well, according tocommentssubmitted by the Southern Environmental Law Center to the EPA, “if PFOA levels are 9.4 parts per billion [as witnessed in sludge tested in Maine], then more than 54 children out of 10,000 who eat 1-2 meals of fish per week on crop farms could get cancer later in life from those meals alone.”In short: if you thought the diarrhea-inducing lettuce was bad, then I’m afraid things only look likely to get worse. If Trump isn’t reined in at the midterms, the whole country is going down the toilet.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionDonald TrumpCyclosporiasis outbreak (US)Trump administrationUS politicsClimate crisisPollutioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Releasing prisoners won’t solve the crisis in English and Welsh jails. Here’s what will | Enver Solomon | The Guardian
description: Ministers need to level with the public about current prison sentences, who needs to be locked up and for how long, says Enver Solomon of Nacro
Author: Enver Solomon
Headline: Ministers need to level with the public about current prison sentences, who needs to be locked up and for how long, says Enver Solomon of Nacro
Content: ‘Ministers need to be much more transparent about the importance of rehabilitation as well as punishment.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Ministers need to be much more transparent about the importance of rehabilitation as well as punishment.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyOpinionPrisons and probationReleasing prisoners won’t solve the crisis in English and Welsh jails. Here’s what willEnver SolomonMinisters need to level with the public about what current prison sentences look like – who needs to be locked up and for how longEnver Solomon is chief executive of Nacro, the criminal justice charity‘Thank you Andy Burnham’: prisoners react as they begin to leave under early release schemeThu 1 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTShareThe flipchart in the corner of the staff meeting room, deep inside a prison in the south-east ofEngland, tells its own story about what our overcrowded jails are having to deal with, day in day out. Under the heading “Challenges”, it lists gangs, the destruction of cells, prisoners exploiting each other and complex behaviours.Committed, hard-working staff talk about the high levels of psychosis, often combined with drug abuse. They provide examples of people actually committing crimes to go back into jail to get some respite from their chaotic, dysfunctional lives.To tackle the current prisons crisis in England and Wales, plannedchanges to sentencingwill see almost 2,000 peoplereleased early from Thursdayand over the following month. It is the first tranche of the estimated 5,000 releases that will take place in phases over the coming year.This will address the immediate crisis, but by the government’s own admission it isnot a permanent fix.If it wants to ensure that the new approach to early releases does not need to be further accelerated, wider reforms will be needed across the system.As a first step, we need to address the staggering increase in people recalled to prison. The power that probation officers have to send someone back behind bars plays an important role in protecting the public, but with recall now accounting forone in sevenof the prison population compared with one in 13 a decade ago, it is neithersustainable nor effective. Cases of people being recalled for missing probation appointments because transport was delayed or for moving out of their accommodation to get away from drug dealers and gangs, are too often punished with a return to custody. A justice secretary under the last Labour government tells me it’s a ludicrous approach that must change if prisons aren’t going to stagger from crisis to crisis.Second, we need to focus on the probation service. It is critical to fixing prisons and too often undervalued. Today it is a long way from its original social-work ethos to advise, assist and befriend those once described as clients but now always labelled offenders. The focus is much more on surveillance and compliance. Consecutive reports by the Chief Inspector of Prisons during the last two weeks reveal how, after years of being run down, the service is struggling to get the basics right. Electronic tags are a critical and expanding part of supervision on release from custody, but theinspector foundthe “systems, processes and frontline practice needed to make it effective have not kept pace”. The standard of probation work isnot consistentlywhat it should be, with staff shortages, poor information sharing and gaps in the capability of probation officers to keep people safe.The government is committed to recruiting thousands more probation staff and to improving practice but, faced with people who have a complex mix of needs and behaviours, a more person-centred approach closer to the profession’s social-work roots is needed. Those coming out of custody whom we work with say they want probation officers to get alongside them and build trusting relationships so they can get their lives back on track.We need to be more open with the public. Prisons and probation are there to keep the public safe, but to do that, ministers need to be much more transparent about the importance of rehabilitation as well as punishment. The justice secretary’sspeech to Labour conferencethis week started this, but far too many are still leaving prison to commit further offences because the system does not provide the drug treatment, access to employment, training and education – and then stable accommodation on release – that will help turn them away from crime. The fact thathalf of those rough sleepingin England and Wales have spent time in prison is a stark reminder of what’s not working.The services need connecting. Fixing this cannot be achieved by the justice system alone. Public bodies from the NHS to local councils have a role to play in giving people the support they need to stay out of prison. Beyond those, community providers can step in where state agencies are not best placed to reach people.In his party conference speech, Andy Burnham spoke of the importance ofbeing honest with the country. To be honest about our prisons would be to recognise that continuing to lock up more and more people on longer sentences in overcrowded jails will not deliver rehabilitation, nor will it protect communities. This means levelling with the public about what current sentences look like, who needs to be locked up and for how long.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is a precedent that shows it can be done. When Labour was last in government, in 2010, there were more than2,000 childrenbehind bars in England and Wales. Today there arefewer than 500. Where there is a will …Enver Solomon is chief executive of Nacro, the criminal justice charityExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justiceHomelessnessLabourSocial exclusionEnglandWalescommentShareReuse this content

title: War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess  | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and decline, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and decline, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Donald Trump addresses the 81st United Nations general assembly in New York on 22 September.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump addresses the 81st United Nations general assembly in New York on 22 September.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersOpinionUnited NationsWar, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a messNesrine MalikUkraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and declineThu 1 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.36 EDTShareUN general assembly meetings are not usually riveting occasions. But this year’s encapsulated a world in flux and crisis, an international law and organisation structure that is falling apart, and a humanitarian order machine running hot. What unfolded was less a gathering for resolution and resolve than a display of showboating, frustration and fractiousness.It was a snapshot for the history books of four huge destabilising conflicts for which there seems to be no means of, or interest in, resolution – Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan. Volodymyr Zelenskyydeliveredan account of five years of Russian aggression: the staggering loss of life – hundreds of thousands killed on both sides – the porousness of the sanctions on Russia, the “madness” of it all. Donald Trump once againthreatenedto “annihilate” Iran if it did not make a deal, a promise that has now been made so many times its restating only reveals its hollowness. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, responded in his own speech by saying that Iran has been the victim of US terrorism and aggression, and would defend itself with the “utmost strength”. The sole US delegation representative in the roomwalked out.In the middle of this unbridled, unseemly pugnaciousness, pleas to restate facts were trampled over by power-lust. The Israeli government’s sense of impunity “has reached terrifying levels”,saidJordan’s King Abdullah II. “It no longer feels compelled to ask, ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”“If international law can be ignored for decades,” he added, “then what exactly is that law worth?” As if to answer that question, Benjamin Netanyahu became the only ICC indicted leader to address the UN general assembly, with a characteristically belligerent speech. Nothing – that law is worth nothing.And on international law meaning nothing, the assembly was subjected to the farce of the United Arab Emirates, the key player in Sudan’s war, piouslypreachingabout how Sudanese people deserve peace and civilian rule, while the UAE’s leaders are accused of arming and funding theRapid Support Forces(RSF), itselfaccused of genocide and ethnic cleansing. A close ally of the US and the UK, the UAE has managed to extend Sudan’s war into a calamitous conflict, without even a breath of censure, or even acknowledgment from its friends. A $500minvestmentin the Trump family’s cryptocurrency scheme, and multibillion-pound partnerships with the UK, have seemingly captured the two states. Indeed, the silence it has bought is so compliantly observed that the US’s senior adviser on African and Arab affairs (Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law) acknowledged foreign interests but refusedto name any of the countries.Even procedurally, the ground was tilted by those who have the power and shamelessness to do so. The Trump administration invoked its sovereign ability to decide who could attend and who could not, wielding a sort of weaponisation of the visa system that rendered the UN not a neutral body with its own rules and protocols, but a tool to be leveraged for the interests of the US and its allies because it sits in US territory. Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas (not ICC-indicted) and 80 other Palestinian officials weredeniedvisas to attend for the second time under Trump’s watch. The head of the Sudanese government and Sudanese armed forces, the antagonists to the UAE-backed RSF, was denied a visa, seemingly an indication of successful Emirati manoeuvrings in Washington. The dynamics were an expression of how foreign policy and conflict are managed today, with constant gaming of the system to amplify one side over the other and produce outcomes friendly to regional and global powers.Amid the collapse there was Tom Fletcher, the UN undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs, darting energetically from meeting to meeting, with a grittily sunny disposition. He posted a hectic flurry of social media clips talking about what could be done in the middle of the fire, a sort of diplomatic “this is fine” meme. And God bless him. Inone, he is on a walk with Alexander De Croo, administrator of the UN development programme, who talks about the problem being “crises piling up on one another”. “The answer,” Fletcher says, “to a lot of what we do is actually diplomacy. Getting those chokepoints open, Bab al-Mandab, the Black Sea, the strait of Hormuz, because otherwise we both have a much bigger development caseload and humanitarian caseload.”He represents an emerging new model of international and humanitarian worker – navigating funding cuts, a lack of interest in peace and politicised drawdown of international aid to at least maintain some traffic of funds. To make sure some support gets to the millions labouring under war, the climate crisis, disease, poverty, hunger and predation. The wars will carry on, and now the strategy is to negotiate with powers to un-choke and unblock what can be opened to get supplies and relief in, from winter aid in Gaza to containing the Ebola outbreak.But where we are now isn’t just a matter of earnest diplomats and cynical, irresponsible warring powers. A far more complex problem is upon us: the rapidly changing nature of military conflict itself. Wars are becoming vastly less containable through the spread, sophistication and low cost of AI and drones. They are now conducted remotely, veering between high-intensity and low-grade assaults that render their beginnings and ends less decisive. They are more likely to just suspend normal life with dispensable drones, the sort that have held the Gulf hostage to Iran’s response to US attacks, Sudan’s war without a clear frontline, and the “ceasefire” in Gaza essentially just a lower-grade assault.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe UN general assembly meeting of 2026 was a study in so many things – the degradation of international law, the rickety system it has bequeathed, the acceleration of the demise of international community, and the importance of resolve to somehow attend to the victims. But we are also entering an era in which belligerents themselves are coming to grips with asymmetrical warfare and an elusive status quo. There is much talk of “what comes next”: an equilibrium ofmiddle powersin compact, a rupture with the US and within Nato, a nihilistic free for all? We as humans tend to think in clear-cut scenarios. What is more likely is what was demonstrated last week in New York – a messy prolonged state of constant stress under careless leaders giddy with what they realise they can get away with, no exit plan, and the rest of the system given no option but to work with and around them to somehow alleviate the consequences of their actions. The new world order is one of active resignation.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionInternational lawHumanitarian responseDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Margot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here’s why | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: I don’t flip a table every time this happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: I don’t flip a table every time this happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion
Content: ‘Last week my tolerance was tested again when it was revealed that after a decade of marriage, Margot Robbie has changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.’Photograph: Image Press Agency/NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Last week my tolerance was tested again when it was revealed that after a decade of marriage, Margot Robbie has changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.’Photograph: Image Press Agency/NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockOpinionMargot RobbieMargot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here’s whyRebecca ShawI don’t flip a table every time this happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussionThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.24 EDTShareBeing a lesbian in a heretofore heteronormative society means having to go along with lots of things that don’t make sense to your beautiful lesbian brain. One such thing for me is the ongoing expectation that women who marry men should change their surname to their husband’s.Last week my tolerance was tested again when itwas revealedthat after a decade of marriage,Margot Robbiehas changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.Margot Ackerley – it simply rolls off the tongue. She will remainMargot Robbiein her public life, and we don’t know why she has done this, but it has nonetheless caused a stir. We got the usual discourse of blah blah tradition, blah blah patriarchy, blah blah women’s individual choice and so on.We all know how it goes and Margot is not alone in doing this, of course. The statistics are hard to pin down (bearing in mind I dropped out of psychology at uni because of the statistics part) but I think it’s safe to say that in the overwhelming majority of straight marriages, the woman changes her name to the man’s. I see this in every part of my social life, from friends back home who married directly out of high school to my cabal of highly educated urban feminist friends. I play my part by putting all my married male friends in my phone under their wives’ surnames.In a world determined to isolate us, friendship may be the best way to keep each other alive | Rebecca ShawRead moreOf course I have no personal sense of the societal pressure and systems that inform such decisions, which is why I don’t flip a table every time it happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion.There are plenty of reasons a woman might want to change her name. She might hate her dad. She might feel no attachment to her name. Her husband might have a meaningful attachment to his and so she might just think it’s a nice thing to do.I’m not an unreasonable lesbian. My issue isn’t with women taking their man’s surname, the problem comes when there is nochoosing. When it’s a foregone conclusion, when it hasn’t been actively decided. That’s your name!If there is discussion, if there is equal respect for both people, if someone has a reason, then that’s fine with me. I once had a colleague whose future husband told her it was a dealbreaker if she didn’t take his name. That’s not a reason. That should have been the dealbreaker itself.I don’t really careaboutthe reasoning, I just care that thereisa reason. That said, when it comes to which surname a baby gets, that’s when I really get irritated. If we really have stopped considering a man’s wife and children his property, why on earth is giving them his name still the default?Womencarry and birth the babies. Women are still far more likely to do the lion’s share of childcare. Hello?? The lesbian mind boggles.But never fear, because I have a solution. And you may be surprised that it doesn’t involve any gender politics whatsoever! My solution is that we throw tradition out the window and that if a couple wants to share a name, we make the decision based on … which surname is cooler. Which surname sounds better, which surname will offer more success – that’s the one you should both use.In an ideal world, this would be done in a courtroom setting, where each couple comes in and sees me sitting high above them like Judge Judy, ready to bang my gavel. Congratulations, Mr Brown, you are now Mr Beaumont. Sorry, Mrs Jones, you’re now Mrs Wilder. Mr Cheeseman, I release you from your prison.No longer would awesome surnames be swallowed by the crap oesophagus of patriarchy. No longer would it be considered weak or weird for a man to take his wife’s last name – instead it would be cool and wise. Even though my loyalty always lies with women, I am willing to maintain neutrality in the courtroom.And sorry, Mr Ackerley, which sounds a bit like a cat throwing up – you’re now Mr Robbie.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsMargot RobbieOpinionCelebrityMarriageFamily filmsRelationshipsFamilyFeminismcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Grenfell prosecutions: at last, survivors have a date | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Prosecutors will decide who to charge within eight months. But ministers should also re-examine the law
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Prosecutors will decide who to charge within eight months. But ministers should also re-examine the law
Content: The Grenfell Tower memorial wall. ‘The police’s decision to let the public inquiry run before concluding their own investigation has been criticised.’Photograph: Ben Bauer/PAView image in fullscreenThe Grenfell Tower memorial wall. ‘The police’s decision to let the public inquiry run before concluding their own investigation has been criticised.’Photograph: Ben Bauer/PAOpinionGrenfell Tower inquiryThe Guardian view on Grenfell prosecutions: at last, survivors have a dateEditorialProsecutors will decide who to charge within eight months. But ministers should also re-examine the lawThu 1 Oct 2026 14.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.55 EDTSharePolice have at last asked prosecutors to consider charges relating to the Grenfell Tower fire in 2017. The suffering of those who survived or were bereaved by the blaze, which killed 72 people, has been exacerbated by the extraordinary length of time that the investigation has taken. But they can nowlook forward to a decisionabout who will face criminal charges. The Crown Prosecution Service has promised that this will be before the 10th anniversary next June.The names of the 20 organisations and 54 individuals in the police files will not be released by prosecutors unless they are charged. But the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and Kensington and Chelsea council have both announced that they are on the list. Angela Rayner promised on Wednesday that the government would cooperate fully whatever decision is reached regarding a potentialbreach of the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. Kensington and Chelsea council revealed that acharge of corporate manslaughteragainst it is being considered alongside health and safety and fire regulation breaches.The police’s decision to let thepublic inquiryrun before concluding their own investigation has been criticised. Some of the bereaved and survivors would have preferred criminal justice to take precedent. But the thoroughness of the inquiry at least means that well-evidenced findings of wrongdoing have already been made. Arconic, Kingspan and Celotex – three suppliers of materials involved in the tower’s refurbishment – were judged to have behaved dishonestly, although this does not mean that the inquiry’s findings were made to a criminal “burden of proof” level. An architecture practice, Studio E, and two building contractors, Rydon and Harley Facades, were each said to bear responsibility for the fire.Arconic was also criticised for its disgraceful refusal to send witnesses to the inquiry. The Metropolitan police have warned that trials are unlikely to take placebefore 2028, meaning that an end to this painful process remains years away.Corporate manslaughter casesare widely recognised as being very difficult due to the need to prove gross negligence with management playing a substantial role. The government and the judiciary must do all they can to expedite the next stages.Beyond any trials, theHillsborough lawwill at long last create an obligation on public officials to be truthful. There are other steps that ministers should take, regardless of what happens in court. Survivors are right to object to thepublic contractsawarded to Rydon and Saint-Gobain (owner of Celotex), given the inquiry’s findings about their conduct. Theexplanationsgiven so far as to why the Procurement Act 2023 cannot be used to bar them on grounds of poor past performance are not good enough.The government should also consider changing the law to enablepunitive damagesto be awarded against companies that harm people.Proposals for a new, independent bodyto monitor the implementation of recommendations from public inquiries and inquests also deserve serious consideration. The current position, in which multiple independent reviews have been accepted but not implemented, is harmful to those affected by tragedies such as Grenfell. It also undermines public trust in the system’s capacity to put things right.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherent | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Three-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the US
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Three-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the US
Content: A protest against the death penalty at the Tennessee state capitol in Nashville on 27 September.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenA protest against the death penalty at the Tennessee state capitol in Nashville on 27 September.Photograph: George Walker IV/APOpinionCapital punishmentThe Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherentEditorialThree-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the USThu 1 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.55 EDTShareWhat is the kindest way to kill? That’s the question being asked once more following Tennessee’sfailed attempts to execute Christa Pikefor the brutal murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. The 50-year-old was taken to a medical facility, her condition unknown, with witnesses describing her snoring loudly around 40 minutes after receiving two injections of pentobarbital on Wednesday. It is the second botched killing in months, prompting Tennessee’s governor to order a halt to executions.Lethal injection was supposed to be the humane alternative to firing squads and electric chairs. They in turn were seen as an improvement on hanging, whichlooked much like lynchingin a system disproportionately handing the death penalty to black men. The age and ill health of those executed, and theethical refusal of most medical staffto be involved, may contribute to botched injections. But analysis of autopsy results has providedcompelling evidencethat suffering is inherent; injections – especially those involving paralytic drugs – have merely disguised it. What is described as safeguarding the dignity of prisoners is really about reducing the discomfort of witnesses who would otherwise see their suffering.Pressure from campaigners on pharmaceutical companies has curbed the supply of lethal drugs, but it has not stopped executions. Donald Trump’senthusiasm for the death penaltyhas spurred on state officials, with thehighest number of executions for 16 yearsin 2025. Some states have found alternative drugs, which may increase the suffering of those killed. Others are using different techniques. In June, the supreme court stopped Alabama from executing a prisonerwith nitrogen gas, which it has used in other cases. The use of firing squadshas resurged. Experts say such deathscan be “excruciating”, especially where marksmen miss the heart of the condemned, with allegations that some executions could even have been deliberately botched.The US is in a shameful minority.Three-quarters of countrieshave got rid of capital punishment in law or practice – with Lebanon this year becoming thefirst Middle Eastern countryto abolish it.Only 17 countries executed prisoners last year, though the total number killed rose to more than 2,700 – the highest since 1984. (The figures do not include China, believed to carry out the most executions.) But while Mr Trump and others champion capital punishment, the American publicare turning away from it. In 1994,80% supported it; by last year that had fallen to 52%. A majority of younger people oppose it.High-profilemiscarriages of justicehave contributed to growing disquiet. So have casessuch as Pike’s. She endured sexual abuse and rape by three perpetrators in childhood, as well as beatings and neglect – yet her experiences and age were not adequately put forward by lawyers at her trial. Her bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder were diagnosed only afterwards. Sandra Babcock, an expert on the death penalty who has acted on Pike’s behalf, argued that her execution would confirm that it was reserved “not for the worst of the worst, but for the most damaged and vulnerable among us”.The ultimate problem, however, is not that the wrong people are being executed, but that anyone is being executed. The search for a humane way to kill is inherently preposterous. It is not just lethal injection, the firing squad or electrocution that should be rejected – but the death penalty itself.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Specialist services are vital to help people with ME/CFS | ME / Chronic fatigue syndrome | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to George Monbiot’s article about how those with myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome, have been failed by the health system
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to George Monbiot’s article about how those with myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome, have been failed by the health system
Content: ‘When I first claimed sickness benefits, I had to pay privately to see a consultant as the DWP would not accept evidence from GPs.’Photograph: Tek Image/Science Photo Library/Getty Images/Science Photo Library RFView image in fullscreen‘When I first claimed sickness benefits, I had to pay privately to see a consultant as the DWP would not accept evidence from GPs.’Photograph: Tek Image/Science Photo Library/Getty Images/Science Photo Library RFME / Chronic fatigue syndromeLettersSpecialist services are vital to help people with ME/CFSReaders respond to George Monbiot’s article about how those with myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome, have been failed by the health systemThu 1 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareGeorge Monbiot (Abandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayed, 24 September) is right about one important thing: people with severe ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome) deserve much better care than many have received. But two different questions are being conflated: how patients have been treated, and what the evidence tells us about the causes and treatment of ME/CFS.The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence no longer recommends the old form of graded exercise therapy, in which activity was increased according to a predetermined schedule regardless of symptoms.That is an important change, particularly given the significance of post-exertional malaise. But it does not establish that exercise is inherently dangerous or that all forms of physical rehabilitation are useless. Clinical trials have found improvements in fatigue and physical functioning in some people following exercise-based interventions, albeit with important limitations.Similarly, cognitive behavioural therapy should not be presented as a cure for ME/CFS or treatment for an assumed psychological cause. But helping someone manage anxiety, depression or the consequences of a disabling chronic illness does not imply that the illness itself is psychological.The growing evidence of biological abnormalities is important, but does not establish whether individual abnormalities are causes, consequences, adaptations or part of a feedback loop. Monbiot’s patient testimonies deserve attention, but a self-selected group responding to a Bluesky appeal cannot establish how common particular experiences are.As a GP, I believe that there is a much simpler failure to address: specialist ME/CFS provision remains remarkably limited. Many chronic conditions, including rheumatological and neurological illnesses, have no cure but still have specialist services for diagnosis, symptom management and support.Patients deserve to be believed and treated with respect. They also deserve honesty about what is known, what is uncertain and what the evidence actually shows.Name and address suppliedI had a mild (undiagnosed) form of ME for 20 years, triggered by a virus, before another virus caused my illness to worsen. My otherwise excellent GP advised me to go for a walk every day, which left me so ill that I barely left the house for more than three years.Twenty-four years later, not only are there no treatments for ME but in some places, such as where I live, there is no support at all. When I first claimed sickness benefits, I had to pay privately to see a consultant in infectious diseases with a special interest in ME as the Department for Work and Pensions would not accept evidence from GPs.I cannot plan anything, as I never know when I will be so ill that I will be confined to the house again. Most people I speak to have never heard of ME/CFS. If we weren’t so ill, those of us with this awful disease would be shouting it from the rooftops.Eleanor DentCardiffGeorge Monbiot is right to draw attention to the “shocking social crisis playing out behind closed doors” for people living with ME. Not only is ME a devastating condition, but too often those affected are failed by the very systems meant to care for them.The level of political attention the issue has received is nowhere close to the scale of the problem. Thegovernment’s strategy on ME, published over a year ago, lacked both substantive funding and outcome targets. Its key action for those affected by the most severe form of ME – “exploring”whether a specialised service could be commissioned – is now delayed until April 2027. We hope that, as a first step, the health and social care select committee will take up this critical issue as a matter of urgency.Karen Hargrave and Emma Gore-LloydCo-founders, ThereForME charityHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Disinformation is just one symptom of the authorities’ failure to regulate social media | Social media | The Guardian
description: Letter: Responding to an editorial on Russian threats, Aneet Morar says companies that profit from spreading harmful content need to face real consequences
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Responding to an editorial on Russian threats, Aneet Morar says companies that profit from spreading harmful content need to face real consequences
Content: ‘We know that engagement-driven feeds are damaging young people’s mental health.’Photograph: Chainarong Prasertthai/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘We know that engagement-driven feeds are damaging young people’s mental health.’Photograph: Chainarong Prasertthai/Getty Images/iStockphotoSocial mediaLettersDisinformation is just one symptom of the authorities’ failure to regulate social mediaResponding to an editorial on Russian threats,Aneet Morarsays companies that profit from spreading harmful content need to face real consequencesThu 1 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTShareYour editorial (The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity, 23 September) is right that Andy Burnham’s warning about the Kremlin only tells half the story. I would go further: disinformation is one symptom of a wider failure to regulate the platforms that now function as critical national infrastructure.The harms are evident across a wide spectrum. We know that engagement-driven feeds are damaging young people’s mental health. The same amplification mechanics that carry foreign propaganda also accelerate far-right radicalisation at home, as your analysis of the disorder in Belfast and Southampton showed. The new generation of wearable devices, such as Meta’s smart glasses, makes recording people without their knowledge or consent a routine part of life.Yes, the government must step up its response to disinformation, but this alone is not enough. Platforms that profit from spreading harmful content need to face real consequences: enforceable duties of care, penalties proportionate to their scale, and transparency about how their algorithms decide what we see.I have spent my career in the payments industry, where infrastructure operating at this scale would never be allowed to run without clear rules, independent oversight and liability when things go wrong. There is no good reason to hold these platforms that shape what millions of people believe to a lower standard.Tackling the Kremlin’s bot armies matters, but until these platforms are held responsible for what they amplify, across every segment of society, we will keep treating the symptoms rather than the cause.Aneet MorarLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
