title: How poor public transport policy is putting the brake on cities | Road transport | The Guardian
description: Letters: David Andrews suggests a tram network could be the answer to London’s clogged streets, while V Narayanan says unused cycle lanes are a waste of valuable road space
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: David Andrews suggests a tram network could be the answer to London’s clogged streets, while V Narayanan says unused cycle lanes are a waste of valuable road space
Content: ‘Transport policy in London is guided by publicity rather than practicality.’Photograph: Justin Kase z12z/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Transport policy in London is guided by publicity rather than practicality.’Photograph: Justin Kase z12z/AlamyRoad transportLettersHow poor public transport policy is putting the brake on citiesDavid Andrewssuggests a tram network could be the answer to London’s clogged streets, whileV Narayanansays unused cycle lanes are a waste of valuable road spaceThu 1 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTShareYour analysis of slowing buses in global cities sets out the mechanism exactly, and the remedy follows from it (London buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised, 23 September).Transport for London’s own calculation that a 10% fall in speed costs 6% of demand and Imperial College London’s finding of the same decline across 15 cities show what happens to buses as the traffic thickens around them. Retiming the lights will not reverse it, and London is already trying. The phrase to notice in the article is one used by TfL: signals will give more buses priority “where possible”.There lies the difficulty. On a route running a bus every two minutes, the signals are asked to intervene 30 times an hour in each direction, and the junction cannot recover between calls before the next bus arrives.Bristol city council’s engineers found precisely this when they reviewed their bus priority: in the most congested parts of the city, priority delivered no journey-time saving at all.This is a bigger brake on the economy than it looks. What holds a city back is the plain difficulty of getting across it to work, to customers, to the shops. A firm can recruit from a smaller area, a worker can reach fewer jobs, and a high street can be reached by fewer people. Much of the decline of the high street is a decline in how easily people can get to it.The cure is to carry the same people in fewer vehicles. One tram carries as many people as three or four buses, so it can be given priority junction after junction, and the crossing traffic still gets its turn.About 30 French cities have put trams through their centres since Nantes started in 1985, and they rebuilt those centres around them. Their central streets are visibly busier for it. Sheffield’s trams share a shopping street with cars and vans, and run to the same timetable in the peak as at midday.David AndrewsChair, Light Rail Transit Association; lead author, Bristol Area Bus and Tram Business CaseYour article onLondonbuses in decline highlights poor transport policy in London, which is guided by publicity rather than practicality.Buses have slowed down as dedicated bus lanes have been largely replaced by a poor choice of cycle lanes. London is an old city with narrow lanes and, with individual cycle transport given priority over mass public transport, it’s no wonder that buses have slowed and become erratic in service.One only needs to observe the utilisation of cycle lanes that are empty except during the peak hours of 7.30am-9am and 4pm-5pm on weekdays. That is a gross waste of valuable road space that could be used by buses.Having a dedicated bus lane instead of a cycle lane would speed up buses and make them more reliable. The bus lane could be shared by cycles and during peak times be dedicated to them, while being free for buses rest of the day.Sadly, politicians rarely look beyond elections, and fail to prioritise buses over bicycles. The authorities have wasted millions on cycle lanes while failing spectacularly to improve mass public transportation.V NarayananLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: It’s cruel to delay ADHD and autism assessments for children | NHS | The Guardian
description: Letter: Anna Bird says the decision by some NHS integrated care boards to impose a two-year minimum wait is harmful to young people and their families
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Anna Bird says the decision by some NHS integrated care boards to impose a two-year minimum wait is harmful to young people and their families
Content: ‘Delays in diagnosis prevent young people receiving the medical and practical assistance they need.’Photograph: Iryna Tolmachova/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Delays in diagnosis prevent young people receiving the medical and practical assistance they need.’Photograph: Iryna Tolmachova/AlamyNHSLettersIt’s cruel to delay ADHD and autism assessments for childrenAnna Birdsays the decision by some NHS integrated care boards to impose a two-year minimum wait is harmful to young people and their familiesThu 1 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTShareBlocking assessments of children with neurodivergent conditions for over two years is cruel to children, deeply damaging to families and ultimately more costly to taxpayers (NHS bodies in England impose two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments, 25 September).Imagine the long-term harm inflicted on a six-year-old child forced to wait two years for an assessment of a physical condition. Waiting for a diagnosis of autism or ADHD is no different. That’s a quarter of a child’s life, and ultimately their potential, put on hold by state bodies that should be supporting all children. It prevents young people receiving the medical and practical assistance they need to learn, make friends and achieve the ordinary things that other children can every day.We know that three-quarters of parents have had to reduce working hours or stop work because of a lack of support that can be put in place with a diagnosis. It’s no wonder that young people and their families reach our members’ services in or near crisis because of protracted waits for information.We have strongly voiced our concerns about the lack of engagement from the Department ofHealthand Social Care with the government’s reform ambitions on special educational needs. The NHS’s rationing of assessments is the exact opposite of the Department for Education’s principle of ensuring early help for young people.This is not joined-up government. It must be sorted out before another generation of children is failed.Anna BirdChair, Disabled Children’s PartnershipHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Borthwick’s England reign remains full of contradictions with World Cup a year away | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: England’s identity under Steve Borthwick is not as clear as it should be this close to the tournament
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: England’s identity under Steve Borthwick is not as clear as it should be this close to the tournament
Content: Steve Borthwick has been praised for his ‘Spock-like approach’, but criticised as a coach who ‘thinks like a machine’ and ‘chases trends’Photograph: Insidefoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSteve Borthwick has been praised for his ‘Spock-like approach’, but criticised as a coach who ‘thinks like a machine’ and ‘chases trends’Photograph: Insidefoto/ShutterstockEngland rugby union teamBorthwick’s England reign remains full of contradictions with World Cup a year awayEngland’s identity under Steve Borthwick is not as clear as it should be this close to the tournamentGerard MeagherThu 1 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was not so long ago that the Rugby Football Union would host an annual Christmas bash. Executives, head coaches, assistants, members of staff and an invitation to the press pack. Mince pies and mulled wine, even a touch of merriment if we were lucky. Eddie Jones would sometimes make an appearance, but the mind goes back to one year when he did not.To give him his dueSteve Borthwick, his assistant at the time, did. He would probably rather have been anywhere else, but one of the more clear-eyed RFU employees, who had long-since figured out that the then forwards coach was destined for the top job, did their utmost to involve him. Alas, Borthwick soon had a long-distance train to catch and hours of in-depth analysis on a laptop ahead of him.Rugby union power rankings: how the teams stand a year from World CupRead moreThat anecdote feeds a narrative about England’s head coach. That he is astonishingly diligent when it comes to analysis, but struggles with the more human elements of the job. Speak to anyone who has shared a dressing room with him and there are countless more. Equally, however, there is the time he surprised the 2023 World Cup squad by inviting their families to a training session and the compassion shown toJamie GeorgeandMaro Itojewhen his two captains were dealing with bereavements.The point here is that Borthwick is much more complex than the robotic stereotypes that persist. Data-obsessed, yet a far more bold selector than his supposedly maverick predecessor. Full of contradictions.So, too, are his England side. The players queue up to defend him and his gameplan. Yet they have produced their best performances when taking matters into their own hands and slipping the straitjacket.Even the RFU’s recent public pronouncements about Borthwick have vacillated.A vote of confidenceafterthe historic Italy defeatwas unprecedented and read like an ultimatum. Less than two months later, Borthwick’s position had been strengthened afterone of the union’s cloak-and-dagger reviews. A few weeks ago, we learnedhis contract was being extended.All of which makes it hard to assess where England stand, almost four years into his tenure and with one year to go until the 2027 World Cup. Are they contenders any more than they were in the final throes of Jones’s reign?View image in fullscreenEngland have won 58% of their matches since Steve Borthwick was appointed in 2022.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APBorthwick leans heavily on statistics, but his record does not stand up to much scrutiny. He has overseen 28 victories from 48 matches, a 58% winning percentage, marginally worse than Stuart Lancaster.It is a feature of Borthwick’s term that records achieved along the way have been unwanted.Theirheaviest home defeat at the hands of France, firstlosses to Fijiand Italy and the worst Six Nations performance in England’s history. At the same time, there was the 12-match winning run and glimpses of what this team are capable of, occasions when Twickenham has rocked the rafters, but, in perhaps the greatest indictment, the absence of a statement victory away from home.Borthwick did not want to take overas England head coach in December 2022– nine months before he was supposed to – but could not say no. It is to his credit that he guided England to third place in the World Cup,losing to South Africain the semi-finals by a point, all the more so after a catastrophic warm-up campaign. That he held his nerve despite losing at home to Fiji is a testament to his resilience because there were times he looked as if he might crumble.It is also true that England could not have wished for a more straightforward draw in France, but then Borthwick had insisted his side “were not good at anything” soon after taking over. In many ways, a short-term run-up to a World Cup campaign is perfect for someone whose coaching credentials, in the true sense of the word, cannot be questioned.Asthe ever excitable Jonny May saidafterEngland’s third-place win over Argentina: “We’re starting to see what a genius Steve is. You won’t find a harder working man and his approach to the game is a little bit like Alan Turing. If anybody is going to crack the code to rugby, it will be Steve. He’s got an analytical brain, evidence-based, scientific, Spock-like approach.”View image in fullscreenSteve Borthwick is said to be data-driven but often makes bold selections.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe trouble is that the manner in which England’s third-place finish was achieved has entrenched the prevailing narrative. Rassie Erasmus has hit upon a similar theme, if not as complimentary as May, the South Africa coach describing Borthwick as a coach who “thinks like a machine” and as one who “chases trends”. The obvious inference being that he is not one who sets them.The second part of Borthwick’s tenure began at the 2024 Six Nations. He insisted English rugby had turned a corner, effectively signalling this was when he was initially expecting to take over. Two steps forward, two steps back would be a better way to describe the ensuing period. It is hard to argue that any corners have been turned.The championship began well enough, Borthwick was quick to put out new faces and in Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, who made his debutagainst Italy in Rome, you could argue there is no more important player to England’s hopes in Australia than the Exeter winger.In round three, England arrived in Edinburgh with two wins from two but the wheelscame off spectacularly at Murrayfield. Borthwick said his team had “played small”, that the jersey had weighed heavy and Itoje bemoaned “tip-tap, hot-potato rugby”. A week’s soul-searching at a training camp in York, when Borthwick is understood to have been implored to give the players more time to learn attacking structures, followed.It paid off witha thrilling win over Irelandand though the campaign ended witha narrow defeat in France, the performance suggested England were rounding the bend.Two more narrow defeats in New Zealand were greeted with optimism, but then came the departures of Aled Walters andFelix Jones, key members of the backroom staff. Beginning the 2024 autumn with three defeats, each more demoralising than the next, turned the pressure dial up, but Borthwick survived his first crisis, helped because the RFU chief executive, Bill Sweeney, was busy trying, and failing,to quell a revoltover his seven-figure salary and bonus.The 2025 Six Nations began with another narrow defeat, but England broke the damat home to Franceand proceeded to embark on a 12-match winning run. It is the most prosperous period of Borthwick’s tenure and included a stunning68-14 win in Walesand an autumn clean sweep.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPull back the curtain, however, and fundamental to England’s winning streak was that they had stolen a march on their rivals in adapting to law tweaks around the aerial contest. When the rest caught up, England could not cope, lost four straight Six Nations matches and Borthwick was suddenly clinging on again.A heavy defeat by South Africathis summer before winsover FijiandArgentinahave done little to move the needle. Hitting out at the “negativity committee” when asked about England’s indiscipline suggests Borthwick is still feeling the heat.Wallabies dare to dream of Rugby World Cup glory as momentum builds under Les KissRead moreWhen it comes to coaching, he clearly knows his onions. Well-placed sources often describe him as a “world-class forwards coach”, which is a compliment, but again infers he is not quite up to the top job. Listen to the players wax lyrical about his methods, witness the fight that they demonstrated in patches against the Springboks and they have not all given up on him yet, however.It is said there is a generational divide in the camp and a split of opinions along those lines about how best to play. Perhaps that explains the crossed words between Itoje and Fin Smith during the loss to Italy in March. But there is no mutiny yet and George was unequivocal after this year’s Six Nations: “Steve is one of the best coaches I’ve ever worked under. Under Steve I think we will be right up there with the favourites to win the World Cup in 2027.”It is said he treats his players like princes, but is considerably more strict with his staff. A close look at his staff certainly says a lot about Borthwick and his tenure. The most pivotal moment of this World Cup cycle could be the departures of Walters and Felix Jones in the summer of 2024.Walters’ reasons for heading to Ireland are easier to understand. His wife is Irish and he had strong ties from his time with Munster. Those of Jones are far more opaque, but clearly Walters’ decision to leave influenced his own, so, too, a difference of opinion with Borthwick in New Zealand. That Jones was forced to work out his notice by the RFU underscored what an odd situation it was.Equally strange is that Borthwick has steadfastly appointed assistants of a certain type. Nick Evans, Byron McGuigan, Tom Harrison, Lee Blackett, Kevin Sinfield and Joe El-Abd had no experience of international coaching. All of which adds fuel to the argument that when it comes to coaching Borthwick struggles to relinquish control.At other times, however, he has impressed with a willingness to delegate. Walters was a clever appointment because he is a vibes man, which Borthwick clearly isn’t. George was a clever choice of captain because he can connect with supporters in a way Borthwick can’t. Sinfield serves as a pastoral figure to the squad in ways Borthwick does not. The problem is, when these people either move, or are moved on, from their roles, they leave a void.The contradictions continue to mount as we enter World Cup year – even the performance in their last outing, against Argentina, was Jekyll and Hyde. Sensational for 40 minutes, substandard thereafter and it all leaves you with the feeling that England’s identity is not as clear as it should be this close to a World Cup.That first half against Argentina, the sense of liberation in defeat in Paris – admittedly when they had little to lose – must be the blueprint if Borthwick is to win over the public in the next 12 months. “If we have a pretty ropey autumn, on the back of building some momentum over the summer, I think we will need to have a pretty hard look at ourselves,” said the fly-half Smith recently.View image in fullscreenSteve Borthwick (right) joined Kevin Sinfield (centre) on day three of Sinfield’s 7 in 7: The Grand Finale 2026 Challenge. Sinfield is one of many of his coaches who arrived without international experience.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAO’Shea has said it is “not even remotely” a possibility that Borthwick is sacked before next year’s World Cup, but he underestimates the power of the fanbase, whose disapproval did for Eddie Jones. Whether Sweeney has the appetite for change so close to another World Cup is another question.It would be misguided to believe Borthwick’s contract extension through to the following Six Nations has raised the temperature any higher. It merely buys the union time when deciding whether or not to sack Borthwick and who to replace him with.Make no mistake, his tenure hinges on the World Cup in Australia, assuming he makes it that far.Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamSteve BorthwickRugby World Cup 2027Rugby World CupRugby unionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Neco Williams fires revitalised Wales to fightback win against 10-man Norway | Nations League | The Guardian
description: A much-improved Wales came from behind to win 2-1 against a Norway side who had Torbjørn Heggem sent off straight after half-time
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: A much-improved Wales came from behind to win 2-1 against a Norway side who had Torbjørn Heggem sent off straight after half-time
Content: Neco Williams celebrates after putting Wales 2-1 up early in the second half.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenNeco Williams celebrates after putting Wales 2-1 up early in the second half.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersNations LeagueNeco Williams fires revitalised Wales to fightback win against 10-man NorwayBen Fisherat Cardiff City StadiumThu 1 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a night when Erling Haaland moped around the pitch, dragging his hulking frame across the Cardiff turf, Wales registered a welcome victory over 10-man Norway and their first this year. Was this just one of those games where the game’s deadliest finisher was stuck on the fringes or was it a case of115 things occupying his mind? Either way, this defeat proved a humbling experience. “You’re just a shit Kieffer Moore,” was the chant aimed at Haaland from the locals.Daniel James cancelled out Oscar Bobb’s well-worked opener in the first half and 17 seconds after the restart Torbjørn Heggem was sent off for fouling James as the Leeds winger streamed towards goal, resulting in a free-kick from which Neco Williams earned Craig Bellamy a timely win with an unerring strike.Nations League: Ronaldo-less Portugal prosper while Klopp gets first win as Germany coachRead more“It feels a bit like the first punch in the face in a long, long time,” said theNorwayand Arsenal captain Martin Ødegaard after his country lost successive games for the first time in four years. “Now we have to respond, stick together and fight back.”For Bellamy, a first win since last November eased the mounting negativity after a bruising run of results, chiefly theirWorld Cup playoff defeatto Bosnia and Herzegovina in March and alistless display in Denmarklast Sunday. “I felt my own disappointment since Bosnia and I’ve felt the stick as well,” the Wales head coach said. “The summer wasn’t easy. These games weren’t easy. But I’ve seen it … I’ve seen managers before me get it. I’ve seen the abuse the previous manager [Rob Page] got. It’s been a really difficult couple of months but it’s ‘welcome to this’ if you want to step into this … this is it. I do think we could be kinder to each other.”It was plain to see Bellamy had been hurting and he cited his daughter receiving abuse on social media. “I chose to live back down here because I wanted to be on the ground, I wanted to be called a wanker to my face,” he added.View image in fullscreenTorbjørn Heggem sees red straight after half-time.Photograph: Nick Potts/PA“The World Cup [playoff defeat] moved, I just felt the shift … Look, I am a strong person, I think we all are, but it’s the people around me I’m conscious of. It’s just society. What are we? Eight prime ministers in the space of 11 years? It’s nuts ... We’re such a small country, why can’t we have each other’s backs? Why don’t we look after each other more? The others can go at us. We’re too quick [to criticise].”View image in fullscreenDan James brings Wales level in the first half.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAWales bounced off the canvas after Ødegaard’s cute ball released Bobb on goal to open the scoring on 11 minutes. Liam Cullen, now of third-tier Leicester, pinched the ball from Sander Berge after the Fulham ­midfielder was sluggish to claim Fredrik Aursnes’s pass andWalesraced away from the scene.Cullen and Lewis Koumas burst forward and Sorba Thomas zipped a low cross into the box, where James beat David Møller Wolfe to the punch. Thomas, who by his own admission loves staying wide to get chalk on his boots, was a constant threat.Norway were punished for being slow out of the blocks in the second half, Heggem hauling James down after the restart. James does everything at speed and Heggem knew he was in trouble. The Spanish referee Alejandro Hernández awarded a free-kick on the edge of the box and ­Williams dispatched a wonderful right-foot strike to Ørjan Nyland’s right, to the surprise of the former Aston Villa and Reading goalkeeper.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPro-Palestine protests interrupt game as Ireland pass up 2-0 lead in draw against AustriaRead moreBobb played draught excluder behind a white wall of Norway shirts and Nyland stepped to his left. Nyland was out of position when he had to shuttle across his goalline when Williams thrashed the ball into the bottom corner.Haaland had one of those games; he was on the periphery and recorded just 11 first-half touches, the fewest of any player, including the Borussia Dortmund full-back Julian Ryerson who was forced off through injury after 16 minutes. Ethan Ampadu easily won what, technically, will go down as a duel on halfway but in truth Haaland just stuck out a leg in the hope of claiming the ball. His first whiff of goal came a couple of minutes before the interval but Ryerson’s replacement, Marcus Pedersen, misread Haaland’s movement and the move collapsed.The substitute Josh Sheehan spurned a golden chance to extend Wales’s advantage, sending a weak shot at Nyland after more fine craftsmanship from Thomas to release the Bolton midfielder on goal. Up the other end, Haaland ambled across the box in preparation for another Pedersen cross. When it arrived Haaland soared high but unmarked sent a header straight at Danny Ward. Then came a puff of the cheeks, a look to the turf. It has been that kind of week.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueWalesNorwaymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Pro-Palestine protests interrupt game as Ireland pass up 2-0 lead in draw against Austria | Republic of Ireland | The Guardian
description: Alexander Prass and Michael Gregoritsch cancelled out Troy Parrott’s double in Austria’s 2-2 draw against the Republic of Ireland in the Nations League
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alexander Prass and Michael Gregoritsch cancelled out Troy Parrott’s double in Austria’s 2-2 draw against the Republic of Ireland in the Nations League
Content: Tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text “#StopTheGame” were launched on the pitch.Photograph: Paul Phelan/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text “#StopTheGame” were launched on the pitch.Photograph: Paul Phelan/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesRepublic of IrelandPro-Palestine protests interrupt game as Ireland pass up 2-0 lead in draw against AustriaPress AssociationThu 1 Oct 2026 17.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProtests halted events in Dublin twice before theRepublic of Irelandwere forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium.Despite a significant security presence, the contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a “limited tennis ball protest”, when – around the 20th minute – tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text “#StopTheGame” were launched on the pitch.‘A lot of lies’: Ireland manager hits out over coverage of Bazunu exit from Israel gameRead moreThen around the 35th minute a man ran on to the field of play from the opposite side carrying what appeared to be a Palestinian flag and was immediately tackled by security and carried off.It has been a tumultuous week for the Republic. Their two Nations Leaguefixtures against Israelhave divided opinion in the country, sparking protests, including one which took place pre-match outside the stadium. The Republic’s behind-closed-doors “home” game against Israel in Backa Topola, Serbia, is scheduled for Sunday, and the manager Heimir Hallgrímsson on Wednesday confirmed it was their intention to play.Troy Parrott got the hosts under way with a sensational 12th-minute opener and added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.A pair of substitutes proved the Republic’s undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.View image in fullscreenMichael Gregoritsch (left) points to the sky after scoring Austria’s second goal.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAHallgrímsson’s men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behindAustriaand Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.Hallgrímsson made three changes, including the re-introduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.The goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, who had made himselfunavailable for the Israel meetings, was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhín Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before the Republic enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors’ half.It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah’s glanced-on header from a goal kick.View image in fullscreenTroy Parrott slots home the Republic of Ireland’s opening goal in the 12th minute.Photograph: Evan Treacy/EPAThe Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts before nutmegging Philipp Lienhart and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.Play was briefly paused just before the 20th minute to clear up the tennis balls, a pause both teams used for a hydration break. The second stoppage of play took place around the 35th minute.Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead. Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a video assistant referee check and blasted it past the Austria keeper.Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed by VAR.The Brentford keeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch, guessing the wrong way as the Augsburg forward fired into the corner.The Republic captain, Dara O’Shea, was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar, and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.Explore more on these topicsRepublic of IrelandAustriaNations Leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League: Ronaldo-less Portugal prosper while Klopp gets first win as Germany coach | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Portugal pulled away late on for a 4-2 win in Denmark while Jürgen Klopp’s Germany beat Serbia 2-0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Portugal pulled away late on for a 4-2 win in Denmark while Jürgen Klopp’s Germany beat Serbia 2-0
Content: João Félix kicks the ball away after it rebounds from the net after he seals Portugal’s 4-2 victory over Denmark in the 87th minute.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJoão Félix kicks the ball away after it rebounds from the net after he seals Portugal’s 4-2 victory over Denmark in the 87th minute.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNations LeagueNations League: Ronaldo-less Portugal prosper while Klopp gets first win as Germany coachPortugal pull away to 4-2 win in DenmarkJürgen Klopp’s Germany beat Serbia 2-0Press AssociationThu 1 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 20.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortugalmaintained their perfect start toNations LeagueGroup A4 as Jorge Jesus’s squad showed little signs of missing Cristiano Ronaldo with a 4-2 victory overDenmarkin Copenhagen.The 41-year-old Al-Nassr forward and five-time Ballon d’Or winner left the camp before the match amidreports of a falling out with Jesus, his former club manager, having been left on the bench throughout a victory in Norway.Neco Williams fires revitalised Wales to fightback win against 10-man NorwayRead moreJoão Cancelo gavePortugala 13th-minute lead before Brentford midfielder Mikkel Damsgaard equalised.Gonçalo Ramos swiftly put Portugal back in front after 25 minutes, with Napoli forward Rasmus Højlund levelling things up at 2-2 early in the second half following a swift counter.Vitinha’s header, his first Portugal goal, and a late strike by João Félix made it three straight wins.“A victory of the highest quality,” said Jesus. “This Portugal team scored four goals and put in a performance which, in my opinion, was of a very high standard – and that cannot be overlooked. Of course, this is more important than anything else that has happened.”NewGermanyhead coach Jürgen Klopp got his first win with a 2-0 Group A2 victory overSerbiain Munich. Bayern Munich midfielder Tom Bischof fired in his first senior international goal and Liverpool forward Florian Wirtz then added a second in the 61st minute.Germany produced a disciplined and intensive game, illustrating the high-pressure soccer Klopp wants to instill in the team. “That’s going in my archive. We’ll make a video out of it now,” Klopp said. “That’s how we want to play.”View image in fullscreenJürgen Klopp (right) applauds fans alongside Tom Bischof, who scored his first international goal in the victory over Serbia.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersSpeaking to public broadcaster ZDF, he added: “The mix of football and attitude was top level today. I told the boys that this has to be our benchmark.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWirtz said: “It was important to win again, just for the spirit in the team, and to send a signal out that we’re good football players and also a good football nation. Definitely a step in the right direction.”In the same group, Tijjani Reijnders scored a late equaliser as theNetherlandsfought back to draw 2-2 withGreece, who remain top. Fotis Ioannidis and Giorgos Masouras had the home side 2-0 up at the break.Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk powered in a header from a corner on the hour. After Denzel Dumfries had seen his goal ruled out by VAR for offside, Reijnders lashed home a rebound in the 89th minute to secure a point.In Group B3,IsraelandKosovoplayed out a goalless draw in Debrecen, Hungary. In Group D1,MaltaandGibraltardrew 1-1 while in Group D2,Azerbaijanwere held to a goalless draw byLiechtensteinin Baku.Explore more on these topicsNations LeaguePortugalDenmarkGermanySerbiaNetherlandsGreecenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shaw secures WCL draw against Real Madrid as Manchester City show spirit after week of turmoil | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Khadija Shaw’s 51st-minute goal earned Manchester City a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, who led through Linda Caicedo, in the Women’s Champions League
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Khadija Shaw’s 51st-minute goal earned Manchester City a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, who led through Linda Caicedo, in the Women’s Champions League
Content: Mary Fowler reacts during the Women’s Champions League draw with Real Madrid in Manchester City’s first game since the verdict against the club was announced.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenMary Fowler reacts during the Women’s Champions League draw with Real Madrid in Manchester City’s first game since the verdict against the club was announced.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAWomen's Champions LeagueShaw secures WCL draw against Real Madrid as Manchester City show spirit after week of turmoilTom Garryat Joie StadiumThu 1 Oct 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrée Jeglertz, the Manchester City head coach, said the noise surrounding theguilty verdict dished outby the Premier League had zero impact on his women’s team’s performance after they played out a high-quality draw with Real Madrid in the Women’s Champions League.Khadija ‘Bunny’ Shaw’s ruthless finish earned City a point against an impressive Real Madrid side on a night when the hosts were surely glad for attentions to turn – however briefly – towards on-pitch matters after a week when the wider football club has dominated the headlines for the wrong reasons.Manchester City 1-1 Real Madrid: Women’s Champions League – liveRead more“Of course there is a lot of noise but the players are very calm – I haven’t seen or noticed anything that will take any percentage out of the players’ performance,” Jeglertz said.The result – which was a fair reflection of an even but entertaining game – left both sides with two points from their opening two fixtures but City will know their league phase opponents should theoretically become less challenging from hereon after their opening draw at Bayern Munich. The Swedish coach added: “It is OK, it’s an OK start in the Champions League. It’s not ideal but it’s a good start and we know what is needed from us in the rest of the tournament.”Quick GuideWCL roundup: PSG pummel LeuvenShowThe day after Paris FC played their first Women’s Champions League home game at Stade Jean-Bouin, across the road from Paris Saint-Germain’s Parc des Princes,PSG’s women’s team entertainedLeuven20km away at the club’s suburban training centre.Rasheedat Ajibade put the hosts ahead from close range after nine minutes against the Belgian side. Naomie Feller (pictured) then scored a quick-fire double, before Sakina Karchaoui and Vitória Yaya completed PSG's 5-0 rout.In the early games, Modesta Uka scoredAustria Vienna’s first goal in the WCL but Inter's captain, Ivana Andrés, levelled in the fourth minute of added time to earn a 1-1 draw. Inter dropping points left Barcelona, who thrashed Roma on Wednesday, as the only WCL team with six points after two games.In a match between two teams that had lost in the opening round,HBKøgecrushed visiting Swiss teamServette5-1 in Denmark.PAPhotograph: Benoît Tessier/REUTERSWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Jeglertz had been at pains to insist that it has been “business as usual” for his team despite the damning guilty verdict released by the Premier League towards the men’s side. There was a strange mood around this stadium in the buildup to kick-off with opinions mixed.Speaking to supporters on the bridge that connects this venue with the neighbouring Etihad Stadium, some appeared relaxed about the situation and unsure what it had to do with the women’s team, while others were clearly troubled and looking forward to watching some football as a form of escapism.View image in fullscreenKhadija Shaw fires home Manchester City’s equaliser early in the second half.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAn elderly City fan, who did not wish to be named, said pre-match: “We’ve been through rough times before, we’ll come through rough times again,” in a matter-of-fact manner. Another simply demonstrated what appears to be a growing dislike for reporters asking about the 115 charges when they said angrily “you’re from the media?” before using an expletive and promptly walking away.A much politer, younger woman simply expressed her sadness and her hopes that it wouldn’t cause the players stress.Once the match started, there were occasional references to the news from the stands; midway through the first half one home fan sang ‘Sheikh Mansour, my lord, Sheikh Mansour, oh lord, Sheikh Mansour’, to the tune of Kumbaya, although nobody else appeared to join in. There was also a small group of men carrying an inflatable banana in one corner defiantly chanting about ‘City going down with a billion in the bank’.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn general, though, the regular Women’s Super League match-going fans who are members of the supporters club seemed focused on their usual repertoire of fan chants to encourage the players, whether singing about the brilliance of Aoba Fujino and later chanting the name of Mary Fowler, who hit the crossbar with a header before the break.By then Real Madrid were already ahead courtesy of Linda Caicedo’s clinical, low finish into the bottom corner after a lethal burst of pace. The visitors could have scored as early as the first minute, when a sloppy mistake by Carlotta Wamser allowed Felicia Schröder to shoot but her effort flew narrowly wide and bounced off the stanchion, rippling the net but from the wrong side. It was a sign of the Spanish team’s intent and they looked sharp throughout.City’s play was significantly more urgent and incisive after the break and – after Yui Hasegawa spurned a volleyed chance when she was in space inside the box – it did not take long for the hosts to equalise. Shaw turned and clinically fired into the corner of the net with great technique after good pressing from City led to Hasegawa winning the ball in midfield and feeding Shaw in the area. It was the Jamaica striker’s fifth goal of the season in all competitions and her first of this Champions League campaign.Suddenly the WSL champions were dominating the territory, although Caicedo did go close at the other end with a diagonal shot that bounced wide. The introductions of Beth Mead, Sam Coffey and Grace Clinton from City’s bench only seemed to further strengthen the hosts.Hasegawa volleyed just wide again, this time from the second phase after a half-clear corner, in another let-off for Real Madrid, who had gone close themselves at the other end when Ayaka Yamashita did well to save from Caicedo. The home fans were on their feet to applaud Yamashita and chant her name when she later produced a quick reaction save to keep out Irune Dorado’s close-range effort and keep the score level.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueManchester City WomenReal Madrid WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton backs Vasseur but believes Ferrari leadership structure could change | Lewis Hamilton | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton has backed his Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, as the best person to lead the team, but believes the leadership structure above and around the Frenchman could be overhauled
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton has backed his Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, as the best person to lead the team, but believes the leadership structure above and around the Frenchman could be overhauled
Content: Lewis Hamilton is 103 points behind the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, in the championship standings.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton is 103 points behind the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, in the championship standings.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockLewis HamiltonLewis Hamilton backs Vasseur but believes Ferrari leadership structure could changeTeam principal under scrutiny after underperformance‘Fred is the guy to take this team in the right direction’Giles RichardsThu 1 Oct 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has backed his Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, as the best person to lead the team, but believes the leadership structure above and around the Frenchman could be overhauled.Hamilton was speaking before this weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the race being held at the Sepang circuit but branded as a replacement for the meeting that was cancelled earlier in the season because of the war in the Middle East.Ferrarigo into the race with Vasseur under scrutiny, given the team have been underperforming and with the former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner having stated last week that taking over at Ferrari would be his dream job.Lando Norris targeted by online abuse after calling for Franco Colapinto banRead moreSpeculation over Vasseur’s future had reached such a level that Ferrari issued a statement on Tuesday saying they hadfull confidence in the Frenchman, which was echoed by Hamilton on Thursday in Sepang. “Structure is very important and so is stability and everyone rowing in the same direction is key in any business,” he said. “There often seems to be a lot of focus on one individual and one role here. Fred is a fantastic leader and he really is the guy to take this team in the right direction.”However, above Vasseur at Ferrari are the executive chair, John Elkann, and Benedetto Vigna, the chief executive officer, and Hamilton suggested the broader management could be addressed, referencing his experience with Toto Wolff at Mercedes. “There is a structure that has been there for some time and whether or not that needs looking at moving forwards? There are obviously also people above Fred and it is not about one person,” he said.“There are changes I would make but I am not going to talk about what those are. Toto is in a different position to Fred. The structure is a lot different.”View image in fullscreenFerrari issued a statement on Tuesday saying they had full confidence in Fred Vasseur.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAHamilton took his first win for Ferrari at Barcelona this year and his teammate, Charles Leclerc, won at Silverstone. Although they are second in the constructors’ championship, they are 160 points behind Mercedes and Hamilton trails the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, by 103 points.While Ferrari started the season strongly with what was considered one of the strongest chassis on the grid their performance has dropped off as McLaren and Red Bull have developed their cars, increasing the pressure on Vasseur. Hamilton conceded he felt the scrutiny and criticism around the team was disheartening.“It is frustrating to see all the negativity. You see other teams making mistakes and no one says too much about it. We make the same mistake, and we know we are not perfect, but it is 10 times worse for Ferrari.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t read all the stuff, so it has zero effect on me, but when I come into the room I can see it definitely affects individuals on the team.“They don’t know what is happening behind closed doors and they don’t know how hard everyone is working and it is all done by assumptions and opinions.“We are going to focus on doing the best job we can regardless of what is written. I knew it wasn’t going to be in my second year [at Ferrari] where we would be where we want to be, but I am hoping and praying that we will get there.”Explore more on these topicsLewis HamiltonFerrariFormula OneFormula One 2026Motor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s tennis tour announces prize money parity with men’s events | Tennis | The Guardian
description: The WTA has announced a ‘major milestone’, with all combined WTA 1000 events to award equal prize money
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The WTA has announced a ‘major milestone’, with all combined WTA 1000 events to award equal prize money
Content: Elina Svitolina won her share of an Italian Open prize money pot totalling £8.3m with final victory this year – the men played for a share of $9.6m.Photograph: Claudia Greco/ReutersView image in fullscreenElina Svitolina won her share of an Italian Open prize money pot totalling £8.3m with final victory this year – the men played for a share of $9.6m.Photograph: Claudia Greco/ReutersTennisWomen’s tennis tour announces prize money parity with men’s eventsWTA announces ‘major milestone’ in fight for equalityCombined WTA 1000 events to award equal prize moneyAgenciesThu 1 Oct 2026 15.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll combined WTA 1000 tournaments will award women equal prize ⁠money to the men from 2027, the Women’sTennisAssociation has announced, ⁠with the Italian ⁠Open ​and other major events joining the rest of the category in offering the ⁠same payouts.Billie Jean King has often said that she was moved to form the women’s professional tennis circuit after earning $600 for her 1970 Italian Open title while Ilie Nastase took home $3,500 for winning the men’s tournament the same year.Laver Cup 2026: Topknots and top shots as Team Europe triumph – in picturesRead moreIn 2027 – nearly six decades after King’s title at the Foro Italico – the Rome clay-court event will finally award women the same amount of total prize money as men, as part a “major milestone” for the women’s tour.The initiative means that all combined WTA 1000 events will award equal prize money for the first time. Besides the Italian Open, the holdouts had been the Canadian Open and the Cincinnati Open. The other combined 1000 events in Indian Wells, California; Miami; Madrid and Beijing; as well as all four Grand Slams, already offer equal prize money.“Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis,” WTA chair Valerie Camillo said. “It demonstrates the WTA’s continued commitment to leading the sports industry in delivering our athletes competitive and financial equality and is a testament to the enduring nature of the founding vision of the WTA.”In 2023, Italian Open organisers pledged to have equal prize money starting in 2025 but didn’t carry through on the promise. The total men’s prize money this year in Rome was $9.6m while the women got $8.3m.Also announced for next year was an expanded WTA 250-level tournament in Manila, Philippines, amid massive interest surrounding home player Alex Eala, who is ranked 18th.Also, the number of annual WTA 500 level tournaments required for players ranked in the top 50 was reduced from six to four, resulting in a total base playing commitment of 14 WTA tournaments plus the four grand slams in 2027.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe WTA relied heavily on its tour architecture council, a working group chaired by third-ranked Jessica Pegula. “As players, we’re on the road most of the year, so having more flexibility in our schedules and commitments makes a real difference,” Pegula said. “The 2027 changes give us more ability to build our seasons around our own goals – competitively and personally. That’s an impactful step forward for players.”The WTA said the updates “will be implemented as a one-year pilot” for 2027, allowing it to “evaluate the impact of the changes across the tour to inform decisions for 2028 and beyond”.Explore more on these topicsTennisEqual paynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hitting the sweet spot: bear treats itself to baked goods at Colorado farmers’ market | Colorado | The Guardian
description: Shoppers and vendors in Aspen surprised by unusual customer as it stretched to sample stall offerings
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Shoppers and vendors in Aspen surprised by unusual customer as it stretched to sample stall offerings
Content: Bear eats pastries at the Aspen farmers market - loopColoradoHitting the sweet spot: bear treats itself to baked goods at Colorado farmers’ marketShoppers and vendors in Aspen surprised by unusual customer as it stretched to sample stall offeringsGuardian staffThu 1 Oct 2026 17.23 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarmers’ market shoppers might not usually pay much attention to the local resident devouring fresh bread and pastries at one of the stalls with extra gusto – but some certainly did last weekend when they realized it was a hungry bear.Onlookers on Saturday reached for their phones to take photos and videos of the bear in downtown Aspen,Colorado, after it wandered through the stalls and got up on to its hind legs to dig into the baked goods.At one point it jumped up on to the table to get better access to the pastries.The bear, bulking up for winter hibernation, initially appeared as vendors were setting up their stalls, the Denver Postreported, according to Joey Livingston, a Colorado parks and wildlife (CWI) spokesperson. Livingston told the paper a police officer took steps to scare the bear away from the humans – and the baked goods – while a CWI officer was on the way. The bear climbed a tree and then later left the area.Bears are particularly active and hungry ahead of hibernation as record drought has reduced food sources,pushing up the numbers of contacts with the public.Explore more on these topicsColoradoAnimalsWildlifenews

title: Tennessee suspends executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says failed lethal injection leaves her in critical condition | Tennessee | The Guardian
description: Independent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murder
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Independent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murder
Content: 1:35Witnesses recount Christa Pike's survival of two lethal injections – videoTennesseeTennessee suspends executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says failed lethal injection leaves her in critical conditionIndependent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murderChrista Pike: what we know so far about Tennessee woman’s failed executionRichard LuscombeThu 1 Oct 2026 17.44 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTennessee’s governor on Thursday said it was “deeply disturbing” that his state botched the execution of a death row prisoner who remained alive and snoring 40 minutes after receiving a double dose of the lethal drug that should have quickly killed her.Bill Lee, a Republican, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after Wednesday night’s failed attempt to put to death Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder, at the execution chamber inNashville.Meanwhile, Pike, 50, remained in the hospital on Thursday afternoon. “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care,” Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said at an afternoon press conference.“She is in critical condition receiving life-saving care. That is the extent of what we have at the moment.”Spivey, of the office of the post-conviction defender, condemnedTennesseeauthorities for the manner in which the failed attempt unfolded. He said officials used seven needles, one of which became bent as it was removed from Pike’s arm.“Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel and it was torturous. It was also predictable,” he said, adding that he saw no life-saving care given after the execution attempt was abandoned at about 8.25pm.Speaking to reporters on Thursday morning, Lee said he had spoken with Frank Strada, secretary of the Tennessee department of correction, but did not have an update on the condition of Pike, who was taken to an off-site medical facility after surviving two doses of pentobarbital.“This is a tragedy,” Lee said, adding that he had not yet spoken to the families of Pike or the teenager she killed in 1995. “There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened.11:05Death row inmate Christa Pike survives two lethal injections in Tennessee - The Latest“It’s the most difficult of circumstances as it relates to the sentence that should have been carried out by the state. It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better than that.”Lee added, in comments reported bythe Tennessean, that he had not yet chosen an investigator to lead a “comprehensive, third party review” he announced in a statement late Wednesday.“There are a lot of questions,” he said. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered. I’m highly disappointed, along with Tennesseans, about what happened.”Cameron Sexton, the Republican speaker of Tennessee’s house of representatives, said on Thursday in a social media post that he and other lawmakers would also be investigating what went wrong with the attempted execution. He added that they would look at other ways to prevent executions from failing.“We will look at all options – expanding the alternatives, and changing the current medications to include potassium chloride,” he said. “Thirty years is too long for justice.”Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said her group was aware of seven other people that have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but nobody had remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions.“This failed attempt is the worst we’ve ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” she said in a statement.“What happened to Christa Pike can be attributed to the extreme secrecy Tennessee officials have maintained about their execution procedures, their refusal to answer reasonable questions and their unwillingness to accept responsibility for their mistakes.”In May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, another convicted murderer, after failing for more than an hour to place an intravenous line into his arm.Pike, who was sentenced to death for the brutal 1994 killing of a teenage classmate, was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.The execution attempt was allowed to proceed only after the US supreme court intervened late on Wednesday to lift a federal court stay issued earlier in the day, a delay it said was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her 1996 sentencing.Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee supreme court after the second pentobarbital dose was administered asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony”, and that the state was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.A representative of the state corrections department defended its handling of the unsuccessful execution attempt.“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the spokesperson, Dorinda Carter, said in a statement.“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”According to the AP, Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.Seven journalists who were present at the Riverbend maximum security institution as witnesses described what they saw during a livestream hosted by WVLT television station soon after curtains in the execution chamber were lowered for the final time.They said Pike was snoring as corrections officials escorted them out.John North, of ABC News affiliate WBIR, said: “It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go. When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.”Pike and her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp were 18 and 17 when they and another female friend tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in January 1995, using boxcutters and a rock.The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder, in which Shipp carved a pentagram into their victim’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of her skull.Pike never denied the killing, and was later diagnosed with mental health disorders.“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she said in a clemency petition that Lee and the US supreme court denied.Lee’s suspension order affects the only other execution set in Tennessee this year.Gary Wayne Suttonhas been on death row since 1996 for the murder of a friend, and was scheduled to be put to death on 3 December.The Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsTennesseeCapital punishmentUS crimeNashvillenewsShareReuse this content

title: NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems
Content: A scene from NAZA. The producers said the team had carried out scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA. The producers said the team had carried out scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.Photograph: The GuardianNAZANAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in GazaTeam behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systemsPeter BeaumontThu 1 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary.In its response, which the IDF said was based on statements made by the film-makers and a review made by a representative who had attended a viewing, the Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on interviews with two dozen intelligence and other troops who had only a partial picture of the target approval process.NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiereRead moreAt the centre of the IDF’s rebuttal was its often repeated claim that its rules of engagement explicitly distinguish between militants and civilians and prohibit deliberately targeting civilians, while requiring commanders to take steps to minimise civilian harm, claims that have long been challenged over the years by critics.While acknowledging that it used AI to help recommend potential targets inGaza, the IDF also said final decisions made on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.The IDF also denied that it had approved, planned or carried out an attack anticipating 500 civilian casualties in pursuit of a single Hamas target.The IDF statement follows previous efforts by Israeli politicians to dismiss NAZA – a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike – which have accompanieddeath threats against the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and calls by the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,for them to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship.It also echoed previous complaints by some Israeli critics – including journalists – that the film’s military sources were anonymised, despite the fact that source protection in media investigations is commonplace and regarded by much of the media as an ethical requirement.“The filmNAZApresents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal,” the statement added.Responding to the IDF statement, the Guardian, which produced the film, disclosed further details of how the team had verified the allegations which involved scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.A spokesperson said: “The IDF’s attempt to portray the 24 participants in NAZAas junior-ranking officers involved only in the early stages of the targeting process is false.“They include officers and soldiers who were involved in multiple stages of the targeting process in Gaza, including intelligence, operations and the final authorisation process.View image in fullscreenPeople walk past the rubble of destroyed buildings in Jabaliya in the northern Gaza Strip.Photograph: Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters“The process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.“Over the past three years we have together interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes.“The Guardian stands fully behind the film, which builds on three years of detailed reporting by the Guardian and our partners. Several highly respected news organisations have subsequently confirmed the IDF’s use of AI-driven systems in the Gaza offensive and the loosening of safeguards to protect civilians, including the New York Times, Washington Post and Associated Press.”While Netanyahu has claimed that Israeli military safeguards have led to one of the lowest civilian-combatant ratios in modern warfare, that has been challenged by the IDF’s own leaked casualty assessments, by the UN’s commission of inquiry in 2024 and research by NGOs including Action on Armed Violence.--1:55NAZA - official trailerExplore more on these topicsNAZAGazaPalestineIsraelDocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Water yes, mining no!’: the 87-year-old farmer who became a nature hero in Colombia | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Porfirio Garcés is one of the ‘Jerico 11’, who face kidnapping charges after opposing a copper mine. Now, with a far-right president prioritising extraction, their fight has become more urgent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Porfirio Garcés is one of the ‘Jerico 11’, who face kidnapping charges after opposing a copper mine. Now, with a far-right president prioritising extraction, their fight has become more urgent
Content: Porfirio Garcés, 87, at his home in Palo Cabildo in Jericó, Antioquia. A small sign reads ‘Si al agua’ (Yes to water). Porfirio is one of 11 farmers facing charges.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoView image in fullscreenPorfirio Garcés, 87, at his home in Palo Cabildo in Jericó, Antioquia. A small sign reads ‘Si al agua’ (Yes to water). Porfirio is one of 11 farmers facing charges.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanColombia‘Water yes, mining no!’: the 87-year-old farmer who became a nature hero in ColombiaPorfirio Garcés is one of the ‘Jerico 11’, who face kidnapping charges after opposing a copper mine. Now, with a far-right president prioritising extraction, their fight has become more urgentSupported byAbout this contentLuis Bernardo Cano in BogotáThu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the rural hamlet of Palo Cabildo inColombia’s western Andes, 87-year-old farmer Porfirio Garcés tends to his anthuriums in the garden of his small house. He talks with passion about his vinyl record collection, which ranges from classical to pop music, but his main interest now lies elsewhere: his homeland, to which he feels a deep connection – and his desire to protect it.Numerous water sources originate in the area, supplying not only Jericó, where Garcés lives, but also several neighbouring towns in the Antioquia region. A sign with a clear message hangs on the main porch of his property: “Yes to water.”“We don’t want to wake to the roar of machinery drilling into and destroying our land, destroying the poetry of the landscape,” says Garcés. “We must defend our water sources. Without water, we will die of thirst.”View image in fullscreenThe countryside around the farming village of La Soledad in Jericó, which is affected by the proposed mine.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoSince last year, Garcés and 10 other local farmers have faced formal charges for opposing the Quebradona copper mining project, promoted by the multinational AngloGold Ashanti through its subsidiaryMinera de Cobre Quebradona. He has since become a symbol of the resistance movement against Quebradona in Jericó.Social protests in support of the “Jericó 11” gained strength in August as the nature defenders awaited new court hearings. “Water yes, mining no!Wateryes, mining no!” the crowd chanted before the hearings, which postponed sentence until March 2027.The charges against the 11 farmers are “simple” kidnapping (the moving of someone against their will, without factors such as ransom or serious bodily harm), aggravated theft and assault. Although the judge at the initial hearings on 13 May 2025 rejected the prosecutors’ request to keep the 11 farmers under house arrest, they are still awaiting trial.View image in fullscreenPeople protest in Jericó to oppose the Quebradona mining project and support the 11 farmers.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoAngloGold Ashanti arrived in the region 15 years ago to extract copper in an area traditionally known for agriculture, where crops such as coffee, plantains, cassava, beans and corn are cultivated. Its first exploration licence was granted in 2007, covering nearly 8,000 hectares (about 19,800 acres).This initial stage was extended for 11 years – the maximum permitted byColombia’s mining code– after which the company consolidated the properties to apply for an exploitation licence to start extraction. However, in 2019, theNational Environmental Licensing Authorityarchived the application due to lack of technical information, requiring the company to conduct new studies before it could begin mining.In August, Colombia’s National Mining Agency approvedan extension of the exploration phaseat Quebradona until 8 December 2027. Mining has not yet begun, as the company still needs to addresssocial and environmental concernsand complete additional studies, but Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’sfar-right presidentsince August, has aggressively prioritised expanding oil, gas and mineral extraction, including fracking, as a core part of his economic platform.View image in fullscreenA T-shirt with an illustration of the 11 farmers who face charges related to opposing the mine.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoLast month, 281 local organisations signed an open letter declaring AngloGold Ashanti and Minera de Cobre Quebradonaunwelcome entities(“entidad no grata”), and arguing that the project endangers the environment, water sources and Jericó’s local agricultural economy. Many campaigners feel AngloGold Ashanti is using the lawsuit as an attempt to suppress dissent over the Quebradona project.The kidnapping charge arose in 2023 on public land owned by the municipality of Jericó, which is designated for safeguarding underground water sources. According to the community, mining employees entered the land without authorisation to carry out excavations. In response, the farmers say they went to the site to halt the works and alerted the police, the ombudsperson’s office and the mayor’s office to request the workers’ removal. After this, the employees filed complaints alleging they were held against their will.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGustavo Arboleda is one of the 11 farmers facing charges.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoGustavo Arboleda, 62, another of the farmers facing charges, says the community became concerned about the direct impact on their water resources after the company installed an exploration drilling platform on the La Fea stream,which provides water to the area. That event, he says, sparked their resistance campaign.The rural village of La Soledad sits on the mountain where mining is planned and where most of the accused live. Gustavo says its name honours thePiaya cayanabird, locally known as soledad. From the village, you can see the Cauca River basin, one of the nation’s major waterways.“Since the mine had not completed its studies to obtain exploitation permits, it started bringing in machinery at night and paid some farmers to rent land. We noticed and did not let the machinery in; that was when we received further charges,” Arboleda says.View image in fullscreenRodolfo Tobón, 44, president of the La Soledad community action board, shows the dirt on his hands from farming. The area has always been agricultural.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoRodolfo Tobón, 44, also facing charges, lives in La Soledad with his family on a farm where he grows cassava, bananas, plantains, coffee and beans, crops that ensure subsistence for his household and the wider region. “This land is very fertile; whatever is planted grows,” he says. “This is life – not just for us, but for many more people.”Tobón, who is president of the village’s community action board,questions how the company has engaged with them since it arrived. He says local people do not want to see Jericó turned into a mining town, “because mining has never existed here”.“When the mine arrived, they didn’t say they were a mining company. They used other methods, saying they would conduct soil studies to see what could be produced in Jericó,” he says. “Later on, we realised it was for large-scale mining. The company acted wrongly; they didn’t arrive stating exactly what they were going to do.”View image in fullscreenTobón looks out over the Cauca valley from his farm in La Soledad. The village is directly above where the mine tunnels are planned.Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoAngloGold Ashanti has publicly said its Quebradona project fully complies with Colombian law and does not encroach on restricted zones. In a three-page statement to the Guardian, the company says its activities pose no threat to local water sources, citing environmental studies by Colombian authorities showing no impact on groundwater or surface water.It also says protests and actions by the activists are illegal and disruptive, prompting it to file criminal complaints for kidnapping, theft and personal injury, and highlights its commitment to dialogue and transparency with local communities.“We believe in frank, open dialogue, free from clandestine or malicious methods, and regret narratives that unfairly affect our reputation and that of our employees,” says AngloGold Ashanti.View image in fullscreenA sticker on Tobón’s house reads: ‘Take off your mask, AngloGold – it’s our turn.’Photograph: Luis Bernardo CanoIn 2025, the company also announced the Quebradona Biodiversity Initiative, aiming to regenerate more than 2,500 hectares (6,000 acres) of Indigenous tropical dry forest and high-mountain forest in Antioquia and to restore ecosystems affected by land use.Although water still flows abundantly through Antioquia’s mountains, the Jerico 11 believe that only collective action can prevent drastic changes to their environment. Argiro Tobón, another of the accused farmers, says they are trying to preserve their way of life and landscape by keeping their region focused on food production.“We take care of the forests, we take care of nature, and we take care of the water,” he says.Explore more on these topicsColombiaSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanMining (Environment)WaterNatural resources and developmentAccess to waterEnvironmental activismLand rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan population | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: The global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknown
Author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
Headline: The global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknown
Content: Abu, the eight-month-old baby of Mama Abu, who are being monitored after they were trapped by smoke from forest and land fires in a palm oil plantation area in West Kalimantan, Indonesia.Photograph: Muffidz Ma'sum/Yiari-Ministry of ForestryView image in fullscreenAbu, the eight-month-old baby of Mama Abu, who are being monitored after they were trapped by smoke from forest and land fires in a palm oil plantation area in West Kalimantan, Indonesia.Photograph: Muffidz Ma'sum/Yiari-Ministry of ForestryThe age of extinctionIndonesia‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan populationThe global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknownSupported byAbout this contentRebecca RatcliffeWed 30 Sep 2026 23.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 23.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe mother’s hands were peeling from walking on the torched ground. Her eight-month-old baby, which clung to her side, was dehydrated and thin. The pair, named Mama Abu and Abu (“ash” in Indonesian), were found in an oil palm subsidiary estate, rescuers say.The orangutan pair were saved last month from wildfires that aredevouring Indonesia’s forestsand peatland, unleashing thick smog, and destroying the habitat of some of the planet’s most vulnerable species.Primate specialists from the International Union forConservationof Nature (IUCN) have called for urgent international assistance to help control the fires, warning this week that thousands of orangutans could be killed, injured or displaced.Wildfires happen every year in Indonesia, where fire is often used to clear land to make way for palm or pulp plantations. But the arrival of a supercharged El Niño has brought especially dry conditions,causing blazes to spread rapidlyacross parts of Sumatra, Kalimantan (the Indonesian part of Borneo) and Papua.The fires have also taken hold across peatland, which is extremely hard to extinguish as it smoulders underground. In its natural state, it should be waterlogged, but over recent decades, vast areas have been drained by industrial agriculture, leaving it highly flammable.Habitat containing 52% of the total Bornean orangutan population is now affected by the fires, according to a statement from the IUCN’s primate specialists.They are not the only animals affected, however. Blazes have also spread into the habitats of five gibbon species, all of which are listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List.
