Geopix, an environmental NGO,warned earlier this monththat 4,500 fires had been detected across 21 Sumatran elephant habitats over recent months.View image in fullscreenA fire burning on peatland and forest in Sungai Putri village, West Kalimantan, Indonesia, in August.Photograph: Garry Lotulung/The Guardian“I believe that the toll on wild animals being burned, dead, because of the fires is huge,” says Dr Karmele Llano Sanchez, a veterinarian and co-founder and CEO of Yiari, a non-profit focused on primate and habitat conservation, which rescues orangutans and other species from torched forests.View image in fullscreenDr Karmele Llano Sanchez in a rescue operation for orangutans caught up in wildfires in Pemangkat village in West Kalimantan province.Photograph: Muffidz Ma’Sum/Yiari/AFP/Getty ImagesEven animals that survive the catastrophe can face long-term consequences. Food availability falls in the aftermath of fires as forests struggle to recover, and the risk of conflict between animals can rise if they are displaced and forced to live closer to each other. Experts believe that, as with humans, there will also be health impacts for animals that have lived with months of dense smog.So far, more than 20 orangutans, as well as other species such as pangolin, have been evacuated from the fires by Yiari, which is working alongside West Kalimantan’s Natural Resources Conservation Agency, searching the forests for animals in need and responding to reports from the public.One of the rescued orangutans died, probably due to smoke inhalation.Others have been found with burns on their hands after touching the scorching ground, or are hungry and dehydrated.“It hasn’t rained in 80 days here, and everything is dried and burned,” says Sanchez. “[There are] no leaves and no fruits – nothing they can eat.”Animals that are evacuated are given sedatives through a dart, which can be fired as high as 30 metres into the trees. A team of about 10 people will hold a net to catch the animal as it tumbles from the branches. An adult male orangutan can weigh about 70kg.View image in fullscreenRescuers hold a net to catch a sedated orangutan as it comes down from the trees.Photograph: Muffidz Ma’Sum/Yiari/AFP/Getty ImagesIf a mother is carrying very young offspring, they usually fall together, with the baby clinging to its mother.Such evacuations are a last resort, says Sanchez, undertaken when the area of forest is destroyed: “Otherwise they will for sure die.”Indonesian wildfires threaten leading orangutan research site in BorneoRead moreThere are many animals in peril that simply can’t be reached:proboscis monkeys, which are endangered, Sunda pangolin and snakes – including a python and king cobra – have all been found dead, according tolocal media reports.Forestry ​minister Raja Juli Antoni told media the wildfires could continue until early November, with the rainy season expected to arrive late. An estimated 600,000 hectares (1.4 million acres) were damaged by fire in August, according to the environmental group YKAN.View image in fullscreenA Nasa satellite of Borneo with red dots indicating where fires have been detected. Peat fires are a recurring challenge in Indonesia.Photograph: Modis/NasaResearchers have observed that large fire events have been followed by unusually high litterfall, where leaves and small branches drop from trees. This is probably because smog has blocked sunlight, preventing photosynthesis, says Dr Susan Cheyne, co-director of Borneo Nature Foundation International, which has conducted studies on the trend.“Even though the fires are out at this point there is still a knock-on effect on food,” says Cheyne, who is also vice-chair for the International Union for Conservation of Nature primate specialist group section on small apes.Such die-offs of leaves occur just as dry season returns, just when species such as orangutan need to eat more, as they rely on flowers and leaves rather than the sugary fruits and pulp that are abundant during the rainy season.Erin Vogel, professor at Rutgers University in New Jersey, says the forest can take years to recover, with trees producing less fruit afterwards, possibly due to a decline in pollinators.In the longer term, tree diversity across burned peat forests can remain suppressedeven 12 years on, research has shown. If fires recur, this risks trapping forests in a permanently degraded state.View image in fullscreenMama Abu’s scorched hands after her rescue from forest fires in West Kalimantan.Photograph: Muffidz Ma’sum/Yiari-Ministry of ForestryThe full extent of the long-term impact of the fires on surviving orangutans’ health is unknown. During smoky periodsorangutans show ketosis, a sign of increased fat breakdown. It’s believed this is because the smoke raises energy demands, probably by forcing the immune system to work harder.Research published after the 2015 firesfound orangutans called less in heavy smoke, and that they had reduced vocal quality. Most vocal changes persisted for two months after the smoke had cleared and probably signalled changes in health, researchers concluded.Gibbons, which rely on song to attract mates, cement bonds and defend territory, have also been found tosing less when exposed to heavy smoke.“We know how [smog] impacts humans in the long term – it can lead to medical problems, breathing problems, asthma, cancer, infections, future lung capacity issues,” says Vogel. “So, I think, there’s no reason to predict that it wouldn’t affect them the same way.”Further studies are needed, but for now, research sites themselves are threatened by the flames. Both the Tuanan orangutan research station in Central Kalimantan, andRangkong research stationin West Kalimantan, have been threatened by fires in recent weeks. Staff and local people have worked to halt the spread, setting up improvised sprinkler systems and clearing the ground cover. Localised rains have brought some relief at Rangkong, though staff fear this may only be temporary. At Tuanan, where there is still no rain, the fire fighting continues day and night.View image in fullscreenConservation agency and Yiari staff evacuating a mother orangutan and her baby trapped by smoke in a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan.Photograph: Yiari/AFP/Getty ImagesWhat is killing Sumatra’s elephants? The battle to save one of our rarest animalsRead moreDecades of research are at risk, says Vogel, who is co-director of the Tuanan orangutan research programme. Academics there have studied the same trees, 2,500 in total, and the same individual orangutans for 23 years, accumulating a crucial body of long-term data.The IUCN says “urgent technical and financial support” are needed, but that the emergency response must be followed by greater investment in re-wetting peatland, addressing deforestation, and ensuring burned forests are restored, not converted into plantations.View image in fullscreenMama Abu is treated by Yiari rescuers after she and her baby were trapped by smoke from forest fires.Photograph: Muffidz Ma’sum/Yiari-Ministry of ForestryFor now, rescuers continue to search the forests for wildlife at risk. The mother and baby rescued last week are now being held at a quarantine centre run by Yiari.When it is safe, they will be released in a new location – one with enough food and no other orangutan populations that might compete with them for territory. “We need to look for a location that is safe, that is a good forest,” says Sanchez. “It is not easy. But we are trying to do our best to find a place that is suitable for them.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldon the app for all the latest news and featuresExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaThe age of extinctionWildfiresEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisPrimatologyWildlifeAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US datacenter discharged large amounts of pollution for almost a year with no permits | Pollution | The Guardian
description: Records show Vineland facility in New Jersey emitted health-harming pollution before regulators stepped in
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Records show Vineland facility in New Jersey emitted health-harming pollution before regulators stepped in
Content: One of the largest data centers on the East Coast, DataOne is the first in New Jersey seeking to build its own power plant.Photograph: Evan Simon / FloodlightView image in fullscreenOne of the largest data centers on the East Coast, DataOne is the first in New Jersey seeking to build its own power plant.Photograph: Evan Simon / FloodlightFloodlightPollutionUS datacenter discharged large amounts of pollution for almost a year with no permitsRecords show Vineland facility in New Jersey emitted health-harming pollution before regulators stepped inEvan Simon of FloodlightThu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a$1m finefor running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight.The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August aftera Floodlight/Guardian visual investigationfound them operating without permits. The New Jersey department of environmental protection last week fined the company over the fleet but did not disclose how long the generators had been operating nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year.Floodlight sent technical data about the generators – obtained through public records requests – to a Rutgers professor and a former EPA air division chief.“Our best estimate is that the generators emitted about 140 tons of NOx,” said Xiaomeng Jin, an assistant professor at Rutgers department of environmental sciences. Her analysis would rank DataOne in the state’s top five NOx polluters of 2025, per EPA data.NOx are a dangerous group of smog-producing gaseslinked to asthma,heart attacksand evenpremature death. It was “the most important air pollutant in the US that affects most people”, Jin said.Longtime Vineland resident Tiffany Leone-Vespa lives about a mile from the data center and said the noise from the generators sounded like an airplane in the back of her house.“What health problems might I face in the future? Because I’ve been exposed to all of that. My kids have been exposed to it,” she said.The site’s potential NOx emissions are even larger, according to Jin and Bruce Buckheit – a former EPA air enforcement division chief. Both concluded that at full use, DataOne’s fleet could emit more than 1,500 tons of NOx per year. That is nearly twice the amount that the Linden Cogeneration gas-fired power plant, New Jersey’s largest NOx emitter, is allowed to emit.Operating the generators “results in very high levels of air pollution” and the fleet’s potential emissions are “well over the regulatory threshold for a new major source”, said Buckheit.New Jersey labels any facility capable of emitting more than 25 tons of NOx per year a “major source”. Obtaining a major source permit requires extensive environmental reviews, best available pollution controls and public comment periods – all before construction can even begin.That didn’t happen at DataOne, despite the operation being capable of emitting more than half the NOx put out by New Jersey’s entire power sector.Drone video shows heat signature of datacenter generators“That is basically offsetting some of the air quality improvements [regulators] have achieved for decades,” Jin said.DataOne did not respond to Floodlight’s emissions analysis. Instead, its spokesperson sent the same statement as they did in response to NJDEP’s decision to fine them, saying the company was “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site’s permanent power solution and have the necessary approvals in place for this solution”.The company disagrees with NJDEP’s determination and had argued the generators did not require permits – but plans to apply for them now.A Microsoft spokesperson wrote that “we expect our suppliers and partners to meet all applicable legal and regulatory obligations” and the company was working with DataOne “to support their completion of the facility’s transition to its permanent long-term power solution”.In press releases, New Jersey regulators said the tractor-trailer-sized generators were detected during a 29 July 2026, site inspection but not during an earlier visit in December. However, the fleet was there to find, according to a letter DataOne later sent NJDEP.The letter, obtained by Floodlight through a public records request, notes the generators first began to arrive in July 2025. Sixteen generators started operating in October 2025, with another 16 brought online in early February. By June, all 62 had been fired up.By the time state inspectors noticed them, the unpermitted fleet had collectively run for more than 46,000 hours in total, according to the letter.“How did 62 generators get installed and operated and nobody did anything until now? That blows me away,” Leone-Vespa said. “Clearly somebody wasn’t doing their job.”A spokesperson for NJDEP declined to comment.For many Vineland residents, confirmation that DataOne’s generators have been running for nearly a year is a bittersweet vindication. Locals have reported strange noises emanating from the facility for months, with more than 100 noise complaints submitted to the Cumberland county department of health since March, according to records obtained by Floodlight. Many of the complaints list generators as the suspected source.“They’re just running these monster generators. And they think, by right, they have every ability to do so at the expense of anyone else,” said local flower farmer Michael Atkinson.Atkinson’s family has been farming a patch of land beside the datacenter for more than 70 years. He said DataOne was “one of the richest and worst neighbors that I have ever had to deal with in my entire life”.During a Vinelandtown hall meeting in late January, DataOne’s chief executive, Charles Beyney, told residents that his datacenter would be “polluting less than a farm”.“I’m too French to just kill my lungs, the lungs of your kids and all the community around us,” he told the crowd.Beyney confirmed during that speech that DataOne was running generators, and he said NJDEP was aware – the agency had been at the site that same morning and was “on us big time”.While the generators may have evaded state regulators for almost a year, local officials knew about them for much longer.A City of Vinelandinspection activity reportnoted that “phase 1 generators are online” in early February. And in May, a Cumberland county health department inspector responding to a noise complaint visited the site and reported that the source of the noise appeared to be two generators, “possibly more”.The inspector noted that the noise “exceeded night-time violation”.As part of the record fine levied against DataOne, the state is mandating the company apply for and obtain the required permits or cease operations, but is allowing them 45 days to do so, according to a NJDEP spokesperson.During that time, regulators are allowing the facility to continue running the generators – which are capable of emitting more than four tons of NOx in nearby neighborhoods each day.“I just don’t understand how this is being allowed,” Leone-Vespa said. She hopes independent air monitoring can help protect her community in the future. Until then, she has little faith in New Jersey regulators to watch out for them.“It’s like they don’t care about the residents.This story is fromFloodlight, a non-profit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’snewsletter hereExplore more on these topicsPollutionFloodlightDatacenters – USNew JerseynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years  | Glaciers | The Guardian
description: Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution
Content: Rhône Glacier in the Swiss AlpsGlaciers‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five yearsAlpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollutionAjit NiranjanThu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwitzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say.Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%.View image in fullscreenGlaciologist Matthias Huss records changes in the Scex Rouge glacier above Les Diablerets, western Switzerland.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/GettyMatthias Huss, a glaciologist at ETH Zürich and lead author ofthe report, said many people do not realise how fast glaciers are retreating, or that just one generation ago some now-barren sites used to sit beneath hundreds of metres of ice. The scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones.“I visited one last week and it’s so impressive to stand in this moonlike landscape where there was a big layer of ice – an extensive glacier – just a few years ago,” said Huss. “And now it’s a rock desert where there’s some scattered blocks of old ice still lying around and melting on the hot rocks.”The report, a collaboration between the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation, found the mean thickness of individual glaciers fell by between 2.5 metres and 4 metres in 2026. Huss said scientists were increasingly seeing glaciers collapse from the inside – the result of internal streams beneath the ice that excavate caverns – rather than simply retreating from surface heat.Graph showing declining ice volume in Switzerland's glaciers“You have huge holes like cheese in the middle of the ice that have collapsing roofs,” said Huss. “These are processes that tear the glaciers apart and make them retreat even faster.”Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average from the heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution and the destruction of nature, with Alpine regions experiencing some of the most dramatic changes.View image in fullscreenMatthias Huss looks at the ice on the Rhône glacier in Obergoms, Switzerland.Photograph: Pierre Albouy/ReutersAnalysis published by MeteoSwiss on Tuesday found the summer half-year from April to September was the hottest and driest it had been since records began in 1864. In that time, humanity has filled the atmosphere with 1.8tn tons of carbon dioxide and heated the planet by about 1.4C.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe heat this summer was worse than in 2022 but Swiss ice loss just missed the record-breaking levels set that year. The scientists attributed this to limited deposits of Saharan dust, which foul the snow and prevent it from reflecting sunlight, as well as slightly greater snow cover at the end of winter and more sunlight in the summer.Huss visited the formerPlattalvafirn, or Griess glacier, in September, which used to cover a mountain flank but lost 99% of its area in just 20 years. The glacier was the subject of some of the most detailed monitoring in the world in the 1950s and Huss worked with its data when he was a PhD student.View image in fullscreenTwo mountaineers hiking on the Rhône Glacier, above Gletsch, in the Swiss Alps.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty“What was different at that time, is that the rates of retreat were still kind of at a normal level,” said Huss. “What we are seeing now is a complete explosion of these melt rates, leading to the disintegration of glaciers. They’re really just falling apart.”Explore more on these topicsGlaciersSwitzerlandEuropeIceFossil fuelsClimate crisisClimate sciencenewsShareReuse this content

title: David Sullivan sues BBC for £150m over Panorama’s sexual misconduct claims | BBC | The Guardian
description: West Ham co-owner and former pornographer lodges high court claim over episode, in which several women accused him of abusing power
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: West Ham co-owner and former pornographer lodges high court claim over episode, in which several women accused him of abusing power
Content: Three women alleged Sullivan had abused his power as the owner of the Sport newspapers to prey on them for sex when they were seeking work.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenThree women alleged Sullivan had abused his power as the owner of the Sport newspapers to prey on them for sex when they were seeking work.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PABBCDavid Sullivan sues BBC for £150m over Panorama’s sexual misconduct claimsWest Ham co-owner and former pornographer lodges high court claim over episode, in which several women accused him of abusing powerMichael SavageMedia editorThu 1 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Sullivan is suing the BBC for £150m over multiple claims of sexual misconduct made in a documentary.Lawyers acting for Sullivan, who remains West Ham United’s co-owner, have lodged a high court claim against the corporation over its Panorama investigation Predator: The Billionaire Football Boss, which was broadcast in June.It featured three women who alleged Sullivan had abused his power as the owner of the Sport newspapers to prey on them for sex when they were seeking work.A further four women accused Sullivan of exploitative and predatory behaviour, including allegations he had tried to pressure them into sex during business meetings.As part of a joint investigation, theBBCand the Times said their reporters had spoken to dozens of former models and industry insiders, with some sources alleging Sullivan was known for “casting couch” behaviour.The former pornographervowed to take legal action against the BBC even before the programme had aired. In a statement in which he also resigned as West Ham’s co-chair, he said the accusations were “factually incorrect and entirely false”.“The false allegations levelled against me have been sensationalised by the media,” he said. “After a lifetime spent building businesses in the adult industry in which I have met thousands of women, it is sadly inevitable that a small number of improper conduct claims are being made against me. I categorically deny these claims.”Sullivan’s high court claim, first seen by the Telegraph, accuses the BBC of “libel and malicious falsehood” in airing the documentary. It states the show caused Sullivan “grave, catastrophic, and irreparable harm” to his reputation and business interests.It states that the programme’s claims opened the 77-year-old up to “profound public hatred, universal ridicule, and global opprobrium”, as well as “immediate and severe commercial alienation, banking disruption, and quantifiable financial destruction”.The BBC declined to comment.While Sullivan has resigned as West Ham’s co-chair, he remains the Championship club’s largest shareholder, owning 39% of its shares.It has also emerged that Sullivan has faced restrictions on his contactwith West Ham’s women’s and youth teamssince 2023 because of a safeguarding investigation.The Football Association began an inquiry three years ago after receiving a complaint, which the Guardian understands involves an allegation of sexual misconduct unrelated to football.Sullivan said through lawyers that the restrictions were part of a “negotiated and temporary agreement” and that the safeguarding investigation related to a “single anonymous complaint” from an event in 1981. He said the alleged incident “never happened”.After the BBC documentary, the presenter Tony Liveseystepped back from the broadcaster. Earlier in his career, Livesey had been the editor-in-chief of Sullivan’s Sport newspapers. TheBBC investigationraised questions for the 62-year-old, with one alleged victim saying he had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan.Livesey has said he has “no recollection” of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was “not part” of his job to do so. He said he had had “practically zero” contact with anyone appearing in the paper, such as female models.Another high-profile legal case would be a blow for the BBC, which is already fighting a claim brought against it by Donald Trump. The US president has taken legal action over an episode of Panorama that spliced together two parts of a speech.The BBC has apologised for the edit, but has always maintained the programme did not defame Trump.Explore more on these topicsBBCDavid SullivannewsShareReuse this content

title: Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releases | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Seven hundred offenders from dozens of prisons in England and Wales expected to be freed on Thursday
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Seven hundred offenders from dozens of prisons in England and Wales expected to be freed on Thursday
Content: People celebrate as they leave HMP Bristol in Horfield, north Bristol.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenPeople celebrate as they leave HMP Bristol in Horfield, north Bristol.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAPrisons and probationPrisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releasesSeven hundred offenders from dozens of prisons in England and Wales expected to be freed on ThursdayEnver Solomon: Releasing prisoners won’t solve the crisis in English and Welsh jails. Here’s what willUK politics live – latest updatesRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 1 Oct 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrisoners have thankedAndy Burnhamas they celebrated walking free from jail early.The first wave of releases began on Thursday, with 700 offenders walking out acrossEnglandand Wales under the government’s plan to ease prison overcrowding.Those released from dozens of prisons under the government’s latest early release scheme on Thursday were greeted by huddles of journalists requesting their personal messages for the prime minister.Some offenders said they would soon return to jail, because they had nowhere to live and would breach their licence conditions.View image in fullscreenA man leaving HMP Brixton on Thursday.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesIt follows the damagingearly release scheme under Keir Starmer in 2024when offenders were photographed holding bottles of champagne while saying: “Big up Starmer”.Prisoners freed early in England and Wales risk living on the streets, say probation officersRead moreAmong the first releases, a former bus driver turned shoplifter, Michael Bogle, 38, from Brent, north London, stepped into the sunlight outside HMP Wandsworth, a south London prison notable for a string of recent scandals.View image in fullscreenUkrainian national Vladimir Hudzyk, 38, celebrates leaving HMP Wormwood Scrubs, in White City, London.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAHaving served 78 days in prison after breaching a 32-week suspended sentence for shoplifting, he was released early and was pleased that he had been given a place in a bail hostel in south-east London.Asked for his message to Burnham, he said: “Keep the early release going. It’s good.”Bogle, who has been jailed five separate times for 100 convictions, said he had been driven to shoplift “so he could eat” after being made homeless.Prison was “terrible”, Bogle said, adding that there were “too many drugs”. He said there was a risk he would shoplift again, “but hopefully not”.View image in fullscreenA man wears a bag over his head as he walks away from HMP Brixton.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesA man leaving HMP Cardiff, who was asked if he had a message for the prime minister, said: “Thank you very much and don’t get me back here again, bro.”People near the end of their time behind bars are meant to be given help to prepare for life outside prison, which includes advice on finding somewhere to live, getting a job and looking after money.Parole officers have said that they have not been able to find temporary accommodation for many of those being released.Tom, 32, who was released from HMP Cardiff after being jailed for burglary, admitted he would “probably be back in the next month or two”. He has been in and out of prison 30 times since he was 15 years old.“I have always said the easiest part is being in jail, the hardest part is getting out. I’d happily spend my time in [jail]. I’ve got nothing better to do with myself, I’m homeless.”David Elliott, 50, who served seven weeks of a 20-week sentence in HMP Brixton, south London, showed reporters a four-page document of licence conditions, which he feared he would breach without a fixed address.“One of my conditions is I’ve got to be in an address to get my alcohol tag put on my foot,” he said. “I’ve got nowhere to live; I’ll be getting recalled back to prison because I’ve got nowhere to put my tag on.”The prisoners are among thousands the government has been forced to let out to free up space in overcrowded jails and stop the collapse of the justice system.Starmer and previous Tory administrations presided over similar plans.View image in fullscreenPeople released from HMP Brixton on Thursday.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesAbout 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are to be freed over the next month, with another 3,000 in stages over the next year to ease overcrowding. The number was reduced from 6,000 after anintervention by Burnham.Prisoners guilty of manslaughter will also be excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.The number of people behind bars has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England andWaleswas 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data. This is up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.The MoJ said released offenders would be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history”.The victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan “is not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.Alice Russell-Harris, public affairs lead at the domestic abuse charity Refuge, said some survivors had “no alternative” than to seek help in refuge centres to escape released perpetrators. “While we appreciate the need to ease pressure on prison estates, women and girls should not be left to pay the price,” she said.View image in fullscreenThe MoJ said released offenders would be monitored under the ‘toughest supervision in British history’.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesThe justice secretary, Alex Norris, said: “We understand the anxiety victims face ahead of offenders’ release dates, but the greatest danger to victims would be prisons running out of cells for dangerous criminals, which was the crisis this government inherited.“Our plan will make sure this never happens again by building 14,000 prison places while subjecting offenders to the toughest-ever controls, leaving them nowhere to hide and under no doubt that we are watching them.”The move coincides with the justice secretary being sworn in as lord chancellor at a ceremony at the Royal Courts of Justice in central London on the first day of the new legal year, where he vowed to the most senior judges in England and Wales that he would be “ambitious” in his effort to cut the backlog of court cases.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesAndy BurnhamShareReuse this content

title: Bedford rail crash: train sped up after red light warning, say investigators | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: Driver of East Midlands train, who died in June crash, received automatic warning after passing red light but train continued to accelerate
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Driver of East Midlands train, who died in June crash, received automatic warning after passing red light but train continued to accelerate
Content: Investigators and police officers at the scene on 20 June, a day after the collision.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenInvestigators and police officers at the scene on 20 June, a day after the collision.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPARail transportBedford rail crash: train sped up after red light warning, say investigatorsDriver of East Midlands train, who died in June crash, received automatic warning after passing red light but train continued to accelerateGwyn TophamTransport correspondentThu 1 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe train that ran into the back of another in theBedford rail crashsped up after the driver received a warning he had passed a red light, rail investigators have reported.The driver of the East Midlands train, who died in the crash in June, acknowledged the automatic warning but did not appear to act after passing a danger signal that was rarely ever red.According to an updated report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch, the train continued to accelerate before the driver applied the emergency brakes when the stationary train in front came into view.The train, a southbound Luton airport express from Corby, could not stop in time, and the collision killed the driver,60-year-old Shaun Burton, who was described by his employers as a “dedicated railway professional”.Investigators had been seeking to establish if the automatic warning system (AWS) had worked properly, after an initial report found the train hadpassed a red signal.The latestinterim reportpublished on Thursday concluded that the driver had acknowledged the warning, which had not previously displayed a red light during all of 2026, but continued to accelerate to 76mph. After braking, the train slowed to 49mph before it collided with a stationary Nottingham-London train on the same track.1:00Emergency services attend to injured after two trains collide near Bedford – videoThe first train had stopped after braking when an AWS warning incorrectly sounded after passing a green signal. The train was a new Aurora class 810 model built by Hitachi, brought into service within the past six months on East Midlands Railway.In a cab with an unfamiliar layout, when no warning signal was expected, the RAIB report said that “neither the driver nor driving instructor recognised this sound as being an AWS warning indication”. Without an acknowledgment in 2.7 seconds, the system applies an emergency brake.The accident inspectors reported that in the weeks after the crash, another class 810 train had also incorrectly received an AWS warning indication at the same signal on green.The RAIB said it would continue to seek to understand why the Corby train had passed a red light, and whether its safety systems had been functioning correctly, as well as the reason why the first Nottingham train had come to a halt.The report said 160 people had also been injured in the crash, which happened at about 5.13pm on 19 June. It was the fourth involving passenger trains on the UK railway since 2020, after more than a decade without any similar serious incident.Explore more on these topicsRail transportTransportTrain crashesPublic transportEnglandBedfordshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles | International trade | The Guardian
description: Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies
Content: The UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAInternational tradeBritain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpilesMinisters discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US suppliesAlex DanielThu 1 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after theTrump administrationtold Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trumpconsiders a potential wider banto help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November.Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves.Bessent flagged the potential diesel cuts in a social media post, writing: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday.The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks.Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices.It was unclear whether the UK would be included in such a ban, but the loss of US supply would drive prices up sharply at the pumps because the UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.The averageprice of a litre of dieselin the UK hit a new all-time high on Wednesday of 199.72p, according to the motoring body the RAC.John Healey, the chancellor, admitted earlier this week that UK diesel prices were “extreme” and said the government was in discussion with the US over trying to stop a ban.EC commission spokesperson Anna Kaisa Itkonen confirmed that EU member states will hold urgent talks with the commission on Friday to discuss a coordinated response.“The commission … is closely coordinating with EU member states to take stock of the situation and examine appropriate measures to tackle these high prices,” Itkonen added. Discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency.The US energy secretary Chris Wright said ​he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global fuel ⁠prices by drawing down its emergency diesel inventories.“This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go ⁠into to harvest season and we ​go ​into winter heating oil season,” he told Fox ⁠News. “Now’s the time to ​bring more ‌diesel to the ​market, ​and that diesel is available.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMiatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy secretary, has been in contact with Wright to raise concerns.Earlier, a US official told reporters it was “in Europe’s best interest” to ⁠work with the US as it pursues options to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers.The US war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies via the strait of Hormuz and sent the price of oil soaring. Before the war, in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It was above $101 on Thursday.Releasing more stocks wouldrepresent a problem for European countries,which need to balance the need to bring down domestic fuel prices with keeping high stocks for a potential worsening energy crisis over the winter if the Iran war continues.“The UK continues to need fuels – from transport to chemicals, agriculture and defence,” said Elizabeth de Jong, the chief executive of the trade group Fuels Industry UK. The latest US threat showed the UK “cannot solely rely on overseas production for domestic energy security”, she added.Trump has said he was “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, topause strikes on Russian oil refineriesover concerns that they could further push up prices. Russia had already extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October after Ukrainian attacks on refining companies.A government spokesperson said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”Explore more on these topicsInternational tradeEuropean CommissionOilTrump administrationEuropeGlobal economyEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (left) is facing off in the presidential election against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump (right).Composite: AFP, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva (left) is facing off in the presidential election against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump (right).Composite: AFP, Getty ImagesBrazilBrazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealedJorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to pollsTom Phillipsin Rio de Janeiro,Andrew RothandJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 1 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after aGuardian report revealedhow the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court.Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added.Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused oftrying to influence– where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls.According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story.Last year, the Trump administration useda campaign of sanctions and tariffsin a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.3:43How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainerIn recent months, the Trump administration has again been accused ofmeddling in Brazilian affairsby using tariffs and the designation of two Brazilian organised crime groups as foreign terrorist organisations to boost Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign and weaken Lula.Writing on Thursday, Messias said: “Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations. What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.”Messias added: “It is the right of each generation of Brazilians to freely decide their destiny, protect their institutions, and hand over to their children a country that does not accept decisions about Brazil being made outside of Brazil. Our democracy belongs to Brazilians. And so it must remain.”The attorney general’s comments came in response to a report that theTrump administrationwas pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa and the campaign against Brazil’s supreme court.A $1m award titled “Countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court.Bolsonaro’s far-right movement considers the supreme court – and in particular justiceAlexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s trial – its greatest foe.Moraes is widely seen to have played a key role in thwarting Jair Bolsonaro’s authoritarian plot, which culminated in the8 January 2023riots in Brasília, despite concerns about the judge overstepping hisconstitutional authority in his crusade to protect democracy.During the rightwing riots, hardcore Bolsonaro supporters trashed the presidential palace, congress and supreme court. The court sustained the most severe damage.0:49Brazil’s presidential palace left in ruins after Bolsonaro’s supporters storm the building – videoBolsonaro supporters continue to claim their leader’s imprisonment is unjust and that he is the victim of a politically motivated sham driven by a corrupt “judicial dictatorship”.Their criticism of Moraes and the supreme court has been bolstered by a recent scandal linking several judges, including him, to Daniel Vorcaro, the playboy banker at the centre of Brazil’s biggest banking scandal. Vorcaro has also been linked to the Bolsonaro family.The banker reportedly gave the family more than £9m, supposedly to produce a biopic aboutJair Bolsonarostarring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s film The Passion of the Christ. On the eve of Vorcaro’s arrest last November, Flávio Bolsonaro messaged him to say: “Brother, I’ll always be with you.”Vorcaro is being held in federal police custody in Brasília. His legal team has consistently denied wrongdoing. On Wednesday, his lawyers said he was not involved in “any kind of illicit activity or criminal practice”.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS foreign policyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: SpaceX launches crew to ISS successfully: ‘Thanks for an amazing ride’ | Florida | The Guardian
description: Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit, is making her second trip to the space station
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit, is making her second trip to the space station
Content: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft lift off carrying astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney, Canada’s Joshua Kutryk and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov from Florida’s Cape Canaveral space force station on Thursday.Photograph: Joe Skipper/ReutersView image in fullscreenA SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft lift off carrying astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney, Canada’s Joshua Kutryk and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov from Florida’s Cape Canaveral space force station on Thursday.Photograph: Joe Skipper/ReutersFloridaSpaceX launches crew to ISS successfully: ‘Thanks for an amazing ride’Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit, is making her second trip to the space stationAssociated PressThu 1 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour astronauts rocketed into orbit on Thursday on a space station mission that will stretch until spring, among them a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he is away.SpaceXlaunched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew forNasaafter a three-week delay to fix the capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff.Although their stay at the InternationalSpaceStation will last a long six months, the flight there promised to be the quickest yet for Elon Musk’s company: a mere eight-hour transit with an arrival well before bedtime.With the late morning liftoff from Cape Canaveral space force station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with Nasa’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022.“Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed after reaching orbit.The others are newcomers to space: Nasa’s Luke Delaney, a retired marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian air force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.“We feel like some of the luckiest people in the world,” Kutryk said ahead of the launch.This was the 13th crew launched bySpaceXfor Nasa, not counting 2020’s test flight. All four embrace their Crew-13 designation that pays homage in their mission patch to Apollo 13. The harrowing 1970 moonshot ended with the astronauts’ safe return.“We really wanted to honor their legacy, honor their resilience and their grit, and bring a little bit of that with us,” Watkins said. She and her crewmates rode to the pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13”.Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth. Wife Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November. The Canadian Space Agency promises plenty of support for the entire family when the big day comes.“A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” Nasa manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency would do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family.In 2004, Nasa provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit.The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehböck. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.Explore more on these topicsFloridaNasaSpaceXSpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: White House removes CNN from press pool for second time in a week | CNN | The Guardian
description: Network was listed as primary TV pool covering Thursday’s presidential activities but then was abruptly removed
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Network was listed as primary TV pool covering Thursday’s presidential activities but then was abruptly removed
Content: Donald Trump speaks to reporters while aboard Air Force One on 13 September.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks to reporters while aboard Air Force One on 13 September.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesCNNWhite House removes CNN from press pool for second time in a weekNetwork was listed as primary TV pool covering Thursday’s presidential activities but then was abruptly removedJeremy Barrin WashingtonThu 1 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a second time in a week, the White House has unilaterally removedCNNfrom its assignment as the primary television pool representative coveringDonald Trump.CNN wasexcluded on Saturdayfrom pool duty onboard Air Force One, despite a district judge’s ruling – two days earlier –overturning the White House’s banon the network and two other media organizations.But on Sunday, in what appeared to be a thawing of tensions, the White Housepublished a pool assignment listthat listed CNN as in-town pooler for Thursday’s activities, with the conservative network Real America’s Voice serving as secondary pooler.Then, on Wednesday night, the White Houseabruptly removedCNN from pool duty for the following day, leaving Real America’s Voice as the only pooler as the president travels to Texas and Oklahoma. The country’s largest broadcast and cable television news networks have not aired Real America’s Voice footage, though the network haswidely broadcast its availability.The five networks that serve in the primary television pool have taken it day by day since the White House originallybannedCNN on 18 September, initially suspending operation before tentativelykicking back into actionthis past Friday.Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’Read moreAs they did on Saturday,none of the other four networkswill take CNN’s place on Thursday, meaning there will be no primary pool footage, though networks could cover individual parts of his trip.CNN did not comment on the network’s exclusion on Thursday.A White House official sent a statement touting Trump’s accessibility and referring to television networks as “performative and dishonest”.Earlier this week, lawyers for CNN, MS Now and Politico – the three outlets targeted by Trump’s ban – formally asked a judge to extend his ruling overturning the White House ban for a period of 14 days.The judge in the case will soon hold a hearing to weigh arguments from both sides about whether the networks should be granted a preliminary injunction that would block the ban untilthe network’s 21 September lawsuitagainst the White House plays out.“As we explain in our latest brief, the White House is persisting in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing the President’s unconstitutional ‘ban on the free press’ by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as a designated television network pooler – to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public,” Theodore J Boutrous, who is representing the networks in their lawsuit, said in a statement on Thursday.Explore more on these topicsCNNDonald TrumpUS press and publishingTrump administrationUS politicsTV newsThe news on TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Travelodge guests are still at risk, finds review launched after sexual assault | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Report finds complaints of room intrusions at nearly one in 10 hotels, after woman attacked by man given a copy of her key
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Report finds complaints of room intrusions at nearly one in 10 hotels, after woman attacked by man given a copy of her key
Content: Despite Travelodge strengthening its key security policy, Greaney found it was ‘not being applied with anything anything like sufficient consistency’.Photograph: Steve Taylor/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDespite Travelodge strengthening its key security policy, Greaney found it was ‘not being applied with anything anything like sufficient consistency’.Photograph: Steve Taylor/SOPA Images/ShutterstockTravel & leisureTravelodge guests are still at risk, finds review launched after sexual assaultReport finds complaints of room intrusions at nearly one in 10 hotels, after woman attacked by man given a copy of her keyKalyeena MakortoffThu 1 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn independent review into Travelodge after a serious sexual assault has found that guests are still at risk, with room intrusions reported at nearly one in 10 of its hotels this summer.The damning findings werepublished in a 70-page report on Thursday, which was commissioned earlier this year after a man was convicted of a serious sexual assault against a Travelodge guest in Maidenhead in 2022.The perpetrator was handed a copy of the victim’s room key, having falsely claimed to be her boyfriend, andsexually assaulted her in her hotel bed. The victim – referred to as “Lily” in the report – was later offered what she described as an “insulting” £30 refund.The incident prompted further reports of security failings at the hotel chain, eventually leading to theresignation of Joanna Boydellas chief executive in August.Paul Greaney KC, the barrister who led the review, said Lily “was treated by Travelodge in a way that was inappropriate and unfair; indeed, it was disgraceful” He said the hotel’s response to her complaint “was driven by a desire to get rid of the complaint as quickly and cheaply as possible”.The report said: “Travelodge’s treatment of Lily, following her complaint in writing, fell short of every standard the public would expect of an organisation such as Travelodge. It was simply appalling.“Overall, these failings are extremely serious and rest principally with the organisation, rather than with any individual [member of staff].”Greaney acknowledged that Travelodge had been trying to improve its room security policies and training since March. However, he said not enough had yet been done to ensure guests were safe.Despite Travelodge strengthening its key security policy, Greaney found it was “not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground. In other words, it has not sufficiently embedded.”“Even in this period of strong improvement, there were reports by guests of room intrusion across nearly one in 10 of Travelodge hotels, which represents around 60 hotels,” the report said.“I am not satisfied that enough has yet occurred to make guests as safe as they should be when staying in a Travelodge,” Greaney added.Although the review was focused on the budget chain’s failings, the KC said guests were suffering unacceptable security breaches in hotels across the country and room intrusions “are a problem across the hotel sector”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe review put forward a series of recommendations, including:Creating a new policy to address violence against women and girls.Improving safety policies for staff working alone.Introducing body cameras for all reception staff.Installing consistent CCTV systems across all its hotels.Introducing mystery shoppers to test its key security policy.Travelodge said it welcomed the report’s recommendations, had put together a new board committee to ensure they were implemented and planned to track their progress over the next six to 12 months.In a statement released alongside the review, Travelodge’s interim chief executive, Ray Reidy, said: “I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed, and particularly to Lily. We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go.“We are working hard to transform our customer service so we respond appropriately when things don’t go right. We will continue to improve so customers get the right level of support and empathy when they need it most.”Explore more on these topicsTravel & leisureHospitality industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Google rolls out new Gemini AI model but restricts access over safety concerns | Google | The Guardian
description: Tech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers
Content: Google's AI Mode feature.Photograph: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoogle's AI Mode feature.Photograph: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle rolls out new Gemini AI model but restricts access over safety concernsTech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackersAgence France-PresseThu 1 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle on Wednesday said it would withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.“Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach,” wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google’s chief AI architect, in a blogpost announcing the model.Google said it was voluntarily giving the US government early access to the model and would gather feedback from testers before making it widely available.The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rivalAnthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organizations.Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release.The announcement came a day after Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including the Google chief, Sundar Pichai, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own AI systems.Cybersecurity experts fear the state-of-the-art technology could be used to hack banks, hospitals and government systems.Google said Argon excelled at complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work and cyber-defense, with a leading ability to find and fix critical software flaws.Early testers used Argon to uncover a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information – something other advanced models had missed, Google said.Google said Argon was designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyber-attacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic and ChatGPT-makerOpenAIhave built similar safeguards into their most advanced models.Google said it was monitoring the model’s reasoning to stop it from straying beyond what users intended, a risk researchers call misalignment.The issue has taken on new urgency since OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models, including one not yet released, broke out of a sealed test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked into the servers of the AI company Hugging Face.Explore more on these topicsGoogleAlphabetAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicOpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when promptedGuardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photoJohana BhuiyanThu 1 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen prompted,AIchatbots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.The Guardian askedChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. BothOpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt.Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or -generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab.Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab.A fake image of a Georgia mayor kissing a person went viral. Can US voters trust everything they see?Read moreThe Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress.It was unclear which software or AI model Odoul used or even whether he modified the image himself, but experts say the MP’s actions were part of a growing pattern of tech-enabled anti-Muslim hatred around the world.In India, where anti-Muslim sentiment is rampant, generative AI is playing an increasingly significant role in producing images that, among other things, sexualize Muslim women or dehumanize Muslims generally, according to astudyby non-profit US thinktank the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH). The CSOH also found that there are similar types of AI-enabled hatred being directed at prominent female Muslim politicians in the US such as Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib.“This is just part of an ongoing trend of how we see Muslim communities, and particularly Muslim women, being targeted and abused,” said Eviane Leidig, the director of research and outreach at the CSOH.While Grok promptly complied with a request to edit an image of a woman wearing a hijab, the chatbot declined to take the dress off an AI-generated image of a woman. When asked what the difference was, the chatbot replied, “Removing the hijab was treated as a relatively straightforward clothing/hair change.” However, the chatbot said it would be willing to do a “less explicit version” of the edit and “change the dress to underwear, a different outfit or a partial reveal”.In May, xAI announced it had implemented technological measures that would not allow its AI image generator to comply with requests to digitally undress “images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis”.ChatGPT similarly declined to remove a dress off the AI-generated woman, saying that the “distinction is that removing a hijab changes a head covering, while removing a dress would expose the person’s body”. However,ChatGPTeventually conceded that for someone who wears hijab, exposing their hair “can be a meaningful violation of privacy or religious practice”.“The fact that an edit doesn’t create nudity doesn’t mean it can’t violate someone’s privacy, dignity or religious boundaries,” ChatGPT responded.These distinctions show the gaps in community guidelines that dictate how AI chatbots can behave, said Leidig, as platforms such as X soften its enforcement of existing rules, emboldening far-right figures. The de-veiling of Muslim women “may not be distinctly violative [of platform rules] but it’s still harmful”, she said.OpenAI, Google,xAI and Anthropic declined to comment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian conducted similar tests for other religious head coverings like a turban traditionally worn by Sikh men and a Catholic nun wearing a habit. ChatGPT readily created new images removing both the habit and turban off the AI-generated people.Gemini initially declined to create a new image of the man without a turban. However, just as in the case of the image of the woman wearing hijab, when asked to make the AI-generated image of the man wearing a turban more western, Gemini created a new image of the man without a turban.Despite initially claiming that it couldn’t remove a hijab from an image of a woman because “attempting to remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people relies entirely on artificial generation to guess what lies underneath”, Gemini removed the habit off of the AI-generated image.Claude, for its part, said that if it could edit images, it would not edit an image of a real woman to remove her hijab regardless of the requester’s intent.“That kind of edit changes how a real person is depicted in a way tied to their religious dress and identity, and it could be used to embarrass, harass or misrepresent them – that’s true whether the woman is a public figure or someone private,” the chatbot responded.Publicly available AI chatbots and third-party “nudify” apps have been used broadly to disrobe women, and in some cases minors. InJanuary, sexualized images of women proliferated across X as users realized they could ask the Grok chatbot, developed by the Elon Musk-owned xAI, to undress images of women posted on the social media platform. The spread of these images prompted countries like France toinvestigateX. Malaysia temporarily restricted the use of Grok in the country.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsChatGPTOpenAIIslamophobiaIslamComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn | Motoring | The Guardian
description: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports
Content: Cars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said.Photograph: Tamer Adel/AlamyView image in fullscreenCars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said.Photograph: Tamer Adel/AlamyMotoringTech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warnHostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese importsAlex DanielThu 1 Oct 2026 06.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations.It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK.Three-quarters of UK’s popular plug-in hybrid cars unable to use rapid chargersRead moreIn a translateddocumentreleased on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet.“On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added.The alert followsreports last yearthat British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’sbestselling car in March.MPs have raisedconcernsthat China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested.The UK Ministry of Defencehas saidit is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles.This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, includingRAF Wytonin Cambridgeshire and theDorset headquartersof Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”.The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”.It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere.On Wednesday, MI5issued a rare public warningto UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.Explore more on these topicsMotoringAutomotive industryEspionageNetherlandsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Orgy, apocalypse and exorcism: Faye Driscoll’s revolving bed puts everyone in a spin | Stage | The Guardian
description: The US performance-maker’s Weathering, which evokes people clinging to a life raft, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences. As it arrives in the UK, she reflects on creating a sensory environment to involve us all
Author: Tim Etchells
Headline: The US performance-maker’s Weathering, which evokes people clinging to a life raft, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences. As it arrives in the UK, she reflects on creating a sensory environment to involve us all
Content: ‘The spinning is the thing’ … Weathering.Photograph: Kevin Monko/Fierce FestivalView image in fullscreen‘The spinning is the thing’ … Weathering.Photograph: Kevin Monko/Fierce FestivalStageOrgy, apocalypse and exorcism: Faye Driscoll’s revolving bed puts everyone in a spinThe US performance-maker’s Weathering, which evokes people clinging to a life raft, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences. As it arrives in the UK, she reflects on creating a sensory environment to involve us allTim EtchellsThu 1 Oct 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFaye Driscoll is in Stockholm, developing a new work forCullberg’s entire 15-dancer ensemble titledflesh chariot, chariot of flesh. In the process she is negotiating the shift from independent projects in New York and Los Angeles to the framework of a large European dance institution. “There are so many people in the rehearsal room, sometimes it feels like I’m running a small corporation,” she jokes on our video call. Thankfully there’s nothing corporate about Driscoll’s work, which comes from a deep, intuitive set of questions about dance, human connection, perception, ecology and community.Since premiering in New York in 2023, her extraordinary and best-known performance, Weathering, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences on its journey from the choreographer’s base in NY/LA to festivals across Europe and farther afield. The work’s UK premiere is a substantial coup for Birmingham’s groundbreakingFierce festival.Weathering begins at a glacial pace, with 10 performers assuming still positions on a rotating central platform, the audience gathered around on four sides. What follows is a compelling and challenging mix of kinetic sculpture and uncanny ritual, long-forgotten orgy, exuberant collective exorcism and intimate apocalypse. A slow build from the stillness in the first scene rises to a chaotic transformative and desperate group exertion. Rooted in techniques and understandings from choreography itself, Driscoll’s work is also dance by way of Butoh and performance art. At the same time, it stands as a nuanced and profoundly impactful wordless reflection on the state of the world, the climate and our tangled place in it.View image in fullscreenNuanced and profoundly impactful … Faye Driscoll’s Weathering.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesAs might be expected, Driscoll’s journey to choreography was a patchwork of influences and permissions. “My parents met in New York as performer-dancers in an all-nude musical –Oh! Calcutta!– so I guess that does feel important; when I wanted to dance, I had no problem with access to it.” After learning ballet and modern dance, she undertook conservatory training in New York.
