Being exposed to the city’s downtown performance scene – shows by legendary figures such asRichard Foremanand invitations to choreograph for up-and-coming radicals like playwrightYoung Jean Lee– had a big effect. “Collaboration really affected my making, pushing me away from the preciousness that can be so strong when you work alone.”Caught in what Driscoll calls “a collective ongoing”, the figures on stage in Weathering are a mix of ages, ethnicities, genders, body types, and presences. We could be seeing strangers plucked at random from city streets, caught off balance together on the performance podium that frames their journey. The rotating platform itself begins as stage or museum plinth but constantly takes on new connotations through the work; a bed, an improvised life raft to which people are clinging, a fragile spinning world.It’s an irony perhaps that such a physical project as Weathering began life during Covid, with Driscoll and team researching remotely. “We couldn’t touch each other or even be in the same rooms. We were using text to figure things out – taking from fight scenes and erotica, mixing the Iliad with bits of Rocky, first world war battle descriptions and porn, mashing everything together.” Although none of this material made the completed work, it’s present as a reference, says Driscoll: “I was thinking a lot about moments in daily life where we push outside ourselves and go into another body – try to be with it, to change it, where our borders as human beings blur in the most intimate ways, in fighting or in sex.”View image in fullscreen‘I was thinking about where our bodies as human beings blur in the most intimate ways’ … Faye Driscoll.Photograph: Valerian MazataudEcological thematics ghost the piece, especially the tangled relation between humans and the nature they claim to oversee. Driscoll explains: “We are nature … we aren’t inside any weather system that we’re trying to fix … We’re part of these systems with every breath and every piss we take.” At the same time, it’s the profound malleability of the image and the audience role in making meaning that grips Driscoll. Her pieceflesh chariot, chariot of fleshalso leans into the question of connectivity in the contemporary context, considering events in the world and how they affect us profoundly from a distance – how can things that reach us via the world-flattening device of screens still be felt as bodily experience, as trauma. “In Weathering, the spinning is the thing. As a spectator, you’re never going to get the whole picture, like in life, maybe we never do. So as the platform spins, you’re constantly re-engaging with things as they come back around, grappling with your own idea about what you’re seeing or what you might have missed.”Indeed, perhaps the most obdurate obsession for Driscoll is the audience. “Previously, I spent eight years doing a project that asked how you sense and feel your culpability in the room when you’re watching a show. To do that, the project dealt a lot with audience participation, which I found completely horrifying.” But her struggle with participation revealed a deeper desire that still compels her: “How do I create a sensory environment that makes you understand that you are already involved in everything? That idea is the DNA of all my work.”As Weathering intensifies towards its ending – “there’s a shedding of clothes, a kind of peeling that occurs … there are hands in mouths, hands in each other’s clothing … ” – we enter a physically and sonically overwhelming zone. The scene, flirting with the limits of control, is grotesque, passionate, tender and urgent, all at the same time. “It might look referential, like bodies from art history. Or it might look imagistic, like moments drawn from life,” says Driscoll. “You think for some time that you could know what this is that you’re looking at … but that certainty dissolves.” She pauses, a small silence on the video call, then adds, as if by way of conclusion: “I love the slipperiness of unknowing.”Weatheringis at Midland Arts Centre, Birmingham, 14-16 October as part ofFierce festival.flesh chariot, chariot of fleshis touring until 6 February. Forced Entertainment’sCold Sweat, devised with and directed by Tim Etchells, is at Sheffield Theatres, 2-3 October; Southbank Centre, London, 9-10 October; and Lancaster Arts, 14 October.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreDancePerformance artfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I will see you in the parking lot after this’: when book clubs get dramatic | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Book clubs can be fun, fulfilling and interesting – but many members have seen a meeting or group go down in flames
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Book clubs can be fun, fulfilling and interesting – but many members have seen a meeting or group go down in flames
Content: Book club dramaWell actually‘I will see you in the parking lot after this’: when book clubs get dramaticBook clubs can be fun, fulfilling and interesting – but many members have seen a meeting or group go down in flamesStephanie McNealThu 1 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.54 EDTShareFor four years, Laura has been in a book club with other young mothers from her church. You might be picturing a docile scene of women drinking sweet tea – they live in the US south – and discussing a life-affirming family novel or chaste romance.But you probably didn’t account forwerewolf smut.“One mom wanted to be a dictator and pick every book,” Laura, who requested a pseudonym so as not to cause another blow-up, told me. “She only readsspice[romance fiction with sexual content] … and there’s different levels of comfortability. Some women clutch their pearls at [her] mere suggestions.”Every meeting started to devolve in the same way. The member would fight hard for her pick – always something spicy – and everyone would give in. But no one was reading the books, and finally, they decided to set some “content guidelines” going forward: no smut and no violence. This did not go well.“She went to every single individual in the group and said she felt like we were kicking her out … but she still shows up every month, just doesn’t read the book and doesn’t participate,” she said. “She sits in a corner and sulks.”Despite fears about AI’s toll oncritical-thinking skillsand articles bemoaning the end ofreading, we may be in the golden age of book clubs. According toAxios, book club events jumped by 33% on the Eventbrite platform in 2026, driven by the popularity of reading formillennialsandgen Z, and a 2025 report from the digital reading platformEverandfound that readers are meeting up more frequently in person, with in-person clubs rising 8% since 2024.Book clubs are fun, fulfilling and interesting. But while they evoke a wholesome image, many members have seen a meeting gone bad or a group that went down in flames.The 100 best novels of all timeRead moreWhen freelance writer and editorSteph Auterithinks of her previous, now disbanded book clubs, she can name all the ways in which they met their demise.“People who don’t read the book, people who don’t prioritize putting [the meeting] on their calendars, people who are all into different sorts of books,” she said. “So then, every book feels like homework … There’s too many books in the world, and too little time in my life to waste on books that I don’t actually want to read.”Once, she moderated a virtual book club during a Covid-19 lockdown. Everyone absolutely hated the book. Unfortunately, the author had been invited to their discussion.“The person who had brought the author on was like: ‘Oh my God, I wish we had read the book before[hand],’” said Auteri.Book club attenders often fall into one of two groups. Auteri is the first kind: a dedicated reader who relishes in-depth discussions about prose and plot. The second type comes for the vibes; they enjoy hanging out but never read the book. These groups can clash if they end up at the same gathering.“As much as I love a time to get together and drink wine and snack, I’m a book nerd, so I want to be talking about the book,” she said. “When two people haven’t read the book, it’s like: ‘What are we doing here?’”View image in fullscreen‘As much as I love a time to get together and drink wine and snack, I’m a book nerd, so I want to be talking about the book.’Photograph: monkeybusinessimages/Getty Images/iStockphotoBut even if everyone is a serious reader, that doesn’t mean it’s smooth sailing.Barbara VanDenburgh, a former books editor for USA Today who runs theFirst Draft Book Club in Phoenix, said it was normally a docile gathering. But in August, that changed – as she chronicled in a Substack post calledWhy my book club almost broke into fisticuffs over Ann Patchett.For the first 30 minutes, discussion of Patchett’s latest novel,Whistler, was “perfectly lovely”, VanDenburgh wrote. Then one attender, Alex, advanced a theory about the book. (It’s a spoiler, so I won’t reveal it here.) “The room erupted. I mean,erupted,” wrote VanDenburgh. “It was the most bonkers book club meeting I’ve ever moderated.“We were yelling theories across the room,” she said over the phone. “Somebody at one point was like: ‘I will see you in the parking lot after this meeting, Alex, you and me.’” (They were joking.)VanDenburgh has been running her club for more than a decade, and the Whistler incident aside, has a few ground rules for keeping the peace. In her club, she always chooses the book. This once caused minor discontent.More than a decade ago, she selectedEileen by Ottessa Moshfeghas December’s book since it was set during the Christmas season. But Eileen, which tells the tale of a troubled young woman who becomes obsessed with an older co-worker at the prison where she works, is decidedly not an uplifting holiday season read. “People are mad to this day,” VanDenburgh said. “At the very last meeting, in fact, people brought up Eileen, like: Don’t you dare ever do that to us again.”Yet VanDenburgh still believes a book “dictatorship”, where one person controls the selection and the flow of the conversation, may actually be the key to success.“It doesn’t have to be the same person every time, but I think whoever has ownership needs to be a benevolent dictator who’s done the work,” she said. “When book clubs don’t work, in my experience, is when everybody sits around and hopes the conversation happens organically.”Erin Pepler, a writer from Toronto, also believes that to have a good book club, someone has to be in charge – because when that’s not the case, she’s seen various members take criticisms of their picks as insults. Like Auteri, she’sjoinedand left countless book clubs over the years, and is tempted every so often to start one up again. Then, she remembers the drama.“I know art is subjective, so I never truly care if people like what I like. But not everyone feels that way,” she said. “People take criticism personally, as if you’re speaking negatively about the people who chose or enjoyed the book rather than just having a conversation about art.”Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Jenn, who requested only her first name be used to avoid more drama, said that the book club she’s in had had a “heated” discussion of politics. The group, based in New York, is a hodgepodge of acquaintances from various friend groups; Jenn was invited by a casual friend who knew she liked to read. But a meeting quickly turned tense when one of the founders accused the group of being too liberal.“After that meeting, she sent a note to everyone ‘dissolving’ the book club,” she told me. “We just continued on without her.”It may be impossible to eliminate interpersonal drama or disagreements. But most of the book club leaders I spoke to have etiquette guidelines. Bittina Sheen, who owns theAway With Words Bookshopin Poulsbo, Washington, and runs its book club, said a key to success was ensuring each club pick is relevant to the group.“Our genres are contemporary fiction and historical fiction,” she said. “It’s quite a mixed group: women who are in their 60s, women who are in their 30s, 40s, 50s. Now that we have our established group of people who regularly come, I don’t want to be like: ‘Oh surprise, we’re gonna read this spicy romance book.’”Most people interviewed said it was OK not to read every book every time. But if you don’t read the book, you can’t stop the discussion in order to avoid “spoilers”.“Oh no, get out of here,” said VanDenburgh. “If you don’t want to have the ending revealed because you didn’t finish the book, don’t show up.”Romantasy, Bridgerton, audio porn apps: it’s a great time for horny ladiesRead moreOlivia Alatorre’s Florida-based fantasy book club, Wings & Flings, used to jokingly shame its members if they showed up with the book unread and took it a step further: those whofail the assignmentmust wear a dunce hat.“Some book clubs can be so strict with their structures and dynamics, and this was kind of a play on that, as our book club is a lot more relaxed and inclusive,” Alatorre said.If you’re worried about joining a local club and being forced to read a textbook-sized tome on second world war battles, it’s never been a better time to join a specialized club like hers. Though theme-agnostic clubs still dominate, ones that center on a particular genre or focus on diversity in perspectives or characters are rapidly growing among 18- to 44-year-old readers, according to a2024 survey by Penguin Random House. According toAxios, “hyper-niche” book meetups, with themes like “romantasy” and “weird girl”, were mostly responsible for the increased popularity of these events.Despite these dramatic tales, most book clubs are like Alatorre’s – they want people to feel welcomed and excited about reading. If you want to start or join a book club, it’s incredibly easy to do. Just gather some friends, pick a book and don’t overthink it.And if it goes down in flames, well, at least you’ll have a good story.“Think of it as a hangout with your friends, with a book at the center of it, and just see what happens,” she said.Stephanie McNeal is a writer and editor based in Brooklyn. She’s the author ofSwipe Upfor More: Inside the Unfiltered Lives of Influencersand writes the newsletterSide Chaton Substack.

title: The Last First: Winter K2 review – race up second highest mountain reveals fatal cost of human ambition | Movies | The Guardian
description: Amir Bar-Lev’s doc covering competing climbers trying to achieve something that has not been done before uncovers a fascinating tapestry of aspiration and folly
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Amir Bar-Lev’s doc covering competing climbers trying to achieve something that has not been done before uncovers a fascinating tapestry of aspiration and folly
Content: Deadly summit … The Last First: Winter K2.Photograph: Apple TV/PAView image in fullscreenDeadly summit … The Last First: Winter K2.Photograph: Apple TV/PAMoviesReviewThe Last First: Winter K2 review – race up second highest mountain reveals fatal cost of human ambitionAmir Bar-Lev’s doc covering competing climbers trying to achieve something that has not been done before uncovers a fascinating tapestry of aspiration and follyCatherine BrayThu 1 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the Covid pandemic in 2021, a “last first” in mountaineering was achieved:the forbidding K2 mountain was scaled in winterfor the first time. Amir Bar-Lev’s mountain-climbing doc tells the story of the competing climbers simultaneously hoping to reach the summit, several of whom do not survive the attempt. Far from being the straightforward survival-against-the-odds account that you might expect, this is a microcosm of some of humanity’s more regrettable traits, which rub up alongside each other in fascinatingly thorny ways.To take just one example: the Nepalese push for the summit comes at the cost of sacrificing the chummy camaraderie among the international climbers; but then again, Nepal is a nation rich in indigenous mountaineering expertise that has been relegated for decades to the role of humble assistant in a series of records set by foreigners. On the other hand, did all the climbers in the Nepalese team get equal credit, or was the lion’s share of the glory allotted toNirmal Purja, AKA Nims, the Nepalese social media rock star who spoke fluent English and knew how to craft a headline-worthy soundbite? (In a further strange twist,Nims was killed in an avalanche this yearin between the film’s world premiere at Sundance and wider release.) Did Nims’ record disrupt old patterns of privilege, subtly reinforce them in new ways – or both?This is just one thread in a tapestry of human ambition and folly. The starkly indifferent environment of the mountain makes for a sharp counterpoint to such concerns. K2 doesn’t know or care about national pride, commercial imperatives, underdog narratives, or what a person’s life might mean to those they leave behind. Even at base camp, temperatures on K2 in the winter can fall to -40C. Tents are torn from the ground like wings from a fly by gale-force winds. Bar-Lev’s film balances compassion for the surviving relatives of those who lose their lives with a clear-eyed view of the realities of nature. It’s a salutary lesson in the climate-change era, when a small percentage of humanity is taking a risky gamble, betting that human ingenuity will win out against physics.The Last First: Winter K2 is on Apple TV from 2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMountaineeringNepalSouth and central AsiareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Don’t hate the movie, hate the critic! Digger’s new PR push is a risky bet for film that was never meant to be divisive | Tom Cruise | The Guardian
description: ‘SAME FILM – DIFFERENT TRUTH’ is the marketing solution for the film’s poor reception by critics. Or, as Cruise says in the ad, ‘Fuck those people!’
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: ‘SAME FILM – DIFFERENT TRUTH’ is the marketing solution for the film’s poor reception by critics. Or, as Cruise says in the ad, ‘Fuck those people!’
Content: In a hole … Tom Cruise at the Digger press conference in South Korea.Photograph: Steve Cho Kyewoong/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIn a hole … Tom Cruise at the Digger press conference in South Korea.Photograph: Steve Cho Kyewoong/ShutterstockTom CruiseDon’t hate the movie, hate the critic! Digger’s new PR push is a risky bet for film that was never meant to be divisivePeter Bradshaw‘SAME FILM – DIFFERENT TRUTH’ is the marketing solution for the film’s poor reception by critics. Or, as Cruise says in the ad, ‘Fuck those people!’Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.37 EDTShare‘You know what? Fuck those people!” The speaker is Tom Cruise in his serious-fatsuit role of Digger, inthe bold new online adwhich gives the finger to his film’s bad reviews and the haters. His words are now repurposed to address loathsome critics. The ad’s message is that a provocative, passionate film like this is divisive. You should make your own mind up. Which is true of course. Although it is just as true for films getting across-the-board raves.The last movie to try this was Francis Ford Coppola’s Megalopolis: it too ran an ad campaign rebranding the existence of bad reviews (though like Digger it also had plenty of good reviews) as evidence of genius which had yet to be appreciated. This campaign went terribly wrong when it was pointed out that bad reviews it had quoted for Apocalypse Now and The Godfatherwere in fact made up.Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satireRead moreWe have to assume that Digger’s PR team have done their homework. Their ad punches out quotes matching superlatives to abuse: “UNPLEASANT – MASTERPIECE”; “BAFFLING – BRILLIANT”; “VERY GOOFY – EXCELLENT”; “MAGNIFICENT – INSUFFERABLE”; “SAME FILM – DIFFERENT TRUTH” it concludes.But who is it being quoted? The answer seems to be: entertainment journalists on social media, reporters who are today startled and tickled pink to be cited in this way. The ad does not deign to quote the reviews as such, the actual longform reviews whose failure to line up unanimously behind this prestige film may have been hurtful. Their dissent is of more consequence in a movie-marketplace where theRotten Tomatoes aggregation scoreis taken very seriously. And of course the good reviews are where the Oscar buzz is supposed to begin. So the narrative has to be changed to debate. Praise and mockery have to be mulched together and offered as a weird kind of controversy-clamour. But the awful truth is that Digger wasn’t supposed to be divisive. It was supposed to be a sophisticated film with glamorous stars and an impeccably liberal message that we could all get behind.Director Alejandro Gonzaléz Iñárritu and producer-star Tom Cruise are naturally entitled to disdain the critics. I myself have raved about crazy high-risk films, like Darren Aronofsky’s much-scorned, much-mocked surreal freakoutMother!which have met with derision from the rest of press. But disdaining the press means following the example of the British Royal Family and ignoring them. And letting the film speak for itself.Explore more on these topicsTom CruiseFilm criticismcommentShareReuse this content

title: East of Eden review – Florence Pugh in soapy Steinbeck adaptation is brilliant, compelling TV | Television | The Guardian
description: This take on the 1952 novel is lavishly shot and full of excellent performances. It lacks the heft to be a full examination of human nature, but it’s a high-quality family saga
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This take on the 1952 novel is lavishly shot and full of excellent performances. It lacks the heft to be a full examination of human nature, but it’s a high-quality family saga
Content: Brotherly love … Mike Faist as Charles Trask, Christopher Abbott as Adam Trask and Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenBrotherly love … Mike Faist as Charles Trask, Christopher Abbott as Adam Trask and Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewEast of Eden review – Florence Pugh in soapy Steinbeck adaptation is brilliant, compelling TVThis take on the 1952 novel is lavishly shot and full of excellent performances. It lacks the heft to be a full examination of human nature, but it’s a high-quality family sagaLucy ManganThu 1 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is rarely difficult to distinguish between a John Steinbeck novel and a ray of sunshine. The new adaptation of his 1952 book East of Eden doesn’t buck the trend and wastes no time plunging us into the murk. The opening scene follows a beaten, bloodied woman as she crawls across a muddy field towards the only house for miles around. Out of the house come two brothers. One rushes to rescue her. The other takes one look and announces: “This is a mistake.” Brother, you have no idea.The rescuer is Adam Trask (Christopher Abbott), the sceptic Charles (Mike Faist). Cut back 25 years to watch them being raised in misery in an essentially motherless household by their monstrous father, Cyrus (Tracy Letts), a civil war veteran and ceaseless recounter of his heroics therein. Charles longs to follow in his footsteps. Adam is beaten for his lack of aggressive instinct. But it is Adam whom Cyrus sends to enlist and Charles he forces to stay behind and work on the family farm. “Because,” he says to Adam in a rare instance of paternal wisdom, “there are loose things in him that should be reined down.”As a resentment-fuelled Charles nearly kills Adam the night before he leaves for the army, you can see Cyrus’s point. But years later, Dad is dead, leaving behind an almost certainly ill-gotten fortune. Adam comes home; the brothers put the past behind them and begin to carve out a decent life on the farm.And then comes Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh), the battered, bloodied woman crawling across the field to damn them all.View image in fullscreenEvil just for kicks? … Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in East of Eden.Photograph: NetflixEast of Eden was Steinbeck’s penultimate major work; he thought it his finest. Critics disagreed. They thought its examination of good and evil – whether we are born to be one or the other, whether we have a choice, how much we can fight our instincts – was heavy-handed and the author guilty of an intrusive moralism that prevented the book from ringing true. The public, however, took it to heart as a soapy family drama – Cain and Abel, but out west and set over three generations. Perhaps this was not what Steinbeck intended, but it made the novel an instant bestseller.It’s on this plane that the new version, by Zoe Kazan (the granddaughter of Elia, who directed the 1955 film adaptation starring an unknown actor called James Dean) works best. Lavishly shot, full of emotional and physical incident and fine performances, there is little chance to be distracted.Adam falls hopelessly in love with Cathy while the far more worldly-wise Charles looks on with contempt and despair.The second episode unpacks her torrid backstory – the born manipulator, leaving desperate boys and suicidal men in her wake, who moves into prostitution as a pragmatic business move and specialises in practices that most 19th-century whorehouses were hoping wouldn’t make it that far west until the internet age, betraying benefactors, committing arson, faking her death and abandoning husbands and eventually babies in her quest for riches and freedom. Or possibly just for kicks.Cathy’s sociopathy or psychopathy was part of the critical rejection of the book – a woman couldn’t possibly! – that feels dated now, but it doesn’t mean it has become much more interesting in the years since. Pugh does what she can with the part – but Cathy remains a spectacle to be ogled rather than a fully fledged character.View image in fullscreenA welcome chance to breathe … Hoon Lee as Lee with Ciarán Hinds as Samuel Hamilton in East of Eden.Photograph: Kristy Griffin/NetflixThe men – some things never change – fare better. The brothers have much to get their teeth into, as they struggle with their love and hate for each other, for her, for their lives and for their father. One of the most finely drawn and touching relationships grows gradually between Adam’s neighbour Samuel Hamilton (Ciarán Hinds), once Adam and Cathy have moved to the Salinas valley, and Adam’s manservant, Lee (Hoon Lee) ; it gives us a welcome chance to breathe. A lovely performance from Martha Plimpton as the unexpectedly vulnerable brothel madam Faye – first Cathy’s boss, then another of Cathy’s victims – helps aerate things, too.As a high-quality family saga, then, it’s brilliant, compelling entertainment. As an excoriation of human nature, as an examination of how helpless we are before our inborn proclivities, it perhaps cannot help but lack the heft it needs.East of Eden is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewFlorence PughreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Break Clause review – you’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll never want to live with anyone again | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Lara Ricote’s tale of a couple who break up after moving in together is weird, hugely funny and uncomfortably true-to-life at times
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Lara Ricote’s tale of a couple who break up after moving in together is weird, hugely funny and uncomfortably true-to-life at times
Content: Uncomfortably true-to-life … Lil (Lara Ricote) and Ben (Samuel Bottomley) in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/ erry SpicerView image in fullscreenUncomfortably true-to-life … Lil (Lara Ricote) and Ben (Samuel Bottomley) in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/ erry SpicerTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewBreak Clause review – you’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll never want to live with anyone againLara Ricote’s tale of a couple who break up after moving in together is weird, hugely funny and uncomfortably true-to-life at timesHannah J DaviesThu 1 Oct 2026 06.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 22, you move from Leeds to London for your first proper job, and get the keys to a flat with your uni boyfriend. But on day one, you break up, and are then stuck living together for the next six months as “friends” until you can wriggle out of your tenancy. We’ve all been there, right? Well, maybe we haven’t but, watching Break Clause, it’s easy to feel as though you have. This six-part comedy-drama harks back to the peak sadcom era of the late 2010s, when pretty much every show on TV was being referred to as “the new Fleabag”, and tears were de rigueur. It will make you laugh, it might make you cry and, at the very least, it will make you think twice about moving in with anybody ever again.Break Clause is the creation of Jess Bray, who has worked on Big Boys and We Might Regret This, and is directed by Alice Snedden, co-writer and star in Starstruck. Unlike that series, Break Clause isn’t a whimsical romcom, despite a very whimsical romcom opening in which Ben (Samuel Bottomley) chooses the exact moment that his girlfriend, Lil (Lara Ricote), is about to walk across the stage at graduation to tell her that he will move down to London with her after all (men, amirite?). Don’t let the soundtrack fool you, either; you may be singing along to Baby, Now That I’ve Found You by the Foundations and Sylvester’s disco bop You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real), but it will be out of habit rather than unbridled joy.It is not unrelentingly bleak, but Break Clause captures post-university malaise in a way that is almost uncomfortably true-to-life. While Lil has a job lined up with an architectural practice, Ben is an unemployed writer, and resorts to skip diving to save on groceries. He won’t do a medical trial for money – it’s “morally dodgy”, he says – although he quickly changes his mind when he finds out that it’s £800 for each study. Much like the real world – where, post-graduation, friends’ circumstances can change seemingly magically and without warning and the word “broke” can lose all meaning – there is also a class element at play. Ben resents Lil – who, like Ricote, is Mexican-American – for coasting down to the capital with her “big fucking bank account”, while he has spent all summer working in an ice-cream van to be able to make the move. It’s a little heavy-handed at times, a little too north/south divide (Ben is a northerner, who grew up in Leeds and went to university there), but it makes its point on privilege. Not least when Ben admits to their Thanksgiving dinner guests that the turkey they are eating was sourced from a bin.View image in fullscreenDeadpan weirdness … Liam (Jack SheP), Ben (Samuel Bottomley) and Lil (Lara Ricote) in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4 / Kerry SpicerLuckily, it is also very funny, with a weird bent that updates the sadcom premise for our current golden age of deadpan weirdness (think: Saturday Night Live UK). Speaking of SNL, there is much crossover here: Jack Shep plays Lil and Ben’s apparently guileless mate Liam (part of a winning crew that also includes Assa Kanouté and Tamika Bennett), while Hammed Animashaun plays a terrible estate agent who doesn’t even own a pen that works. Nathan Foad – one of the writers of SNL – was also in the writers room here and plays Lil’s boss, Owen, who is desperate to ingratiate himself with his team. Really, though, the best and weirdest (meant, of course, lovingly) thing here is Ricote, whose quirky comic chops make her the perfect candidate for scenes such as the one in which Lil gyrates against a wall while asking her date: “Do you like this?” (“I’d actually quite like it to stop,” he says). Her lines are among the best, in writing and delivery: “You were always so fucking negative about London,” she reminds Ben, mid-fight. “What if the water tasted weird? What if it was too loud? What aboutterrorism?!”Saturday Night Live UK review – it didn’t fail and it could have been a lot worseRead moreIt’s not a romcom, but it does end with something of a romcom scenario: Lil is offered a transfer abroad, and the pair have to figure out whether to enact their break clause (the clue was in the title, I suppose). The final episode pulls its punches a little when it comes to this dilemma, and the pair’s “quarter-psychic” stirrer neighbour, Frances (Charly Clive), who clearly has the hots for Ben. Still, things have been left open for series two, and I sincerely hope it gets made. “You have to be a lot of different people when you’re in a long relationship,” Ben’s dad, Alan (John Thomson), tells him, and it feels as though there are more versions of these two – maybe even some happier ones! Please! – that we are yet to meet.Break Clause is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Conrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63 | Metal | The Guardian
description: Singer and bassist helped turn Newcastle band into hugely influential force on thrash and black metal subgenres
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Singer and bassist helped turn Newcastle band into hugely influential force on thrash and black metal subgenres
Content: Conrad Lant, aka Cronos, of Venom performing at the Sweden Rock festival in June.Photograph: Anne-Marie Forker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConrad Lant, aka Cronos, of Venom performing at the Sweden Rock festival in June.Photograph: Anne-Marie Forker/Getty ImagesMetalConrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63Singer and bassist helped turn Newcastle band into hugely influential force on thrash and black metal subgenresBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 1 Oct 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConrad Lant, the British heavy metal musician who fronted Venom and ensured the Newcastle band became a huge influence on the genre, has died aged 63.“For more than four decades, Conrad’s voice, bass and vision were at the heart of Venom,” reads a statement from the band. “He created something that changed heavy music for ever. Venom never followed the rules. They forged their own path. And Conrad was there at the centre of it all – uncompromising, fearless and unmistakable.” No cause of death was given.Using the stage name Cronos, with an eerie pallor and dressed in showboating leather ensembles as he made theatrical declarations about witches, Satan and the underworld, Lant brought great showmanship to the group, for whom he also played bass.While they never reached the commercial heights of forebears such as Black Sabbath or the thrash bands that followed – they reached the UK Top 75 only once – Venom had a big impact, and their album Black Metal ended up giving a name to one of metal’s most important subgenres.Lant was born in Chelsea, London but moved with his family to Newcastle aged seven. His brothers were also musicians, one a drummer who joined Prefab Sprout (“they were shite,” Lant would later opine), and another who drummed for Venom in the band’s 21st-century period.Venom began as Guillotine, which Lant joined aged 16, initially on guitar, then bass and graduating to vocalist after a previous frontman left. Renamed Venom, the lineup solidified around Lant, guitarist Jeff Dunn (AKA Mantas) and drummer Tony Bray (AKA Abaddon), and they released their debut album Welcome to Hell in 1981. It featured the controversy-baiting single In League with Satan, which featured reversed speech about the devil and helped bring satanic imagery into metal.Inspired by punk, Venom intensified the heaviness of early British heavy metal bands by playing at a furious pace. The Sabbath frontman Ozzy Osbourne “was singing about the devil”, Lant said. “I wanted tobethe devil.”He told the Guardian in 2019: “I had that snot and piss and shit element, which I wanted to put back into metal. I saw more and more bands shoving socks down their pants and putting lipstick on, and I just was disgusted by that, to tell you the truth. Fucking hell, if heavy metal was anything it had to be raw and dangerous and in your face.”View image in fullscreenVenom pictured in 1984.Photograph: Fin Costello/RedfernsThat impulse came to bear on five more albums during the 1980s, including Black Metal, whose demonic cover art and raw, hellish sound “carved in stone some of the essential features” of the black metal genre, according to scene historians Michael J Moynihan and Didrik Søderlind in their book Lords of Chaos. Lant, who co-produced the album, said the making of it was “pure mayhem from start to finish”, with instrumentation including steel plates being cut into with a chainsaw, and a makeshift coffin having earth dumped on to it.Venom went on hiatus in 1988 and Lant – after pondering a career change in forestry – went solo as Cronos, putting out two early 1990s albums. Venom then reformed for another seven LPs, the most recent being 2018’s Storm the Gates. There was another, shorter hiatus in the early 2000s while Lant recovered from a climbing injury.He trained as a fitness instructor in the 1990s (“I did loads of classes, I played rave,” he later said) and also began parallel careers in computer engineering and graphic design, though Venom continued to tour, including at festivals in summer 2026.Venom’s pace, ferocity and darkness all proved seductive to a new generation of metalheads in the 1980s, particularly thrash bands such as Metallica, Slayer and Anthrax. “It was so, so evil. This was a new kind of insanity,” Scott Ian of Anthrax said admiringly of Welcome to Hell.Lant collaborated with another admirer, Dave Grohl, for Grohl’s metal supergroup Probot in 2004.Lant’s son Nathan thanked Venom’s fans after his father’s death. “I know he really appreciated you all. He has laid down his soul, and his music will live on. The legend of Cronos will never die.”Explore more on these topicsMetalPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: The Mercy Step by Marcia Hutchinson audiobook review – a Caribbean child’s-eye view of 60s Bradford  | Books | The Guardian
description: The author captures the comedy and cruelty in this tenderly written coming-of-age tale
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author captures the comedy and cruelty in this tenderly written coming-of-age tale
Content: Marcia Hutchinson.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverView image in fullscreenMarcia Hutchinson.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewThe Mercy Step by Marcia Hutchinson audiobook review – a Caribbean child’s-eye view of 60s BradfordThe author captures the comedy and cruelty in this tenderly written coming-of-age taleFiona SturgesThu 1 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis Women’s prize-nominated novel from Marcia Hutchinson is told from the perspective of Mercy Hanson, a girl born in Bradford in 1962 to a mother she adores and a father she fears. We follow Mercy, their spirited fifth child, from birth through her toddler years to primary education. There she discovers books for the first time, in which she finds delicious escape.In her first week at school, she flees the classroom and runs all the way home after a teacher inadvertently kicks her in the forehead and then denies it. This prompts her God-fearing mother to march to school and into the classroom where she threatens the teacher with hellfire if she touches her daughter again. But Mercy’s mother is unable to protect herself or her children from her short-tempered husband who is “very tall, a proper giant” and smokes Capstan Full Strength cigarettes. Mercy’s father slaps her in her crib when she cries, and viciously beats her mother.The narrator is Hutchinson, whose reading draws out the comic and the unhappy elements of Mercy’s story and who moves seamlessly between her young protagonist’s Yorkshire tones and her mother’s Jamaican Patois. Tenderly written, with moments of sweetness and levity, the novel is named after the stair on which Mercy sits at home, clutching her beloved toy Dolly and surveying the goings on in the household. Her child’s-eye view of the world is effective here not only in showing us the preoccupations that shape childhood but in revealing the cost of the cruelty inflicted by adults.Available via Recorded Books, 9hr 3minFurther listeningFamesickLena Dunham,4th Estate, 11hr46minThe creator of the hit millennial TV series Girls narrates her memoir in which she reflects on her career, controversies, relationships and addictions along with multiple health challenges which include OCD, early menopause and endometriosis.Son of NobodyYann Martel, Canongate, 7hr 32minAaron Willis and Robin Wilcock are the narrators of this novel by the Life of Pi author. It tells of a Canadian classicist who stumbles across a lost epic poem about the Trojan war which is told from the perspective of a common soldier.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Beth Taylor: The Deeps Have Music album review – seamless legato and a gift for storytelling | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Scottish mezzo-soprano makes this programme of sea-themed songs gleam and shimmer. Her account of Elgar’s Sea Pictures holds its own against classic accounts by Janet Baker and Sarah Connolly.
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The Scottish mezzo-soprano makes this programme of sea-themed songs gleam and shimmer. Her account of Elgar’s Sea Pictures holds its own against classic accounts by Janet Baker and Sarah Connolly.
Content: Considered contemplation … Beth Taylor.Photograph: Courtesy of Olivia CostaView image in fullscreenConsidered contemplation … Beth Taylor.Photograph: Courtesy of Olivia CostaClassical musicReviewBeth Taylor: The Deeps Have Music album review – seamless legato and a gift for storytellingTaylor/Brown(Linn)TheScottish mezzo-soprano makes this programme of sea-themed songs gleam and shimmer. Her account of Elgar’s Sea Pictures holds its own against classic accounts by Janet Baker and Sarah ConnollyClive PagetThu 1 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScottish mezzo-soprano Beth Taylor was a standout in the finals of the 2023 BBC Cardiff Singer of the World and has since become something of a go-to in Handel. Her debut solo album, smartly curated with pianist Hamish Brown, brings together a satisfyingly salty programme of art song, culminating in an intrepid account of Elgar’s Sea Pictures.View image in fullscreenBeth Taylor and Hamish Brown: The Deeps Have Music.Photograph: Courtesy of Helena MarionTaylor’s is an instantly identifiable instrument. At its ruby-red bottom she has the breadth of a true contralto, yet there’s an upper extension that brands her a mezzo. Her seamless legato, cushioned lower register and gift for storytelling come into their own in Schubert songs like Meeres Stille and in the spellbinding opener, Hamilton Harty’s arrangement of My Lagan Love. Her gleaming top is shown off in delicate musical aquarelles by Hedwige Chrétien. Brown is a resourceful partner throughout, bringing imaginative depths to even the briefest of songs.Chrétien, a professor at the Paris Conservatoire but barely remembered today, isn’t the only rarity here. Taylor makes an excellent case for Ethel Smyth’s reflective Three Moods of the Sea and Harty’s melancholy Sea Wrack. Cameron Biles-Liddell’s luminous The Breakers, written for Taylor herself, is another find.The Elgar, with piano accompaniments embellished by Brown, is full of telling details and sung with demonstrable passion. Listen to the lilt she brings to In Haven, or the tempestuous way she attacks The Swimmer. These considered interpretations hold their own against classic accounts by Janet Baker and Sarah Connolly.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Meshell Ndegeocello: Synonym review – vivid all-star reinventions of everyone from Bob Dylan to J-Lo | Music | The Guardian
description: In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyond
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyond
Content: Restlessly inventive … Meshell Ndegeocello.Photograph: Charlie GrossView image in fullscreenRestlessly inventive … Meshell Ndegeocello.Photograph: Charlie GrossAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewMeshell Ndegeocello: Synonym review – vivid all-star reinventions of everyone from Bob Dylan to J-Lo(Blue Note)In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyondAlexis PetridisThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s fair to say that Meshell Ndegeocello has made a career out of declining to stay in one place too long. Since helping spark the neo soul genre with her 1993 debut album, Plantation Lullabies, she has variously worked in the fields of jazz, R&B, alternative rock, reggae, fusion and gospel. Her last album, No More Water: The Gospel of James Baldwin, seemed intent on defying any kind of classification, leaping from Afrobeat funk to electronic abstraction to a closing track that sounded not unlike the xx: it won a Grammy for best alternative jazz album, which slightly smacked of the awards’ organisers throwing up their hands in defeat after a lengthy and fruitless attempt to decide in which category it might belong.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Synonym.Even if you knew absolutely nothing about Ndegeocello’s eclectic musical history, you could get a sense of her restlessness just from looking at the back cover of Synonym, a collection of cover versions rendered as duets. The source material picks from the oeuvres of Bob Dylan, Jennifer Lopez, the Human League, Barbra Streisand and Chris Cornell’s short-lived grunge supergroup Temple of the Dog, among others. Her collaborators range from Bill Callahan and Cat Power to Chaka Khan andCynthia Erivo, by way of jazz pianist Robert Glasper.There is a certain unifying thread in Ndegeocello’s desire to make Synonym “an expression of queer liberation as a synonym for liberation of all kinds”. A lot of the tracks were formerly male-female duets, but are sung here by two women, occasionally altering their meaning in the process: the chorus of Streisand’s Guilty is transformed into an anthem of defiance when performed by Ndegeocello and Ink (a singer-songwriter best known as co-author of Beyonce’s Texas Hold ’Em). Even that unifying thread, though, occasionally snaps, as if Ndegeocello were too restive to stick with an overarching concept.It doesn’t fit her and Callahan’s closing version of Dylan’s With God on Our Side, which sets the oldBob Dylanbroadside against a backing that initially carries a trace of the song’s acoustic roots – accompanied by mandolin and piano, Callaghan and Ndegeocello’s harmonies are slightly out of step, as if they’re belting it out live in a folk club – but gradually becomes consumed by hissing electronic noise and distorted guitar. Ndegeocello has suggested the idea was to match the sound to the aggression of the lyrics; the end result feels more like a protest song struggling to be heard amid the noise of modern life. It’s potent either way.Certainly, Ndegeocello is far too restive an artist to leave a song much as you remember it. Her selections are the work of someone with great taste: Be Real Black for Me is far from the best-known of Flack and Hathaway’s duets, but its blend of politics and sexual charge is extraordinary. Yet Synonym deals not so much in cover versions as reinventions, and frequently stunning ones at that.Her version of Don’t You Want Me withCat Powerrecasts the song as reggae, an idea that sounds a lot better coming out of the speakers than it looks on paper, and there’s a mood-shifting alteration in the vocal delivery that goes far beyond the obvious gender-swap. Ndegeocello sings Phil Oakey’s lines with a slightly halting phrasing; they suddenly sound fragile and vulnerable rather than how-dare-you? huffy. And Cat Power delivers Susan Ann Sulley’s as if she couldn’t, and indeed never did, care less: she sounds as if she’s singing “the five years we have had have been such good times, I still love you” over her shoulder while bolting for the door.Meshell Ndegeocello: ‘Making music is the rare moment that I feel raceless and genderless’Read moreNdegeocello takes such liberties with the melody, tempo and even lyrics ofDylan’s It Ain’t Me Babe that it’s almost unrecognisable (you could argue that has pretty much been Dylan’s approach to his back catalogue for the last thirtysomething years). The result here is not just startling but beautiful, a strange, dream-like mass of electric guitar arpeggios, musical box tones and mandolin.You could read Ndegeocello’s version of Yarborough and Peoples’ old soul weekender classic Don’t Stop the Music as a comment on the devaluing of music in the streaming era: the electronic voice now feels ominous and menacing, less as though you’re being invited to dance the night away than cajoled into consuming more and more, regardless of its quality. It’s a marked contrast to Ndegeocello’s plaintive vocal and acoustic guitar.Sometimes, Synonym’s approach falters. The restructuring of Sonny and Cher’s I Got You Babe is impressively radical:Anohnitakes Cher’s role, while Ndegeocello deploys her lowest register to render Sonny’s part, and the music is restructured as sparse jazz, with deeply un-pop chords performed on brass and woodwind. The end result doesn’t quite hold together emotionally, though: the tumbling, folk-rock fatalism of the original has vanished, but it’s unclear what has replaced it.Equally, the odd experiment not entirely coming off feels a very small price to pay for an album as fascinating as this: proof both of Ndegeocello’s unique, personal approach to what she does, and of pop’s infinite malleability in the right hands. It might celebrate collaboration, but Synonym feels like an entirely singular achievement.This week Alexis listened toHermanos Gutiérrez – Canto AndinoThe Hermanos brothers’ latest Dan Auerbach-produced album is intended to evoke the landscape of the Andes, and whether you’re familiar with South America or not, the guitar shimmer of Canto Andino will certainly transport you somewhere.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPop and rockSoulJazzR&BBob DylanBill Callahanalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

Content: View image in fullscreenWhat we're readingBooksWhat we’re reading: China Miéville, Sebastian Barry, Derek Owusu and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in SeptemberWriters and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsChina Miéville, Sebastian Barry, Derek Owusu, andGuardian readersThu 1 Oct 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina Miéville, authorI was sideswiped by Giada Scodellaro’sRuins, Child. A brilliant, strange book that challenged me in the most exhilarating way, with its fractured language and dream-cinema visions, the sense it bestowed of walking through a corridor full of echoes. Echoes of a less elliptical but no-less political kind haunt Jordy Rosenberg’s astoundingNight Night Fawn. I guess you could call it a family novel? But it’s at least as much about fascism as it is about the family – as well as about unsettling linkages between the two. And for horrors and rage in a nonfiction register, Jonas Marvin’sThe Breaking of the English Working Classis an indispensable – and beautifully written – essay on decades of structural, economic and psychic violence. The feeling it provoked in me brought to mind John Berger’s phrase “undefeated despair”.The Rouse by China Miéville is published by Picador (£35). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Linda, Guardian readerI was totally immersed inWhale Fallby Elizabeth O’Connor, a beautifully written story describing a short time in the life of a young woman and her fishing community on an island off the coast of Wales in the 1930s. The simplicity of this tale is underpinned with intriguing moral issues when two anthropologists visit the island to study the lives and history of the islanders. The book is the most poetic I’ve read in a while.Derek Owusu, authorI’ve enjoyed so many books recently. Two I now claim as favourites of all time. The first isBelovedbyToni Morrison. Incredibly late to the party because I was resistant to reading her again having had such a hard time with Sula. But Beloved, in my opinion, is the perfect novel. The second isPedro Páramoby Juan Rulfo, one of the founding texts of the Latin American tradition of magical realism. It was hard work but so enjoyable, a reminder that challenging can be fun and that it’s possible to tell a story in a variety of ways. Last, I want to mentionThe Bridge of San Luis Reyby Thornton Wilder. I’ve only just finished it, so coherent feelings are still working themselves out, but in the mix I know there is admiration, pleasure, something life affirming and something ineffable sparked by the religious elements of the novel. I’m almost certain it’s going to join the others as one of my favourites. I’m having a great run.The Recovery House by Derek Owusu is published by Merky Books (£16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Fiona, Guardian readerIn the day,Mario Vargas Llosaby Gerald Martin, a giant ship of a book which, at nearly a thousand pages, will probably steer me through the remains of 2026. In the night, when I cannot sleep, I do as I always do around the date of my birthday: a re-read of all of Jean Rhys. With her, I am on the moonlit deck of the ship and we watch the darkness of a deep sea rush by. For sanity,The Practice of Not Thinkingby Ryunosuke Koike: the antidote to botched CBT therapy. For inspiration,For Nowby Eileen Myles, concerning the loss of part of their archive and the struggle to hold on to a rent controlled apartment of 40 years. AndMy Life on the Roadby Gloria Steinem. Of course.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSebastian Barry, authorIf anyone is in a mood to have their psyches calmed and their reading synapses restored, thenThe Last Chronicle of Barsetby Anthony Trollope is the cat’s pyjamas. I was nodding my head recently when Marlon James was saying somewhere that he rated Trollope above Dickens. Not that D is any slouch. I am rereading a book I read for work, and now again just because it’s so excellently done,Army Life in a Black Regiment, by Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Emerson said it was a masterpiece by a writer not known for writing masterpieces(!) The Penguin Classics reissue in the late 1990s also has his correspondence with Emily Dickinson and an account of his one meeting with her, revelatory on many levels. She spoke as she wrote. I was also very admiring of a little book of poems by Kayleigh Jayshree calledMango and Starblush, which Miss Dickinson might have called true poems.The Newer World by Sebastian Barry is published by Faber (£20).
