title: The Long Cloud by Hector MacKenzie review – there’s only so much depth to a himbo | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This wry debut novel about a male model’s inner life, written in lowercase fragments, has tender insights but isn’t as profound as it aims to be
Author: Jack Callil
Headline: This wry debut novel about a male model’s inner life, written in lowercase fragments, has tender insights but isn’t as profound as it aims to be
Content: In Hector Mackenzie’s novel The Long Cloud, the central character Xander is ‘as comically vapid as he is at times poignantly reflective’.Composite: Madeleine Ryan/ScribeView image in fullscreenIn Hector Mackenzie’s novel The Long Cloud, the central character Xander is ‘as comically vapid as he is at times poignantly reflective’.Composite: Madeleine Ryan/ScribeAustralian book reviewsFictionReviewThe Long Cloud by Hector MacKenzie review – there’s only so much depth to a himboThis wry debut novel about a male model’s inner life, written in lowercase fragments, has tender insights but isn’t as profound as it aims to beSupported byAbout this contentJack CallilThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShould you care about a vape-loving, philandering male model who just goes with the flow because that’s life? Yes, says The Long Cloud, the wry debut novel ofNew Zealandartist and photographer Hector MacKenzie. Is it convincing? Well, sort of.Xander, a 30-year-old former jock ageing out of the modelling industry and into an existential crisis, is a tabula rasa of sorts – a way for readers to glimpse reflections of themselves. And in an age dominated by how we’re perceived, what exactly is that “self”, anyway?The first thing that’s immediately striking about MacKenzie’s novel is how it’s written: lowercase fragments of sparse punctuation; a stream of consciousness spewing forth Xander’s inner conflicts, reflections and insecurities, his polished surface belying an inner turmoil. His success is waning as a model working in London, where he lives with his emasculatingly successful actor girlfriend, Tessa. He hasn’t “really felt anything for a long time”. Life is something that happens to him.I Can’t Tell You But I Will by Magda Szubanski review – an insightful, elegant, anti-celebrity memoirRead moreAt Tessa’s insistence, Xander flies home to Hawkes Bay in New Zealand, his first trip back in a decade. He’s apprehensive, though: the place and its past, inhabited by everyone he left for greener pastures, is the one big mirror he doesn’t like looking at. Once home, he feels unmoored. He spends time with his divorced parents: his paranoid, doting mother, and his father and his new girlfriend. The latter live on the family farm – Xander’s totemic “home” (and the “envy of rich people everywhere”) – which he learns will soon be sold. He sees former friends and former lovers, one of whom seems keen to rekindle things.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsAdrift and alienated, Xander begins to splinter: “who the fuck was i? was i a farm boy? or was i a handsome boy? or was i just a washed-up big-dog jock of the year with nothing to my name.” Here, MacKenzie astutely shows how nostalgia becomes a siren’s song, luring us back to the familiar only to dash us upon the rocks. Xander falls into reveries about his past relationships, wondering about what might have been, the person he could have become. He then meets Charlotte, a woman 10 years younger than him, who he thinks may solve his woes.The long cloud of the novel’s title (a nod to the Māori word Aotearoa, meaning long white cloud) feels like a culmination of the lives we leave unlived, both past and future: a spectre that casts shadows over our choices and thus who we are. Via Xander – as comically vapid as he is at times poignantly reflective – we see how the anxieties of adulthood are born from the anxieties of youth; how, as we strive to define ourselves, fleeing what shaped us so that we may carve out something new, we can wake suddenly, years later, feeling estranged. We become newborns again, distressed at having lost what’s familiar. As Xander laments, “how dare the world force us to decide what we’ll do as adults when we are only children.”For these tender insights, The Long Cloud is an enjoyable novel, but it isn’t a great one. There’s only so much depth to a himbo. Which is fine! Beautiful, simple men have beautiful, simple thoughts. But when you’re stuck at the party with one, you can eventually get bored. There is a sense, too, that the novel is missing its ending: it’s only just as the edges of Xander’s world properly begin to fray that we leave him, leaving things feeling a bit prematurely tied off.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBig Little Truths by Liane Moriarty review – Big Little Lies sequel shoots for high drama but fails to deliverRead moreBut what MacKenzie renders well is the fading of youth, the throes of nostalgia, the disorientation of displacement – and all in the prose of a friend’s late-night Facebook message. There may have been a version of this book that, while staying true to Xander and his internal tensions, tookitto the profound, but it doesn’t quite get there.Xander is indeed like one big mirror. In all the ill-considered decision-making that wreaks the very devastation he laments, amid all the stumbling and posturing and multiple redrafts of a 10-word flirty SMS, there are many glimpses of our own flawed, unsure selves. When Xander is at one point beaten up, his face finally looking how he feels inside, he finds relief. So too is there some comfort in recognising the “collage of mild anxiety” that Mackenzie’s debut pieces together.The Long Cloud by Hector MacKenzie is out now (via Scribe in the UK and Australia)Explore more on these topicsFictionAustralian book reviewsNew ZealandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong | Europe | The Guardian
description: In a new book, German artist and writer Philipp Ruch argues that viewing the ascent of Hitler’s NSDAP through the prism of the Third Reich has distorted our understanding of fascism’s electoral breakthrough
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: In a new book, German artist and writer Philipp Ruch argues that viewing the ascent of Hitler’s NSDAP through the prism of the Third Reich has distorted our understanding of fascism’s electoral breakthrough
Content: ‘I had grown up seeing Hitler as a monster’ … Adolf Hitler near Garmisch, Bavaria, Germany, 1936.Photograph: Print Collector/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I had grown up seeing Hitler as a monster’ … Adolf Hitler near Garmisch, Bavaria, Germany, 1936.Photograph: Print Collector/Getty ImagesEuropeInterview‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrongPhilip OltermannIn a new book, German artist and writer Philipp Ruch argues that viewing the ascent of Hitler’s NSDAP through the prism of the Third Reich has distorted our understanding of fascism’s electoral breakthroughThu 1 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith your art collective Centre for Political Beauty youfamouslybuilt areplica of theHolocaustmemorial on a property next to the home of an AfD politician. Now you’ve written a history book about the Nazis’ rise to power. Don’t we already know everything there is to know about the 1932 elections, the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act of 1933?About three years ago I became interested in how Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ party (NSDAP) rose to prominence whenGermanywas still a democracy, because I hoped it could tell us something about the success of rightwing extremist movements today. From looking at historical sources, I realised that the Reichstag elections of 14 September 1930 were in many ways more important than what happened in 1932 and 1933. And I expected it to be an open-and-shut case. But the more I looked into it, the more I realised that most of the theories we have to explain the rise of the Nazis don’t make sense – the data tells a completely different, far darker story.View image in fullscreenTelling a darker story … Philipp Ruch.Photograph: Zuma Press/AlamyWhy were the 1930 elections so important?The numbers behind the vote were astonishing. In 1928, the NSDAP got 800,000 votes and 12 seats in the Reichstag. A few weeks before the 1930 election, Hitler’s propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels, history’s grand master of exaggeration, still thought they had a chance of going up to 50 to 60 seats at best. Yet on the night, the Nazis got 6.4 million votes and 107 seats. That’s a ninefold increase over the space of two years. In one night, a small splinter party from the political fringes overtook the three established parties of the right – the Centre Party, the DVP and the DNVP – coming in second place behind the Social Democrats. It was an enormous shock. It was the moment at which a racist sect of loudmouths and club-wielders, a party of absolute cranks, came to be politically legitimised.View image in fullscreenOut in front … Otto Wels, chair of the Social Democrats, in 1930.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyYou call the NSDAP a “party of cranks”. Didn’t Hitler have a certain dark charisma?Among German historians, this has long been the dominant theory to explain the Nazi party’s success: that Hitler had an irresistible inner aura that captured the masses. There’s a second theory that is very similar, theführerkultidea. It argues that the NSDAP was so irresistible because it had a leader that spoke to Germans’ yearning for authoritarianism. The problem is: I couldn’t find any evidence before the 1930 vote to support those theories. Because in 1930, every party was practising a star cult around their own political leader, even the Social Democrats. The Nazi party didn’t have a USP in that respect. And the Nazis didn’t even seem to be wholly on board with theführerprinciple themselves at this stage. Several people in the party complained about the “Byzantine” star cult around Hitler, which is also why the campaign wasn’t really tailored around him as a personality. Let’s remember that in 1930 Hitler wasn’t even on the ballot, because he wasn’t a German citizen: he was a foreigner who had a criminal record for trying to mount a coup and was at risk of being deported.I had grown up seeing Hitler as a monster, but one with a certain political talent. And after 1930, that’s not entirely untrue. But when you focus on 1928 to 1930, even his biographer Ian Kershaw concludes that the NSDAP’s success had very little to do with Hitler. He was going through an absolute dip in form. He only held 29 speeches in 1929, half of what was customary, and 21 of them were all in Bavaria. In 1930 Goebbels spent half the year complaining about Hitler’s prevaricating: when he travelled to Munich to track down the NSDAP leader, he didn’t even bother looking at the party headquarters. “The Reich leadership is at [Hitler’s favourite coffeehouse] Café Heck or the cinema,” Goebbels wrote sarcastically. In 1930, Hitler wasn’t a political genius. He was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon.View image in fullscreenAdolf Hitler speaks at the Nuremberg rally, 1938.Photograph: Sueddeutsche Zeitung Photo/AlamyIf not Hitler, was propaganda chief Goebbels thekeyfigure behind the rise of the Nazis? One explanation being revisited these days is that political crises tend to go hand-in-hand with media crises: that the Nazis pounced expertly on new forms of media like illustrated news, radio and film.When we talk about the Nazis, everyone has these images in their head that point to this slick propaganda machine: the Nuremberg rally, the cathedral of light, all these awe-inspiring spectacles. And it’s true that pre-1930 Goebbels invested a lot of effort into building up propaganda newspapers inspired by American formats, such as Der Angriff, Völkischer Beobachter and Illustrierter Beobachter. But early Nazi propaganda was an embarrassing, amateurish joke. I’ve looked through every edition of Illustrierter Beobachter, and the images they presented to the reader were laughable, such as SA men dressed as advertising pillars. It just wasn’t professional. The sales figures were pathetic: nobody was reading these newspapers. Compare it to the means that the other parties had at their disposal: they put up neon signs on street corners and hired planes for aerial advertising. Propaganda just doesn’t explain the NSDAP’s success.View image in fullscreenEmbarrassing … A human advertising pillar, pictured in Nazi party newspaper Illustrierter Beobachter on 17 November 1928.Photograph: Philipp RuchWhat about the economy? Thestock marketon Wall Street hadcrashed a year beforehand, German exports were collapsing and unemployment was on the rise.It’s always tempting to fall back on economic factors when explaining the rise of fascist movements. We are hearing it again in Germany now: the economy is crumbling, the trains aren’t running on time, so people are going to fall for the fascists again. But if I look at historical sources from the run-up to 1930, I come away thinking that voters weren’t that stupid. Take the unemployed. Over the last 30 years, historians have established a pretty good picture of who voted for the NSDAP. And we can say with certainty that in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience. And as to the idea that the Nazis managed to attract young first-time voters, the same applies: the NSDAP also performed badly in areas with high rates of first-time voters. The young were also running away from this party.The global economic crisis may explain why the NSDAP managed to double its support in 1932 and attain 37.3% of the vote. But as an explanation for the ninefold boost in 1930, it falls short. Wall Street’s Black Thursday didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931, when several major banks collapsed – 10 months after the Nazis got 107 seats in the Reichstag. The Weimar Republic’s GDP went into a tailspin, with a 36.6% collapse, only over the course of the two years that followed – by the end of 1930, it had merely shrunk by 7.1%, and we don’t know how much of that was as a result of the election outcome. There’s a risk here of confusing cause and effect.What if we look at the democratic parties instead?One of the central tenets of the Nazi party’s campaign was the alleged corruption of the established parties, but there is very little evidence that this was actually the case. The most striking – and also the most puzzling – thing I learned was that all of the three big rightwing parties of the Weimar Republic had put political hardliners in charge between 1928 and 1929. If voters had really been desperate for tough rightwing policies, they could have voted for the Catholic Centre party, the nationalist liberal DVP or the monarchist DNVP – all parties in a pole position to turn their promises into practice.Didn’t they just experience what many conservative parties are finding out now: that when they copy the positions of thefar right, voters tend to prefer the original?I think that’s a platitude that simply isn’t true. Because in 1930 Hitler wasn’t the original, he was a washed-out copy of what was offered by the DVP or the DNVP. The DNVP ran a more antisemitic campaign than Hitler, and yet it was the biggest loser of the election, shedding 7.3% of the vote. What strikes me as much more important is credibility. In 1930, the nationalist-liberal DVP was attacked by its own party newspapers for betraying the legacy of its former leader Gustav Stresemann, who had died a year earlier. It’s not unlike the situation we now have with Germany’s Christian Democrats: a party that under Merkel was absolutely centrist and managed to retain loyal voters but then picked a figure from its right wing as their new leader in Friedrich Merz. And voters are switching to the AfD. The central lesson to me is that conservative parties can only win from the centre.You say credibility iskey. Then why do corruption scandals barely seem to hurt the modernfar-rightparties railing loudest against ‘the system’?It’s true that the NSDAP in 1930 was absolutely riddled with scandals: back-stabbing, power struggles, corruption, the whole spectrum. And many German journalists at the time believed they were just one more scandal away from complete collapse. There were some excellent and brave journalists leading some really good investigations. But it didn’t work.I look at far-right parties acrossEuropenow, and I see undercover reporters revealing the AfD’s remigration plans, leading to the biggest protests in postwar German history. And these kinds of investigations are extremely important. But fascist or rightwing extremist parties seem to be immune to this kind of stuff. They are like lightning rods: the scandal is a flash of energy that passes straight through them into the ground and then it’s gone. A corruption scandal might temporarily damage a party, like the “Ibiza affair” did to the Austrian Freedom party, but five years later they are back at double their strength.So whydidthe Nazis perform so strongly in 1930?As paradoxical as it sounds, it might be for the same reason that voters turned away from the Nazis in 1928: its propensity to violence. Ever since Hitler had been in the NSDAP, he had talked about one thing: executing his political opponents. And the Nazi party remained absolutely consistent in that respect. In the run-up to the 1930 vote, it didn’t talk about social policy, it didn’t talk about building the autobahn. It just had murder plots.View image in fullscreenBook cover: Philipp Ruch, Der Ruckfall.Photograph: HeyneHow does that help us understand the rise of fascist orrightwingextremist movements today?It’s hard to admit this from a modern perspective, but historical fascism’s lust for violence didn’t make it repulsive but extremely attractive to a lot of German voters. And we are seeing similar things with the AfD today, where fantasies of violent retribution seem to be integral to campaign events on market squares. We are witnessing the poisoning of an entire society, and as a democracy we should ask ourselves whether criminal law shouldn’t apply when political parties communicate that way. Communication is one thing, political plans are another. The NSDAP had both. But we know that the AfD is a radical party that seems to want to ethnically cleanse Germany. If the AfD is voted into power, one of the most highly advanced economies in the world could experience something similar to what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina.Philipp Ruch’s Der Rückfall (The Relapse) is published by PenguinExplore more on these topicsEuropeHistory booksGermanyAdolf HitlerNazismThe far rightSocial historyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dodge City by Patrick deWitt review – a wild draft-dodging road trip | Patrick deWitt | The Guardian
description: This tale of a 60s college dropout driving across the US to avoid being sent to Vietnam is committed to both readerly pleasure and literary artifice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This tale of a 60s college dropout driving across the US to avoid being sent to Vietnam is committed to both readerly pleasure and literary artifice
Content: Patrick deWitt.Photograph: Ray BidegainView image in fullscreenPatrick deWitt.Photograph: Ray BidegainBook of the dayPatrick deWittReviewDodge City by Patrick deWitt review – a wild draft-dodging road tripThis tale of a 60s college dropout driving across the US to avoid being sent to Vietnam is committed to both readerly pleasure and literary artificeKeshava GuhaThu 1 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanadian author Patrick deWitt broke through with a western, 2011’s Booker-shortlistedThe Sisters Brothers. Now, he has taken on another hallowed American genre: the road novel. Recent works by Miranda July and Ben Markovits have, in very different ways, used the idea of the road trip as a way to dramatise midlife crisis. As befits a writer who is, in so many ways, a throwback, Dodge City returns the genre to its roots: the 1960s, and youth as opposed to middle age. A short précis – a cross-country journey undertaken by a UCLA drop-out armed only with a bag of amphetamines – makes the book sound like an Easy Rider tribute. It is typical for deWitt novels to be compared to films rather than other books. But in this case, something very different transpires.The novel opens with our protagonist, Leland “Lee” Clarke, receiving his draft notice – he is to be sent to Vietnam. He has just been expelled from UCLA for assaulting a fellow student, a rich hippy who condescends to him. This “event of violence” (a “one-punch wonder”, as Lee’s father calls it) costs him his draft deferment. Lee doesn’t consider himself a conscientious objector – that is only another form of heroism, and “the myth of the hero is at the heart of my critique of the entire exercise”. But nor does he want to go to Vietnam. He decides, instead, to dodge – to head to Canada. Younger readers may note with envy that being kicked out of college mattered a lot less when you weren’t tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt.He has, in any case, been thinking of ending things with Cal, short for Calliope, the beautiful blond daughter of east coast intellectuals. Lee is the unglamorous product of a broken home in Concrete, Washington. Cal finds him exotic: “a patrician redneck”, meaning someone who irons his T-shirts. Over time, their class differences have begun to grate. The hippy he punches is a friend of Cal’s.To raise money for the journey, he sells his own car and signs up to a “drive-away” service, delivering a brand-new Jaguar E-Type to its owner. Since he may be saying goodbye to his country for good, he plots an L-shaped route from Los Angeles to New Jersey that will allow him to say individual farewells to his father in Concrete, his mother in Montana, and his sister, a trainee nurse, in Manhattan. His brother Harry, in Minnesota, he plans to avoid. There is ancient history there.DeWitt is a throwback because he has never been near a master of fine arts programme (he dropped out of high school) and because he writes what is unquestionably “literary fiction” for a large audience, and makes a living from doing so. To Chad Harbach’s dilemma for the young North American writer, “MFA v NYC”, deWitt’s triumphant answer is “neither”. You see this in his simultaneous commitment to readerly pleasure and literary artifice; and above all in his prose.double quotation markThe reader can expect vivid minor characters, hijinks, and a tone on the margin between silliness and miseryWith his puns, archaisms, tics (“certain of the” for “some”), fondness for the passive voice and tendency to use two or three words more than strictly needed, deWitt violates almost every current MFA norm. Like one of his favourite writers, Ivy Compton-Burnett, he is a master of arch dialogue: more eloquent, and usually more enjoyable, than the naturalistic kind. DeWitt’s idiosyncrasies are not always euphonious – he can take his preference for Latin over Anglo-Saxon verbs to irritating lengths – but they remind us of the difference between having style and havingastyle.Where deWitt is most contemporary is in his preoccupation with the past. Almost all his novels have historical settings, and his protagonists are stalked by old traumas. This is why Dodge City is no Easy Rider. If the essence of hippiedom is living in the present, and the special privilege of youth is ownership of the future, Lee Clarke’s business is with his past. The visits to his parents and siblings – in the end, he finds that he can’t avoid Harry – are not token goodbyes, but attempts to settle emotional accounts.The journey itself is less one of self-discovery than of the reader discovering Lee, who is from the Hans Castorp school of hero. “Perfectly ordinary, if engaging” is how Thomas Mann described Hans. The reader sees Lee’s ordinariness right away, and over the course of the book grows more and more engaged. This is a deWitt novel, of course, and so the reader can expect – and is supplied with – vivid minor characters, hijinks, and a tone that lives confidently on the margin between silliness and misery.Patrick deWitt: ‘Poetry is good in moments of crisis’Read moreOver the course of his career, however, deWitt has changed. His books have become more contemplative, less rambunctious; if he has always trafficked in real feelings in slightly unreal settings, the settings are growing realer, and the feelings softer. Dodge City is not exactly optimistic, but its emotional tendency is towards something few would have expected of the author of The Sisters Brothers: tenderness.Dodge City by Patrick deWitt is published by HarperCollins (£18.99). title: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring | Games | The Guardian
description: E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Content: Big shoulder-pads and motor-powered blades are en vogue once again … Marcus in Gears of War E-Day.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosView image in fullscreenBig shoulder-pads and motor-powered blades are en vogue once again … Marcus in Gears of War E-Day.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosGamesReviewGears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boringXbox, PC (version tested); The Coalition/Xbox Game StudiosE-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointingKirk McKeandThu 1 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery Gears of War game released in the last 20 years has made reverent reference to Emergence Day, when alien creatures emerged from the earth, single-minded in their savagery. In E-Day, you’re there to witness it: the police lights, flipped cars, ground tremors, civilians running, aliens pouring out of fissures in the earth and ripping faces off. You’re at ground zero in a squad of four soldiers called Gears – Marcus Fenix, the leader; Dom, who wants to retire; Lucas, a green cadet with a buzzcut; and the dishonourably discharged Mags. Only this dysfunctional quartet can turn the tide. With guns. Lots of ’em.Instead of answering questions raised by the ending of2019’s Gears 5, we’re back to the start to find out why Marcus has a scar on his lip and why these soldiers started strapping chainsaws on to their assault rifles. Anything that was left to the imagination is here, for you to point at and say: “I understood that reference. This is a thing that I have seen.”This series has lost its way a bit over the years, but the opening hours of E-Day will have you believing that big shoulder pads and ripping into gollum-esque freaks with motor-powered blades are en vogue once again. There are flashes of the horror and grimness of the first couple of Gears games as you’re funnelled between urban fighting arenas, with bountiful flanking routes and chunks of fallen buildings to take cover behind. But then it keeps going. And going. Long after you realise it’s all out of ideas, it’s still going.Because it’s set during and immediately after E-Day, the squad is stuck. You spend most of your time running back and forth across the city in various states of destruction. You cross the same section of bridge three times before the credits roll. Levels are flipped, daytime turns to night and you run through them again. E-Day’s two attempts at switching things up involve putting you on the gunner seat of a helicopter or making you walk slowly while people talk to you. The setting is a ball and chain that the developers are tethered to.E-Day is at its best when it turns off the lights, cranks up the horror, and forces you into enclosed spaces, but these moments make up a tiny portion of the game. The bulk of it is spent in large, open areas stuffed to the gills with collectibles. There are hundreds of them and you get a little audio chime whenever one is close. At one point, there was a particularly poignant cutscene where one of the emotionally stunted characters finally lets it all out and, just as the game transitioned from this emotional beat back to gameplay, the chime drowned out the character’s trauma to tell me there was something to pick up nearby.These open levels are big enough to require a map to navigate and they’re even peppered with side objectives (usually mini horde missions where you hold off waves of enemies after setting up defences). In Gears 5, you at least had a vehicle to zip between points of interest. Here you’re just hoofing it on foot, trying to cover as much of the map as possible without triggering the next cutscene. If you do happen to stray into the main objective by accident and try to backtrack, you’re hit with a big “mission failed” message for stepping out of bounds. You basically die. For exploring. In a game that constantly tells you to explore.View image in fullscreenEmotionally stunted … Gears of War E-Day’s full squad.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosIt’s a shame because if you rip a chainsaw through all the fat and wipe the blood spray from your eyes, there’s good meat on the bones here. Combat-wise, this is the best the series has ever felt. Characters move much less clunkily, heaving into cover, sliding under chunks of rubble, even leaping around with grace that the older Marcus Fenix and his creaky knees could only dream of.Environments crack and splinter as you fight, with glass smashing into shards that litter on the ground. Cars wobble as they take a hit, petrol stations explode and pillars crumble like the Matrix corridor scene. Blood and entrails cover everything when the dust settles after a firefight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCover feels more naturalistic and combat arenas blend nicely into the open sections, blurring the lines between exploration and fighting elegantly. Guns feel hefty and dangerous – especially the shotgun that spits acid. Active reloading, which asks you to time a button press for faster weapon reloads and more powerful bullets, remains a smart bit of game design that keeps you locked in as you fight.There’s a reason Gears of War has survived as a series long enough to earn a prequel. Its specific flavour of bloody, tactical, cover-based combat isn’t done better anywhere else. Unfortunately, E-Day is let down by everything around that fighting, resulting in a safe and repetitive experience that shows you all its ideas in the opening hours and never dares to build on them in any meaningful way.Gears of War: E-Day is out 6 Oct; £59.99Explore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesShooting gamesPCreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? review – Gillian Anderson fights tooth and nail in marital meltdown | Theatre | The Guardian
description: There is no shortage of sparring between Anderson and Billy Crudup in Edward Albee’s classic, though its comedy has an air of George and Mildred
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: There is no shortage of sparring between Anderson and Billy Crudup in Edward Albee’s classic, though its comedy has an air of George and Mildred
Content: Squaring up … Gillian Anderson as Martha in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? at @sohoplace, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenSquaring up … Gillian Anderson as Martha in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? at @sohoplace, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewWho’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? review – Gillian Anderson fights tooth and nail in marital meltdown@sohoplace, LondonThere is no shortage of sparring between Anderson and Billy Crudup in Edward Albee’s classic, though its comedy has an air of George and MildredArifa AkbarThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThose who want to moan about the toxic reliance on celebrity casting and screen stars in the West End can stop right there: Billy Crudup andGillian Andersonboth began their careers on stage. Here they are now, glittering up Edward Albee’s conflagration of a play about unhappy marriage and its necessary illusions, immortalised on screen by Richard Burton and Elizabeth Taylor.Anderson and Crudup can hold their own against that landmark adaptation of the play about George, a middle-aged history professor with a sagging academic libido, and Martha, his frustrated, ceaselessly needling wife. They are confident performers and it makes sense that this 1962 American classic about conjugal warfare is taken on by two Americans, albeit under the aegis of British directorial powerhouse Marianne Elliott. If Elliott’s previous production,Les Liasons Dangereuses at the National Theatre,had what some considered an anaemic connection between its leading lovers, there is no shortage of sparks and sparring for the central couple here. They are shouty and jousting, although it does not feel dangerous or emotionally eviscerating enough between them for rather too long.View image in fullscreenThe chemistry of rivalry … Josh Dylan, Billy Crudup, Phoebe Horn and Gillian Anderson in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?Photograph: Johan PerssonTheir night-long fight at home begins after a faculty party thrown by Martha’s university president father. The pair’s guests are a younger couple – biology academic Nick (Josh Dylan) and his wife, Honey (Phoebe Horn), who first watch Martha and George play their emotional games, then get sucked in.Elliott preserves the play’s original setting, with Miriam Buether’s set an elegant 1960s-era living room complete with the all-important drinks trolley. The couples are drunk but intent on getting drunker, each refill raising the stakes.Anderson makes a formidably angry Martha as she needles away, poking George in every place it hurts. She is all hard edges and armour, agitating for a fight from the off, with a big, dirty laugh and a bawdy flirtation with Nick. Crudup is put-upon, dusty, literally all (in) grey. He initially leads with passive aggression, mansplaining Martha’s behaviour to the room and batting off her barbs with intellectual superiority or sarcasm, before entering into more confrontational territory.It ends in hand-to-hand combat but before that, laughter is eked out of the first act, which emanates a deliberately upbeat lightening of tone. George and Martha have more than a touch of George and Mildred, their game-playing a little cartoonish at times.View image in fullscreenCartoonish at times … Billy Crudup and Gillian Anderson.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe chemistry of rivalry and one-upmanship between the men is at first stronger. In between Nick and George’s Darwinian fight to be the bigger chest-beater, there is banter and a sharing of confidences – which in one of this production’s most brutal moments is used agonisingly against Nick and Honey.Horn and Dylan play their relationship with less comedy and are always compelling, Nick seeming like an overgrown frat-boy, Honey quietly tragic. They make a subtle mirror reflection of George and Martha, both with their own versions of phantom children.The most savage moments between Martha and George keep their queasily comic edges: her groin-thrusting dance with Nick which graduates to boastful “necking” in the hope to get a rise from George and her digs at his academic underachievement, delivered with bent-kneed, pointy-fingered, almost panto-like drunken accusation.Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? is a misunderstood masterpieceRead moreThe play, while exquisitely written and structured, feels tortuously long at over three hours, and though this is the point – to watch how two people destroy each other yet love each other – it still feels like a punishment. Staged in the round, it leaves little room for hiding. There is a revolve, slow for the most part, which shows their marriage up close, from every angle.For all the comedy and nervous laughs, this couple does combust and the end is devastating. Martha stops her high-pitched attack and becomes vulnerable. George lets go of his emotional cruelty. They have finally stopped the power games and play-acting of their marriage. Or have they?At@sohoplace, London, until 19 DecemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreWest EndGillian AndersonEdward AlbeeMarianne ElliottMiriam BuetherreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Balraj Khanna: Lines of Flight review – plenty of dazzle, but where is the darkness? | Art | The Guardian
description: This six-decade survey is a riot of biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacle – but the quieter works pack the biggest punch
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: This six-decade survey is a riot of biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacle – but the quieter works pack the biggest punch
Content: Verdant … A Grasshoppers Eye’s View (1966), oil on canvas, by Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryView image in fullscreenVerdant … A Grasshoppers Eye’s View (1966), oil on canvas, by Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryArtReviewBalraj Khanna: Lines of Flight review – plenty of dazzle, but where is the darkness?Ikon, BirminghamThis six-decade survey is a riot of biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacle – but the quieter works pack the biggest punchBen EasthamThu 1 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe work of Balraj Khanna will be familiar to many residents ofBirmingham, whether they know it or not. Displayed on the safety curtain at the Hippodrome, his monumental painting Astral Dance has prepared countless theatregoers for the evening’s performance since it was completed in 2001. Khanna produced a dreamlike vision of biomorphic forms – pulsing blobs, splayed fingers, blooming whorls – set against variegated orange hues. Its delightful colours and benign shapes conjure a palpable sense of magic and wonder, while also containing little that might disturb the audience’s mind beyond the curtain’s raising.This show is likewise one of flash and spectacle. The introductory text makes a point of the fact that, having been born in Punjab in 1939, Khanna witnessed the 1947 partition of India as a young boy. But if that generational trauma influenced his work as an artist, then it is apparent only in a turning away from horror towards the consolations of fantasy. He moved to London in 1962, just in time for the invention of sex (in Philip Larkin’s account), but the social revolutions of the era are no more obvious. Instead, his practice as an artist (and a picaresque novelist) summons more innocent memories: the astonishments of street entertainment and the glamorous artifice of theatre.View image in fullscreenOtherworldly … Festival (1970), acrylic and sand on canvas, Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryOne tantalising early work hints at darkness behind the dazzle. In a mulch-green landscape, a body struggles to unwrap itself from a winding shroud. Composed during the artist’s rehabilitation from a motorcycle accident, the puzzlingly titled Ladies With Qualification is so direct in its expression of suffering that you wonder whether this otherwise effervescent artist abandoned figuration because he found it too revealing. The surrounding abstractions struggle to match its charge, shoehorning blustery squiggles into strict grids that can impose only the most superficial measure of control. This is an issue that will dog the work.A standout is A Grasshopper’s Eye View, the title of which was suggested by the enduringly great Indian painter FN Souza, an early supporter of Khanna. Colourfully striped, spotted and dotted globules float through a field of verdant colour structured by regular vertical struts and subtle horizontal balances that allow the eye to wander at leisure around the picture without fear of getting lost in the confusion. The title is apt: a grasshopper might not be able to see how the wider world is organised, but can be confident enough in the prevailing rules (of gravity, of the distribution of forces) to jump from one stalk to the next.View image in fullscreenBombastic … Big Bang (2004-07), acrylic and sand on canvas, Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryThis balance is difficult to maintain. Unravelled, which presents a tangle of white lines against a night-blue background, might seem to meet Paul Klee’s maxim that making a drawing is like “taking a line for a walk”. The problem is that this walk should ideally take the artist into strange and unexpected places. Khanna’s line, by comparison, meanders around the canvas, turning back politely when it veers too close to the edges. His line feels a little too well behaved to drag its owner down into the depths of the unconscious, as artists including Klee (a clear influence) hoped it might do.It is nonetheless entertaining to see an artist try on so many styles: an abrupt diversion into hard-edge minimalism; a rhapsody in pink scattered with footprints (perhaps in homage to Jackson Pollock’s Blue Poles); a gloss finish anticipating the vogue for spray paint (it seems Khanna achieved the effect by blowing paint through a straw). But two significant paintings from 1970 show an artist getting a grip on the compositional dynamics – the systems of push and pull – that would govern the fabulous world of his paintings. In Splash and Festival this takes the form of an invisible force pulling forms resembling glistening scales and fading petals into a central vortex. They promise much.View image in fullscreenRemarkable … Sunset in Sinai (1980-81), acrylic on canvas, Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryOn the second floor, Khanna settles into a style. Characterised by forms resembling amoebas, tropical fish and bioluminescent invertebrates floating through candy-coloured galaxies, the style is cosmic in its ambitions and bombastic in scale. The late painting Big Bang is typical: a vaguely celestial landscape in which the attempts of Klee, Miró or Kandinsky to pull archetypal forms out of the primordial soup have been replaced by shapes like children’s toys drifting through a Day-Glo ether. Like magic tricks, these paintings attract your gaze but do not hold it for long. My lingering feeling was that this was no longer a failure: the artist preferred, for reasons of temperament, to excite the eye rather than trouble the mind.Nothing wrong with this, of course: paintings can do all kinds of things. Yet three remarkable works are so at odds with the general bravado that no one seems sure they were finished (the artist died in 2024, and the wall text calls them “almost studies”). Sunset in Sinai is a grainy landscape of depressions and folds that might equally be the surface of Mars or the fabric of spacetime; Dunes, in gorgeous bright pastel tones, is embedded with trails of string (a characteristic technique) that pull the colour off a series of gentle ripples; Ocean is a marvellously delicate interplay of scintillating pinks and greens. These strangely melancholy close studies of the natural world strike me as far more transcendent than the aggressively cosmic scenes by which they are surrounded. Because they are so much less eager to impress, I found myself wanting to spend time with them. They made me wish that Khanna had more often resisted the urge to entertain.Balraj Khanna: Lines of Flightis at Ikon, Birmingham, until 21 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArtPaintingExhibitionsBirminghamreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? review – when John Home outdid Stratford’s Bard | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Brian Logan revisits the 18th-century production of Home’s Douglas in a shouty comedy about nationalism, religion and the power of theatre
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Brian Logan revisits the 18th-century production of Home’s Douglas in a shouty comedy about nationalism, religion and the power of theatre
Content: Promising premise … Fraser Sivewright, Gavin Jon Wright, Kevin Lennon and Lewie Watson in Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? at Òran Mór, Glasgow.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenPromising premise … Fraser Sivewright, Gavin Jon Wright, Kevin Lennon and Lewie Watson in Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? at Òran Mór, Glasgow.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanTheatreReviewWhaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? review – when John Home outdid Stratford’s BardÒran Mór, GlasgowBrian Logan revisits the 18th-century production of Home’s Douglas in a shouty comedy about nationalism, religion and the power of theatreMark FisherThu 1 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the most famous heckle in Scottish theatre history. In an exclamation of nationalist zeal after a performance of Douglas at Edinburgh’s Canongate playhouse in 1756, an audience member declared playwright John Home to be better than England’s most revered dramatist. “Whaur’s yer Wullie Shakespeare noo?” went the cry.Safe to say posterity cares for Shakespeare more than Home, but the performance of Douglas remains a symbolic flashpoint. As presented by Brian Logan, writer, director and Guardian comedy critic, the play – and its excited reception – exemplifies the national and religious schisms that have played out inScotlandever since. It is one of those theatrical events that meant more politically than it did artistically.On the one hand, we find a post-Union Scotland both beholden and resistant to a dominant England. Logan shows an Edinburgh establishment eager for the success of Douglas almost as a matter of principle even before it is put in front of an audience, not least after its brusque rejection byDavid Garrickin London.All at Sea review – faked death of ‘canoe man’ inspires waves of intrigueRead moreOn the other hand, we find a post-John Knox church torn between being “o’er pagan for you, o’er pious for me,” as Home (Lewie Watson) puts it in the play. Under pressure from those who see plays as sinful, regardless of how wholesome their message, Home is forced to resign his ministry in East Lothian.All this makes a promising premise but it is a shouty, one-note production, co-presented by A Play, a Pie and a Pint with Aberdeen Performing Arts and the Traverse. Written in Scots, the play switches from a soft-target send-up of 18th-century acting to a two-dimensional debate about art and morality. The play is on fertile ground, but fails to settle on the characters and conflict that would give the factionalism of the early Scottish Enlightenment due dramatic weight.At Òran Mór, Glasgow, until 3 October, then touring until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreScotlandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s frustrating to see immoral videos do so well’: how YouTube sensation Half-Asleep Chris sent a rollercoaster to space and made Bella the cat a star | Culture | The Guardian
description: His videos of cats, loopy contraptions and theme park rides round the heavens (and his back garden) have notched up a billion views. We meet Chris Burton in the suburban home where it all happens
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: His videos of cats, loopy contraptions and theme park rides round the heavens (and his back garden) have notched up a billion views. We meet Chris Burton in the suburban home where it all happens
Content: ‘Usually, the longer I spend on something, the fewer people watch it’ … Chris with one of his creations and kitten Henry.Photograph: Sarah Lee/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Usually, the longer I spend on something, the fewer people watch it’ … Chris with one of his creations and kitten Henry.Photograph: Sarah Lee/the GuardianCultureInterview‘It’s frustrating to see immoral videos do so well’: how YouTube sensation Half-Asleep Chris sent a rollercoaster to space and made Bella the cat a starCatherine ShoardHis videos of cats, loopy contraptions and theme park rides round the heavens (and his back garden) have notched up a billion views. We meet Chris Burton in the suburban home where it all happensThu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 04.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChris Burton is getting ready to redecorate his house. The first reason for this is quite sad. His beloved cat Bella died recently, aged 17, and the indignities of old age mean a new carpet is in order. The other reason is that Burton, AKA Half-Asleep Chris, is turning his dining room into a re-creation of London’s Rainforest Cafe (also RIP – it closed in 2023). There will be temple walls and a talking tree, a fish tank and fronds. Thunderstorms every 20 minutes.He’s doing most of the work himself, he explains, as we edge past an 8ft fibreglass tapir in the hall. But he’ll need an electrician to rig the starry ceiling and a plumber to check the waterfall for leaks. I sneak a feel of the tapir: firm yet squishy, foam and five layers of silicone over a steel frame. Most people will only see rather than touch it, yet it has exactly the same amount of give as – I imagine – the real deal. This lack of half-measures is very Half-Asleep Chris.It is from this detached house on a suburban estate in London’s commuter belt that Burton, 31, makes the videos that have turned him into an unlikelyYouTubesensation: more than a billion views, five million subscribers, a PO box deluged with drawings and knitted hats, Instagram DMs full of requests to hang out for the day, or take children to Legoland. “It’s like, ‘You’re just giving your child away?’”The videos are mostly about his cats. Or Lego. Or a combination of the two. Or loopier contraptions he finds creatively fulfilling yet usually prove to be of more niche appeal. “It’s very important to me not to be driven by videos that will perform well,” he says. “But usually, the longer I spend on something, the fewer people watch it.”He spent 14 months, off and on, constructing ajungle boat ridethrough his garden that has notched up 9.1m views – five times fewer than avideo in which he plays hide and seek with Bella and fellow cat Ralph, which got 49mviews.(Kitten Henry joined the family last year.) He sent aworking Lego rollercoaster into space, which “took months and had loads of people involved – and it’samazing”. But while that has 2.4m views,Giant Cat Destroys Lego City(basically just Bella inspectingoneof hisglorious model villages) has 21m.Who watches the videos? About 45% of his audience are in the US, another 10% from the UK, with Canada, France and the Philippines following behind. Data protection makes it hard to tell what proportion are children, but he does know his biggest demographic is 25 to 40-year-olds – ie, those most likely to be fairly new parents. His hope is that the videos encourage co-watching.“It’s hard to tell,” he says, “because I think an adult is less inclined to draw a picture of your cat and send it to you. But I want my videos to be family friendly. Nothing rude or obnoxious but not dumbed down.Childrencan learn and infer a lot more than we give them credit for. But a lot of content is patronising, and that’s a great loss. It’s very much about the most popular thing, which is often the most excessive or in-your-face.”View image in fullscreenPerfect fit … Burton’s working Lego rollercoaster in space.Photograph: Half-Asleep ChrisBurton keeps more distance. He is gentle, geeky, self-effacing: an anti-Blippi. Think Tony Hart or Mister Rogers, but young, with cats. His videos are kind and silly, with whimsical theme tunes and unambitious stopmotion graphics. There is charm and the cast-iron certainty that, should you stop co-watching for a bit to see to the peas, your child will be in safe hands.Does he consider himself a role model? “Absolutely. The version of yourself you put in a video is job interview best-behaviour. But it’s very important. A lot of YouTube content that appeals to children is awful and you wouldn’t want your kid to watch it. A lot of the big names are big because they’re outlandish and I don’t think their content has any value whatsoever.” He chucks Henry a ball. “It’s frustrating watching videos that are so immoral do so well.”The calm, articulate version of Burton that he puts forward today seems, in most ways at least, identical to the job interview version. It’s the school holidays and I’ve brought my nine-year-old son Laurie along; Burton answers his questions with patience and respect, before handing him lollipop sticks and a spatula.View image in fullscreenAdventure time … the theme park boat ride in Burton’s garden.Photograph: Half-Asleep ChrisWith these, Laurie has a crack at one of the activities from Burton’s first book, The Unordinary Book of Ideas: Everywhen Projects for Rainy Days. Some of these have been trialled in videos (massive domino run round your house using household items;fiery obstacle course for a remote control car); others (make your own transit map, track your life in strange statistics) not yet. The manual also represents a manifesto against the perils of modern-day childhood. It seeks to stretch attention times. Many activities require a day to complete, others rather longer – in theory, the stone circle one needs 4,000 years.Sometimes phones are used to film things, but otherwise it’s rigorously luddite, a celebration of the homemade that delights in domestic detail. “Things can seem mundane now, but one day they’ll seem remarkable,” says Burton, getting out his collection of unusual paperclips. He’s particularly keen on coins, banknotes and stamps – tactile markers of a country’s self-projection. One activity involves resending vintage used postcards. “Something like a third of kids in the UK have never sent or received a letter,” he says, “and last year theDanish postal system closed downafter 400 years. We should grieve for it.”Burton’s fame may have digital origins, but his allergy to TikTok is pronounced and AI brings him out in hives. “It’s awful and dangerous. It doesn’t teach you anything. So much of a project is the journey. With the Rainforest Cafe, I have a very clear idea in my head of how it’s going to go. But it’s not going to go like that. It’s going to go wrong. I’m going to have to learn loads of random skills I didn’t anticipate. But AI is just A to B.”View image in fullscreenFiery … an obstacle course built by Burton.Photograph: Half-Asleep ChrisYes, there’s a data-entry benefit, he concedes, but “AI shouldn’t be anywhere near creativity or art”. On Ralph’s last birthday, among the sketches and paintings sent in were a couple of AI-generated cards. “That’s so sad,’” he says, shaking his head. “It’s heartbreaking.”Burton’s strong and sometimes surprisingly stern moral core comes, he says, not from “a particular set of beliefs” but rather a sense of the importance of “doing the right thing, being a kind person and making something that isn’t awful”. After university, he worked in a clothes store, which he hated, then part-time in a travel agency, which he liked. He began making videos “very arrogantly, because I saw a lot of people doing it and thought I could do it a lot better”.After quite a lot ofcontentabout foreign currency, he began his Lego binge series. He doesn’t do those now, he says: too clickbaity, too much conspicuous consumption. And indeed the likes ofI Built 250 Lego Sets in 24 Hours(16m views) do feel discordantly grabby next to, say,I Picked up a Ton of Trash (Literally!)(8m views).Burton is not sanctimonious, yet his conscience is something of a selling point. “I find it very frustrating when YouTubers encourage you to donate and don’t donate anything themselves. When you go to Tesco and they want you to round up for charity – they’re taking credit without donating anything themselves. That’s not really a good deed. You need to lead by example.” So the jungle boat ride video includes a brief explanation of the clean-water crisis in Cambodia, to which Burton duly donated enough to fund a whole school.Profits from Bella plushies, meanwhile, have been diverted to the RSPCA since her death. Announcing that to his fans was a challenge, he says: “I knew I was going to make a lot of people very sad.” Thirty-three thousand bereft YouTubecommentsprove him right.Stepping into Burton’s house is an odd and exciting experience. All around are familiar sights and previous projects: thecatio! Thecat mansion! Theceiling train! But there is also evidence of life that doesn’t make it into shot, and the shock of this is testimony to his broadcasting skills. The intimacy he projects on screen is genuine, yet it’s also curated. His world, it turns out, is richer than cats and Lego alone.“I’m kind of strict with privacy, and people seem to not see this because I involve the cats and that seems hyper-personal. But there are certain rooms that are never filmed in and a lot of other personal details I don’t talk about, or emotions, or any kind of relationships or family life.”View image in fullscreenBella, whose death inspired 33,000 comments on YouTube.Photograph: Half-Asleep ChrisThis is something he learned on the job. A former girlfriend featured in some of his previous videos; when they broke up, Burton felt the need to issue a statement, including details on custody of the cats. “It creates something awkward,” he says. Viewers “feel they have the right to know and I guess they do have a right to know because you’ve kind of shared that. But it’s unfair on other people. I’ve chosen to be in the public eye but they haven’t, and I need to protect their privacy.”Cats don’t care what strangers project on to them, he says, but humans are less immune. “I’m massively against kids being in YouTube videos. I think it’s an exploitative thing by the parents. Christopher Robin grew up to really hate his dad. He resented that he’d sold out his childhood.”View image in fullscreenHalf-Asleep Chris, Henry and a plaque to Bella.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianIt’s time to leave. Burton ushers us out, past an Aardman-themed bathroom and giant 3D printed Lego bricks. What’s next? After the Rainforest Cafe, there are plans for a train around the garden that will navigate a greenhouse, mushroom tunnel, giant sandcastles and jets of coloured water.And then? “A claw-machine litter tray,” he grins. “I think these inventions are often best when they’re a little impractical.” The carpet-fitters may need to plan a return visit.The Unordinary Book of Ideas by Half-Asleep Chris is published byDorling Kindersley Ltd(£24.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsCultureYouTubeCatsPetsChildrenFamilyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Peta claimed victory when fashion stopped using fur – so why are they back hijacking catwalks? | Peta | The Guardian
description: The animal welfare group has revived their runway-storming tactics from the naughts, now targeting the use of wool
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: The animal welfare group has revived their runway-storming tactics from the naughts, now targeting the use of wool
Content: Josie Knowles, an activist with Peta UK, crashes London fashion week on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Peta UKView image in fullscreenJosie Knowles, an activist with Peta UK, crashes London fashion week on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Peta UKPetaPeta claimed victory when fashion stopped using fur – so why are they back hijacking catwalks?The animal welfare group has revived their runway-storming tactics from the naughts, now targeting the use of woolHannah MarriottThu 1 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.38 EDTShareHer walk was poised, her outfit – crop top, tailored trousers, high heels – so on point that when Josie Knowles strutted down aLondonFashion Week catwalk last month she could have passed for a model. That is, had it not been for the sign the Peta protester held saying “H&M: Wool is Bloody Cruel.”Still, asone social media commentator put itwhen praising her strut: “you cant tell me Peta didn’t know what they were doing when they hired this diva”.The diva in question, Josie Knowles, 26, actually hired herself as part of her role leading fashion campaigns atPetaUK. Though she would not reveal how she got into last month’s H&M show (rumours of industry plants and sympathizers abound), she would confirm that dressing to “look the part” was part of her prep. For the record, Knowles’s clothes were all vegan and secondhand; the trousers were Spacegirlz, a now defunct early 2000s label; her high-heeled boots were from the Peta prop cupboard.double quotation markI love expressing myself through fashion, but never at an animal’s expenseJosie KnowlesKnowles admits that she did practise her walk a bit (“I can’t say that I didn’t walk up and down my bedroom a few times”) but the main thing she practised was getting her sign out and unfolding it, because “obviously, for me, the most important part was getting my message seen, even if it would just be for a second”, she says.She was also aware that looking good would boost the chances of her protest going viral. “Unfortunately, we live in a shallow world, and I think people are often more willing to listen to people that they find attractive,” she says.And go viral it did: one post alone had 40m views. Many of the comments were complimentary, with some even demanding fashion credits (“a lot of people were like, ‘where are the pants from?’” she says).The model Adwoa Aboah even complimented her walk. Even though it’s a shame, says Knowles, that “she’s not talking about the message, the fact that there is someone in the fashion world who isn’t angry or annoyed at what we’re doing, is, I suppose, encouraging.”View image in fullscreenPeta models dressed in faux-wool clothing during a protest outside the H&M London fashion week show at Olympia London on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Christian Vierig/Getty ImagesOne of the reasons Knowles’s catwalk moment engaged so many was because it felt unlikely that someone clearly steeped in fashion’s visual codes would also be prepared to protest against the industry so fiercely.Knowles has never worked in fashion. She studied philosophy at university, went vegan after falling into an internet rabbit hole, appalled by what she saw about the treatment of animals. She interned at Peta for six months before she was hired there. But she has always been into personal style. “Social media gave me access to countless creators who inspired me. It also introduced me to thrifting, which I love because it lets me be creative with what I wear while giving clothes a second life. I love expressing myself through fashion, but never at an animal’s expense,” she says.Runway protestshave been a staple of Peta campaigning for decades, with memorable moments including a naked runway invasion at Oscar de la Renta’s 1991 show in New York, and an astonishing visual tableaux created at a Victoria’s Secret show in 2002, when Gisele Bündchen posed in her smalls while four Peta protesters behind her each held an all-caps signs saying “Gisele: Fur Scum”.View image in fullscreenPeta activists rush the stage as Gisele Bündchen struts on the runway during the Victoria’s Secret fashion show on 14 November 2002 in New York.Photograph: Stephen Chernin/APThe tactic waned at the tail end of Peta’s I’d Rather Go Naked Than Wear Fur campaign in the late 2010s, largely because the fashion industry had accepted Peta’s position and removed fur from new lines. Now though, it has burst back on to the catwalk.Since 2023, activists have rushed the catwalks of top fashion shows including Burberry, Gucci, Hermès, Victoria Beckham and Fendi. Many of them have been young men and women who could pass for models themselves. Peta activists often blend in so well that before some recent catwalk ambushes, they have mingled with show-goers and even sat front row before leaping to action.Modelesque Peta activists also do other visual stunts outside shows and boutiques, such as posing in reptilian body paint to protest against the use of crocodile skins.Presumably this is all strategic casting. Though when I asked Peta activists why many fashion protesters looked runway ready, they all cited confidence and the vegan diet.Knowles’s catwalk moment was one of two Peta viral moments of fashion month so far. The first was more ugly: atNew York fashion week, Steven Kolb, who has since resigned from his role as head of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA), wrestled a protester to the ground with his hand clamped over her mouth at a runway show for H&M Group-owned brand Cos.Steven Kolb physically restraining a Peta protester at a Cos New York fashion week show on 13 September 2026.Photograph: @Fashionista/InstagramThe Cos debacle took place at the first officially fur-freeNew Yorkfashion week – an initiative announced by Kolb himself.But Peta still protested because the organization is shifting emphasis. It’s now calling for the eradication of nearly all animal-derived fabrics including, perhaps most divisively, wool.H&M became a target for Peta’s anti-wool efforts last year, when Peta captured footage of extreme cruelty to sheep at a wool operator that supplies H&M through a broker. That farm was Nativa- and Responsible Wool Standard-certified, accreditations designed to reassure customers that the fibre has been sourced ethically and traceably; Peta has described such certifications as “humanewashing”. Though many in the wool and fashion industry claim such cases are bad apples, Peta claims to have evidence of extreme crueltyfrom 150 wool operations globallyand argue that such mistreatment is systemic.Peta’s assertions are challenging to many of us, at odds with the cosy associations we have with wool farming – associations Peta’s activists say are based on misinformation.For a fashion world patting itself on the back for dropping fur, calls to ban wool have been met with “a breath of exasperation from some fashion insiders, and confusion from others” according to aVogue Businesspiece which ran in response to the protests.Peta is not the only organization to express concern about sheep welfare. Studies had found sheep to exhibitan acute stress response during shearing. TheAustralia branch of RSPCA, the world’s largest animal welfare charity, has also spoken out about shearing injuries.One big concern, says Melanie Lary, research and campaigns manager at global animal welfare organization Four Paws, is that80% of the merino wool used for clothing globally comes from Australia, the only country in the world where mulesing – the practice of cutting skin from a lamb’s hindquarters to prevent the condition flystrike – is still legal. “That practice is very cruel, and it is widespread within the system.”double quotation markIt does kind of bring you back to those earlier tactics of really having to drag an issue into the headlinesAshley ByrneHow widespread cruelty is, more broadly, is debated: the Guardian spoke to several experts in animal welfare, some of whom said that they see far fewer injuries in UK farms than in Australia and China. Many expressed particular concern about the prioritization of speed over care when producing wool at a low cost.Many farmers, fashion brands and wool producers, meanwhile, maintain that they adhere to ethical standards. They flag social and environmental concerns inherent in abandoning wool production, and argue that – because sheep have been bred for generations to grow very thick fleeces – not shearing them would also be cruel. A spokesperson for Textile Exchange, the organization responsible for the Responsible Wool Standard certification, said that it believed that responsibly produced animal-derived materials, “can play an important role in a more resilient textile and apparel industry”.Clearly, though, the ethical certifications designed to reassure consumers are imperfect: H&M said that they “rely on some of the strictest certifications in the industry when sourcing animal fibers for our products”. But after Peta’s recent investigation, “licenses for one wool farm have been suspended”. Nativa said that the events shown in the footage were unacceptable and added: “We take this breach of our protocol as an opportunity to further tighten the control measures on all of our certified farms.”‘It gives Shein’: how did polyester become the world’s most-hated material?Read moreSome have also accused Peta of pushing synthetic fibres just when the environmental nightmare of polyester use needs to be abated, though Peta say that’s a false dichotomy. The Peta activists I spoke to were advocates for vegan plant-based alternatives such as bamboo, cotton, hemp and tencel. Peta US spokesperson Ashley Byrne points out that her favourite boots aremade from cactus leather. Such fabrics aren’t always widely available, which Byrne says ties in to “another part of the message: we have these other incredible, innovative materials at our fingertips”. Big fashion houses, she says, have a responsibility to invest in them.Peta would assert that, even under the best of circumstances, the process is cruel, because any animals raised for commercial purposes are killed before the end of their natural life (usually about seven years old, while sheep could live to 10-15 years old, says Dwyer). For Peta, any system in which animals are considered to be products for human use, before their own needs as living creatures is considered, is unacceptable.View image in fullscreenPeta protests the use of wool at New York fashion week at Manhattan’s Rockefeller Center.Photograph: Milo Hess/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockByrne, a Peta US campaigner of 19 years, who recently stood outside a Coach show “wearing a backless evening gown, appearing to get my skin ripped off and screaming”, in protest against leather – is convinced that it’s “only a matter of time” before wool goes the same way as fur.“If people saw the footage that Peta was obtaining of what’s happening behind the scenes in industries like the wool industry, they would reject it,” she says. Being at the beginning of the road of what Peta hopes will be a change in public opinion, however, and feeling that “we’re starting from scratch”, explains the recent influx of catwalk invasions. “It does kind of bring you back to those earlier tactics of really having to drag an issue into the headlines in a different way,” she says.Gen Z activists will be a big part of this. Having grown up with unfettered access to information online, Byrne says they are “less surprised than other generations when they learn that wool and leather are a product of cruelty”.For younger activists, says Byrne, catwalk invasions almost feel like part of the Y2K revival. Many of them have “a fascination with archival fashion”. Looking back at fashion imagery from the naughts, they see Peta and think: “We’re going to take these early tactics that worked and apply them now.”View image in fullscreenA Peta activist demonstrates at a Dolce & Gabbana store on 15 January 1998 in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/ReutersHarry Morris, who works in youth outreach for Peta, also rushed the H&M catwalk in London, and invaded the runway at a Paul Smith show in Milan this summer, protesting about the use of mohair. He passed for a model with Knowles’s help. He is, he says “the least fashionable person in the world” but “she dresses me and tells me what looks good”.Morris says the issue of cognitive dissonance feels particularly pertinent to fashion; designers are sometimes keen to talk about the semiotic meaning of a garment, while avoiding going too deep into the reality of how materials are made.Morris, like Knowles, says the stunts are “nerve-racking” and always a “last resort” after attempts to negotiate with companies. Like the other activists I spoke to, Morris watched Peta’s footage from farms just before leaping on to the catwalk – “so you have that to spur you on,” he says. With that in mind, “it’s very easy to say, ‘oh, what about the models that you’re disrupting, and the hard work that’s been put into these shows’ – and that is something to think about – but it’s so insignificant in terms of the harm that comes to these animals.Animalsare losing their lives over an item of clothing.”Even now, as security is tightening as awareness of Peta’s presence rises, Morris says Peta will keep on storming the catwalk. “The thing is with Peta, if there’s a will, there’s a way. We will find a way to get in, and to stand up for animals.”

title: My wife obsessively consumes US news. She’s so stressed but can’t turn off. What should I do? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Instead of asking her to step away from her distress, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith, could you suggest she channel it into action?
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: Instead of asking her to step away from her distress, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith, could you suggest she channel it into action?
Content: ‘The general collapse of everything is distressing. So it can seem like an obligation of responsible citizenship tobedistressed,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Miranda and The Tempest by John William Waterhouse.Illustration: Wikimedia CommonsView image in fullscreen‘The general collapse of everything is distressing. So it can seem like an obligation of responsible citizenship tobedistressed,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Miranda and The Tempest by John William Waterhouse.Illustration: Wikimedia CommonsLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleMy wife obsessively consumes US news. She’s so stressed but can’t turn off. What should I do?Instead of asking her to step away from her distress, writes advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smith, could you suggest she channel it into action?Read moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy wife is obsessed with everything that’s happening in the US. She literally spends all day sitting on the couch, watching videos and reading opinion pieces. She’s originally from America and has beenliving abroad for 25 years and she has familyin the US, so I get that she needs to feel connected to what’s happening. But it’s constant. Whether we’re eating, watching a TV show or movie, when we’re talking about something completely unrelated – everything, every topic, either starts or ends with outrage.I’ve told her she needs to take at least one day off all social media, but she won’t do that even for an hour. It stresses her out more and more every day, but she just keeps going back to it – and it has been really affecting me, more lately than ever.On weekends I stay up late playing games (my way of winding down after a week of work) and she’ll go to bed early. And during those times sometimes I just sit and cry. Everything that’s happening is so stressful, and there’s nothing we can do about it. I just wishI could rip away her phone andlet her breathe! I don’t know what to say or do. Is there anything that could help?Eleanor says:It’s so easy to feel that if you’re a politically engaged person youhaveto stay tuned in and upset. The general collapse of everything is distressing. So it can seem like an obligation of responsible citizenship tobedistressed.My friend keeps sending me unsolicited conspiracy theory material. Should I ask them to stop? | Leading questionsRead moreBut a lot of thinkers say that in politically distressing times it’s also our jobto cultivate hope.We have to husband our emotional resources carefully, to guard our capacity for real action. And you don’t do that by endlessly scrolling platforms that want you to stay transfixed in horror, because that’s how they get their ad dollars.I can think of two things that might help here. One is to repeat your request for less time on social media – but this time, instead of sayingsheneeds a day off, could you make it about how it’s affectingyou?When a partner’s choice negatively affects us it’s tempting to litigate the choice itself: “You shouldn’t elect to live like that; it’s bad for you, objectively.” But then the other person just disagrees. “It isn’t bad; I value it; who are you to tell me what I need?”There’s one thing she can’t disagree with, though, and that’show this affects you.Using your recreation time to weep alone is a desperately poignant place to have wound up. Asking her to put her phone away for hersake invites questions about why you’re the authority. But you’re the authority on your own needs. Could you ask again, appealing for your own sake?The other strategy might be to meet her in – but rechannel – her distress. It’s clearly important to her to know about this stuff. It involves her home, it affects her family, and facing up to grim truths can feel like a civic imperative. I can even imagine that you asking for time away from distressing news might seem to herlike a bourgeois wish to be unperturbed: “I don’t want to be disturbed in my citadel by the knowledge of the horrors outside.” But you don’t necessarily have to ask her to step awayfrom her distress – you could suggest shedosomething with it, besides consuming information and looking at the screen.Could you encourage her to act on what’s distressing her? Organise, campaign, do things in your local area, give time, with others, regularly? Otherwise she’s paying all the emotional costs of “responsible political engagement” without making much gain for causes she actually cares about. Consuming information and feeling feelings do not actually discharge the burdens of political engagement. Doing things, even small things, does. It’s also a bit of an antidote to despair. It gets you back in touch with good people. It gets you out of the house; it gets you small victories.If you could suggest that the best use of her intelligence and empathy is not scrolling and debating butacting,that might make her feel less like you want her to not care about something important to her – while helping you feel less like you’ve lost your wife. You can be saying: “I agree this is important, so let’s make sure we have the energy to actuallydothings about it, and not let it eat our home and relationship too.”Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose.
