For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleLeading questionsFamilyHealth & wellbeingRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best dishes to come out of a roasting tin | Food | The Guardian
description: Baked pasta, gnocchi, chicken, meatballs and greens perfectly served straight from the oven
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Baked pasta, gnocchi, chicken, meatballs and greens perfectly served straight from the oven
Content: A roasting tin favourite … Meera Sodha’s baked pasta, with sweet potato, spinach and miso.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA roasting tin favourite … Meera Sodha’s baked pasta, with sweet potato, spinach and miso.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianFeastFoodThe best dishes to come out of a roasting tinBaked pasta, gnocchi, chicken, meatballs and greens – all perfectly served straight from the ovenSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastRachel RoddyThu 1 Oct 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs I have mentioned before, we live directly above a takeaway pizzeria andtavola calda(a canteen-like spot that translates as “hot table”). My desk is by the window, so the writing and editing of my next book (a collection of regional recipes that is only two years late) has been accompanied by the smell of whatever is cooking in their kitchen downstairs, before being arranged, in big roasting trays, behind a glass counter. Occasionally, I have to shut the window, but mostly the steady stream of pizza, baked pasta, braised meat, meatballs, roast potatoes and green vegetables shining with olive oil inspires me. And that is the inspiration for this newsletter: ideas for easygoing dishes that are best served straight from their rectangular roasting tins.As I write this, it is almost lunchtime, so, driven by my own hunger, I would like the first serving from a roasting tray to be Angela Hartnett’smacaroni cheese: al dente pasta mixed with béchamel and various cheeses, then baked until golden brown and bubbling at the edges. Just as welcome would be a plate of baked pasta inspired by one of my friend Cinzia’s dishes: meze maniche, rigatoni, penne or macaroni with a rich tomato sauce, basil, lots of mozzarella and pecorino. Or a slice of Meera Sodha’svegan sweet potato, miso and wholemeal lasagne, which, she promises, takes 15 minutes to put together and uses good, flavourful, ready-made ingredients such as miso, sun-dried tomato paste and passata.Moving from short tubes and sheets of pasta to gnocchi, Rukmini Iyer, author ofthe hugely successful Roasting Tin series, has a great (and great-value) recipe forcreamy baked gnocchi with tomatoes, mozzarella and basil. I have a similar recipe, known in Italy asgnocchi alla Sorrentina,which begins on the stovetop (where the gnocchi is boiled and the sauce made) and is then transferred to a roasting tin. Mozzarella and parmesan are added, and the cooking is finished in the oven. The dish is also known asgnocchi filanti alla Sorrentina– filanti means “stringy”, after the way the mozzarella melts into long strings and pulls into a game of cat’s cradle as you eat, a reminder to enjoy it while the gnocchi is still hot.View image in fullscreenComforting one-pot dinner … Thomasina Miers’ falling-apart chicken cacciatore.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The GuardianFarther along the counter, I would hope to see a big tray of braised chicken, the meat visibly tender, the sauce thick enough to be called gravy. In Rome, this way of cooking chicken or rabbit is generally known asalla cacciatora, or hunters’ style, because this was how the hunters themselves, or their wives (or whoever else was in the kitchen) cooked what they had shot; the name persists even when the hunting involves buying the meat at the butcher or supermarket. Or maybe it is simply a term concocted by city trattorias to evoke the countryside? Either way, alla cacciatora is a good way to cook and eat chicken. I have written several cacciatora recipes over the years, including one forchicken with rosemary, tomatoes and olives. Another version is Thomasina Miers’ falling-apartchicken cacciatore, with tomatoes, peppers, and fennel, and coriander seeds rubbed into the chicken skin (though she says to leave them out if you’re a stickler for authenticity). Yotam Ottolenghi, meanwhile, gives a recipe for veryslow-braised chicken with celeriac and lemon. Next to the chicken, there must be a tray of roast potatoes, each chunk golden and roughly the size of a domino.The next tray along should contain meatballs. Felicity Cloake has suggestionsfor perfect ones, as does Thomasina Miers, notably in her recipe forgiant pork meatballs in tomato sauce. Alternatively, borrow either meatball recipe, then poach them in Dara Klein’srich tomato sauce. Another option is Andy Baraghani’skufteh, orIranian meatballs, a different kind of meatball altogether, being tennis ball-sized and made with lamb, pork or turkey mince, herbs, rice and turmeric, or Tom Hunt’s brilliantstale bread turned into vegetarian “meatballs”. Next to those meatballs, there must be a tray of greens – spinach, chard, peas – that have been boiled then cooked again, briefly, with olive oil, garlic and a bit of chilli.My week in foodView image in fullscreenThe language of cheese … Jenny Linford has written a guide for cheese lovers.Photograph: Marion Bernet/The GuardianSay cheese|Having enjoyed her writing and podcasts for two decades now, I was happy to receive a copy of Jenny Linford’sThe Cheese Lover’s Guide: A Flavour-Focused Approach to Cheese. It is an approachable book with a large scope, and it’s also immensely detailed, intelligent and full of Jenny’s expertise. Her short but bright essays explore the origins and principles of cheesemaking, the global cheese scene today and the language of cheese, followed by a useful and enlightening guide (with pictures) to 100 iconic cheeses from around the world.Nice ice|Two days in London was not nearly enough. I did, however, fit in a visit to Jacob Kenedy’sGelupoin Soho for a cup of fig cremolato with double cream. Jacob describes cremolato as the more luxurious cousin of granita, but I think it sits more at the crossroads of sorbet, granita and a sweetened crush of semi-frozen fruit. Gelupo’s version is every bit as good as Mario De Angelis’s atLa Casa del Cremolato in Rome, which is sublime.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHoly smoke!|AtBeppe e i Suoi Formaggi, a Roman cheese and wine shop, they offer a butter tasting that includes three varieties: dairy butter, smoked dairy butter and butter produced from cows grazing while on holiday in the mountains. All of them are made by the Giovale family in Piedmont, and they are all great, but it’s the smoked butter – rich, toasted, tarry and like caramel-hickory – that has stayed with me and introduced me to a whole world of smoked butter, for spreading on toast or stirring through pasta. In the UK,Curing Rebels’ own English butter, slowly smoked over a two-day process, sounds divine.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastItalian food and drinkAutumn food and drinkMeatChickenPastaMain coursenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: From breakfast pancakes to dinner sides and pudding: Alissa Timoshkina’s apple recipes | Autumn food and drink | The Guardian
description: Fried in pancakes, braised with duck, pickled with a roast chicken or baked for pudding, apples are one of autumn’s star ingredients
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fried in pancakes, braised with duck, pickled with a roast chicken or baked for pudding, apples are one of autumn’s star ingredients
Content: Photograph: Laura Edwards / The Guardian/Photographer - Laura Edwards /The Guardian. Food Styling - Joss Herd. Prop Styling - Tabitha HawkinsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Laura Edwards / The Guardian/Photographer - Laura Edwards /The Guardian. Food Styling - Joss Herd. Prop Styling - Tabitha HawkinsAutumn food and drinkFrom breakfast pancakes to dinner sides and pudding: Alissa Timoshkina’s apple recipesFried in pancakes, braised with duck, pickled with a roast chicken or baked for pudding, apples are one of autumn’s star ingredientsAlissa TimoshkinaThu 1 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew ingredients are as familiar as apples, yet few carry such symbolic weight. Peaking just as the season’s begin to turn, they are the ultimate symbol of nature’s abundance, imbued with a sense of nostalgia for the retreating sunlight. The symbolism became unexpectedly tangible to me during a recent autumn apple-picking trip with my family: surrounded by branches heavy with fruit, I found myself seeing the humble apple with fresh awe. It looked nothing short of nature’s miracle. Native to the mountains of central Asia, near the modern Kazakhstan-China border, it has travelled further than perhaps any other fruit, becoming at home in cuisines from Normandy to New York, Caucasus to Kashmir. Sweet or savoury, everyday or celebratory, the apple is truly universal. Its versatility always reminds me of the simple joy of cooking with the seasons.Breakfast appleoladky(pictured top)Prep10 minCook25 minMakes24, to serve6200g plain flour,sifted1 shy tspbaking powder¼ tspbicarbonate of sodaA pinch of cinnamonA pinch of fine sea salt1 medium egg (50g)200ml whole milk50g unsalted butter,melted, plus extra for frying3 sweet apples,cored, then 1 grated and 2 thinly sliced on a mandoline2 tbsprunny honey, plus extra for servingNeutral oil,for fryingGreek yoghurt, for servingIn a bowl, mix all the dry ingredients together, then in a separate bowl whisk the wet ones, including the grated apple.Gently fold the wet and dry ingredients together with a silicone spatula – make sure you don’t over mix it. Leave to rest at room temperature for five minutes, or until you see bubbles appear.Heat a frying pan on a low-medium heat, and add enough oil to coat it evenly. Scoop up the batter (about 15-20g per oladky) and drop it into the pan – it should start sizzling straight away. Depending on the size of your pan, you should be able to cook around four oladky at the same time.Fry them on one side for 40 seconds, adding a few slices of apple on top halfway through cooking.Flip them over, adding a teaspoon of butter to help the apples soften and caramelise, and continue cooking undisturbed for 90 seconds to two minutes, until the pancakes have puffed up and the apples are caramelised.Repeat with the remaining batter and apple slices. Serve with Greek yoghurt and a drizzle of honey.Roast chicken salad with kale, fennel, pickled apples and tahini ‘mayo’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Photography: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.Prep20 minRest30 minCook15 minServes4For the salad150-200g kale,washed and stalks removed2 tbspextra-virgin olive oilFlaky sea salt andblack pepperJuice of ¼ lemon1grannysmith apple,thinly sliced on a mandolin2 celery sticks,sliced diagonally into long wedges1 small fennel bulb,trimmed and thinly sliced on a mandoline25gflat-leaf parsley,leaves picked, plus extra to garnish1 roast chicken breast(about 200g), or equivalent chicken meat leftover from a roast, shredded2 tbsptoasted sunflower seeds,to garnishFor the pickle4 tbspapple cider vinegarJuice of ½ lemon1 tbsprunny honeyA pinch of flaky sea salt1granny smith,finely dicedFor the tahini mayo150mltahini3 tbspextra-virgin olive oilJuice of ½ lemon1 tbsprunny honey1 tbspapple cider vinegarFlaky sea salt, to tastePickle brine(see above)1 ice cube,or 2 tsp of ice-cold waterStart by making the pickle. In a medium jar, mix two tablespoons of cold water, the vinegar, lemon juice, honey and salt. Add the diced apple and shake well to combine. Leave to rest in the fridge for about 30 minutes.Next, prep the kale. Massage the kale with the olive oil, salt and lemon juice in a large bowl until wilted. Set aside.To make the tahini mayo, add the first six ingredients into a mixing bowl, finishing with all the apple pickle brine. Start mixing slowly with a fork; if the paste gets too thick or splits, add an ice cube or ice-cold water and continue stirring gently, until you reach a silky consistency (you will!).Back to the salad. To the bowl with the kale, add the fresh and pickled apples, celery, fennel, parsley and chicken. Add a third of the tahini dressing and give everything a gentle toss.Transfer the salad to a large bowl or sharing platter, drizzle over the tahini sauce in wriggly lines, then scatter over the sunflower seeds and extra torn parsley leaves. Finish with an extra sprinkle of sea salt and a generous crack of black pepper. You will have some tahini dressing left over; serve this in the jar alongside.Duck legs with braised sauerkraut, apples and cranberriesView image in fullscreenPrep10 minCook2 hrServes41-2 tbspduck fat4 duck legs,at room temperatureSea salt and black pepper2 red onions,peeled and thinly sliced1 tsp caraway seeds1 tspdried thyme200ml red wine½ small red cabbage,shredded650g jarsauerkraut with brine3 red apples,sliced into chunky wedges (about 6-8 each)1 orange,zest and juice2 tbspdried cranberries1 tspsugar4 bay leaves400ml stock (vegetable or chicken)Melt a tablespoon of the duck fat in a heavy-based casserole. Pat the duck legs dry and salt on both sides, then place them in the casserole skin side down and sear on a medium-high heat for 10 minutes, to achieve a seductive crispy skin. Transfer the legs to a plate and set aside while you get on with the rest.Depending on how fatty the duck legs are, add another tablespoon of duck fat to the casserole. Lower the heat to medium, and fry the onion with a pinch of salt, the caraway and thyme for eight to 10 minutes.Deglaze the pan by adding the wine and scraping off any delicious bits of fat and onion that might be stuck to the pan. Cook with the lid off for a minute. Next, add the remaining ingredients, stir well to combine and bring to a gentle simmer.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the duck legs on top of the cabbage, skin side up, cover with a lid, and put in theoven for 90 minutes, or until tender.The dish goes down a treat as is (with a glass of red wine, of course), or add some creamy mash or roast potatoes for an extra comforting autumnal meal.Fermented apple salsaView image in fullscreenThis is a very versatile ferment: add it to salads or egg mayo (instead of capers), use it to top avocado or layer into a cheese toastie filling.Prep15 minCook15 minFerment3 days+Makes1 x 1.5L jarFor the apple salsa3 largegrannysmithapples,cored and diced2 spring onions,trimmed, white and green parts finely sliced100g white grapes,quartered2 celery sticks,diced1 jalapeño,seeds and pith removed, flesh finely diced10g fresh dill,stems and fronds finely chopped1 tspfennel seedsFor the brine7g fine, non-iodized sea salt(roughly 1½ level tsp)350ml filtered waterSterilise a 1.5L jar by running it through the dishwasher, then let it cool down before handling. Mix all the apple salsa ingredients in a bowl to make sure everything is well distributed. Make the brine by dissolving the salt in the water.Pack the jar tightly with the apple mix, and top with the brine, leaving about two fingers’ worth of space at the top (for the weight). Put a fermentation weight on top, close the lid and place in a small bowl to catch any leakages. Leave at room temperature and out of direct sunlight for three to six days, depending on how warm the room is.The salsa is ready when the brine becomes effervescent and the apples acquire a pleasant, piquant, sour quality. At this point, remove the weight, and transfer to the fridge. The salsa will keep in the fridge for up to three months.Ukrainian baked rice pudding with apples, cinnamon and raisinsView image in fullscreenPrep5 minCook1 hrServes4200glong-grain rice750mlwhole milkA pinch of salt50gunsalted butter,plus extra for greasing and dotting2 medium apples (gala,cox’s, braeburn, for example),cored and diced50graisinsZest of 1 medium orange1 tsp ground cinnamon,plus extra for dusting2 large eggs50gcastersugar1 tsp vanilla extractRinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear. Then, in a saucepan, combine the rice with the milk and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 18–20 minutes, until the rice is soft and creamy and most of the milk has been absorbed. It might feel like a lot of milk at first, but it will work.Meanwhile, melt the butter in a frying pan and saute the diced apples with the raisins, orange zest and cinnamon for five to seven minutes, until slightly softened. In a large bowl, beat the eggs with the sugar and vanilla extract.When the rice is cooked, let it cool slightly before stirring it into the egg mixture, followed by the sauteed apples, raisins and orange zest, until well combined.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/400F/gas 6 and grease a 20cm × 30cm ovenproof dish with butter. Pour the rice mixture into the dish, smoothing the top and dotting with small pieces of butter. Bake for 30–40 minutes, until the top is golden and set. Cool slightly before serving, dusted with extra cinnamon, if desired.Lozhka by Alissa Timoshkina is published in October by Quadrille at £28. To order a copy for £25.20, visitguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsAutumn food and drinkFruitFoodPickling, fermenting and preservingMeatChickenDuckrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Heart-meltingly good: the best cooking chocolate to buy | Food | The Guardian
description: Those cookies and cakes will only be as tasty as the chocolate you use in their baking. Here are my favourites
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Those cookies and cakes will only be as tasty as the chocolate you use in their baking. Here are my favourites
Content: You cannot make Edd Kimber's double chocolate olive oil cookies with bad chocolate. Just don’t.Photograph: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.View image in fullscreenYou cannot make Edd Kimber's double chocolate olive oil cookies with bad chocolate. Just don’t.Photograph: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.The chocolate diariesFoodHeart-meltingly good: the best cooking chocolate to buyThose cookies and cakes will only be as tasty as the chocolate you use in their baking. Here are my favouritesAnnalisa BarbieriThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf course, you can bake with any sort of chocolate, and I do, but being Chocolate Correspondent means I have a lot of it spare, despite giving much away. I once made mychocolate rye cookiesand served them to a friend. She went away and made her own. “Mine were nice,” she said, “but not as nice as yours.” Mine had about £40’s worth of craft chocolate in them.Clearly this is madness and outside the remit of all but the privileged, but the quality of chocolate you use in baking really does make a difference. Although I can and do use chocolate bars chopped up post-testing, having specific cooking chocolate (which may have more cocoa butter in it for easier melting) makes life easier, because it often comes either in pastilles or little chocolate buttons, which are bliss for the lazy. The go-to for a lot of professional chefs isValrhona. I love the pastilles: for rich chocolate baking, the Ghana 80% is my favourite (I also love it as an eating chocolate), but theGuanaja 70%is more readily available. There are lots of variations in each cacao percentage, from 29%-85%, with different flavour profiles. For white-chocolate cooking, theDulcey, biscuity and caramelly, is hard to beat.Formy little breakfast briochesorItalian breakfast cake, and if you’re serious about baking (because it comes in 2kg bags), my go-to is Islands, which has micro chocolate buttons (in75% darkor55% milk) that are brilliant.View image in fullscreen‘Ideal as inclusions in cakes or cookies’: Pierre Marcolini cooking chocolate buttons.Photograph: Juan Vrijdag/Pierre MarcoliniPierre Marcolini recently launched anexcellent cooking chocolate rangefrom 45% cocoa to 82%. They come in small button shapes (but not as small as the Islands minis), which are ideal as inclusions in cakes or cookies, or for easy melting. They also make rather excellent munchies: I mix mine with salted popcorn for a relatively healthy snack.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe chocolate diariesChocolatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A perry respectable alternative to wine – in praise of pear cider  | Food | The Guardian
description: Beyond Babycham there is a whole cottage industry of small-batch fine perries that are surprisingly perfect for pairing with food
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Beyond Babycham there is a whole cottage industry of small-batch fine perries that are surprisingly perfect for pairing with food
Content: Wilding ciderproduces “November,” a limited-release sparkling perry made with late-season, hand-pressed pears.Photograph: Olivia Estebanez/The Fine Cider CompanyView image in fullscreenWilding ciderproduces “November,” a limited-release sparkling perry made with late-season, hand-pressed pears.Photograph: Olivia Estebanez/The Fine Cider CompanyFoodA perry respectable alternative to wine – in praise of pear ciderBeyond Babycham there is a whole cottage industry of small-batch fine perries that are surprisingly perfect for pairing with foodMina HollandThu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“They’re gorgeous little beasts,”Eddie Izzard said on the subject of pearsin her mid-1990s show Definite Article, “but they’re ripe for half an hour and you’re never there!” Little did she know that she was touching on one of the difficulties of making perry – the fermented juice of perry pears – a drink that remains, in comparison with cider, a relative cottage industry.There are some notable exceptions to that rule (anyone familiar withBabychamandLambriniwill have tried a commercial perry, albeit an industrially made one), but the perry I’m interested in is made from specific perry pears grown on vast trees in ancient, biodiverse orchards in the British West Country and northern France; it is made in small batches, because, as Izzard points out, pears are ripe for a notoriously short time; additionally, they begin to rot from the inside out and, such is the height of those gnarly branches, they can be difficult to pick, too. “Perry-making is hard to do well,” says Felix Nash ofthe Fine Cider Company, a retailer that specialises in craft drinks made from apples and pears.Nash holds that “fine perry”, a term he uses to distinguish his perries from the industrial kind, is a blank slate; unlike cider, it has no mass-market presence beyond the likes of Babycham, which is largely seen as a kitsch anachronism. The fine perries that Nash sells run the gamut from medium-dry and sparkling to sweet and still; aperitifs to pudding accompaniments. He lists vintage perries, single-varietals and blends of pears with names that make me want to take up wassailing: hendre huffcap, butt, green horse, thorn, gin … Perry-making dates back centuries in Gloucestershire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, and is said to have been one of Elizabeth I’s favoured tipples.Historic perry may be, but, as we head into 2026’s harvest season, it occurs to me that there is much to love about it for the modern drinker. It has a naturally low ABV (usually 5-6%) and pears contain sorbitol, a non-fermentable sugar alcohol that can leave even a technically dry perry with an impression of sweetness. It’s also surprisingly food-friendly; Nash cites the classic pairing with oysters or cheese, while I enjoyed a bottle of Tom Oliver’s sparkling medium-dry We Aren’t Stopping Now with chilli paneer; it would also be a doozy with most oily fish.Then there’s the price. The production of fine perry has all the elements of fine wine, Nash says, reflecting fruit varietal, terroir, vintage and skill (some of his perries are made using the champagne method, others have tannins with the grip of red wine): “It’s largely the little known nature of great perry that has helped keep the cost where it currently is.” Without wine’s prestige, and with relatively minimal transport costs and, at those ABVs, considerably lower UK alcohol duty than wine, some of the bottles in today’s picks are nothing short of a giveaway.Six perries - and what to pair with themOliver’s Fine Perry Wild Ferment Rolling Blend£3.50 (330ml) Secret Bottle Shop, 6.5% A great introduction to fine perry, this has notes of elderflower and is happy with everything from butter to spice.Ross On Wye Cider & Perry Company Red Longdon Perry 2025£12 (750ml) Fine Cider, 5.8%. Dry enough for an aperitif, grippy enough for a roast or a cheeseboard – extraordinary and moreish.Little Pomona FaussetPét Nat Perry2023£15 (750ml) Little Pomona, 6%. Juicy, aromatic and sparkling single-varietal perry. I drank it with mapo tofu.Wilding Cider Moorcroft 2022£25 (750ml) Fine Cider, 10.1%. Acid, structure, tannin and an unusually high ABV make this single-varietal perry an excellent stand-in for pudding wine.Eric Bordelet Poiré Authentique£16.50 (750ml) Gnarly Vines, 5%. A Norman perry made by a one-time sommelier, this is off-dry, biodynamic and bloody lovely.Oliver’s We Aren’t Stopping Now 2024£14 (750ml) Fine Cider, 5.5%. Struggling to find a wine pairing for your curry night? Look no further than this elegant, medium-dry perry made by a titan in British cider- and perry-making.Explore more on these topicsFoodCiderBritish food and drinkFrench food and drinkFruitfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my girlfriend let me hang my football calendar in her flat? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Kitty is buying a flat and Henry is moving in with her, but they’re already having decor disagreements. You decide who needs to get over their hang-ups?
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Kitty is buying a flat and Henry is moving in with her, but they’re already having decor disagreements. You decide who needs to get over their hang-ups?
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my girlfriend let me hang my football calendar in her flat?Kitty is buying a flat and Henry is moving in with her, but they’re already having decor disagreements. You decide who needs to get over their hang-ups?Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 1 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prosecution: Henrydouble quotation markIt’s not a showroom; it’s a home. Both people should get a chance to display their personalitiesMy girlfriend Kitty was preparing to buy a flat and I was so proud of her. We were going to move into it together after living in a shared house. I was going to contribute to the mortgage.The purchase fell through, but our conversations about it highlighted an issue of control. I think I should have some say over what goes into any new home, but when I said I wanted to hang my Liverpool-themed calendar, Kitty put her foot down. She said it was ugly, childish and not her aesthetic.double quotation markKitty says she lets me have loads of things, but they tend to be things that she also likesKitty works in interiors and has brilliant taste, but this was supposed to be our shared living space. It’s not a showroom; it’s a home. In shared spaces, both people should get a chance to show off their personalities, but also put up with bits that your partner wants. The calendar is a bit of my personality. My mum bought it for me, so it’s not completely trivial, and I love football. It gives me a sense that it’s my home, and I can keep an eye on the dates of the fixtures.Kitty says she lets me have loads of things, but they tend to be things she also likes. When you move into a home with someone, you have to accept that your partner will bring things you don’t like. There are things of Kitty’s I wouldn’t choose. She ordered a chaise longue and loads of other furniture without asking whether I liked it. But I wouldn’t veto those things because they make her feel at home.This is bigger than the calendar – it made me realise I had a complete lack of agency.I’m hardly demanding a shrine to Liverpool FC. The calendar is only A4-sized. It could go on the back of the kitchen door and add some colour. Kitty will only allow it to go in a cupboard or a wardrobe. The crux of the issue is that Kitty has to accept some things her partner loves even when she doesn’t love them herself. Otherwise, it’s not really our home.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThe defence: Kittydouble quotation markIt’s juvenile and garish. It would be like me sticking a Dua Lipa poster on the wallI don’t want a home that is entirely dictated by my taste, and I already make lots of compromises. For example, Henry has a passion for first world war art, as well as a piano, guitars … We’ve already got lots of his things I wouldn’t have chosen, including his old cigarette packet painting and dining room chairs.I’m not so strong-minded that I can’t be flexible. But the Liverpool calendar is a step too far. It reminds me of living with a teenage boy. And the flat I was buying was tiny, so the calendar would have really affected the overall vibe. It’s juvenile and garish. It would be like me sticking a Dua Lipa poster on the wall.Of course, as an interior designer I care more about such things than the average Joe. And I’m in my 30s and I’d saved up for this flat on my own, so I wanted it to feel like an adult space that combines our tastes. The calendar feels individualistic, so putting my foot down on this occasion shouldn’t be interpreted as super-controlling.double quotation markIf I’m buying stuff, it kind of has to lean towards my tastesHe’s complaining about the stuff in our current shared home now, but he moved in with me and my friend, who owns it. Henry knew what he was getting into. With the new flat, I put my life savings into it, spending hours planning it and doing it alone. It was incredibly stressful. I felt there was a lack of support and excitement from Henry generally. He made the calendar into a big deal in the middle of all that, which I thought trivial.I understand that he felt he lacked control, but I also need to make an investment that is right for me, in case he turns around and says he doesn’t want to be with me. It’s my responsibility to furnish and pay for everything, so it kind of has to lean towards my tastes.I’m still a hard no on the calendar – he’s never even written on it. We can hang it in a wardrobe. I think that’s a good compromise, but if people vote against me here, I will reconsider.The jury of Guardian readersKitty, if you are planning to build a life with Harry, you need to accommodate his passions and interests. Hanging a calendar on the back of the kitchen door is hardly a “test of your investment”. If he moves out, the calendar obviously goes too. If you can’t accept this, you may not be living together for much longer.Maria, 40skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile I get that Kitty probably has a more of an aesthetic eye than Henry, calling his calendar “juvenile” seems a bit much. The fact it’s Liverpool-themed brings a bit of his character to the space they’ve chosen to share. You’ll never walk alone, Henry!Dean, 46While neither is “guilty”, the calendar seems to have become symbolic of the couple lacking a shared perspective on buying/moving. Kitty sees her new financial freedom, whereas Henry is solely focused on making it theirs.Lotte, 33Henry doesn’t deserve to feel like a lodger when he is contributing to the mortgage. It appears he is only allowed things on Kitty’s terms. Compromise is key: Henry, stop badgering and support Kitty whilst she is stressed; Kitty, let the guy have his Liverpool calendar!Gemma, 27The flat is Kitty’s – she is investing her life’s savings while accommodating Henry’s choices, so the financial burden justifies her aesthetic authority. The wardrobe compromise is reasonable – calendars are temporary and functional anywhere.Amira, 35Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: is Kitty’s refusal to put up Henry’s football calendar an own goal?The poll closes on Wednesday 7 October at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked ifNed is ruining the wokby whacking up the heat when he cooks.45%of you said yes –Ned is guilty55%of you said no –Ned is innocentNames have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgeRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The zero-bills home: how one family is beating the energy price hikes | Renewable energy | The Guardian
description: The Naylors’ four-bedroom home in Milton Keynes acts like a mini-power station after retrofitting solar panels, a battery and a heat pump
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: The Naylors’ four-bedroom home in Milton Keynes acts like a mini-power station after retrofitting solar panels, a battery and a heat pump
Content: Clare Naylor’s home in Milton Keynes has been retrofitted with the most modern heating equipment, including a heat pump and solar panels, to reduce her monthly energy bills to zero.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClare Naylor’s home in Milton Keynes has been retrofitted with the most modern heating equipment, including a heat pump and solar panels, to reduce her monthly energy bills to zero.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianRenewable energyThe zero-bills home: how one family is beating the energy price hikesThe Naylors’ four-bedroom home in Milton Keynes acts like a mini-power station after retrofitting solar panels, a battery and a heat pumpShane HickeyThu 1 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClare Naylor paid close attention to how much energy she and her family were using last winter, filling hot-water bottles and bringing out extra blankets to ensure they didn’t go over budget. This year, she won’t have to worry as she is guaranteed not to receive a bill.While millions of British households face the highest energy charges in three years from todayafter a 4% rise in the price cap,and predictions of a 16% increase in January, upgrades to Naylor’s home mean she will not have to pay anything.The four-bedroom detached home inMilton Keyneswas recently fitted with a heat pump and 17 solar panels, and a large battery was installed in the garage to manage the energy generated.The new technology, as well as four new radiators, means the house can use an energy tariff which guarantees she will not pay any bills for five years. In effect, the house behaves like a mini-power station that feeds excess energy back to the grid.View image in fullscreenThe heat pump at the rear of Clare Naylor’s home.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianAs long as the Naylor family stay within a “fair usage” limit,Octopus Energyguarantees they will not be billed for heating, lighting or any of the devices that a family with three children under 10 use.“We were always fairly careful,” says Naylor. “Our heating was only ever set to 18C [although] we might boost it if the family were coming around. “Otherwise [it was] slippers, hot-water bottle, jumpers – that’s how you get through the winter.”This year, she says she will heat the house before the children come home from school, which is something that did not used to happen.The family’s energy bills were relatively low – she says they were about £130 a month, a sum they now plan to spend on holidays.View image in fullscreenThe hot water cylinder installed in the garage.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianThe house, which was built in the 1980s, was retrofitted for free by Santander as part of a project to examine how to fund homes towards better energy efficiency. If Naylor had to pay for the works, the solar panels, heat pump and battery would have come to just under £20,000 after a government grant was applied.TheOctopus “Zero Bills” tariffis operating in hundreds of new-build homes around the country since it was launched five years ago. The company is now testing how it works in houses, such as the Naylors’, that are older and need to be retrofitted.Properties need to have good insulation, solar panels, a heat pump and a battery so that they can generate more energy than is being used. “Typically the homes generate slightly more energy over a year than we’d expect them to use,” said Nigel Banks, the technical director of Zero Bills atOctopus Energy. “One of the fundamental requirements is we need to make enough revenues from selling power back to the grid.”To qualify for the tariff, homes must have no gas, even for cooking, so the Naylors had to have their gas boiler removed. The zero-bill promise does not cover charging electric vehicles (EVs).Typically, the best candidates for the retrofitting work are homes built in the last 10 years with good insulation levels, said Banks. The usage cap will be different for each house and is set depending on how much energy they would normally use, with a margin on top.View image in fullscreenThe four-bedroom home, built in the 1980s, was retrofitted for free by Santander as part of a project to examine how to fund homes towards better energy efficiency. If Naylor had to pay for the works, the cost would be £20,000 after a government grant.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianSantander is working on how to offer financing for households who need to borrow money to fund retrofitting projects. In the meantime, using its home improvement loan, at a 6.4% interest rate over five years, would mean repaying £389 a month for a £20,000 project.Mick Taylor from Santander said: “We’ve got a big challenge. We’ve got 1.5m mortgage accounts and the vast majority of those are paying monthly energy bills. Consumers are concerned that energy bills are only going one way – they’re probably the second- or third-biggest outgoing for most households,” he said.“What can we do to help the country move towards net zero with such a big mortgage portfolio? We’ve obviously got a role to play.”Naylor says that she will try to keep the home at a constant warm temperature during the coming winter. “And then train my children to keep the door shut, which will be fun,” she adds.Explore more on these topicsRenewable energyEnergy (Environment)EnglandOctopus EnergyEnergy billsEnergy efficiencyEnergy industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 20 fascinating facts about hair: why baldness is super-masculine – and a pubic bush could be a ‘cheating detector’ | Health | The Guardian
description: Judy Wearing has spent much of her life studying our follicles. She explains how our armpits betray our emotions, why some gentlemen really do prefer blondes and the reason we evolved to have eyebrows
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Judy Wearing has spent much of her life studying our follicles. She explains how our armpits betray our emotions, why some gentlemen really do prefer blondes and the reason we evolved to have eyebrows
Content: Balding is ‘about as male as it gets’ …Photograph: ozgurdonmaz/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenBalding is ‘about as male as it gets’ …Photograph: ozgurdonmaz/Getty Images/iStockphotoHealth20 fascinating facts about hair: why baldness is super-masculine – and a pubic bush could be a ‘cheating detector’Judy Wearing has spent much of her life studying our follicles. She explains how our armpits betray our emotions, why some gentlemen really do prefer blondes and the reason we evolved to have eyebrowsElle HuntThu 1 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a PhD student at Oxford studying mating behaviour, Judy Wearing was suddenly struck by a thought: what was the purpose of pubic hair? The point of armpit hair? The function of each of our body’s furry patches? When the published literature failed to produce satisfying answers, Wearing began her own investigation. Her aim was to shed light on why exactly we evolved these particular patches, with pubic hair the most puzzling of all: was it for warmth, protection … or something else?Wearing is still tangling with those questions, some 30 years after her student days. Now an author and editor (largely in the education sector), she has revisited her fascination with hair in Anxious and Hairy: The Evolution and Culture of Human Hair, exploring its unexpectedly dense and layered place in our history and psyche. Even Wearing was surprised by the places her research on hair took her, and the mysteries that still remain to be solved. “A lot of these questions, no one’s actually looked at,” she says over Zoom. Here is a mere snip of the fascinating facts she’s uncovered about hair.View image in fullscreenJudy Wearing was surprised where her research on hair took her.Photograph: Mike Wing1. Hair originated with giant furry lizardsHair, or fur, evolved about 245 million years ago with cynodonts, the warm-blooded reptilian ancestors of all mammals, including humans. They had fur for insulation, preventing heat from escaping their bodies. Fossil evidence of the wolf-likeCynognathussuggests it also had whiskers: super sensitive, tactile hairs that provide valuable sensory input.2. Hairy or scaly, we’re made of the same stuffYou may have heard of the protein keratin, integral to human hair, skin and nails. It’s also the basis for cat claws, bird feathers, sheep wool and much else besides. Hair growth is an evolutionary modification of an ancient skin-development process by which reptiles grow scales, Wearing explains, joining the dots with our reptilian ancestors. “You can think of hair as kind of long, thin scales, in a way. Both are made of keratin.”3. Your crowning glory is a pile-up of dead cellsCells called keratinocytes are generated from the very base of the hair root, pushing older cells higher inside the tubular follicle. As they pile up, dead keratin cells fuse into shafts, breaking the skin and becoming visible as hair. Each hair follicle functions like a “mini organ”, Wearing says, with its own set schedule of growth and resting phases.4. It’s not just ‘breast or bottle’Like fur, the ability to produce milk is another defining trait of mammals. The two are more closely associated than you may think: mammary glands evolved as an adaptation of certain hair follicle glands. In Australia, the echidna and the platypus (both monotremes) embody the evolutionary path, before it diverged. Though they lay eggs, they also nurse their young via specialised milk-secreting patches of fur on their bellies.View image in fullscreenWe’ve got just as many follicles as chimps.Photograph: Alamy5. We are not-so-naked apes …Though we might appear wildly less furry than our primate relatives,Homo sapienshave the same number of follicles, found everywhere, in fact, except the palms and soles. “We have as many hair follicles as chimpanzees: two to four million of them,” Wearing says. The difference is that the majority of human hairs are very thin and fine.6. … and terminally patchyThese shrunken “vellus” hairs that cover the body are distinct from “terminal” hairs: the thicker, stiffer and more pigmented strands growing in what Wearing terms “strategic locations” across the human body, such as the eyebrows, armpits and groin. The constellation of these patches is unique to our species, but “there is logical function” underpinning each one, Wearing says.7. The eyes have itEyebrows evolved to protect our eyes and communicate social information. “When was the last time you remember flashing your eyebrows? We don’t know we’re doing it, but we’re reading those signals all the time,” she says. There is also a rich history of refining them through beauty practices. Shaping eyebrows to be thinner, as has often been the style for women, gets “interpreted as submissive and friendlier”, Wearing says. In ancient China, there was a 1,000-year-old tradition of removing all the hairs to paint on an altogether new shape, in painstaking symmetry and often non-natural colours.View image in fullscreenBotox is being studied as a potential treatment for depression.Photograph: Posed by model; Dimensions/Getty Images8. Botoxcurbs empathyToday, one fashion for brows is to stop them from moving, using Botox to prevent wrinkles. But, as Wearing points out, this has indirect implications for our communication too. Psychologists have found that the popular cosmetic procedure impairs our ability to mimic others’ emotional expressions, which curbs empathy. It sounds dystopian, but “there might actually be positive consequences”, Wearing adds. Botoxis being studiedas a potential treatment for depression, by interrupting the feedback loop by which we experience and express emotions.9. Body odour is a broadcast“Underarm and body odour are huge in our social communication,” says Wearing. Our armpit strands are stiffer than those in other places, causing them “to stick out” and broadcast our particular chemical blend. Research suggests we can sniff out not only each other’s genetic differences, but emotional states and even health. This exchange largely happens below our conscious awareness, Wearing says. “Most of us never think, ‘You smell anxious’ – but we might think, ‘You look afraid.’”10. What about beards?Though men and women have the same average number of follicles on their faces, the majority of adult men grow terminal hairs rather than the more typically female peach fuzz. The density is determined by genetic and hormonal differences, with beard and moustache hairs regulated by testosterone and dihydrotestosterone. It is likely that facial hair evolved as a means to compete against sexual rivals and communicate dominance. There is even a suggestion that beards – thick, strong, oilier hair – provide some protection to the jaw in the event of a punch-up.View image in fullscreenHair loss can be a source of distress for men.Photograph: Posed by model; agrobacter/Getty Images11. Balding is not so badHair loss is commonly a source of distress for men, associated with higher rates of anxiety, depression and even suicide. Yet it is a natural and even widespread experience, with more than 70% of Caucasian men experiencing thinning on top (50% by the age of 40). “There’s this notion that it’s pathological, but there’s nothing wrong with it; it’s exceedingly common and evolved for a reason.” Balding can be considered an expression of masculinity, with hair loss regulated by dihydrotestosterone, the same hormone that regulates the growth of the male genitalia. “It’s testosterone with a punch,” says Wearing, “and about as male as it gets.”12. Hair is a health indicatorIn many diverse cultures, long hair in men has been historically associated with strength – think Samson from the Bible. This isn’t just apocryphal: hair is strongly associated with age and health, among people with the genes to grow it long. It grows longer and faster through adolescence and young adults, then slows from around age 25 by about 0.4cm a year. Hair health can also reflect nutritional deficiency, with a lack of protein, iron and vitamins D and B producing more dull and brittle strands. The association between long, shiny hair and good health may be why some women tend to grow hair faster and lose it more slowly (resulting in generally longer hair) than men: it signals a healthy potential mate. Nowadays, of course, we can fake the effect and achieve sleeker, shinier strands with products.13. HairhealsHair doesn’t just reflect good health; it also functions a bit like the body’s sticking plaster. Stem cells, found at the base of every follicle, support skin regeneration and repair. “They’re like mini emergency kits, all over our bodies,” Wearing says.View image in fullscreenStyling dates back to the bronze age for women.Photograph: Sergii Kolesnikov/Getty Images14. Styling has a long history …Evidence of hair styling in women dates back to the bronze age. “If you look at the earliest statuettes and human images, You see hairstyles, braids, buns,” says Wearing. “The ancient Egyptians were just wild about wigs, curls, dyes, extensions.” Throughout history, these went in trends, and took off when commercial styling became big business, from the late 17th century. The enormous “poufs” favoured by the Parisian upper classes in the time of Marie Antoinette, sometimes reaching as far as 40cm above the scalp, were followed by short layered styles, known as Titus cuts.15. … and not just for the richFourteenth century BCE remains excavated from a cemetery in Egypt show evidence of adornments in working-class people. One woman had 70 extensions in varied colours; another elderly woman had dyed her locks with henna not long before her death. Ramses II, who ruled a century later, also covered his greys. “Like today, everyone was doing it,” Wearing says.16. Some gentlemen did prefer blondesBlond is consistently the most popular shade of hair dye for women, despite theeffort and expenseinvolved with maintenance. This speaks to its desirability in some quarters: “It does have some deep association with sexuality, femininity and youth,” Wearing says. In ancient Greece and Rome, “blond hair was part of a prostitute’s uniform”, at one stage required by law to distinguish sex workers from respectable women – until the upper classes started desiring lighter locks, too. Like styles, shades have moved in trends. During the 18th century in England, blond hair was considered disagreeable and best rectified with black dye.View image in fullscreenBlond is consistently the most popular shade of hair dye for women.Photograph: Posed by model; Group4 Studio/Getty Images17. Lighter hair may let in more lightThe first humans had dark hair; it is still the most widespread shade on the planet. But lighter shades have evolved multiple times. DNA sequencing of Neanderthals found evidence of red hair and pale skin in Europe, and a different mutation from that found in modern humans. One theory is that fair hair – containing less UV-blocking melanin – evolved in Europe to permit more sunlight to reach the scalp, supporting the production of vitamin D in regions where deficiency is likely, but this might not explain all natural blonds. About 10% of the dark-skinned Indigenous people of the Melanesian Islands, and some Aboriginal Australians, have blond hair as children due to a unique genetic mutation.18. Hair can express, and oppressThe hair on our head is a powerful means of self-expression, and also oppression and control. There is a long history of forced hair removal as a means of removing cultural identity or dehumanisation, such as in Nazi concentration camps and residential schools for Indigenous children in North America. The ancient Maya shaved or ripped the hair off their enemies before cutting off their heads. Through history, and across cultures, enslaved people and criminals had their heads forcibly shorn to express their lower status. On the flipside, among men in particular, shaving the skull has been a way of demonstrating purity and devotion to God, with Buddhist and Jain monks the best-known examples. It demonstrates the importance of hair to belonging, Wearing says, with its removal a sign of “removal from society”.19. A ‘Hollywood wax’ is not so LAWhether or not to remove pubic hair continues to be debated, with the contemporary trend (at least for women) for sweeping removal often attributed to our pornified culture. However, Wearing says, pubic hair removal has always fallen in and out of favour. “There’s this back and forth we can see, through western history and cross-culturally.”20. So … whatisthe purpose of pubic hair?Of all the questions that persist about hair, this one remains one of the biggest, at least for Wearing. Both men and women grow hair around their genitalia from puberty, complicating a search for an answer as to why it evolved: “You need an explanation that works for both sexes,” Wearing says. This particular patch is also unique to humans. Wearing’s favoured theory, “almost by process of elimination”, is that pubic hair evolved to collect smells from sexual intercourse, communicating a current or potential mate’s activities. Wearing describes it as a “cheating detector … It’s really the only plausible idea, so far, that makes any sense – although again, it’s unproven.” Though many questions remain, the long and short of it is that hair is more fascinating than we might think.Anxious and Hairy: The Evolution and Culture of Human Hair by Judy Wearing is published on 8 October (Icon Books, £20).
