title: Terrible idea or major coup? Galliano’s Zara collection launches after Met controversy | Zara | The Guardian
description: Collaboration regarded as ‘really big thing’ for retailer in some quarters despite backlash around designer’s antisemitic remarks in 2011
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Collaboration regarded as ‘really big thing’ for retailer in some quarters despite backlash around designer’s antisemitic remarks in 2011
Content: John Galliano's first collection for Zara.Photograph: Steven MeiselView image in fullscreenJohn Galliano's first collection for Zara.Photograph: Steven MeiselZaraTerrible idea or major coup? Galliano’s Zara collection launches after Met controversyCollaboration regarded as ‘really big thing’ for retailer in some quarters despite backlash around designer’s antisemitic remarks in 2011Ellie Violet BramleyThu 1 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmonth after it was announced that a planned exhibition dedicated to fashion designerJohn Gallianoat New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art would not proceed, his debut collection for fast fashion company Zara has been released.Called Re{form}, it was, according to a press release, “authored by the couturier John Galliano. Built from our memory. Made for now.”Its launch in shops comes after controversy over plans to honour the former Dior designer, whowas found guiltyof a hate crime in 2011 after a series of racist and antisemitic rants, with an exhibition of his work at the Met and a corresponding Met gala – a juggernaut of popular culture viewed by billions globally online. The exhibitionwas cancelledbut had it gone ahead, it would have been only the third time such an honour had been bestowed on a living designer. The only others being Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo of Comme des Garçons in 2017.View image in fullscreenA young John Galliano, pictured in 1986.Photograph: E Hamilton West/The GuardianThe backlash to the plans were vehement and widespread, with Met patrons, New York politicians and prominent Jewish leaders objecting.Writing in the New York Times, his biographer Dana Thomaslabelled it a “terrible idea”, saying that “choosing this moment to glorify the life’s work of someone who was convicted of making antisemitic remarks … is downright bizarre”, and noting that “his infamous antisemitic rants were not an aberration”.Met Gala exhibition honoring John Galliano is cancelled after backlashRead moreIn other quarters in the fashion industry, not least in Anna Wintour’s corner, support for Galliano has been similarly full-throated. Many argue he has sufficiently atoned for his crimes. Others point out that it has been 15 years since Galliano, who was struggling with addiction at the time, committed them and that there ought to come a time for forgiveness.Gallianosaid in his statement withdrawing from the exhibition: “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it.”Given this fraught atmosphere and renewed attention on Galliano’s past, why hasZarapushed ahead with its plans?For Zara, says Orsola de Castro, designer and author, this is “the coup of their career, their life, their brand”. Fashion critic Philippe Pourhashemi agrees: “For Zara it’s still a major coup that they managed to get [Galliano] on board.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Steven Meisel“That’s a really, really big thing because if we really look at it from a rational point of view, it doesn’t really make sense that someone like him would work with a platform like that.”More tangibly, there are logistics. The collection, which was shot by acclaimed fashion photographer Steven Meisel, has been years – and a lot of money – in the making and for some, even in the immediate wake of the Met cancellation, Zara following suit was an unrealistic prospect. Online, and in the form of queues outside the Zara store on Bond Street on Thursday morning,there was huge excitement for the unveiling of the designs.Galliano has been working elsewhere in the fashion industry for years. Sacked by Dior in 2011, by 2013 he had returned to work, doinga short residency with New York designer Oscar de la Renta. From 2014 onwards he spent a decade as creative director of Margiela, bowing out on a final show in 2024 that waswidely celebrated in the industry as legendary and history-making. His designs have continued to appear even on the Met Gala red carpet: in 2024 Kim Kardashian wore a chainmail, corseted Galliano creation to walk the steps.The venerable Met and the high street are different beasts. Zara, which is owned by Inditex, the largest fashion retailer in the world, is a fast fashion brandthat has previously been criticised over allegations of unethical treatment of workers. “Zara has done a really good job at whitewashing its image, and Galliano is also a part of that,” says Pourhashemi.Why the Met’s John Galliano reversal shocked the fashion world: ‘There hadn’t been this much excitement since camp’Read moreIn terms of grappling with Galliano’s past, according to fashion expert and historian Tony Glenville: “His antisemitism and problems are something that in discussions I suspect they just thought, ‘this is fashion and we want his name on some clothes,’ simply a business deal.” Fashion as an industry isn’t inherently known for its ethics.Zara will be hoping that it bolsters its perceived fashion chops. The collection, prices for which run from £17.99 to £699, is being positioned as a dialogue between Galliano and the Zara archive – conceived from archival Zara garments, it will be produced in all new materials, rather than pre-existing stock.The collection is also being seen as a pitch by Zara to be seen as the brand of affordable luxury. In the age of Shein, Temu, Primark and supermarket fashion, it is, according to Pourhashemi, “vital, from a business standpoint, for Zara to distance itself”. It will also be hoping to differentiate itself from its own cut-price brand,Lefties, which launched in Liverpool last month. For Glenville, “all this is Inditex leaving the bottom price line to Lefties to do the hard work – and elevating Zara”.For Zara the move is likely more about reputation than actual sales. “It’s an absolute hook to draw us in,” says Glenville, noting that many garments from these designer collaborations never actually make it to the shop floor.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Steven MeiselGalliano is known for his theatrical, storybook designs, not for clothes that are inherently wearable. The designs are inspired by characters fromhis notorious 1984 graduate collection titled Les Incroyables: “Les Incroyables and les Merveilleuses – the defiant dandies and divas of post-revolutionary France.”Speaking to Vogue, Galliano said he “had no intentions to dumb down” for a more mainstream market.Galliano has signed a two-year contract, so the stakes are relatively low. “If he does a couple of collections a year in small quantities, they get the cachet without too much risk,” says Glenville. “If it’s phenomenally successful, they’ll extend his contract.”Zara declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsZaraJohn GallianoFashion industryShops and shoppingAntisemitismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley’s October style essentials: glam jeans, an irresistible coat and my shoes of the year | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Ready to fall back in love with getting dressed? Our fashion expert’s favourites bring layers, colour and just the right amount of drama
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Ready to fall back in love with getting dressed? Our fashion expert’s favourites bring layers, colour and just the right amount of drama
Content: JCM October EditView image in fullscreenJCM October EditGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley‘s editFashionJess Cartner-Morley’s October style essentials: glam jeans, an irresistible coat and my shoes of the yearReady to fall back in love with getting dressed? Our fashion expert’s favourites bring layers, colour and just the right amount of dramaThe best women’s autumn wardrobe updatesJess Cartner-MorleyThu 1 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOctober is when getting dressed starts to get interesting again. It is not yet cold enough for the full swaddling, but there is bandwidth for layers, texture, colour, a little drama. This month’s edit has all of the above. There is an irresistible coat, a tomato-red jumper to wake up everything you already own, and the bag I think may be the answer if you want something roomy that still feels neat. Also, stirrup leggings!Elsewhere, I’ve finally located the right sheer shirt for anyone ready to dip a toe into transparency, some extremely glamorous Marks & Spencer jeans and a lovely ring that looks much more special than its price. And because October is also the month when staying in starts to sound as appealing as going out, there are candles for the kitchen table. A sensible autumn shopping list, but with a little soul.A pop of redBodenCamilla cotton crew sweaterfrom£65£65 at Boden£65 at NextView image in fullscreenBoden Camilla cotton crew sweater in crimson red£65 at Boden£65 at NextA classic tomato-red sweater will give your wardrobe a lift. Layer it over a stripe with the collar and cuffs showing, or tie it over the shoulders of your blazer for a flash of colour and a potential extra layer if it gets chilly later. This is a cotton blend, so it won’t swelter you, and it has slightly full sleeves so you can layer it over a shirt without the sleeves bunching.BodenCamilla cotton crew sweaterfrom£65£65 at Boden£65 at NextAnother M&S winnerM&SHigh-waisted embellished barrel jeans£75£75 at M&SView image in fullscreenM&S high-waisted embellished barrel jeans£75 at M&SI was in M&S stalking a brilliant skirt I saw at the press day that doesn’t seem to be in store yet (will let you know when I find it!) and found these jeans, which look so fancy, all embellished with black beads and gems, and would make a knockout but easy-to-wear party outfit with a camisole and a tuxedo jacket.M&SHigh-waisted embellished barrel jeans£75£75 at M&SMy first new-season crushRixoMicah embroidered jacket£395£395 at RixoView image in fullscreenRixo Micah embroidered jacket£395 at RixoI am not going to pretend this is the most practical coat in the world, and you’ll have to wait for it because it’s on preorder for delivery in December. But look at it! Absolutely delicious. You probably already know Rixo for its brilliant dresses – it has a capsule collaboration coming toJohn Lewislater this month; I have seen it, and I think you will love it – and the coats are great too. With vintage-style embroidery, kimono-width sleeves and deep faux fur trim, you can wear this over a party dress to make a dramatic entrance, but it will also look brilliant over a T-shirt and jeans.RixoMicah embroidered jacket£395£395 at RixoI may have found your perfect bagKurt GeigerChelsea large slouch flap bag£289£289 at Kurt GeigerView image in fullscreenKurt Geiger Chelseaflap bag£289 at Kurt GeigerKurt Geiger has been London-based since the 1960s, when it opened a store on Bond Street. Lots of rainbow stripes, which I fully endorse as a brand-values symbol of kindness and inclusivity but don’t necessarily want to wear on a handbag. But the quality is great – details like adjustable shoulder straps, which really matter – and there are always classic colours as well as the rainbow. This shape is perfect if you want a large bag that still feels neat.Kurt GeigerChelsea large slouch flap bag£289£289 at Kurt GeigerMy shoe of the yearL’AgenceArleen kitten heel mules£345£345 at L’AgenceView image in fullscreenL’Agence Arleen kitten heel mules£345 at L’AgenceWhen I got these shoes I thought they were a classic I would wear occasionally, but I’ve worn them more than any other non-flat shoe for months now. I hate shoes that slow me down, so I generally ignore mules, but these are comfortable and secure, so you can walk at a normal speed. They are the perfect travel shoe because they take up so little room, weigh almost nothing, and make every outfit look better. They also come in leather, which would arguably be more practical, but the suede is so soft, and you can’t be sensible all the time.L’AgenceArleen kitten heel mules£345£345 at L’AgenceStirrup leggings: discussVuoriStirrup leggings£120£120 at VuoriView image in fullscreenVuori stirrup leggings£120 at VuoriI saw another fashion editor at Heathrow during the recent month of catwalk shows, wearing stirrup leggings and ballet pumps and a crew-neck sweater, and I believe I have finally found my version of what the youngsters call an Airport Fit. Yes, stirrup leggings are kind of silly, but that’s sort of the point – they turn leggings (boring) into a look. And they tie the leggings to your shoe, visually, I mean, so the silhouette is more elegant. This won’t be for everyone, but, you know, putting it out there. These are mine: I am a big fan of Vuori; the fabrics are so comfortable yet hold their shape.VuoriStirrup leggings£120£120 at VuoriA great sheer shirt and it’s on sale!ArketSilk organza shirt£81£81 at ArketView image in fullscreenArket silk organza shirt£81 at ArketSheer clothes aren’t just for red-carpet exhibitionists any more. Sheer layers are happening in real life. I think they work right now because they stop oversized, untucked outfits from drowning you. A sheer shirt is a good place to start: you can wear it over a tank top during the day, but it will also look dead chic and modern for evening over a lace bra if you are feeling slightly racy. Found this organza one in Arket, and I love the deep grey shade.ArketSilk organza shirt£81£81 at ArketPut a ring on itCarrie ElizabethVintage crest ring£59.50£59.50 at Carrie ElizabethView image in fullscreenCarrie Elizabeth vintage crest ring£59.50 at Carrie ElizabethCarrie Elizabeth jewellery has been around for a decade and is gaining traction – it is in Liberty for the first time this season – because in a market that often feels divided into cheap trend-led baubles and eye-wateringly expensive fine jewellery, it offers affordable pieces that feel personal and special. This 14-carat gold vermeil ring is beautifully detailed – it makes you want to look closer, which I love – with an elegant, slim band.Carrie ElizabethVintage crest ring£59.50£59.50 at Carrie ElizabethIdeal autumnal skirt situationNobody’s ChildHerringbone pleated skirtfrom£79£79 at Nobody’s Child£79 at AsosView image in fullscreenNobody’s Child herringbone pleated skirt£79 at Nobody’s Child£79 at AsosThis perfect, kicky little skirt has amatching herringbone blazer. The suit has a cute Cher-in-Clueless energy to it, but I’d wear this with a rugby shirt, black tights and biker boots.Nobody’s ChildHerringbone pleated skirtfrom£79£79 at Nobody’s Child£79 at AsosIt is candle seasonSøstrene GreneBi-colour candles£4.12£4.12 at Søstrene GreneView image in fullscreenSøstrene Grene bi-colour candles, set of two£4.12 at Søstrene GreneScented candles get all the love these days, but I love an old-fashioned taper candle as a cheap and cheering way to brighten up the kitchen table. The shell pink and electric blue colour combination is giving Roksanda energy.Søstrene GreneBi-colour candles£4.12£4.12 at Søstrene GreneFor more, readthe best women’s autumn wardrobe updates (some are even free)Explore more on these topicsFashionJess Cartner-Morley‘s editWomen's coats and jacketsWomen's topsWomen's shoesAccessoriesHandbagsWomen's shirtsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pierpaolo Piccioli presents ‘most personal show’ at Balenciaga | Balenciaga | The Guardian
description: Italian designer imbues collection with signature flourishes and style rooted in the craft of the couture atelier
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Italian designer imbues collection with signature flourishes and style rooted in the craft of the couture atelier
Content: Pierpaolo Piccioli wore his signature coral necklace and placed a huge sculpture of undersea coral crafted from fabric in the middle of the catwalk.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPierpaolo Piccioli wore his signature coral necklace and placed a huge sculpture of undersea coral crafted from fabric in the middle of the catwalk.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesBalenciagaPierpaolo Piccioli presents ‘most personal show’ at BalenciagaItalian designer imbues collection with signature flourishes and style rooted in the craft of the couture atelierJess Cartner-MorleyThu 1 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was “the most personal show I have done here”, the designer Pierpaolo Piccioli said after his Balenciaga presentation atParis fashion weekon Thursday.Piccioli, who always wears a coral necklace, placed a monumental sculpture of undersea coral crafted from fabric in the middle of the catwalk. Like CristóbalBalenciaga, Piccioli is both a maximalist and a minimalist. He likes boldness but not fuss, each look one audacious idea executed cleanly. A floor-length ivory cape fastened with a simple gold clasp. A black suit with one bold slash of tangerine at the jacket hem. A gown covered from neck to ankle in bubbles of organza.View image in fullscreenBold: a model wears a black suit with a slash of tangerine at the jacket hem at the Balenciaga fashion show.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty Images“I like surfaces to be either entirely embellished or super clean,” he said. He loves colour for how instinctively we react to it, because “how you feel in your clothes is much more important than how you look in them”.A year into the job, Piccioli has his reasons to feel the need to stake Balenciaga’s territory as his own. He used the show to remind the Paris audience that his way of making clothes, which is rooted in the craft of the couture atelier rather than in contemporary obsessions with branding and virality and the attention economy, is what Cristobal himself would have wanted for his house.View image in fullscreenAudacious: a model in a dramatic floor-length ivory cape fastened with a simple gold clasp.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesWith Balenciaga sales declining, particularly in menswear, which had become a key source of revenue under the previous designer, Demna, there have been rumblings around Piccioli’s future. A departure after such a brief tenure would be unusual, but in a bleak global market luxury houses are jittery and impatient for results.Demna’s Balenciaga, with its catwalk shock tactics and apocalypse-cosplay high-end hoodies, was polarising but undeniably compelling. The arrival of Piccioli, a charming Italian couturier whose show notes, signed with kisses, speak of “joy and light” and “mutual nourishment”, whose passion is for making women look beautiful, was a radical change of direction. In March, Balenciaga collaborated with teen drama Euphoria, an unlikely tie up which suggested the designer was being encouraged to re-engage a streetwear-loving clientele who were drifting away.View image in fullscreenMaximalist: Piccioli says he wants to share his enthusiasm for Balenciaga’s couture heritage with customers who are not in the market for ballgowns.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesPiccioli wants to share his enthusiasm for Balenciaga’s couture heritage with customers who are not in the market for ballgowns. He brought couture techniques to work on wardrobe basics, giving a white shirt a dramatic peplum hem and a pair of ripped jeans a moulded hourglass waist. “I like shirts, I like jeans – I like the dignity of them,” he said. “This job is about creating desirability in something familiar, by presenting it in a different way.”Explore more on these topicsBalenciagaLuxury goods sectorFashion weeksParis fashion weekParisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stepping back in time: a historic walk along Dorset’s Jurassic Coast | Dorset holidays | The Guardian
description: A ride in a water taxi transforms a stunning hike from Lyme Regis to West Bay into a perfect circular route
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A ride in a water taxi transforms a stunning hike from Lyme Regis to West Bay into a perfect circular route
Content: Golden Cap, the highest point on the crumbling, fossil-rich cliffs of the Jurassic Coast.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyView image in fullscreenGolden Cap, the highest point on the crumbling, fossil-rich cliffs of the Jurassic Coast.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyDorset holidaysStepping back in time: a historic walk along Dorset’s Jurassic CoastA ride in a water taxi transforms a stunning hike from Lyme Regis to West Bay into a perfect circular routeJon WoolcottThu 1 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany favour a circular walk, but you can give a linear one new shape with the addition of a novel form of transport. My wife Helen, our friend Tom Cox and I take the water taxi – a rigid inflatable boat (Rib) – from West Bay on Dorset’s coast to Lyme Regis, with a plan to walk back to our starting point.The rain stops as the boat leaves the harbour, the views open along Chesil Beach to low-lying Portland to the east, and west to Lyme Regis; on the far horizon, we can see Start Point on the Devon coast. Our skipper, Nick, is highly knowledgable and takes time to stop and point out the history of the shoreline and the treacherous waters of Lyme Bay. The seabed is studded with wrecks – fishing boats and smugglers’ ships, but some are from the two world wars.View image in fullscreenThe Cobb at Lyme Regis.Photograph: Martin Augustus/AlamyOn New Year’s Day 1915, the battleshipHMS Formidablewas torpedoed by a German submarine. Of its crew of 750, no more than 200 survived. In the second world war, the Dorset coast was a huge mustering station for the allied forces in preparation for D-day. During Exercise Tiger, a large-scale rehearsal for the Normandy landings, hundreds of American service personnel were killed in an attack by German boats later known as theBattle of Lyme Bay– the wreck sites are now designated war graves.At Lyme Regis, we disembark on to the Cobb, the harbour wall that snakes unsteadily into the bay and was made famous by Jane Austen, who had Louisa jump from it in Persuasion,and by John Fowles, who lived in Lyme. The movie adaptation of his novel The French Lieutenant’s Woman starred Meryl Streep as Sarah Woodruff.Its famous trailerbegins with the actor sweeping across the Cobb, the hood of her cloak covering her face. For the filming, many buildings in the town were given a 19th-century facade. For a film that plays with time, it seems appropriate that the town’s bookshop kept its temporary fascia for many years.double quotation markIn 1725, Henry Fielding, then aged 17, attempted to abduct his cousin Sarah, with whom he was infatuated, from LymeOur walk back to West Bay is 10 miles long and begins not along the coast but by heading inland. The west Dorset coast is friable – the cliffs keep falling on to the beaches, and the path to Charmouth takes a diversion through a golf course. It wasn’t always like this: once there was a coastal road, Long Entry, between the two settlements. In 1725, Henry Fielding, then aged 17, attempted to abduct his cousin Sarah, with whom he was infatuated, from Lyme. The future novelist made his escape along Long Entry before being stopped by her guardian.View image in fullscreenThe statue of Mary Anning in Lyme Regis.Photograph: Darren Galpin/AlamyOur walk back to the coast is interrupted bya sculpture on the path. The shape of a woman, angular and determined, a hammer in her outstretched right hand, the other holding above her head the skeleton of a prehistoric animal. There’sanother recent sculptureof the same subject, Mary Anning, in Lyme Regis, recording her importance to palaeontology and to the town, but this upland creature, made by Greta Berlin, is wilder, perfectly suited to its woodland setting. The representation of the fossil held aloft is Anning’s discovery:Ichthyosaurus anningae. One cannot walk this section of Dorset’s coast without being aware of its ancient past and the fragile geology close to the surface. Our boat trip began on crumbly sandstone, which gave way to fossil-rich clay as we travelled west.Charmouth is a pretty village with no harbour; its shallow waters make it popular with those learning to swim or paddleboard. This next section of the South West Coast Path, to West Bay, coincides with theMonarch’s Way, the route that Charles II took to flee to mainland Europe after the civil war. Our day is more peaceful but the path is steep. We’re grateful for Tom’s company – his latest novel,Everything Will Swallow You,is infused with the history and landscape of the Dorset coast and his knowledge enlivens our walk, as do the pasties he brings, baked by his wife, Ellie.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Anchor Inn at Seatown.Photograph: Darren Galpin/AlamyWe pass the remains ofSt Gabriel’s Church, which fell into disuse in the 18th century, although smugglers found within its walls useful shelter for their contraband. Soon we’re onGolden Cap, the highest point on the south coast – 191 metres (627ft) above sea level, with extraordinary views over Lyme Bay. At Seatown, we stop at theAnchor Innfor refreshments, meeting friends who have opted for a shorter walk. From Thorncombe Beacon, we descend to Eype Mouth – in Old English Eype is “Steep Place”; the church in this secluded village was chosen by PJ Harvey to record Let England Shake, a Mercury prize-winning album rich with the echoes of war.There are further reminders of the coast’s fragility on the final stretch to West Bay – one sign references a cliff fall in 2020, and the path is frequently redirected to safer routes. West Bay, a small stone town, was once the harbour from where Bridport exported its rope and was originally called Bridport Harbour, but had its name changed by the railway company hoping to attract tourists. The railway is long gone – its station now hosts a restaurant in railway carriages – but West Bay, with its stalls for chips and views back towards Lyme, is a fitting place to end, a town out of time.OS Explorer 116(Lyme Regis & Bridport) covers the entire walk from Lyme Regis to West Bay.TheLyme Bay Water Taxioperates during the summer months;there is a year-roundbus servicebetween West Bay and Lyme Regis.Jon Woolcott is the author ofReal DorsetandThe Tattooed Hills, Journeys to Chalk FiguresExplore more on these topicsDorset holidaysWalking holidaysWalkingEngland holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I went to America’s largest gathering of astrologers. It was a battle over how to read the stars | History of science | The Guardian
description: Now a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?
Author: Katherine Rowland
Headline: Now a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?
Content: ‘Astrology is really an art form,’ said one practitioner at the United Astrology Conference in Chicago. ‘There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.’Illustration: Dajah Callen/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Astrology is really an art form,’ said one practitioner at the United Astrology Conference in Chicago. ‘There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.’Illustration: Dajah Callen/The GuardianHistory of scienceI went to America’s largest gathering of astrologers. It was a battle over how to read the starsNow a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?Katherine RowlandThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTShare“The dwarf planets change everything,” said the woman with the smart haircut as she made amind blowngesture with her fingertips, temples to air.I am at the United Astrology Conference, the largest professional gathering of astrologers in the world, in downtownChicago. Around me, vendors are hoping to excite the 1,500 attenders, flogging books, tracts, affiliations, proprietary apps and various software programs that have replaced the laborious chart-drawing of yore.I admit, I had come expecting a crowd flaunting amulets and sweeping cloaks. But apart from the occasional streak of purple hair and wispy wizard beard, what I encountered was an even weirder normcore of podiatry-sensible footwear and Oxford button-downs. At a glance, it could almost have been a trade convention of insurance adjusters: experts gathered to contemplate the future, assess risk, gauge the impact of events beyond our control.double quotation markThe single biggest problem astrologers have is that they believe in astrology too muchMark JonesIn that sense, the room reflected astrology’s broader transformation. Astrology is now a $15bnindustry. From the marginal, it has crept into the mainstream. A 2025 Pew Researchreportfound that 30% of American adults consult astrology, tarot or a fortune teller at least once a year, and 43% of women under 50 claim to “believe in astrology”.But its influence on the zeitgeist has hardly made astrology more settled. As I sat down with my interlocutor, her companion Alan Clay, founder of Dwarf Planet University, tells me the mainstays of the solar system can only get you so far. Recent astral discoveries, he said, have enriched the picture, offering a view into the unconscious through bodies drifting in theKuiper belt, billions of miles beyond the sun.On the wall behind his booth, the price of a reading has been slashed from $29 to $9.He pulled my chart, a term that I learn carries tremendous weight, something between destiny and the template of my very being. There is the dwarf planetMakemakein my fifth house (I too, had to look this up), which carries bold implications for creative expression and, less attractively, secret or potentially bruising sexual affairs.Some of this resonated. And therein lies the problem. Part of astrology’s current appeal is how quickly it can make itself feel personal – and persuasive.Like any sufficiently established field, modern astrology has developed its own hierarchies, factions and grudges. There are fights over tradition and fears about AI; impatient zoomers butting heads with baffled boomers; older men with reputations for harassment; and quieter epistemic disputes. (Has no one noticed, for instance, that almost all the planets are male?)Beneath all of it was a more fundamental question: who gets to interpret the stars?“Astrology is the oldest of the occult sciences,” writes scholar Benson Bobrick in his 2005 history, The Fated Sky. “It is also the origin of science itself.”For millennia, people have looked to the heavens for guidance and meaning: when to hunt and harvest, how to navigate the seas. The night presents a tapestry of gods and heroes, myths and parables. The stars are indifferent to these projections, of course, but they reveal a great deal about the people making them.The basic premise of astrology is that the configuration of the sky at the moment of your birth leaves its imprint on your constitution and life trajectory. As above, so below. If in the past, the stars reflected a collective social order, today they are more often treated as a vast personal mirror.The principle is straightforward. What astrologers make of it is not.I arrived at theconference, which sold out of its advance weekend passes, with what seemed like a simple question: what does astrology mean to the practitioner in 2026? Moving from room to windowless room, I quickly realized the question was less simple than naive.“Astrology is really an art form,” said one seasoned practitioner. “There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.”To another, it was a spiritual practice, a means of communing with the ancients. It was unscientific, and also “notnota science”. It was a field of infinite study: “We’ll never get to the bottom of it.” It was moreover a language, composed of symbols and competing dialects, but nonetheless extant. “No one questions whether Spanish is real,” the astrologer Samuel Reynolds told me.We asked astrologers about major life decisions they’ve made because of astrology – videoAnd yet, in one lecture I attended, Mark Jones, an astrologer and psychotherapist, opened with the controversial claim: “Astrology is not real.” At his words, a murmur rolled through the room, before he elaborated: “not in the sense that you are”. By his telling, the planets exert their influence on the psyche through a theory of object relations. He clicked through slides, and spoke with great authority on the spatial impact of Neptune and the role of the moon in the developmental self.But that notwithstanding, he said: “The single biggest problem astrologers have is that they believe in astrology too much.”Just what to believe in and what methods to follow are open and contentious questions. “There are as many branches of astrology as there are astrologers,” one attender told me, before rattling off a list. There’s horary astrology, an oracle for a single moment –is the person I made eyes with on the subway someone special?– and electional astrology, dealing with the timing of events (one woman told me that, much to the chagrin of her friends and family, her chart dictated a 7.30am wedding.)Geminis get colds, Scorpios get STDs: inside the ‘science’ of medieval astrologyRead moreThere’s also evolutionary astrology, which maps the soul over lifetimes; mundane astrology, concerning politics and society; and medical astrology. It goes on: relational, predictive, Jungian (the Jungian vibes are strong).Above all, it was presented to me as a kind of security blanket: a system for understanding the inexplicable, a way to make sense of a shitty day, a means to grasp the contours of current upheavals and find solace in their eventual end. During Covid, one astrologer explained: “People were really looking for answers. They were like, ‘Sky, tell me what’s going on.’”The 185 experts who presented were doing what people at conferences do: establishing hierarchies and professionalizing a crowded, competitive field. A conference, after all, is an occasion for conferring legitimacy and codifying the rules of the trade.In astrology, this raises some obvious complications. If you are claiming to see something about a person’s future, what are you responsible for telling them?Some clients, I was told, “just want the good stuff”. Other practitioners prefer to rip off the Band-Aid – if dark days lie ahead, it’s better to make an ominous prognostication so the afflicted can prepare or hunker down as necessary.But what happens when you get it wrong?“There is no wrong,” Clay told me. “There are different interpretations. Right or wrong is a Saturnian construct, it’s useful but doesn’t help us understand these new energies.”That is not, however, the abiding consensus. One of the conference seminars was devoted to learning from readings that went awry.“When people are giving predictions, there is at least a five or 10% chance that it’s not right, and the stakes are huge,” said Kay Taylor, president of the UAC and the Organization for Professional Astrology.Another astrologer illustrated the stakes with a story from her own practice. Based on her reading of a client’s chart, she concluded that both of the client’s parents would die within the year. She felt obliged to convey this information, whereupon the client quit their job and moved across the country to be with their parents for the end.“But they didn’t die!” She exclaimed with surprising pride.That was years ago. Mom and dad are still alive and well. Yet the astrologer assured me that even though the prediction was off, the message remained sound. Her client got to enjoy some bonus time with her parents.double quotation markEvery person is a complicated mathematical formulaCeleste Nash-WeningerGaffes like this are what make training critical, I was told. No fewer than six professional organizations were sponsoring this year’s gathering – the National Council for Geocosmic Research is the only one without “astrology” in its name – and they offered various routes to affiliated credentialing and curricula, ranging from astrological markers of ADHD to advanced training in asteroids.Celeste Nash-Weninger, from the American Federation of Astrologers, told me: “Every person is a complicated mathematical formula.” She used to be intimidated by the graphs and numbers, but after taking recommended courses – “and they’re tough: eight hours of math and delineation” – she has confidence in “how the heavens move”.Whether advanced math is required for mastery is open to debate. But there is one thing nearly everyone here agrees on: technology has made astrology more accessible – but also, some practitioners worry, diluted its expertise.“Before, people had to do it all by hand,” said Leslie Benson, an astrologer who works for AstroGraph, maker of the popular TimePassages app. “You had to have an ephemeris, where you looked up every placement. You had to draw it all. Now it’s instant.”Most have eagerly embraced the new tools; after all, if software can do the calculations, practitioners have more time for the interpretive work. But they also remove one of the barriers by which skill was once recognized.Artificial intelligence is where most everyone here draws the line. Of course, AI was inevitable: Pluto is in Aquarius and Uranus is in Gemini – yikes – but the contemporary astrologer, at least according to one seminar, must safeguard the personal and spiritual component of the work. “Embracing Uranus,” it advised, referring to the dark trickster of the cosmos, “without losing your soul.”Co-Star, the astrology app that has brought personalized charts and algorithmic readings to millions of users, is notably absent from the conference, and attenders clucked in disapproval overnewsof its recent acquisition by the AI startup Midjourney. The technology that made astrology accessible to anyone with a phone is also the technology that threatens to make the astrologer – the human interpreter, the trained practitioner, the person who knows what all those symbols mean – obsolete.Throughout the conference I asked around why astrology inspires such avid faith, why it appears to “work”. Some practitioners offered explanations involving gravity – the extremely subtle but no less palpable effects of celestial bodies on our own bodies. Or perhaps it is about the moon, whose effects on the tides might somehow produce corresponding swells within us. “We’re 80% water,” one astrologer offered.On three separate occasions I was told, “the proof is in the pudding”. and so with an equal mix of trepidation and enticement I agreed when Nash-Weninger, of the American Federation of Astrologers, volunteered to give me a cold read. Though she assured me she was a “professional” and could tell me “some things” about myself, I could not imagine how, on the basis of my scant data – birth date, time and location – she could uncover anything about my life. But in the name of research I let her plug my information into an app on her phone.“Ooh!” she exclaimed. I experienced an instant tingle – was this a good chart? I was born, she pronounced, in a great conjunction year, “just like Jesus Christ … in theory.”My sun is conjunct with Mercury – “that’s the writer” – and my north node indicates that “if you did something creatively you would probably be known for it later”, she said.It was hard to resist the ego bath of it all, especially when she said: “I’m going to take a chance and say your career might get really big. You might have opportunities that are huge.”At the time, I confess, I didn’t preoccupy myself with the caveating “might”, hearing only the allusions to success. The mere fact that I was born in time and place conferred a thrill: the universe had designs forme.But then she paused and squinted at a corner of my chart.“One thing I want to say: take good care of your liver and kidneys.” She gave me a pointed look and gravely intoned, Jupiter lords over my house of health issues.And then, graver still, she said she was “a little concerned about this dark moon” in my house of love.When I mentioned my recent divorce, she nodded in anof coursesort of way.Maurice Fernandez, a popular evolutionary astrologer, was giving a lecture on Chiron in Taurus. Astronomically, Chiron is an icy body discovered in 1977 that travels in a long ellipse between Saturn and Uranus, taking roughly 50 years to circle the sun.It was named for the centaur of Greek mythology – and this is where the afternoon’s drama began.Fernandez assured the audience that Chiron was not an “add on” to the chart but a “central part”. In myth, Chiron was the immortal son of the titan Cronos and the sea nymph Philyra. When a poisoned arrow struck him, he suffered unbearable pain and eventually chose to surrender his perpetuity.In astrological terms, Fernandez explained, Chiron represents a confrontation with mortality: the “wound of invisibility”, “hubris” and “the freedom to be sovereign”.View image in fullscreen‘Astrology is not therapy, but it is therapeutic,’ writes astrologer Chani Nicholas.Illustration: Dajah Callen/The GuardianAs he spoke a logic came into focus, wherein a celestial body receives a name, the name summons a story, and the story reaches through the light years to our fragile, earthbound lives.Chiron was just leaving Aries, Fernandez said, a transit that explained the #MeToo movement and the rise of the manosphere. George Floyd’s death and Black Lives Matter were also, he said, the stuff of Chiron. He needed to check the numbers, but Chiron in Aries had seen “a greater statistic of political violence”. Myth is a capacious place.What was coming as Chiron entered Taurus could be glimpsed via the past: sustainability, finances, land, resources. Stalin’s agrarian policies, Fernandez stated, also bore the hallmark of the roving centaur. He drew out the words: “Three to 5 million people died because of a manmade food crisis.” Gasps rippled through the room.Then the stock market crashed. A decade of poverty. More gasps.What gripped the audience was not necessarily the work of the stars, but rather the stunning facts of history, which, like myth, is a generous tool in astrology. A pattern is imposed on a bygone moment, and that pattern, once established, lends credibility to the prediction of what comes next.While figures like Fernandez swam through a field of palpable adoration, some of the greatest gusts of enthusiasm were reserved for the conference’s plenary speaker,Chani Nicholas, whose star is among the most ascendant in the field – at least to some.Nicholas, who has nearly 700,000 followers on Instagram, has built a devoted following around a blend of astrology and social justice. In an August post announcing Virgo season, she called for readers to “Abolish ICE and data centers and billionaires! … Manifesting a socialist utopia! Life is short! Let Gaza Live! There’s another eclipse coming!”Her company, Chani, promises employees a salary floor of $80,000 and comprehensive benefits, including “unlimited menstrual leave for people with uteruses”.double quotation markThere’s something going on that is too accurate for me to dismiss [astrology] out of handIan Anthony WallerRather than delivering a conventional keynote, Nicholas sat in conversation with Samuel Reynolds, a former fundamentalist Baptist youth minister who came to astrology as a skeptic and, in the course of trying to debunk it, found himself converted.“Extremes are extreme-ing,” Nicholas told the room, citing floods in Nepal, rising inequality, and populations straining precious resources. “If Pluto in Aquarius is about a revolution, then the robots are definitely out to get us.”Nicholas spoke directly to a younger generation that had shown up in Chicago in droves. “We’ve never had so many newcomers,” one of the conference organizers observed, not without ambivalence.The tensions were already thrumming before Nicholas took the stage. A scheduled speaker had been removed from the program after using the N-word on a podcast over the summer, prompting a small but vocal schism among attenders. For some, the episode represented an overdue reckoning; for others, it was evidence that astrology was being remade according to the dictates of a younger, more censorious culture. An antiracism panel followed.At Nicholas’s keynote, the divide became harder to miss. When she mentioned white supremacy, a handful of people got up and left. But the overwhelming number applauded when she described astrology as an essential tool for organizing in the fight against fascism – and AI.It was tempting to see this as a generational culture war imported wholesale into a trade convention. But it was also about something more fundamental: who gets to decide what astrology is for, who gets to speak for it, and what counts as knowledge in the first place.That question has particular force in a field that has never had much institutional authority to begin with. You don’t need a degree to practice astrology. You don’t need a license to create a chart, or credentials to interpret one. This makes astrology unusually democratic – and unusually susceptible to the creation of new gatekeepers.In times of uncertainty, the argument goes, people reach for systems that offer, if not certainty, then comfort: faith, mysticism, pop psychology protocols for surviving the collapse of familiar structures.“Astrology is not therapy, but it is therapeutic,” writes Nicholas. “It’s a relentless reminder that we are the way that we are on purpose.” If the self has become a more demanding and illegible creature, here is another way to make sense of it.There is something to this. When the world feels chaotic, when our purpose seems opaque, it is appealing to believe that chaos has a pattern, that this crappy stretch will end, that the planets are moving and so, eventually, will you.But the explanation is also too easy. We are always living in “interesting” times. Astrology has survived wars, plagues, depressions and the scientific method.How astrology paved the way for predictive analyticsRead moreReynolds, the former Baptist minister, offered another possibility. Young people who came of age with Donald Trump and Covid, he said, may have a different relationship to authority. They spent crucial developmental years watching institutions struggle to explain the present, while science was often hauled off to the chopping block. Truth itself became unstable.Perhaps, he suggested, they are simply more comfortable inhabiting several systems of knowledge at once: data and mysticism, evidence and meaning.In this sense, astrology is not necessarily an alternative to facticity so much as a parallel language, asking a different set of questions. It does not have to win an argument with physics to be useful to someone trying to understand why their marriage ended.Before leaving Chicago, I found myself in conversation with the sociologist Ian Anthony Waller, who was there to research the gendered nature of astrological belief. He also described himself as a “solid seven” on his own scale of faith.I had come to see astrology less as an impossible-to-validate predictive model than a cool caress of reassurance. The stars see you and whatever happens is happening for a reason.But how, I wondered, as a scholar, did he manage to maneuver between a healthy skepticism and an embrace of a system of elaborately calculated comforts?“Sometimes astrologers will say things and I’m like, ‘that is madness,’” Waller said. “But then other times, things that I read and then see in the world – there’s something going on that is too accurate for me to dismiss out of hand.”It was incumbent for him as a scholar to understand why it appears to work. “If anybody ever really figures it,” Waller said, “it’s probably not going to be an astrologer, it’s probably going to be an astrophysicist or a physicist or somebody from Nasa who makes a connection between launch failures and Mercury or something like that.“And that’s going to be the big eureka moment – or the big Uranian innovation, as we would say in this culture.”

title: Country diary: Which tree sounds the best in the wind? Take a bough, the poplar | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Frome, Somerset: With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the trees
Author: Derek Niemann
Headline: Frome, Somerset: With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the trees
Content: Riverside poplars, Frome.Photograph: Sarah NiemannView image in fullscreenRiverside poplars, Frome.Photograph: Sarah NiemannCountry diaryTrees and forestsCountry diary: Which tree sounds the best in the wind? Take a bough, the poplarFrome, Somerset:With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the treesDerek NiemannThu 1 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe wind-catchers along the bottom of the valley miss nothing. Even the lightest breath has them whispering. And when the wind strengthens, they do a good imitation of the river streaming over boulders below their feet. Truly, when it blows, it pours.Pass a poplar and you are enjoying the best example of psithurism, the sound of wind in trees. All this growing season, I have listened politely to oaks, alders and willows, but if I rocked up in a pub looking for chatty company, I’d want a poplar on the bar stool next to me.View image in fullscreenThe noisy leaves of a poplar.Photograph: Sarah NiemannThe name psithurism seems to have been conjured up from Greek roots as recently as the 19th century, yet the practice is as old as humanity. It exposes a curious and inescapable fact – wind itself has no voice. The explorer‑conservationistJohn Muirtramped many a mile through America’s wild lands, observing that “winds are advertisements of what they touch”.He may well have been thinking of talkative, animated aspens, but all members ofthe poplar clanare physiologically equipped to shoot the breeze with a wide range of sound and movement. Every broad leaf,shaped like an ace of spades, is well separated from its neighbour on a long stem. Every leaf is therefore washing on a line. Blow, wind, blow.Right now, conditions are what meteorologists call a fresh breeze, enough to bring out a sway and a swoosh, the noise a tide over fine pebbles, the sight upper trunks tilting back and forth to the rhythm.The top boughs are visible evidence of wind as wave, for each sprig springs to life in turn, hundreds of leaves twirling at once. The overall effect is something akin to a host of green glitterballs. Close up, each leaf appears to be spinning in agony or ecstasy, desperate to break free or stay attached. Photosynthesis must be quite a giddy wonder, for how do rotating cells catch the sun?Over the coming weeks, these wind chimes will break, their leaves raining down. And up above, in the so-tall trees, there will be a new percussion, the click-clack creak of branch on branch, the incoming drumbeat of winter.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsTrees and forestsCountry diaryRural affairsAutumnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire
Content: Al-Mawasi in Rafah in 2023 (left) and 2026, with huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline.Composite: GoogleView image in fullscreenAl-Mawasi in Rafah in 2023 (left) and 2026, with huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline.Composite: GoogleGazaNew Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in GazaSatellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefireJason BurkeandEithne StauntonThu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn update toGoogle Mapshas revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants.The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago.Gaza 2023-2026: al-Mawasi, RafahThey show huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline, often within a few metres of the sea. Gaza’s once busy main port, now badly damaged and empty of fishing boats, is surrounded by makeshift accommodation. Any available open space inGazaCity is packed with shacks, tents and huts.Gaza 2023-2026: Tel al-Sultan, RafahThe images also show massive damage to northern towns such as Beit Lahiya and Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Major neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable.Swaths of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed to the ground.Gaza 2023-2026: Istiqlal Mosque, Khan YounisMore than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where about 82% of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.A recentUN assessmentestimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025.Gaza 2023-2026: Beit Lahiya“The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestinetold the Guardianlast month. The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian problems.More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, mostly civilians. The conflict was triggered by a surprise attack by Hamas into Israel in October 2023, in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineGoogle MapsIsraelUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Inside the undersea kingdom: the secret, sinister battle to control what lies beneath the waves | Books | The Guardian
description: Every day, trillions of dollars, oil and gas and 99% of the world’s web traffic move through undersea pipelines under no state’s protection. With superpowers and corporations now vying for control, should we be worried about this potential new wild west of geopolitical power?
Author: Aida Edemariam
Headline: Every day, trillions of dollars, oil and gas and 99% of the world’s web traffic move through undersea pipelines under no state’s protection. With superpowers and corporations now vying for control, should we be worried about this potential new wild west of geopolitical power?
Content: ‘In this environment of geopolitical tension, it feels like an incredible vulnerability’ … undersea security expert Elisabeth Braw.Photograph: Greg Funnell/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘In this environment of geopolitical tension, it feels like an incredible vulnerability’ … undersea security expert Elisabeth Braw.Photograph: Greg Funnell/The GuardianThe ideas interviewBooksInterviewInside the undersea kingdom: the secret, sinister battle to control what lies beneath the wavesAida EdemariamEvery day, trillions of dollars, oil and gas and 99% of the world’s web traffic move through undersea pipelines that bear no state’s protection. With superpowers and corporations vying for control, should we be worried about this new wild west?Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Christmas Day 2024, six weeks before Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were due to disconnect themselves from Russia’s power grid, a Finnish engineer was just about to sit down to lunch when his phone rang. He was responsible for the Finnish side of the undersea cables that keep Finland and the Baltic states supplied with electricity, and one was malfunctioning. Within a couple of hours, authorities knew that a Cook Islands-registered tanker called the Eagle S, part of the shadow fleet carrying sanctioned Russian oil, in this case to Egypt, had sailed over the cable at the moment and location at which it had stopped working. The coastguard hailed the Eagle S. Were their anchors up? Yes, they replied – though they did not seem to check – and sailed on.Three hours later the ship hit another four cables in quick succession, nearly hobbling internet provision in Finland and Estonia – and was minutes away from a major electricity cable and the Balticconnector, which supplies the two countries with gas. Finland scrambled the border guard, which pulled up alongside the tanker and demanded the crew take up its anchor. But the Eagle S was not in Finnish territorial waters: the authorities could not force the captain to comply, and they did not know who or what might come to his aid.View image in fullscreen‘It makes no sense’ … Seized oil tanker Eagle S in Porvoo, Finland.Photograph: Jussi Nukari/Rex/Shutterstock“It makes no sense,” says Swedish security expert Elisabeth Braw, leaning over a table in a well-upholstered corner of a private members’ club steps away from the Bank of England. She has spent the last couple of years talking to undersea engineers and coastguards about this and other similar incidents, rootling through accident investigation documents and court transcripts and Zoom-calling the small, specialised crews who have to go out and repair the damaged cables, often under extremely challenging conditions, asking them to show her what they are doing out there at sea. Now she has written it all up into a book bristling with enough incident to supply several action movies. “It makes no sense that you would drag your anchor across five cables, dozens of kilometres. No trained seafarer would do that. And they can say, ‘Well, I had no idea. We didn’t notice a thing.’ And how can you prove that that’s not the case?”The Undersea War paints an extraordinary picture of the bottom of the ocean, of fish and plant life threading through shipwrecks and junk thrown overboard – and especially of the “undersea spaghetti bowl” made of miles and miles of gas and oil pipes and electricity, telegraph and fibreoptic cables, thelongest of which is 45,000km longand some of which are so delicate “even an inquisitive fish could damage them”. Vast amounts of electricity and oil, 95-99% of global internet traffic and $10tn (£7.75tn) of financial transactions travel through this system every day. “We assume the cloud is in the sky,” Braw writes, “but it’s underwater.” It is a system both incredibly fragile – take out a few cables off the coast of New York and New Jersey, and “Wall Street could become kneecapped in very short order”, as a Republican senator told her – and a source of great power, not least to anyone inclined to sabotage.View image in fullscreen‘We assume the cloud is in the sky, but it’s under water’ … Elisabeth Braw.Photograph: Greg Funnell/The GuardianBraw, who has a direct, unfussy confidence and a dry sense of humour, began as a journalist before retraining in national security and specifically in so-called “grey zone” or sub-threshold threats (disinformation, election interference, cyber-attacks, cable sabotage). A government adviser (she won’t say which governments, only that they’re in Nato), and senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, she traces her interest back to watching Polish lorries loitering with intent around a cold war airbase near her childhood home in southern Sweden. The first newspaper article she remembers – she had just learned to read – was about a Soviet submarine that ran aground off the nearby city of Karlskrona in 1981, “the Soviet captain standing on top of the submarine” – she raises her arms as if in surrender.double quotation markWhat if Trump got mad at Spain, which he often does, and told Google to disconnect it?A couple of years ago she was called as an expert witness to aHouse of Commons Defence Committee inquiryinto grey-zone threats and was struck that while the parliamentarians were serious, and knowledgable about the subject, they were “taken aback by the realisation that it’s very hard to protect undersea infrastructure. It’s not like you can say, ‘Oh, well, here’s what we should do. It’s expensive, but it’s going to happen.’ That solution doesn’t exist.” The thing that still amazes her is that “behind every email, credit card payment, and Zoom call is an ocean worker” – and just how few of them there are.Talking to Braw, it’s impossible not to be struck by how oblivious most people are to what she calls the “undersea kingdom”. “Well, it’s out of sight, out of mind, right? And undersea cables and pipelines arereallyout of sight.” Even the most sophisticated organisations in the world seem to have based everything on blind trust that everything will be OK, that everyone will behave.“We don’t have a global government and the entire structure is based on countries committing to doing something and then following through, abiding by the rules they’ve agreed to follow” – ie the 1994 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos). “We don’t have a higher authority that can force them to follow the rules. And it’s extraordinary that it has worked so well, that we’ve been able to build the entire modern economy on that assumption.”View image in fullscreen‘New order of impunity’ … French President Emmanuel Macron addresses the UN in New York earlier this month.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/CNP/Kyle Mazza - CNP/ShutterstockAll that trust is quite touching, really. Except, increasingly, powerful people and states are seemingly choosing what Emmanuel Macron, addressing the UN in New York last week, called “the new order of impunity”. In an ideal world, or even the world of 15 years ago, you might say, “Well, we are going to set up a global flotilla led by the United States, with Russia, China, Germany, the UK, France, to make sure these pirates, whoever they are, who are harming cables, don’t do it,” says Braw. But that, clearly, is a pipe dream, one that is now further complicated by big tech laying its own cables. “Since the very first cable [in 1858] it has been, you know, one road for everybody. We’ve all travelled, our traffic has travelled, on those communal roads.” But now Google, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are planning about 60 of their own;Meta’s Waterworth cablewill be the longest ever, at 50,000km, and wrap around the world.There was an interesting moment in the parliamentary hearing, says Braw, when Mike Martin MP worried about the “absolute insanity that a key piece of critical national infrastructure is going to be delivered and owned by tech giants, over which we have no control”.double quotation markIreland is the original cable junction. It has bet the house on globalisation and peace … it’s so exposed“On one hand, it’s business,” Braw says now. “If they can create these cables, then more power to them. On the other hand, in this environment of geopolitical tension, it does feel like an incredible potential vulnerability. What if Trump got mad at Spain, which he often does, and told Google to disconnect Spain? Because Google has this super-duper cable between Spain and the US East Coast. Or what if Google thought that the way to please Trump on some other matter would be to suspend traffic?” There has already, she writes, been a kind of precedent, when in 2023 Elon Musk momentarilyblocked Starlink access to Crimea.Then there areall the pinch points: off the east coast of the US, for instance, off Japan, off Ireland. About 75% of transatlantic cable trafficgoes through Irish waters, in which Russian vessels have recently been seen lurking – while the Irish navy is tiny.“They are so defenceless,” says Braw. “Ireland is the original cable junction and it’s still a cable junction because of its location. It has bet the house on globalisation, and peace” – and headquartering big tech. “And now that can no longer be taken for granted, Ireland is so exposed.” What if something happened? They’d probably have to turn to the Royal Navy, Braw replies, bluntly. Which would “obviously be hugely humiliating”.Iran hasrecently opened a whole new frontby suggesting it might impose tolls on cables traversing the strait of Hormuz.And underneath all this is the question of what, exactly, constitutes an act of war. Because defining what is going on is the first step in working out how to respond. Suppose, Braw says, that a cable company reports an issue. Then the coastguard sails out to the approximate site. They might identify a suspect, but then they have to decide, while that is happening, whether it’s just an accident, or “whether it’s the first step towards something much bigger” – which would involve the navy, and thus a military response, and who knows what after that.In the case of the Eagle S, Finnish authorities ordered the boat in towards their coast and abseiled on to it – knowing, all the while, that as it was carrying Russian oil, they could be setting something far bigger in motion. (Thankfully, this did not happen. The crew were arrested and although eventually found guilty of criminal damage, Finnish law could not be applied and no sentence enforced because the incident had happened outside their territorial waters.)And in fact, the interception, some months later, of a tanker called the Jaguar, which was sailing under no flag at all, prompted aRussian fighter jet to enter Estonian airspace.There has been, in recent weeks, an increase in chatter about a possible imminent attack by Russia on European soil. Braw largely dismisses this – not least because she can’t see why Russia, already overstretched in Ukraine, would do something so expensive when all it takes is an errant anchor and plausible deniability. And “if you engage in sabotage, disinformation, election interference, arson, using drones, then what is the target country supposed to do?” There is a kind of very dark humour in the fact that the only people properly intent on defining what exactly counts as war at the moment seem to be “insurers, the companies they insure – and district judges. It is extraordinary.”View image in fullscreenSea change … TransPacific communication cables on the ocean floor off the island of Guam, Micronesia.Photograph: David Fleetham/AlamyThere is another type of sabotage to contend with, too. It has been known for decades that the ocean contains treasure – specifically, potato-shaped nodules containing elements such as manganese, iron, aluminium, nickel, copper, cobalt, potassium, titanium, barium and rare earths – that can, in theory, simply be picked off the ocean floor. Some of them, the larger ones, have been there for up to 15m years. Especially attractive are the nodules in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, an abyssal (deep and flat) plain between Hawaii and Mexico in the Pacific, which contains vast amounts of minerals, and over which no country has jurisdiction. But when theLaw of the Seacame into force in 1994, the International Seabed Authority was also created: any mining has to be agreed to by all members (170 countries plus the EU). The US never ratified the law of the sea, but this has until recently been largely a technicality, because the American navy has sailed the world enforcing it, and the US government, understanding the importance of the ISA, has attended its meetings.Thirty-one licences for exploration have been issued, but no one has mined – in fact, a bloc of 40 countries, including the UK, think there should be a moratorium on any commercial mining, not least because it is such a complex and fragile ecosystem, poorly understood, and no one has any idea what damage would be done. (A position underlined when, earlier this year, scientists announced the discovery of a wholenew family of crustacean speciesin the Clarion-Clipperton.)But last April Donald Trump signed an executive orderallowing mining in international waters, including outside US jurisdiction. Five days later they received their firstapplication, a request to mine the Clarion-Clipperton zone. Braw believes the main impetus is the Trump administration’s wish to reduce their dependence on China, especially for therare earths used in digital devices. The trouble is, “processing will still have to happen in China unless America wants to set up processing plants, and it’s very dirty, which is why China specialises in it. Nobody wants to have processing plants in their community, in their backyard.”View image in fullscreen‘The undersea kingdom has everything’ … sunset over the Baltic Sea.Photograph: Jorg Greuel/Getty ImagesAn even larger risk is the precedent it sets. “The thing about America launching unilateral deep-sea mining is that China can say, ‘Since this arrangement clearly doesn’t work, we’ll start mining unilaterally as well.’ And how do you then figure out who gets what? It’s completely outside an international legal framework. It’s the wild west. You can have two companies backed by two different countries fighting for the same pile of nodules.” Or, as Braw puts it in her book: “A battle for commercial domination of the undersea realm could turn into a surface war between the world’s most powerful fleets.” Instead, she argues, we could just recycle our tech and aim to use no new rare earths at all: “That’s what the European Union is focusing on.”“The undersea kingdom has everything,” says Braw. “It is such a combination of mystery and hi-tech. And the hi-tech that sits there, it functions, it works well, it doesn’t harm anybody. But I think if we start messing with this undersea kingdom, either for hostile purposes or for selfish reasons, then we risk upsetting it, and it’s to the detriment of the maritime environment but also to the detriment of our modern life, because the balance is so delicate.”Surely we can stop this happening? With deep-sea mining specifically, says Braw, you would need to “plead with the next US president to reverse the executive order, since it’s based on an executive order, not legislation”. And is the international law simply no longer fit for purpose? Given that the US cannot be trusted, what should happen next?“Well, the first thing that needs to happen is the world needs to realise who the heroesare. It’s the cable crews that go out defying the elements, but now also having to worry that when they go to cable repair sites they themselves could become some sort of target.”As for the larger picture, the seahas been called the “blue commons”; it belongs to all of us, and we need, Braw argues, “the countries of the world that believe in maritime order to get together and show that we are the majority. Yes, you big countries may decide to violate rules that don’t suit you, but we are the majority, and we will stick together, even though we are very different – not because we are more virtuous than everybody else, but because it’s in everybody’s interest that thereberules, which is why countries have wanted to establish rules of governance of the oceans going back to the ancient Greeks. And we managed to do it with Unclos. How can it be that we’re letting this slip now? The cables are just an extremely dramatic illustration of what can happen if we let it slip.”The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World is published by John Murray on 8 October. We want to hear from people about what happened nextGuardian community teamThu 1 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOocyte cryopreservation, more commonly known as egg freezing, has been around for decades but the procedure stopped being considered experimental in 2012. Since then, elective egg freezing has boomed. Often represented as an insurance policy against age- or illness-related fertility decline, the process can be costly and complex.While figures vary, research suggests most people who undergo egg freezing never access their eggs and results are mixed for those who do. Long-term storage poses its own costs and questions.We want to hear from people who froze their eggs five, 10 or even 15 years ago about what happened next. Did the “insurance” buy you peace of mind? Content: Esther Rantzen in Edinburgh in 2003.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen in Edinburgh in 2003.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianEsther RantzenShare your tributes and memories of Esther RantzenWe would like to hear your tributes and memories of TV presenter and Childline founder Esther Rantzen – whether you met her, or appreciated her workGuardian community teamThu 1 Oct 2026 05.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEsther Rantzen, the Bafta-winning TV presenter and founder of Childline,has died aged 86. She announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and becamea vocal campaigner to change the law around assisted dying.Ranzten hosted That’s Life! for 21 years from 1973 until 1994, which drew more than 20 million viewers at its peak. She presented Hearts of Gold in 1988, a series focusing on people responsible for outstanding acts of kindness, and hosted the chatshow Esther from 1994. In later years, she was a contributor to the One Show and hosted a podcast with Adrian Mills.Outside of broadcasting, Rantzen is known for her wide-ranging charity work. She founded Childline in 1986, a helpline for children, and in 2010 launched the Silver Line, a free confidential helpline for older people, which led to her being made a dame for services to children and older people.We would like to hear your tributes and memories ofEsther Rantzen– whether you met her, or appreciated her work.Share your experienceYou can share your response using this form.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (left) is facing off in the presidential election against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump (right).Composite: AFP, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva (left) is facing off in the presidential election against far-right Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump (right).Composite: AFP, Getty ImagesBrazilBrazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealedJorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to pollsTom Phillipsin Rio de Janeiro,Andrew RothandJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 1 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after aGuardian report revealedhow the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court.Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added.Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused oftrying to influence– where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls.According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story.Last year, the Trump administration useda campaign of sanctions and tariffsin a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.3:43How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainerIn recent months, the Trump administration has again been accused ofmeddling in Brazilian affairsby using tariffs and the designation of two Brazilian organised crime groups as foreign terrorist organisations to boost Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign and weaken Lula.Writing on Thursday, Messias said: “Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations. What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.”Messias added: “It is the right of each generation of Brazilians to freely decide their destiny, protect their institutions, and hand over to their children a country that does not accept decisions about Brazil being made outside of Brazil. Our democracy belongs to Brazilians.
