And so it must remain.”The attorney general’s comments came in response to a report that theTrump administrationwas pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa and the campaign against Brazil’s supreme court.A $1m award titled “Countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court.Bolsonaro’s far-right movement considers the supreme court – and in particular justiceAlexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s trial – its greatest foe.Moraes is widely seen to have played a key role in thwarting Jair Bolsonaro’s authoritarian plot, which culminated in the8 January 2023riots in Brasília, despite concerns about the judge overstepping hisconstitutional authority in his crusade to protect democracy.During the rightwing riots, hardcore Bolsonaro supporters trashed the presidential palace, congress and supreme court. The court sustained the most severe damage.0:49Brazil’s presidential palace left in ruins after Bolsonaro’s supporters storm the building – videoBolsonaro supporters continue to claim their leader’s imprisonment is unjust and that he is the victim of a politically motivated sham driven by a corrupt “judicial dictatorship”.Their criticism of Moraes and the supreme court has been bolstered by a recent scandal linking several judges, including him, to Daniel Vorcaro, the playboy banker at the centre of Brazil’s biggest banking scandal. Vorcaro has also been linked to the Bolsonaro family.The banker reportedly gave the family more than £9m, supposedly to produce a biopic aboutJair Bolsonarostarring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s film The Passion of the Christ. On the eve of Vorcaro’s arrest last November, Flávio Bolsonaro messaged him to say: “Brother, I’ll always be with you.”Vorcaro is being held in federal police custody in Brasília. His legal team has consistently denied wrongdoing. On Wednesday, his lawyers said he was not involved in “any kind of illicit activity or criminal practice”.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS foreign policyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration
Author: Camille Rodríguez Montilla
Headline: Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration
Content: An image of Venezuela’s former president Hugo Chávez in Mario Silva’s home studio in La Guaira.Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn image of Venezuela’s former president Hugo Chávez in Mario Silva’s home studio in La Guaira.Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The GuardianVenezuela‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of TrumpDiehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administrationCamille Rodríguez Montillain Caracas andTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroThu 1 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade.Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist.View image in fullscreenSilva’s tattoos.Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The GuardianBut nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy,Delcy Rodríguez.“[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas.Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US.Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking“the biggest oil deal in world history”with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly,posing for a smiley photographthat left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast.“I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumedon YouTubeas a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him.View image in fullscreenMario Silva in his home studio in La Guaira state, Venezuela.Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian“They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.”In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!”Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January.Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”.View image in fullscreenVenezuela’s interior minister Diosdado Cabello addressing a crowd during a march in support of Delcy Rodríguez last week.Photograph: Diko Betancourt/Anadolu/Getty ImagesJuan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!”“The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said.Rodríguez hasdefendedthe deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast.Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently.​Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people ​joined a pro-government rall​y in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”).View image in fullscreenEx National Assembly deputy and television presenter Mario Silva in his home studio.Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian“No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, ​told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released.The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear.Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.”But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power.“If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said.“Beyond whatever ideological position they might have…I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.”However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash.“They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned.View image in fullscreenA Venezuelan government supporter carries dolls depicting Hugo Chávez and the pro-government comic-book characters Super Bigote and Cilita at a march in Caracas backing Delcy Rodríguez’s participation in the UN general assembly in New York.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesSo far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests.“Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”.Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself.The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told.Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaHugo ChávezDelcy RodríguezNicolás MaduroAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Daredevil Jaan Roose completes slackline walk high above central Seoul | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Estonian completed first of two attempts to navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace on Thursday
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Estonian completed first of two attempts to navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace on Thursday
Content: 1:33Jaan Roose amazes crowds with 120 metre-high slackline walk above Seoul - videoSouth KoreaDaredevil Jaan Roose completes slackline walk high above central SeoulEstonian completed first of two attempts to navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace on ThursdayRaphael Rashidin SeoulThu 1 Oct 2026 02.04 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 20.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe lunchtime crowds drifted slowly back to their offices along central Seoul’s main boulevard, heads up and phones raised to the sky.High above, a narrow ribbon ran between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, a few hundred metres from the capital’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace and Gwanghwamun square.A countdown ticked down on a big screen, and at 1pm, a figure stepped off the roof of the Koreana and out over the drop.Livestream of Jaan Roose slackline attempt in SeoulJaan Roose, an Estonian aerial athlete and three-time slackline world champion, was in Seoul to cross a 160-metre long highline suspended 120 metres above the city, in what organisers called South Korea’s first high-altitude slackline performance.The 34-year-old has made a name for himself slacklining dramatic urban environments, such as his 185-metre high featbetween Qatar’s Katara towers.In 2024, he became thefirst person to slackline the strait of Messinabetween mainland Italy and Sicily, completing the 3.6km traverse despite a fall near the end, caught by his safety harness. Last month, he covered 14.7km over 12 hours on a line above the Danube in Bratislava, Slovakia.View image in fullscreenA woman in Warsaw, Poland, watches Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose cross a highline suspended above the city in 2026.Photograph: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBelow Roose, the Seoul traffic kept moving and the crowd held its breath each time he wobbled.“Just looking at him makes my legs go weak,” said Kim Young-sook, an office worker. “I can’t imagine how he can do that without being scared. It’s incredible.”Midway across, Roose sat cross-legged on the line, then lay flat on his back, drawing gasps from below, before the daredevil rose and continued.“I’m worried he might fall”, said Choi Eun-jung, who came out to see Roose. “I know he’s a professional, but it’s still a little frightening to watch.”On reaching Dong-A Media Center, he turned around, and started his return to the hotel rooftop.At the halfway point, he again dropped down and waved at the crowd. But this time he hung from the line with one arm and then dangled by his feet.When he finished his performance, the crowds clapped, some clearly relieved.At nearby Cheonggye plaza, people tried out their skills on slacklines, but these were set a mere 30cm and 50cm off the ground. Roose was scheduled for a second performance at 4pm.Roose said a visit in 2022 toSouth Koreainspired his Gwanghwamun walk.On that trip, Roose encounteredjultagi, Korea’s traditional tightrope walking, which Unesco added to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011.Unlike tightrope walking elsewhere,jultagiis as much comedy as acrobatics. The walker sings, jokes and dances on the rope, trading banter with a clown on the ground as musicians play.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaAsia PacificExtreme sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Underlying causes of recurrent bacterial vaginosis identified by Australian scientists | Health | The Guardian
description: Melbourne researchers behind previous BV transmission breakthrough turn attention to understanding why some cases are harder to cure
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Melbourne researchers behind previous BV transmission breakthrough turn attention to understanding why some cases are harder to cure
Content: The study identified two distinct pathways to recurring BV: persistence of the condition despite a weeklong course of antibiotics and re-infection.Photograph: alvarez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe study identified two distinct pathways to recurring BV: persistence of the condition despite a weeklong course of antibiotics and re-infection.Photograph: alvarez/Getty ImagesHealthUnderlying causes of recurrent bacterial vaginosis identified by Australian scientistsMelbourne researchers behind previous BV transmission breakthrough turn attention to understanding why some cases are harder to cureDonna LuAssistant editor, climate, environment and scienceThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian scientists have identified two contributors to recurrent bacterial vaginosis infections, a common sexual health condition that affects about one in four women globally.The condition, commonly called BV, is characterised by an imbalance of naturally occurring bacteria in the vagina, in which there is a reduction of “good” bacteriaand an overgrowth of other mixed bacteria.In March last year, researchers published alandmark studywhich found that BV can besexually transmitted to women by male partners.Concurrently treating women with the condition and their male sexual partners with antibiotics reduced BV recurrence rates by more than 60%, they found.In new research, the same group of scientists set out to understand why about 20% of women treated concurrently with their partners were not cured of BV.The study, published inThe Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women’s Health, involved 188 couples: the women were given a weeklong course of oral antibiotics, while the men were treated with both oral and topical antimicrobials.It identified two distinct pathways to recurring BV: persistence of the condition despite a weeklong course of antibiotics, and re-infection.‘Paradigm shift’: Australian researchers discover key to treatment of bacterial vaginosisRead moreStudy lead author Dr Lenka Vodstrcil, a senior research fellow at Monash University and Bayside Health’s Melbourne SexualHealthCentre, said: “For about two-thirds of women, the day after they finish treatment, they return to … an optimal vaginal microbiome”, which is characterised by an abundance of healthyLactobacillibacteria.The other third of women had microbiomes suggesting “they may not have cleared their BV” before couples resumed sex after treatment, and were nearly three times more likely to get the condition again within four weeks.A better understanding of “persistence of infection … helps us develop new strategies to cure more women from BV,” Vodstrcil said.BV can be asymptomatic or can cause vaginal itching, burning and discomfort. Treatment is essential as the condition can increase susceptibility to other infections and is linked to complications in pregnancy and childbirth.The study – which the researchers believe is the largest to date involving heterosexual couples receiving concurrent BV treatment – found that persistence and reinfection from partners were “distinct, but not mutually exclusive, pathways”.Of the female participants, 30% used an intrauterine device, which the study found “could enhance the persistence of bacterial vaginosis following treatment in some women” but noted that further research was needed.The scientists now plan to trial longer treatment lengths and combinations of multiple antibiotics.“Our aim is to stop women from having two, three, four courses of antibiotics throughout the year, which was happening previously,” Vodstrcil said.Study senior author Prof Catriona Bradshaw, head of research translation and mentorship at Monash University and the Melbourne Sexual Health Centre, said: “Using partner-treatment to mitigate re-infection and more intensive strategies that target persistence of BV-bacteria, we hope to create more effective treatment approaches that can be tailored to an individual and achieve higher levels of cure.”Though the ethnicities of participants were “representative of urban Australia”, the study noted that its results “might not be generalisable to other global populations, including those in low-income and middle-income countries and in other settings with a high burden of bacterial vaginosis”.Explore more on these topicsHealthWomen's healthSexual healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Million-dollar public servants: 11 staff at Australia’s Future Fund paid significantly more than the PM | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: One executive received a $1.5m package last year, while 10 other staff received remuneration exceeding $1m each
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: One executive received a $1.5m package last year, while 10 other staff received remuneration exceeding $1m each
Content: The generous remuneration of 11 Australian public servants employed at the Future Fund has been criticised as insulting during a cost-of-living crisis and amid job cuts across the public service.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe generous remuneration of 11 Australian public servants employed at the Future Fund has been criticised as insulting during a cost-of-living crisis and amid job cuts across the public service.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPBreaking News AustraliaAustralian politicsMillion-dollar public servants: 11 staff at Australia’s Future Fund paid significantly more than the PMOne executive received a $1.5m package last year, while 10 other staff received remuneration exceeding $1m eachFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly a dozen federal public servants were paid more than $1m last year, with one receiving a $1.5m package worth more than double Anthony Albanese’s base salary.The generous remuneration – which includes bonuses and allowances – has been criticised as insulting during a cost-of-living crisis and amid job cuts across the public service.The 11 staff are employed by Australia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Future Fund, and have direct oversight and responsibility for its investments, worth $350bn.One Future Fund manager employed at an “executive level 2” rank was paid $1.5m of taxpayer money last year, which is significantly more than the prime minister’s $622,000 salary.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAll 11 staff are paid more than federal cabinet ministers and all but one department secretary, including the heads of Australia’s domestic intelligence agency and the federal police.Their pay emerged after Greens senator Barbara Pocock asked the minister for the public service, Katy Gallagher, to justify the high remuneration in a question on notice in August.Future Fund spent $20,000 to send CEO’s executive assistant on business class trip to scope hotels in USRead moreA response from Gallagher’s office, tabled in parliament this week, said the fund operated in a “highly competitive global market” and the generous wages were needed to attract the best possible talent.“The Future Fund delivered a return of 14.8% in the 12 months to June 2026, adding $37.4bn to increase the value of the investment portfolio to over $350bn,” the spokesperson said.In the private sector, senior managers at major Australian bankscommonly receive annual bonuses of more than $1m. But these salariesremain controversial with shareholders.The spokesperson said the salaries were within government rules that state performance bonuses can only be used in limited circumstances.“This includes positions that involve significant, at-risk investment outcomes and for Commonwealth entities and companies whose primary purpose is to operate in commercial markets – both of which apply to the Future Fund.”Pocock was not satisfied by the response, and said “most taxpayers would be questioning if these payments are good value for money”.“In a cost-of-living crisis, Australians are suffering and many would be outraged to learn that a dozen public servants are earning over a million dollars, and in some cases double what the prime minister earns,” said Pocock.“What kind of public service work warrants a salary of $1m or 1.5m dollars? We’re not talking about secretaries running government departments but employees. How can the government justify this?”The Future Fund declined to comment.It comes amid budget pressures that last month resulted in the National Disability Insurance Agency announcing voluntary redundancies for the first time since its 2013 creation.Several other government departments have also announced job cuts in recent months, including in the prime minister’s own department, home affairs and the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water.In December, the Future Fund wascriticised for spending $20,000to send the chief executive’s then-assistanct on a scoping trip to assess hotels in the US and negotiate rates.2:50Future Fund CEO questioned over staffer’s $20,000 US hotel scoping trip – videoThe fund told a Senate estimates hearing the trip led to annual savings of $30,000. The executive assistant and another person flew business class to the US.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsBreaking News AustraliaAustralian economynewsShareReuse this content

title: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting | France | The Guardian
description: About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
Content: Students take part in a blockade outside Voltaire high school in Paris's 11th arrondissement.Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStudents take part in a blockade outside Voltaire high school in Paris's 11th arrondissement.Photograph: CLPRESS/ABACA/ShutterstockFranceFrance school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meetingAbout 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the countryJon Henleyin ParisThu 1 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfast-growing protestby high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.View image in fullscreenThe pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves.Photograph: CLPress/Abaca/ShutterstockNearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured.The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils.Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.View image in fullscreenRiot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”.Studentswere protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.View image in fullscreenInjuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles.Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty ImagesWhile many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”The government has accused the radical left LaFranceInsoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestSchoolsEuropeStudentsYoung peopleHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles | International trade | The Guardian
description: Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies
Content: The UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAInternational tradeBritain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpilesMinisters discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US suppliesAlex DanielThu 1 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after theTrump administrationtold Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trumpconsiders a potential wider banto help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November.Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves.Bessent flagged the potential diesel cuts in a social media post, writing: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday.The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks.Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices.It was unclear whether the UK would be included in such a ban, but the loss of US supply would drive prices up sharply at the pumps because the UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.The averageprice of a litre of dieselin the UK hit a new all-time high on Wednesday of 199.72p, according to the motoring body the RAC.John Healey, the chancellor, admitted earlier this week that UK diesel prices were “extreme” and said the government was in discussion with the US over trying to stop a ban.EC commission spokesperson Anna Kaisa Itkonen confirmed that EU member states will hold urgent talks with the commission on Friday to discuss a coordinated response.“The commission … is closely coordinating with EU member states to take stock of the situation and examine appropriate measures to tackle these high prices,” Itkonen added. Discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency.The US energy secretary Chris Wright said ​he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global fuel ⁠prices by drawing down its emergency diesel inventories.“This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go ⁠into to harvest season and we ​go ​into winter heating oil season,” he told Fox ⁠News. “Now’s the time to ​bring more ‌diesel to the ​market, ​and that diesel is available.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMiatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy secretary, has been in contact with Wright to raise concerns.Earlier, a US official told reporters it was “in Europe’s best interest” to ⁠work with the US as it pursues options to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers.The US war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies via the strait of Hormuz and sent the price of oil soaring. Before the war, in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It was above $101 on Thursday.Releasing more stocks wouldrepresent a problem for European countries,which need to balance the need to bring down domestic fuel prices with keeping high stocks for a potential worsening energy crisis over the winter if the Iran war continues.“The UK continues to need fuels – from transport to chemicals, agriculture and defence,” said Elizabeth de Jong, the chief executive of the trade group Fuels Industry UK. The latest US threat showed the UK “cannot solely rely on overseas production for domestic energy security”, she added.Trump has said he was “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, topause strikes on Russian oil refineriesover concerns that they could further push up prices. Russia had already extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October after Ukrainian attacks on refining companies.A government spokesperson said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”Explore more on these topicsInternational tradeEuropean CommissionOilTrump administrationEuropeGlobal economyEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Putin says ‘all weapons at disposal’ if there’s an attack on Russia – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: The president said it was a warning if any countries were considering an attack on Russia
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: The president said it was a warning if any countries were considering an attack on Russia
Content: 12.25 EDTRussia's Putin confirms 'all weapons at disposal' in case of attack on Russia, but says it would not attack firstIn the Q&A after his speech, Russia’s Putin also got asked about Moscow’s widely reported nuclear threat over Kaliningrad(Europe Live, yesterday).Russian president Vladimir Putin attends a plenary session of the 23d annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, Russia.Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/EPAPutinconfirms thatRussiaissued a statementand letters to some embassies on this point.But he claims:“This is not us threatening, but this is a response to attempts to threaten us.”He continues:“These statements, statements by the western politicians and European politicians about the need and possibility and preparation for the war with Russia in 2029 and 2030.It’s not us saying these words, but we hear it from the other side, constantly.”He eventually confirms that “if it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation– in this case we mean Kaliningrad, but may be some other territories as well – of course, naturally,immediately what will be on the agenda is the use … of all weapons that we are the disposal of our country.”He says that with Nato a potential adversary “exceeding us,” Russia would not have “many means to counter such a threat,” and would need to use its “competitive advantages.”But Putin says that the risk of using nuclear weapons is only serious if Nato’s threats against Russia are serious.And then he goes on a rant about taking his words out of context, so let’s quote him in full:“I think that this constant increased tension by many European countries; it has to do with a great deterioration of economic and domestic political situation in the countries.Look at their economy, what’s happening in terms of social policy and living standards of citizens in major European countries. Amid such conditions, they have to shift the focus of attention of their citizens from domestic issues towards outside issues.Now, I have to respond to the questions that you asked me, and I think that they were waiting for us to respond.Right now,they will cut it out of context, and they will abuse and exploit this notion that Russia is threatening us with nuclear weapons to distract the attention of their citizensfrom the fact that they are conducting their own aggressive policy against Russia, that they’re pushing their citizens towards a dangerous line towards confrontation against Russia.We’re not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050, but if we come across an aggression, we will have to respond.The citizens of the European countries should be fully aware of that and make the distinction between our position and the position of incumbent governments of their countries.”Curiously, a moment later, he also appears to play down tensions a bit as he says “I do not think we are going to conduct strikes on the territory of countries procuring weapons forUkraine, but this is a threat, and we are monitoring it closely.”ShareUpdated at12.38 EDT

title: Finnish PM says suspected break-ins at MPs’ homes could be work of foreign power | Finland | The Guardian
description: Police investigating reports of politicians’ homes being broken into in last year with nothing being stolen
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Police investigating reports of politicians’ homes being broken into in last year with nothing being stolen
Content: Petteri Orpo said Russia had sought to influence elections in several European countries.Photograph: Kaisa Siren/EPAView image in fullscreenPetteri Orpo said Russia had sought to influence elections in several European countries.Photograph: Kaisa Siren/EPAFinlandFinnish PM says suspected break-ins at MPs’ homes could be work of foreign powerPolice investigating reports of politicians’ homes being broken into in last year with nothing being stolenMiranda BryantNordic correspondentThu 1 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, has said a foreign power could be responsible for a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of several members of parliament.Police said on Thursday they were investigating multiple reports of MPs’ homes being broken into in the Helsinki area in the last year in which nothing was stolen but subtle signs of breaking and entering were left.When asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the alleged intrusions, Orpo said: “It is very possible. Quite possible in this day and age.“If someone tries to destabiliseFinland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity.”He said the incidents would be investigated by police and within government and would be “taken very seriously”.With the Finnish parliamentary elections just six months away, Orpo said the risk of election interference must be taken seriously. “We see in several European countries thatRussiahas sought to influence elections,” he said.Finland shares a long border with Russia that has been closed for years amid a rapid deterioration of relations since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Finland joining Nato.The Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, said when asked about the suspected incidents: “An attack on a member of parliament is an attack on democracy.“It should not be allowed or accepted in any form … I stand in support of every member of parliament.”At a press conference in parliament, the speaker, Jussi Halla-aho, said he did not have an exact number of suspected cases but that it was “significant”. He said it was the kind of behaviour associated with state actors.“It is known that state actors sometimes engage in activities that resemble suspected cases, but we have no information to comment on at this time and there is no point in speculating,” Halla-aho said.Observations had been made “drop by drop”, he said. “It is possible that the marks were left visible on purpose.”According to the broadcaster Yle, suspected cases include doors being left open to homes and lights being left on.Helsinki police said they had received information from parliament about suspected intrusions at the homes of MPs and had begun a preliminary inquiry. The force said in a statement: “The Helsinki police department is working closely with the national bureau of investigation in clarifying the matter. The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time.”Explore more on these topicsFinlandEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems
Content: A scene from NAZA. The producers said the team had carried out scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenA scene from NAZA. The producers said the team had carried out scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.Photograph: The GuardianNAZANAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in GazaTeam behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systemsPeter BeaumontThu 1 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary.In its response, which the IDF said was based on statements made by the film-makers and a review made by a representative who had attended a viewing, the Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on interviews with two dozen intelligence and other troops who had only a partial picture of the target approval process.NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiereRead moreAt the centre of the IDF’s rebuttal was its often repeated claim that its rules of engagement explicitly distinguish between militants and civilians and prohibit deliberately targeting civilians, while requiring commanders to take steps to minimise civilian harm, claims that have long been challenged over the years by critics.While acknowledging that it used AI to help recommend potential targets inGaza, the IDF also said final decisions made on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.The IDF also denied that it had approved, planned or carried out an attack anticipating 500 civilian casualties in pursuit of a single Hamas target.The IDF statement follows previous efforts by Israeli politicians to dismiss NAZA – a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike – which have accompanieddeath threats against the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and calls by the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,for them to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship.It also echoed previous complaints by some Israeli critics – including journalists – that the film’s military sources were anonymised, despite the fact that source protection in media investigations is commonplace and regarded by much of the media as an ethical requirement.“The filmNAZApresents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal,” the statement added.Responding to the IDF statement, the Guardian, which produced the film, disclosed further details of how the team had verified the allegations which involved scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.A spokesperson said: “The IDF’s attempt to portray the 24 participants in NAZAas junior-ranking officers involved only in the early stages of the targeting process is false.“They include officers and soldiers who were involved in multiple stages of the targeting process in Gaza, including intelligence, operations and the final authorisation process.View image in fullscreenPeople walk past the rubble of destroyed buildings in Jabaliya in the northern Gaza Strip.Photograph: Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters“The process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.“Over the past three years we have together interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes.“The Guardian stands fully behind the film, which builds on three years of detailed reporting by the Guardian and our partners. Several highly respected news organisations have subsequently confirmed the IDF’s use of AI-driven systems in the Gaza offensive and the loosening of safeguards to protect civilians, including the New York Times, Washington Post and Associated Press.”While Netanyahu has claimed that Israeli military safeguards have led to one of the lowest civilian-combatant ratios in modern warfare, that has been challenged by the IDF’s own leaked casualty assessments, by the UN’s commission of inquiry in 2024 and research by NGOs including Action on Armed Violence.--1:55NAZA - official trailerExplore more on these topicsNAZAGazaPalestineIsraelDocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Co-pilot in flight stabbing had ‘Islamic radical indoctrination’, says Netanyahu | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
Author: William Christou
Headline: Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
Content: Yaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers who intervened on the flydubai plane, is welcomed at Ben Gurion airport.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APView image in fullscreenYaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers who intervened on the flydubai plane, is welcomed at Ben Gurion airport.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APFlydubai plane incidentCo-pilot in flight stabbing had ‘Islamic radical indoctrination’, says NetanyahuAlleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opensWilliam ChristouandJonathan YerushalmyThu 1 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, has claimed.Israeli passengers intervened tostop the attackon Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia.The plane had more than 170 people onboard and Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened, announcing that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a “heroism” award for preventing a potential disaster.A ‘hero’ pilot, plumber and dentist among those who saved flydubai flight to IsraelRead moreNetanyahu told Fox News: “We know that he underwent Islamic radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information.”The co-pilot, whose identity is still not known, was being interrogated by Saudi security services, which arrested him on the plane’s arrival in Tabuk, in the north-west of the country.Saudi investigators were cooperating with theUnited Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker’s motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” they told the Associated Press.GraphicTwo Israeli security officials said that Israel’s initial assessment was that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, Reuters reported.Netanyahu said that the co-pilot was probably suicidal, citing preliminary “indications”.“It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue,” he said, emphasising that final conclusions had yet to be made.Netanyahu had previously said it was “too early to say” if there was any state backing – namely Iranian – of the attack. Two Israeli security sources told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.The attack came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election. The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat and the opposition leader Yair Lapid said that a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat.Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a “terror attack”, with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE.Map of flight pathDonald Trump suggested the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, and told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length.Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel’s involvement in the investigation.Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.3:28How the stabbing incident unfolded on Israel-bound flydubai plane | DeconstructedThe UAE announced on Thursday that it would conduct its own investigation into the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai. It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker’s motive and if he had any links to any “terrorist purpose”.Passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – putting the captain of the plane on the floor, after which the plane began to plummet. The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane’s descent.A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard had played out.Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India’s ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain’s family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said.Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk,but was in good health and recovering well, according to the Indian embassy in the UAE, which said the ambassador had visited the pilot.“Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,” Modi said, in a post on social media. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentIsraelUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuAir transportSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels | Oil | The Guardian
description: Alternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrained
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Alternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrained
Content: Iran has sought to exert its authority on the strait since the war began, but its control appears to have declined in recently as oil exporters find workarounds.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreenIran has sought to exert its authority on the strait since the war began, but its control appears to have declined in recently as oil exporters find workarounds.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAOilCrude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levelsAlternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrainedJoanna PartridgeThu 1 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of theIranwar, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.Pipeline exports and ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used, according to analysts tracking the situation, while the US militarycontinues to escort some vessels. However, flows of refined products such as diesel remain constrained, pushing prices higher.At least 16.5m barrels per day (bpd) left the region in September, according to figures from the global trade intelligence firm Kpler, equalling the pre-war average, excluding Iran. The figure is 10.5m bpd higher than the monthly average for March, during the first weeks of the Iran war.A graphic comparing oil transits through the strait of Hormuz to other routes in the GulfSince the conflict began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has sought toexert its authorityon the strait of Hormuz and has at times evendeclared the strategic waterway closed.However, Iran’s control appears to have declined in recent weeks, as oil exporters have found workarounds to address the disruption.About 40% of the region’s crude is now transported without transiting the strait, compared with just 17% before the war, through Saudi and Emirati pipelines, according to Kpler analysis. Saudi Arabia was able to restart operations on its east-west pipeline in late September,after it was damaged during drone attacks, allowing exports from resume from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.In a sign of the other adaptations, the majority of crude transported through the strait of Hormuz is carried on a shuttle fleet mostly comprising very large crude carriers, sailing with their satellite transponders turned off. The cargo is moved on to different tankers in open water, usually off the coast of Oman or Fujairah in theUnited Arab Emirates.View image in fullscreenTankers and merchant vessels anchor off Fujairah. Ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used to transport oil.Photograph: Barry Iverson/AlamyMore than 70% of the crude that passed through the strait in August changed tankers, whereas before the war almost no Gulf crude changed ships in the Gulf ofOman.However, the recovery in exports from the region remains unbalanced, and supplies of refined products remain constrained.This poses a problem for businesses and households that depend on refined products such as diesel to run their cars, vans and lorries.The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time highof 199.18p a litre on Monday, with many motorists already reporting prices above £2 on some forecourts.“Diesel carries the sharpest risk,” said Kpler analysts, who found that less than 20% of pre-war levels of refined products shipped through Hormuz were being transported.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday.Photograph: Jacob King/PAThey recorded a seven-day average of 677,000 bpd of refined products as of Monday, compared with 3.6m before the conflict.Even as oil exports from the region have increased, the level of threat to ships operating around the strait of Hormuz has not disappeared.“New routes emerge, cargos are rerouted, risk is priced in and absorbed. The danger is assuming that resilience equals security. It doesn’t,” said Richard Meade, the editor in chief of shipping publication Lloyd’s List. “Oil flows have recovered because the market participants have accepted greater operational complexity and higher costs. The underlying threat remains.”The danger to vessels and their crew was highlighted on Tuesday, when three Liberian-flagged tankers werehit by projectileswhile transiting the strait.The price of crude remains at elevated levels and moved higher again on Thursday, as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports withuncertainty over a long-term solutionto the conflict and reopening of the strait.The price of Brent crude briefly was back above $100 a barrel on Thursday, up 3% to $101.The rise came after reports that China had suspended exports of oil products to regions beyond Hong Kong and Macau, a move that would add further pressure to oil markets. Oil analysts said China’s decision could suggest it was concerned about the availability of domestic products.Explore more on these topicsOilStrait of HormuzEnergy industryShipping industryUS-Israel war on IranIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Israelis divided as vote that could oust Netanyahu only weeks away | Israel | The Guardian
description: Some on streets of Jerusalem pledge their support to prime minister while others hope for change
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Some on streets of Jerusalem pledge their support to prime minister while others hope for change
Content: A campaign poster for Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s far-right national security minister, at the Machane Yehuda market in Jerusalem.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA campaign poster for Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s far-right national security minister, at the Machane Yehuda market in Jerusalem.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsraelIsraelis divided as vote that could oust Netanyahu only weeks awaySome on streets of Jerusalem pledge their support to prime minister while others hope for changeLorenzo TondoandQuique Kierszenbaumin Jerusalem; graphics byAna Lucía González PazThu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious nationalists, settlers, Palestinians, and soldiers returning from deployments, uncertainty hangs over an election less than a month away that could mark a turning point for a country profoundly changed after the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 and nearly three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.The political battle remains on a knife-edge.For over two years most polls have predicted that the coalition of parties led by prime ministerBenjamin Netanyahuwill collectively slip below the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government.But there is no clear path to power for his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of theIsraelDefense Forces, even if he maintains current levels of support, because he has ruled out going into coalition with any of the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who are projected to claim a critical 12 seats.For Netanyahu to stay in power, he would have to either put together a different coalition or pull off an unprecedented election night surprise. Another deeply fragmented Knesset seems likely, in whichneither side is close to securing a majority.Thelatest Channel 13 poll, published last week, captured that deadlock: Jewish Israeli parties opposed to Netanyahu were projected to win 52 seats, against 51 for the prime minister’s bloc, with both falling short of the 61 required for a majority.Eisenkot’s Yashar party topped the poll with 22 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to take 18. The lack of clarity over the next government – with both main blocs on the right – is fuelling unease among Israelis, some of whom believe little will change whoever becomes prime minister.“I’m not going to vote because I don’t trust anyone,” said Rachel, 42, an Israeli citizen living in West Jerusalem. “I used to vote for Yair Lapid,” she added, referring to the leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party. “The party’s name means ‘there is a future’. But today, I don’t see any future for this country.”Average public trust across the eight Israeli institutions measured consistently by the Israel Democracy Institute, a statistics body, stood at 34% in 2025, compared with 61% in 2012.A graph showing levels of public trust between 2003 and 2025An atmosphere of pessimism and indecision is palpable in Jerusalem, where tensions between Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem – the majority of whom cannot vote in Israeli national elections – and rightwing Jewish Israelis have deepened since 7 October. The Hamas attack is likely to weigh heavily on the ballot: arecent poll by the Israel Democracy Institutefound that 68% of Jewish respondents said 7 October would be a central factor in deciding how they voted.A graphic showing how 7 October will affect the way Israeli Jews and Israeli Arabs vote“After 7 October, everyone in this government has to take the blame,” said Ilda, who owns a clothing shop on Jaffa Street, one of Jerusalem’s oldest and busiest thoroughfares. Referring to a Haaretz investigation claiming Netanyahu had been warned about the possibility of a major Hamas attack, which he denies, she said: “After journalists exposed what happened, look what they did: they attacked the journalists instead of taking responsibility.”West Jerusalem has long been considered fertile ground for Netanyahu and the Israeli right. Yet Israel’s growing diplomatic isolation and the prospect of seemingly endless conflict on multiple fronts are beginning to worry voters even here, a few steps from the bustling Mahane Yehuda market, where giant election posters for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister known for his anti-Palestinian rhetoric andchampioning a racist death penalty lawthat in practice applies only to Palestinians, loom over the streets.View image in fullscreenAnother advert showing Ben-Gvir at the Machane Yehuda market in Jerusalem.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian“This country needs radical change. I think I’ll vote for Naftali Bennett,” said Yosef, 26, a religious Israeli, referring to the rightwing former prime minister who now leads the B’Yachad alliance and is one of Netanyahu’s main political rivals.On one side are tens of thousands of Netanyahu supporters – called “Bibi-ists” in reference to the prime minister’s nickname – as well as backers of the far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who want to return the current coalition to power to “finish the job” in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon and the West Bank.On the other are tens of thousands of voters who believe Israel is losing its standing in the world and needs a change of direction – something many see as embodied by the centre-right Eisenkot. His supporters argue that he would place greater emphasis on education, social policy and the economy, areas they say have been neglected by the current government.“I’ll vote for anyone but the prime minister of 7 October,” said Turgeman as he enjoyed a coffee with his wife at a cafe in Jaffa during the Jewish high holiday season. “I’ve never voted Likud in my life, and I’m certainly not going to start now. I’ll vote for Eisenkot. We need a normal prime minister – someone who also cares about the economy and about prices, which have soared because of the war.”Food prices in Israel havereached record highsamid the regional conflict and supply chain disruption, with food inflation outpacing the broader consumer price index. The cost of food, including fresh fruit and vegetables, hasrisen by 9.5% over the past two years.“They think about wars, while nobody is dealing with the economic crisis,” Turgeman said. “And what has Netanyahu done? He has continued to provide financial support that benefits the Haredi [ultra-Orthodox] community.”Since 7 October, Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community has been at the centre of abitter dispute over military conscription. While most Jewish Israelis serve, Haredi men studying in religious seminaries have long been largely exempt.In 2024, amid war and growing pressure on reservists, the supreme court ruled there was nolegal basis to continue the exemption, fuelling anti-draft protests, roadblocks and clashes with police. Haredi parties have blamed Netanyahu for failing to pass legislation to protect the exemption.Ultra-Orthodox Jews, who make up about 14% of Israel’s population, have traditionally voted for parties backed by their rabbis, including the two main Haredi parties in Netanyahu’s coalition. Butanger among younger Haredim over conscriptionand the policing of protests could lead some to defy their religious leaders this time.A graph showing how Jewish Israelis define their religiosity over time“All the options in this election are junk, but I think I will vote for Eisenkot,” said Pinchas, 24, an ultra-Orthodox student who recently completed his military service. “I have the impression that this time people my age won’t vote according to what the rabbis tell them. Many are angry about the way Netanyahu handled the conscription law, and especially about the crackdown on those who protested against it.”As the Guardian conducted interviews near Jerusalem’s central bus station, an elderly passerby called out: “There is only one prime minister – Bibi!” It was a reminder that, despite the uncertainty and the opposition’s narrow lead in the polls, the Israeli leader retains a loyal base.View image in fullscreenAn advert for Gadi Eisenkot, a retired chief of staff of the Israeli army, on a bus in Jerusalem.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian“I’m sure Netanyahu will win,” said Avraham Levy, 76, a Likud supporter and fruit seller at Mahane Yehuda market. “We’ll have the majority. We need to support Netanyahu because he has to finish the job. If he doesn’t, who will?” he said, referring to Israel’s wars on several fronts.Among those still backing Netanyahu’s coalition partners are supporters of the far right, including Jakub, 23, who was due to begin his military service soon. “I’ll vote for Moshe Feiglin,” he said, referring to anextreme far-rightformer Israeli Knesset member who declared in 2025 that the conflict in Gaza was not against Hamas butagainst every child and baby in the territory, and is now running jointly with the far-right Religious Zionist party. “Because he represents my values, and he has never changed his principles,” Jakub said.The field is wide open and the divide is also generational: by 2019, support for a Palestinian state stood at about 20%-30% among the youngest Jewish Israeli cohorts, compared with roughly 40%-55% among older generations, reflecting a longer-term shift towards more hawkish attitudes. No more recent comparable data was available.A graph showing how hawkish attitudes are more prevalent among younger generations of IsraelisThe difficulty for the anti-Netanyahu camp is that it remains fragmented and has struggled to agree on a coherent political platform or a common strategy capable of uniting its different factions.Parties representing Palestinian citizens, known as Arab parties inside Israel, could push Eisenkot’s coalition over the 61-seat threshold, but amid acampaign ofracism and Islamophobia, he has ruled out going into government with them.They could potentially support a minority government.But last week, the Central Elections Committeevoted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List, the country’s two main Palestinian parties, from the election, after the far-right Otzma Yehudit party filed a petition arguing that they support terrorism and deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.The opposition Democrats party filed a similar petition arguing for Otzma Yehudit to be banned for incitement to racism and negating the existence of Israel as a democratic state, because of racist policies pursued in power under its leader Itamar Ben Gvir. That was not upheld.The decision is being challenged in the supreme court, which has overturned similar bans in past elections.If allowed to run in the elections, the Arab parties will be crucial to the opposition’s prospects of forming a government and to Eisenkot’s chances of replacing Netanyahu.Tensions between Palestinian citizens of Israel and the state have deepened since 7 October amid arrests, interrogations and other legal action against Arab citizens, often over protests or social media posts.View image in fullscreenAvraham Levy at his fruit stall in the Mahane Yehuda market. Behind him is an image of Menachem Begin, a co-founder of the Likud party.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianFor these reasons, Palestinian citizens of Israel are often reluctant to express their voting preferences. In the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index survey, 70% said they preferred to remain silent about their political views in the presence of strangers, up from 45% in 2016 and compared with 53% of Jewish respondents.But Palestinian citizens of Israel remain divided over how best to respond, with many pessimistic that any future government will defend rights they say have too often been denied. The Joint List has maintained a more oppositional stance, signalling it could support an anti-Netanyahu minority government from outside while stopping short of joining a coalition, although it has done so in the past.A bar chart showing the proportion of Israeli Jews and Israeli Arabs who agree it is ‘preferable’ to keep quiet about political opinions“These elections are about our strength as an Arab community and our ability to have an influential political voice,” said Amir, 34, from Mashhad in northern Israel, who plans to vote for the Joint List. “We need strong, united Arab representation on equality, discrimination and the Palestinian cause, while cooperating when it benefits our community.”Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, has instead made political pragmatism its defining strategy. In 2021 it became the first independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, seeking budgets, services and greater influence for Palestinian citizens of Israel.“Arab society is being torn apart by crime and violence, while relations with Jewish Israelis are becoming more hostile,” said Abu Mahmoud, 33, from Kafr Kanna, also in the north of the country. “That’s why I’ll vote for Ra’am: negotiate, secure budgets and work with Jewish Israelis where possible.”He added: “I want politics that can actually improve people’s lives.”Jamal Risheqcontributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIsraelBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire
Content: Al-Mawasi in Rafah in 2023 (left) and 2026, with huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline.Composite: GoogleView image in fullscreenAl-Mawasi in Rafah in 2023 (left) and 2026, with huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline.Composite: GoogleGazaNew Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in GazaSatellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefireJason BurkeandEithne StauntonThu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn update toGoogle Mapshas revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants.The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago.Gaza 2023-2026: al-Mawasi, RafahThey show huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline, often within a few metres of the sea. Gaza’s once busy main port, now badly damaged and empty of fishing boats, is surrounded by makeshift accommodation. Any available open space inGazaCity is packed with shacks, tents and huts.Gaza 2023-2026: Tel al-Sultan, RafahThe images also show massive damage to northern towns such as Beit Lahiya and Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Major neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable.Swaths of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed to the ground.Gaza 2023-2026: Istiqlal Mosque, Khan YounisMore than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where about 82% of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.A recentUN assessmentestimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025.Gaza 2023-2026: Beit Lahiya“The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestinetold the Guardianlast month. The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian problems.More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, mostly civilians. The conflict was triggered by a surprise attack by Hamas into Israel in October 2023, in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineGoogle MapsIsraelUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: British Sikh activist released from Delhi jail after nine-year detention | India | The Guardian
description: Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal
