Content: Jagtar Singh Johal after being released from prison on bail in India.Photograph: FreeJaggiNow campaign/PAJagtar Singh Johal after being released from prison on bail in India.Photograph: FreeJaggiNow campaign/PAIndiaBritish Sikh activist released from Delhi jail after nine-year detentionIndian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh JohalPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorThu 1 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.Explore more on these topicsIndiaForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeForeign policySouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Enter Shikari announce indefinite hiatus from 2027: ‘We don’t think we’re splitting up’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next 12 months, but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next 12 months, but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’
Content: Rou Reynolds on stage with Enter Shikari in Leeds in 2024. The rock band have announced they are taking a break.Photograph: Georgina HarrisonView image in fullscreenRou Reynolds on stage with Enter Shikari in Leeds in 2024. The rock band have announced they are taking a break.Photograph: Georgina HarrisonMusicEnter Shikari announce indefinite hiatus from 2027: ‘We don’t think we’re splitting up’Rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next year but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’Press AssociationThu 1 Oct 2026 19.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British rock band Enter Shikari have announced they will go on hiatus at the end of 2027, a decision that may result in the band’s “extinction”.The St Albans band, who formed in 1999 as Hybryd, are due to tour the UK in November, Europe and the US next year, and said they hoped to play some of their favourite places “one last time”.A statement from band reads: “As of December 31, 2027, Enter Shikari will fall dormant as a recording and performing entity. This dormancy may eventually end with an eruption back into activity, or may end with extinction, we have no idea which.“As everyone keeps reminding us, 2027 will be 20 years since the release of our debut album. We’ve been playing music together since we were 15, and friends longer still, but there’s no doubt this is a huge milestone.Enter Shikari review – sensory overload by a British band hitting the big leaguesRead more“For the past two decades, we’ve run amok in a cultural landscape that elevates easily-pigeonholed art, so being an Enter Shikari hasn’t always been easy, professionally or personally, with obvious negative impact on one’s mental health when tasked with coming up with the goods.“But we do this because we love it, and we are lucky enough to have built an audience who understand that the less-trodden path is sometimes the more interesting journey. However, it gets to the point where the often difficult terrain of that path starts to frazzle and drain the humble traveller.“We are far from being the same kids who recorded that debut album, and as much as we love what we do, and still love being in each other’s company, as humans our priorities and capacities have changed.”The band said their lead singer, Rou Reynolds, had suffered “recent illness” but they had already had “difficult conversations” about their future before that.“To then see a friend in trouble made those conversations more pertinent,” the statement reads. “While we don’t think we’re splitting up, we do not have a diary that extends beyond 2027 … Maybe we’ll be like Fugazi and just get together to rehearse for fun, without feeling the need to make anyone else listen to it.“All we really know is after two decades of being a professional band, not having plans three years in advance is liberating.”The band also said they were working on new music, which fans “should get to hear sooner rather than later, along with another thing we’ve just finished filming”.Enter Shikari added that they would not be announcing a “farewell world tour”.The statement concludes: “It’s not the sort of statement we thought we’d be making if you’d asked us a year ago, but we felt it was time to let you know our headspace.“We really hope we’ll be seeing you over the next 14 months or so, somehow. But if not, all that remains to be said is thank-you for your support, your sweat, your passion, your energy.”Since forming in 1999, the band have released six UK top 10 albums, including a No 1 with A Kiss for the Whole World in 2023.They have also scored a handful of hit singles including Anything Can Happen in the Next Half, Juggernauts and Sssnakepit.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Falling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plants  | Edinburgh | The Guardian
description: After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done
Content: The £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburghFalling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plantsAfter five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be donePatrick GreenfieldThu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early autumn sunlight, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh’s extensive plant collection appears safe in their glass enclosures. But danger lurks from above for the tropical ferns, cycads and rare alpine heathers.Soon the September sunshine will give way to the storms and gales of the Scottish winter, which can bring hundreds of glass panels crashing to the greenhouse floor on the windiest days. Nobody is allowed inside when the wind is above 30mph.“We’ve had plants that have essentially been decapitated by falling bits of glass,” says Sadie Barber, the glasshouse curator at RBGE. “You go into one of these tropical spaces in winter and there’s icy air coming in. It’s traumatic for those of us who put decades into caring for these plants. A storm can literally just wipe them out.”View image in fullscreenProf Julia Knights, regius keeper and CEO of RBGE, officially opening the doors.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBut this week, change is in the air for the creaking infrastructure at the 356-year-old botanic garden, the second oldest in Britain after Oxford. On Friday, the palm houses are reopening after five years of painstaking restoration work, complete with 5,750 panels of toughened glass to keep out the elements.Before they closed for renovation works, the horticultural team had installed a net in case panels fell from the weathered structure. The new ones are not bulletproof – but they are strong enough to resist a bird strike.View image in fullscreenDamage to one of the glasshouses after a storm.Photograph: Helen Pugh PhotographyPart-Georgian, part-Victorian, the £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell. Inside, more than 600 temperate plants have returned to the building. The air is clean and crisp, purified by ferns that naturally remove toxins from the air. Its temperature and humidity is still controlled by the original pulleys and winches.“We have made it one vast cathedral-like space for temperate plants,” says Prof Julia Knights, the garden’s regius Keeper and the royally appointed chief executive. She points out her favourite tree fern, which comes from Tasmania and has a Scottish liverwort growing on its woody stem. “They can grow outside in our botanic garden in Logan on the west coast ofScotlandbecause of the oceanic climate,” she says.View image in fullscreenExtensive work has been done to replace and strengthen panels at the greenhouse.Photograph: Helen Pugh PhotographyFounded by two physicians in 1670 to teach doctors about medicinal plants, RBGE has morphed into one of the most important collections of plant biodiversity in the world. Its research glasshouses are stuffed with rare ginger species, bananas, blueberries and dozens of begonias.It is a global authority on rhododendrons and ferns, houses rare plant species that have gone extinct in the wild, and its scientists have helped pioneer new technology, such as DNA barcoding which is used to identify plant species. Arthur Conan Doyle studied here, infusing Sherlock Holmes novels with his botanical knowledge. Today, conservation is its primary focus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Our conservation collections are so important to have. The threats are extreme in the wild,” said Prof Pete Hollingsworth, RBGE’s director of science. “The driver[s] for environmental damage are so strong, so having these ex situ safe sites is really important,” he said.View image in fullscreenNew display benches in the restored building.Photograph: RBGEBut the restored palm houses aside, many of the glasshouses used to care for the plants are decades past their originally intended lifespan and are waiting for upgrades. Leaks from Scottish rain rot the rootstock of plants, sometimes killing them. Last year, horticulturalists were not allowed inside the greenhouses for 20 days due to high winds. In 2026, they have been shut out 15 times. When they return, they have often worn hard hats and safety gear to pick out the broken glass.“The glasshouses are the one thing we don’t want to break. It’s the plants inside that suffer,” said Barber. “I was looking at one of our records the other day of a plant we lost in the lowland tropical house. It just had ‘storm’ written next to it. It had either suffered from the cold, or even been cut by falling glass.”Explore more on these topicsEdinburghScotlandPlantsGardensConservationBiodiversitynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’
Content: The change would require airlines to seat passengers under 14 next to their parents.Photograph: Viacheslav Iakobchuk/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe change would require airlines to seat passengers under 14 next to their parents.Photograph: Viacheslav Iakobchuk/AlamyAirline industryUK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with childrenPlanned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’Nadeem BadshahThu 1 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans.The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake.It is understood that ministers will try to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister,Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays.MPs are in the process of debating a new set of rules for travel companies, as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament. The proposed law will give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports.Burnham dodges questions on Heathrow third runway as project faces four-year delayRead moreBurnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”An arrangement to sit together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey, according to the Department forTransport.Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights. The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children aged between two and 11 to pay to reserve what was referred to as a mandatory family seat.Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge. The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority watchdog found.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRyanair will dispute passenger’s claim he was sucked out of windowRead moreUnder the new policy, parents will still have the option of paying to reserve a seat of their choosing and have their children alongside them free of charge.The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the government, airlines and trade unions working on a new system for sharing information about disruptive passengers.Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.Using the new system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryAndy BurnhamBooking feesAir transportTransportConsumer affairsChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: How success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in power | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: PM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformation
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: PM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformation
Content: Andy Burnham, then the mayor of Greater Manchester, speaks to a reporter after watching a match at the Etihad Stadium in May 2021.Photograph: Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham, then the mayor of Greater Manchester, speaks to a reporter after watching a match at the Etihad Stadium in May 2021.Photograph: Alamy Live NewsAndy BurnhamHow success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in powerPM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformationJosh HallidayNorth of England editorThu 1 Oct 2026 14.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn July 2016, theManchester Cityplayer Yaya Touré ambled into a small bar near Beijing’s Workers’ Stadium and offered a bemused smile as dozens of Chinese fans rushed towards him.Manchester City had just won their sixth trophy under the big-spending ownership of Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group and the blues were international megastars. They were also magnets for investment.On a trade mission led by Sir Howard Bernstein, the architect of modernManchester, civic leaders rolled out club legends such as Mike Summerbee and Sun Jihai in a charm offensive to football-mad Chinese businessmen who saw that the club and the city were on the rise.A decade on, Manchester istransformed. Estate agents advertise £15,000-a-month penthouses in a city-region growing faster economically than any other in Britain, while the success of “Manchesterism” has powered its mayor, Andy Burnham, to Downing Street.Yet the city’s close ties with Abu Dhabi United Group are now facing fresh scrutiny, after Manchester City’s owners were found guilty ofmore than 100 breachesof Premier League financial rules.Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier LeagueRead moreIn a surprising intervention on Wednesday, Burnham praised Abu Dhabi United Group as “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” and said he would be “really concerned” to lose them as the club’s owners.View image in fullscreenSheikh Mansour.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAThe prime minister went on to say that he would not get involved in the Premier League’s disciplinary process, but appeared to express some sympathy for City’s plight by referring to a similar investigation into Everton, the club he supports.“I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,” he said.Burnham’s comments raised eyebrows given the continuing disciplinary process – the Premier League is considering a range of sanctions – and because it turned the spotlight on to Abu Dhabi United Group’s wider investments inGreater Manchester, where he was mayor from 2017 until June this year.One Burnham ally said it was “absolutely mad” for the prime minister to comment and risk being seen to be influencing a disciplinary process, describing it as his “biggest mistake so far”.In an attempt to clarify the prime minister’s remarks on Thursday, a No 10 spokesperson said: “As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process.“It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.”When Mansour’s Abu Dhabi group took over Manchester City in 2008, the grounds for success had already been laid.The club had a gleaming new stadium, built with taxpayers’ money for the Commonwealth games just four years earlier, and council bosses were eager for a reliable long-term investor in a city battling the financial crash.View image in fullscreenManchester City's Etihad stadium.Photograph: Jon Super/APIn 2014, Manchester city council announced a “£1bn deal” with Mansour, one of the world’s richest men, to transform a large stretch of land between the stadium and the edge of the city centre. Richard Leese, then the council leader, promised it to be “a world-class exemplar of regeneration”.The partnership between the council and Manchester City’s owner, which was called Manchester Life, included more than 1,000 private rented apartments and 395 built-for-sale homes – but not one social or affordable home.In a sharply critical assessment of the Manchester Life partnershippublished in 2024, researchers at the University of Sheffield said it appeared that the council had leased the land to Abu Dhabi at a much cheaper rate than many comparable developments – they had “sold the family silver too cheaply”, the academics said – and did not appear to be receiving any rental income or revenue from the property sales.All of the property, with an estimated worth of £350m, is controlled by Jersey-domiciled subsidiaries and ultimately owned by Abu Dhabi interests, the researchers found.They described it as a “transfer of public wealth to private hands that is difficult to justify as prudent”.Dr Richard Goulding, who co-authored the University of Sheffield research, said on Thursday that the Manchester Life development raised “questions about what type of Britain we’re trying to build and who the type of Manchester that we’ve built works for”.He added: “On the one hand, [the Abu Dhabi deal] was bringing money in. On the other hand, a lot of that money was flowing into flats whose rents, according to our research, are being taken offshore.”In July, Manchester city councilpublished a reviewof its deals with private developers. It found that while these agreements had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals.A Manchester city council spokesperson said: “We do not recognise the criticisms linked to the disposal of public land and the idea that there is no financial benefit to the council through this partnership.View image in fullscreenSkyscrapers have transformed Manchester’s skyline over the past decade as the city’s population has grown to nearly 100,000 people.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“The tired claim that working in partnership with Manchester City FC’s owners has not been a good deal for the council or the city has been debunked repeatedly. It is a one-sided perspective that fails to take into account the positive impact of investment in Ancoats and New Islington as well as the wider east Manchester area.”The council added: “Claims that some land was sold too cheaply to Manchester Life ignore the fact that there was zero market interest at the time of the sale, that the land is worth more now precisely because of Manchester Life’s investment and the significant financial return the council is receiving through profit-sharing arrangements.”Gleaming skyscrapers have transformed Manchester’s skyline over the past decade, as the city’s population has grown bynearly 100,000 peopleand become one of Europe’s most attractive destinations for foreign money.Yet born-and-bred Mancunians have felt increasingly pushed out. A report publishedearlier this yearby Greater Manchester combined authority, which Burnham led until June, revealed that of the 10,974 homes built across the region in the nine years to 2024, only 679 (6%) were classed as affordable.Hayley Flynn, an anti-gentrification campaigner who leads tours of Manchester, said development of luxury flats in Ancoats, the home of the Manchester Life project, had not benefited the area’s existing community.“What provisions have we got for them? They’re not going to spend £7 on a loaf of bread in Pollen [a trendy bakery], but that’s their nearest bakery,” she said. “All these apartments for influencers – it’s quite a forceful erosion that’s just pushing the community out.”Tim Heatley, a co-founder of the Manchester developer Capital & Centric, said the city had benefited from Abu Dhabi’s riches and that the success of City had “put Manchester on the map internationally”.Under the ownership of Mansour, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and one Champions League, becoming one of the world’s elite clubs.The club, whichcontinues to denyany wrongdoing, won eight trophies, including three Premier League titles between 2009 and 2018, the period under investigation.Heatley said Abu Dhabi had had “a major impact on that particular area of the city” between the Etihad Stadium and Manchester city centre, but that he believed the region’s economic upturn would have happened without the football investment.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamManchester CityGentrificationGreater ManchesterSheikh MansourLocal politicsCity mayorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes | Welfare | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment
Content: The plans are part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16- to 24-year-olds not in work, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe plans are part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16- to 24-year-olds not in work, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWelfareKey disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changesExclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employmentRowena Mason,Pippa CrerarandPatrick ButlerThu 1 Oct 2026 14.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned.Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work.The move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion byLabourMPs. But ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade them the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned.The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviewsby Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, andthe Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs.However, a central option under consideration for young people is removing the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month, and offering intensive support for people to get into work. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is being looked at.The extra support will include subsidised jobs for younger people, more targeted “back to work” schemesand support with mental health, as part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace.As part of the same package, officials are looking at a new system to replace the Pip, which is claimed by four million people, after attempts to change existing eligibility criteria were rejected by MPs last year.One possible plan is for a separate regime to apply to the under-25 agegroup, with reduced or withdrawn entitlements – although those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities would not lose any money.View image in fullscreenProtests were held last summer outside parliament against proposals to change the personal independence payment (Pip). Officials are looking at a new system for Pip, which could involve a separate regime for under-25s.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianMore broadly, officials are working up plans under the replacement system for a new set of eligibility criteria and assessments for the extra costs of disability, and looking at whether this would apply to all claimants of working age, or those below a cut-off point such as 50 or 60. Again, those with the most severe conditions would not lose money or be reassessed.Officials have also been returning to the idea of cuts to the Motability scheme at a future budget, after axing tax breaks worth £300m. The scheme allows disabled people to use their Pip benefit to lease new cars for three years.One Whitehall source said removing or further cutting the health element of universal credit for those older than 25 had been considered, but government sources said this was not on the table.Officials have looked at systems in other countries, such as Denmark, which restricts access to its “disability pension” for under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they have no ability permanently to work.A government source said: “We will be bringing forward a comprehensive package of support and reform to tackle the scandal of a million young people not in education, employment or training. The details are yet to be decided, but we are committed to enabling work and opportunity, while always protecting those unable to work.”The significant changes would need legislation, with ministers and officials looking at a bill encompassing the replacement for Pip and changes to the under-25 system to be presented in the next session of parliament next year.Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, used his conference speech this week to describe changing the welfare system asa “moral crusade”, saying too many younger people were stuck claiming benefits for too long.However, the scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the impact on the cost of living for disabled people, particularly when Pip is a non-means-tested benefit that is unrelated to a person’s employment status.Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has gone further by saying she would ban young people from signing straight on to the benefits system if her party won the next election, aspart of a planto cut £23bn from the welfare bill. Under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment would no longer be able to claim universal credit and would instead have to undergo intensive job coaching.Reform UK plans to cut the overall welfare bill by £50bn, with Pip replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”, while “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by local authorities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the cost of living for disabled people.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianPolling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe thattackling the root causesof joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts”, and used hisparty conference speechto signal an overhaul of the welfare system to pay for an expansion of youth jobs and training support.UK welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people including Neets – but not children – about 2.5%. Milburn said it was “shameful” the government spent 25 times as much on benefits for them than it did on supporting them into work.More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities warned ministers earlier this year against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.The disability charity Scope has estimated about half of households with an under-22 receiving the universal credit health element are already in poverty, which it said could rise to more than nine in 10 if support was removed.Campaigners warned that any move to cut benefits or increase conditionality rules was likely to drive many youngsters further away from the jobs market.Lucy Schonegevel, the director of impact at Action for Children, said: “We are deeply concerned by reports that disability benefits for under-25s could be cut. If confirmed, that would be at odds with the prime minister’s recent warning against ‘crude cuts’ … Serious investment in high quality, tailored employment support is vital, but employment support alone cannot overcome a lack of jobs.”A DWP spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews, due in the autumn, will lay the foundation for sustainable reform, and we will not pre-empt their findings.“We are already changing the system through the youth guarantee, narrowing the gap between universal credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing a record £3.5bn in employment support for disabled people and those with long-term conditions. We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.”Milburn has said that too few young people who moved on to disability benefits received help into work. Many became “trapped” on benefits, with evidence showing half were not in work 15 years later, an outcome he called a “catastrophic failure”.He appeared to hint at the potential political risks of cuts to benefits at a Labour party conference fringe meeting on youth employment on Monday, saying “when it comes to benefit cuts it will be tricky” – but added that not acting would be financially unsustainable and worse for young people.About 184,000 young people in the UK aged 16-24 receive the universal credit health element. The government has already cut this benefit, having previously announced a 50% reduction to £217 a month for most new claimants from next April.Explore more on these topicsWelfareBenefitsUniversal creditDisabilityYoung peopleYouth unemploymentState benefitsnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Washington DC law bans landlords from imposing dog breed restrictions | Washington DC | The Guardian
description: Landlords can no longer refuse pit bulls, rottweilers, dobermans or other breeds considered ‘scary’
Author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
Headline: Landlords can no longer refuse pit bulls, rottweilers, dobermans or other breeds considered ‘scary’
Content: Rooftop dog park at City Market at O Street apartments in Washington DC.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRooftop dog park at City Market at O Street apartments in Washington DC.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesWashington DCNew Washington DC law bans landlords from imposing dog breed restrictionsLandlords can no longer refuse pit bulls, rottweilers, dobermans or other breeds considered ‘scary’Alba Asenjo DomínguezThu 1 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLandlords inWashington DCwill no longer be able to refuse a tenant’s dog based on its breed, size or weight, nor can they impose special charges related to these factors.At least, that’s what a new law that took effect on Thursday aims to achieve. Animal welfare organizations and animal shelters applauded the legislation, emphasizing the benefits of reducing barriers to pet ownership in the US capital.Dog breeds considered “scary” used to face restrictions, especially pit bulls, rottweilers and dobermans. Property owners could ban certain breeds, regardless of their behavior. With these restrictions, landlords tried to avoid incidents with aggressive dogs that could damage property or harm other tenants or pets.However, animal groups challenged this claim, explaining that breed bans penalize responsible dog owners and that in the vast majority of cases, aggressive behavior is linked to owner management and control, and not to the dog’s breed. Also, they warned that exorbitant pet fees and breed restrictions were putting housing out of reach for people.What takes effect this Thursday is the last part of the pets in housing amendment act, or “Roscoe’s Law”, brought forward by councilmember Robert White in honor of his dog. The first part has been partially in effect since 2025. It included caps on pet-related fees:under that first part of the legislation, pet security deposits cannot exceed 15% of a tenant’s monthly rent, pet rent is capped at 1% of the monthly rent, and all other non-refundable fees are prohibited.While organizations like the DC Landlord Association acknowledged that the law’s intent “to help keep families together and prevent the separation of pets from their owners due to restrictive housing policies”, they expressed concerns. In May, they worried that the security deposits and rent caps included in the law might not cover the costs associated with pet-related damages, and called for “adequate” deposits and rent.Although breed and weight restrictions are prohibited in all residential leases beginning after 1 October 2026, immediate changes may not be evident. Real estate websites commonly include pet restrictions on their property listings.In a quick search on Zillow on Thursday, many “pet-friendly” DC listings included a “pet essentials” section where it stated if the property allowed cats or dogs and their weight limit, and it was sometimes set at a maximum of 75lb.Explore more on these topicsWashington DCAnimalsDogsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US borrowing costs hit 24-year high as global bond sell-off intensifies | Government borrowing | The Guardian
description: Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
Content: Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAView image in fullscreenTraders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAGovernment borrowingUS borrowing costs hit 24-year high as global bond sell-off intensifiesFears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998Business live – latest updatesPhillip Inman,Graeme WeardenandJoanna PartridgeThu 1 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 04.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.The threat of a renewed round of inflation fromthe persistently high cost of oilhas spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike ratesRead moreStock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”A graphic showing the yield, or interest rate, on UK 30-year bonds since 1996The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAxel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz havelargely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports withuncertainty over a long-term solutionto the conflict and reopening of the strait.Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.Explore more on these topicsGovernment borrowingBondsUS Government borrowingEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: I went to America’s largest gathering of astrologers. It was a battle over how to read the stars | History of science | The Guardian
description: Now a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?
Author: Katherine Rowland
Headline: Now a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?
Content: ‘Astrology is really an art form,’ said one practitioner at the United Astrology Conference in Chicago. ‘There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.’Illustration: Dajah Callen/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Astrology is really an art form,’ said one practitioner at the United Astrology Conference in Chicago. ‘There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.’Illustration: Dajah Callen/The GuardianHistory of scienceI went to America’s largest gathering of astrologers. It was a battle over how to read the starsNow a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?Katherine RowlandThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTShare“The dwarf planets change everything,” said the woman with the smart haircut as she made amind blowngesture with her fingertips, temples to air.I am at the United Astrology Conference, the largest professional gathering of astrologers in the world, in downtownChicago. Around me, vendors are hoping to excite the 1,500 attenders, flogging books, tracts, affiliations, proprietary apps and various software programs that have replaced the laborious chart-drawing of yore.I admit, I had come expecting a crowd flaunting amulets and sweeping cloaks. But apart from the occasional streak of purple hair and wispy wizard beard, what I encountered was an even weirder normcore of podiatry-sensible footwear and Oxford button-downs. At a glance, it could almost have been a trade convention of insurance adjusters: experts gathered to contemplate the future, assess risk, gauge the impact of events beyond our control.double quotation markThe single biggest problem astrologers have is that they believe in astrology too muchMark JonesIn that sense, the room reflected astrology’s broader transformation. Astrology is now a $15bnindustry. From the marginal, it has crept into the mainstream. A 2025 Pew Researchreportfound that 30% of American adults consult astrology, tarot or a fortune teller at least once a year, and 43% of women under 50 claim to “believe in astrology”.But its influence on the zeitgeist has hardly made astrology more settled. As I sat down with my interlocutor, her companion Alan Clay, founder of Dwarf Planet University, tells me the mainstays of the solar system can only get you so far. Recent astral discoveries, he said, have enriched the picture, offering a view into the unconscious through bodies drifting in theKuiper belt, billions of miles beyond the sun.On the wall behind his booth, the price of a reading has been slashed from $29 to $9.He pulled my chart, a term that I learn carries tremendous weight, something between destiny and the template of my very being. There is the dwarf planetMakemakein my fifth house (I too, had to look this up), which carries bold implications for creative expression and, less attractively, secret or potentially bruising sexual affairs.Some of this resonated. And therein lies the problem. Part of astrology’s current appeal is how quickly it can make itself feel personal – and persuasive.Like any sufficiently established field, modern astrology has developed its own hierarchies, factions and grudges. There are fights over tradition and fears about AI; impatient zoomers butting heads with baffled boomers; older men with reputations for harassment; and quieter epistemic disputes. (Has no one noticed, for instance, that almost all the planets are male?)Beneath all of it was a more fundamental question: who gets to interpret the stars?“Astrology is the oldest of the occult sciences,” writes scholar Benson Bobrick in his 2005 history, The Fated Sky. “It is also the origin of science itself.”For millennia, people have looked to the heavens for guidance and meaning: when to hunt and harvest, how to navigate the seas. The night presents a tapestry of gods and heroes, myths and parables. The stars are indifferent to these projections, of course, but they reveal a great deal about the people making them.The basic premise of astrology is that the configuration of the sky at the moment of your birth leaves its imprint on your constitution and life trajectory. As above, so below. If in the past, the stars reflected a collective social order, today they are more often treated as a vast personal mirror.The principle is straightforward. What astrologers make of it is not.I arrived at theconference, which sold out of its advance weekend passes, with what seemed like a simple question: what does astrology mean to the practitioner in 2026? Moving from room to windowless room, I quickly realized the question was less simple than naive.“Astrology is really an art form,” said one seasoned practitioner. “There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.”To another, it was a spiritual practice, a means of communing with the ancients. It was unscientific, and also “notnota science”. It was a field of infinite study: “We’ll never get to the bottom of it.” It was moreover a language, composed of symbols and competing dialects, but nonetheless extant. “No one questions whether Spanish is real,” the astrologer Samuel Reynolds told me.We asked astrologers about major life decisions they’ve made because of astrology – videoAnd yet, in one lecture I attended, Mark Jones, an astrologer and psychotherapist, opened with the controversial claim: “Astrology is not real.” At his words, a murmur rolled through the room, before he elaborated: “not in the sense that you are”. By his telling, the planets exert their influence on the psyche through a theory of object relations. He clicked through slides, and spoke with great authority on the spatial impact of Neptune and the role of the moon in the developmental self.But that notwithstanding, he said: “The single biggest problem astrologers have is that they believe in astrology too much.”Just what to believe in and what methods to follow are open and contentious questions. “There are as many branches of astrology as there are astrologers,” one attender told me, before rattling off a list. There’s horary astrology, an oracle for a single moment –is the person I made eyes with on the subway someone special?– and electional astrology, dealing with the timing of events (one woman told me that, much to the chagrin of her friends and family, her chart dictated a 7.30am wedding.)Geminis get colds, Scorpios get STDs: inside the ‘science’ of medieval astrologyRead moreThere’s also evolutionary astrology, which maps the soul over lifetimes; mundane astrology, concerning politics and society; and medical astrology. It goes on: relational, predictive, Jungian (the Jungian vibes are strong).Above all, it was presented to me as a kind of security blanket: a system for understanding the inexplicable, a way to make sense of a shitty day, a means to grasp the contours of current upheavals and find solace in their eventual end. During Covid, one astrologer explained: “People were really looking for answers. They were like, ‘Sky, tell me what’s going on.’”The 185 experts who presented were doing what people at conferences do: establishing hierarchies and professionalizing a crowded, competitive field. A conference, after all, is an occasion for conferring legitimacy and codifying the rules of the trade.In astrology, this raises some obvious complications. If you are claiming to see something about a person’s future, what are you responsible for telling them?Some clients, I was told, “just want the good stuff”. Other practitioners prefer to rip off the Band-Aid – if dark days lie ahead, it’s better to make an ominous prognostication so the afflicted can prepare or hunker down as necessary.But what happens when you get it wrong?“There is no wrong,” Clay told me. “There are different interpretations. Right or wrong is a Saturnian construct, it’s useful but doesn’t help us understand these new energies.”That is not, however, the abiding consensus. One of the conference seminars was devoted to learning from readings that went awry.“When people are giving predictions, there is at least a five or 10% chance that it’s not right, and the stakes are huge,” said Kay Taylor, president of the UAC and the Organization for Professional Astrology.Another astrologer illustrated the stakes with a story from her own practice. Based on her reading of a client’s chart, she concluded that both of the client’s parents would die within the year. She felt obliged to convey this information, whereupon the client quit their job and moved across the country to be with their parents for the end.“But they didn’t die!” She exclaimed with surprising pride.That was years ago. Mom and dad are still alive and well. Yet the astrologer assured me that even though the prediction was off, the message remained sound. Her client got to enjoy some bonus time with her parents.double quotation markEvery person is a complicated mathematical formulaCeleste Nash-WeningerGaffes like this are what make training critical, I was told. No fewer than six professional organizations were sponsoring this year’s gathering – the National Council for Geocosmic Research is the only one without “astrology” in its name – and they offered various routes to affiliated credentialing and curricula, ranging from astrological markers of ADHD to advanced training in asteroids.Celeste Nash-Weninger, from the American Federation of Astrologers, told me: “Every person is a complicated mathematical formula.” She used to be intimidated by the graphs and numbers, but after taking recommended courses – “and they’re tough: eight hours of math and delineation” – she has confidence in “how the heavens move”.Whether advanced math is required for mastery is open to debate. But there is one thing nearly everyone here agrees on: technology has made astrology more accessible – but also, some practitioners worry, diluted its expertise.“Before, people had to do it all by hand,” said Leslie Benson, an astrologer who works for AstroGraph, maker of the popular TimePassages app. “You had to have an ephemeris, where you looked up every placement. You had to draw it all. Now it’s instant.”Most have eagerly embraced the new tools; after all, if software can do the calculations, practitioners have more time for the interpretive work. But they also remove one of the barriers by which skill was once recognized.Artificial intelligence is where most everyone here draws the line. Of course, AI was inevitable: Pluto is in Aquarius and Uranus is in Gemini – yikes – but the contemporary astrologer, at least according to one seminar, must safeguard the personal and spiritual component of the work. “Embracing Uranus,” it advised, referring to the dark trickster of the cosmos, “without losing your soul.”Co-Star, the astrology app that has brought personalized charts and algorithmic readings to millions of users, is notably absent from the conference, and attenders clucked in disapproval overnewsof its recent acquisition by the AI startup Midjourney. The technology that made astrology accessible to anyone with a phone is also the technology that threatens to make the astrologer – the human interpreter, the trained practitioner, the person who knows what all those symbols mean – obsolete.Throughout the conference I asked around why astrology inspires such avid faith, why it appears to “work”. Some practitioners offered explanations involving gravity – the extremely subtle but no less palpable effects of celestial bodies on our own bodies. Or perhaps it is about the moon, whose effects on the tides might somehow produce corresponding swells within us. “We’re 80% water,” one astrologer offered.On three separate occasions I was told, “the proof is in the pudding”. and so with an equal mix of trepidation and enticement I agreed when Nash-Weninger, of the American Federation of Astrologers, volunteered to give me a cold read. Though she assured me she was a “professional” and could tell me “some things” about myself, I could not imagine how, on the basis of my scant data – birth date, time and location – she could uncover anything about my life. But in the name of research I let her plug my information into an app on her phone.“Ooh!” she exclaimed. I experienced an instant tingle – was this a good chart? I was born, she pronounced, in a great conjunction year, “just like Jesus Christ … in theory.”My sun is conjunct with Mercury – “that’s the writer” – and my north node indicates that “if you did something creatively you would probably be known for it later”, she said.It was hard to resist the ego bath of it all, especially when she said: “I’m going to take a chance and say your career might get really big. You might have opportunities that are huge.”At the time, I confess, I didn’t preoccupy myself with the caveating “might”, hearing only the allusions to success. The mere fact that I was born in time and place conferred a thrill: the universe had designs forme.But then she paused and squinted at a corner of my chart.“One thing I want to say: take good care of your liver and kidneys.” She gave me a pointed look and gravely intoned, Jupiter lords over my house of health issues.And then, graver still, she said she was “a little concerned about this dark moon” in my house of love.When I mentioned my recent divorce, she nodded in anof coursesort of way.Maurice Fernandez, a popular evolutionary astrologer, was giving a lecture on Chiron in Taurus. Astronomically, Chiron is an icy body discovered in 1977 that travels in a long ellipse between Saturn and Uranus, taking roughly 50 years to circle the sun.It was named for the centaur of Greek mythology – and this is where the afternoon’s drama began.Fernandez assured the audience that Chiron was not an “add on” to the chart but a “central part”. In myth, Chiron was the immortal son of the titan Cronos and the sea nymph Philyra. When a poisoned arrow struck him, he suffered unbearable pain and eventually chose to surrender his perpetuity.In astrological terms, Fernandez explained, Chiron represents a confrontation with mortality: the “wound of invisibility”, “hubris” and “the freedom to be sovereign”.View image in fullscreen‘Astrology is not therapy, but it is therapeutic,’ writes astrologer Chani Nicholas.Illustration: Dajah Callen/The GuardianAs he spoke a logic came into focus, wherein a celestial body receives a name, the name summons a story, and the story reaches through the light years to our fragile, earthbound lives.Chiron was just leaving Aries, Fernandez said, a transit that explained the #MeToo movement and the rise of the manosphere. George Floyd’s death and Black Lives Matter were also, he said, the stuff of Chiron. He needed to check the numbers, but Chiron in Aries had seen “a greater statistic of political violence”. Myth is a capacious place.What was coming as Chiron entered Taurus could be glimpsed via the past: sustainability, finances, land, resources. Stalin’s agrarian policies, Fernandez stated, also bore the hallmark of the roving centaur. He drew out the words: “Three to 5 million people died because of a manmade food crisis.” Gasps rippled through the room.Then the stock market crashed. A decade of poverty. More gasps.What gripped the audience was not necessarily the work of the stars, but rather the stunning facts of history, which, like myth, is a generous tool in astrology. A pattern is imposed on a bygone moment, and that pattern, once established, lends credibility to the prediction of what comes next.While figures like Fernandez swam through a field of palpable adoration, some of the greatest gusts of enthusiasm were reserved for the conference’s plenary speaker,Chani Nicholas, whose star is among the most ascendant in the field – at least to some.Nicholas, who has nearly 700,000 followers on Instagram, has built a devoted following around a blend of astrology and social justice. In an August post announcing Virgo season, she called for readers to “Abolish ICE and data centers and billionaires! … Manifesting a socialist utopia! Life is short! Let Gaza Live! There’s another eclipse coming!”Her company, Chani, promises employees a salary floor of $80,000 and comprehensive benefits, including “unlimited menstrual leave for people with uteruses”.double quotation markThere’s something going on that is too accurate for me to dismiss [astrology] out of handIan Anthony WallerRather than delivering a conventional keynote, Nicholas sat in conversation with Samuel Reynolds, a former fundamentalist Baptist youth minister who came to astrology as a skeptic and, in the course of trying to debunk it, found himself converted.“Extremes are extreme-ing,” Nicholas told the room, citing floods in Nepal, rising inequality, and populations straining precious resources. “If Pluto in Aquarius is about a revolution, then the robots are definitely out to get us.”Nicholas spoke directly to a younger generation that had shown up in Chicago in droves. “We’ve never had so many newcomers,” one of the conference organizers observed, not without ambivalence.The tensions were already thrumming before Nicholas took the stage. A scheduled speaker had been removed from the program after using the N-word on a podcast over the summer, prompting a small but vocal schism among attenders. For some, the episode represented an overdue reckoning; for others, it was evidence that astrology was being remade according to the dictates of a younger, more censorious culture. An antiracism panel followed.At Nicholas’s keynote, the divide became harder to miss. When she mentioned white supremacy, a handful of people got up and left. But the overwhelming number applauded when she described astrology as an essential tool for organizing in the fight against fascism – and AI.It was tempting to see this as a generational culture war imported wholesale into a trade convention. But it was also about something more fundamental: who gets to decide what astrology is for, who gets to speak for it, and what counts as knowledge in the first place.That question has particular force in a field that has never had much institutional authority to begin with. You don’t need a degree to practice astrology. You don’t need a license to create a chart, or credentials to interpret one. This makes astrology unusually democratic – and unusually susceptible to the creation of new gatekeepers.In times of uncertainty, the argument goes, people reach for systems that offer, if not certainty, then comfort: faith, mysticism, pop psychology protocols for surviving the collapse of familiar structures.“Astrology is not therapy, but it is therapeutic,” writes Nicholas. “It’s a relentless reminder that we are the way that we are on purpose.” If the self has become a more demanding and illegible creature, here is another way to make sense of it.There is something to this. When the world feels chaotic, when our purpose seems opaque, it is appealing to believe that chaos has a pattern, that this crappy stretch will end, that the planets are moving and so, eventually, will you.But the explanation is also too easy. We are always living in “interesting” times. Astrology has survived wars, plagues, depressions and the scientific method.How astrology paved the way for predictive analyticsRead moreReynolds, the former Baptist minister, offered another possibility. Young people who came of age with Donald Trump and Covid, he said, may have a different relationship to authority. They spent crucial developmental years watching institutions struggle to explain the present, while science was often hauled off to the chopping block. Truth itself became unstable.Perhaps, he suggested, they are simply more comfortable inhabiting several systems of knowledge at once: data and mysticism, evidence and meaning.In this sense, astrology is not necessarily an alternative to facticity so much as a parallel language, asking a different set of questions. It does not have to win an argument with physics to be useful to someone trying to understand why their marriage ended.Before leaving Chicago, I found myself in conversation with the sociologist Ian Anthony Waller, who was there to research the gendered nature of astrological belief. He also described himself as a “solid seven” on his own scale of faith.I had come to see astrology less as an impossible-to-validate predictive model than a cool caress of reassurance. The stars see you and whatever happens is happening for a reason.But how, I wondered, as a scholar, did he manage to maneuver between a healthy skepticism and an embrace of a system of elaborately calculated comforts?“Sometimes astrologers will say things and I’m like, ‘that is madness,’” Waller said. “But then other times, things that I read and then see in the world – there’s something going on that is too accurate for me to dismiss out of hand.”It was incumbent for him as a scholar to understand why it appears to work. “If anybody ever really figures it,” Waller said, “it’s probably not going to be an astrologer, it’s probably going to be an astrophysicist or a physicist or somebody from Nasa who makes a connection between launch failures and Mercury or something like that.“And that’s going to be the big eureka moment – or the big Uranian innovation, as we would say in this culture.”

title: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn | Motoring | The Guardian
description: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports
Content: Cars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said.Photograph: Tamer Adel/AlamyView image in fullscreenCars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said.Photograph: Tamer Adel/AlamyMotoringTech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warnHostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese importsAlex DanielThu 1 Oct 2026 06.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations.It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK.Three-quarters of UK’s popular plug-in hybrid cars unable to use rapid chargersRead moreIn a translateddocumentreleased on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet.“On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added.The alert followsreports last yearthat British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’sbestselling car in March.MPs have raisedconcernsthat China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested.The UK Ministry of Defencehas saidit is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles.This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, includingRAF Wytonin Cambridgeshire and theDorset headquartersof Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”.The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”.It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere.On Wednesday, MI5issued a rare public warningto UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.Explore more on these topicsMotoringAutomotive industryEspionageNetherlandsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK house price growth halves amid rising mortgage interest rates | House prices | The Guardian
description: Prices fell by 0.2% month on month in September as average price of a home slipped to £274,251, says Nationwide
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Prices fell by 0.2% month on month in September as average price of a home slipped to £274,251, says Nationwide
Content: Nationwide said there was ‘upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing’.Photograph: BMD Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenNationwide said there was ‘upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing’.Photograph: BMD Images/AlamyHouse pricesUK house price growth halves amid rising mortgage interest ratesPrices fell by 0.2% month on month in September as average price of a home slipped to £274,251, says NationwideBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffandGraeme WeardenThu 1 Oct 2026 03.51 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 02.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnnual house price growth halved in the UK last month, as economic uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East continued to deter homebuyers.The average price of a British home rose 0.8% in the year to September to £274,251,according to Nationwide. That washalf the rate recorded in August, when house prices grew 1.6% year on year. It also marked the slowest pace of home price growth since December last year.House prices across the UK fell 0.2% month on month, after taking account of seasonal effects.What you need to know about Your First Home scheme for first-time buyersRead moreThe housing market has been subdued in recent months, as the US-Israel war with Iran and resulting disruption to Gulf oil and gas flowsdrive up energy costs and inflation fears.That has fed through to higher interest rates on mortgages, making it more expensive for people to buy new homes.“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns,” the Nationwide chief economist, Robert Gardner, said.“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank [of England] rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.”Moneyfacts reported earlier this week that the average interest rate on a two-year fixed mortgage in the UK had risen to its highest level since July 2024, while the average rate on a five-year fixed rate mortgage hit its highest level since October 2023. Both were sitting above 5.9%.That could rise further, given that investors are pricing in a 92% chance that the Bank of England will raise interest rates, from 3.75% to 4%, at its next meeting on 5 November. Markets expect the Bank to institute at least three further rises in 2027, taking the base rate to 4.75% by the end of next year.Threadneedle Street is trying to bring inflation,now at 3.1%, back down to its 2% target. However, it predicted last month that the consumer price index of inflation could rise above 4% in the first quarter of 2027.Nationwide said that across the regions East Anglia posted the biggest hit to house prices, logging an annual decline of 0.7%. Northern Ireland was an exception, experiencing the strongest house price growth at an annual rate of 5.9%.The house price slowdown has improved affordability for some homebuyers, Gardner said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Underlying affordability is improving, as house price growth has been well below earnings growth for some time,” he said. “These gains have been only partially offset by higher mortgage rates. This suggests that activity should regain momentum in the quarters ahead, providing the energy shock fades and confidence returns – especially if market interest rates fall back to pre-conflict levels.”Meanwhile, prospective homeowners are preparing for the launch ofthe government’s Your First Home scheme, which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have the luxury of being able to call on the “bank of mum and dad”.The scheme involves a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price, with the buyer having to put down a minimum deposit of only 2.5%, which meanings taking out a standard mortgage for just 77.5% of the property’s value.The scheme applies only to England and new-build flats or houses. News of its launch has already increased the share price of housebuilders including Persimmon, Barratt Redrow, Taylor Wimpey, Crest Nicholson and Vistry.Explore more on these topicsHouse pricesPropertyHousing marketnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s sad seeing players promote it’: Wembanyama says he will never endorse gambling companies | Victor Wembanyama | The Guardian
description: Spurs star says it is ‘very sad’ to see NBA players promote gambling companies and insists money no longer drives his sponsorship decisions
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Spurs star says it is ‘very sad’ to see NBA players promote gambling companies and insists money no longer drives his sponsorship decisions
