Content: Spurs star Victor Wembanyama speaks to reporters during the team’s media day at the Victory Capital Performance Center in San Antonio on Monday.Photograph: San Antonio Express-News/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSpurs star Victor Wembanyama speaks to reporters during the team’s media day at the Victory Capital Performance Center in San Antonio on Monday.Photograph: San Antonio Express-News/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesVictor Wembanyama‘It’s sad seeing players promote it’: Wembanyama says he will never endorse gambling companiesSpurs star says he will ‘never’ promote bettingWembanyama says endorsements must reflect his valuesJames, Durant and Antetokounmpo have gambling tiesGuardian sportThu 1 Oct 2026 17.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVictor Wembanyama has ruled out ever endorsing a sports betting company, saying he was saddened to see fellow NBA players lend their names to gambling platforms.TheSan Antonio Spursstar was unequivocal when asked after Thursday’s training camp workout if he would consider partnering with a sportsbook.“Absolutely not,” Wembanyama said. “I will never do that. Honestly, I think it’s very sad to see some players promote it. Everybody does whatever they want, but without me.”Wembanyama said his approach to sponsorships has evolved during his ascent to one of basketball’s biggest stars. While money once factored into his thinking, he said he has come to prioritize whether potential partnerships align with his personal values.“In the past, there was a dimension of money,” he said. “Not anymore.”Wembanyama added that he has rejected offers worth considerably more than the endorsement deals he has accepted because he did not feel comfortable with what he would be promoting.“Obviously, we earn millions and millions. This is not our biggest strength. Our biggest strength is inspiring. I want to inspire in a good way. That’s the strongest thing I can do.”Wembanyama’s position stands in contrast to several of the NBA’s most prominent stars, who have established relationships with sportsbooks or prediction-market companies.LeBron James announced a partnership with Polymarket in September after previously working with DraftKings. Kevin Durant has an endorsement deal with FanDuel and is an investor in the prediction market Kalshi, while Giannis Antetokounmpo announced earlier this year that he had become a Kalshi shareholder. Three-time NBA MVP Nikola Jokić has served as an ambassador for Superbet in Serbia since 2023.NBA players are permitted to endorse sports betting companies under the league’s collective bargaining agreement, subject to restrictions. They cannot promote wagering on NBA-related markets but can enter broader endorsement arrangements and hold limited investments in gambling companies.The French center enters his fourth NBA season after helping San Antonio reach the NBA finals for the first time since 2014. He was unanimously voted Defensive Player of the Year last season after leading the league in blocked shots for a third consecutive year.Wembanyama, who also finished third in MVP voting, made clear Thursday that his increasing prominence will not change where he draws the line on endorsements.“I want to promote things that have a good impact, have a good influence with who I can share messages and values,” he said.Explore more on these topicsVictor WembanyamaSan Antonio SpursNBABasketballLeBron JamesShareReuse this content

title: Pro-Palestine protests interrupt game as Ireland pass up 2-0 lead in draw against Austria | Republic of Ireland | The Guardian
description: Alexander Prass and Michael Gregoritsch cancelled out Troy Parrott’s double in Austria’s 2-2 draw against the Republic of Ireland in the Nations League
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alexander Prass and Michael Gregoritsch cancelled out Troy Parrott’s double in Austria’s 2-2 draw against the Republic of Ireland in the Nations League
Content: Tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text “#StopTheGame” were launched on the pitch.Photograph: Paul Phelan/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text “#StopTheGame” were launched on the pitch.Photograph: Paul Phelan/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesRepublic of IrelandPro-Palestine protests interrupt game as Ireland pass up 2-0 lead in draw against AustriaPress AssociationThu 1 Oct 2026 17.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProtests halted events in Dublin twice before theRepublic of Irelandwere forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium.Despite a significant security presence, the contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a “limited tennis ball protest”, when – around the 20th minute – tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text “#StopTheGame” were launched on the pitch.‘A lot of lies’: Ireland manager hits out over coverage of Bazunu exit from Israel gameRead moreThen around the 35th minute a man ran on to the field of play from the opposite side carrying what appeared to be a Palestinian flag and was immediately tackled by security and carried off.It has been a tumultuous week for the Republic. Their two Nations Leaguefixtures against Israelhave divided opinion in the country, sparking protests, including one which took place pre-match outside the stadium. The Republic’s behind-closed-doors “home” game against Israel in Backa Topola, Serbia, is scheduled for Sunday, and the manager Heimir Hallgrímsson on Wednesday confirmed it was their intention to play.Troy Parrott got the hosts under way with a sensational 12th-minute opener and added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.A pair of substitutes proved the Republic’s undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.View image in fullscreenMichael Gregoritsch (left) points to the sky after scoring Austria’s second goal.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAHallgrímsson’s men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behindAustriaand Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.Hallgrímsson made three changes, including the re-introduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.The goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, who had made himselfunavailable for the Israel meetings, was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhín Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before the Republic enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors’ half.It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah’s glanced-on header from a goal kick.View image in fullscreenTroy Parrott slots home the Republic of Ireland’s opening goal in the 12th minute.Photograph: Evan Treacy/EPAThe Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts before nutmegging Philipp Lienhart and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.Play was briefly paused just before the 20th minute to clear up the tennis balls, a pause both teams used for a hydration break. The second stoppage of play took place around the 35th minute.Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead. Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a video assistant referee check and blasted it past the Austria keeper.Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed by VAR.The Brentford keeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch, guessing the wrong way as the Augsburg forward fired into the corner.The Republic captain, Dara O’Shea, was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar, and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.Explore more on these topicsRepublic of IrelandAustriaNations Leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: From Super Bowl champ to master architect: Mike Tomlin’s sprawling Minecraft city is magnificent | NFL | The Guardian
description: The former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach took 12 years to build a city filled with stadiums, skyscrapers and bespoke homes. It is a marvel
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: The former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach took 12 years to build a city filled with stadiums, skyscrapers and bespoke homes. It is a marvel
Content: Mike Tomlin's Minecraft city includes a baseball field as well as an MLS stadium.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenMike Tomlin's Minecraft city includes a baseball field as well as an MLS stadium.Photograph: YouTubeNFLFrom Super Bowl champ to master architect: Mike Tomlin’s sprawling Minecraft city is magnificentThe former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach took 12 years to build a city filled with stadiums, skyscrapers and bespoke homes. It is a marvelAlex KirshnerThu 1 Oct 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe may finally have cracked the case as to why thePittsburgh Steelersstagnated so much over the final years of Mike Tomlin’s tenure as head coach: he was focused on virtual urban planning.I’m kidding, of course. It’s good when people in high-pressure jobs have creative hobbies. Count this writer (and his interior designer wife) among those who were gobsmacked on Wednesday night by Tomlin’s reveal of a 12-year-long project in Minecraft, the world-building game. Tomlin had teasedthat during his coaching career, he took up Minecraft city-building as a way to connect with his young children. We have now seen the fruits of that labor,and they are magnificent. Look my my works, Terry Bradshaw, and despair.“More than anything, it was therapeutic for me,” Tomlin says at the video’s outset. One can see how this sort of “mindless entertainment” would’ve been helpful to a man in his position. Tomlin was building up hisMinecraftcity (whose name is still unclear) during a tumultuous period in Steelers history. When star tailback Le’Veon Bell declined to sign his franchise tag in 2018, keeping the Steelers offense in limbo all season? Tomlin had Minecrafting. When Antonio Brown blew up his relationship with Ben Roethlisberger and ultimately forced a trade to the Raiders? Tomlin had Minecrafting. When the Pittsburgh sports media turned on him for not winning any playoff games in nearly a decade? Minecrafting, still.Where Tomlin’s description of his Minecraft experience doesn’t make sense, however, is when he calls the experience “mindless”. It’s clear that Tomlin’s project was anything but.The city is built around a central body of water, not terribly unlike the city where the coach built hisNFLlegend. (Pittsburgh has three rivers meeting at Point State Park. Tomlin’s city has a big lake from which the whole urban landscape flows outward.) “This is kind of where it all started, around this body of water,” the coach deadpans. “I thought it was appropriate to just give you that perspective of where I wanted to get started from.” He sounds like he’s about to read off his team’s Week 4 injury report, but no. Tomlin is about to take us through his universe, one he crafted over the years with evidentlypainstakingdetail.Tomlin tells us about the first building he ever constructed, ostensibly around 2014, when the Steelers won the AFC North behind a 1,700-yard receiving season from Brown and 1,300 on the ground from Bell. It’s a “boutique hotel” with an executive spa off the main lobby, featuring therapy rooms. He takes us into a multipurpose conference room on the other side, with tall windows and a glass roof.“I was very lighting conscious,” Tomlin tells us. “You’ll consciously see me do things with glass ceilings where appropriate.”We see more and more as Tomlin flies us around. He breezes right past a virtual CVS and into an aquarium-themed apartment highrise. “I did it because it was across the street from the aquarium that I built in the city,” he explains, in case anyone thought the water features were out of place. Tomlin promises that we will see the aquarium in a future episode and that it will be “crazy”. His son and producer Dino, a former college wide receiver, tells us that it took a lot of time for his dad to get the water all situated.“That was a nightmare,” Mike says.It goes on and on. Tomlin explains that he was “fixated” on providing details in bedrooms. He is also conscious that not everyone in his city will be an NFL fan: Tomlin built an MLS stadium as well as a baseball field that fits neatly into the cityscape, not terribly unlike Pittsburgh’s PNC Park. He relishes in the fact that one of his highrises has a good view of the ballpark. Tomlin tells us that he is “view-conscious”, and indeed, the man seems to take a special pleasure in a city vista.The finer details are not left to chance, either. In office and multipurpose space, we learn of the coach’s passion for providing an “appropriate number of public restrooms.” Tomlin built his city with the well-roundedness of a good gameplan, understanding that a successful operation means not just acquiring glitzy wide receivers (or swanky apartment complexes) but also good linemen (toilets).We also see touches of Tomlin’s family life. He built a collegiate apartment complex called “The View”, which shares the name with a particularly grungy complex in College Park, Maryland, where Dino began his college career. (Your correspondent had many long nights in the same complex, one he hopes to never revisit for the rest of his life.) We get the sense that there will be much more to see.View image in fullscreenMike Tomlin’s city is built around water.Photograph: YouTubeIn some dark corners of the internet, Tomlin’s hobby was met with condescension.“There is a tension between trying to appreciate people’s widely diverse passions, and the feeling that some people are wasting all of their ambition and energy,”tweetedone person with the job title “chief economist”. It was a bizarre sentiment about a man whowon a Super Bowland became one of the most decorated coaches in the history of the NFL before going on to a lucrative career in broadcasting.Fortunately, it was also a minority view. The overarching response to Tomlin’s Minecraft build could only be described as adulation. People found it refreshing that a 54-year-old with one of the most high-profile, pressurized jobs in the US would develop a personal hobby that bakes in as much creativity and thoughtfulness as this one. The city of Pittsburgh should hire Tomlin as a planning consultant.Explore more on these topicsNFLMinecraftGamesUS sportsPittsburgh SteelersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pleasant surprises of the NFL season so far: Brock Purdy for MVP and actual Raiders competence | NFL | The Guardian
description: It’s still early in the 2026 season but a number of teams and players have found unexpected levels of success in the last few weeks
Author: Doug Farrar
Headline: It’s still early in the 2026 season but a number of teams and players have found unexpected levels of success in the last few weeks
Content: Kirk Cousins drops back to pass, Case Keenum and Brock Purdy have all boosted their teams this season.Composite: APView image in fullscreenKirk Cousins drops back to pass, Case Keenum and Brock Purdy have all boosted their teams this season.Composite: APNFLPleasant surprises of the NFL season so far: Brock Purdy for MVP and actual Raiders competenceIt’s still early in the 2026 season but a number of teams and players have found unexpected levels of success in the last few weeksDoug FarrarThu 1 Oct 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 04.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast season ended with a Super Bowl in which neither team – the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots – had been expected to participate. Before that, we had a 44-year-old grandfatherreturning from a four-season layoffto give the Indianapolis Colts unexpected cheer in an otherwise miserable season, while the Chicago Bears and Jacksonville Jaguars rebounded from bad 2024 seasons to win their divisions.It’s early to state which surprises will be the most fun to recall this time around, but here are four to watch as things progress.Brock Purdy playing at an MVP levelUnder an obscure Santa Clara bylaw, we are legally obliged to point out that Purdy has outplayed his status as the last pick in the 2022 draft. But last season, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback was caught up in his team’s horrible injury luck (which continues unabated), missing eight games. Purdy still played well when healthy, but nobody was quite prepared for how good he has been in 2026.The 49ers are 3-0 despite all the injury hits, and Purdy is the primary reason. He has completed 60 of 83 passes (72.3%) for 789 yards (9.5 yards per attempt), nine touchdowns, one interception, no sacks, and a passer rating of 133.1, whichleads the league quite comfortably(in second place is Drew Lock, more on which later).Moreover, Purdy is doing all of this without the superhuman traits attributed to thelikes of Lamar Jackson and Josh Allen. He’s a decent runner, has an above-average arm, and moves well in the pocket, but Purdy is really beating opponents with his mind. He’s reading defenses like they’re first-day third-grade stuff, and his ability to throw with anticipation (“throwing his receivers open” in football parlance) is unmatched. No matter who’s healthy enough to block for him or catch his passes,the big plays are coming in bunches.It’s why everyone is on the Purdy bandwagon right now, and as long as he can avoidthe Substation Curse, that should continue.Backup quarterbacks saving games for teams in needIt’s not just starting quarterbacks who are making things better for their injury-ravaged teams. 2026 has already been a banner year for backups too.The defending champion Seattle Seahawks lost starter Sam Darnold five plays into the new season when he suffered a glute injury. Backup Drew Lock, who has rarely resembled a starting-level quarterback in an NFL career that goes back to 2019,turned himself into exactly thatin Weeks 1 and 2. The Seahawks beat the New England Patriots and the Arizona Cardinals with Lock, who completed 35 of 48 passes (72.9%) for 422 yards (8.8 YPA), four touchdowns, no interceptions, and a league-high passer rating of 127.3 – yes, even higher than Purdy’s 125.6 through those two games.View image in fullscreenMarcus Mariota helped his team to a shock win over the Super Bowl champions.Photograph: Nick Wass/APDarnold returned to the field for Seattle’s Week 3 game against the Washington Commanders, but the Seahawks ran into another example of this phenomenon when they were upended by Marcus Mariota. Starter Jayden Daniels suffered a dislocated left elbow in Week 2 against the Dallas Cowboys, and Mariota was back – he had started eight games for the Commanders in 2025 when Daniels had a similar elbow injury – but he had never played like this. In Washington’s shock 33-31 win over Seattle, Mariota completed 19 of 31 passes (61.3%) for 183 yards (5.9 YPA), three touchdowns, no interceptions, and a passer rating of 110.0. Not quite as impressive until you consider that from Week 1 of the 2025 season to Week 2 of the 2026 season,Seattle’s defense had allowed a cumulative passer rating of 77.8.Still, it was up to the Chicago Bears’ Case Keenum to write the ultimate backup story of the new season. Against the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night, Chicago’s 38-year-old third-stringer (behind injured starter Caleb Williams and ostensible No. 2 man Tyson Bagent) completed 24 of 34 passes (70.6%) for 247 yards (7.3 YPA), two touchdowns, no interceptions, and a passer rating of 110.8.Bears’ 38-year-old backup Case Keenum rolls back the years to ground EaglesRead moreNot bad for a guy who hadn’t started an NFL game since December 2023, when he was with the Houston Texans. Most delightfully, Keenum had his family at Soldier Field,which led to a fascinating discussionabout whether Keenum’s kids would prefer to watch game highlights on Tuesdayor revert to their usual staple, Bluey.We’re guessing it was a mixture of the two.The Las Vegas RaidersThe Raiders haven’t made the playoffs since the 2021 season, their second in Las Vegas. Before that, they hadn’t made the playoffs since the 2016 season, when they were the Oakland Raiders. And the franchise hasn’t actually won a playoff game since the 2002 season, seven years after they moved back to Oakland from Los Angeles.No matter where they are, the Raiders have been hapless for most of this century. But, based on the early returns with new head coach Klint Kubiak, that could be about to change. Kubiak’s new Raiders are one of five undefeated teams remaining (the Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs,Minnesota Vikings, and the 49ers are the others), and they’re getting it done on both sides of the ball. And we haven’t even seen Fernando Mendoza, the first overall pick in the 2026 draft, on the field for the Raiders yet, because veteran Kirk Cousins is playing at such an unexpectedly high level.The Raidersrank ninth in DVOA, FTN’s efficiency metric, after ranking 31st in 2025. They’ve already won as many games as they did last season, and between Kubiak’s brilliance as an offensive playcaller and what defensive coordinator Rob Leonard has done with a bunch of relative no-names (edge-rusher Maxx Crosby excepted), few teams are benefiting from better coaching than the Raiders right now.When was the last time anybody could say that? Kubiak is only the third coach in franchise history to start his first season 3-0. Before him, there was Bill Callahan in 2002, and the legendary John Madden in 1969.Of course, we don’t actually know what Kubiak’s Raiders will do over time. It could go either way. Callahan lasted just two seasons with the team after he followed a Super Bowl XXXVII appearance with a 4-12 season in 2003, while Madden was one of the most successfulNFLcoaches ever. But as things stand right now, Kubiak is coaching his guys as well as anybody in the league.The Minnesota Vikings’ unconventional defenseMinnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is absolutely one of one. While most coaches prefer to treat blitzing opposing quarterbacks as if it’s something to pull out of the quiver in obvious passing situations, Flores prefers to make the entire plane out of the black box.The former Bill Belichick assistant in New England, who was also the Miami Dolphins’ head coach from 2019 to 2021, is going to do things his way, and it generally works. Since he became the Vikings’ DC in 2023, Flores’s defenses have led the NFL in blitz rate every season,and they’re topping out at an insane 66.4% so far in 2026.How far off the grid is that? The Chicago Bears rank second in blitz rate… at 39.8%.So, why don’t more coaches blitz more often? Because when you send extra defenders after the quarterback, said quarterback can exploit the obvious openings in coverage. But Flores has answers for that as well.The Vikings have also led the league every year since 2023 in simulated pressures, in which a defense looks like it’s going to blitz, and then several defenders drop into coverage post-snap.So, you wind up with a playbook in which the Vikings are generally among the top of the NFL in both six-man-or-more rushes, and three-man-or-fewer rushes.In less capable hands, that kind of binary approach wouldn’t work as well – not only because opposing coaches would figure out how to attack it, but also because few other defensive coaches have Flores’s understanding of what his players do well, and how best to utilize them. The Vikings’ roster is filled with players who embrace Flores’s approach wholeheartedly, because they love it, and because it works.The Vikings have the NFL’s best defense per DVOAby a comfortable margin, and the team would be even more of a juggernaut if their offense didn’t rank 30th. As brilliant as he is, Flores isn’t able to manufacture a quarterback for head coach Kevin O’Connell. Flores is more of a quarterback destroyer than a quarterback creator.Explore more on these topicsNFLSan Francisco 49ersChicago BearsWashington CommandersMinnesota VikingsLas Vegas RaidersSeattle SeahawksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The ultra-rich face … accountability? Manchester City and Clippers verdicts show it’s possible | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The sports world has accomplished a rare feat: calling out industrial-scale cheating on both sides of the Atlantic
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The sports world has accomplished a rare feat: calling out industrial-scale cheating on both sides of the Atlantic
Content: Manchester City’s achievements over the last decade have come under question.Photograph: Molly Darlington/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester City’s achievements over the last decade have come under question.Photograph: Molly Darlington/ReutersSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester CityThe ultra-rich face … accountability? Manchester City and Clippers verdicts show it’s possibleLeander SchaerlaeckensThe sports world has accomplished a rare feat: calling out industrial-scale cheating on both sides of the AtlanticSign up for our free newsletter hereThu 1 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTShareThe first stage of billionaire exposure to accountabilityis vociferous denial.The second is bafflement that such an earthly and proletarian problem should even be allowed to happen to you, titan of industry, pillar of society, master of man and beast alike.The third is a milquetoastnon-apology apology“for the distraction and distress this matter has caused”, after issuinga totalandbelligerent denialthrough your proxies.The fourth stage? We’ll know soon enough.Manchester City timeline: trophies, transfers and more than 100 chargesRead moreWithin the last month, we have traipsed, on tiptoes, into a strange new age where some modicum of repercussion may occasionally threaten the billionaire class – albeit strictly limited to the confines of sports, where nothing actually matters. It’s a new and funny feeling in an age when it seems that the 1% don’t just get a bespoke business climate, where taxation and regulation are administered on an opt-in basis, but their own concierge service from the justice system, too.Setting aside for the moment the argument of whether billionaires should exist at all, or whether they are a flagrant failure of fiscal policy, this is a remarkable turn of events.On 2 September, the NBA released the findings of an investigation: The Los Angeles Clippers and their owner Steve Ballmer were officially caught paying star forward Kawhi Leonard $28m off the books for a no-show job with a supposed sponsor, circumventing the league’s salary cap. The Clippers weredocked five first-round picks and fined $30m. Ballmer, the ninth richest man in the world, was suspended from involvement with his team for a year. Initially, the Clippersissued a statement, snarling that they “vehemently reject the NBA’s findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence”.Then, the team accepted the punishment.View image in fullscreenClippers owner Steve Ballmer at a game in April.Photograph: Allen Berezovsky/Getty ImagesAfter all, they were caught bang to rights, after a year-long investigation by journalist Pablo Torre and his podcast, Pablo Torre Finds Out, which won a Pulitzer Prize for its work. The podcast unfurled its findings over several episodes and faced deep skepticism, including from Mark Cuban, Dallas Mavericks minority owner and Ballmer’s fellow billionaire. “I’m on Team Ballmer,” Cubanhad previously postedin an act of class solidarity. “Steve isn’t that dumb.”Ballmer, it should be noted, was only allowed to buy the Clippers when the team’s previous owner, Donald Sterling, was more or less expelled from the league over racist comments; another rare time that an owner was brushed back, especially by their own kind.Then, last week, a similar hammer dropped; Manchester Cityhas been found guiltyof more than 100 charges of cheating the Premier League’s financial regulations from 2009 to 2018 and obstructing the subsequent investigation from 2019 to 2023. They’re not at the apology stage yet,insisting on their innocence, as they have all along, taking an aggressively defiant posture.Still, it seems that in any of the plausible ways this may play out, after several more years of appeals and lawsuits surely, the club’s Abu Dhabi ownership will emerge from the ordeal bruised. Its entire footballing body of work, backed by untold billions in investment turning a humdrum club into a world-beating one, will have been tarnished. And if the entire point of the project – in the club administrator parlance – was a soft power PR play by the oil-rich nation state, it will have backfired catastrophically. No matter what happens next, the UAE-owned club will be remembered for cheating on an industrial scale, with a colossal scope, subverting the world’s most popular sporting competition and a British cultural institution for almost a decade.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWill the Clippers’ $30m fine tame the NBA’s billionaire class? We’re about to find outRead moreIt’s worth pausing and taking that in. These are the very rare occasions in a modern society, which has carved out a friction-free fast lane for the very rich and the very, very rich, that anyone in that stratus should be made to pay a price for anything at all.Like that time New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was allegedly caught paying for sex in a Florida massage parlor; prosecutors dropped the charge. Or the current status of theridiculousandspitefulNew York Knicks owner James Dolan, whofaces a lawsuitby a former employee over discrimination in which it’s alleged that he spied on the team’s own fans illegally – this, too,had been reported by Torre. It feels unlikely that Dolan will ever feel any effects from the accusations.And this is in addition to innumerable examples outside sports – including a certain resident of the White House, and a lot of his friends and allies.Time will probably mark out the Clippers and City cases as outliers. But that, for now, is what makes them so notable, so newsworthy. People of power and means running into the consequences of their own decadent and crooked decisions. A true novelty in our time.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsManchester CitySoccer with Jonathan WilsonNBABasketballUS sportsLos Angeles ClippersBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: Phil Mickelson’s reps say he sought treatment for family trauma and addiction | Phil Mickelson | The Guardian
description: The six-time major winner, who has spoken in the past of his struggles with gambling addiction, has not played in an event since March
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The six-time major winner, who has spoken in the past of his struggles with gambling addiction, has not played in an event since March
Content: Phil Mickelson’s most recent event was at LIV Golf South Africa in March.Photograph: Siphiwe Sibeko/ReutersView image in fullscreenPhil Mickelson’s most recent event was at LIV Golf South Africa in March.Photograph: Siphiwe Sibeko/ReutersPhil MickelsonPhil Mickelson’s reps say he sought treatment for family trauma and addictionGolfer has spoken of gambling issues in pastSix-time major winner has not played since MarchGuardian sportThu 1 Oct 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhil Mickelson sought treatment earlier this year for “family trauma and addiction”, his representatives confirmed to multiple outlets on Wednesday.The 56-year-old golfer voluntarily entered a treatment facility and has since returned home. Mickelson’s representatives did not say when he sought treatment or how long he stayed at a facility.TMZ was the first to report the news. The six-time major winner, who hasspokenin the past about gambling addiction,withdrewfrom the Masters in April and several LIV Golf events this year due to a “family health matter”.In June, Mickelsondeniedallegations of nonconsensual and inappropriate physical conduct with a female employee at a San Diego golf club. A report by Golf Digest claimed Mickelson was challenged on an incident mid-round and left the property soon after. His lawyer confirmed he hadresignedfrom the Farms Golf Club amid the allegations and said he was working on recovery.“Some of the allegations circulating about Mr Mickelson are false, and others revisit mistakes he has already acknowledged, publicly or privately,” a spokesperson for MickelsontoldPeople magazine in June, in response to an article on golf website Skratch about alleged misconduct.“Recovery is not a straight line. Throughout their 35-year relationship, his wife, Amy Mickelson, has supported Mr Mickelson and their family with extraordinary grace, unwavering love, and the belief that people are measured not only by their failures, but by what they do to make them right. Mr Mickelson’s priority is to become the husband, father, and man his family deserves. Right now, that means giving his full attention to a private family health matter. He understands that parts of his life are public, but his family’s private matters are not,” the statement concluded.Mickelson has played just one tournament with LIV Golf this season, in South Africa in March. When he withdrew from the Masters in April, he said he would be out for an “extended period of time”, and he later pulled out of May’s PGA Championship. His plans to return to the sport are unclear, given theuncertaintyaround the future of the Saudi-backed LIV circuit.He spoke publicly of his struggles with gambling addiction in 2023 after renowned gambler Billy Walters claimed in his book that Mickelson had wagered more than $1bn over three decades. He said he was “in recovery” after betting had alienated him from loved ones.“After many years of receiving professional help, not gambling, and being in recovery from my addictions, I’m now able to sit still, be present in the moment and live each day with an inner calm and peace,” Mickelson wrote on social media in September 2023. “I still have a lot of cleaning up to do with those I love the most but I’m doing it slowly and as best I can.”Explore more on these topicsPhil MickelsonGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s tennis tour announces prize money parity with men’s events | Tennis | The Guardian
description: The WTA has announced a ‘major milestone’, with all combined WTA 1000 events to award equal prize money
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The WTA has announced a ‘major milestone’, with all combined WTA 1000 events to award equal prize money
Content: Elina Svitolina won her share of an Italian Open prize money pot totalling £8.3m with final victory this year – the men played for a share of $9.6m.Photograph: Claudia Greco/ReutersView image in fullscreenElina Svitolina won her share of an Italian Open prize money pot totalling £8.3m with final victory this year – the men played for a share of $9.6m.Photograph: Claudia Greco/ReutersTennisWomen’s tennis tour announces prize money parity with men’s eventsWTA announces ‘major milestone’ in fight for equalityCombined WTA 1000 events to award equal prize moneyAgenciesThu 1 Oct 2026 15.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll combined WTA 1000 tournaments will award women equal prize ⁠money to the men from 2027, the Women’sTennisAssociation has announced, ⁠with the Italian ⁠Open ​and other major events joining the rest of the category in offering the ⁠same payouts.Billie Jean King has often said that she was moved to form the women’s professional tennis circuit after earning $600 for her 1970 Italian Open title while Ilie Nastase took home $3,500 for winning the men’s tournament the same year.Laver Cup 2026: Topknots and top shots as Team Europe triumph – in picturesRead moreIn 2027 – nearly six decades after King’s title at the Foro Italico – the Rome clay-court event will finally award women the same amount of total prize money as men, as part a “major milestone” for the women’s tour.The initiative means that all combined WTA 1000 events will award equal prize money for the first time. Besides the Italian Open, the holdouts had been the Canadian Open and the Cincinnati Open. The other combined 1000 events in Indian Wells, California; Miami; Madrid and Beijing; as well as all four Grand Slams, already offer equal prize money.“Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis,” WTA chair Valerie Camillo said. “It demonstrates the WTA’s continued commitment to leading the sports industry in delivering our athletes competitive and financial equality and is a testament to the enduring nature of the founding vision of the WTA.”In 2023, Italian Open organisers pledged to have equal prize money starting in 2025 but didn’t carry through on the promise. The total men’s prize money this year in Rome was $9.6m while the women got $8.3m.Also announced for next year was an expanded WTA 250-level tournament in Manila, Philippines, amid massive interest surrounding home player Alex Eala, who is ranked 18th.Also, the number of annual WTA 500 level tournaments required for players ranked in the top 50 was reduced from six to four, resulting in a total base playing commitment of 14 WTA tournaments plus the four grand slams in 2027.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe WTA relied heavily on its tour architecture council, a working group chaired by third-ranked Jessica Pegula. “As players, we’re on the road most of the year, so having more flexibility in our schedules and commitments makes a real difference,” Pegula said. “The 2027 changes give us more ability to build our seasons around our own goals – competitively and personally. That’s an impactful step forward for players.”The WTA said the updates “will be implemented as a one-year pilot” for 2027, allowing it to “evaluate the impact of the changes across the tour to inform decisions for 2028 and beyond”.Explore more on these topicsTennisEqual paynewsShareReuse this content

title: US soccer’s youth system is expensive, chaotic and overdue for reform | Soccer | The Guardian
description: World Cup setbacks have renewed concern over America’s costly, fragmented youth system. The real test is whether the urgency survives the next news cycle
Author: Beau Dure
Headline: World Cup setbacks have renewed concern over America’s costly, fragmented youth system. The real test is whether the urgency survives the next news cycle
Content: The cost and fragmentation of the development system in the US have renewed questions over how the country identifies and nurtures young talent.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe cost and fragmentation of the development system in the US have renewed questions over how the country identifies and nurtures young talent.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesSoccerUS soccer’s youth system is expensive, chaotic and overdue for reformWorld Cup setbacks have renewed concern over America’s costly, fragmented youth system. The real test is whether the urgency survives the next news cycleBeau DureThu 1 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA few years ago, the idea that the US soccer community at large was neglecting youth soccer was met with silence or ridicule.At a May 2022 conference call announcing a new collective bargaining agreement that effectively ended the “equal pay” saga, players were asked how they would build bridges with grassroots organizers who, in afit of anger over perceived slights, nearlyrestored Carlos Cordeiroto US Soccer’s presidency not long after he resigned under heavy pressure. They could have offered any vague platitudes about how they valued youth and amateur soccer. Theyfell silent.Meanwhile, in the social media sphere, suggestions that US Soccer should be paying its able-bodied national teams a bit less and redistributing more resources to development – as is the case in more successful soccer countries – found a hostile reception. The heavily memed Simpsons reference “Won’t somebody please think of the children?!” was a typical sarcastic response.Today, everyone’s thinking of the children. But the thoughts are as chaotic and self-contradictory in the soccer world as they were when Helen Lovejoy squealed out her “think of the children” plea repeatedly on The Simpsons.When the US men’s World Cup campaign ended with a whimper this summer, fingers were pointed atthe “pay-to-play” systemand economic barriers that keep a lot of players out of elite youth soccer. The US Under-20 women’s lackluster World Cup performance in September was partially blamed on clubs refusing to release players (or, more broadly, blamed on Fifa fornot scheduling such eventsduring appropriate windows), but the result wasn’t an outlier alongside other recent US youth results.Simply put, the kids aren’t all right. And it’s a problem that has been addressed not with a sustained effort to improve matters but with intermittent cries for help, often followed by simplistic solutions.In 2026, the most prominent voice sounding the alarm isUS women’s coach Emma Hayes, whose track record of success at Chelsea and with the gold medal-winning US women in the 2024 Olympics commands attention.In 2018, the most prominent voices were the nine candidates who sought US Soccer’s presidency after the US men failed to qualify for the World Cup.In between, various forces have yanked the discussion from one overarching solution to another. Claudio Reyna, US Soccer’s youth technical director at the time,unveiled a curriculumat the NSCAA (now United Soccer Coaches) convention in 2011 that was heavily influenced by Barcelona’s tiki-taka approach. Three years later, at the same convention, one of the sessionsgrappled with the questionof reconciling threedifferentorganizations’ curricula.Most countries don’t have such chaos. In Germany, if the DFB wishes to embark on a massive overhaul such as the heralded “Das Reboot” of the early 2010s, it can do so. US Soccer simply doesn’t have that power. Nor does it have the money, especially given the vastness of a country that would make a US equivalent of Germany’s regional training-center system impossible.Incoherence is just one obstacle preventing a US youth system overhaul. The biggest obstacle is one that most of the US soccer community, Alexi Lalasnotwithstanding, agrees upon: Youth soccer costs too much. It’s an easy problem to identify but much more difficult to solve.It’s not that it’s difficult to find affordable soccer in the USA. Recreational soccer costs about the same as youth clubs in England, Spain, Germany and other more established soccer powers. Professional academies are generally free – in men’s soccer, anyway. Most high school soccer teams are free to anyone who can make the team. For all the fretting over barriers to entry in soccer, participation levelshave roared back to lifeafter the pandemic.The problem is the middle tier that is largely unique to the USA – “travel” soccer that costs anywhere from the low four figures to the low five figures. Unfortunately, this tier is the only one that matters to professional and college scouts. Travel soccer is the key to any sort of future in the game and/or a ticket to admission to a school that rejects high school valedictorians but welcomes promising left backs. College and pro coaches may talk a good game about lowering barriers to entry, but they and their scouts are noticeably absent from high school and recreational games that would harbor the supposed thousands of outstanding players who can’t pay for travel soccer.Travel soccer also appeals to parents who recognize their kids have little to no chance of making the cut in college. The snazzy uniforms are appealing to kids. The games are better because those with no aptitude for the sport are weeded out in tryouts. Teams are supposedly better because they have professional coaches, but whether they’re really better than parent coaches who have more experience dealing with kids is up for some debate. It’s also a social endeavor for kids and their parents, who wear their long-distance drives and depleted bank accounts as badges of honor.While all of this may sound frustrating and pointless, it’s worth noting that travel soccer generates a lot of money that might not otherwise be available. That money goes toward suitable fields – and scholarships for players who couldn’t play without financial help.So the soccer-industrial complex will be difficult to dismantle. A better bet is to reform it, in part by limiting the “travel” aspect of “travel soccer”. Players don’t get better in a car or an airplane.The bold reforms of 2018 may have fallen flat. But US Soccer is making incremental progress. The federation is starting to tame the alphabet soup of youth organizations byintegrating with US Youth Soccer, which had already joined up with rival US Club Soccer tomerge a couple of redundant competitionsinto the new National 1 League. These changes should make it easier for neighboring clubs to play each other instead of traveling farther to play a club in League XYZ while the neighboring club is in League ZYX. The reorganization may also bring a halt to the incessant arguments over which “elite” league in a given area is more “elite”.Parsing out how much US Soccer invests in youth soccer as opposed to senior-level national teams isn’t particularly straightforward. The federation spends well into nine figures on its “national teams”, but that includes everything from the able-bodied men’s and women’s teams to youth squads, futsal, beach soccer, deaf soccer, 7-a-side soccer for players with cerebral palsy or similar conditions, and power soccer (players in electric wheelchairs). What wedoknow is that US Soccergives its players80% of World Cup prize money while other federations take a majority of their winnings and reinvest into development so they can come back and beat the USA again in the next Cup.The federation has a grant program that isn’t particularly well-funded. The 2025 tax form says the federation gavenearly $4m in grant moneyover that fiscal year -- less than it spent to pay five members of the women’s team. An offshoot foundation, Soccer Forward, is geared toward harnessing the legacy – read: money – of the World Cups and Olympics being hosted in the USA from 2026 (men) to 2031 (women) toward the next generation. Soccer Forward’s biggest endeavor so far is “Soccer at Schools”, which aspires to “make soccer possible in every school in the United States”.That alone is a major change in US youth soccer programming, which has been divorcing itself from schools for a few decades now. It’s also sensible on a basic level. Every kid in the United States goes to school. Only a handful of kids can afford to play travel soccer, which takes place after the school day and on weekends.But the biggest challenge for US Soccer (the federation) and US soccer (the community) will be sustaining the interest in making things better. If youth development is given the priority it deserves, the country can overcome some – not all, but some – of the challenges it faces as a sprawling nation in which soccer isn’t the most popular sport. If the soccer community only springs into action with every World Cup loss and otherwise sneers at the idea that the youth game matters, the game will stagnate. Or worse.Explore more on these topicsFootballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jürgen Klopp disgusted by claims his Germany team are ‘not white enough’ | Germany | The Guardian
description: Jürgen Klopp has reacted with disgust to a social media debate questioning whether the Germany team he is in the process of forming are ‘white enough’
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Jürgen Klopp has reacted with disgust to a social media debate questioning whether the Germany team he is in the process of forming are ‘white enough’
Content: Jürgen Klopp said his Germany squad ‘could not be better united’.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJürgen Klopp said his Germany squad ‘could not be better united’.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Getty ImagesGermanyJürgen Klopp disgusted by claims his Germany team are ‘not white enough’Says social media claims are ‘nonsense’ and ‘idiocy’Coach sees ‘no reason to pay attention to these people’Kate Connollyin BerlinThu 1 Oct 2026 06.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJürgen Klopp has reacted with disgust to a social media debate questioning whether the Germany team he is in the process of forming are “white enough”. Klopp said he believed there was no point in giving room to “such people and their utterances”, dismissing them as “complete nonsense”.Asked to respond to the debate as to whether the national team were “not German enough” or “not white enough”, he said: “There is absolutely no reason to pay attention to these people. You won’t get my thoughts on this. I have little time in everyday life for idiocy – and even less on social media.Jürgen Klopp wants his Germany team to reclaim national pride from ‘the wrong people’Read more“The great crux of our lives is that everyone is allowed to express their opinion … it’s insane when something like that exists.”Klopp said watching sportspeople interact with each other was proof to him that mutual respect was still possible. “The world could learn a thing or two from a sports changing room … There, everyone is respected based on the facts and not discredited based on false opinions.”Klopp, whose plans for Germany since hetook over as coachin the summer have attracted huge attention, said the players he had gathered at the national team camp, including several players with a migrant background, “could not be better united than they are”.The barrage of racist and generally offensive commentaries on social media followed Germany’s 1-0 defeat by Greece last Sunday, in the Nations League, marking the first time Greece had beatenGermany.It is also reflective of plenty of utterances from MPs of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the largest opposition party in the Bundestag, who have repeatedly and consistently criticised the diversity and ethnic makeup of the national team, often referring to the squad in derogatory terms such as a “politically correct mercenary force”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKlopp, who has a four-year contract running until the end of the 2030 World Cup, was speaking before Germany’s Nations League match on Thursday against Serbia.Explore more on these topicsGermanyJürgen KloppEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier League | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister
Content: Andy Burnham accused the Premier League of ‘abuse of process’ when it punished Everton in 2023.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham accused the Premier League of ‘abuse of process’ when it punished Everton in 2023.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAManchester CityAndy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier LeagueGovernment said to be unhappy at lack of warningTreasury committee chair wants HMRC involved in City caseMatt HughesThu 1 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s intervention in theManchester Citydebate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister.Government officials are ­understood to be unhappy they were not given notice that the ­independent commission’s damning judgment of £900m offinancial manipulation and “sham contracts”would be published shortly after Burnham’s address at the Labour party ­conference on Tuesday, and his response has not gone down well with several ­Premier League clubs concerned by his ­relationship with City’s owners.Manchester City fans are right to feel angry – now they need to direct it at the owners | Will UnwinRead moreIn a series of interviews on Wednesday Burnham saidhe would be “really concerned”if City’s owners were forced to sell after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.Such was the reaction that ­Downing Street felt compelled to ­clarify ­Burnham’s position on ­Thursday, with a No 10 ­spokesperson saying the prime minister had made clear that “the initial judgment is ­serious” and “there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules”.With City appealing against the verdict, the spokesperson noted the process had to be allowed to run its course but said: “If wrongdoing is established those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.” That phrase raised eyebrows given City have been found guilty by an independent commission after a 42-day hearing that produced 7,000 pages of witness evidence, eight years after thePremier Leaguebegan investigating the club.Burnham’s apparent sympathy for City, with a warning about ­jumping to conclusions and praise for the ­owners’ investment in ­Manchester, has alarmed some clubs but the ­Premier League declined to respond.HMRC is facing calls to get involved, with Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury committee, asking for its response to the commission’s judgment. In a letter to John-Paul Marks, the permanent secretary of HMRC, Hillier sought assurances that the tax authority was “seized of the importance” of the case and asked whether it had requested an unredacted copy of the commission’s verdict.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe Times and Daily Mail have reported that City’s appeal will be based on evidence the club claim proves their sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club. Thecommission rejected that argumentas “untrue”.Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and ­conceal the realities of the Disguised ­Funding Scheme.”Burnham has history with the ­Premier League, which he ­mentioned in Wednesday’s ­interviews by ­referencing his criticisms of its ­prosecution of his club, Everton, for financial rule breaches afterthey were docked 10 points–reduced to six on appeal – by an independent commission three years ago.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with the Manchester City chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at Vincent Kompany’s testimonial in 2019.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Live NewsIn November 2023, Burnham, when mayor of Greater Manchester, wrote to the Premier League chair, Alison Brittain, accusing the league of an “abuse of process” and claimedEvertonwere being used as a pawn in efforts to show an independent ­regulator was not required in football.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham made similar ­complaints on Wednesday despite ­Everton ­having admitted ­breaching ­profitability and sustainability rules, with the club contesting only the extent of the breach and sanction. “I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,” he said. “I still hold the view very firmly that they weren’t fairly treated in that process.”The Premier League was unhappy with Burnham’s behaviour in 2023, particularly as his office posted on X two letters of complaint he sent to the league, but did not publicise replies sent by Brittain that explained the competition’s financial regulations governance process.The Independent Football Regulator chief executive, David Kogan, has made clear he will not tolerate political interference in his role, telling the Times last year that he would resign if he sensed ­government pressure.The City case has the potential to present an early test of his ­mettle and the IFR’s powers, given ­Burnham’s previous working relationship with the club’s owner, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), and the £25bn annual UK-Abu Dhabi ­trading ­relationship. One of Burnham’s first calls after he succeeded Sir Keir Starmer in July was with Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, ­president of the United Arab ­Emirates and the ultimate owner of ADUG.Kogan confirmed the IFR was monitoring the case and has powers “to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives” to protect “honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals”.City’s owners are unlikely to fall foul of the licensing system that will be introduced next season, because that is an assessment of financial sustainability and separate from the new owners, directors and senior executives test, which the IFR uses to examine honesty and integrity.The Premier League and IFR declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityAndy BurnhamPremier LeagueEvertonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Neco Williams fires revitalised Wales to fightback win against 10-man Norway | Nations League | The Guardian
description: A much-improved Wales came from behind to win 2-1 against a Norway side who had Torbjørn Heggem sent off straight after half-time
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: A much-improved Wales came from behind to win 2-1 against a Norway side who had Torbjørn Heggem sent off straight after half-time
Content: Neco Williams celebrates after putting Wales 2-1 up early in the second half.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenNeco Williams celebrates after putting Wales 2-1 up early in the second half.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersNations LeagueNeco Williams fires revitalised Wales to fightback win against 10-man NorwayBen Fisherat Cardiff City StadiumThu 1 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a night when Erling Haaland moped around the pitch, dragging his hulking frame across the Cardiff turf, Wales registered a welcome victory over 10-man Norway and their first this year. Was this just one of those games where the game’s deadliest finisher was stuck on the fringes or was it a case of115 things occupying his mind? Either way, this defeat proved a humbling experience. “You’re just a shit Kieffer Moore,” was the chant aimed at Haaland from the locals.Daniel James cancelled out Oscar Bobb’s well-worked opener in the first half and 17 seconds after the restart Torbjørn Heggem was sent off for fouling James as the Leeds winger streamed towards goal, resulting in a free-kick from which Neco Williams earned Craig Bellamy a timely win with an unerring strike.Nations League: Ronaldo-less Portugal prosper while Klopp gets first win as Germany coachRead more“It feels a bit like the first punch in the face in a long, long time,” said theNorwayand Arsenal captain Martin Ødegaard after his country lost successive games for the first time in four years. “Now we have to respond, stick together and fight back.”For Bellamy, a first win since last November eased the mounting negativity after a bruising run of results, chiefly theirWorld Cup playoff defeatto Bosnia and Herzegovina in March and alistless display in Denmarklast Sunday. “I felt my own disappointment since Bosnia and I’ve felt the stick as well,” the Wales head coach said. “The summer wasn’t easy. These games weren’t easy. But I’ve seen it … I’ve seen managers before me get it. I’ve seen the abuse the previous manager [Rob Page] got. It’s been a really difficult couple of months but it’s ‘welcome to this’ if you want to step into this … this is it. I do think we could be kinder to each other.”It was plain to see Bellamy had been hurting and he cited his daughter receiving abuse on social media. “I chose to live back down here because I wanted to be on the ground, I wanted to be called a wanker to my face,” he added.View image in fullscreenTorbjørn Heggem sees red straight after half-time.Photograph: Nick Potts/PA“The World Cup [playoff defeat] moved, I just felt the shift … Look, I am a strong person, I think we all are, but it’s the people around me I’m conscious of. It’s just society. What are we? Eight prime ministers in the space of 11 years? It’s nuts ... We’re such a small country, why can’t we have each other’s backs? Why don’t we look after each other more? The others can go at us. We’re too quick [to criticise].”View image in fullscreenDan James brings Wales level in the first half.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAWales bounced off the canvas after Ødegaard’s cute ball released Bobb on goal to open the scoring on 11 minutes. Liam Cullen, now of third-tier Leicester, pinched the ball from Sander Berge after the Fulham ­midfielder was sluggish to claim Fredrik Aursnes’s pass andWalesraced away from the scene.Cullen and Lewis Koumas burst forward and Sorba Thomas zipped a low cross into the box, where James beat David Møller Wolfe to the punch. Thomas, who by his own admission loves staying wide to get chalk on his boots, was a constant threat.Norway were punished for being slow out of the blocks in the second half, Heggem hauling James down after the restart. James does everything at speed and Heggem knew he was in trouble. The Spanish referee Alejandro Hernández awarded a free-kick on the edge of the box and ­Williams dispatched a wonderful right-foot strike to Ørjan Nyland’s right, to the surprise of the former Aston Villa and Reading goalkeeper.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPro-Palestine protests interrupt game as Ireland pass up 2-0 lead in draw against AustriaRead moreBobb played draught excluder behind a white wall of Norway shirts and Nyland stepped to his left. Nyland was out of position when he had to shuttle across his goalline when Williams thrashed the ball into the bottom corner.Haaland had one of those games; he was on the periphery and recorded just 11 first-half touches, the fewest of any player, including the Borussia Dortmund full-back Julian Ryerson who was forced off through injury after 16 minutes. Ethan Ampadu easily won what, technically, will go down as a duel on halfway but in truth Haaland just stuck out a leg in the hope of claiming the ball. His first whiff of goal came a couple of minutes before the interval but Ryerson’s replacement, Marcus Pedersen, misread Haaland’s movement and the move collapsed.The substitute Josh Sheehan spurned a golden chance to extend Wales’s advantage, sending a weak shot at Nyland after more fine craftsmanship from Thomas to release the Bolton midfielder on goal. Up the other end, Haaland ambled across the box in preparation for another Pedersen cross. When it arrived Haaland soared high but unmarked sent a header straight at Danny Ward. Then came a puff of the cheeks, a look to the turf. It has been that kind of week.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueWalesNorwaymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League: Ronaldo-less Portugal prosper while Klopp gets first win as Germany coach | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Portugal pulled away late on for a 4-2 win in Denmark while Jürgen Klopp’s Germany beat Serbia 2-0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Portugal pulled away late on for a 4-2 win in Denmark while Jürgen Klopp’s Germany beat Serbia 2-0
Content: João Félix kicks the ball away after it rebounds from the net after he seals Portugal’s 4-2 victory over Denmark in the 87th minute.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJoão Félix kicks the ball away after it rebounds from the net after he seals Portugal’s 4-2 victory over Denmark in the 87th minute.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNations LeagueNations League: Ronaldo-less Portugal prosper while Klopp gets first win as Germany coachPortugal pull away to 4-2 win in DenmarkJürgen Klopp’s Germany beat Serbia 2-0Press AssociationThu 1 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 20.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortugalmaintained their perfect start toNations LeagueGroup A4 as Jorge Jesus’s squad showed little signs of missing Cristiano Ronaldo with a 4-2 victory overDenmarkin Copenhagen.The 41-year-old Al-Nassr forward and five-time Ballon d’Or winner left the camp before the match amidreports of a falling out with Jesus, his former club manager, having been left on the bench throughout a victory in Norway.Neco Williams fires revitalised Wales to fightback win against 10-man NorwayRead moreJoão Cancelo gavePortugala 13th-minute lead before Brentford midfielder Mikkel Damsgaard equalised.Gonçalo Ramos swiftly put Portugal back in front after 25 minutes, with Napoli forward Rasmus Højlund levelling things up at 2-2 early in the second half following a swift counter.Vitinha’s header, his first Portugal goal, and a late strike by João Félix made it three straight wins.“A victory of the highest quality,” said Jesus. “This Portugal team scored four goals and put in a performance which, in my opinion, was of a very high standard – and that cannot be overlooked. Of course, this is more important than anything else that has happened.”NewGermanyhead coach Jürgen Klopp got his first win with a 2-0 Group A2 victory overSerbiain Munich. Bayern Munich midfielder Tom Bischof fired in his first senior international goal and Liverpool forward Florian Wirtz then added a second in the 61st minute.Germany produced a disciplined and intensive game, illustrating the high-pressure soccer Klopp wants to instill in the team. “That’s going in my archive. We’ll make a video out of it now,” Klopp said. “That’s how we want to play.”View image in fullscreenJürgen Klopp (right) applauds fans alongside Tom Bischof, who scored his first international goal in the victory over Serbia.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersSpeaking to public broadcaster ZDF, he added: “The mix of football and attitude was top level today. I told the boys that this has to be our benchmark.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWirtz said: “It was important to win again, just for the spirit in the team, and to send a signal out that we’re good football players and also a good football nation. Definitely a step in the right direction.”In the same group, Tijjani Reijnders scored a late equaliser as theNetherlandsfought back to draw 2-2 withGreece, who remain top. Fotis Ioannidis and Giorgos Masouras had the home side 2-0 up at the break.Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk powered in a header from a corner on the hour. After Denzel Dumfries had seen his goal ruled out by VAR for offside, Reijnders lashed home a rebound in the 89th minute to secure a point.In Group B3,IsraelandKosovoplayed out a goalless draw in Debrecen, Hungary. In Group D1,MaltaandGibraltardrew 1-1 while in Group D2,Azerbaijanwere held to a goalless draw byLiechtensteinin Baku.Explore more on these topicsNations LeaguePortugalDenmarkGermanySerbiaNetherlandsGreecenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shaw secures WCL draw against Real Madrid as Manchester City show spirit after week of turmoil | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Khadija Shaw’s 51st-minute goal earned Manchester City a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, who led through Linda Caicedo, in the Women’s Champions League
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Khadija Shaw’s 51st-minute goal earned Manchester City a 1-1 draw against Real Madrid, who led through Linda Caicedo, in the Women’s Champions League
Content: Mary Fowler reacts during the Women’s Champions League draw with Real Madrid in Manchester City’s first game since the verdict against the club was announced.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenMary Fowler reacts during the Women’s Champions League draw with Real Madrid in Manchester City’s first game since the verdict against the club was announced.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAWomen's Champions LeagueShaw secures WCL draw against Real Madrid as Manchester City show spirit after week of turmoilTom Garryat Joie StadiumThu 1 Oct 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrée Jeglertz, the Manchester City head coach, said the noise surrounding theguilty verdict dished outby the Premier League had zero impact on his women’s team’s performance after they played out a high-quality draw with Real Madrid in the Women’s Champions League.Khadija ‘Bunny’ Shaw’s ruthless finish earned City a point against an impressive Real Madrid side on a night when the hosts were surely glad for attentions to turn – however briefly – towards on-pitch matters after a week when the wider football club has dominated the headlines for the wrong reasons.Manchester City 1-1 Real Madrid: Women’s Champions League – liveRead more“Of course there is a lot of noise but the players are very calm – I haven’t seen or noticed anything that will take any percentage out of the players’ performance,” Jeglertz said.The result – which was a fair reflection of an even but entertaining game – left both sides with two points from their opening two fixtures but City will know their league phase opponents should theoretically become less challenging from hereon after their opening draw at Bayern Munich. The Swedish coach added: “It is OK, it’s an OK start in the Champions League. It’s not ideal but it’s a good start and we know what is needed from us in the rest of the tournament.”Quick GuideWCL roundup: PSG pummel LeuvenShowThe day after Paris FC played their first Women’s Champions League home game at Stade Jean-Bouin, across the road from Paris Saint-Germain’s Parc des Princes,PSG’s women’s team entertainedLeuven20km away at the club’s suburban training centre.Rasheedat Ajibade put the hosts ahead from close range after nine minutes against the Belgian side. Naomie Feller (pictured) then scored a quick-fire double, before Sakina Karchaoui and Vitória Yaya completed PSG's 5-0 rout.In the early games, Modesta Uka scoredAustria Vienna’s first goal in the WCL but Inter's captain, Ivana Andrés, levelled in the fourth minute of added time to earn a 1-1 draw. Inter dropping points left Barcelona, who thrashed Roma on Wednesday, as the only WCL team with six points after two games.In a match between two teams that had lost in the opening round,HBKøgecrushed visiting Swiss teamServette5-1 in Denmark.PAPhotograph: Benoît Tessier/REUTERSWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Jeglertz had been at pains to insist that it has been “business as usual” for his team despite the damning guilty verdict released by the Premier League towards the men’s side. There was a strange mood around this stadium in the buildup to kick-off with opinions mixed.Speaking to supporters on the bridge that connects this venue with the neighbouring Etihad Stadium, some appeared relaxed about the situation and unsure what it had to do with the women’s team, while others were clearly troubled and looking forward to watching some football as a form of escapism.View image in fullscreenKhadija Shaw fires home Manchester City’s equaliser early in the second half.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAn elderly City fan, who did not wish to be named, said pre-match: “We’ve been through rough times before, we’ll come through rough times again,” in a matter-of-fact manner. Another simply demonstrated what appears to be a growing dislike for reporters asking about the 115 charges when they said angrily “you’re from the media?” before using an expletive and promptly walking away.A much politer, younger woman simply expressed her sadness and her hopes that it wouldn’t cause the players stress.Once the match started, there were occasional references to the news from the stands; midway through the first half one home fan sang ‘Sheikh Mansour, my lord, Sheikh Mansour, oh lord, Sheikh Mansour’, to the tune of Kumbaya, although nobody else appeared to join in. There was also a small group of men carrying an inflatable banana in one corner defiantly chanting about ‘City going down with a billion in the bank’.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn general, though, the regular Women’s Super League match-going fans who are members of the supporters club seemed focused on their usual repertoire of fan chants to encourage the players, whether singing about the brilliance of Aoba Fujino and later chanting the name of Mary Fowler, who hit the crossbar with a header before the break.By then Real Madrid were already ahead courtesy of Linda Caicedo’s clinical, low finish into the bottom corner after a lethal burst of pace. The visitors could have scored as early as the first minute, when a sloppy mistake by Carlotta Wamser allowed Felicia Schröder to shoot but her effort flew narrowly wide and bounced off the stanchion, rippling the net but from the wrong side. It was a sign of the Spanish team’s intent and they looked sharp throughout.City’s play was significantly more urgent and incisive after the break and – after Yui Hasegawa spurned a volleyed chance when she was in space inside the box – it did not take long for the hosts to equalise. Shaw turned and clinically fired into the corner of the net with great technique after good pressing from City led to Hasegawa winning the ball in midfield and feeding Shaw in the area. It was the Jamaica striker’s fifth goal of the season in all competitions and her first of this Champions League campaign.Suddenly the WSL champions were dominating the territory, although Caicedo did go close at the other end with a diagonal shot that bounced wide. The introductions of Beth Mead, Sam Coffey and Grace Clinton from City’s bench only seemed to further strengthen the hosts.Hasegawa volleyed just wide again, this time from the second phase after a half-clear corner, in another let-off for Real Madrid, who had gone close themselves at the other end when Ayaka Yamashita did well to save from Caicedo. The home fans were on their feet to applaud Yamashita and chant her name when she later produced a quick reaction save to keep out Irune Dorado’s close-range effort and keep the score level.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueManchester City WomenReal Madrid WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: US lined up instead of Qatar to host inaugural Women’s Club World Cup  | Women's football | The Guardian
description: The United States is poised to host the first women’s Club World Cup in January 2028, becoming the latest in a series of Fifa tournaments staged in North America
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The United States is poised to host the first women’s Club World Cup in January 2028, becoming the latest in a series of Fifa tournaments staged in North America
Content: SoFi stadium in Los Angeles could stage the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028Photograph: Dirk Waem/Belga/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSoFi stadium in Los Angeles could stage the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028Photograph: Dirk Waem/Belga/ShutterstockWomen's footballUS lined up instead of Qatar to host inaugural Women’s Club World CupLA and San Diego are among favoured host citiesJanuary 2028 tournament would include 19 teamsExclusive byNick AmesandMatt HughesThu 1 Oct 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US is poised to host the first Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028, becoming the latest in a series of majorFifatournaments staged in North America. Discussions to take the competition to the US are at an advanced stage, with Los Angeles and San Diego among the favoured host cities.It will follow the men’s tournament,whose expanded version debuted last year,in being staged by a country that also hostedthe men’s World Cup this summer.Moving the Goalposts | Women’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will a new winner be crowned?Read moreWhile a deal is yet to be confirmed, the path has cleared for the US to hold the 19-team event without going through a formal bidding process, eventhough Qatar was in talks with Fifaabout hosting.The winter scheduling will avoid a clash with the men’s Copa América, which the US is the frontrunner to host in June and July 2028, but raises the prospect of a hectic year-round calendar for the world’s top players. The Club World Cup is placed squarely between the 2027 Women’s World Cup and the 2028 Olympics, which will demand full-strength squads. A number of top clubs are in favour of a rule change limiting players to one international tournament per year, whether for club or country.Fifa is keen to use the Club World Cup as a dry run for the 2031 Women’s World Cup, which the US will hostin conjunction with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaicain a decision to be formally approved at an Extraordinary Fifa Congress on 23 November.Football’s global body is eager to assess the stadium venues, pricing and demand for tickets at the smaller 19-team Club World Cup before the 48-team World Cup three years later.
