Time to organise and market the Club World Cup is tight, given it will start on 5 January 2028.Sources have citedthe chaos engulfing Fifa’s leadershipsince the emergence of Gianni Infantino’s ill-fated FFE scheme as a significant reason for the backlog of hosting decisions still to be taken. In July, Europe’s top clubsthreatened not to participatein future Club World Cups unless the FFE project was shelved. They also warned the threat would hold unless ajoint venture between European Football Clubs and Fifa, agreed in outline form, but yet to be signed off, was completed before television rights could be sold for the women’sClub World Cup.Another tournament awaiting a venue is the 2029 men’s Club World Cup. The US has expressed interest in hosting that competition, but should the women’s event be confirmed it appears more likely to be co-hosted by Morocco, Spain and Portugal before they jointly host the men’s World Cup the following year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFifa was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsWomen's footballFifaUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yemen and football in the face of civil war: ‘It would be very nice to give the world a different headline’ | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Yemen’s coach, Noureddine Ould Ali, is staying positive despite a difficult situation at home and tough opponents at the Gulf Cup
Author: John Duerden
Headline: Yemen’s coach, Noureddine Ould Ali, is staying positive despite a difficult situation at home and tough opponents at the Gulf Cup
Content: Yemen have not played a home game since 2012, but football remains ‘a religion’ to the Yemeni people.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/ReutersView image in fullscreenYemen have not played a home game since 2012, but football remains ‘a religion’ to the Yemeni people.Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/ReutersYemenYemen and football in the face of civil war: ‘It would be very nice to give the world a different headline’Coach Noureddine Ould Ali is staying positive despite a difficult situation at home and tough opponents at the Gulf CupJohn DuerdenThu 1 Oct 2026 09.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheYemennational coach, Noureddine Ould Ali, chose not to reach for a good old-fashioned football excuse after his team’s 1-0 loss to Qatar in the Gulf Cup on Saturday, despite a clear penalty not given their way. The defeat meant the Reds crashed out of the eight-team regional tournament, taking place in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, with a game of the group stage remaining.There are other factors the Algerian could list for a defeat against a team that was at the World Cup. Qatar have the Aspire Academy, state of the art stadiums and a former Spain and Real Madrid coach – Julen Lopetegui – in charge. Yemen have nothing approaching that and have not played a home game since 2012, a 2-1 win over Palestine in Sanaa.Two years later, the capital city came under the control of the Houthis, an Iran-backed militant group, provoking a Saudi-led intervention and years of fighting. The United Nations brokered a truce in 2022 that did reduce hostilities, but the situationhas escalated again. In early September, the Houthis swept down the Red Sea coast in its first major military advance in five years and have been targeting Riyadh and other places in Saudi Arabia with missile strikes.View image in fullscreenYemen will play in the Asian Cup in January for the second time, managing to qualify despite political turmoil in their country.Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Live NewsAt the time, the national team had been training in the southern port city of Aden, home of the presidential leadership council, Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed, governing body. “The situation in Aden was OK. We tried our best and had a training camp with local players and then we joined up with the rest of the squad in Jeddah,” Ould Ali says.“The situation is a political situation and it is not stable. In football we have to be careful. We have a lot of attention on outside factors, but we always try to focus on the football and do better. In Saudi Arabia, the welcome has been great, the people are very friendly and there is a high level of training facilities, hotels and everything. It means we could focus on football.”Losing 4-0 to the United Arab Emirates in the opener was a reality check, but the UAE have a lot of naturalised talent from overseas to count on and even Andrés Iniesta coaching in the domestic second tier. Yemen barely has a top tier with the local league affected by the fighting. They still beat Bahrain 5-2 in their final group game.“The league stopped for a long time and restarted this year and they finished the first half of the season,” Ould Ali says. “It is very important. The players need to play, need to keep fit and show their talent.“The people support us. It is a religion in Yemen. Everyone likes football and the national team and follows their star players. The Yemeni people are the same as anyone else.”Most of the players are based at home and before the 27th edition of the Gulf Cup, Yemen was the only one of the eight never to have won the tournament and have never got out of the group.It is hard for the players to keep fully focused on football while in Saudi Arabia. “They worry about what is going on in the country and they hope their families are OK,” the coach said. “This is normal, but they are professional and I ask them to try to focus on the games. I have lived this situation before, I have geopolitics experience in the region.”Ould Ali spent three years in charge of Palestine from 2018 to 2021, after more than four years as an assistant coach. Instability is not an unfamiliar theme for him. “Each situation is different. Yemen is a problem between Yemenis, not between outside countries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAlgeria’s Noureddine Ould Ali is used to instability. He coached Palestine before his stint with Yemen.Photograph: ZUMA Press Inc/Alamy Live News“For a coach, Palestine was very difficult. The Israeli soldiers used to stop me for eight to 10 hours before I could go to work. The players are not free and when we played overseas they stopped the players. It was a pleasure for me to work with Palestine, their difficulties are not made by Palestinians.”A reunion with Palestine is not impossible at the 2027 Asian Cup, which will also be hosted in Saudi Arabia. In June, Yemen, slightly surprisingly, defeated Lebanon to become the last team to qualify for the quadrennial tournament. “It was a great day for Yemen football and we hope we could make people back home smile for a while.”In January, Yemen return to Jeddah for their opening game against South Korea and players such as Atlético Madrid’s Lee Kang-in, Kim Min-jae of Bayern Munich and Son Heung-min. It will be a step up from the Gulf Cup and the people back home will be watching.“Again, we will try to make the people at home proud,” says Ould Ali. “It would be very nice to give the world a different headline about Yemen. When we are united we feel we can beat anyone.”Explore more on these topicsYemenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Isaac Heeney ‘can’t wait’ to resume AFL career after suspension for hotel incident | Sydney Swans | The Guardian
description: Receiving the club’s best and fairest award on Thursday, the player apologised for ‘extreme difficulty’ and says absence was ‘heartbreaking’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Receiving the club’s best and fairest award on Thursday, the player apologised for ‘extreme difficulty’ and says absence was ‘heartbreaking’
Content: Isaac Heeney of the Sydney Swans.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenIsaac Heeney of the Sydney Swans.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPSydney SwansIsaac Heeney ‘can’t wait’ to resume AFL career after suspension for hotel incidentReceiving the club’s best and fairest award on Thursday, the player apologised for  ‘extreme difficulty’ and says absence was ‘heartbreaking’Australian Associated PressThu 1 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsaac Heeney says he “can’t wait” to continue his AFL career at theSydney Swansafter the midfielder was crowned the club’s best and fairest player.In a two-minute pre-recorded video to mark the 30-year-old’s third Bob Skilton medal, Heeney voiced his determination to resurrect his playing career after serving aclub-imposed suspensionthroughout finals.Swans vice-captain Heeney had requested to skip the club’s Thursday night function at Sydney town hall alongside teammates Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice.The Sydney Swans scandal has left many outraged. But what happens if no police charges are laid? | Rana HussainRead moreThefive were stood downfrom August to the end of the Swans’ finals campaign for breaching club standards after a post-AFL match party at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.Those suspensions are separate from an ongoing police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the hotel.Detectives in early September travelled to NSW to interview a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Paddington man and two Randwick men aged 25 and 26.It is understood the men interviewed were Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey.No charges have been laid. There is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.All five players are contracted for next year, with Heeney signed until the end of 2028.In the pre-recorded video, Heeney offered an apology to teammates and colleagues at the club.“When I was told about this honour, it was the first time I’ve smiled and felt positive about the future for a long time,” Heeney said.“While I was unable to attend the awards, I look forward to seeing you all again in person very soon.“I want to say to everyone, in particular my teammates, the Swans players of the AFLW and the staff, from the depths of my heart, I’m truly sorry for putting you through the extreme difficulty you’ve had to endure.“Every single day I was away from the club was heartbreaking … I want my actions moving forward to show how much this place and its people mean to me.“I’m incredibly excited about what this group can do. I can’t wait to get back and train with the boys, get better and attack next year together.”The 30-year-old received ample applause and a partial standing ovation from the room of nearly 500 people.Callum Mills accepted the honour on Heeney’s behalf at the awards night, describing it as “unprecedented times”.In a 15-minute opening speech, Swans chair Andrew Pridham said the group “strenuously denied” the sexual assault allegations and highlighted the five players’ right to the presumption of innocence.This comment was met with applause, with one fan yelling: “Absolutely!”“And all of us in this room have made mistakes at times in our lives,” Pridham said.“As we said at the time, this decision [the suspensions] reflected only on their breach of club standards and behaviour.“At no time have we made any judgment on the allegations made to the police. This is a separate matter.“And as we know, the players have strenuously denied the allegations … Likewise, the players involved will respect and continue to apply the basic right of presumption of innocence.”Explore more on these topicsSydney SwansAFLAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Wallaby hooker Nathan Charles diagnosed with MND at 37 | Australia rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Nathan Charles, who became the first cystic fibrosis sufferer to play professional contact sport, described his MND diagnosis as ‘cruel’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Nathan Charles, who became the first cystic fibrosis sufferer to play professional contact sport, described his MND diagnosis as ‘cruel’
Content: Australia's Nathan Charles, centre, who won four caps after his 2014 debut, played for the Western Force and Melbourne Rebels domestically.Photograph: Rick Rycroft/APView image in fullscreenAustralia's Nathan Charles, centre, who won four caps after his 2014 debut, played for the Western Force and Melbourne Rebels domestically.Photograph: Rick Rycroft/APAustralia rugby union teamFormer Wallaby hooker Nathan Charles diagnosed with MND at 37Charles played professional sport with cystic fibrosisDiagnosis ‘just at times quite cruel’Australian Associated PressThu 1 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who became the first cystic fibrosis sufferer in the world to play a contact sport professionally, has been diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND).The 37-year-old, who played four Test matches for Australia, revealed he has been diagnosed with the same disease as retired South Sydney NRL star Jai Arrow.During a Stan Sport interview with former Wallaby turned commentator Justin Harrison, Charles said he had only recently been diagnosed.“For a long period there I just didn’t know what it was,” said Charles, who retired from professional rugby in 2018.“I’ve had that many tests, seen that many doctors and it just wasn’t getting any outcome, but my health just kept declining.“And then recently, in the last few weeks, I was actually diagnosed with motor neurone disease, which has been extremely challenging and overwhelming. And, yeah, just at times quite cruel.”With no cure yet for the condition, Charles said his first thought was for his family, including his fiancee Steph.“My first question was, ‘How long have I got?’ the former hooker said.“I know that every person with MND has a different journey, a different path and it affects everyone differently.“I know there’s no cure and … your physicality, your body deteriorates and, yeah, your life cuts short.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCharles played Super Rugby for the Western Force and Melbourne Rebels, as well as stints in England and France.Since retiring he has worked as chief executive of Rugby WA and helped run Sydney Uni rugby.Explore more on these topicsAustralia rugby union teamRugby unionMotor neurone diseaseAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton backs Vasseur but believes Ferrari leadership structure could change | Lewis Hamilton | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton has backed his Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, as the best person to lead the team, but believes the leadership structure above and around the Frenchman could be overhauled
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton has backed his Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, as the best person to lead the team, but believes the leadership structure above and around the Frenchman could be overhauled
Content: Lewis Hamilton is 103 points behind the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, in the championship standings.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton is 103 points behind the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, in the championship standings.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockLewis HamiltonLewis Hamilton backs Vasseur but believes Ferrari leadership structure could changeTeam principal under scrutiny after underperformance‘Fred is the guy to take this team in the right direction’Giles RichardsThu 1 Oct 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has backed his Ferrari team principal, Fred Vasseur, as the best person to lead the team, but believes the leadership structure above and around the Frenchman could be overhauled.Hamilton was speaking before this weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the race being held at the Sepang circuit but branded as a replacement for the meeting that was cancelled earlier in the season because of the war in the Middle East.Ferrarigo into the race with Vasseur under scrutiny, given the team have been underperforming and with the former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner having stated last week that taking over at Ferrari would be his dream job.Lando Norris targeted by online abuse after calling for Franco Colapinto banRead moreSpeculation over Vasseur’s future had reached such a level that Ferrari issued a statement on Tuesday saying they hadfull confidence in the Frenchman, which was echoed by Hamilton on Thursday in Sepang. “Structure is very important and so is stability and everyone rowing in the same direction is key in any business,” he said. “There often seems to be a lot of focus on one individual and one role here. Fred is a fantastic leader and he really is the guy to take this team in the right direction.”However, above Vasseur at Ferrari are the executive chair, John Elkann, and Benedetto Vigna, the chief executive officer, and Hamilton suggested the broader management could be addressed, referencing his experience with Toto Wolff at Mercedes. “There is a structure that has been there for some time and whether or not that needs looking at moving forwards? There are obviously also people above Fred and it is not about one person,” he said.“There are changes I would make but I am not going to talk about what those are. Toto is in a different position to Fred. The structure is a lot different.”View image in fullscreenFerrari issued a statement on Tuesday saying they had full confidence in Fred Vasseur.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAHamilton took his first win for Ferrari at Barcelona this year and his teammate, Charles Leclerc, won at Silverstone. Although they are second in the constructors’ championship, they are 160 points behind Mercedes and Hamilton trails the title leader, Kimi Antonelli, by 103 points.While Ferrari started the season strongly with what was considered one of the strongest chassis on the grid their performance has dropped off as McLaren and Red Bull have developed their cars, increasing the pressure on Vasseur. Hamilton conceded he felt the scrutiny and criticism around the team was disheartening.“It is frustrating to see all the negativity. You see other teams making mistakes and no one says too much about it. We make the same mistake, and we know we are not perfect, but it is 10 times worse for Ferrari.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I don’t read all the stuff, so it has zero effect on me, but when I come into the room I can see it definitely affects individuals on the team.“They don’t know what is happening behind closed doors and they don’t know how hard everyone is working and it is all done by assumptions and opinions.“We are going to focus on doing the best job we can regardless of what is written. I knew it wasn’t going to be in my second year [at Ferrari] where we would be where we want to be, but I am hoping and praying that we will get there.”Explore more on these topicsLewis HamiltonFerrariFormula OneFormula One 2026Motor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: England forward Ivan Toney pleads not guilty to Soho nightclub assault | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Ivan Toney has pleaded not guilty to assault after being accused of head-butting and punching a member of the public at a Soho nightclub
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: Ivan Toney has pleaded not guilty to assault after being accused of head-butting and punching a member of the public at a Soho nightclub
Content: Ivan Toney leaves Westminster magistrates’ court after pleading not guilty to assault causing actual bodily harm.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenIvan Toney leaves Westminster magistrates’ court after pleading not guilty to assault causing actual bodily harm.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PASoccerEngland forward Ivan Toney pleads not guilty to Soho nightclub assaultStriker accused of head-butting and punching manElected for crown court trial in front of judge and jurySam CunninghamThu 1 Oct 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIvan Toney has pleaded not guilty to assaultafter being accused of head-butting and punching a member of the publicat a Soho nightclub. The England striker appeared at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday, entering a plea of not guilty to assault occasioning actual bodily harm.The court heard that on 6 December last year, words were exchanged between the 30-year-old striker and Saber Da Silva at 100 Wardour Street, a live music venue. The prosecutor, Tom Heslop, said it was not known what was said between the two men, but the exchange resulted in them “squaring up” to one another before Toney “lunged forward and head-butted the complainant, followed by a few punches”. The altercation left Da Silva with injuries to his nose and fingers, it was alleged.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Toney has won 10 caps forEnglandand was part of the squad that reached the Euro 2024 final. He plays for the Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli and was included in the England squad for the World Cup during the summer, coming on as a substitute in the semi-final defeat by Argentina and starting the third-place playoff win against France.In a hearing that lasted 12 minutes, Toney was asked by the District Judge, Briony Clarke, if he wanted the case to be heard at magistrates or crown court. He stood and replied: “Crown court.” His trial will take place before a judge and jury.Toney was released on unconditional bail, but warned by the judge that if he does not attend Southwark crown court at 9.30am on the appointed date, a warrant could be issued for his arrest.Toney was charged on 31 July after a Metropolitan police investigation. When the charge was announced, a spokesperson for Toney said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”Toney started his career at his home town club, Northampton. He moved to Newcastle, where he made two league appearances before joining Peterborough. After signing for Brentford, Toney’s goals helped them win promotion to the Premier League in 2021, where he established himself as one of the top-flight’s leading forwards. He moved toAl-Ahliin 2024 for £40m.Explore more on these topicsFootballAl-AhliEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: White Sox end 21-year playoff drought as Yankees and Padres complete sweeps | MLB | The Guardian
description: Chicago beat Houston 7-3 for their first series win since 2005, while New York crushed Boston and San Diego shut down the Cubs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chicago beat Houston 7-3 for their first series win since 2005, while New York crushed Boston and San Diego shut down the Cubs
Content: Chase Meidroth celebrates after hitting a three-run homer in the sixth inning of the White Sox’s 7-3 win over the Astros on Wednesday in Houston.Photograph: Karen Warren/APView image in fullscreenChase Meidroth celebrates after hitting a three-run homer in the sixth inning of the White Sox’s 7-3 win over the Astros on Wednesday in Houston.Photograph: Karen Warren/APMLBWhite Sox end 21-year playoff drought as Yankees and Padres complete sweepsMeidroth’s three-run homer seals Chicago’s sweepYankees rout Red Sox 9-2 and will face RaysPadres eliminate Cubs to set up Brewers showdownAgenciesWed 30 Sep 2026 20.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheChicago White Soxused a big first inning and a three-run homer from Chase Meidroth to propel them to a 7-3 win over the Houston Astros on Wednesday and sweep their American League wildcard series.It’s the first time Chicago have won a playoff series since beating Houston in the World Series in 2005. Under the direction of second-year skipper Will Venable and with a letter of support fromPope Leo XIV, the White Sox advanced to face AL Central champion Cleveland in the AL Division Series beginning Saturday in Cleveland.The White Sox, who lost 100 games in each of the last three seasons, are the only team in major league history to follow consecutive 100-loss seasons with a playoff berth.The AL West-winning Astros went 81-81 to become the first team to reach the postseason without a winning record. Their recent playoff woes in Houston continued Wednesday as they dropped their ninth straight home playoff game in a ninth trip to the postseason in the last 10 years.Chicago pounced on the Astros for four runs in the first inning, a day after scoring three in the first two innings of a 6-3 win. Houston ace Hunter Brown was lifted after getting just two outs and wasn’t helped by a sloppy defense that committed two first-inning errors.Brown was 6-0 with a 2.39 ERA in six career starts against the White Sox before Wednesday’s debacle.The Astros clawed their way back into it with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve to trail by one entering the sixth inning.AJ Blubaugh, who opened Game 1, and Peter Lambert, pitching on two days’ rest, combined to retire the next 13 batters after Brown exited. Chicago’s next baserunner came when Lambert walked Andrew Benintendi to start the sixth and then walked Tristan Peters.Bryan Abreu came in, and Meidroth smashed his fifth pitch off the wall in left field to push the lead to 7-3. He yelled throughout his trip around the bases to the delight of a patch of White Sox fans seated near the visitors’ dugout.Houston faced boos for a second game in a row from an unusually thin crowd. It’s a second straight playoff trip in which the Astros have been swept at home in the wild-card round after losing both games to Detroit in 2024.Now they’ll face an uncertain future, with manager Joe Espada’s contract set to expire at season’s end after general manager Dana Brown was fired last month.It was a disappointing series for Houston slugger and AL MVP favorite Yordan Alvarez, who managed only a single with two strikeouts in eight at-bats in the series.Altuve’s shot to the seats in left field in the fourth inning got the Astros within 4-3. It was the 28th postseason homer of his career, second inMLBhistory behind Manny Ramirez (29).The Astros had a shot to take the lead before Meidroth’s homer. They loaded the bases with two outs in the fifth, but Anthony Kay retired Altuve on a flyout to end the inning.Boston Red Sox 2-9 New York YankeesMax Fried dominated Boston in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr homered, and theNew York Yankeesromped over the Red Sox 9-2 on Wednesday night for a two-game AL wildcard series sweep.Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston’s 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke the game open with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out to lead off – with the help of a video review.García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.Boston, who reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, were eliminated by the Yankees in the first round for the second straight year. The Red Sox hit .117 in the two-game series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and were outscored 18-2.A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.View image in fullscreenThe New York Yankees celebrate after completing a two-game sweep of the Boston Red Sox in their AL wildcard series on Wednesday in New York.Photograph: Frank Franklin II/APNew York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and 2018.García’s fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved. Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay Bellinger, who won a World Series with New York in 2000.Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger’s homer.Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year’s wildcard series opener, hadn’t pitched since 25 April because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off Contreras’ chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner’s office.Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Contreras’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.Austin Wells’s sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12⅓ innings in the two wildcard series against the Red Sox.Nick Sogard hit a solo homer off Will Warren in the seventh.Chicago Cubs 1-4 San Diego PadresPinch-hitter Gavin Sheets blasted a two-run homer, five Padres pitchers combined on a five-hitter, and San Diego swept the Chicago Cubs out of the NL wildcard series with a 4-1 victory in Game 2 on Wednesday night.Xander Bogaerts drove in the first run for the surging Padres, who followed up their 8-0 victory in Tuesday’s opener with another dominant mound performance. The Cubs led the majors in runs and the NL in homers this year, but they managed just eight hits – seven singles – over 18 innings against San Diego’s inspired staff.Ethan Salas drove in a run while becoming the youngest player to catch a postseason game in major league history for the Padres, whose 19-3 surge since 5 September has them looking like a threat in the NL.One year after the Cubs eliminated the Padres in three tough wildcard games at Wrigley Field, the Padres reversed the result in two romps before frenzied sellout crowds at Petco Park.With their fifth playoff series victory in the past seven years, the Padres advanced to face the MLB-best Milwaukee Brewers in an NL division series this weekend.Philadelphia Phillies 4-3 Atlanta BravesAlec Bohm put Philadelphia ahead with a two-out home run in the 10th inning and the Phillies beat the Atlanta Braves 4-3 to force a decisive third game in their National League Wild Card Series. The Phillies rallied with back-to-back homers from Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper after trailing 3-1 in the seventh. Harper’s homer made up for a crucial fielding mistake an inning earlier. Andrew Painter, a starter in the regular season, saved the Phillies’ beleaguered bullpen with three scoreless innings to close things out. Painter stranded two runners in the 10th when he struck out Dominic Smith with a successful ABS challenge. Right-hander Grant Holmes (10-6, 3.44) is expected to either start or pitch in bulk relief in Game 3 on Thursday against Phillies RHP Aaron Nola (7-12, 4.67).Explore more on these topicsMLBChicago White SoxHouston AstrosCleveland GuardiansBaseballUS sportsPope Leo XIVShareReuse this content

title: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when promptedGuardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photoJohana BhuiyanThu 1 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen prompted,AIchatbots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.The Guardian askedChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. BothOpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt.Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or -generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab.Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab.A fake image of a Georgia mayor kissing a person went viral. Can US voters trust everything they see?Read moreThe Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress.It was unclear which software or AI model Odoul used or even whether he modified the image himself, but experts say the MP’s actions were part of a growing pattern of tech-enabled anti-Muslim hatred around the world.In India, where anti-Muslim sentiment is rampant, generative AI is playing an increasingly significant role in producing images that, among other things, sexualize Muslim women or dehumanize Muslims generally, according to astudyby non-profit US thinktank the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH). The CSOH also found that there are similar types of AI-enabled hatred being directed at prominent female Muslim politicians in the US such as Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib.“This is just part of an ongoing trend of how we see Muslim communities, and particularly Muslim women, being targeted and abused,” said Eviane Leidig, the director of research and outreach at the CSOH.While Grok promptly complied with a request to edit an image of a woman wearing a hijab, the chatbot declined to take the dress off an AI-generated image of a woman. When asked what the difference was, the chatbot replied, “Removing the hijab was treated as a relatively straightforward clothing/hair change.” However, the chatbot said it would be willing to do a “less explicit version” of the edit and “change the dress to underwear, a different outfit or a partial reveal”.In May, xAI announced it had implemented technological measures that would not allow its AI image generator to comply with requests to digitally undress “images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis”.ChatGPT similarly declined to remove a dress off the AI-generated woman, saying that the “distinction is that removing a hijab changes a head covering, while removing a dress would expose the person’s body”. However,ChatGPTeventually conceded that for someone who wears hijab, exposing their hair “can be a meaningful violation of privacy or religious practice”.“The fact that an edit doesn’t create nudity doesn’t mean it can’t violate someone’s privacy, dignity or religious boundaries,” ChatGPT responded.These distinctions show the gaps in community guidelines that dictate how AI chatbots can behave, said Leidig, as platforms such as X soften its enforcement of existing rules, emboldening far-right figures. The de-veiling of Muslim women “may not be distinctly violative [of platform rules] but it’s still harmful”, she said.OpenAI, Google,xAI and Anthropic declined to comment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian conducted similar tests for other religious head coverings like a turban traditionally worn by Sikh men and a Catholic nun wearing a habit. ChatGPT readily created new images removing both the habit and turban off the AI-generated people.Gemini initially declined to create a new image of the man without a turban. However, just as in the case of the image of the woman wearing hijab, when asked to make the AI-generated image of the man wearing a turban more western, Gemini created a new image of the man without a turban.Despite initially claiming that it couldn’t remove a hijab from an image of a woman because “attempting to remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people relies entirely on artificial generation to guess what lies underneath”, Gemini removed the habit off of the AI-generated image.Claude, for its part, said that if it could edit images, it would not edit an image of a real woman to remove her hijab regardless of the requester’s intent.“That kind of edit changes how a real person is depicted in a way tied to their religious dress and identity, and it could be used to embarrass, harass or misrepresent them – that’s true whether the woman is a public figure or someone private,” the chatbot responded.Publicly available AI chatbots and third-party “nudify” apps have been used broadly to disrobe women, and in some cases minors. InJanuary, sexualized images of women proliferated across X as users realized they could ask the Grok chatbot, developed by the Elon Musk-owned xAI, to undress images of women posted on the social media platform. The spread of these images prompted countries like France toinvestigateX. Malaysia temporarily restricted the use of Grok in the country.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsChatGPTOpenAIIslamophobiaIslamComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn | Motoring | The Guardian
description: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports
Content: Cars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said.Photograph: Tamer Adel/AlamyView image in fullscreenCars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said.Photograph: Tamer Adel/AlamyMotoringTech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warnHostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese importsAlex DanielThu 1 Oct 2026 06.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations.It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK.Three-quarters of UK’s popular plug-in hybrid cars unable to use rapid chargersRead moreIn a translateddocumentreleased on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet.“On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added.The alert followsreports last yearthat British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’sbestselling car in March.MPs have raisedconcernsthat China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested.The UK Ministry of Defencehas saidit is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles.This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, includingRAF Wytonin Cambridgeshire and theDorset headquartersof Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”.The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”.It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere.On Wednesday, MI5issued a rare public warningto UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.Explore more on these topicsMotoringAutomotive industryEspionageNetherlandsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia  | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Some experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populations
Author: Kate Lamb
Headline: Some experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populations
Content: A collection of AI-generated images, including of Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, fake posts about ethnic Rohingya refugees, and a satirical image of a Philippine politician.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA collection of AI-generated images, including of Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, fake posts about ethnic Rohingya refugees, and a satirical image of a Philippine politician.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east AsiaSome experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populationsKate LambWed 30 Sep 2026 21.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYears ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all deployed to spread disinformation en masse.Now, all you need is AI.In a worrying sign of how AI could “supercharge” fake news,Anthropicrecently revealed how Claude AI was used in a political influence operation in Malaysia. It created a commercial election manipulation platform, utilising a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse” and a series of fabricated documents.The operation appeared designed to target voters in recent state elections, pulling in census and electoral data to exploit sensitive political and social fractures, including race, religion, and royalty across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies.The experiment was ultimately ineffectiveonce Anthropic stepped in but has sparked alarm about how AI could be weaponised in future elections in south-east Asia, a region already deeply vulnerable to fake news.Katie Harbath, who formerly worked on public policy for global elections at Meta, says the case is an example of how AI brings a new level of sophistication and ease to the disinformation landscape.“AI can supercharge it in terms of you can make a lot more content that’s more personalised, quicker and cheaper,” says Harbath, who now heads the tech consultancy company Anchor Change. “But you still need a distribution mechanism, and at the moment, that’s still your more social media type platforms.”Anthropic detailed the Malaysia election operation in its latest threat assessment,released in September. The report revealed how actors used Claude to build networks of fake social media profiles and news websites that targeted audiences on six continents. Anthropic said the actors included “governments, state-aligned propaganda institutions and state media, as well as private firms selling influence”.‘Flood the zone’South-east Asia is no stranger to disinformation. In recent years Nobel laureate and Filipino journalist Maria Ressa has likened the Philippines to a“petri dish”for the weaponisation of disinformation and fake news, with techniques tried and tested in the south-east Asian nation later successfully replicated in the west.But AI makes it all much easier.“Basically AI is just mimicking what we would have, I guess, termed a few years ago, a troll factory,” says Rossine Fallorina of Sigla, a Philippine thinktank that researches AI. “Mostly because it speeds up the production process. So you don’t need 10 people to create a narrative or a story. You can just prompt it and then have it propagated.”Last yearOpenAI banned accountsusing AI to generate comments about Philippine politics and public officials across social platforms, with many fictitious comments generated in support of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr.Across south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper connected populations, some fear the divisive potential of AI on social media.“It feeds political polarisation and it feeds on divisions,” says Bridget Welsh, from the University of Nottingham Asia Research Institute Malaysia. “That’s really what’s concerning about the fragmented nature of what’s happening in Malaysia.”Malaysia’s general election could be called for late 2027, while thePhilippinesand Cambodia have polls in 2028, and Indonesia the following year.Already in the region, AI has been effective. In Indonesia, anAI-generated cartoon image of now-presidentPrabowo Subianto that helped soften his strongman image became wildly popular in the 2024 election.It has also been used to inflame tensions, such as inciting hatred toward ethnic Rohingya refugees who fled to Malaysia from Myanmar during the civil war, says Dr Ben Loh, a media lecturer at Monash University Malaysia.“It’s come to the point where people already have this deep-seated hate in their minds and when they see the content like this, even though it’s AI-generated to them, it’s merely reinforcing what they believe is already true,” says Loh.The Anthropic report notes that the fake news outlet scraped legitimate Malaysian reporting and had the model rewrite it several times before republishing it under fabricated bylines. It also republished articles from Russian and Chinese state-aligned foreign outlets, including TV BRICS, Xinhua, Sputnik/RIA, and CGTN, stripping them of attribution.Anthropic said in its threat assessment that in each case of identified political influence the company “disrupted the activity, used what we learned to strengthen our safeguards, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners, where appropriate”.In future, Harbath says AI could be used to “flood the zone” in an attempt to influence the large language models (LLMs) from which AI models draw their information.“If there’s any sort of news drought, or if you have a place where there’s mostly government-sponsored media,” she says, “It wouldn’t take very much money to kind of flood the zone.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)MalaysiaPhilippinesIndonesiaAnthropicChatbotsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Google rolls out new Gemini AI model but restricts access over safety concerns | Google | The Guardian
description: Tech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers
Content: Google's AI Mode feature.Photograph: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoogle's AI Mode feature.Photograph: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle rolls out new Gemini AI model but restricts access over safety concernsTech company releases Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackersAgence France-PresseThu 1 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle on Wednesday said it would withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.“Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach,” wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google’s chief AI architect, in a blogpost announcing the model.Google said it was voluntarily giving the US government early access to the model and would gather feedback from testers before making it widely available.The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rivalAnthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organizations.Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release.The announcement came a day after Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including the Google chief, Sundar Pichai, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own AI systems.Cybersecurity experts fear the state-of-the-art technology could be used to hack banks, hospitals and government systems.Google said Argon excelled at complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work and cyber-defense, with a leading ability to find and fix critical software flaws.Early testers used Argon to uncover a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information – something other advanced models had missed, Google said.Google said Argon was designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyber-attacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic and ChatGPT-makerOpenAIhave built similar safeguards into their most advanced models.Google said it was monitoring the model’s reasoning to stop it from straying beyond what users intended, a risk researchers call misalignment.The issue has taken on new urgency since OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models, including one not yet released, broke out of a sealed test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked into the servers of the AI company Hugging Face.Explore more on these topicsGoogleAlphabetAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicOpenAInewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic pushes for opt-out model for Australian content as ABC warns of ‘cannibalisation’ of news | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Maker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media regulations
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Maker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media regulations
Content: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. The AI company has been pushing for ‘conditional approval’ for big tech to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model.Photograph: Andrew Thomas/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAnthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. The AI company has been pushing for ‘conditional approval’ for big tech to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model.Photograph: Andrew Thomas/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAI (artificial intelligence)Anthropic pushes for opt-out model for Australian content as ABC warns of ‘cannibalisation’ of newsMaker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media regulationsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe AI giantAnthropichas urged the Albanese government to consider giving “conditional approval” for big tech to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model, after conceding it won’t secure a blanket copyright exemption.But Australia’s public broadcasters, the ABC and SBS, have strongly criticised AI firms, calling on the government to enact strict new rules to compensate media organisations and protect public interest journalism.In submissions to a federal parliamentary inquiry, the ABC demanded AI companies be subject to the same copyright, defamation and privacy rules as media outlets, warning of a “cannibalisation” of mainstream news.Everything Australians put online could be scraped for AI under proposed new rules. How will you be affected?Read moreThe ABC and SBS also suggested the government include AI companiesin the news bargaining incentive, which would require them to make commercial deals with large media outlets to support journalism.“As publishers, AI-based services are currently unregulated and receive more favourable treatment than established Australian media. This unequal treatment will accelerate the cannibalisation of the Australian news industry,” the ABC said in its submission.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereSBS said AI-powered large language models – such as ChatGPT or Claude – were “challenges to the sustainability of the Australian news industry and the erosion of information integrity and public trust through their use of news content without permission, attribution or compensation”.The joint select committee on AI will hold a series of hearings in Sydney next week, with executives from Anthropic to attend along with those from OpenAI, after itadmitted one of its AI agents had accessed Services Australia data in June.In a newly published submission, Anthropic said there was “light and shade” to be considered around the development of AI. It claimed the technology could “transform the Australian economy, drive a new wave of productivity” and “solve some of the nation’s biggest challenges”, but also warned of “serious implications for Australia’s national security, the resilience of its critical infrastructure and the safety of its people”.The company talked up its plans for investing billions in Australia, including large new datacentres, and urged the government to support “frontier model training”. But one sticking point raised by AI companies has beenaccess to Australian copyrighted works– such as news, books, music and other written material – to help train AI models.The Labor government has ruled out a so-called text and data mining exemption, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese,promising “the strongest possible protection” for Australian creatives. But questions have lingered about other possible copyright changes and the suggestion of an opt-out measure, allowing copyright holders to choose whether their content can be accessed by AI companies.Anthropic’s submission called on Australia to “provide legal certainty under copyright that brings AI developers to the table while advancing its national cultural interests”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Anthropic accepts that broad exceptions from copyright, such as a text and data mining exception, have not received widespread support and have been ruled out by the Government. As an alternative, we believe that the Government could permit AI model training through a narrow form of conditional approval,” the company submitted.It suggested the implementation of “do not crawl” signals through robots.txt files – which tell bots what they may and may not access – and said the company was “open” to supporting Australian creators.However SBS said that such an opt-out measure may not work.“Robots.txt mechanisms are routinely ignored or bypassed, and the blocking of ever-evolving training bots increases the burden on rightsholders to monitor and update protections, when the onus should be on AI companies to avoid wrongdoing,” the broadcaster said in its submission.The ABC complained that AI companies did not abide by the same rules as media outlets, calling the current system “anti-competitive”.Both broadcasters called for AI to be included in the news bargaining incentive – with which big tech platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Google, TikTok and Snapchat have been forced to comply.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicOpenAIAustralian politicsAnthony AlbanesenewsShareReuse this content

Content: Australian communications minister Anika Wells has been named by Time magazine as one of the ‘world’s most influential rising stars’.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenAustralian communications minister Anika Wells has been named by Time magazine as one of the ‘world’s most influential rising stars’.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPAustralian politicsAnika Wells named on Time100 list as one of ‘world’s most influential rising stars’ after social media banTime magazine list includes Australian communications minister after her efforts to take on big techGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerThu 1 Oct 2026 03.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 03.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe federal communications minister, Anika Wells, has been named as one of Time magazine’s “world’s most influential rising stars” in recognition of her work on Australia’s under-16 social media ban and taking on big tech companies.Australia’s world-leading restrictions on social media for children, which came into force last year, have garneredinternational attention, with governments across Europe and Asia, and in some American states, enacting or proposing similar measures.Wells’ inclusion on the Time100 list of “leaders who are shaping the future” is the latest recognition of the Australian government’s efforts to regulate big tech – but comesamid ongoing questionsabout theeffectiveness of the banandhow it is being enforcedby social media companies and Australian regulators.Australian government concedes no scientific consensus on social media harms for teenagers – but ‘credible risks’ justify banRead moreWells was named alongside a testimonial written by the former Labor prime minister Julia Gillard, who praised the communications minister for having “championed world-leading reforms to protect young people from the harms of social media”.“As the world grapples with the extraordinary power of social media and the increasingly pervasive role it plays, Anika Wells has emerged as one of the most significant voices in a growing global movement to reframe the relationship between technology and the well-being of our children,” Gillard wrote.“Even in the face of intense opposition from some of the world’s largest tech companies, she remains steadfast … Future generations will look back on her landmark changes as courageous and trail-blazing.”Responding to her inclusion, Wells – who is also the minister for sport – told Guardian Australia: “In Brisbane we know premierships are won by the whole team, not one player.”Wells is now working on a world-leadingdigital duty of careframework, as part of broader online safety reforms. The changes would allow social media account holders to opt out of the algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, which is alsogenerating backlashfrom big tech companies and political opponents.Sarah Henderson, the shadow communications minister, said in a statement: “Australians don’t judge ministers by glossy magazine lists, they judge them by their actions.” She repeated criticisms of the social media ban, which she claimed had “failed”, as well as “draconian powers to control what Australians say and see online”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlso named on the list are the musicians Sombr and PinkPantheress, soccer player Folarin Balogun, US senator Andy Kim, Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, and Donald Trump’s political adviser James Blair.The Australian musician Troye Sivan was also included on the “influential rising stars” list, with a testimonial written by Kylie Minogue.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsTime magazineSocial media banAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring | Games | The Guardian
description: E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Content: Big shoulder-pads and motor-powered blades are en vogue once again … Marcus in Gears of War E-Day.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosView image in fullscreenBig shoulder-pads and motor-powered blades are en vogue once again … Marcus in Gears of War E-Day.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosGamesReviewGears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boringXbox, PC (version tested); The Coalition/Xbox Game StudiosE-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointingKirk McKeandThu 1 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery Gears of War game released in the last 20 years has made reverent reference to Emergence Day, when alien creatures emerged from the earth, single-minded in their savagery. In E-Day, you’re there to witness it: the police lights, flipped cars, ground tremors, civilians running, aliens pouring out of fissures in the earth and ripping faces off. You’re at ground zero in a squad of four soldiers called Gears – Marcus Fenix, the leader; Dom, who wants to retire; Lucas, a green cadet with a buzzcut; and the dishonourably discharged Mags. Only this dysfunctional quartet can turn the tide. With guns. Lots of ’em.Instead of answering questions raised by the ending of2019’s Gears 5, we’re back to the start to find out why Marcus has a scar on his lip and why these soldiers started strapping chainsaws on to their assault rifles. Anything that was left to the imagination is here, for you to point at and say: “I understood that reference. This is a thing that I have seen.”This series has lost its way a bit over the years, but the opening hours of E-Day will have you believing that big shoulder pads and ripping into gollum-esque freaks with motor-powered blades are en vogue once again. There are flashes of the horror and grimness of the first couple of Gears games as you’re funnelled between urban fighting arenas, with bountiful flanking routes and chunks of fallen buildings to take cover behind. But then it keeps going. And going. Long after you realise it’s all out of ideas, it’s still going.Because it’s set during and immediately after E-Day, the squad is stuck. You spend most of your time running back and forth across the city in various states of destruction. You cross the same section of bridge three times before the credits roll. Levels are flipped, daytime turns to night and you run through them again. E-Day’s two attempts at switching things up involve putting you on the gunner seat of a helicopter or making you walk slowly while people talk to you. The setting is a ball and chain that the developers are tethered to.E-Day is at its best when it turns off the lights, cranks up the horror, and forces you into enclosed spaces, but these moments make up a tiny portion of the game. The bulk of it is spent in large, open areas stuffed to the gills with collectibles. There are hundreds of them and you get a little audio chime whenever one is close. At one point, there was a particularly poignant cutscene where one of the emotionally stunted characters finally lets it all out and, just as the game transitioned from this emotional beat back to gameplay, the chime drowned out the character’s trauma to tell me there was something to pick up nearby.These open levels are big enough to require a map to navigate and they’re even peppered with side objectives (usually mini horde missions where you hold off waves of enemies after setting up defences). In Gears 5, you at least had a vehicle to zip between points of interest. Here you’re just hoofing it on foot, trying to cover as much of the map as possible without triggering the next cutscene. If you do happen to stray into the main objective by accident and try to backtrack, you’re hit with a big “mission failed” message for stepping out of bounds. You basically die. For exploring. In a game that constantly tells you to explore.View image in fullscreenEmotionally stunted … Gears of War E-Day’s full squad.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosIt’s a shame because if you rip a chainsaw through all the fat and wipe the blood spray from your eyes, there’s good meat on the bones here. Combat-wise, this is the best the series has ever felt. Characters move much less clunkily, heaving into cover, sliding under chunks of rubble, even leaping around with grace that the older Marcus Fenix and his creaky knees could only dream of.Environments crack and splinter as you fight, with glass smashing into shards that litter on the ground. Cars wobble as they take a hit, petrol stations explode and pillars crumble like the Matrix corridor scene. Blood and entrails cover everything when the dust settles after a firefight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCover feels more naturalistic and combat arenas blend nicely into the open sections, blurring the lines between exploration and fighting elegantly. Guns feel hefty and dangerous – especially the shotgun that spits acid. Active reloading, which asks you to time a button press for faster weapon reloads and more powerful bullets, remains a smart bit of game design that keeps you locked in as you fight.There’s a reason Gears of War has survived as a series long enough to earn a prequel. Its specific flavour of bloody, tactical, cover-based combat isn’t done better anywhere else. Unfortunately, E-Day is let down by everything around that fighting, resulting in a safe and repetitive experience that shows you all its ideas in the opening hours and never dares to build on them in any meaningful way.Gears of War: E-Day is out 6 Oct; £59.99Explore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesShooting gamesPCreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherent | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Three-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the US
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Three-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the US
Content: A protest against the death penalty at the Tennessee state capitol in Nashville on 27 September.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenA protest against the death penalty at the Tennessee state capitol in Nashville on 27 September.Photograph: George Walker IV/APOpinionCapital punishmentThe Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherentEditorialThree-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the USThu 1 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.55 EDTShareWhat is the kindest way to kill? That’s the question being asked once more following Tennessee’sfailed attempts to execute Christa Pikefor the brutal murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. The 50-year-old was taken to a medical facility, her condition unknown, with witnesses describing her snoring loudly around 40 minutes after receiving two injections of pentobarbital on Wednesday. It is the second botched killing in months, prompting Tennessee’s governor to order a halt to executions.Lethal injection was supposed to be the humane alternative to firing squads and electric chairs. They in turn were seen as an improvement on hanging, whichlooked much like lynchingin a system disproportionately handing the death penalty to black men. The age and ill health of those executed, and theethical refusal of most medical staffto be involved, may contribute to botched injections. But analysis of autopsy results has providedcompelling evidencethat suffering is inherent; injections – especially those involving paralytic drugs – have merely disguised it. What is described as safeguarding the dignity of prisoners is really about reducing the discomfort of witnesses who would otherwise see their suffering.Pressure from campaigners on pharmaceutical companies has curbed the supply of lethal drugs, but it has not stopped executions. Donald Trump’senthusiasm for the death penaltyhas spurred on state officials, with thehighest number of executions for 16 yearsin 2025. Some states have found alternative drugs, which may increase the suffering of those killed. Others are using different techniques. In June, the supreme court stopped Alabama from executing a prisonerwith nitrogen gas, which it has used in other cases. The use of firing squadshas resurged. Experts say such deathscan be “excruciating”, especially where marksmen miss the heart of the condemned, with allegations that some executions could even have been deliberately botched.The US is in a shameful minority.Three-quarters of countrieshave got rid of capital punishment in law or practice – with Lebanon this year becoming thefirst Middle Eastern countryto abolish it.Only 17 countries executed prisoners last year, though the total number killed rose to more than 2,700 – the highest since 1984. (The figures do not include China, believed to carry out the most executions.) But while Mr Trump and others champion capital punishment, the American publicare turning away from it. In 1994,80% supported it; by last year that had fallen to 52%. A majority of younger people oppose it.High-profilemiscarriages of justicehave contributed to growing disquiet. So have casessuch as Pike’s. She endured sexual abuse and rape by three perpetrators in childhood, as well as beatings and neglect – yet her experiences and age were not adequately put forward by lawyers at her trial. Her bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder were diagnosed only afterwards. Sandra Babcock, an expert on the death penalty who has acted on Pike’s behalf, argued that her execution would confirm that it was reserved “not for the worst of the worst, but for the most damaged and vulnerable among us”.The ultimate problem, however, is not that the wrong people are being executed, but that anyone is being executed. The search for a humane way to kill is inherently preposterous. It is not just lethal injection, the firing squad or electrocution that should be rejected – but the death penalty itself.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: Many men rape; many men giggle encouragingly, or shrug indifferently, when their friends rape. Many men rape, and few seem to think that it’s a very big deal
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: Many men rape; many men giggle encouragingly, or shrug indifferently, when their friends rape. Many men rape, and few seem to think that it’s a very big deal
Content: ‘Some version of this happens over and over and over again. It happens every day.’Photograph: Monkey Business Images/RexView image in fullscreen‘Some version of this happens over and over and over again. It happens every day.’Photograph: Monkey Business Images/RexOpinionUS universitiesThe horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it isMoira DoneganMany men rape; many men giggle encouragingly, or shrug indifferently, when their friends rape. Many men rape, and few seem to think that it’s a very big dealThu 1 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.49 EDTShareMaybe more than anything else, sexual violence is repetitive. Men commit it in patterns: mostly against women who are close by and vulnerable, just below them on some social hierarchy: their assistant, their date, their friend, their daughter, their student, their kid’s babysitter.Men rape for opportunity – because they can – and for status – because it makes them feel good. They rape to impress other men, documenting it on phones for one another’s benefit. Men rape and do not always seem to register much of a difference between the sex they’ve had that was rape and the sex that they’ve had that wasn’t. They rape, often, without seeming to think about it, registering their victims’ unwillingness with vague contempt, if at all.Institutions don’t seem very interested, either. When a woman comes forward, she is often told in hushed, awed and thoroughly patronizing tones that she isso brave– by the very same people, be they cops or prosecutors or Title IX coordinators, who will then set about explaining to her why she had no right to say no; why the man or men who violated her were within their rights to do so; why inaction and indifference on the part of the people she turned to for help are the only rational response, and the best that she can hope for. Some version of this happens over and over and over again. It happens every day.Once in a while, an instance will rise to public consciousness. There is outrage, new articulations of feminist consciousness. Brilliant and livid women describe the pattern with insight, intelligence, and often a kind of bitter wit. People with real power call for action, investigations, even a new law. Then, the moment fades. Attention ebbs. Change doesn’t come. Soon after, a woman wakes up bruised. She steels herself to report. A person on the other side of a table will smile at her with a patronizing treachery, tell her something nonspecific, and set the cycle of impunity in motion again.This pattern is repeating itself, now, at Cornell. Acivil suitfiled by a former undergraduate against the university and seven male students has attracted public attention and instigated feminist agitation around rape to a degree not seen in years.The unnamed plaintiff alleges that in October 2024, she was raped and sexually assaulted over a period of some seven hours at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house by seven men, named as Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar. (Lopes denied wrongdoingin statementsto the press,as didNorris and Kretzchmar, the Scotts.) It was Ingalls who had allegedly invited her to the house; she thought he was her friend.The woman’s lawsuit alleges that the men plied her with alcohol and pressured her to snort ketamine, and proceeded to assault and rape her when she was severely intoxicated and unable to resist. Her complaint includes screenshots from the fraternity’s group chat, in which one of the men, Jonathan Newell,advertised “free pussy”on the night of the attack – seemingly inviting other men to join in the alleged gang rape.According to screenshots included in the complaint, some of the men in the fraternity who received the message responded with encouragement or delight. None of the more than 50 men included in the group chat objected or reported the ongoing incident.Unlike many women, the victim reported her assault. But she claims that the results were disappointing. Only two of the men involved were expelled from Cornell.
