All of the other five soon returned to classes; some werebriefly suspended, or required to attend a workshop. According to the student-runCornell Daily Sun, which broke the story of the lawsuit, the accused were asked, as part of their punishment, to write an essay. I would like to read those essays. Their alleged victim dropped out; according to her attorney, she has not returned to college.For his part, the local district attorney in Cornell’s Tompkins county, Matthew Van Houten, declined to pursue charges – claiming,nonsensically, that the woman who came to the police to report a rape did not assert that the encounter was nonconsensual or that she was drugged against her will. Van Houten says that allegations from this month’s civil lawsuit are “dramatically different” from Jane Doe’s statement two years ago. In her interview with police at that time, Doe said: “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.” When asked about this byCBS News, Van Houten replied: “I’m going to follow up on this because this is news to me.”None of the men were ever arrested; it’s not clear that they were interviewed by police at all. Van Houten has now reversed that decision and reopened the case following a public outcry, and subsequently gone on something of a press tour defending his initial decision not to investigate. But one wonders about his integrity and soundness of judgment in handling such cases. Sadly, his behavior here is not an outlier.It is often observed that sexual violence is so common that most women have experienced some form of it, and more women than you’d like to think have experienced the worst forms. The obvious corollary to this is even less comfortable to acknowledge: the fact that so many women have experienced sexual violence is only possible because many, many, many men are committing it.Many men rape; many men giggle encouragingly, or shrug indifferently, when their friends rape. Many men rape, and few seem to think that it’s a very big deal. If anything, cases like the alleged incident at Chi Phi – and many others – show that rape can be a bonding activity for men, a way they celebrate their own shared status as men.Complicity, too, is typical, not uncommon, for responding institutions. Impunity for rapists is cast as good sense, or as responsibility; as fairness, or compassion.Today, Chi Phi, Cornell, and the Tompkins county district attorney are under fire as the Cornell case has come to light. All appear to have behaved abominably. None behaved unusually. The next time a case like this arises – and it will arise, with the certainty of the tides – will we have learned anything?Texts about alleged Cornell gang-rape released after investigation reopenedRead moreI began my writing career as a feminist, in the midst of the #MeToo movement, and I’ve often thought that that early education in sexual violence advocacy was good preparation for the Trump era, both with its malignant cultural products and its collapse of the rule of law. Sexual violence is intimate, but impersonal: when someone rapes or assaults you, they both force access to the most private parts of your body and also negate your individual qualities, rendering your own thoughts and personality largely moot. So, too, with authoritarianism, which on the one hand seems to seep into the minute corners of our lives, inflecting our thoughts and conversations with its logic, but is also hostile to individualism, blurring citizens into subjects, types.Sexual assault, like the Trump era, reveals that law is applied selectively, according to the needs of power. Every court and every university, and every institutionwill say: “We take sexual violence extremely seriously.” And every one will find, with uncanny consistency, reasons not to take it very seriously at all.And sexual assault, like Trumpist authoritarianism, is ideologically incoherent. It is perpetrated by men against women in every race and class category, in every region and industry, in every school, and among people of every strain of politics. Its only rule, and its only value, is domination.If you understand all this – that domination is the rule of much of men’s interaction with women, that the law is mutable and does not protect you, and that beyond the effort to hurt and humiliate, there is no agenda and no rules – you will understand much of the Trump regime, and just about everything there is to know about rape. You’ll never be surprised by either one of them again. When I hear, now, about a new and pointlessly sadistic Trump policy, or a new high-profile rape case, I can often guess the details without being told. I’m never shocked any more. I wish that meant that I was never heartbroken.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistInformation and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUS universitiesOpinionUS politicsRape and sexual assaultNew YorkTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: The ultra-rich face … accountability? Manchester City and Clippers verdicts show it’s possible | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The sports world has accomplished a rare feat: calling out industrial-scale cheating on both sides of the Atlantic
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The sports world has accomplished a rare feat: calling out industrial-scale cheating on both sides of the Atlantic
Content: Manchester City’s achievements over the last decade have come under question.Photograph: Molly Darlington/ReutersView image in fullscreenManchester City’s achievements over the last decade have come under question.Photograph: Molly Darlington/ReutersSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester CityThe ultra-rich face … accountability? Manchester City and Clippers verdicts show it’s possibleLeander SchaerlaeckensThe sports world has accomplished a rare feat: calling out industrial-scale cheating on both sides of the AtlanticSign up for our free newsletter hereThu 1 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTShareThe first stage of billionaire exposure to accountabilityis vociferous denial.The second is bafflement that such an earthly and proletarian problem should even be allowed to happen to you, titan of industry, pillar of society, master of man and beast alike.The third is a milquetoastnon-apology apology“for the distraction and distress this matter has caused”, after issuinga totalandbelligerent denialthrough your proxies.The fourth stage? We’ll know soon enough.Manchester City timeline: trophies, transfers and more than 100 chargesRead moreWithin the last month, we have traipsed, on tiptoes, into a strange new age where some modicum of repercussion may occasionally threaten the billionaire class – albeit strictly limited to the confines of sports, where nothing actually matters. It’s a new and funny feeling in an age when it seems that the 1% don’t just get a bespoke business climate, where taxation and regulation are administered on an opt-in basis, but their own concierge service from the justice system, too.Setting aside for the moment the argument of whether billionaires should exist at all, or whether they are a flagrant failure of fiscal policy, this is a remarkable turn of events.On 2 September, the NBA released the findings of an investigation: The Los Angeles Clippers and their owner Steve Ballmer were officially caught paying star forward Kawhi Leonard $28m off the books for a no-show job with a supposed sponsor, circumventing the league’s salary cap. The Clippers weredocked five first-round picks and fined $30m. Ballmer, the ninth richest man in the world, was suspended from involvement with his team for a year. Initially, the Clippersissued a statement, snarling that they “vehemently reject the NBA’s findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence”.Then, the team accepted the punishment.View image in fullscreenClippers owner Steve Ballmer at a game in April.Photograph: Allen Berezovsky/Getty ImagesAfter all, they were caught bang to rights, after a year-long investigation by journalist Pablo Torre and his podcast, Pablo Torre Finds Out, which won a Pulitzer Prize for its work. The podcast unfurled its findings over several episodes and faced deep skepticism, including from Mark Cuban, Dallas Mavericks minority owner and Ballmer’s fellow billionaire. “I’m on Team Ballmer,” Cubanhad previously postedin an act of class solidarity. “Steve isn’t that dumb.”Ballmer, it should be noted, was only allowed to buy the Clippers when the team’s previous owner, Donald Sterling, was more or less expelled from the league over racist comments; another rare time that an owner was brushed back, especially by their own kind.Then, last week, a similar hammer dropped; Manchester Cityhas been found guiltyof more than 100 charges of cheating the Premier League’s financial regulations from 2009 to 2018 and obstructing the subsequent investigation from 2019 to 2023. They’re not at the apology stage yet,insisting on their innocence, as they have all along, taking an aggressively defiant posture.Still, it seems that in any of the plausible ways this may play out, after several more years of appeals and lawsuits surely, the club’s Abu Dhabi ownership will emerge from the ordeal bruised. Its entire footballing body of work, backed by untold billions in investment turning a humdrum club into a world-beating one, will have been tarnished. And if the entire point of the project – in the club administrator parlance – was a soft power PR play by the oil-rich nation state, it will have backfired catastrophically. No matter what happens next, the UAE-owned club will be remembered for cheating on an industrial scale, with a colossal scope, subverting the world’s most popular sporting competition and a British cultural institution for almost a decade.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWill the Clippers’ $30m fine tame the NBA’s billionaire class? We’re about to find outRead moreIt’s worth pausing and taking that in. These are the very rare occasions in a modern society, which has carved out a friction-free fast lane for the very rich and the very, very rich, that anyone in that stratus should be made to pay a price for anything at all.Like that time New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was allegedly caught paying for sex in a Florida massage parlor; prosecutors dropped the charge. Or the current status of theridiculousandspitefulNew York Knicks owner James Dolan, whofaces a lawsuitby a former employee over discrimination in which it’s alleged that he spied on the team’s own fans illegally – this, too,had been reported by Torre. It feels unlikely that Dolan will ever feel any effects from the accusations.And this is in addition to innumerable examples outside sports – including a certain resident of the White House, and a lot of his friends and allies.Time will probably mark out the Clippers and City cases as outliers. But that, for now, is what makes them so notable, so newsworthy. People of power and means running into the consequences of their own decadent and crooked decisions. A true novelty in our time.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsManchester CitySoccer with Jonathan WilsonNBABasketballUS sportsLos Angeles ClippersBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: As the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking point
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: As the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking point
Content: ‘The Trump administration seems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe.’Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The Trump administration seems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe.’Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Is Trump to blame for Americans getting explosive diarrhea?Arwa MahdawiAs the midterms approach, Americans’ digestive health has become a bizarre talking pointThu 1 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.27 EDTShareDonald Trump seems to spend an unusual amount of time thinking about toilets.Back in 2019, he bizarrelyclaimed: “People are flushing toilets 10 times, 15 times as opposed to once.” He repeated this claim at a Michigan rally the followingyear. “Ten times, right, 10 times,” Trump complained. “Not me, of course not me, but you,” he added while pointing at an unfortunate audience member.A couple of years later, he was back to the toilet talk: angrilydisputing claimsby the New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman that he’d once clogged a White House toilet by attempting to dispose of documents in it.I regret to inform you that the president is once again responsible for a national conversation about toilets. In a fitting encapsulation of Trumpism, explosive diarrhea has become a midtermtalking point. Food recalls and stomach-churning parasites have been a mainstay of the news this year and Democrats are milking the issue.Food-borne illnesses, funding cuts and layoffs: Maha movement’s glaring limitations are now showingRead moreIn August, for example, the Democratic party’s official Twitter/X accounthighlightedthe number of foods that have been recalled in 2026 and demanded that RFK Jr resign from his role as health secretary. Last month (which happened to be Food Safety Month – who knew?), the Rhode Island congressman Gabe Amoarguedthat Trump’s cuts to the federal workforce had contributed to decreased food safety. Senator Elizabeth Warrensimilarly accused“slashed food safety agencies” of contributing to the “cyclospora outbreak” and demanded Trump be held accountable in November.To be fair, the number offood recallsduring Trump’s second term is not remarkably different than it was under Joe Biden. What is different, however, is the scale of the problem. The US only recently declared the end of thelargest ever recordedcyclosporiasis outbreak, which was linked to contaminated lettuce. That resulted in 570 hospitalizations and two ⁠deaths.Also different is the fact that, as Warren noted, theTrump administrationseems hellbent on dismantling the regulations and systems that help keep consumers safe. Ever since 1995, there has been a federal-state partnership called the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet) which tracks infections caused by various pathogens, including Cyclospora.Starting on 1 July, however, the CDCdowngradedthis program so that mandatory surveillance for the 10 state health departments that participate in the program was limited to salmonella andEcoli. This downgrading of pathogen surveillance didn’t cause the cyclospora outbreak, but it might have made it harder for health authorities torespond to it.And it’s not just food that the current administration is making less safe: the air we breathe and the water we drink are all getting more dangerous in the name of maximizing corporate profits.On Monday, for example, the Trump administrationannouncedit was relaxing rules that govern how fuel-efficient auto companies have to make their new gasoline-powered cars and light trucks. The rationale given by Sean Duffy, the reality show star turned transportation secretary, is that removing stringent pollution-control requirements will reduce the average costs of new vehicles by $1,300.We’ll see if that actually happens (corporations are not keen on passing on cost savings), but even if it does reduce car prices, it’s going to cost consumers and the environment in other ways. Reduced efficiency will increase fuel spending, for one thing. And the change is poised to create more air pollution and worsen climate change.Donald Trump’s Maga cult is finally crumbling | Arwa MahdawiRead moreThe Trump administration is also working toroll back regulationof toxic air pollutants. Earlier this year the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed weakening air pollution limits on ethylene oxide (EtO), a knowncarcinogenthat is used to clean medical devices. A Biden-era rule finalized in 2024 required stringent testing for hazardous emissions and required emitters to cut the amount of EtO they were producing.If the EPA is successful in overturning these rules, then tons of the carcinogenic gas will continue to be released into the community. And it’s obviously not people in the vicinity of Mar-a-Lago breathing in the brunt of this poisonous air, is it? It’s people in largely low-income neighborhoods.Then there’s our water supply. A Biden-era rule set drinking-water limits for several Pfas (commonly known as “forever chemicals”). You know what happened next, don’t you? The Trump administration is trying to roll backthose limits, arguing that the standards are expensive and legally flawed.They’ve also terminated a regulatory review of Pfas-contaminatedsewage sludgefertilizer that is used on farmland. What does that mean? Well, according tocommentssubmitted by the Southern Environmental Law Center to the EPA, “if PFOA levels are 9.4 parts per billion [as witnessed in sludge tested in Maine], then more than 54 children out of 10,000 who eat 1-2 meals of fish per week on crop farms could get cancer later in life from those meals alone.”In short: if you thought the diarrhea-inducing lettuce was bad, then I’m afraid things only look likely to get worse. If Trump isn’t reined in at the midterms, the whole country is going down the toilet.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionDonald TrumpCyclosporiasis outbreak (US)Trump administrationUS politicsClimate crisisPollutioncommentShareReuse this content

title: From Robert Kraft to Netanyahu, Israel’s supporters keep helping its critics | Peter Beinart | The Guardian
description: These men’s actions aren’t just morally loathsome; they’re politically stupid. Social science may explain the phenomenon
Author: Peter Beinart
Headline: These men’s actions aren’t just morally loathsome; they’re politically stupid. Social science may explain the phenomenon
Content: ‘It’s hard to imagine anything more likely to intensify fury towards the Aipac class.’Photograph: Steven Senne/APView image in fullscreen‘It’s hard to imagine anything more likely to intensify fury towards the Aipac class.’Photograph: Steven Senne/APOpinionIsraelFrom Robert Kraft to Netanyahu, Israel’s supporters keep helping its criticsPeter BeinartThese men’s actions aren’t just morally loathsome; they’re politically stupid. Social science may explain the phenomenonThu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShareIsrael’s supporters keep proving its detractors right. Over the last couple of years, Americans from across the ideological spectrum – from Bernie Sanders to Tucker Carlson – have grown increasingly enraged by the way pro-Israel billionaires restrict Americans’ free speech. So, last month, along comes the New York England Patriots owner Robert Kraft,allegedlyin tandem with other stadium owners, and pushes Ed Sheeran to drop Macklemore from his US tour because the rapper uttered “Free Palestine” on stage. It’s hard to imagine anything more likely to intensify fury towards the Aipac class.Then Benjamin Netanyahu does something equally self-defeating. Since 2018, Israel’s favorability rating among Americans hasdroppedby an astonishing 67 points. A plurality of Democrats with views on the subjectconsiderIsrael to be “a state with segregation similar to apartheid” rather than a democracy. Yet faced with an American public that increasingly rejects Israel’s self-presentation as a bastion of freedom, Benjamin Netanyahu’s party haspushedto ban Arab parties, undercutting claims about Israel being a democracy for its Palestinian citizens. He’s undermining his own hasbara.Kraft and Netanyahu’s actions aren’t merely morally loathsome. They’re politically stupid. Were pro-Israel leaders savvy, they would greet the turn in American opinion with tactical concessions aimed at salvaging Israel’s reputation. Instead, they’re doubling down.Social science may offer an explanation. In 1979, the behavioral economists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tverskyobservedthat people care more about losing what they already have than gaining what they don’t. Most people react more strongly to accidentally dropping a $10 bill into the gutter than to finding one on the street.I was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a stand | Darializa Avila ChevalierRead moreAnd because people are “loss averse”, they take greater risks to avoid losing than they take to win. If you’re already down $1,000 at the casino, you’re more likely to gamble aggressively to get the money back than you would be if you hadn’t lost it in the first place.Since Kahneman and Tversky’s essay, social scientists have expanded their findings into realms beyond money. In a 2013 essay, the political scientists Jeffrey D Berejikian and Bryan R Earlyfoundthat US foreign policy makers were loss averse when it comes to national power. In negotiations with other countries, they took greater risks “to avoid losses” than they did “to acquire new gains”.This tendency may shape the way ordinary Americans view foreign policy as well. In 2018, the political scientist Diana Mutzdiscoveredthat, all other things being equal, Americans who felt the US was losing its global dominance were more likely to vote for Donald Trump. Supporting a reality television star who vowed to restore American greatness but had no governmental experience was risky. But Americans who felt the US was losing its international position were more willing to take that risk than those who did not.Now Trump himself is doing something similar: the more American power declines, the more he belligerent he becomes. He tariffs Canada, which leads its government toseek membershipin the European Union, which leads Trump tothreatenit even more.You can see the same dynamic in Kraft and Netanyahu’s behavior. Both men have spent their careers in a political environment in which US support for Israel was largely uncontested. The shrewder political decision would be to accept that this is no longer true, and to adapt their behavior accordingly – for instance, by acting in less thuggish ways towards Israel’s critics.But loss aversion suggests that when faced with the loss of something people have taken for granted, they don’t become more prudent. They become more aggressive.There are exceptions to this rule. Last summer, former Democratic congressman Rahm Emanuel, a longtime supporter of Israel, went to Tel Aviv University and did exactly what Kraft and Netanyahu have not: he threw Israel’s critics a bone. Heproposedthat Israel respond to its growing isolation by changing course and supporting a Palestinian state.But Kraft and Netanyahu’s obduracy is more common. Consider Aipac’s response to Tom Malinowski. Earlier this year, the former congressman – who was seeking the Democratic nomination in a special House election –suggestedplacing conditions on US support to Israel.Given thatalmost three-quartersof Democratic voters now oppose such aid, and that Malinowski has apro-Israel voting record, Aipac would have been wise to treat him as an ally. They instead spentmillionstrying to defeat him and inadvertentlyhelped electa progressive who is more hostile to the Jewish state.Israel and the US have battered the international legal order. The impunity must stop | Varsha GandikotaRead moreThis is loss aversion in action, and it’s part of the reason that Israel’s public standing keeps declining.This dynamic may not continue forever. If the US and Europe stop selling Israel weapons or cut if off from chunks of the international economy, Israeli leaders and their American defenders may have no choice but to offer concessions. They will be like the person at the casino who has lost, doubled down, lost again and eventually stops trying to recoup their losses because they have run out of money.But that scenario, while possible, remains years away. In the meantime, Israel’s champions are likely to keep answering its critics in ways that strengthen the very criticisms they are trying to quash. In a 2014speechat Columbia, when Israel’s reputation was just beginning to slide, the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions leader Omar Barghouti noted: “When I went to school here, Zionists used to be very smart” but now “they’re really not thinking straight.”That’s even more true today. And, ironically enough, two Israel-born economists help explain why.Peter Beinart is a contributing opinion writer atthe New York Times, editor at large atJewish Currents, a professor at theNewmark School of Journalism at the City University of New York, and the author ofThe Beinart Notebook, a weekly newsletter. His most recent book isBeing Jewish After the Destruction of GazaExplore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Americans are paying millions for a batch of pro-Trump ads | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: The spots, including a recycled campaign ad, are funded by taxpayers and present the president as a hero
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: The spots, including a recycled campaign ad, are funded by taxpayers and present the president as a hero
Content: ‘The ads do make a twisted kind of Trumpian sense.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘The ads do make a twisted kind of Trumpian sense.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APOpinionTrump administrationAmericans are paying millions for a batch of pro-Trump adsMargaret SullivanThe spots, including a recycled campaign ad, are funded by taxpayers and present the president as a heroThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTShareThe US government is spending millions of taxpayer dollars to get a blatantly partisan message in front of voters as the midterm elections loom.And while theseTV adsaren’t explicitly campaign ads, they might as well be.They featureDonald Trumpas a hero. They try to scare people into thinking that the US could become a communist country. They take shots at the news media and at vaguely described political enemies.Two Democratic senators, Patty Murray and Chris Murphy, on Tuesday aptlycalled them“a shockingly corrupt use of taxpayer dollars”.Their funding, through the Department of Homeland Security,may be illegal, according to experts, and is certainly unethical. They lack any hint of the public service message that the White House claims.Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics sayRead moreIn fact, they closely fit the defining characteristics of propaganda, as described by the government accounting office, including “self-aggrandizement” or “puffery”.But the agencies or institutions thatcoulddo something about them, including the supposedly independent FCC, are eager to do the president’s bidding. Brendan Carr, the FCC chair, is a proud Trump toady, with his thumb on the scale for every Trump project.Carr hasshrugged offquestions about the ads. They don’t raise any red flags for him; they are quite normal, and nothing that his agency intends to investigate.And with both houses of Congress held by Republican majorities, this startling use of taxpayer money will probably go unpunished – at least for now.“The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress,”saidDonald Sherman, who heads Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics (Crew) in Washington. However, as he told CNN, Congress “has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable”. Some Republican members of Congress have questioned the ads, but there’s no groundswell of bipartisan outrage so far.TheTrump administrationis responding to the criticism with its usual defiance, even planning to double down in the next few weeks.“This is just the beginning,” one administration officialtoldAxios.The argument that these are not political ads is contradicted by an undeniable reality: one of them is a straight-up rerun of a Trump campaign commercial from before the 2024 presidential election. It differs, though, with the addition of an Orwellian coda, “paid for by the US government”.With its weirdly menacing tone, it shows black-and-white images of Trump walking as he promises to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and pledges to “rout out the fake news media”.Another ad shows images of Trump at public events with a voiceover insisting that “America will never be a communist country,” while the song Love Me plays in the background. (The R&B artist JMSN has said he didn’t authorize this use of his song and has made acease-and-desist demand.)Another ad,reportedRobert Tait of the Guardian, shows images of Mount Rushmore and has Trump bragging: “The United States of America is the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.”Donald Trump’s midterm strategy? Make it all about him | Robert ReichRead moreThe White House described that “love me” ad as “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. And, in a statement, it termed the various ads as “public service announcements”.They are playing to a big-tent crowd that Trump apparently thinks (or hopes) is persuadable. They’ve aired everywhere from pro-football games to Saturday Night Live.The Wall Street Journal reported that the ads, by last weekend, had aired more than 90 times across various networks – and political leanings – including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now and CBS.As corrupt as they appear to be, the ads do make a twisted kind of Trumpian sense.They are probably illegal and have garnered plenty of legitimate criticism. But what’s missing is accountability with actual teeth.As usual, he’s getting away with it.But the midterm elections could change that. With Trump’s approval ratings low and voters unhappy with misguided Iran war and soaring costs, Democrats could seize a majority in one or both houses of Congress.That might mean some restraints on Trump’s never-ending cascade of malfeasance.It’s no wonder he’s pulling out all the stops to make that nightmare go away.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionDonald TrumpUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month | Timnit Gebru and Emily M Bender | The Guardian
description: The risks of AI aren’t what we think they are, as a recent security incident between China and the United States reveals
Author: Emily M Bender
Headline: The risks of AI aren’t what we think they are, as a recent security incident between China and the United States reveals
Content: ‘As the former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us, there is no exemption to the law when it comes to AI.’Photograph: US Navy/Zuma Wire/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘As the former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us, there is no exemption to the law when it comes to AI.’Photograph: US Navy/Zuma Wire/Rex/ShutterstockOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this monthTimnit Gebru andEmily M BenderThe risks of AI aren’t what we think they are, as a recent security incident between China and the United States revealsThu 1 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTShareAmid a barrage of news stories warning about superintelligent machines rendering humanity extinct, a CNN story describing the opposite scenario – one in which the US military’s reliance on brittle chatbots almost brought the US into war with China – went mostly unnoticed by the public.The biggest international AI news of the past three weeks was the Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon’s resignation. According to him, OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Coxon’s description of a “terminator” scenario, a machine becoming much smarter than humanity and deciding to wipe us out, captured the public’s, journalists’ and politicians’ attention, stirring waves of fear-inducing, credulous reporting, and policy actions.The California governor, Gavin Newsom, issued a mandate to create an “AI kill-switch”; New York’s governor,Kathy Hochul, is similarly exploring the possibility of having “AI kill-switches”; and Senator Bernie Sanders and Congressman Greg Casar introduced legislation to “ban artificial superintelligence”.While so many of us were focused on fictional superintelligent machines that we were told could hypothetically cause human extinction, however, there was a more serious story being reported.A series of events almost got us to armageddon, not caused by “rogue, superintelligent AI”, but bygovernment relianceon error-prone systems that are marketed by their manufacturers as being close to superintelligent.ACNN reportpublished on 18 September, which hasn’t been verified by other major outlets, describes how the US “almost started a war” with China, based on an intelligence report that claimed a Chinese ship was transporting components of nuclear weapons. Military personnel made plans to intercept the Chinese vessel, complete with aircraft and soldiers ready to board the ship. A military skirmish of this kind between China and the US could quickly escalate and spiral into world war three.It was only moments before executing on the plan that American officials further investigated the intelligence report and found that it had been generated with the use of a chatbot and contained erroneous information about the vessel’s contents.Unlike the terminator, “rogue AI”, scenario, this incident didn’t galvanize lawmakers into announcing calls for regulation so as to avoid potential human extinction. Media outlet after media outlet didn’t warn the public that we almost triggered a war against a nuclear superpower because of our military’s reliance on error-prone chatbots.We describe the large language models (LLMs) powering these chatbots as stochastic parrots, that is, models that are designed to regurgitate the patterns of the data they are trained on. News coverage describing them as “powerful” “rogue” models that could render humanity extinct all on their own, bolsters perceptions of tools based on these models being infallible enough to merit usage in stakes as high as warfare.Even CNN’s more critical coverage describes the chatbot used by the US military as presenting “profound risks” because it is “powerful, new and relatively poorly understood technology”.In fact, today’s LLMs and the chatbots they power are not poorly understood, nor are they powerful in the sense of being effective tools for this use case. They are systems for generating plausible-looking text, built out of enormous, haphazardly collected datasets and then “fine-tuned” (that is, further trained) to be especially appealing to their intended users.CNN wasn’t able to learn which chatbot product was used in this case, but the LLM powering the product was probably fine-tuned to output text with the stylistic hallmarks of intelligence reports. Both the basic functionality and the risks of such a model have been well-understood and well-documented for years, including in our 2021 paperOn the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?Claims that system behavior is mysterious arise fromdeliberate mystificationon the part of those selling those systems, and a misapprehension of what their output is by those procuring and using it.Unlike the unscientific and fantastical claims of OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs and those who uncritically repeat their talking points, the harmful, and well-documented, impacts of these companies’ products have arisen because peoplebelievethat the products are superintelligent, not because they actually are.From“AI” scribesused by hospitalserroneously classifying patientsas illicit drug users, to governments killing children after relying on “intelligence analysis” systems whichmistake schools for military facilities, we are seeing the predictable harms that come from misplaced faith in unreliable automated software.Meanwhile, the marketing campaigns from the companies selling this software warn of impending superintelligence, directing our attention away from the real risk to their fantasies of doom.It is high time for us to regulate usage of systems sold as “AI”, not because they are magical machines, but because they are error-prone products that shouldn’t be used in high-stakes scenarios. Any automation used in military, medical or other life-and-death situations must be thoroughly evaluated within its use case and paired with usage norms that keep accountability with people who have actual power to make decisions.As the former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us,there is no exemption from the law when it comes to AI: there are existing laws that federal agencies and other regulators can enforce to protect the public against the AI industry’s unsafe and unscientific practices of pushing unsound products while marketing them as “magic intelligence in the sky”.Going along with company executives and describing their products as beings with agency allows these executives to evade accountability while deceiving the public. We call on journalists and lawmakers to hold companies accountable rather than parrot their marketing talking points.Timnit Gebru is executive director of Dair and author of the forthcoming bookDeep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, which is available for preorders now and set to publish on 16 February.Emily M Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and co-author ofThe AI Con.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess  | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and decline, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and decline, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Donald Trump addresses the 81st United Nations general assembly in New York on 22 September.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump addresses the 81st United Nations general assembly in New York on 22 September.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersOpinionUnited NationsWar, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a messNesrine MalikUkraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and declineThu 1 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.36 EDTShareUN general assembly meetings are not usually riveting occasions. But this year’s encapsulated a world in flux and crisis, an international law and organisation structure that is falling apart, and a humanitarian order machine running hot. What unfolded was less a gathering for resolution and resolve than a display of showboating, frustration and fractiousness.It was a snapshot for the history books of four huge destabilising conflicts for which there seems to be no means of, or interest in, resolution – Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan. Volodymyr Zelenskyydeliveredan account of five years of Russian aggression: the staggering loss of life – hundreds of thousands killed on both sides – the porousness of the sanctions on Russia, the “madness” of it all. Donald Trump once againthreatenedto “annihilate” Iran if it did not make a deal, a promise that has now been made so many times its restating only reveals its hollowness. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, responded in his own speech by saying that Iran has been the victim of US terrorism and aggression, and would defend itself with the “utmost strength”. The sole US delegation representative in the roomwalked out.In the middle of this unbridled, unseemly pugnaciousness, pleas to restate facts were trampled over by power-lust. The Israeli government’s sense of impunity “has reached terrifying levels”,saidJordan’s King Abdullah II. “It no longer feels compelled to ask, ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”“If international law can be ignored for decades,” he added, “then what exactly is that law worth?” As if to answer that question, Benjamin Netanyahu became the only ICC indicted leader to address the UN general assembly, with a characteristically belligerent speech. Nothing – that law is worth nothing.And on international law meaning nothing, the assembly was subjected to the farce of the United Arab Emirates, the key player in Sudan’s war, piouslypreachingabout how Sudanese people deserve peace and civilian rule, while the UAE’s leaders are accused of arming and funding theRapid Support Forces(RSF), itselfaccused of genocide and ethnic cleansing. A close ally of the US and the UK, the UAE has managed to extend Sudan’s war into a calamitous conflict, without even a breath of censure, or even acknowledgment from its friends. A $500minvestmentin the Trump family’s cryptocurrency scheme, and multibillion-pound partnerships with the UK, have seemingly captured the two states. Indeed, the silence it has bought is so compliantly observed that the US’s senior adviser on African and Arab affairs (Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law) acknowledged foreign interests but refusedto name any of the countries.Even procedurally, the ground was tilted by those who have the power and shamelessness to do so. The Trump administration invoked its sovereign ability to decide who could attend and who could not, wielding a sort of weaponisation of the visa system that rendered the UN not a neutral body with its own rules and protocols, but a tool to be leveraged for the interests of the US and its allies because it sits in US territory. Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas (not ICC-indicted) and 80 other Palestinian officials weredeniedvisas to attend for the second time under Trump’s watch. The head of the Sudanese government and Sudanese armed forces, the antagonists to the UAE-backed RSF, was denied a visa, seemingly an indication of successful Emirati manoeuvrings in Washington. The dynamics were an expression of how foreign policy and conflict are managed today, with constant gaming of the system to amplify one side over the other and produce outcomes friendly to regional and global powers.Amid the collapse there was Tom Fletcher, the UN undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs, darting energetically from meeting to meeting, with a grittily sunny disposition. He posted a hectic flurry of social media clips talking about what could be done in the middle of the fire, a sort of diplomatic “this is fine” meme. And God bless him. Inone, he is on a walk with Alexander De Croo, administrator of the UN development programme, who talks about the problem being “crises piling up on one another”. “The answer,” Fletcher says, “to a lot of what we do is actually diplomacy. Getting those chokepoints open, Bab al-Mandab, the Black Sea, the strait of Hormuz, because otherwise we both have a much bigger development caseload and humanitarian caseload.”He represents an emerging new model of international and humanitarian worker – navigating funding cuts, a lack of interest in peace and politicised drawdown of international aid to at least maintain some traffic of funds. To make sure some support gets to the millions labouring under war, the climate crisis, disease, poverty, hunger and predation. The wars will carry on, and now the strategy is to negotiate with powers to un-choke and unblock what can be opened to get supplies and relief in, from winter aid in Gaza to containing the Ebola outbreak.But where we are now isn’t just a matter of earnest diplomats and cynical, irresponsible warring powers. A far more complex problem is upon us: the rapidly changing nature of military conflict itself. Wars are becoming vastly less containable through the spread, sophistication and low cost of AI and drones. They are now conducted remotely, veering between high-intensity and low-grade assaults that render their beginnings and ends less decisive. They are more likely to just suspend normal life with dispensable drones, the sort that have held the Gulf hostage to Iran’s response to US attacks, Sudan’s war without a clear frontline, and the “ceasefire” in Gaza essentially just a lower-grade assault.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe UN general assembly meeting of 2026 was a study in so many things – the degradation of international law, the rickety system it has bequeathed, the acceleration of the demise of international community, and the importance of resolve to somehow attend to the victims. But we are also entering an era in which belligerents themselves are coming to grips with asymmetrical warfare and an elusive status quo. There is much talk of “what comes next”: an equilibrium ofmiddle powersin compact, a rupture with the US and within Nato, a nihilistic free for all? We as humans tend to think in clear-cut scenarios. What is more likely is what was demonstrated last week in New York – a messy prolonged state of constant stress under careless leaders giddy with what they realise they can get away with, no exit plan, and the rest of the system given no option but to work with and around them to somehow alleviate the consequences of their actions. The new world order is one of active resignation.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUnited NationsOpinionInternational lawHumanitarian responseDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Flipping public opinion on the triple lock was Burnham magic – he’ll need more of it to see his social care plans through | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Rebuilding a complex and broken system into one that’s fair for all, and in the face of steely opposition: that will be the PM’s real challenge, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Rebuilding a complex and broken system into one that’s fair for all, and in the face of steely opposition: that will be the PM’s real challenge, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andy Burnham speaks to residents, care workers and volunteers during visit to a care home in London, 29 July 2026.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/Pool AP/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaks to residents, care workers and volunteers during visit to a care home in London, 29 July 2026.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/Pool AP/APOpinionSocial careFlipping public opinion on the triple lock was Burnham magic – he’ll need more of it to see his social care plans throughPolly ToynbeeRebuilding a complex and broken system into one that’s fair for all, and in the face of steely opposition: that will be the PM’s real challengeThu 1 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTShareHere is rare clearcut proof of the power of political persuasion. Party conference speeches, the lifeblood of political obsessives, rarely reach the public beyond a brief news clip. But this time was different.Andy Burnham’s speechspun the dial on public opinion on several political hot potatoes, defining who he is.The pensions triple lock, which guarantees that pensions rise faster than average incomes, has been a no-go electoral minefield despite a groundswell of economists (and even aTimes leader) calling for reform to prevent pensions skyrocketing. Touching this live rail was an act of bravery – or recklessness.Polls over the years strongly supported the lock: a Persuasion UK poll this week found65% in favourof keeping it, more among over-65s. A Times YouGov poll this month went as high as93% of pension-age peopledefending it. So the sudden change in public opinion after the speech has been astonishing. YouGovnow reportsthat 48% support the Burnham plan, with just 28% against. Survation finds64% backing itwith only 15% against. The magic was linking reform of the lock with creating a national care service. Never mind that it barely begins to cover the cost, it makes an emotional link between the two policies.I can’t think of any other conference speech that reversed public opinion on such a sensitive policy. Kemi Badenoch’s Tories protested that it was just “robbing Peter to pay Paul”, whileNigel Farage’s party vowed, “Reform UK will always protect our pensioners and maintain the triple lock.” Both are out of touch with the public (at least, for now).But this is only week one on a long and winding journey to 2030, when plans for the triple lock and a national care service have appeared in the nextLabourmanifesto – and fickle voters have reelected a Labour government. When the world so often turns upside down in the blink of an eye (Burnham keeps reminding himself he is the seventh PM in a decade), 2030 can feel light years away.We don’t yet know what a national care service is. But the most moving and easiest to implement promise in Burnham’s speech is to improve the lives and status of care workers like those he watched looking after his father: “Caring for other people’s parents on poverty pay, but doing it with huge skill, humour and humanity.” He pledged, “I promise you, I won’t leave this job without doing everything I can to change things for you.” Starmer’s fair-pay agreement for care workers is already on its way, to be agreed between trade unions and employers. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary,this week announcedthe first national pension scheme for care workers. Next, they need training, pay and career ladders the same as NHS healthcare assistants, merging the two together.But the rest of Burnham’s “landmark policy as significant as the creation of the NHS itself” looks perplexingly difficult. He promised “care that is about people, not profit”, but Margaret Thatcher privatised care, breaking it into fragments by denying central funds to any council keeping its own service. There are now about19,000 organisationsproviding adult care in England, some big, most small, some good, some pretty terrible, some voluntary, many understaffed. In theory, they are inspected by the regulator, but the Care Quality Commission, knowing the shortage of beds and services, sets alow bar in standards. Could that be in-sourced?But here’s the biggest conundrum of all. Who pays for social care goes right to the heart of social justice and fair taxation. Currently, most people in England already have their care paid for by the state, because they have less than £23,250 in savings and no property that is not lived in by a partner. But23% of peoplein England who get at-home careand 37% of thosein residential careare self-funders. Between them, they pay £14bn a year. Burnham seemed to imply they would be relieved of that burden, NHS style – but if so, that would be a whopping £14bn given to better-off elderly people, paid for by taxpayers. That’s unthinkably expensive and unfair to younger working people, a generation with less income and less property. So it won’t and shouldn’t happen.Instead, as hastily explained afterwards, self-payers will only get their care paid for, but they will stillpay for their bed and boardin care homes – as in Scotland, where standard weekly costs of about £1,000 are mitigated by the statecontributing £260 for care. Burnham said that people should no longer lose their homes to pay care costs; they still do in Scotland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritons are not ageing healthily – we need to learn from countries that have made it a priority | Devi SridharRead moreAnd rightly. Only 21% of people think the state should pay for it all, regardless of the recipient’s wealth, according to aKing’s Fund survey. Keeping an empty home to pass on as inheritance is not something the state should subsidise, when every spare penny is needed to pay for better social care. More than 400,000 are on officialcare waiting listsin England, while Age UK says2 million older peoplehave unmet care needs, putting a huge burden on families. Burnham himself talked of the miserably inadequate 15-minute homecare visits. Meanwhile, the NHS desperately needs a better care service to save the13,000 beds a dayfilled with those waiting for a care package.At any one time, few people use social care, so few understand the system, according to the King’s Fund. Simon Bottery, who leads its work on adult social care, says, “Frailty and dementia in later life are issues that most people just don’t want to think about until they really need to.” But it’s about to become a hot political battleground, with its fiendish complexities and its difficult moral and political choices.When problems look insoluble, the last five prime ministers have summoned the great troubleshooterLouise Casey. She reports next year on what should be done. With the political right preparing for war, her job is to find answers acceptable enough to most. But that’s unlikely to include a carbon copy of the free NHS, nor should that be on the table.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSocial careOpinionOlder peopleNHSLabourHealthAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Margot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here’s why | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: I don’t flip a table every time this happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: I don’t flip a table every time this happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion
Content: ‘Last week my tolerance was tested again when it was revealed that after a decade of marriage, Margot Robbie has changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.’Photograph: Image Press Agency/NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Last week my tolerance was tested again when it was revealed that after a decade of marriage, Margot Robbie has changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.’Photograph: Image Press Agency/NurPhoto/Rex/ShutterstockOpinionMargot RobbieMargot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here’s whyRebecca ShawI don’t flip a table every time this happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussionThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 21.24 EDTShareBeing a lesbian in a heretofore heteronormative society means having to go along with lots of things that don’t make sense to your beautiful lesbian brain. One such thing for me is the ongoing expectation that women who marry men should change their surname to their husband’s.Last week my tolerance was tested again when itwas revealedthat after a decade of marriage,Margot Robbiehas changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.Margot Ackerley – it simply rolls off the tongue. She will remainMargot Robbiein her public life, and we don’t know why she has done this, but it has nonetheless caused a stir. We got the usual discourse of blah blah tradition, blah blah patriarchy, blah blah women’s individual choice and so on.We all know how it goes and Margot is not alone in doing this, of course. The statistics are hard to pin down (bearing in mind I dropped out of psychology at uni because of the statistics part) but I think it’s safe to say that in the overwhelming majority of straight marriages, the woman changes her name to the man’s. I see this in every part of my social life, from friends back home who married directly out of high school to my cabal of highly educated urban feminist friends. I play my part by putting all my married male friends in my phone under their wives’ surnames.In a world determined to isolate us, friendship may be the best way to keep each other alive | Rebecca ShawRead moreOf course I have no personal sense of the societal pressure and systems that inform such decisions, which is why I don’t flip a table every time it happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion.There are plenty of reasons a woman might want to change her name. She might hate her dad. She might feel no attachment to her name. Her husband might have a meaningful attachment to his and so she might just think it’s a nice thing to do.I’m not an unreasonable lesbian. My issue isn’t with women taking their man’s surname, the problem comes when there is nochoosing. When it’s a foregone conclusion, when it hasn’t been actively decided. That’s your name!If there is discussion, if there is equal respect for both people, if someone has a reason, then that’s fine with me. I once had a colleague whose future husband told her it was a dealbreaker if she didn’t take his name. That’s not a reason. That should have been the dealbreaker itself.I don’t really careaboutthe reasoning, I just care that thereisa reason. That said, when it comes to which surname a baby gets, that’s when I really get irritated. If we really have stopped considering a man’s wife and children his property, why on earth is giving them his name still the default?Womencarry and birth the babies. Women are still far more likely to do the lion’s share of childcare. Hello?? The lesbian mind boggles.But never fear, because I have a solution. And you may be surprised that it doesn’t involve any gender politics whatsoever! My solution is that we throw tradition out the window and that if a couple wants to share a name, we make the decision based on … which surname is cooler. Which surname sounds better, which surname will offer more success – that’s the one you should both use.In an ideal world, this would be done in a courtroom setting, where each couple comes in and sees me sitting high above them like Judge Judy, ready to bang my gavel. Congratulations, Mr Brown, you are now Mr Beaumont. Sorry, Mrs Jones, you’re now Mrs Wilder. Mr Cheeseman, I release you from your prison.No longer would awesome surnames be swallowed by the crap oesophagus of patriarchy. No longer would it be considered weak or weird for a man to take his wife’s last name – instead it would be cool and wise. Even though my loyalty always lies with women, I am willing to maintain neutrality in the courtroom.And sorry, Mr Ackerley, which sounds a bit like a cat throwing up – you’re now Mr Robbie.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsMargot RobbieOpinionCelebrityMarriageFamily filmsRelationshipsFamilyFeminismcommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham is right that ‘hope comes from honesty’. That’s why Labour must make the case for rejoining the EU | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: Brexit was a disastrous act of national self-harm. Britain needs EU membership to bring growth and security in an increasingly volatile world, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: Brexit was a disastrous act of national self-harm. Britain needs EU membership to bring growth and security in an increasingly volatile world, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: Andy Burnham meets with European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, at the UN general assembly, in New York, 22 September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham meets with European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, at the UN general assembly, in New York, 22 September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersOpinionBrexitBurnham is right that ‘hope comes from honesty’. That’s why Labour must make the case for rejoining the EUSadiq KhanBrexit was a disastrous act of national self-harm. Britain needs EU membership to bring growth and security in an increasingly volatile worldThu 1 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTShareHope again. That was theprime minister’s messageto the country this week. Anational social care system, greater public control of water and energy, help for first-time buyers and a crackdown on rogue landlords and empty homes. With clarity and conviction, Andy Burnham set out a bold plan to put Britain on a new path, steeped in Labour values.It felt like a conference speech that would be remembered for years to come, marking a decisive break with a broken political model that has let British people down for decades. And perhaps most encouraging of all was the prime minister’s promise torethink Britain’s relationship with the EU.Burnham’s words were simple but stark: “Brexit has done more harm than good.” He is right – and the reality of the vote’s impact on the UK is sobering. Researchcommissioned by City Hall in 2024showed that London’s economy was £30bn smaller than it would have been without Brexit and that there were nearly 2m fewer jobs overall in the UK as a result of us leaving. Earlier this year, weset out new analysisshowing that our country has grown more slowly than our comparable European counterparts since 2016. If that trend continues, our economy could be £250bn smaller than similar EU countries’ by 2030.Ten years after the referendum, the sunlit uplands promised by the Brexiters have proven to be a total fiction. Instead, Britain finds itself battling an economic and geopolitical storm.Earlier this year,I warned thatDonald Trump’s bombing of Iran could have catastrophic consequences for Londoners, and it gives me no pleasure to be proved right. The folly of this reckless war of choice is now clear for all to see. The conflict is sending shock waves through the global economy, hiking up mortgage costs and pushing up fuel prices. The price of diesel hashit an all-time highat nearly £2 per litre, while energy bills are forecastto rise 25% this winter, piling unbearable pressure on many households across the UK already grappling with a cost-of-living crisis.I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen JonesRead moreAt the same time, Trump’s fondness for unilateralism has shaken the foundations of the transatlantic alliance on which our national security depends. As Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, persists with his illegal and unconscionable full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Trump’s unpredictable actions and unsettling ambivalence towards European security can no longer be ignored.In this geopolitical storm, Europe offers us not just a safe harbour, but a huge opportunity for growth. The EU is our biggest trading partner and our most reliable ally. That’s why, at the UK-EU summit in November, I will call on the government to lay the groundwork for Britain’s swift return to both the customs union and the single market – a move that should happen within this parliament.Rejoining the customs union and the single market would deliver an immediate boost to economic growth, improving living standards for communities across the country and helping to grant Londoners some respite from the most acute cost of living pressures. In the long term, however, we must raise our ambitions higher still. Our party must immediately start making the case for rejoining the EU, so we can fight and win a general election with EU membership effectively on the ballot paper in 2029.The brutal truth is that leaving the EU was the biggest act of economic and geopolitical self-harm in our country’s history. Rejoining is the only viable path to long-term prosperity and security. Anything less will fail to undo the severe damage that’s been done.For far too long, theLabourparty’s debate about Europe has been constrained by “red lines” that make rebuilding our relationship with the EU impossible. But Burnham has now recognised that these lines were drawn up for a different world.In Canada,Mark Carney has set out his planto partner much more closely with the EU on defence, critical minerals and energy security, with the country now on the path to becoming the bloc’s first associate member. In this multipolar world, middle powers such as Canada, the UK and our European neighbours must come together, both to safeguard our own security and economies and to stand up for free trade and our liberal democratic values.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDeeper integration can – and will – unlock a new age of growth and productivity, but it will also provide us with a louder voice on the world stage. From bolstering our military defences to safely developing AI and combating the climate crisis, if we are to make ourselves heard, we must speak as one. And in a world whose superpowers appear ever more comfortable with throwing their weight around, the EU is the only organisation with the economic and geopolitical heft to hold its own.For me, the most memorable line inBurnham’s speechcame a couple of minutes in: “Hope comes from honesty.” They were the words of a leader unafraid to change the terms of Britain’s dysfunctional political debate by taking on the seemingly intractable problems that too many would be inclined to avoid.Today, Brexit is foremost among those problems. If we are to bring back hope, we must be honest about the disastrous costs of our decision to leave the EU. And we must be honest about the fact that reversing it is the best chance we have to get Britain back on track – and get the country firing on all cylinders again.Sadiq Khan is mayor of LondonExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionAndy BurnhamEuropean UnionLabourEuropeForeign policyLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Releasing prisoners won’t solve the crisis in English and Welsh jails. Here’s what will | Enver Solomon | The Guardian
description: Ministers need to level with the public about current prison sentences, who needs to be locked up and for how long, says Enver Solomon of Nacro
Author: Enver Solomon
Headline: Ministers need to level with the public about current prison sentences, who needs to be locked up and for how long, says Enver Solomon of Nacro
Content: ‘Ministers need to be much more transparent about the importance of rehabilitation as well as punishment.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Ministers need to be much more transparent about the importance of rehabilitation as well as punishment.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyOpinionPrisons and probationReleasing prisoners won’t solve the crisis in English and Welsh jails. Here’s what willEnver SolomonMinisters need to level with the public about what current prison sentences look like – who needs to be locked up and for how longEnver Solomon is chief executive of Nacro, the criminal justice charity‘Thank you Andy Burnham’: prisoners react as they begin to leave under early release schemeThu 1 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTShareThe flipchart in the corner of the staff meeting room, deep inside a prison in the south-east ofEngland, tells its own story about what our overcrowded jails are having to deal with, day in day out. Under the heading “Challenges”, it lists gangs, the destruction of cells, prisoners exploiting each other and complex behaviours.Committed, hard-working staff talk about the high levels of psychosis, often combined with drug abuse. They provide examples of people actually committing crimes to go back into jail to get some respite from their chaotic, dysfunctional lives.To tackle the current prisons crisis in England and Wales, plannedchanges to sentencingwill see almost 2,000 peoplereleased early from Thursdayand over the following month. It is the first tranche of the estimated 5,000 releases that will take place in phases over the coming year.This will address the immediate crisis, but by the government’s own admission it isnot a permanent fix.If it wants to ensure that the new approach to early releases does not need to be further accelerated, wider reforms will be needed across the system.As a first step, we need to address the staggering increase in people recalled to prison. The power that probation officers have to send someone back behind bars plays an important role in protecting the public, but with recall now accounting forone in sevenof the prison population compared with one in 13 a decade ago, it is neithersustainable nor effective. Cases of people being recalled for missing probation appointments because transport was delayed or for moving out of their accommodation to get away from drug dealers and gangs, are too often punished with a return to custody. A justice secretary under the last Labour government tells me it’s a ludicrous approach that must change if prisons aren’t going to stagger from crisis to crisis.Second, we need to focus on the probation service. It is critical to fixing prisons and too often undervalued. Today it is a long way from its original social-work ethos to advise, assist and befriend those once described as clients but now always labelled offenders. The focus is much more on surveillance and compliance. Consecutive reports by the Chief Inspector of Prisons during the last two weeks reveal how, after years of being run down, the service is struggling to get the basics right. Electronic tags are a critical and expanding part of supervision on release from custody, but theinspector foundthe “systems, processes and frontline practice needed to make it effective have not kept pace”. The standard of probation work isnot consistentlywhat it should be, with staff shortages, poor information sharing and gaps in the capability of probation officers to keep people safe.The government is committed to recruiting thousands more probation staff and to improving practice but, faced with people who have a complex mix of needs and behaviours, a more person-centred approach closer to the profession’s social-work roots is needed. Those coming out of custody whom we work with say they want probation officers to get alongside them and build trusting relationships so they can get their lives back on track.We need to be more open with the public. Prisons and probation are there to keep the public safe, but to do that, ministers need to be much more transparent about the importance of rehabilitation as well as punishment. The justice secretary’sspeech to Labour conferencethis week started this, but far too many are still leaving prison to commit further offences because the system does not provide the drug treatment, access to employment, training and education – and then stable accommodation on release – that will help turn them away from crime. The fact thathalf of those rough sleepingin England and Wales have spent time in prison is a stark reminder of what’s not working.The services need connecting. Fixing this cannot be achieved by the justice system alone. Public bodies from the NHS to local councils have a role to play in giving people the support they need to stay out of prison. Beyond those, community providers can step in where state agencies are not best placed to reach people.In his party conference speech, Andy Burnham spoke of the importance ofbeing honest with the country. To be honest about our prisons would be to recognise that continuing to lock up more and more people on longer sentences in overcrowded jails will not deliver rehabilitation, nor will it protect communities. This means levelling with the public about what current sentences look like, who needs to be locked up and for how long.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is a precedent that shows it can be done. When Labour was last in government, in 2010, there were more than2,000 childrenbehind bars in England and Wales. Today there arefewer than 500. Where there is a will …Enver Solomon is chief executive of Nacro, the criminal justice charityExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionUK criminal justiceHomelessnessLabourSocial exclusionEnglandWalescommentShareReuse this content

title: Would I want my child to study for a social media influencer degree? No, but it’s the way of the world  | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: What next, you might think, as you consider the UK university course: a BA in the manosphere? Take a look at media job listings to set yourself straight, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: What next, you might think, as you consider the UK university course: a BA in the manosphere? Take a look at media job listings to set yourself straight, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: Kim and Khloe Kardashian in Venice, Italy, June 2025.Photograph: Luigi Costantini/APView image in fullscreenKim and Khloe Kardashian in Venice, Italy, June 2025.Photograph: Luigi Costantini/APOpinionUniversitiesWould I want my child to study for a social media influencer degree? No, but it’s the way of the worldEmma BrockesWhat next, you might think, as you consider the UK university course: a BA in the manosphere? Take a look at media job listings to set yourself straightThu 1 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTShareSometimes you read a story in the news that seems designed to wind up as many people as possible. This week, that story involves adegree in content creationfrom Nottingham Trent University. Otherwise known as the “influencer degree”, this three-year course comes with BA (Hons) status and a top-tier price tag of almost £10,000 a year, for which students will learn “hands-on technical production”, “analytics, branding and commercial strategy” and collaboration with brands and “industry partners”. Course leaders are at pains to point out it won’t turn them into overnight social media stars, but of course, while reading, I felt the cold drag of undertow forces pulling me towards world-gone-mad outrage.We’ve been here before, obviously: media studies, women’s studies, anything that hasn’t been on the syllabus of the ancient universities for at least 500 years is vulnerable to accusations of dumbing down – and this is no different. The course was launched in 2022, meaning its first cohort of graduates are out there looking for jobs right now, while giving interviews about whether or not it was worth it. One very sensible-sounding graduate, talking to the BBC this week in what one assumes is an application of the all-publicity-is-good-publicity principle learned from her course, said that the £30,000 spend was worth it for the networking opportunities alone – an absolutely valid point and half the reason why people strive towards Oxbridge.Still, there will be eyebrows twitching. That price tag seems punchy for a course that iscurrently in clearing. But the bigger issue is the triggering effect the words “social media” and “influencer” will have on parents mired in data supporting the view that their children’s lives are in constant peril from the forces unleashed by online platforms and the jobs that go with them. What next? A degree course in dropshipping?! How about an MPhil in manosphere studies? And so on and so on: all modern versions of the sinking spirits that have traditionally attended a child announcing they want to go to drama school.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBill Gates predicts AI will kill a billion people – but saying he’s been wrong before is quite the understatement | Arwa MahdawiRead moreIn general, we’ve always been quite sniffy about vocational degrees in this country. Look at the prestige that comes, for example, from attending Columbia Journalism School in the US, despite much laughter from journalists in this country who think the best way to study journalism is to get a job in journalism. British friends with jobs in marketing hold similar views about degrees in that subject: “Get a job, it’s stupid to pay to study it.” If degree courses are supposed to teach critical thinking, so the argument goes, then these courses don’t qualify as suitably academic – not a concern anyone ever raises about medicine or law.It’s snobbery, then, and in this case also conditioning. Influencing is empty, pointless, evil and grifty, underscored by narcissism and fulfilling no useful human or social need – an assessment that might just as easily be applied to the careers in banking that so many top graduates head towards. If anything, it seems to me that influencing is a clever spin from Nottingham Trent (and Brighton University, which also offers the course) in response to the terrible state of traditional media careers. Going forward, it’s fair to assume that for those going into the media, the smart move is to be an independent contractor rather than hold a traditional job without bonus structures or opportunities for profit-sharing.Prosecco pratfalls and coffee catastrophes: Neets are missing out on formative first-job experiences | Isabel BrooksRead moreIn case you haven’t noticed, I’m trying hard here to argue against the gravitational pull exerted by my own experience of doing a traditional degree. I guess the real test would be what any of us parents would say if our kids came to us with an intention to apply for one of these courses.In my own household, we’d have to go through a whole rigmarole in which I would definitely infuriate my children by suggesting their time might be better spent reading The Wife of Bath’s Tale or, like, the structure and function of proteins.
