I’d be forced to lecture them on the hollow interior life of anyone chasing fame and say the words, “Do we think the Kardashians are actually happy?” Then I’d look at the job market, at all the listings for social media managers, podcast producers and video editors and, if I could get over myself, might work my way to the conclusion that they could do a lot worse. (I’m kidding, I’d be devastated.)Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUniversitiesOpinionSocial mediaHigher educationYoung peoplecommentShareReuse this content

title: Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: Borrowing can be good, there is no such thing as the ‘nation’s credit card’, and, yes, you can buck the markets – as previous governments have shown, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: Borrowing can be good, there is no such thing as the ‘nation’s credit card’, and, yes, you can buck the markets – as previous governments have shown, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: Photograph: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sébastien Thibault/The GuardianOpinionEconomic policyRightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to KeynesLarry ElliottBorrowing can be good, there is no such thing as the ‘nation’s credit card’, and, yes, you can buck the markets – as previous governments have shownThu 1 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTShareAndy Burnham does a nice line in nostalgia. Hisfirst party conference speechas prime minister was full of fond memories for the Britain of the 1950s and 1960s, when working-class families could sense their lives steadily getting better. The underlying message of his address was that, given time, he could rekindle that optimism and return the country to how it was before Margaret Thatcher wrecked everything.Much of what Burnham says is true. The 1980s was a decade of deindustrialisation, asset-stripping and financial deregulation that has shaped modern Britain – and not in a good way.But listen a bit more closely to the speech and it becomes clear that Burnham is struggling to find a way to turn back the clock. For a start, he might not be given time. Energy bills are forecastto rise sharply this winter. John Healey’s first budget, in less than a month’s time, is expected to raise taxes or cut spending – taking money out of an economy that is already struggling.There’s no question that Burnham and Healey would prefer not to be taking these actions but feel they have no choice. Burnham may well rail against 40 years of neoliberalism. He may think neoliberalism was a dud. But his government is constrained by neoliberal ideas and the language used to express them. Burnham and Healey would never use this language themselves, but that’s irrelevant. To make a real difference, they need to tackle head-on the nostrums of the past four decades. Otherwise they will be for ever in thrall to them.Top of the list is the idea that the UK government is no different from a household. That means it should match its spending to its income as closely as possible, borrowing prudently and within tightly defined limits. Otherwise it will“max out the nation’s credit card”and risk spiralling into unsustainable debt.This analogy has the benefit of sounding like a statement of the obvious to many voters, but is actually entirely false. There is no such thing as the nation’s credit card, and a country that prints its own currency can never “max out” or face bankruptcy in the way an individual can.The notion that the government is living well beyond its means is convenient for those on the political right who have an aversion to public spending. The reality is that, as John Maynard Keynesonce said: “Anything we can actually do we can afford.” It was that mentality that allowed the Attlee government to create the welfare state when debt was running at more than250% of national income– more than double today’s level. I don’t know whether Burnham has seen thenew play about Keynesin London’s West End, but it seems as if he ought to.View image in fullscreenRory Kinnear (right) as John Maynard Keynes alongside Luke Cinque White in The Standard of Living.Photograph: Manuel HarlanBy the same token, it makes no sense to talk about “black holes” in the public finances every time the government looks on course to miss its targets for borrowing as set out in its fiscal rules. These rules are treated as totemic when in reality they can be changed at any time – and are ditched altogether when there is a crisis.Again, the idea of a black hole is a convenient fiction for those with an interest in shrinking the size of the state. As with “maxing out the credit card”, it forms part of the inquisition every time a minister goes on the TV or radio with a new spending measure: “That’s all very well but how are you going to pay for it?”Burnham is committed to re-industrialising Britain, but to do so he will have to break with the neoliberal convention that it is not the job of the government to pick winners. As the prime minister should point out, China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea have all built up their manufacturing strength by picking winners, and Britain could do the same. Indeed, the one sector that Thatcher picked out for special care and attention – financial services – has gone from strength to strength. Breaking the taboo on picking winners is central to a successful industrial strategy.Last but not least, Burnham has to address Thatcher’s famous dictum: you can’t buck the market. A cursory glance back at recent economic history shows that governments buck the market all the time. In 2009, the Bank of England responded to the risk of a second Great Depression posed by the global financial crisis by buying government bonds. This provided money to the banking system while cutting the interest rate – or yield – on bonds. This was bucking the market. In 2020, the then Conservative government spent hundreds of billions on a furlough scheme thatpaid up to 80% of the wagesof workers at risk of losing their jobs during the pandemic. This, too, was bucking the market.So when Burnham, in his conference speech, harked back to the Britain in the immediate decades after the second world war, he missed out a key part of the reason working people felt things were getting better. Rather than being constrained by fiscal rules, governments were committed to full employment. Capital controls meant that financial markets were tightly controlled.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBefore we get too nostalgic, it’s worth remembering that things were far from perfect in the so-called postwar golden age. By today’s standards, growth rates were spectacular, but they lagged well behind those of Germany and France. Even so, managed capitalism certainly delivered more for working people than has been the case in the unmanaged capitalism that has followed.The postwar status quo has been turned on its head. Then, financial markets were caged to ensure that governments could pursue domestic economic goals. Now, governments are caged and the markets are free. It is a classic case of the tail wagging the dog.Shifting back to a world where finance is fettered is not going to be easy – but until it happens, governments will remain boxed in. Burnham and Healey will be forced to do things they know will harm the economy because they know any deviation from what is acceptable to the received wisdom risks a backlash from the financial markets.Some new economic thinking is required, and if ever there were a time for an iconoclast like Keynes, it is surely now. He would certainly have no truck with the wrong-headed economic policies of the past half-century and the seemingly commonsense phrases – such as maxing out the credit card – that have been used to disguise just how nonsensical they are.All credit to Burnham. His analysis of what has gone wrong has clearly rattled his political enemies. Even so, he risks becoming the nearly man of British politics: the prime minister who asked the right questions but failed to come up with the right answers.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEconomic policyOpinionAndy BurnhamJohn Maynard KeynesEconomicsLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Jean-Luc Mélenchon will win young French voters – until they realise the size of his Russia blind spot | Alexander Hurst | The Guardian
description: La France Insoumise gives voice to the left-behind, and progressives approve. But many recoil from a leftwing leader whose foreign policy is stuck in 1985, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Author: Alexander Hurst
Headline: La France Insoumise gives voice to the left-behind, and progressives approve. But many recoil from a leftwing leader whose foreign policy is stuck in 1985, says Guardian Europe columnist Alexander Hurst
Content: Jean-Luc Melenchon at a demonstration in Paris, 29 September 2026Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJean-Luc Melenchon at a demonstration in Paris, 29 September 2026Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockOpinionJean-Luc MélenchonJean-Luc Mélenchon will win young French voters – until they realise the size of his Russia blind spotAlexander HurstLa France Insoumise gives voice to the left-behind, and progressives approve. But many recoil from a leftwing leader whose foreign policy is stuck in 1985Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 05.15 EDTShareThéodore Abitbol is a self-described “militant antifascist,” with degrees in political science and comparative literature, and a bookshelf that ranges from the gender and queer theory of bell hooks to the anti-capitalist social analysis of the Marxist theorist Mike Davis.The 34-year-old is a regular participant in pro-Palestine protests, and has a decade of full-time activism under his belt: unions, strikes, protests, civil disobedience and vast protest encampments used to block construction projects, known in France asZAD – for “zone à défendre”.Abitbol should be an in-the-bag vote for Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of La France Insoumise (LFI), a longtime fixture of hard-left French politics and a2027 presidential candidatewho is drawingsignificant supportamong voters under 35.After all, LFI is doing something necessary by focusing on some of France’s most left-behind urban areas and giving voters in them a voice: Bally Bagayoko faced downracist abuseto win the mayoral race in Paris’s inner banlieue of Saint-Dénis. David Guirauddefeated the rightfor the first time since 1983 in Roubaix, one ofFrance’s poorest large cities. The party’s success in these heavily working-class and minority areas is due its willingness to draw new lines around old identity debates, and an intransigent anti-capitalist attitude. LFI parliamentarians such as Clémence Guetté are actually making innovative and radical proposals,such as recognising close friendshipsand extendinglegal rightsto them.Yet Abitbol demonstrates the single biggest voter faultline between two incompatible French lefts: Mélenchon himself.I mainly remember Abitbol, an acquaintance from my immediate post-student days, as being staunchly opposed to Macron’s economic policies. That hasn’t changed. But he also can’t stomach voting for Mélenchon, he confided when I reached out to him recently, , because of the LFI leader’s stances on Russia,Ukraineand the EU. “A part of the [French] left retains a cold-war mentality where Russia is an ally against American imperialism, without seeing that Putin and Trump are in agreement about almost everything in their foreign and domestic policies,” he told me.I don’t believe Abitbol is alone. They might not admit it as openly, but I think there are millions of French voters who also crave the kind of rupture with capitalism and the status quo that Mélenchon is proposing, but have no desire to go where he would take France on foreign and European policy. French presidential elections rarely hinge on discussions of France’s place in the world. But the threat posed by Russia to Europe has already dominated the opening days of the 2027 campaign, including a special primetimeTV interview with Macron.Mélenchonconsistently pollsat around 17%, enough to qualify for round two of the presidential election. The combined non-Mélenchon left, split between the Ecologists, Socialist party and Communist party, just trails him, with Raphaël Glucksmann leading a split field with around 10% of a first-round vote. But polling also shows that Marine Le Penwould defeatMélenchon 69% to 31% in a second round run-off.If the divided and riven French left gets this wrong, it could leave millions of pro-European voters in an impossible position, and ultimately put Le Pen in power.The term “zombie lie” is a good way to describe much of Russia’s propaganda about Ukraine. That Nato provoked the 2022 invasion by “expanding”; that Ukraine was full of neo-Nazis; that Ukraine was developing chemical weapons in secret Nato labs; thatRussia– Ukraine’s former coloniser – has legitimate claims to parts of its territory anyway.Since the mid-2010s, Mélenchon has consistently advanced many of these claims. In 2014, Mélenchon denounced the Maidan Revolution – when young Ukrainians filled the streets of Kyiv to demand a European future – saying that Russia would have to defend itself against “anadventurous putschist regime in which neo-Naziswield a thoroughly reprehensible influence”. When Putin annexed Crimea shortly after Maidan, Mélenchon defended it byclaimingthat “Crimea has always been Russian”.He didn’t stop there. In 2015, in response to Putin’s aggression, Francecancelled the saleof two advanced “Mistral-class” helicopter carriers – both are now part of the French Mediterranean fleet based in Toulon. Mélenchon joined Marine Le Pen indecryingthe cancellation as the “vassalisation of France to Nato’s bellicose rhetoric”, and accused the then president, François Hollande, of “unbearable betrayal” for having “devalued the worth of France’s word” by refusing to deliver the warships.That is when Mélenchon lost Abitbol and others like him.“It’s easier [for Mélenchon] to grasp at phantoms than it is to face the reality that Russia is waging a hybrid war on us, and that tomorrow it will be a ‘classic’ war,” he says.Mélenchon filled the next seven years alternately invoking international law to condemn the US’s unilateral action in Syria, and dispensing with the same international law when it came todefendingorminimisingRussia’s unilateral action and war crimes in Syria – which killed, by moderately conservative estimates,20,000 civilians. All while denying Russia’s former Soviet colonies their right – under international law – tofreely chose their alliancesby joining Nato.Accepting Georgia’s request for membership would be,he said, an “offensive and stupid provocation”. As for Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia (EU and Nato members since 2004, and some of Ukraine’slargest donors by GDP), Mélenchon’s dismissalshave been scathing. “I feel nothing in common with them, it’s the end of the world, even the Romans never made it that far!” he said in 2017.Mélenchon seems uninterested in examining why there would have been such huge interest among Russia’s immediate neighbours in joining a defensive military alliance. Apparently, in Mélenchon’s mind, it couldn’t possibly be because they had just been occupied by an aggressive and territorially expansionist petro-oligarchy – it’s because the US, and to a lesser extent western Europe, are the only ones with agency.It’s little surprise, then, that Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine did nothing to rock Mélenchon’s fixed position. Ukraine was “without a doubt” the aggressor,he claimed, whereas Russia felt “humiliated, threatened, aggressed” by the US’s decision “to annex Ukraine into Nato”. (The invasion, of course, hastened Sweden and Finland’s sovereign decisions to join.) In the four years since Putin’s war, Mélenchon’s personal blog and media appearances have been a grab-bag of thesame type ofideas thatXenia Federova, former director of RT France, spewed on the rightwing news network CNews – until Franceissued an expulsion orderand froze her assets. These included bringing Russia “back into the fold”and re-openingthe Nord Stream gas pipelines; castigating Zelenskyy as “president of nothing”while promotingthe Kremlin’s narrative about his lack of political legitimacy; and haranguing other Europeans for having “demonised Putin”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaking common cause with “the enemy of my enemy” – whatever the consequences for the less powerful – as a shortsighted form of “realist” foreign policy is certainly nothing new. (Neither, in Mélénchon’s case, does it end at Europe’s borders: “Taiwan is China,” hetold French TVin May). But how is any of this principled, or leftist?After a summer when France burned and burned and burned, how is the frontrunner for the left a man who is calling for reopening the poison-drip ofnatural gasfrom a state that has been, for years, in an undeclared war hybrid war on France along with the rest of Europe? It seems Mélenchon, who has wanted to withdraw France from Nato for decades, has not updated his worldview since 1985 when he first held public office. But this is not the anti-American position it once was: it is simply to attack from the inside what Putin seeks to dismantle from the outside.Mélenchon is not trying to hide his Eurosceptic ideas any more than he has tried to hide his positions on Ukraine. What he loudly said during the first presidential debate, in late August, is alsoin his programme: he will “assume confrontation with European institutions” and “disobey” EU rules “whenever necessary”.This is not the way to lead and change an EU that, while imperfect, remains among France’s greatest foreign policy achievements. This is the way to destroy from within the best framework for tackling every modern challenge that transcends borders, from the climate crisis to inequality.If the new guiding philosophy is that France can decide to “désobéir” whenever it sees fit, so can everyone else. How do we imagine the EU maintaining its emissions trading scheme, and the carbon border tax meant to protect it? How will these – or any other European-level policies – survive if, as Mark Carney might say, a member state’s word becomes something“written in pencil”?The short answer is: they won’t. The EU will enter an institutional death cycle, of which a deteriorating US is only slowly becoming aware. This is what Europe’s far-right nationalists want. Is it what Mélenchon supporters want?Mélenchon makes no secret of his desire for France to lead some non-aligned coalition of states geographically more remote, with even less coherent common interests than the existing 27 EU countries. What would all these other potential partners conclude if France were to show that it were ready, in a very Trumpian way, to do the very thing Mélenchon accused Hollande of doing? To walk all over its word, ratified in treaty with its closest neighbours, with whom it has shared a political community that France itself built?When it comes to foreign and EU policy, Mélenchon is barely distinguishable from Le Pen: a nationalist who believes that France is too small to do anything but close in on itself – and look to Russia for guidance. If the presidential contest comes down to Mélenchon v Le Pen in the final roundthen Abitbol says he would vote Mélenchon, but “with vomit in my mouth”. Pity him and the others like him who might have to choose between two equally disastrous visions of France in Europe and the world.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoirGeneration Desperationis out nowDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsJean-Luc MélenchonOpinionFranceEuropeEmmanuel MacronMarine Le PenRussiaUkrainecommentShareReuse this content

title: The green light for the largest coalmine in NSW history is shocking proof that our governance systems are betraying Australians | Georgina Woods | The Guardian
description: There is no greater treachery than this failure to face up to the climate crisis. How can we now fend off despair?
Author: Georgina Woods
Headline: There is no greater treachery than this failure to face up to the climate crisis. How can we now fend off despair?
Content: The task of supporting the Hunter through coalmine closure ‘is nothing to the task of adapting to catastrophic global heating’, Georgina Woods writes.Photograph: Lock the GateView image in fullscreenThe task of supporting the Hunter through coalmine closure ‘is nothing to the task of adapting to catastrophic global heating’, Georgina Woods writes.Photograph: Lock the GateOpinionNew South WalesThe green light for the largest coalmine in NSW history is shocking proof that our governance systems are betraying AustraliansGeorgina WoodsThere is no greater treachery than this failure to face up to the climate crisis. How can we now fend off despair?Wed 30 Sep 2026 23.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.23 EDTShareThe Independent Planning Commission’s published reasons forapproving the largest coalmine in New South Wales historyin the context of mounting death, disaster and despair brought on by global heating reads like a hostage statement.In its decision, the commission accepts that the extension of the Hunter Valley Operations’ mine for a further 19 years – resulting 809m tonnes of greenhouse gas pollution – will materially worsen global warming. The panel members cite CSIRO’s finding that climate change is having a growing effect on the lives and livelihoods of all Australians and that the severity of that impact “will depend on the speed at which global greenhouse gas emissions can be reduced”. They reject the idea that keeping HVO’s coal in the ground would make no difference to global warming.Despite all of this, the commission has still found that all of this is “outweighed” by the revenues coalmining makes, its centrality to the Hunter’s regional economy and the livelihoods of 1,500 people.The commission’s jarring and contradictory statement must be read for what it is: an admission that Australia’s governance systems are failing to meet the crisis of climate change. It is a shocking and unsettling admission because our faith in these systems has been the foundation of advocacy for action on the climate emergency for decades.Approval of biggest coal project in NSW planning commission’s history described as ‘infamous betrayal’Read moreWe vote, we make submissions, we go to court, we meet our MPs, we compile and present evidence. All of this activity rests on a belief in the systems of government that have now clearly failed to meet their solemn public duty. We must seriously consider what avenue remains available to us to fend off despair.The commission heard direct,heart-rending testimonyfrom people who are already grappling with the damage and loss brought by the climate crisis, from grandparents in anguish about the lives awaiting the little children they love, from scientists patiently outlining devastating evidence about the mine’s climate change impacts. All of this, they have decided, is less weighty than the economic contribution a rich mining company claims it will make.The argument presented in favour of approval was economic and short-term.There is no doubt that refusing the project would have caused immediate hardship for families, businesses and the wider community in Singleton and Muswellbrook. Had the extension been refused, the mine would have closed at the end of this year. More than 1,000 people would have been stood down from their work and local suppliers would have lost business.The impact of this would be locally severe but it could have been managed. The workforce could have been supported. The region could have been given money and backing to weather that storm. The Hunter has been through such disruption before and come through. The difficult task of supporting it through mine closure is nothing to the task of adapting to catastrophic global heating.Australia is facing a crisis of confidence in its democratic institutions. It is a crisis brought on by the betrayal of the people by those institutions – and there is no greater betrayal than this failure to face up to the climate emergency and protect the community from its worst consequences.The crisis will deepen as the effects of global heating assault communities, infrastructure and the natural and economic systems that underpin our society. In the Hunter region,polling commissioned by Lock the Gatehas shown that 85% of people have experienced extreme weather in the last five years and 80% of them say they believe climate change is influencing it.Young people overwhelmingly understand that their governments are failing to stop pollution from coalmining and coal-burning from fuelling the rising heat, the rising prices, the collapsing ecosystems. My conscience is troubled by having encouraged them to engage politely in the public processes that keep failing them.The approval of the HVO mine continuing is not just another climate failure among many. It is the failure that finally broke my faith in the capacity of public institutions to serve the public interest.Georgina Woods is a joint national coordinator of Lock the Gate AllianceExplore more on these topicsNew South WalesOpinionCoalFossil fuelsClimate crisisEnergy (Environment)Energy (Australia news)New South Wales politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Sex, drugs and amoebic dysentery: the 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, we rate cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenes
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, we rate cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenes
Content: Impossibly ambitious … Romy Schneider in Henri-Georges Clouzot's Inferno.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenImpossibly ambitious … Romy Schneider in Henri-Georges Clouzot's Inferno.Photograph: Publicity imageRankedMoviesSex, drugs and amoebic dysentery: the 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked!From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, we rate cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenesRyan GilbeyThu 1 Oct 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. Document of the Dead (1985)Behind-the-scenes footage from Dawn of the Dead is the highlight of this aficionados-only affair, which follows the 1979 satirical zombie horror all the way through to distribution. Director George A Romero, makeup maestro Tom Savini and the occasional zombie actor shoot the breeze in the deserted shopping mall that provides the movie with its incongruous central location.19. The Death of “Superman Lives”: What Happened? (2015)Imagining what might have been if Tim Burton’s Superman Lives had got off the ground, documentary maker Jon Schnepp cosies up on screen with his interviewees and insinuates himself unforgivably into the story. The material is almost good enough to transcend his vanity: there is test footage of lead actor Nicolas Cage in his Man of Steel duds, plus interviews with Burton, original screenwriter Kevin Smith and producer Jon Peters, who was adamant that Superman should fight polar bears and a giant spider.18. Becoming Bulletproof (2014)A group of actors with disabilities form the bulk of the cast of the short western Bulletproof, shot in the California desert courtesy of the inclusive arts project Zeno Mountain Farm. Crucially, Bulletproof itself isn’t about disability, but rather an attempt to highlight the lack of on-screen representation – and plug the gap. This affectionate documentary tracks the film from preproduction to premiere.17. They’ll Love Me When I’m Dead (2018)Orson Welles spent five years shooting what became his final film, The Other Side of the Wind, with three years elapsing before its star – director and sometime actor John Huston – even stepped in front of the camera. After all that, the footage ended up impounded by the Iranian revolutionary government. A version eventually premiered in 2018 and is now on Netflix, along with this scattershot documentary, presented by Alan Cumming, which strings together archive footage, new interviews and typically Wellesian stories of on-set bluffs, tomfoolery and procrastination.16. Filmmaker: A Diary by George Lucas (1968)A half-hour snapshot by Lucas of his new buddy Francis Ford Coppola, who is hard at work on his fourth film, The Rain People, and not too shy to argue with his lead actor, Shirley Knight. Contains one choice detail: in preparation for driving across the country shooting this road movie, all the men on the crew, Coppola included, shave off their beards to look more presentable for any hippy-hating officials they might encounter along the way.15.Boorman and the Devil(2025)In declining The Exorcist but taking on Exorcist II: The Heretic, John Boorman perhaps displayed a preference for poisoned chalices over champagne flutes. He is candid and good-humoured, if still a little shell-shocked, as he recounts the experience of filming the sequel once derided as “the stupidest major movie ever made”, and the despair that led him to contemplate self-immolation on Hollywood Boulevard. Sand-related illness, a sozzled Richard Burton, locusts and tap-dancing: this has it all.14. Doomed! The Untold Story of Roger Corman’s The Fantastic Four (2015)Filmed in a rat-infested studio on sets recycled from the Jurassic Park rip-off Carnosaur, with special effects entrusted to a local outfit called Mr Film, this cheapo superhero adventure was made in a rush to prevent the rights to The Fantastic Four reverting from producer Bernd Eichinger to Marvel. (“That movie was never supposed to be shown to anybody,” said Stan Lee.) This heartening documentary, which shows the crestfallen cast refusing to let their film die, feels even more pertinent after Warner Bros recently shelved some movies as tax write-offs, including Batgirl and Coyote Vs Acme, the latter rescued only by the skin of its teeth.13. Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013)In trying to adapt Frank Herbert’s Dune in the mid-1970s, cinematic shaman Alejandro Jodorowsky (Santa Sangre, El Topo) bit off more than he could chew, just as David Lynch would when his version came to painful fruition in 1984. But Frank Pavich’s documentary proves that Jodorowsky’s intention to make “a film that gives LSD hallucinations without taking LSD” was not too fanciful. Among those in his corner were the artist HR Giger, who went on to design the monsters in Alien, and a cast including Salvador Dalí, Mick Jagger and Orson Welles, with the latter being bribed to take part with the promise of having his favourite chef on set.View image in fullscreenHallucinatory … concept artwork from Jodorowsky’s Dune.Photograph: Sony classics/Sony Classics12. Lost Soul: The Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley’s Island of Dr Moreau (2014)When the studio New Line tried to ditch South African director Richard Stanley from his own HG Wells adaptation, he asked a warlock called Skip to pull some cosmic strings. That did the trick for a while, helping Stanley to charm the film’s star, Marlon Brando. But black magic was no match for cast member Val Kilmer, who demanded a 40% reduction in his own shooting days, then spent his time on set playing power games. There was nature to contend with, too, in the form of wild animals (a puma pisses on Stanley’s tailored suit) and a hurricane that ravages the location in Cairns, Queensland. Finally replaced by curmudgeonly veteran John Frankenheimer, Stanley refuses to leave Australia, which is when things go from mad to worse.11. No Frank in Lumberton (1988) / Blue Velvet Revisited (2016)Two behind-the-scenes Blue Velvet documentaries from one director. Peter Braatz was still a film student when David Lynch, with whom he had been corresponding for several years, invited him to Wilmington, North Carolina in 1985 to chart the making of what would become his twisted masterpiece. Braatz marshalled just under an hour of the resulting Super-8 material into his 1988 documentary, which straddled the line between orthodox and experimental. He then reshaped it into a full-on ambient head-trip for the 86-minute 2016 version, which mixes flickering footage and crisp black-and-white photographs with a woozy score and the voices of Lynch, Dennis Hopper and others to form an ethereal audiovisual collage.10. The Sweatbox (2002)Disney had high hopes for Kingdom of the Sun, a Prince and the Pauper-style animated musical drama set in the Inca empire. The studio sent Lion King co-director Roger Allers on a research trip to Peru and commissioned a suite of new songs by Sting. But it was back to the drawing board after a calamitous screening of an early rough cut; Allers and Sting were given the heave-ho, and the movie was retooled as the larky comedy The Emperor’s New Groove. Sting’s wife, Trudie Styler, charts every disastrous step in a documentary that Disney hasdone its darnedest to suppress.9. From Darkness to Light (2024)A 10-a-penny title for an account of a once-in-a-lifetime film-making folly: Jerry Lewis’s abandoned, incomplete 1972 Holocaust dramaThe Day The Clown Cried. Directing himself as a former clown who entertains children in a concentration camp, Lewis made a misguided bid to be taken seriously. “It was bad work,” he admits here. It wasn’t only the dubious material that defeated the former Nutty Professor: unbeknown to him, the option on the script had expired, rendering the entire project illegal. It was his decision, though, to hire a repentant former concentration camp guard as part of the crew. “He was a human being!” Lewis protests.View image in fullscreen‘Bad work’ … Jerry Lewis on the set of The Day the Clown Cried.Photograph: Venice Film Festival8. Poultry in Motion: Truth Is Stranger Than Chicken (2008)Seventy-odd fans of horror exploitation studio Troma worked unpaid on Poultrygeist: Night of the Chicken Dead while living in a deserted church in a rundown corner of Buffalo, New York, with one cold shower between them. Meanwhile, the chicken-themed zombie flick was shot at a nearby abandoned McDonald’s. This documentary captures all the on-set horror, from the sexually disinhibited auditions to the hourly cast-and-crew bust-ups. Actors walk off, burst into tears and throw punches; a zombie extra accidentally sets himself on fire; and bilious co-director and Troma boss Lloyd Kaufman proves both lackadaisical and tyrannical.7. Shirkers (2018)When budding film-maker Sandi Tan met the enigmatic Georges Cardona, he cited Fitzcarraldo as his inspiration and claimed to know crew members from Apocalypse Now. Those pictures – famously troubled productions that spawned their own jaw-dropping documentaries – look like red flags considering what came next: Cardona directed Tan’s indie road movie Shirkers, swallowing up $10,000 of her savings when he ran out of money, then vanished with the resulting 70 reels of unprocessed film. She didn’t see the footage until decades later, when those reels were returned to her by Cardona’s widow. Tan’s sobering 2018 documentary attempts to make sense of the betrayal.6. The Peddler (2010)“Good film directors will notice many mistakes,” says prolific camcorder auteur and 67-year-old Santa Claus lookalike Daniel Burmeister. “But I like what I do: making hand-crafted films.” In exchange for a month’s food and accommodation, Burmeister sets up shop in a remote Argentinian village to bring the community together by shooting a movie from one of his own scripts. His budget may be nonexistent but his resourcefulness is boundless: in place of a dolly shot, for instance, he sits on a blanket, camera on his shoulder, while being dragged across the floor. This delightful, deeply humanistic portrait of grassroots DIY cinema has all the charm and idiosyncrasies of a Jared Hess comedy.5.Lost in La Mancha(2002)View image in fullscreen‘We’re fucked!’ … Jean Rochefort and Terry Gilliam in Lost in La Mancha.Photograph: Blue Finch Film ReleasingTerry Gilliam was happy to have documentary makers Keith Fulton and Louis Pepe on set for The Man Who Killed Don Quixote after being impressed by The Hamster Factor, their behind-the-scenes film on the making of his earlier 12 Monkeys. The anguished result shows exactlywhy Quixote was abandonedafter six days’ shooting in Spain in September 2000. Takes were rendered unusable by the roar of F16s from a nearby Nato base; Jean Rochefort, co-lead opposite Johnny Depp, fell seriously ill; and the equipment was destroyed by a merciless storm. Gilliam’s on-set catchphrase sums it up: “We’re fucked!” (When Quixote was eventually made in 2018, Fulton and Pepe documented that shoot, too, inHe Dreams of Giants.)4. Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno (2009)The subgenre of documentaries about unfinished films stretches back to the BBC’s 1965 The Epic That Never Was, which investigated Josef von Sternberg’s planned version of I, Claudius starring Charles Laughton and Merle Oberon. But it reached its apotheosis with Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno, Ruxandra Medrea and Serge Bromberg’s ravishing reflection on an early-1960s Proustian psychological drama from the director of Les Diaboliques. Lavishly funded by Columbia, Clouzot’s vision was impossibly ambitious, with three crews and a trippy array of complicated in-camera special effects. The director, who could not be dissuaded from shooting time-consuming test footage, suffered a heart attack three weeks into the 18-week shoot. The fragments of his vision, cherrypicked here from 15 hours of unseen footage, are intoxicating: where else can you see Romy Schneider covered in glitter, cellophane and olive oil?3.Burden of Dreams (1982)Deep in the rainforests of South America, Werner Herzog battles mud and misery, along with his leading man Klaus Kinski, to make Fitzcarraldo, about one man’s dream of building an opera house in the Amazon. Les Blank’s documentary, which is arguably more compelling than the movie it’s about, enables us to watch in disbelief as a film about a lunatic mission turns into one itself. Herzog’s initial footage has to be abandoned when the lead actor, Jason Robards, falls ill with amoebic dysentery and co-star Mick Jagger is needed on a world tour. Up and running again, the production is forced to relocate more than 1,000 miles away due to a border war, while Herzog’s plans to move a steamship up a hillside provide a textbook example of madness eclipsing method.2.American Movie(1999)Mark Borchardt, a Milwaukee junkyard poet with a mullet and plateglass specs, may be best suited to factory work or serial killing, according to his brother, but he positively glows with a passion for cinema. Lacking the funds to finish his feature debut, he instead tries to complete a short horror film, Coven, undaunted by his inability to pronounce the title. MoreWiseauthan Welles, he has optimism and indefatigability to burn. Not to mention a crew of colourful collaborators, including his mother, whom he enlists as an extra despite her protestations that she needs to go shopping; his bleary, poodle-haired pal and former acid-head Mike; and the gnarled, trailer-dwelling Uncle Bill, who needs 30 takes to deliver four lines. Director Chris Smith (who later made the pricelessFyre festival documentary) rightly portrays Mark as one of cinema’s most inspiring heroes – even if he still hasn’t finished his first feature.1.Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse(1991)View image in fullscreen‘I’m thinking of shooting myself’ … Francis Ford Coppola directing Apocalypse Now, from Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMegadoc, the forthcoming behind-the-scenes film about Francis Ford Coppola’s $120mpassion project Megalopolis, is directed by Mike Figgis, though earlier Coppola-related documentaries tended to be family affairs. The director’s late wife, Eleanor, was responsible for Making Marie Antoinette, released later this month, about their daughter Sofia’s 2006 historical fantasia. And it was Eleanor, too, who co-directed the extraordinary Hearts of Darkness, which draws on her 60 hours of footage and 40 hours of audio recordings, as well as her own diaries, all from the turbulent 238-day shooting of Apocalypse Now. The film reveals her husband arguing on set with Dennis Hopper, frantically typing new scenes just moments before the cameras roll, and negotiating with Marlon Brando, who has piled on the pounds but neglected to learn his lines. “I’m thinking of shooting myself,” the director confides. “This is one crisis I can’t pull myself out of.”Boorman and the Devil is in cinemas in the UK and Ireland now. Making Marie Antoinette is in cinemas in the UK, Ireland and US from 23 October and streaming on Mubi from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmRankedDocumentary filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Shane was rascality personified’: the Pogues on their late frontman, anti-Irish prejudice and the feud over Fairytale of New York | The Pogues | The Guardian
description: The Celtic punk band’s co-founders Spider Stacy and James Fearnley take your questions about Shane MacGowan, ruffling the feathers of trad musicians and putting Laurence Fox in his place
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: The Celtic punk band’s co-founders Spider Stacy and James Fearnley take your questions about Shane MacGowan, ruffling the feathers of trad musicians and putting Laurence Fox in his place
Content: Put on the ritz …(clockwise from bottom left)the Pogues’ Shane MacGowan, James Fearnley, Spider Stacy, Philip Chevron, Terry Woods, Cait O’Riordan, Andrew Ranken and Jem Finer at the Ritz in New York, June 1986.Photograph: Gary Gershoff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPut on the ritz …(clockwise from bottom left)the Pogues’ Shane MacGowan, James Fearnley, Spider Stacy, Philip Chevron, Terry Woods, Cait O’Riordan, Andrew Ranken and Jem Finer at the Ritz in New York, June 1986.Photograph: Gary Gershoff/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewThe PoguesInterview‘Shane was rascality personified’: the Pogues on their late frontman, anti-Irish prejudice and the feud over Fairytale of New YorkAs told toDave SimpsonThe Celtic punk band’s co-founders Spider Stacy and James Fearnley take your questions about Shane MacGowan, ruffling the feathers of trad musicians and putting Laurence Fox in his placeThu 1 Oct 2026 08.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Pogues earned a reputation early on as a ferocious live band. What does it feel like to be in the middle of that whirlwind?VerulamiumParkRangerSpider Stacy [co-founder, tin whistle, vocals]:Last Christmas, we did a secret gig in a pub in Nunhead [in London] and it reminded me of those early days when we were so close to the audience, who were practically on top of each other. The venue that most sticks in my mind is the Hope & Anchor [in Islington, London]. We played there to about 35 people [in 1983], but when we went back a month later the match had been struck and it was absolutely roaring. After that, at gigs, there were clothes landing on stage …James Fearnley [co-founder, accordion]:Medical equipment, crutches …Stacy:On the reunion tour, someone in Sydney threw a prosthetic leg. It still had a boot on.On the first single [1984’s Dark Streets of London],Shane MacGowantalks about hisexperience of electroconvulsive therapy. Did he ever talk about what effect it had on him?BenkoView image in fullscreenFearnley, Stacy and Finer in Sydney in April.Photograph: Ian LaidlawStacy:He didn’t go into detail. As a teenager, it was probably enormously distressing, but Shane had a mordant humour about it. That single drew on personal experience, but an aspect of his genius was to see the unseen and what goes on in people’s hearts. Walking down the street with Shane, he’d be dishing out pocketfuls of change – banknotes if he had them – to homeless people. He was always aware that “there but for the grace of God go I”. A lot of Irish people had come over to London as builders, or whatever, and fallen into the abyss of drink and chronic unemployment, and there was a lot of anti-Irish prejudice. It could get nasty. Then attitudes became less hostile. I don’t know how much that had to do with us, but I’ve a feeling that we played a part.My favourite Pogues’ song isSummer in Siam. Do you each have your own?Philip_Larkin_FanFearnley:Lorca’s Novena, aboutFederico García Lorca[the 20th-century Spanish poet and playwright]. It’s all about freedom of speech and expression.Stacy:The Broad Majestic Shannon. Such a beautiful song about people leaving Ireland and looking back, but it’s so evocative about love and loss. As with so many of Shane’s songs, it speaks to everyone.Listen to The Broad Majestic Shannon.What was the process when Shane brought a new song to the band?MissIdahoPotatoFearnley:It depended on the song. When he came in withA Rainy Night in Soho, we knew it was complete because he’d dressed for the occasion. He had his nice suit on and these latticed sandals and had the whole thing in his head: “You play this; this little hook goes there.” It was an amazing experience. Other times, he’d have the tune and lyrics, but it could be infuriating having to wring the harmonic structure out of him. Then he’d suddenly say: “That’s how it’s supposed to go.”Were you part of the panel discussion with Noel Hill [in which the Irish musician describedthe Pogues’ music as a “terrible abortion of words”] and what was the reaction?RiverboatCaptainStacy:When we went to Ireland for the first time [the band formed in London], we were invited on to RTÉ radio for an audience Q&A with people like Noel Hill, an extremely accomplished concertina player who had very strong opinions about how Irish music should and shouldn’t be played. The traditional Irish music establishment basically thought we were a bunch of chancers who didn’t know what we were doing. It backfired because people like Christy Moore and Paddy Moloney from the Chieftains understood what we were trying to do and felt we’d been shabbily treated. The Dubliners took to us like dogs to a bone, because they’d had similar stick when they started. In the studio, we returned fire with fire. Then we titled an instrumental Planxty Noel Hill, which in that particular context means “fuck off, Noel Hill”.Fearnley:But a gorgeous, fantastic concertina player. He’d be most welcome at our shows.The Pogues have been through so many changes and challenges. Is there a particular period that you think of as the peak, when the songwriting was soaring and the behaviouraland substance issues were under control?RadioFreeNewportView image in fullscreenMacGowan(left)and Fearnley at the Vic theatre, Chicago, in July 1986.Photograph: Paul Natkin/Getty ImagesStacy:Probably ’86 to ’88, until after If I Should Fall from Grace With God. It’s pretty peak now – we’ve no Shane, but we have the songs! – but the wheels always had an amount of wobble. Even at the peaks, you can run out of oxygen or a rope can get frayed.Fearnley:Or like Jon Krakauer says in Into Thin Air, his book about Everest: you go into the death zone, where everything conspires to your demise.How was your relationship with Shane after heleft the Pogues in 1991and how did the reunion come about?PalaceCelticStacy:Shane plainly didn’t want to do it any more and his way of letting us know – which I think reflects really well on Shane – was to get drunk or fucked up. With hindsight, we should have suggested he take a year off, but we gallantly got Darryl [Hunt, bass] to tell him he was sacked. Shane’s relieved response was: “What took you so long?” Then we all went out to dinner.Shane MacGowan’s 10 greatest recordingsRead moreBut both Jem [Finer, co-founder, banjo] and I played on the Shane MacGowan and the Popes album [1994’s The Snake] and I saw Shane quite a lot over those years. In 2000, the band’s accountant asked the promoter Simon Moran about a Pogues reunion. My understanding is that other promoters told him: “God no, don’t go near.” So Simon’s very Mancunian response was to think: let’s do it. It was fucking great. Then Shane went: “I don’t wanna do this any more. It was only meant to be one Christmas. It’s been 14 years.”I saw a fabulous show in Osaka in the early 90s withJoe Strummersinging. Did that experience help to convince you that it was possible to carry on without Shane?NamelessreaderView image in fullscreenThe Pogues with Joe Strummer(back row, second left)at the Ritz in New York City in November 1987.Photograph: Ebet Roberts/RedfernsStacy:Yes. Joe was a real shot in the arm because of his enthusiasm. When he’d previously stood in forPhil Chevron[guitarist and songwriter] on tours in the late 80s, Joe Sellotaped the chord sheets around the body of his guitar, then his eagle eyes would glance down and he’d absorb a lot of information very swiftly. We didn’t announce him. Joe just walked on stage and people thought: “Who’s that? Oh fuck …!”Your band fell off my radar when Shane wasn’t involved until I woke up hungover one morning in the early 90s and heardTuesday Morningon the radio. What a great song. Do you regret not pushing on more without MacGowan?shedexileStacy:By the time we got to Pogue Mahone [1996], we’d driven ourselves into the ground creatively and it increasingly wasn’t the Pogues. We got dropped [by their record company]. I think there was just Jem, Andrew [Ranken, drums] and myself left, so we thought: “Nah.” We’d had our time.How close did you get to writing or recording any new material with Shane in the 2001-14 era and do you have any plans for new releases?TheSeamenBandStacy:Shane came round to Jem’s house, then Jem and Shane came to mine with the idea of writing new songs, but nothing came of it. We’ve just done Gabrielle for Shane’s tribute album [20th Century Paddy, released in November], but I don’t think it would be right to do new original music. Possibly some Irish stuff. I haven’t given any thought to it.Was there ever a lyric where you told Shane he should probably change it?AngryTomatoView image in fullscreenPlaying Sydney in April.Photograph: Ian LaidlawStacy:No, and we never would have. The BBC asked Shane to change a line in the rereleased Fairytale of New York for Top of the Pops [in 1992] and he did. [Later,in 2020, the BBC censored the song on Radio 1.] One thing that caught my eye was a guy saying that he loved the song, but hearing drunk guys bellowing: “You cheap, lousy faggot,” every Christmas reminded him of being persecuted or beaten up for being gay. So I wasn’t going to complain to the BBC. Then Laurence Fox chimed in on Twitter, saying: “Wouldn’t it be nice if we sent the (proper) version to the top of the charts?” and I replied: “Fuck off you little herrenvolk shite” – a line from Brendan Behan’s Borstal Boy – which went viral.But we perform the original, bearing in mind that Phil Chevron was proudly gay in Ireland since 1977 and we had loads of gay friends and gay fans who had no problem with the lyric, because they understood the context. It’s two people having a vile argument, flinging whatever abuse they can at each other. It’s interesting that all the focus was on “faggot”, but “old slut on junk” gets a complete pass.In a TV special about the late Gerry Rafferty, one of his brothers remarked: “Aye, he was a rascal, but he was our rascal.” Would you say Shane was your rascal?ShaunfromWiganView image in fullscreenMacGowan in the 80s.Photograph: Brian Rasic/Getty ImagesFearnley:Shane was rascality personified, but one of the most inspiring people I ever came across. The life I have lived because of him … jeez.Stacy:There was so much going on in his head that he could get cantankerous, but I’m sitting here in New Orleans because of Shane.Fearnley:And I’m in Los Angeles. In a way, I couldn’t get further away from him, but in a weird way we’re all manacled to Shane.It’s great to see a new generation of Irish bands like the Mary Wallopers and Lankumcoming through. How much of an influence do you feel you have had?RaithRaverFearnley:What took them so long?!Stacy:There’s so much great music coming out of Ireland. The first time I sawLankumwas at Shane’s 60th in Dublin. They did The Old Main Drag and I was mesmerised.Lisa O’Neillis a generational talent.One Leg One EyeandØXNare dragging some HP Lovecraftian God up from the nether depths.John Francis Flynnis utterly fantastic.Mary Wallopers.Junior Brother. We’ve been having a blast playing with some of these people and we’ve got some huge talents performing with us now.Fearnley:On stage, they’ll tolerate this trio of 70-year-olds blithely fumbling around in the middle of people half our age. It’s like taking uncle to the playground, but wonderful.The Pogues’ European tourstarts on 19 November at Tempodrom Berlin. Their UK and Ireland tour starts on 28 November at Portsmouth GuildhallExplore more on these topicsThe PoguesFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockFolk musicShane MacGowanPunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hay Fever review – Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski host Coward’s country house shenanigans | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Grant brings shock-haired vigour as a vain novelist forced to welcome his boho children’s surprise guests in comedy of clipped social embarrassment
Author: Emma John
Headline: Grant brings shock-haired vigour as a vain novelist forced to welcome his boho children’s surprise guests in comedy of clipped social embarrassment
Content: Brew haha … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski in Hay Fever at Wyndham’s theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenBrew haha … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski in Hay Fever at Wyndham’s theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewHay Fever review – Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski host Coward’s country house shenanigansWyndham’s theatre, LondonGrant brings shock-haired vigour as a vain novelist forced to welcome his boho children’s surprise guests in comedy of clipped social embarrassmentEmma JohnThu 1 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHay Fever, now one of Noël Coward’s best-known and most-performed works, hasn’t always been a smash hit. British critics who found itsWest Enddebut in 1925 amusing enough nevertheless noted its lack of plot, and the first Broadway production was a flop. A critic for Vogue called it “funny in places”, which sounds like the kind of stinging putdown you’d expect from the playwright’s own hand.A century of performances have proved the play’s lasting power, but its comic effect has always lain less in the words as written than their delivery – it is, after all, about a family that is “artificial to the point of lunacy”. At their centre is diva Judith Bliss, who has retired from the stage to take up the role of country hostess. When she, her husband and their self-consciously bohemian children Sorel and Simon all invite surprise guests for the weekend, the unfortunate attendees find themselves embroiled in a self-serving drama of exquisite embarrassment.View image in fullscreenRadiating charm … Ophelia Lovibond in Hay Fever.Photograph: Marc BrennerThe action takes place on Frankie Bradshaw’s sumptuous set, with corniced ceilings and French windows at the Blisses’ Berkshire pile that are almost an extension of the Wyndham’s ornate interior. The stage is populated with effusions of flowers and a fine cast, not leastRichard E Grantwho seems to be having a heyday of robe-and-slipper roles. He brings his trademark shock-haired vigour to the narcissist-novelist David, bounding down a grand staircase to read his latest work to his family.Will Close’s Simon swings from pretentious artiste – in paint-stained plus-fours and buttoned boots – to Tiggerish lover at the arrival of the experienced Myra (a statuesque Nancy Carroll). And even the seen-it-all-seductress is less in command than she thought as the games progress from after-dinner entertainments to more overtly saucy ones. Charles Edwards, meanwhile, maintains an endless gallantry as the visiting diplomat whose social skills are strained to the limit as he falls beneath Judith’s spell.Judith was inspired by real-life American actor Laurette Taylor – excuse enough, should Christine Baranski have chosen, to play the part in her own accent. Instead, a technically sound RP oddly constrains her. Judith’s combination of pretend languor and genuine vagueness mean that jokes go begging and some lines land too earnestly, as when she tells her daughter: “I’m very glad you’re pretty.” The squabbles and blow-ups are comically theatrical enough, but there’s not enough of Judith’s much-vaunted “vitality” to entirely make sense of them when they come.‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatreRead moreInstead it’s Ophelia Lovibond’s Sorel who emerges as the most vital character. She’s the only one of the bunch with any self-awareness, a smile half-playing on her lips, radiating charm that makes even her own selfishness seem forgivable. Director Emily Burns’s CV majors in farce and she stages some lovely bits of business, including a scene when a servant silently lays a breakfast table to a swellingly romantic soundtrack and a Gone With the Wind-crimson backdrop. On the first of multiple press nights, some of the comic timing isn’t quite up and running – but a stronger second half suggests that when the production beds in, there will be plenty of classic Coward to enjoy.AtWyndham’s theatre, London, until 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreNoel CowardWest EndRichard E GrantComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Celebrity Traitors review – Ross Kemp really needs to get a grip | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: The most hotly anticipated TV show of the year is here! And a number of the stars – ahem Grant Mitchell – are struggling already …
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The most hotly anticipated TV show of the year is here! And a number of the stars – ahem Grant Mitchell – are struggling already …
Content: Clothes and attitude … Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAView image in fullscreenClothes and attitude … Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PATV reviewThe TraitorsReviewThe Celebrity Traitors review – Ross Kemp really needs to get a gripThe most hotly anticipated TV show of the year is here! And a number of the stars – ahem Grant Mitchell – are struggling already …Lucy ManganThu 1 Oct 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWarning: this article contains spoilers for episode one of The Celebrity Traitors.So – have they managed to capture lightning in a franchised bottle again? The new series of The Celebrity Traitors, more hotly anticipated than Nigella entering the Bake Off tent, is here. Twenty-one contestants of varying levels of fame, but never dipping below C-list, have signed up to endure Claudia Winkleman’s tyranny in Ardross Castle, in the hope of winning up to £100,000 for their chosen charity and a place in the nation’s consciousness and possible heart for between one week and a lifetime, depending how things work out.We get our first glimpse of the gang as they file into a church replete with masked guards and floral tributes spelling out RIP and VIP at the altar. Actors, broadcasters, comedians, musicians and some miscellanea start to fill up the pews. Young Sebastian Croft pauses to genuflect before continuing down the aisle, and such is the power of the format that you immediately wonder if this is a tactic to make himself seem trustworthy. Will it work? Or is anyone with a religious belief marked as a weirdo for whom anything is possible these days?If you think that’s sensitivity gone mad, may I introduce you to Ross Kemp? Before the episode is out, he is turning bewildered circles in the castle, convinced that anyone who touches him is trying to murder him in plain sight. Get it together, Kemp. We’ve a long way to go yet.View image in fullscreen‘Already iconic’ … Richard E Grant.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/BBC Creative/PABut this is what we came for, of course. To see behind famous faces to the reality beneath. The hard man who is actually a soft target will do nicely. If mathematician Hannah Fry proves incapable of putting stats to work in her service, it will be noted. If Julie Hesmondhalgh (“I get hungry for friendship with people I see on the telly!”) turns out to be a Machiavellian genius, we will be over the moon. How long can they last in a game that is all about personalities before they have to reveal the true nature of theirs?It’s about 30 seconds for Richard E Grant. Most people – apart from Hannah Fry (“I am dripping with prefect energy”) – want to be chosen as traitors. But Reg publicly longs to be chosen as a traitor (“It would be the jackpot!”). He is chosen as a traitor. He is asked by Joe Lycett whether he is a traitor. “I am a traitor!” he gleefully replies. A drama queen without guile. An actor’s actor. “Already iconic,” says Claudia.View image in fullscreenRed alert … Jerry Hall.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/BBC Creative/PASome choose to ignore this revelation – unprecedented in the history of either Celebrity or peon Traitors. “He’s just acting out because he hasn’t been chosen,” says Jerry Hall, who has known him for 30 years – and you can well imagine him doing so. But in this case, he has just exuberantly shared the truth. Much of his time in the extended opening episode is spent trying to walk it back.From shocking cruelty to the reason Claudia hid in a bush: 10 things you need to know about The Celebrity TraitorsRead moreHis partner in treacherous crime is Love Island presenter Maya Jama (“My villain era has begun!”). Together, in one of the twists that any iteration of the series must serve up to keep participants and audience engaged, they must choose the third traitor from two people they haul in to plead their cases. The loser will be murdered (or, if you are one of the three people who do not know how the game works yet, “murdered”). They agree that they must choose two contestants who have taken Reg at his word and believe him (“I’m a traitor!”) to be a traitor. It’s between journalist Amol Rajan and comedian James Acaster. They wait in coffins – I am not a huge fan of this recurring motif, to be honest – to hear their fates, and we hear one of the lids bang shut as the credits roll.So, the lightning – is it bottled? Not quite as successfully as last time. The law of diminishing returns is brutal in television. The cast feels slightly more muted – the energy is not quite there yet. But Claudia and her clothes and attitude are, and the opening episode of any Traitors outing is always the weakest. It is relationships and alliances that make the show, and they of course take time to build. Seeds have been sown (is Jerry Hall bossy? Is former army captain James Blunt about to reinvent himself as a national hero? Will Romesh Ranganathan and Rob Beckett’s real-life friendship be an asset or a liability?) and will flourish in due course. But it feels as if they are at work in ever so slightly less fertile soil this time round.The Celebrity Traitors aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now. title: Esther Rantzen: one of the UK’s boldest, bravest ever campaigners – right to the very end | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: The TV host, who died this week aged 86, was in recent years one of the most vociferous proponents of assisted dying, but her activism dates back decades to her time on That’s Life!
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The TV host, who died this week aged 86, was in recent years one of the most vociferous proponents of assisted dying, but her activism dates back decades to her time on That’s Life!
Content: Esther Rantzen, after revealing her lung cancer diagnosis in January 2023.Photograph: Esther Rantzen/PAView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen, after revealing her lung cancer diagnosis in January 2023.Photograph: Esther Rantzen/PAEsther RantzenEsther Rantzen: one of the UK’s boldest, bravest ever campaigners – right to the very endWhen she got serious, she got very serious. The TV host boosted organ donations, closed down a school for abuse, founded two revolutionary helplines – and put assisted dying on the agenda for years to comeFrom Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeEsther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in picturesStuart HeritageThu 1 Oct 2026 07.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy no means should That’s Life! have ever worked as a television programme. For more than 20 years it functioned as an absurd grab bag of features that at times seemed specifically designed to induce tonal whiplash in its viewers.To demonstrate this point, That’s Life! was the show that introduced the nation to Prince, a talking dog who could say the word“sausages”, but it was also the show that put pressure on the government to introduce mandatory seatbelt use for children. This was the show that invented a new animal as an April fool’s joke, only for coachloads of tourists to arrive at London Zoo to try to spot it. It was also the show that embarked on a vigorous three-month investigation into allegations of widespread sexual abuse by teachers at a boys’ boarding school, resulting in the school’s closure less than two weeks after the feature aired.All of which makes That’s Life! sound like The One Show on human growth hormones. Yet the show was one of the most popular of its time, regularly pulling in close to 20 million viewers. Key to its success was its producer and presenter,Esther Rantzen.Starting her career as a BBC Radio trainee sound effects assistant, Rantzen rose up the ranks as a researcher on shows such as Ned Sherrin’s BBC-3 before being given her first shot at presenting on Braden’s Week, a magazine show that came to sticky end when its host, Bernard Braden, was fired for advertising margarine on ITV. Nevertheless, that was all the grounding Rantzen needed to start a show of her own.View image in fullscreenRantzen with other members of the That’s Life! cast in 1989.Photograph: Bill Lovelace/Daily Mail/REX/ShutterstockAlong with producer John Lloyd, Rantzen devised That’s Life!, a series that would encompass every issue and indignity known to man. Fronted by Rantzen, with an ever-changing swirl of co-presenters around her, That’s Life would take on everything from dubious advertising to theover-proliferation of crisp flavours. There would be vox pops about theshare of domestic tasks undertaken by menand genuinely nightmarish features where people would pose as waxworks thenburst into songin a bid to inspire more singing in Britain.And Rantzen was the perfect host. This was down to her ability to maintain a sense of ease between all these tonal extremes. It paid off in spades, since when That’s Life! got serious, it got extremely serious. In 1984 it used a story about Ben Hardwick, a two-year-old boy who needed a liver transplant, to push for more widespread organ donation. And it worked – MPs noted in parliament in 1988 that it had directly led to a boom in the number of transplants.Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86Read moreIt also revealed the story of Nicholas Winton, dubbed the British Schindler, a man who assisted in the rescue of 669 children from what was then Czechoslovakia on the eve of the second world war. Winton’s acts went unacknowledged for half a century, until a 1988 episode of That’s Life! sat him in the studio audience, revealing that he was surrounded by dozens of the children he saved, along with their children and grandchildren. It was a profoundly emotional piece of television, and one that Rantzen was rightly proud of; this year she wrote the Guardian a letter of complaint when its list of theBBC’s 100 greatest moments omitted the episode.That’s Life! also focused heavily on child abuse, which resulted in Rantzen setting up Childline, the first national helpline for children in danger or distress. According to the NSPCC, Childline has helped six million children since it was established in 1986.When That’s Life! ended in 1994, Rantzen continued to embody the spirit of the series in all her ventures. She hosted her own talkshow, named Esther, which ran for eight years. And Hearts of Gold, which was inspired by Winton, shone a light on members of the public who had done good deeds, seeking out numerous unsung heroes. She continued to champion consumer rights with the shows Old Dogs New Tricks and Esther Rantzen’s House Trap. She also had stints on Strictly, I’m a Celebrity and Celebrity First Dates.Following the death of her husband, Desmond Wilcox, in 2000, Rantzen increasingly turned her focus towards end of life care. BBC Two’s How to Have a Good Death was a landmark programme about palliative care, and she built on this further after her cancer diagnosis in 2023. When she found out her cancer had reached stage four, she publicly announced that she had joined Dignitas, and used her final stretch of time to campaign heavily for assisted dying. Three weeks ago,MPs voted against an attempt to legalise it in England and Wales.But Rantzen’s relentless campaigning means that the conversation is unlikely to go away. Even in death, she may yet prove to be one of this country’s greatest campaigners.Share your tributes and memoriesYou can share your tributes and memories of Esther Rantzen using this form.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
