title: ‘These early friendships are huge romances’: Extra Geography’s lessons in teenage love | Movies | The Guardian
description: Rose Tremain, along with the cast and crew of the new film updating her 1950s story to the early 00s, remember the intensity of these relationships and explain why its story has not dated
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Rose Tremain, along with the cast and crew of the new film updating her 1950s story to the early 00s, remember the intensity of these relationships and explain why its story has not dated
Content: Big emotions … Minna (Galaxie Clear) and Flic (Marni Duggan) in Extra Geography.Photograph: Brock MediaView image in fullscreenBig emotions … Minna (Galaxie Clear) and Flic (Marni Duggan) in Extra Geography.Photograph: Brock MediaMovies‘These early friendships are huge romances’: Extra Geography’s lessons in teenage loveRose Tremain, along with the cast and crew of a new film updating her 1950s story to the early 00s, remember the intensity of these relationships and explain why its story has not datedCath ClarkeThu 1 Oct 2026 09.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew years ago,Rose Tremainwas asked to name her biggest disappointment. Her reply? The film of her novel Restoration. Despite a Hollywood budget, Robert Downey Jr and Ian McKellen in the cast and a couple of Oscars, it was “a dog’s dinner”. Speaking on the phone from her home in Norfolk, Tremain is far more complimentary about a new British adaptation of her semi-autobiographical short story Extra Geography, set in a boarding school in the 1950s and first published in 2007.View image in fullscreen‘It’s not just a little relic from my past’ … Rose Tremain.Photograph: Mark Bourdillon“I’ve been delighted by this whole project,” she says, still sounding surprised. Tremain adores the script, adapted from her elegant five-page story by playwright and Succession scriptwriter Miriam Battye. At their first meeting, Battye told her it would easily transfer to the modern day: “I felt really pleased about that,” says Tremain. “It’s not just a little relic from my past. It has relevance now.”She is equally delighted with the finished film: “To make a 90-minute movie, Miriam had to do a lot of inventing. And I think all the inventing that she’s done is very, very right for the story. She completely understood it and yet made it her own, which, honestly …” Tremain pauses. “In cinema, I don’t know how often that happens. Usually when somebody says they’re going to write your thing, they take it in a direction which you can’t recognise at all.”The film is set in a boarding school in the north of England in the early 2000s, where Year 10s Minna and Flic rule the school, queens of the common room. Minna is posh and fast becoming a beauty (a dewy faced English rose, think teenage Kate Winslet). Flic is a “scholarship girl”, brainy, but lacking her friend’s effortless confidence. They are gloriously extra. “What happens if we don’t get into Oxbridge?” asks Minna. “Maybe we’ll just die,” sighs Flic. There is no irony. It’s all from the heart.One long afternoon, Minna and Flic decide to make themselves more interesting by falling in love. Borrowing the idea from A Midsummer Night’s Dream (a “rubbish” play, declares Flic) they agree to fall in love with the first person they see. Who happens to be their geography teacher Miss Delavigne, a woman with sturdy ankles and frumpy skirts, played in the film by Alice Englert.But Extra Geography is not about love, rather friendship, which is a recurring theme in her work, says Tremain. “Romance is the staple of fiction and always has been. But I think friendship, which is a kind of poor relation of that, is so interesting.”I call Battye, who explains that she instantly wanted to adapt the story into a film: “It felt very familiar to me, like it was something I’ve gone through. I felt very connected to the character of Flic. I just found it really truthful.”View image in fullscreenGalaxie Clear and Marni Duggan in Extra Geography.Photograph: Brock MediaDid she go to a boarding school? “No. But I went to quite an intense girls’ school in the north. It was extraordinarily ambitious. There was an intense kind of rabid ambitiousness to everyone. And a strong sense that we had to be something, and to do something with ourselves. I brought that out a little more in the film. That was something I was interested in, the impatience and intensity in the girls to make something significant of themselves. I can remember being pretty hard on myself, I think we all were.”Battye was the story editor on Season four of Succession. I tell her that I can see a similarity between the ferociously funny dialogue in the boardroom and the schoolroom in Extra Geography. “Well, I am obsessed with dialogue. I like characters who use their language very intentionally and intensely. It’s not supposed to be improvised or mumblecore.”It was the script that hooked the film’s director Molly Manners, speaking over a video call from her home in Brighton. “Miriam writes in this unbelievably witty and truthful way, very sharp-tongued. Really bold. I was really drawn to the language and the way in which the script explored relationships in very funny but tragic way.”View image in fullscreenMiriam Battye, Marni Duggan, Galaxie Clear and Molly Manners at a photoshoot for Extra Geography.Photograph: Jeff Vespa/ShutterstockThe reviews for Extra Geography have been glowing. One critic described it as Jane Austen updated to a 21st-century boarding school. Another compared the twists and turns in Minna and Flic’s friendship to Elena Ferrante’s My Brilliant Friend. When I mention the Ferrante comment, her eyes widen. “I don’t know if I actually read that one. Imustgo and read this!” she jokes.But in all seriousness, epic emotions are what they were going for, she says. “The scale of the feelings that you have as a teenager are huge. Small things can feel quite world-ending. I wanted the feelings to be huge.” And the biggest feelings Minna and Flic experience are for each other: they are the love of each other’s 15-year-old lives. “A massive part of it was to show what huge romances these early female friendships are,” says Manners.Did she go to boarding school? “No I’m pleased to say. But my experience was an all-girls’ school, having these intense female friendships as you’re forming your world and self-view. The boarding school setting intensifies it further, so it becomes a petri dish.”Extra Geography review – a sweet and spiky coming-of-age debutRead moreThe film is set pre-social media. That was important says Manners: “Mobile phones were around but not many of the girls would have had them. It was like: ‘You can speak on the payphone to your parents for 15 minutes maximum.’ It needed to feel as isolating as possible, no access to the real world. It’s a very sheltered all girls’ experience.” That changes with the rude interruption of lads from a neighbouring all-boys school to work on the end-of-term play. “You get the male gaze and a bit of real world.”View image in fullscreen‘As isolating as possible’ … Minna and Flic.Photograph: Brock MediaExtra Geography is Manners’ cinema debut. She was the lead director on Netflix’s adaptation of One Day, where she oversaw the casting of Ambika Mod and Leo Woodall as Emma and Dexter. To find Extra Geography’s Flic and Minna, she trawled drama clubs up and down the country for months with casting director Lucy Pardee. The shoot took place in a dilapidated country pile in North Yorkshire. “We called the school the ‘cold cradle’, because there’s no pastoral care there. No useful adults.”The actor Marni Duggan, 19, who plays Flic, says she that felt possessive of the character from the get go: “Throughout the audition process I said: ‘If I don’t get this part I’m not going to be able to watch the film.’” What did she connect to? “The intense female friendships was something that I could relate to. When I was 14, 15, I had really intense female friendships that looked romantic almost. It’s not that they were romantic, it was just that they were so intense. When you have that friendship breakup it’s absolutely devastating and it feels worse than a romantic breakup.”Back with Rose Tremain, I ask did she ever actually fall in love with her geography teacher? She laughs. “Well, at girls’ boarding school in the 1950s, there was a lot of dead time.” Usually she spent loose hours writing plays. “But there was an afternoon my friend Heather and I were really bored. We thought it’d be quite nice to fall in love with somebody, and we had a slight crush on the geography teacher, who was called Miss Howard and was very pretty. It didn’t go far. We just tried to do rather well at geography. I don’t think she ever knew that we had this little crush on her.”Extra Geography is in cinemas nowExplore more on these topicsFilmRose TremainFilm adaptationsDrama filmsFriendshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Orgy, apocalypse and exorcism: Faye Driscoll’s revolving bed puts everyone in a spin | Stage | The Guardian
description: The US performance-maker’s Weathering, which evokes people clinging to a life raft, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences. As it arrives in the UK, she reflects on creating a sensory environment to involve us all
Author: Tim Etchells
Headline: The US performance-maker’s Weathering, which evokes people clinging to a life raft, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences. As it arrives in the UK, she reflects on creating a sensory environment to involve us all
Content: ‘The spinning is the thing’ … Weathering.Photograph: Kevin Monko/Fierce FestivalView image in fullscreen‘The spinning is the thing’ … Weathering.Photograph: Kevin Monko/Fierce FestivalStageOrgy, apocalypse and exorcism: Faye Driscoll’s revolving bed puts everyone in a spinThe US performance-maker’s Weathering, which evokes people clinging to a life raft, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences. As it arrives in the UK, she reflects on creating a sensory environment to involve us allTim EtchellsThu 1 Oct 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFaye Driscoll is in Stockholm, developing a new work forCullberg’s entire 15-dancer ensemble titledflesh chariot, chariot of flesh. In the process she is negotiating the shift from independent projects in New York and Los Angeles to the framework of a large European dance institution. “There are so many people in the rehearsal room, sometimes it feels like I’m running a small corporation,” she jokes on our video call. Thankfully there’s nothing corporate about Driscoll’s work, which comes from a deep, intuitive set of questions about dance, human connection, perception, ecology and community.Since premiering in New York in 2023, her extraordinary and best-known performance, Weathering, has left a trail of overwhelmed audiences on its journey from the choreographer’s base in NY/LA to festivals across Europe and farther afield. The work’s UK premiere is a substantial coup for Birmingham’s groundbreakingFierce festival.Weathering begins at a glacial pace, with 10 performers assuming still positions on a rotating central platform, the audience gathered around on four sides. What follows is a compelling and challenging mix of kinetic sculpture and uncanny ritual, long-forgotten orgy, exuberant collective exorcism and intimate apocalypse. A slow build from the stillness in the first scene rises to a chaotic transformative and desperate group exertion. Rooted in techniques and understandings from choreography itself, Driscoll’s work is also dance by way of Butoh and performance art. At the same time, it stands as a nuanced and profoundly impactful wordless reflection on the state of the world, the climate and our tangled place in it.View image in fullscreenNuanced and profoundly impactful … Faye Driscoll’s Weathering.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesAs might be expected, Driscoll’s journey to choreography was a patchwork of influences and permissions. “My parents met in New York as performer-dancers in an all-nude musical –Oh! Calcutta!– so I guess that does feel important; when I wanted to dance, I had no problem with access to it.” After learning ballet and modern dance, she undertook conservatory training in New York. Being exposed to the city’s downtown performance scene – shows by legendary figures such asRichard Foremanand invitations to choreograph for up-and-coming radicals like playwrightYoung Jean Lee– had a big effect. “Collaboration really affected my making, pushing me away from the preciousness that can be so strong when you work alone.”Caught in what Driscoll calls “a collective ongoing”, the figures on stage in Weathering are a mix of ages, ethnicities, genders, body types, and presences. We could be seeing strangers plucked at random from city streets, caught off balance together on the performance podium that frames their journey. The rotating platform itself begins as stage or museum plinth but constantly takes on new connotations through the work; a bed, an improvised life raft to which people are clinging, a fragile spinning world.It’s an irony perhaps that such a physical project as Weathering began life during Covid, with Driscoll and team researching remotely. “We couldn’t touch each other or even be in the same rooms. We were using text to figure things out – taking from fight scenes and erotica, mixing the Iliad with bits of Rocky, first world war battle descriptions and porn, mashing everything together.” Although none of this material made the completed work, it’s present as a reference, says Driscoll: “I was thinking a lot about moments in daily life where we push outside ourselves and go into another body – try to be with it, to change it, where our borders as human beings blur in the most intimate ways, in fighting or in sex.”View image in fullscreen‘I was thinking about where our bodies as human beings blur in the most intimate ways’ … Faye Driscoll.Photograph: Valerian MazataudEcological thematics ghost the piece, especially the tangled relation between humans and the nature they claim to oversee. Driscoll explains: “We are nature … we aren’t inside any weather system that we’re trying to fix … We’re part of these systems with every breath and every piss we take.” At the same time, it’s the profound malleability of the image and the audience role in making meaning that grips Driscoll. Her pieceflesh chariot, chariot of fleshalso leans into the question of connectivity in the contemporary context, considering events in the world and how they affect us profoundly from a distance – how can things that reach us via the world-flattening device of screens still be felt as bodily experience, as trauma. “In Weathering, the spinning is the thing. As a spectator, you’re never going to get the whole picture, like in life, maybe we never do. So as the platform spins, you’re constantly re-engaging with things as they come back around, grappling with your own idea about what you’re seeing or what you might have missed.”Indeed, perhaps the most obdurate obsession for Driscoll is the audience. “Previously, I spent eight years doing a project that asked how you sense and feel your culpability in the room when you’re watching a show. To do that, the project dealt a lot with audience participation, which I found completely horrifying.” But her struggle with participation revealed a deeper desire that still compels her: “How do I create a sensory environment that makes you understand that you are already involved in everything? That idea is the DNA of all my work.”As Weathering intensifies towards its ending – “there’s a shedding of clothes, a kind of peeling that occurs … there are hands in mouths, hands in each other’s clothing … ” – we enter a physically and sonically overwhelming zone. The scene, flirting with the limits of control, is grotesque, passionate, tender and urgent, all at the same time. “It might look referential, like bodies from art history. Or it might look imagistic, like moments drawn from life,” says Driscoll. “You think for some time that you could know what this is that you’re looking at … but that certainty dissolves.” She pauses, a small silence on the video call, then adds, as if by way of conclusion: “I love the slipperiness of unknowing.”Weatheringis at Midland Arts Centre, Birmingham, 14-16 October as part ofFierce festival.flesh chariot, chariot of fleshis touring until 6 February. Forced Entertainment’sCold Sweat, devised with and directed by Tim Etchells, is at Sheffield Theatres, 2-3 October; Southbank Centre, London, 9-10 October; and Lancaster Arts, 14 October.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreDancePerformance artfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meshell Ndegeocello: Synonym review – vivid all-star reinventions of everyone from Bob Dylan to J-Lo | Music | The Guardian
description: In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyond
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyond
Content: Restlessly inventive … Meshell Ndegeocello.Photograph: Charlie GrossView image in fullscreenRestlessly inventive … Meshell Ndegeocello.Photograph: Charlie GrossAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewMeshell Ndegeocello: Synonym review – vivid all-star reinventions of everyone from Bob Dylan to J-Lo(Blue Note)In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyondAlexis PetridisThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s fair to say that Meshell Ndegeocello has made a career out of declining to stay in one place too long. Since helping spark the neo soul genre with her 1993 debut album, Plantation Lullabies, she has variously worked in the fields of jazz, R&B, alternative rock, reggae, fusion and gospel. Her last album, No More Water: The Gospel of James Baldwin, seemed intent on defying any kind of classification, leaping from Afrobeat funk to electronic abstraction to a closing track that sounded not unlike the xx: it won a Grammy for best alternative jazz album, which slightly smacked of the awards’ organisers throwing up their hands in defeat after a lengthy and fruitless attempt to decide in which category it might belong.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Synonym.Even if you knew absolutely nothing about Ndegeocello’s eclectic musical history, you could get a sense of her restlessness just from looking at the back cover of Synonym, a collection of cover versions rendered as duets. The source material picks from the oeuvres of Bob Dylan, Jennifer Lopez, the Human League, Barbra Streisand and Chris Cornell’s short-lived grunge supergroup Temple of the Dog, among others. Her collaborators range from Bill Callahan and Cat Power to Chaka Khan andCynthia Erivo, by way of jazz pianist Robert Glasper.There is a certain unifying thread in Ndegeocello’s desire to make Synonym “an expression of queer liberation as a synonym for liberation of all kinds”. A lot of the tracks were formerly male-female duets, but are sung here by two women, occasionally altering their meaning in the process: the chorus of Streisand’s Guilty is transformed into an anthem of defiance when performed by Ndegeocello and Ink (a singer-songwriter best known as co-author of Beyonce’s Texas Hold ’Em). Even that unifying thread, though, occasionally snaps, as if Ndegeocello were too restive to stick with an overarching concept.It doesn’t fit her and Callahan’s closing version of Dylan’s With God on Our Side, which sets the oldBob Dylanbroadside against a backing that initially carries a trace of the song’s acoustic roots – accompanied by mandolin and piano, Callaghan and Ndegeocello’s harmonies are slightly out of step, as if they’re belting it out live in a folk club – but gradually becomes consumed by hissing electronic noise and distorted guitar. Ndegeocello has suggested the idea was to match the sound to the aggression of the lyrics; the end result feels more like a protest song struggling to be heard amid the noise of modern life. It’s potent either way.Certainly, Ndegeocello is far too restive an artist to leave a song much as you remember it. Her selections are the work of someone with great taste: Be Real Black for Me is far from the best-known of Flack and Hathaway’s duets, but its blend of politics and sexual charge is extraordinary. Yet Synonym deals not so much in cover versions as reinventions, and frequently stunning ones at that.Her version of Don’t You Want Me withCat Powerrecasts the song as reggae, an idea that sounds a lot better coming out of the speakers than it looks on paper, and there’s a mood-shifting alteration in the vocal delivery that goes far beyond the obvious gender-swap. Ndegeocello sings Phil Oakey’s lines with a slightly halting phrasing; they suddenly sound fragile and vulnerable rather than how-dare-you? huffy. And Cat Power delivers Susan Ann Sulley’s as if she couldn’t, and indeed never did, care less: she sounds as if she’s singing “the five years we have had have been such good times, I still love you” over her shoulder while bolting for the door.Meshell Ndegeocello: ‘Making music is the rare moment that I feel raceless and genderless’Read moreNdegeocello takes such liberties with the melody, tempo and even lyrics ofDylan’s It Ain’t Me Babe that it’s almost unrecognisable (you could argue that has pretty much been Dylan’s approach to his back catalogue for the last thirtysomething years). The result here is not just startling but beautiful, a strange, dream-like mass of electric guitar arpeggios, musical box tones and mandolin.You could read Ndegeocello’s version of Yarborough and Peoples’ old soul weekender classic Don’t Stop the Music as a comment on the devaluing of music in the streaming era: the electronic voice now feels ominous and menacing, less as though you’re being invited to dance the night away than cajoled into consuming more and more, regardless of its quality. It’s a marked contrast to Ndegeocello’s plaintive vocal and acoustic guitar.Sometimes, Synonym’s approach falters. The restructuring of Sonny and Cher’s I Got You Babe is impressively radical:Anohnitakes Cher’s role, while Ndegeocello deploys her lowest register to render Sonny’s part, and the music is restructured as sparse jazz, with deeply un-pop chords performed on brass and woodwind. The end result doesn’t quite hold together emotionally, though: the tumbling, folk-rock fatalism of the original has vanished, but it’s unclear what has replaced it.Equally, the odd experiment not entirely coming off feels a very small price to pay for an album as fascinating as this: proof both of Ndegeocello’s unique, personal approach to what she does, and of pop’s infinite malleability in the right hands. It might celebrate collaboration, but Synonym feels like an entirely singular achievement.This week Alexis listened toHermanos Gutiérrez – Canto AndinoThe Hermanos brothers’ latest Dan Auerbach-produced album is intended to evoke the landscape of the Andes, and whether you’re familiar with South America or not, the guitar shimmer of Canto Andino will certainly transport you somewhere.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPop and rockSoulJazzR&BBob DylanBill Callahanalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Conrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63 | Metal | The Guardian
description: Singer and bassist helped turn Newcastle band into hugely influential force on thrash and black metal subgenres
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Singer and bassist helped turn Newcastle band into hugely influential force on thrash and black metal subgenres
Content: Conrad Lant, aka Cronos, of Venom performing at the Sweden Rock festival in June.Photograph: Anne-Marie Forker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConrad Lant, aka Cronos, of Venom performing at the Sweden Rock festival in June.Photograph: Anne-Marie Forker/Getty ImagesMetalConrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63Singer and bassist helped turn Newcastle band into hugely influential force on thrash and black metal subgenresBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 1 Oct 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConrad Lant, the British heavy metal musician who fronted Venom and ensured the Newcastle band became a huge influence on the genre, has died aged 63.“For more than four decades, Conrad’s voice, bass and vision were at the heart of Venom,” reads a statement from the band. “He created something that changed heavy music for ever. Venom never followed the rules. They forged their own path. And Conrad was there at the centre of it all – uncompromising, fearless and unmistakable.” No cause of death was given.Using the stage name Cronos, with an eerie pallor and dressed in showboating leather ensembles as he made theatrical declarations about witches, Satan and the underworld, Lant brought great showmanship to the group, for whom he also played bass.While they never reached the commercial heights of forebears such as Black Sabbath or the thrash bands that followed – they reached the UK Top 75 only once – Venom had a big impact, and their album Black Metal ended up giving a name to one of metal’s most important subgenres.Lant was born in Chelsea, London but moved with his family to Newcastle aged seven. His brothers were also musicians, one a drummer who joined Prefab Sprout (“they were shite,” Lant would later opine), and another who drummed for Venom in the band’s 21st-century period.Venom began as Guillotine, which Lant joined aged 16, initially on guitar, then bass and graduating to vocalist after a previous frontman left. Renamed Venom, the lineup solidified around Lant, guitarist Jeff Dunn (AKA Mantas) and drummer Tony Bray (AKA Abaddon), and they released their debut album Welcome to Hell in 1981. It featured the controversy-baiting single In League with Satan, which featured reversed speech about the devil and helped bring satanic imagery into metal.Inspired by punk, Venom intensified the heaviness of early British heavy metal bands by playing at a furious pace. The Sabbath frontman Ozzy Osbourne “was singing about the devil”, Lant said. “I wanted tobethe devil.”He told the Guardian in 2019: “I had that snot and piss and shit element, which I wanted to put back into metal. I saw more and more bands shoving socks down their pants and putting lipstick on, and I just was disgusted by that, to tell you the truth. Fucking hell, if heavy metal was anything it had to be raw and dangerous and in your face.”View image in fullscreenVenom pictured in 1984.Photograph: Fin Costello/RedfernsThat impulse came to bear on five more albums during the 1980s, including Black Metal, whose demonic cover art and raw, hellish sound “carved in stone some of the essential features” of the black metal genre, according to scene historians Michael J Moynihan and Didrik Søderlind in their book Lords of Chaos. Lant, who co-produced the album, said the making of it was “pure mayhem from start to finish”, with instrumentation including steel plates being cut into with a chainsaw, and a makeshift coffin having earth dumped on to it.Venom went on hiatus in 1988 and Lant – after pondering a career change in forestry – went solo as Cronos, putting out two early 1990s albums. Venom then reformed for another seven LPs, the most recent being 2018’s Storm the Gates. There was another, shorter hiatus in the early 2000s while Lant recovered from a climbing injury.He trained as a fitness instructor in the 1990s (“I did loads of classes, I played rave,” he later said) and also began parallel careers in computer engineering and graphic design, though Venom continued to tour, including at festivals in summer 2026.Venom’s pace, ferocity and darkness all proved seductive to a new generation of metalheads in the 1980s, particularly thrash bands such as Metallica, Slayer and Anthrax. “It was so, so evil. This was a new kind of insanity,” Scott Ian of Anthrax said admiringly of Welcome to Hell.Lant collaborated with another admirer, Dave Grohl, for Grohl’s metal supergroup Probot in 2004.Lant’s son Nathan thanked Venom’s fans after his father’s death. “I know he really appreciated you all. He has laid down his soul, and his music will live on. The legend of Cronos will never die.”Explore more on these topicsMetalPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Rick Ross arrested on domestic battery and strangulation charges | Hip-hop | The Guardian
description: The rapper was arrested in Miami Beach on Thursday, days after an ex-girlfriend accused him of physical abuse
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The rapper was arrested in Miami Beach on Thursday, days after an ex-girlfriend accused him of physical abuse
Content: Rick Ross performs in Chicago, Illinois, in 2019.Photograph: RMV/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRick Ross performs in Chicago, Illinois, in 2019.Photograph: RMV/REX/ShutterstockHip-hopRick Ross arrested on domestic battery and strangulation chargesThe rapper was arrested in Miami Beach on Thursday, days after an ex-girlfriend accused him of physical abuseOwen MyersThu 1 Oct 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 17.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRick Rosshas been arrested on domestic violence charges inMiamiBeach, according to local police.The rapper was booked at Turner Guilford Knight correctional center at 6.10am local time on Thursday and faces one felony count of battery by strangulation as well as a misdemeanor count of battery.Bond has been listed at $6,000, according to Miami-Dade jail and court records.Local authorities have not specified the circumstances that led to Ross’s arrest or details of the alleged incident. They also did not identify the alleged victim.Woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her aged 13 says claims were falseRead moreThe Guardian has reached out to the musician’s representative for comment.The arrest comes days after Rick Ross’s ex-girlfriend Jazzma Kendrick alleged that the rapper was physically abusive to her, People magazinereported.“He saw a punching bag,” she wrote on an Instagram story after sharing images of a swollen lip that she said was caused by Ross. Alongside the picture she wrote: “The day Rick busted my lip and the day I left.”“I don’t know a lot of things, but I do know that a man that puts his hands on me, is a man that never loved me and never will,” Kendrick posted over another image.“It’s always good until it isn’t,” she said. “If a man hits you one time, he will do it again. Don’t give him the opportunity. Value your life and leave.”Rick Ross, born William Leonard Roberts, is a longtime Miami resident with five No 1 albums and hit collaborations with Drake, DJ Khaled and Nicki Minaj, among many others. In July he released his 12th studio album, Set in Stone, which featured Gucci Mane, The-Dream and Yung Miami.Local court records say that Ross has retained attorney Bradley Horenstein. His arraignment is set for 22 October.In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsHip-hopRapUS crimeMiamiFloridanewsShareReuse this content

title: Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson to watch Bafta Scotland awards in separate ‘relaxed’ space | Movies | The Guardian
description: Decision follows independent review into handling of February ceremony, where his involuntary tics caused a BBC crisis
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Decision follows independent review into handling of February ceremony, where his involuntary tics caused a BBC crisis
Content: Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson.Photograph: Matt Baron/BEI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson.Photograph: Matt Baron/BEI/ShutterstockMoviesTourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson to watch Bafta Scotland awards in separate ‘relaxed’ spaceDecision follows independent review into handling of February ceremony, where his involuntary tics caused a BBC crisisAndrew PulverThu 1 Oct 2026 10.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Davidson, the Tourette syndrome campaigner whose outburst at the British Academy film awards in Februaryled to a crisis for Bafta (British Academy of Film and Television Arts) and the BBC, will attend the Bafta Scotland awards and watch the ceremony from a separate “relaxed” space.In a letter sent to Bafta members on Thursday, the organisation’s chair Sara Putt and CEO Jane Millichip said that,after an independent review, Bafta had “strengthened and centralised our safeguarding, risk assessment and compliance processes” and had made arrangements in consultation with “safeguarding and inclusion experts” for Davidson’s attendance at the awards ceremony organised by Bafta’s Scottish branch, which is due to take place in November.For the BaftaScotlandawards ceremony, Bafta says that, in accordance with Davidson’s own suggestion, he will “watch the ceremony via video link from a separate relaxed space within the venue with his family and friends”.I Swear, the film based on Davidson’s life, is the leading contender with seven nominations at the Bafta Scotland awards, including all three nominations in the best film actor category, for Peter Mullan, Robert Aramayo and Scott Ellis Watson, and best film actress for Shirley Henderson. Aramayo unexpectedly won best actor at the national Bafta film awards in February.As executive producer ofI Swear, Davidson had been in attendance at the Baftas and was heard several times shouting during the ceremony, including using the N-word while actors Delroy Lindo and Michael B Jordan were on stage presenting the evening’s first prize. In a statement after the show, Davidson said he was “deeply mortified if anyone considers my involuntary tics to be intentional or to carry any meaning”. He added: “I have spent my life trying to support and empower the Tourette’s community and to teach empathy, kindness and understanding from others and I will continue to do so. I chose to leave the auditorium early into the ceremony as I was aware of the distress my tics were causing.”The crisis became more acute after it emerged thatDavidson’s outburst was audible during the BBC’s coverage of the event, despite the broadcast starting two hours later. The BBC apologised and suggested that producers overseeing the ceremony for the BBC were doing so from a truck and did not hear the slur.Explore more on these topicsFilmI SwearTourette syndromeBaftasScotlandAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jackie Jackson obituary | Toots and the Maytals | The Guardian
description: Toots and the Maytals bass player whose melodic lines drove some of the biggest reggae hits of the 1960s and 70s
Author: David Katz
Headline: Toots and the Maytals bass player whose melodic lines drove some of the biggest reggae hits of the 1960s and 70s
Content: Jackie Jackson, front, with the guitarist Winston ‘Bo Pee’ Bowen at a recording session for Fruits Records in 2017.Photograph: Liza MazurView image in fullscreenJackie Jackson, front, with the guitarist Winston ‘Bo Pee’ Bowen at a recording session for Fruits Records in 2017.Photograph: Liza MazurToots and the MaytalsObituaryJackie Jackson obituaryToots and the Maytals bass player whose melodic lines drove some of the biggest reggae hits of the 1960s and 70sDavid KatzThu 1 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bass player Jackie Jackson, who has died aged 79, was one of the cornerstones of Jamaican popular music. In addition to being the bassist in Toots and the Maytals for more than 50 years, Jackson provided substantial and melodic bass lines underpinning some of the most important reggae hits of the 1960s and 70s, helping tracks such as The Israelites byDesmond Dekker, TheLiquidator by Harry J Allstarsand the Upsetters’Return of Djangoreach the UK Top 10 in 1969.Equally inspired by the pumping approachLloyd Brevettused on his acoustic upright in the Skatalites, and the electric hooks of James Jamerson at Motown, Jackson was also an important part of the rock steady craze that swept Jamaica in the mid-60s. A mainstay of the house band at Duke Reid’s Treasure Isle studio, the Supersonics, he had his first recording session there forAlton Ellis’s smash I Have Got a Date (1966, later re-released as Girl I’ve Got a Date), with Jackson’s buoyant bass a propulsive engine that helped make the song one of the defining releases of the rock steady era.Jackson playing bass on the Toots and the Maytals track Sweet and Dandy in the 1972 film The Harder They ComeThen, in 1968, Jackson helped give birth to the new reggae style at the core of a session band variously known as the All Stars, the Upsetters, the Dynamites and the Crystalites, depending on which producer was hiring them. His fellow players included the drummer Paul Douglas, guitarists Hux Brown and Dougie Bryan, organist Winston Wright and pianist and arranger Gladdy Anderson. These musicians appeared on King Stitt’s Fire Corner for Clancy Eccles, Bob and Marcia’s cover of Nina Simone’s Young, Gifted and Black for Harry J, the Wailers’ Small Axe forLee “Scratch” Perry, Keith and Tex’s Stop That Train for Derrick Harriott and numerous hits for Leslie Kong, includingJimmy Cliff’s Wonderful World, Beautiful People, Hard Road to Travel and Vietnam. The latter inspired Paul Simon to work with Jackson and his peers, on Mother And Child Reunion in 1971.Appearing inPerry Henzell’s ground-breaking feature film The Harder They Come (1972), Jackson is among the players backing Cliff on the title track and Toots and the Maytals on Sweet and Dandy; his playing is also heard on the latter’s hitPressure Drop, as featured on the soundtrack. Jackson also played on the Best of the Wailers album that the group recorded for Kong in 1970, his Motown-inspired lines perfectly suited to the soul-influenced material on the LP.View image in fullscreenJackie Jackson on the cover of Greater Jamaica Moon Walk-Reggay, by the Supersonics.Photograph: Treasure IsleJackson’s calm demeanour, no-nonsense approach and musical adaptivity made him easy to work with, prompting his long working relationship withToots Hibbertof the Maytals. He was also an inspiration to many younger players, notably the Wailers bassistAston “Family Man” BarrettandRobbie Shakespeareof Sly and Robbie.Born Clifton Jackson in Kingston, he was raised by his mother in a single-parent household. His uncle Luther Williams was a pianist who led the popular dance band the Arawaks in the 50s and 60s, and Jackson began learning the piano at a young age before switching to upright bass as a teenager after seeing Brevett perform with the Skatalites at the Bournemouth Club circa 1962.He joined the club act Ty and the Titans around 1964, now playing electric bass, and when the Titans disbanded he shifted to the Cavaliers with the alto saxophonist Lester Sterling of the Skatalites. By the time that the Cavaliers disbanded in late 1966, Jackson’s mastery of his instrument led Tommy McCook to recruit him for the Supersonics at Treasure Isle.Initially earning five shillings per song, Jackson played on significant hits for leading rock steady acts such as the Paragons, the Melodians, the Techniques, Hopeton Lewis and Phyllis Dillon. Moonlighting for various producers, he appeared onPrince Buster’s anti rude boy saga Judge Dread andRoy Shirley’s peculiar rock steady hit Hold Them for upcoming producerJoe Gibbs, as well as the Wailers’ self-produced singles Hypocrites, Nice Time and Pound Get a Blow.From 1968 Jackson was playing regularly with Toots and the Maytals, and by 1973 reduced his session work to concentrate on the group, whose status was on the rise following the release of their Funky Kingston album overseas. Nevertheless, continuing his association with Cliff, he played on the Unlimited and House of Exile albums, and on high-calibre fusion projects made by foreign artists in Jamaica, including the American folk singerPeter Yarrow’s That’s Enough for Me, the New York rocker Garland Jeffreys’ self-titled Atlantic debut, the jazz saxophonistRobin Kenyatta’s Terra Nova, the flautistHerbie Mann’s Reggae and soul singerDoris Troy’s Stretchin’ Out, among others.Tired of the rigours of the road with the Maytals, and of the unreliable nature of session work, Jackson retreated from touring and recording in late 1982, launching a new career as an entertainment consultant specialising in the staging of live music events. Based in Montego Bay on Jamaica’s north coast, he ran the business successfully until 1995, when he rejoined the Maytals, remaining on the road with the group until the restrictions imposed on live music by the Covid-19 pandemic.In 2012 Jackson was awarded the Order of Distinction (Commander class) for his services to Jamaican popular music.His wife, the cabaret singer Karen Smith, whom he married in 1989, died in 2021. He is survived by their daughter, Courtni, and three daughters from other relationships, Marie, Jheanell and Jhanine.Jackie (Clifton Courtney) Jackson, bass player, born 22 March 1947; died 23 September 2026Explore more on these topicsToots and the MaytalsReggaeLee 'Scratch' PerryJimmy CliffJamaicaobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Van Gogh to go on display before sale of ‘almost mythical’ private collection | Vincent van Gogh | The Guardian
description: Châtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and Monet
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Châtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and Monet
Content: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in May 1890. It and the other works have not been seen in public in decades.Photograph: Sotheby's New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionView image in fullscreenChâtaigniers en fleurs was painted in May 1890. It and the other works have not been seen in public in decades.Photograph: Sotheby's New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionVincent van GoghVan Gogh to go on display before sale of ‘almost mythical’ private collectionChâtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and MonetKim Willsherin ParisThu 1 Oct 2026 08.20 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than 50 years it was held in a private art collection with an “almost mythical status” that was likened to a miniature version of Paris’s Musée d’Orsay.But a painting byVincent van Goghcreated during the last two months of his life will go on display this month before being put up for auction with a value of $180m (£136m).Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Flower) was painted in May 1890 shortly after Van Gogh arrived in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise. He died just weeks later.Most Van Gogh works from this period now hang in the world’s leading museums – but Châtaigniers en fleurs is one of 12 impressionist and modern masterpieces from the collection of the Argentinian collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, who died in 2020.View image in fullscreenFleurs dans une coupe by Paul Gauguin is among the 12 works up for sale.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionPhilip Hook, a former director of impressionist and modern art at the auction house Sotheby’s and a regular expert on BBC One’s Antiques Roadshow, said the opening of the collection to buyers was a “historic moment”.“For decades the Blaquier-Arrieta collection has been the stuff of legend: whispered about, kept from public view, it has attained an almost mythical status in the art world,” he said.“One of the last great private collections of impressionist and post-impressionist art, it was formed when major examples by the great names were still within reach.”View image in fullscreenPaul Cézanne’s Arlequin is valued at $150m.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionThe Sotheby’s auction will also include Paul Cézanne’s Harlequin, painted in the late 19th century and valued at $150m.They will be sold along with 10 other significant works by Camille Pissarro, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Claude Monet, Paul Gauguin, Alfred Sisley, André Derain, Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec and Maurice de Vlaminck.The 12 paintings are expected to fetch more than $450m in total. Several of the works went on display at Sotheby’s in London on Wednesday for two days and a number will be flown to Taipei, and then Hong Kong and Paris, before the auction on 18 November in New York.The Van Gogh will be on view in Hong Kong from 13-15 October and in Paris from 19-23 October.View image in fullscreenClaude Monet’s Le Jardin des Tuileries.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionVan Gogh painted at least four major works featuring chestnut trees in Auvers-sur-Oise during a period of optimism and energy after his discharge from a psychiatric hospital at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. After his death in July 1890, Châtaigniers en fleurs passed to his brother, Theo. A subsequent owner was George Gard “Buddy” DeSylva, the US songwriter and film producer who co-founded Capitol Records.It is one of only eight paintings Van Gogh produced in Auvers that are in private hands.View image in fullscreenAndré Derain’s Bâteaux au port de Collioure was painted in 1905.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionSimon Shaw, a senior art adviser at Sotheby’s, said the collection felt “like a small museum – a miniature Musée d’Orsay, now opening its doors for the very first time”.This article was amended on 1 October 2026. Due to information provided, an earlier version said that all 12 paintings would be on show at Sotheby’s in London. In fact, not all the paintings were on display there, including Châtaigniers en fleurs by Vincent van Gogh. The Van Gogh will be on view in Hong Kong from 13-15 October and in Paris from 19-23 October.Explore more on these topicsVincent van GoghPaintingArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dame Esther Rantzen obituary | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: Presenter and producer of That’s Life!, a TV series providing entertainment and consumer reporting, out of which came the Childline service
Author: Stephen Bates
Headline: Presenter and producer of That’s Life!, a TV series providing entertainment and consumer reporting, out of which came the Childline service
Content: Esther Rantzen filming scenes for the BBC show That's Life!, March 1983. The show ran for 21 years.Photograph: Radio Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen filming scenes for the BBC show That's Life!, March 1983. The show ran for 21 years.Photograph: Radio Times/Getty ImagesEsther RantzenObituaryDame Esther Rantzen obituaryPresenter and producer of That’s Life!, a TV series providing entertainment and consumer reporting, out of which came the Childline serviceStephen BatesThu 1 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor four decades Esther Rantzen, who has died aged 86, was one of the most recognisable figures on British television. A pioneering and influential female presenter and campaigner, she also set up theChildline telephone hotlinefor children to report abuse and bullying, and in her later years advocated the right to assisted dying for terminally ill people.Rantzen became a champion of consumer rights and the central figure on the BBC’s That’s Life! programme, which ran for 21 years from 1973. She went on to present other, shorter-running series, including Hearts of Gold (1988-96) and a chatshow, Esther (1994-2002). She also appeared as a contestant on Strictly Come Dancing in 2004 and I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! in 2008.The style of That’s Life! was distinctly populist, even tabloid, in tone; sometimes mawkish and sanctimonious. But the show pioneered television reporting on consumer problems about dodgy builders, fraudulent businessmen and criminal cheats, and it raised important issues such as the sugar content in drinks, human organ donations and rear seatbelts in cars.It also leavened the mix with more jokey items – suggestively shaped vegetables sent in by viewers, singing dogs, street vox-pops with engaging pensioners such as the perennially jolly East End womanAnnie Mizen, silly headlines and comic songs. The show gave a new lease of life to the veteran rhyming comedianCyril Fletcherwith his Odd Odes, and provided an early showcase for new talents such asVictoria Wood, Richard Stilgoe and Lynsey de Paul. At its peak the show attracted 20 million viewers on Sunday nights, and Rantzen became one of the few TV personalities recognisable by her first name alone.View image in fullscreenRantzen presents her one-month-old daughter, Emily, to Annie Mizen, a ‘perennially jolly East End woman’ who had become famous on That’s Life, February 1978.Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesShe was central to the show’s success and was its presiding power. Her onscreen mateyness had a cool edge, and she was not always easy to work with, according to colleagues. Paul Heiney, for a time one of her co-presenters, said: “You were crowded out if you didn’t click. The most annoying thing is that she was always right.”“I am working on humility,” she confided to the Times in 2008. “That’s another new thing I am doing … I may never get there.”Childline,now also an online service, grew out of the programme, which discovered that many children were suffering abuse in silence with no natural outlet to express their fears and gain help. On the line’s first night in 1986 it received 50,000 calls, swamping the system.Rantzen toldthe Scotsman in 2018: “When I look back I am amazed at those very first calls, often from red phone boxes … in the middle of the night, with drunks banging on the glass. For the first seven years or so the most common problem was sexual abuse, because it had been the great taboo. They had not been able to talk about it to anybody else and thought they would not be believed. They thought it was their fault and didn’t know how to ask for help.”By the time the charity wasabsorbed into the NSPCC– the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children – in 2006, Childline claimed to have helped 4 million callers, but acknowledged that one in four of those who called failed to get through.Born in Berkhamsted, in Hertfordshire, Esther was the daughter of liberal Jewish parents. Her mother, Katherine (nee Leverson), ran a nursery in the East End of London, and her father, Harry Rantzen, was a sound engineer for the BBC, rising later to become the corporation’s head of engineering designs. Esther was educated at the private North London Collegiate school and studied English at Somerville College, Oxford, where she became an enthusiastic member of the university dramatic society.Any ambition of a stage career, however, was curtailed by self-consciousness about her appearance, a hang-up that remained decades later when, becoming the first woman to receive a Bafta Richard Dimbleby award in 1988 for her work on factual programmes, she described herself as “the oldest, plainest woman on television”.View image in fullscreenThe 1982 cast of That’s Life, with, from left, Noel Edmonds, Michael Groth, Rantzen, Bill Buckley, Paul Daniels, Gavin Campbell, Joanna Monro and Doc Cox.Photograph: Nils Jorgensen/Rex/ShutterstockAfter graduation she worked briefly at a West End advertising agency before joining the BBC as a secretary, then providing dramatic effects as a radio studio manager (1963) and becoming a programme researcher (1965). In 1967 she joined the BBC2 Man Alive documentary team as a trainee director, and there was spotted by the head of documentaries,Desmond Wilcox, who became her boss. The two began an affair three years later, and eventually married in 1977, following Wilcox’s divorce from his first wife, Patsy.Rantzen’s first onscreen experience came as a reporter from 1968 on the programme Braden’s Week, a gentler precursor of That’s Life!, starring the Canadian-born actor and broadcasterBernard Braden, who lost his job with the BBC when he advertised margarine on ITV in 1972. Rantzen not only presented her own programme from the start, but also became its producer and scriptwriter.The success of That’s Life! owed much to her drive and ambition, and she struggled after it ended in 1994 to find an equally successful replacement. The Rantzen Report, which aimed to continue That’s Life’s investigatory ethos, was described in a letter to the Times as “zoo TV”, consisting as it did of “a boisterous studio audience [applauding] as Esther made her accusations” and ran for only three episodes in 1996, one of which was found by the Broadcasting Standards Commission to be “inaccurate, misleading and unfair” in its allegations of neglect at a home for chronically ill people.As her regular broadcasting career began to wane, Rantzen threw her activities increasingly into charity work, especially for young people. There was support for ME sufferers and the National Deaf Children’s Society, Hospice Care, even a campaign for courtesy: her name was associated with 55 charities in all. She was appointed OBE in 1991, followed by CBE in 2006, and was made a dame in 2015.As someone who had made a career out of discussing the lives of others, Rantzen was also not shy about sharing details of her own. She frequently described her loneliness as a widow following Wilcox’s death in 2000, and that led in time to setting up theSilver Linein 2013, a telephone counselling service for older people similar to Childline. When she started dating potential partners, that got an airing too, including her humiliation when one dinner date ungallantly described her as elderly.View image in fullscreenRantzen with her husband, television producer Desmond Wilcox, in 1998. He died in 2000.Photograph: Julian Makey/ShutterstockShe cheerfully discussed her OCD, her Botox injections, even a brief 1960s fling with the Tory politicianNicholas Fairbairn. Her appearances on Strictly Come Dancing and I’m a Celebrity were justified, she claimed, to keep her name and charities in front of a youthful audience too young to remember her on That’s Life! She also appeared in the first episode of Celebrity First Dates in 2016, and presented a Channel 5 consumer watchdog series, Esther Rantzen’s House Trap, in 2018.In the 2010 general election, outraged by the MPs’ expenses row, Rantzenstood as an independent candidate in the Luton South constituency, where the Labour MP Margaret Moran had featured prominently in the scandal. Rantzen’s high-profile campaign was vitiated slightly by the fact that Moran had already resigned, and she eventually came in fourth, with 4% of the vote, well behind the main party candidates.There were several books, including an autobiography, Esther, in 2001, and two “life guides”: If Not Now, When? (2008) and Older and Bolder: My A-Z of Surviving Almost Everything (2023).In May 2023 Rantzen announced that she had beendiagnosed with stage-4 lung cancer. In December that year she called for a change in the law on assisted dying, revealing that she had joined the Dignitas clinic in Zurich.She welcomed the private member’s bill to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales that was introduced in October 2024, but it failed to get through the House of Lords. In encouraging its revival in September 2026, she announced that she wastoo physically fragile to travel to Switzerland. In the event the bill wasvoted down in the Commons, but she continued to assert that change would come.She is survived by her children, Miriam, Rebecca and Joshua, and five grandchildren, Benjamin, Alexander, Teddy, Florence and Romilly.Esther Louise Rantzen, television broadcaster and campaigner, born 22 June 1940; died 30 September 2026Explore more on these topicsEsther RantzenTelevision industryConsumer rightsBBCobituariesShareReuse this content
