title: East of Eden review – Florence Pugh in soapy Steinbeck adaptation is brilliant, compelling TV | Television | The Guardian
description: This take on the 1952 novel is lavishly shot and full of excellent performances. It lacks the heft to be a full examination of human nature, but it’s a high-quality family saga
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This take on the 1952 novel is lavishly shot and full of excellent performances. It lacks the heft to be a full examination of human nature, but it’s a high-quality family saga
Content: Brotherly love … Mike Faist as Charles Trask, Christopher Abbott as Adam Trask and Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenBrotherly love … Mike Faist as Charles Trask, Christopher Abbott as Adam Trask and Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewEast of Eden review – Florence Pugh in soapy Steinbeck adaptation is brilliant, compelling TVThis take on the 1952 novel is lavishly shot and full of excellent performances. It lacks the heft to be a full examination of human nature, but it’s a high-quality family sagaLucy ManganThu 1 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 19.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is rarely difficult to distinguish between a John Steinbeck novel and a ray of sunshine. The new adaptation of his 1952 book East of Eden doesn’t buck the trend and wastes no time plunging us into the murk. The opening scene follows a beaten, bloodied woman as she crawls across a muddy field towards the only house for miles around. Out of the house come two brothers. One rushes to rescue her. The other takes one look and announces: “This is a mistake.” Brother, you have no idea.The rescuer is Adam Trask (Christopher Abbott), the sceptic Charles (Mike Faist). Cut back 25 years to watch them being raised in misery in an essentially motherless household by their monstrous father, Cyrus (Tracy Letts), a civil war veteran and ceaseless recounter of his heroics therein. Charles longs to follow in his footsteps. Adam is beaten for his lack of aggressive instinct. But it is Adam whom Cyrus sends to enlist and Charles he forces to stay behind and work on the family farm. “Because,” he says to Adam in a rare instance of paternal wisdom, “there are loose things in him that should be reined down.”As a resentment-fuelled Charles nearly kills Adam the night before he leaves for the army, you can see Cyrus’s point. But years later, Dad is dead, leaving behind an almost certainly ill-gotten fortune. Adam comes home; the brothers put the past behind them and begin to carve out a decent life on the farm.And then comes Cathy Ames (Florence Pugh), the battered, bloodied woman crawling across the field to damn them all.View image in fullscreenEvil just for kicks? … Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in East of Eden.Photograph: NetflixEast of Eden was Steinbeck’s penultimate major work; he thought it his finest. Critics disagreed. They thought its examination of good and evil – whether we are born to be one or the other, whether we have a choice, how much we can fight our instincts – was heavy-handed and the author guilty of an intrusive moralism that prevented the book from ringing true. The public, however, took it to heart as a soapy family drama – Cain and Abel, but out west and set over three generations. Perhaps this was not what Steinbeck intended, but it made the novel an instant bestseller.It’s on this plane that the new version, by Zoe Kazan (the granddaughter of Elia, who directed the 1955 film adaptation starring an unknown actor called James Dean) works best. Lavishly shot, full of emotional and physical incident and fine performances, there is little chance to be distracted.Adam falls hopelessly in love with Cathy while the far more worldly-wise Charles looks on with contempt and despair.The second episode unpacks her torrid backstory – the born manipulator, leaving desperate boys and suicidal men in her wake, who moves into prostitution as a pragmatic business move and specialises in practices that most 19th-century whorehouses were hoping wouldn’t make it that far west until the internet age, betraying benefactors, committing arson, faking her death and abandoning husbands and eventually babies in her quest for riches and freedom. Or possibly just for kicks.Cathy’s sociopathy or psychopathy was part of the critical rejection of the book – a woman couldn’t possibly! – that feels dated now, but it doesn’t mean it has become much more interesting in the years since. Pugh does what she can with the part – but Cathy remains a spectacle to be ogled rather than a fully fledged character.View image in fullscreenA welcome chance to breathe … Hoon Lee as Lee with Ciarán Hinds as Samuel Hamilton in East of Eden.Photograph: Kristy Griffin/NetflixThe men – some things never change – fare better. The brothers have much to get their teeth into, as they struggle with their love and hate for each other, for her, for their lives and for their father. One of the most finely drawn and touching relationships grows gradually between Adam’s neighbour Samuel Hamilton (Ciarán Hinds), once Adam and Cathy have moved to the Salinas valley, and Adam’s manservant, Lee (Hoon Lee) ; it gives us a welcome chance to breathe. A lovely performance from Martha Plimpton as the unexpectedly vulnerable brothel madam Faye – first Cathy’s boss, then another of Cathy’s victims – helps aerate things, too.As a high-quality family saga, then, it’s brilliant, compelling entertainment. As an excoriation of human nature, as an examination of how helpless we are before our inborn proclivities, it perhaps cannot help but lack the heft it needs.East of Eden is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewFlorence PughreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Break Clause review – you’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll never want to live with anyone again | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Lara Ricote’s tale of a couple who break up after moving in together is weird, hugely funny and uncomfortably true-to-life at times
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Lara Ricote’s tale of a couple who break up after moving in together is weird, hugely funny and uncomfortably true-to-life at times
Content: Uncomfortably true-to-life … Lil (Lara Ricote) and Ben (Samuel Bottomley) in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/ erry SpicerView image in fullscreenUncomfortably true-to-life … Lil (Lara Ricote) and Ben (Samuel Bottomley) in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4/ erry SpicerTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewBreak Clause review – you’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll never want to live with anyone againLara Ricote’s tale of a couple who break up after moving in together is weird, hugely funny and uncomfortably true-to-life at timesHannah J DaviesThu 1 Oct 2026 06.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 22, you move from Leeds to London for your first proper job, and get the keys to a flat with your uni boyfriend. But on day one, you break up, and are then stuck living together for the next six months as “friends” until you can wriggle out of your tenancy. We’ve all been there, right? Well, maybe we haven’t but, watching Break Clause, it’s easy to feel as though you have. This six-part comedy-drama harks back to the peak sadcom era of the late 2010s, when pretty much every show on TV was being referred to as “the new Fleabag”, and tears were de rigueur. It will make you laugh, it might make you cry and, at the very least, it will make you think twice about moving in with anybody ever again.Break Clause is the creation of Jess Bray, who has worked on Big Boys and We Might Regret This, and is directed by Alice Snedden, co-writer and star in Starstruck. Unlike that series, Break Clause isn’t a whimsical romcom, despite a very whimsical romcom opening in which Ben (Samuel Bottomley) chooses the exact moment that his girlfriend, Lil (Lara Ricote), is about to walk across the stage at graduation to tell her that he will move down to London with her after all (men, amirite?). Don’t let the soundtrack fool you, either; you may be singing along to Baby, Now That I’ve Found You by the Foundations and Sylvester’s disco bop You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real), but it will be out of habit rather than unbridled joy.It is not unrelentingly bleak, but Break Clause captures post-university malaise in a way that is almost uncomfortably true-to-life. While Lil has a job lined up with an architectural practice, Ben is an unemployed writer, and resorts to skip diving to save on groceries. He won’t do a medical trial for money – it’s “morally dodgy”, he says – although he quickly changes his mind when he finds out that it’s £800 for each study. Much like the real world – where, post-graduation, friends’ circumstances can change seemingly magically and without warning and the word “broke” can lose all meaning – there is also a class element at play. Ben resents Lil – who, like Ricote, is Mexican-American – for coasting down to the capital with her “big fucking bank account”, while he has spent all summer working in an ice-cream van to be able to make the move. It’s a little heavy-handed at times, a little too north/south divide (Ben is a northerner, who grew up in Leeds and went to university there), but it makes its point on privilege. Not least when Ben admits to their Thanksgiving dinner guests that the turkey they are eating was sourced from a bin.View image in fullscreenDeadpan weirdness … Liam (Jack SheP), Ben (Samuel Bottomley) and Lil (Lara Ricote) in Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4 / Kerry SpicerLuckily, it is also very funny, with a weird bent that updates the sadcom premise for our current golden age of deadpan weirdness (think: Saturday Night Live UK). Speaking of SNL, there is much crossover here: Jack Shep plays Lil and Ben’s apparently guileless mate Liam (part of a winning crew that also includes Assa Kanouté and Tamika Bennett), while Hammed Animashaun plays a terrible estate agent who doesn’t even own a pen that works. Nathan Foad – one of the writers of SNL – was also in the writers room here and plays Lil’s boss, Owen, who is desperate to ingratiate himself with his team. Really, though, the best and weirdest (meant, of course, lovingly) thing here is Ricote, whose quirky comic chops make her the perfect candidate for scenes such as the one in which Lil gyrates against a wall while asking her date: “Do you like this?” (“I’d actually quite like it to stop,” he says). Her lines are among the best, in writing and delivery: “You were always so fucking negative about London,” she reminds Ben, mid-fight. “What if the water tasted weird? What if it was too loud? What aboutterrorism?!”Saturday Night Live UK review – it didn’t fail and it could have been a lot worseRead moreIt’s not a romcom, but it does end with something of a romcom scenario: Lil is offered a transfer abroad, and the pair have to figure out whether to enact their break clause (the clue was in the title, I suppose). The final episode pulls its punches a little when it comes to this dilemma, and the pair’s “quarter-psychic” stirrer neighbour, Frances (Charly Clive), who clearly has the hots for Ben. Still, things have been left open for series two, and I sincerely hope it gets made. “You have to be a lot of different people when you’re in a long relationship,” Ben’s dad, Alan (John Thomson), tells him, and it feels as though there are more versions of these two – maybe even some happier ones! Please! – that we are yet to meet.Break Clause is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: South Park has ​​AI datacentres​, sentient penises ​and a billionaire problem – in more ways than one | South Park | The Guardian
description: ​M​att Parker and Trey Stone t​ake aim at the obscenely wealthy ​in the latest episode – but it feels harder now to forget how wealthy they are
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: ​M​att Parker and Trey Stone t​ake aim at the obscenely wealthy ​in the latest episode – but it feels harder now to forget how wealthy they are
Content: Butters takles an AI problem in the second episode of South America (aka South Park).Photograph: ParamountView image in fullscreenButters takles an AI problem in the second episode of South America (aka South Park).Photograph: ParamountSouth ParkSouth Park has ​​AI datacentres​, sentient penises ​and a billionaire problem – in more ways than one​M​att Parker and Trey Stone t​ake aim at the obscenely wealthy ​in the latest episode – but it feels harder now to forget how wealthy they areJesse HassengerThu 1 Oct 2026 02.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 02.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA little over a year ago,South Parkcreators Trey Parker and Matt Stone renewed their deal with Paramount after a contentious negotiation that held up production of the 2025 season.That $1.5bn agreement raised questions about whether Paramount, newly owned by David Ellison, would really offer the creators creative freedom – or was the billionaire class solidifying its hold over a comedy series as cover to meddle in other divisions, like CBS News?The deal also made Parker and Stone likely billionaires themselves. Between this renewal and their co-ownership of the South Park intellectual property, they each have an estimated net worth of over $1bn.The second episode of the show’s 29th season examines life from either side of the billionaire/regular people divide. On one hand, Parker and Stone are unsparing of their corporate benefactors, depicting billionaires as tiny, sentient penises with high-pitched voices who are addicted to sharing their stupid opinions on podcasts and social media in their miniature city called Billionaire Weenietown.South Park – I mean, South America – is back, with no Donald Trump in sight (yet)Read moreOn the other hand, Parker and Stone aren’t exactly taking shots from outside Weenietown. Though they were certainly famous before becoming billionaires, they were still outside that world. Being a billionaire is a very different sort of outsider status no matter how much dumber Elon Musk is than you. Keep that in mind when Parker and Stone shrug off the existence of billionaires as no big deal.You can’t accuse them of not giving voice to anti-billionaire sentiment, though. This episode starts with Butters using a school presentation on “My Happy Place” as an opportunity to rant about the datacentre that has sprung up in his back yard, sapping electricity and interrupting his actual happy place: calmly watching Dr Pimple Popper videos online. Butters isn’t just using “my back yard” rhetoric to refer to events in South Park,er, South America. Billionaire Weenietown has literally sprung up in his back yard, and his parents aren’t remotely concerned. Instead, they blindly use billionaire-backed AI to redesign their home and fret that Butters has been made “libtarded” by the measles vaccination he was given as a child. “Nobody’s pissed off except for me!” Butters roars; relatable, honestly.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe other South Park kids are largely absent from this go-round, and even Butters flits in and out of his own episode. Many scenes are devoted to the billionaire weenies themselves – rendered with horrifying live-action puppetry and animation, a nice (well, kind of repulsive) callback to Parker and Stone’s fondness for crude (in both senses of the word) mixed media.View image in fullscreenButters uses a school presentation on ‘My Happy Place’ as an opportunity go on a furious rant about the datacentre literally in his backyard.Photograph: ParamountThe problem, the weenies’ leader insists, is not the preponderance of billionaires, which supposedly have been around for ages. (Technically true, though misleading; the billionaire class isgrowing, and for much of the past century there were as few as a dozen, compared to thousands now.) The real problem is that the billionaires have been ignoring the time-tested strategy of laying low and keeping quiet as they amass wealth. Parker and Stone zero in on the particularly 21st-century compulsion that the rich and powerful have, aided by the internet, to think of themselves as deep thinkers and incredibly cool.As such, the lead weenie must go over the guidelines: flying private jets everywhere, buying huge yachts for the purposes of doing drugs, and spending big on sex workers are all permissible. Going on Joe Rogan’s podcast to talk about peptides, however, is banned, as is using social media to feed Covid conspiracies or pick fights with Mark Ruffalo and Macklemore. But some billionaires just refuse to listen, no matter how many times they’re reminded of how constitutionally unequipped they are to be cool.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe episode’s philosophy eventually circles back to a treasured tenet of South Park, tellingly repeated by a billionaire weenie in this episode: “All you need to do is learn to shut up.” Isn’t that more or less Parker and Stone’s advice to everyone about everything?Indeed, that’s more or less what Butters learns to do by episode’s end. Yes, he does strike a deal to attract the billionaire infestation by putting out a podcast mic and asking for opinions (great gag), vacuuming a bunch of them up, and shuttling them over to Nashville, hoping that they bother another city instead. But his renewed sense of calm at episode’s end, enhanced by the regained ability to watch his YouTube show, does feel kind of like another Parker/Stone lesson about how ultimately, getting worked up over anything is dumb and pointless. Why is Butters repentant about getting angry about this stuff when it helped him get results, however half-arsed?Still, it’s hard to begrudge Parker and Stone their cynicism when they’re offering some solid running gags. Once again, adults want to wait until November because “that’s when Grand Theft Auto 6 comes out”, but are moved to act because the datacentres’ electricity usage threatens their ability to play it. They continually take swings at podcasters, who obviously annoy them way more than datacentres or AI does. Butters’ dad, for example, spends the entire episode on a tangent about how his wife refused to heed nonsensical warnings about vaccines: “You never listen to a single podcast I say!” he screams.As for AI, well, apparently the South Park guys feel like it has its uses, resources be damned. The episode closes with an AI-generated image of Donald Trump trudging into a bathroom stall, pulling down his semi-soiled pants, and then watching as his own billionaire penis detaches from his body and flies away. It’s a wonderfully crude and spiteful postscript – so long as you remember that it’s two funnier, smarter billionaires taking shots at a guy who is, in a sense, one of their own.Explore more on these topicsSouth ParkAnimation on TVTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the British TV event of the year finally arrives!  | Television | The Guardian
description: Let the backstabbing begin in The Celebrity Traitors. Plus: tearjerking searches in Long Lost Family. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Let the backstabbing begin in The Celebrity Traitors. Plus: tearjerking searches in Long Lost Family. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Goth-chic … Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody BurridgeView image in fullscreenGoth-chic … Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody BurridgeTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the British TV event of the year finally arrives!Let the backstabbing begin in The Celebrity Traitors. Plus: tearjerking searches in Long Lost Family. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hannah Verdier,Ali CatterallandSimon WardellThu 1 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Celebrity Traitors8pm, BBC OneWhom willMichael Sheenpretend to be in his latest role? How long before James Blunt gets his guitar out? Will Prof Hannah Fry prove to be too clever? And how well do Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan really know each other? Welcome to the TV event of the year! Last year’s inaugural starry series provided dozens of sublime small-screen moments and made the show the hottest celebrity booking in the business.Can this year’s maintain the standard?Phil HarrisonBreak Clause10pm, Channel 4A comedy built around the housing crisis was only a matter of time. This series follows Lil and Ben as their move to London goes pear‑shaped. In the time it takes Ben to confess to a drunken one-night stand, the couple go from conversations about what colour bedding they’d prefer to labelled sections in the fridge. Unfortunately, they’ve signed a six-month tenancy, so they’re stuck. It’s amusing rather than uproarious, butLara Ricoteand Samuel Bottomley are sweetly bewildered leads.PHSam & Ade Go Birding7pm, Channel 5View image in fullscreenBirds of a feather … Ade Edmondson and Sam West.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/Frank FilmsThis attempt to approximate the magic of Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing returns. It is rather lovely in its own right, even if the actors Sam West and Ade Edmondson lack Bob and Paul’s comic chemistry. They begin in the Yorkshire Dales, where Sam drags Ade out of bed at 3am for the dawn chorus. Ouch.PHLong Lost Family9pm, ITV1Two more tearjerking searches are shepherded by Davina McCall and Nicky Campbell. First comes Anita, who found a photo of a baby in her mother’s wardrobe and is finally searching for the brother who was given up for adoption. Then, Ruth traces her late sister’s son, who was taken into care.Hannah VerdierTaskmaster9pm, Channel 4This customarily spicy mixture of comics is dominated by Richard Ayoade and his disdain for the whole enterprise. However, Chloe Petts also causes problems for Alex this week by hiding something in a very awkward place indeed. Somehow, Taskmaster’s formula is sturdy enough to accommodate everyone it encounters.PHAll Creatures Great and Small9pm, Channel 5Siegfried works the veterinary practice flat out as he tries to “seize the advantage” from his rival Granville Bennett, while James’s devotion to work leaves Dorothy feeling neglected. It’s time to make amends: “Dorothy … would you consider making things between us more permanent?”Ali CatterallFilm choiceBetter Man(Michael Gracey, 2024),8.30am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenVibrant and silly … Better Man.Photograph: Entertainment Film/SkyMichael Gracey’s film about Robbie Williamssticks to the music biopic template of rise-fall-redemption, save for one aspect: he’s portrayed as a chimp. Manifesting Take That’s cheeky chappy as an ape provides a pleasingly surreal edge to the singer’s lairy tale – as well as giving Williams, who narrates, the chance to be amusingly self-deprecating. A fun, vibrant and silly film, with one set-piece, Rock DJ on Regent Street in London, that’s the equal of La La Land’s freeway number.Simon WardellThe Holdovers(Alexander Payne, 2023),9pm, Film4Alexander Payne gets back with his Sideways lead, Paul Giamatti, fora witty, bittersweet story. The actor is on fine misanthropic form as Paul Hunham, a widely disliked classics teacher at a New England boys’ boarding school in 1970. He is ordered to stay on site over the Christmas holidays to supervise the children who can’t go home, most problematically Dominic Sessa’s smart, sardonic teenager Angus. Also stuck there is the grieving canteen manager, Mary (an Oscar-winning Da’Vine Joy Randolph). Forced into uncomfortable proximity, the three slowly eke out an understanding.SWExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightEntertainment TVReality TVTV comedyMichael SheenClaudia WinklemanRomesh RanganathanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Mercy Step by Marcia Hutchinson audiobook review – a Caribbean child’s-eye view of 60s Bradford  | Books | The Guardian
description: The author captures the comedy and cruelty in this tenderly written coming-of-age tale
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The author captures the comedy and cruelty in this tenderly written coming-of-age tale
Content: Marcia Hutchinson.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverView image in fullscreenMarcia Hutchinson.Photograph: Sophia Evans/The ObserverAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewThe Mercy Step by Marcia Hutchinson audiobook review – a Caribbean child’s-eye view of 60s BradfordThe author captures the comedy and cruelty in this tenderly written coming-of-age taleFiona SturgesThu 1 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis Women’s prize-nominated novel from Marcia Hutchinson is told from the perspective of Mercy Hanson, a girl born in Bradford in 1962 to a mother she adores and a father she fears. We follow Mercy, their spirited fifth child, from birth through her toddler years to primary education. There she discovers books for the first time, in which she finds delicious escape.In her first week at school, she flees the classroom and runs all the way home after a teacher inadvertently kicks her in the forehead and then denies it. This prompts her God-fearing mother to march to school and into the classroom where she threatens the teacher with hellfire if she touches her daughter again. But Mercy’s mother is unable to protect herself or her children from her short-tempered husband who is “very tall, a proper giant” and smokes Capstan Full Strength cigarettes. Mercy’s father slaps her in her crib when she cries, and viciously beats her mother.The narrator is Hutchinson, whose reading draws out the comic and the unhappy elements of Mercy’s story and who moves seamlessly between her young protagonist’s Yorkshire tones and her mother’s Jamaican Patois. Tenderly written, with moments of sweetness and levity, the novel is named after the stair on which Mercy sits at home, clutching her beloved toy Dolly and surveying the goings on in the household. Her child’s-eye view of the world is effective here not only in showing us the preoccupations that shape childhood but in revealing the cost of the cruelty inflicted by adults.Available via Recorded Books, 9hr 3minFurther listeningFamesickLena Dunham,4th Estate, 11hr46minThe creator of the hit millennial TV series Girls narrates her memoir in which she reflects on her career, controversies, relationships and addictions along with multiple health challenges which include OCD, early menopause and endometriosis.Son of NobodyYann Martel, Canongate, 7hr 32minAaron Willis and Robin Wilcock are the narrators of this novel by the Life of Pi author. It tells of a Canadian classicist who stumbles across a lost epic poem about the Trojan war which is told from the perspective of a common soldier.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dodge City by Patrick deWitt review – a wild draft-dodging road trip | Patrick deWitt | The Guardian
description: This tale of a 60s college dropout driving across the US to avoid being sent to Vietnam is committed to both readerly pleasure and literary artifice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This tale of a 60s college dropout driving across the US to avoid being sent to Vietnam is committed to both readerly pleasure and literary artifice
Content: Patrick deWitt.Photograph: Ray BidegainView image in fullscreenPatrick deWitt.Photograph: Ray BidegainBook of the dayPatrick deWittReviewDodge City by Patrick deWitt review – a wild draft-dodging road tripThis tale of a 60s college dropout driving across the US to avoid being sent to Vietnam is committed to both readerly pleasure and literary artificeKeshava GuhaThu 1 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanadian author Patrick deWitt broke through with a western, 2011’s Booker-shortlistedThe Sisters Brothers. Now, he has taken on another hallowed American genre: the road novel. Recent works by Miranda July and Ben Markovits have, in very different ways, used the idea of the road trip as a way to dramatise midlife crisis. As befits a writer who is, in so many ways, a throwback, Dodge City returns the genre to its roots: the 1960s, and youth as opposed to middle age. A short précis – a cross-country journey undertaken by a UCLA drop-out armed only with a bag of amphetamines – makes the book sound like an Easy Rider tribute. It is typical for deWitt novels to be compared to films rather than other books. But in this case, something very different transpires.The novel opens with our protagonist, Leland “Lee” Clarke, receiving his draft notice – he is to be sent to Vietnam. He has just been expelled from UCLA for assaulting a fellow student, a rich hippy who condescends to him. This “event of violence” (a “one-punch wonder”, as Lee’s father calls it) costs him his draft deferment. Lee doesn’t consider himself a conscientious objector – that is only another form of heroism, and “the myth of the hero is at the heart of my critique of the entire exercise”. But nor does he want to go to Vietnam. He decides, instead, to dodge – to head to Canada. Younger readers may note with envy that being kicked out of college mattered a lot less when you weren’t tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt.He has, in any case, been thinking of ending things with Cal, short for Calliope, the beautiful blond daughter of east coast intellectuals. Lee is the unglamorous product of a broken home in Concrete, Washington. Cal finds him exotic: “a patrician redneck”, meaning someone who irons his T-shirts. Over time, their class differences have begun to grate. The hippy he punches is a friend of Cal’s.To raise money for the journey, he sells his own car and signs up to a “drive-away” service, delivering a brand-new Jaguar E-Type to its owner. Since he may be saying goodbye to his country for good, he plots an L-shaped route from Los Angeles to New Jersey that will allow him to say individual farewells to his father in Concrete, his mother in Montana, and his sister, a trainee nurse, in Manhattan. His brother Harry, in Minnesota, he plans to avoid. There is ancient history there.DeWitt is a throwback because he has never been near a master of fine arts programme (he dropped out of high school) and because he writes what is unquestionably “literary fiction” for a large audience, and makes a living from doing so. To Chad Harbach’s dilemma for the young North American writer, “MFA v NYC”, deWitt’s triumphant answer is “neither”. You see this in his simultaneous commitment to readerly pleasure and literary artifice; and above all in his prose.double quotation markThe reader can expect vivid minor characters, hijinks, and a tone on the margin between silliness and miseryWith his puns, archaisms, tics (“certain of the” for “some”), fondness for the passive voice and tendency to use two or three words more than strictly needed, deWitt violates almost every current MFA norm. Like one of his favourite writers, Ivy Compton-Burnett, he is a master of arch dialogue: more eloquent, and usually more enjoyable, than the naturalistic kind. DeWitt’s idiosyncrasies are not always euphonious – he can take his preference for Latin over Anglo-Saxon verbs to irritating lengths – but they remind us of the difference between having style and havingastyle.Where deWitt is most contemporary is in his preoccupation with the past. Almost all his novels have historical settings, and his protagonists are stalked by old traumas. This is why Dodge City is no Easy Rider. If the essence of hippiedom is living in the present, and the special privilege of youth is ownership of the future, Lee Clarke’s business is with his past. The visits to his parents and siblings – in the end, he finds that he can’t avoid Harry – are not token goodbyes, but attempts to settle emotional accounts.The journey itself is less one of self-discovery than of the reader discovering Lee, who is from the Hans Castorp school of hero. “Perfectly ordinary, if engaging” is how Thomas Mann described Hans. The reader sees Lee’s ordinariness right away, and over the course of the book grows more and more engaged. This is a deWitt novel, of course, and so the reader can expect – and is supplied with – vivid minor characters, hijinks, and a tone that lives confidently on the margin between silliness and misery.Patrick deWitt: ‘Poetry is good in moments of crisis’Read moreOver the course of his career, however, deWitt has changed. His books have become more contemplative, less rambunctious; if he has always trafficked in real feelings in slightly unreal settings, the settings are growing realer, and the feelings softer. Dodge City is not exactly optimistic, but its emotional tendency is towards something few would have expected of the author of The Sisters Brothers: tenderness.Dodge City by Patrick deWitt is published by HarperCollins (£18.99). title: The Last First: Winter K2 review – race up second highest mountain reveals fatal cost of human ambition | Movies | The Guardian
description: Amir Bar-Lev’s doc covering competing climbers trying to achieve something that has not been done before uncovers a fascinating tapestry of aspiration and folly
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: Amir Bar-Lev’s doc covering competing climbers trying to achieve something that has not been done before uncovers a fascinating tapestry of aspiration and folly
Content: Deadly summit … The Last First: Winter K2.Photograph: Apple TV/PAView image in fullscreenDeadly summit … The Last First: Winter K2.Photograph: Apple TV/PAMoviesReviewThe Last First: Winter K2 review – race up second highest mountain reveals fatal cost of human ambitionAmir Bar-Lev’s doc covering competing climbers trying to achieve something that has not been done before uncovers a fascinating tapestry of aspiration and follyCatherine BrayThu 1 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring the Covid pandemic in 2021, a “last first” in mountaineering was achieved:the forbidding K2 mountain was scaled in winterfor the first time. Amir Bar-Lev’s mountain-climbing doc tells the story of the competing climbers simultaneously hoping to reach the summit, several of whom do not survive the attempt. Far from being the straightforward survival-against-the-odds account that you might expect, this is a microcosm of some of humanity’s more regrettable traits, which rub up alongside each other in fascinatingly thorny ways.To take just one example: the Nepalese push for the summit comes at the cost of sacrificing the chummy camaraderie among the international climbers; but then again, Nepal is a nation rich in indigenous mountaineering expertise that has been relegated for decades to the role of humble assistant in a series of records set by foreigners. On the other hand, did all the climbers in the Nepalese team get equal credit, or was the lion’s share of the glory allotted toNirmal Purja, AKA Nims, the Nepalese social media rock star who spoke fluent English and knew how to craft a headline-worthy soundbite? (In a further strange twist,Nims was killed in an avalanche this yearin between the film’s world premiere at Sundance and wider release.) Did Nims’ record disrupt old patterns of privilege, subtly reinforce them in new ways – or both?This is just one thread in a tapestry of human ambition and folly. The starkly indifferent environment of the mountain makes for a sharp counterpoint to such concerns. K2 doesn’t know or care about national pride, commercial imperatives, underdog narratives, or what a person’s life might mean to those they leave behind. Even at base camp, temperatures on K2 in the winter can fall to -40C. Tents are torn from the ground like wings from a fly by gale-force winds. Bar-Lev’s film balances compassion for the surviving relatives of those who lose their lives with a clear-eyed view of the realities of nature. It’s a salutary lesson in the climate-change era, when a small percentage of humanity is taking a risky gamble, betting that human ingenuity will win out against physics.The Last First: Winter K2 is on Apple TV from 2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMountaineeringNepalSouth and central AsiareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Derek vs Derek review – farmers go head to head in rewilding rivalry with real bite | Movies | The Guardian
description: Two Devon neighbours face off over the future of the countryside in this warm, wry documentary about farming, conservation and some troublesome wild boar
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Two Devon neighbours face off over the future of the countryside in this warm, wry documentary about farming, conservation and some troublesome wild boar
Content: Wellies and bellies … Derek Gow (left) and Derek Banbury in Derek vs Derek, a film by  James Dawson.Photograph: Joss BarrattView image in fullscreenWellies and bellies … Derek Gow (left) and Derek Banbury in Derek vs Derek, a film by  James Dawson.Photograph: Joss BarrattMoviesReviewDerek vs Derek review – farmers go head to head in rewilding rivalry with real biteTwo Devon neighbours face off over the future of the countryside in this warm, wry documentary about farming, conservation and some troublesome wild boarLeslie FelperinThu 1 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis ebulliently accessible but never tacky British documentary finds a delightfully sneaky way to explore debates around environmental damage, agriculture and the countryside without ever being preachy, dry or patronising. The trick is to find engaging characters who happen to have opposing points of view, and while by the end most viewers would reckon that the pro-environmentalists pretty much win the argument, the conservative element of the farming community gets to have its say and make its case, earning sympathy in the process for a way of life that is itself endangered, albeit partly because of its own self-destructive practices.The twosome at the heart of the story are neighbours Derek Gow and Derek Banbury, two men in late middle age in wellies with bellies whose roughly equal-sized allotments of land (about 120 hectares) abut each other inDevon, near Dartmoor. Twinkly eyed, West Country-accented Banbury is a regular farmer like many others across the UK, rearing dairy cows and planting crops, and just about getting by as the price of milk is kept incredibly low thanks to his main customers, the supermarkets. His son works beside him and is set to inherit the spread just as Derek did, while Derek’s wife, Linda, supplements their income by running holiday cottages.Meanwhile, across the road and behind the hedgerows that he insists not be trimmed in order to protect the wildlife living therein, is Derek Gow. He is Scottish and moved to these parts years ago; he gave up sheep farming to become a conservationist, passionately devoted to rewilding his land in order to restore the biodiversity that modern farming is gradually destroying. Salty of tongue but as smart as the beavers he champions, Gow has swapped his ovine flock for wild boar whose rootling naturally reshapes the landscape. Unfortunately, this annoys the neighbours, especially Banbury and Tony to the north, when the boar breach the admittedly flimsy-looking fencing and sometimes eat sheep. (It’s not clear, though, whether the boar killed the sheep or just chowed down on ones that died naturally, a mystery worthy of Miss Marple.) What is clear, though, is that traditional farmers will be even more hopping mad if wolves are introduced to the area, a proposition discussed at a conference that Gow hosts on his land (with guests catered to by Linda Banbury).Director James Dawson started out making TV documentaries and there’s just the right amount of common touch to the way he sets up the antagonism between these two men – only to see it evolve into a more agreeable coexistence, perhaps even a symbiosis by the last act. What seems to win over Banbury is the case that Gow makes about declining insect populations, especially the pollinators, so crucial to farming, whose populations have reduced by as much as 70% in some areas thanks to insecticides and the monocultural green deserts that modern farming creates.In the end, this serves up exactly the kind of film you could sit down and watch with your Countryside Alliance-supporting uncle at Christmas and see what happens. It won’t turn him into a Green party voter all at once, but it gently builds up persuasive arguments, and in any case makes for a lovely viewing experience as a nature movie, with gorgeous shots of bitey little water voles, plucky beavers and elegant storks.Derek vs Derek is in UK cinemas from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsFarmingConservationBiodiversityWildlifeDevonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? review – Gillian Anderson fights tooth and nail in marital meltdown | Theatre | The Guardian
description: There is no shortage of sparring between Anderson and Billy Crudup in Edward Albee’s classic, though its comedy has an air of George and Mildred
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: There is no shortage of sparring between Anderson and Billy Crudup in Edward Albee’s classic, though its comedy has an air of George and Mildred
Content: Squaring up … Gillian Anderson as Martha in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? at @sohoplace, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenSquaring up … Gillian Anderson as Martha in Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? at @sohoplace, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewWho’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? review – Gillian Anderson fights tooth and nail in marital meltdown@sohoplace, LondonThere is no shortage of sparring between Anderson and Billy Crudup in Edward Albee’s classic, though its comedy has an air of George and MildredArifa AkbarThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThose who want to moan about the toxic reliance on celebrity casting and screen stars in the West End can stop right there: Billy Crudup andGillian Andersonboth began their careers on stage. Here they are now, glittering up Edward Albee’s conflagration of a play about unhappy marriage and its necessary illusions, immortalised on screen by Richard Burton and Elizabeth Taylor.Anderson and Crudup can hold their own against that landmark adaptation of the play about George, a middle-aged history professor with a sagging academic libido, and Martha, his frustrated, ceaselessly needling wife. They are confident performers and it makes sense that this 1962 American classic about conjugal warfare is taken on by two Americans, albeit under the aegis of British directorial powerhouse Marianne Elliott. If Elliott’s previous production,Les Liasons Dangereuses at the National Theatre,had what some considered an anaemic connection between its leading lovers, there is no shortage of sparks and sparring for the central couple here. They are shouty and jousting, although it does not feel dangerous or emotionally eviscerating enough between them for rather too long.View image in fullscreenThe chemistry of rivalry … Josh Dylan, Billy Crudup, Phoebe Horn and Gillian Anderson in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?Photograph: Johan PerssonTheir night-long fight at home begins after a faculty party thrown by Martha’s university president father. The pair’s guests are a younger couple – biology academic Nick (Josh Dylan) and his wife, Honey (Phoebe Horn), who first watch Martha and George play their emotional games, then get sucked in.Elliott preserves the play’s original setting, with Miriam Buether’s set an elegant 1960s-era living room complete with the all-important drinks trolley. The couples are drunk but intent on getting drunker, each refill raising the stakes.Anderson makes a formidably angry Martha as she needles away, poking George in every place it hurts. She is all hard edges and armour, agitating for a fight from the off, with a big, dirty laugh and a bawdy flirtation with Nick. Crudup is put-upon, dusty, literally all (in) grey. He initially leads with passive aggression, mansplaining Martha’s behaviour to the room and batting off her barbs with intellectual superiority or sarcasm, before entering into more confrontational territory.It ends in hand-to-hand combat but before that, laughter is eked out of the first act, which emanates a deliberately upbeat lightening of tone. George and Martha have more than a touch of George and Mildred, their game-playing a little cartoonish at times.View image in fullscreenCartoonish at times … Billy Crudup and Gillian Anderson.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe chemistry of rivalry and one-upmanship between the men is at first stronger. In between Nick and George’s Darwinian fight to be the bigger chest-beater, there is banter and a sharing of confidences – which in one of this production’s most brutal moments is used agonisingly against Nick and Honey.Horn and Dylan play their relationship with less comedy and are always compelling, Nick seeming like an overgrown frat-boy, Honey quietly tragic. They make a subtle mirror reflection of George and Martha, both with their own versions of phantom children.The most savage moments between Martha and George keep their queasily comic edges: her groin-thrusting dance with Nick which graduates to boastful “necking” in the hope to get a rise from George and her digs at his academic underachievement, delivered with bent-kneed, pointy-fingered, almost panto-like drunken accusation.Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? is a misunderstood masterpieceRead moreThe play, while exquisitely written and structured, feels tortuously long at over three hours, and though this is the point – to watch how two people destroy each other yet love each other – it still feels like a punishment. Staged in the round, it leaves little room for hiding. There is a revolve, slow for the most part, which shows their marriage up close, from every angle.For all the comedy and nervous laughs, this couple does combust and the end is devastating. Martha stops her high-pitched attack and becomes vulnerable. George lets go of his emotional cruelty. They have finally stopped the power games and play-acting of their marriage. Or have they?At@sohoplace, London, until 19 DecemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreWest EndGillian AndersonEdward AlbeeMarianne ElliottMiriam BuetherreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? review – when John Home outdid Stratford’s Bard | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Brian Logan revisits the 18th-century production of Home’s Douglas in a shouty comedy about nationalism, religion and the power of theatre
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Brian Logan revisits the 18th-century production of Home’s Douglas in a shouty comedy about nationalism, religion and the power of theatre
Content: Promising premise … Fraser Sivewright, Gavin Jon Wright, Kevin Lennon and Lewie Watson in Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? at Òran Mór, Glasgow.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenPromising premise … Fraser Sivewright, Gavin Jon Wright, Kevin Lennon and Lewie Watson in Whaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? at Òran Mór, Glasgow.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanTheatreReviewWhaur’s Yer Wullie Shakespeare Noo? review – when John Home outdid Stratford’s BardÒran Mór, GlasgowBrian Logan revisits the 18th-century production of Home’s Douglas in a shouty comedy about nationalism, religion and the power of theatreMark FisherThu 1 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the most famous heckle in Scottish theatre history. In an exclamation of nationalist zeal after a performance of Douglas at Edinburgh’s Canongate playhouse in 1756, an audience member declared playwright John Home to be better than England’s most revered dramatist. “Whaur’s yer Wullie Shakespeare noo?” went the cry.Safe to say posterity cares for Shakespeare more than Home, but the performance of Douglas remains a symbolic flashpoint. As presented by Brian Logan, writer, director and Guardian comedy critic, the play – and its excited reception – exemplifies the national and religious schisms that have played out inScotlandever since. It is one of those theatrical events that meant more politically than it did artistically.On the one hand, we find a post-Union Scotland both beholden and resistant to a dominant England. Logan shows an Edinburgh establishment eager for the success of Douglas almost as a matter of principle even before it is put in front of an audience, not least after its brusque rejection byDavid Garrickin London.All at Sea review – faked death of ‘canoe man’ inspires waves of intrigueRead moreOn the other hand, we find a post-John Knox church torn between being “o’er pagan for you, o’er pious for me,” as Home (Lewie Watson) puts it in the play. Under pressure from those who see plays as sinful, regardless of how wholesome their message, Home is forced to resign his ministry in East Lothian.All this makes a promising premise but it is a shouty, one-note production, co-presented by A Play, a Pie and a Pint with Aberdeen Performing Arts and the Traverse. Written in Scots, the play switches from a soft-target send-up of 18th-century acting to a two-dimensional debate about art and morality. The play is on fertile ground, but fails to settle on the characters and conflict that would give the factionalism of the early Scottish Enlightenment due dramatic weight.At Òran Mór, Glasgow, until 3 October, then touring until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreScotlandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best theatre to stream this month: Jack Lowden locks horns with Martin Freeman in The Fifth Step | Stage | The Guardian
description: An addict meets his sponsor in David Ireland’s two-hander, Gillian Anderson dazzles in A Streetcar Named Desire and Winsome Pinnock’s audio dramas are revelatory
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: An addict meets his sponsor in David Ireland’s two-hander, Gillian Anderson dazzles in A Streetcar Named Desire and Winsome Pinnock’s audio dramas are revelatory
Content: Darkly humorous … Martin Freeman and Jack Lowden in David Ireland’s The Fifth Step at @sohoplace, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenDarkly humorous … Martin Freeman and Jack Lowden in David Ireland’s The Fifth Step at @sohoplace, London.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe best theatre to stream this monthStageThe best theatre to stream this month: Jack Lowden locks horns with Martin Freeman in The Fifth StepAn addict meets his sponsor in David Ireland’s two-hander, Gillian Anderson dazzles in A Streetcar Named Desire and Winsome Pinnock’s audio dramas are revelatoryChris WiegandThu 1 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Fifth StepFor an addict in the Alcoholics Anonymous programme, the fifth of the 12 steps includes confessing your wrongs to another person, such as your sponsor. That act is at the heart of David Ireland’s characteristically turbulent, darkly humoroustwo-handerin which Jack Lowden and Martin Freeman lock horns. Watch out for a (sort of) cameo from Willem Dafoe as Jesus. OnNational Theatre at Homefrom 1 October.13 Going on 30: The MusicalA year afterits Manchester premiere,here is an original cast recordingled byLucie Jonesfor the musical based on the movie about a frustrated teen who suddenly becomes “30, flirty and thriving”. Earworms include Poise, performed by Jones and Grace Mouat, set in the office of the titular fashion mag: “Time to sharpen up those claws / Photoshopping out those flaws!”A Small and Quiet LightThe British resistance agent Noor-un-Nisa Inayat Khan was the first female wireless operator sent into Nazi-occupied France by the UK during the second world war. Priyanga Burford plays the intrepid hero in this bio-drama by Stephanie Street, staged at Richmond’s Orange Tree.Available 27-30 October.Slant“Not unlike singing along with one’s vacuum cleaner” was composer Nico Muhly’s analogy for his Drones project, which found harmony in ambient-style noise. Choreographer Jules Cunningham matches his works for strings, played live by the Britten Sinfonia, with a magnetic,superbly measured performancethat cuts through.From Sadler’s Wells Digital Stage.A Streetcar Named DesireWith Gillian Anderson back in the West End, starring inWho’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?alongside Billy Crudup, why not revisit her phenomenal performance as Blanche in another explosive American classic, onNT at Home? Anderson also stars in the Streetcar prequel,The Departure, a short film written by Andrew O’Hagan.Leave Taking & Other PlaysWinsome Pinnockmade history in 1994 when her play Leave Taking became the first drama by a black British female playwright to be produced at the National Theatre. This revelatory seven-hour collection brings together her lesser known audio dramas with a first-rate cast including Adjoa Andoh, Marianne Jean-Baptiste and Noma Dumezweni. FromPenguin.AwayIt is 40 years since the premiere of Michael Gow’s enduring dramaAway, about three strung-out Australian families on holiday, who are brought together through a storm. A play of revolutions and revelations, it’s directed by Matthew Lutton for Sydney Theatre Company and Malthouse Theatre. Fromthe Theatre Channel.Leslie Odom Jr: An OfferingIt’s not exactly theatre but let’s make an exception for this concert performed by the OG Aaron Burr on Broadway, whoreturned to Hamiltonin the West End this summer. The album onYouTubeincludes a more delicate, introspective version of Wait for It, contrasting with its polished power on the Hamilton album – he makes it all ripple rather than erupt.Explore more on these topicsStageThe best theatre to stream this monthTheatreDavid IrelandJack LowdenMartin FreemanComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring | Games | The Guardian
description: E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Content: Big shoulder-pads and motor-powered blades are en vogue once again … Marcus in Gears of War E-Day.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosView image in fullscreenBig shoulder-pads and motor-powered blades are en vogue once again … Marcus in Gears of War E-Day.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosGamesReviewGears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boringXbox, PC (version tested); The Coalition/Xbox Game StudiosE-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointingKirk McKeandThu 1 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery Gears of War game released in the last 20 years has made reverent reference to Emergence Day, when alien creatures emerged from the earth, single-minded in their savagery. In E-Day, you’re there to witness it: the police lights, flipped cars, ground tremors, civilians running, aliens pouring out of fissures in the earth and ripping faces off. You’re at ground zero in a squad of four soldiers called Gears – Marcus Fenix, the leader; Dom, who wants to retire; Lucas, a green cadet with a buzzcut; and the dishonourably discharged Mags. Only this dysfunctional quartet can turn the tide. With guns. Lots of ’em.Instead of answering questions raised by the ending of2019’s Gears 5, we’re back to the start to find out why Marcus has a scar on his lip and why these soldiers started strapping chainsaws on to their assault rifles. Anything that was left to the imagination is here, for you to point at and say: “I understood that reference. This is a thing that I have seen.”This series has lost its way a bit over the years, but the opening hours of E-Day will have you believing that big shoulder pads and ripping into gollum-esque freaks with motor-powered blades are en vogue once again. There are flashes of the horror and grimness of the first couple of Gears games as you’re funnelled between urban fighting arenas, with bountiful flanking routes and chunks of fallen buildings to take cover behind. But then it keeps going. And going. Long after you realise it’s all out of ideas, it’s still going.Because it’s set during and immediately after E-Day, the squad is stuck. You spend most of your time running back and forth across the city in various states of destruction. You cross the same section of bridge three times before the credits roll. Levels are flipped, daytime turns to night and you run through them again. E-Day’s two attempts at switching things up involve putting you on the gunner seat of a helicopter or making you walk slowly while people talk to you. The setting is a ball and chain that the developers are tethered to.E-Day is at its best when it turns off the lights, cranks up the horror, and forces you into enclosed spaces, but these moments make up a tiny portion of the game. The bulk of it is spent in large, open areas stuffed to the gills with collectibles. There are hundreds of them and you get a little audio chime whenever one is close. At one point, there was a particularly poignant cutscene where one of the emotionally stunted characters finally lets it all out and, just as the game transitioned from this emotional beat back to gameplay, the chime drowned out the character’s trauma to tell me there was something to pick up nearby.These open levels are big enough to require a map to navigate and they’re even peppered with side objectives (usually mini horde missions where you hold off waves of enemies after setting up defences). In Gears 5, you at least had a vehicle to zip between points of interest. Here you’re just hoofing it on foot, trying to cover as much of the map as possible without triggering the next cutscene. If you do happen to stray into the main objective by accident and try to backtrack, you’re hit with a big “mission failed” message for stepping out of bounds. You basically die. For exploring. In a game that constantly tells you to explore.View image in fullscreenEmotionally stunted … Gears of War E-Day’s full squad.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosIt’s a shame because if you rip a chainsaw through all the fat and wipe the blood spray from your eyes, there’s good meat on the bones here. Combat-wise, this is the best the series has ever felt. Characters move much less clunkily, heaving into cover, sliding under chunks of rubble, even leaping around with grace that the older Marcus Fenix and his creaky knees could only dream of.Environments crack and splinter as you fight, with glass smashing into shards that litter on the ground. Cars wobble as they take a hit, petrol stations explode and pillars crumble like the Matrix corridor scene. Blood and entrails cover everything when the dust settles after a firefight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCover feels more naturalistic and combat arenas blend nicely into the open sections, blurring the lines between exploration and fighting elegantly. Guns feel hefty and dangerous – especially the shotgun that spits acid. Active reloading, which asks you to time a button press for faster weapon reloads and more powerful bullets, remains a smart bit of game design that keeps you locked in as you fight.There’s a reason Gears of War has survived as a series long enough to earn a prequel. Its specific flavour of bloody, tactical, cover-based combat isn’t done better anywhere else. Unfortunately, E-Day is let down by everything around that fighting, resulting in a safe and repetitive experience that shows you all its ideas in the opening hours and never dares to build on them in any meaningful way.Gears of War: E-Day is out 6 Oct; £59.99Explore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesShooting gamesPCreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Balraj Khanna: Lines of Flight review – plenty of dazzle, but where is the darkness? | Art | The Guardian
description: This six-decade survey is a riot of biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacle – but the quieter works pack the biggest punch
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: This six-decade survey is a riot of biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacle – but the quieter works pack the biggest punch
Content: Verdant … A Grasshoppers Eye’s View (1966), oil on canvas, by Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryView image in fullscreenVerdant … A Grasshoppers Eye’s View (1966), oil on canvas, by Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryArtReviewBalraj Khanna: Lines of Flight review – plenty of dazzle, but where is the darkness?Ikon, BirminghamThis six-decade survey is a riot of biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacle – but the quieter works pack the biggest punchBen EasthamThu 1 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe work of Balraj Khanna will be familiar to many residents ofBirmingham, whether they know it or not. Displayed on the safety curtain at the Hippodrome, his monumental painting Astral Dance has prepared countless theatregoers for the evening’s performance since it was completed in 2001. Khanna produced a dreamlike vision of biomorphic forms – pulsing blobs, splayed fingers, blooming whorls – set against variegated orange hues. Its delightful colours and benign shapes conjure a palpable sense of magic and wonder, while also containing little that might disturb the audience’s mind beyond the curtain’s raising.This show is likewise one of flash and spectacle. The introductory text makes a point of the fact that, having been born in Punjab in 1939, Khanna witnessed the 1947 partition of India as a young boy. But if that generational trauma influenced his work as an artist, then it is apparent only in a turning away from horror towards the consolations of fantasy. He moved to London in 1962, just in time for the invention of sex (in Philip Larkin’s account), but the social revolutions of the era are no more obvious. Instead, his practice as an artist (and a picaresque novelist) summons more innocent memories: the astonishments of street entertainment and the glamorous artifice of theatre.View image in fullscreenOtherworldly … Festival (1970), acrylic and sand on canvas, Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryOne tantalising early work hints at darkness behind the dazzle. In a mulch-green landscape, a body struggles to unwrap itself from a winding shroud. Composed during the artist’s rehabilitation from a motorcycle accident, the puzzlingly titled Ladies With Qualification is so direct in its expression of suffering that you wonder whether this otherwise effervescent artist abandoned figuration because he found it too revealing. The surrounding abstractions struggle to match its charge, shoehorning blustery squiggles into strict grids that can impose only the most superficial measure of control. This is an issue that will dog the work.A standout is A Grasshopper’s Eye View, the title of which was suggested by the enduringly great Indian painter FN Souza, an early supporter of Khanna. Colourfully striped, spotted and dotted globules float through a field of verdant colour structured by regular vertical struts and subtle horizontal balances that allow the eye to wander at leisure around the picture without fear of getting lost in the confusion. The title is apt: a grasshopper might not be able to see how the wider world is organised, but can be confident enough in the prevailing rules (of gravity, of the distribution of forces) to jump from one stalk to the next.View image in fullscreenBombastic … Big Bang (2004-07), acrylic and sand on canvas, Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryThis balance is difficult to maintain. Unravelled, which presents a tangle of white lines against a night-blue background, might seem to meet Paul Klee’s maxim that making a drawing is like “taking a line for a walk”. The problem is that this walk should ideally take the artist into strange and unexpected places. Khanna’s line, by comparison, meanders around the canvas, turning back politely when it veers too close to the edges. His line feels a little too well behaved to drag its owner down into the depths of the unconscious, as artists including Klee (a clear influence) hoped it might do.It is nonetheless entertaining to see an artist try on so many styles: an abrupt diversion into hard-edge minimalism; a rhapsody in pink scattered with footprints (perhaps in homage to Jackson Pollock’s Blue Poles); a gloss finish anticipating the vogue for spray paint (it seems Khanna achieved the effect by blowing paint through a straw). But two significant paintings from 1970 show an artist getting a grip on the compositional dynamics – the systems of push and pull – that would govern the fabulous world of his paintings. In Splash and Festival this takes the form of an invisible force pulling forms resembling glistening scales and fading petals into a central vortex. They promise much.View image in fullscreenRemarkable … Sunset in Sinai (1980-81), acrylic on canvas, Balraj Khanna.Photograph: Andrew Judd/Balraj Khanna/Jhaveri ContemporaryOn the second floor, Khanna settles into a style. Characterised by forms resembling amoebas, tropical fish and bioluminescent invertebrates floating through candy-coloured galaxies, the style is cosmic in its ambitions and bombastic in scale. The late painting Big Bang is typical: a vaguely celestial landscape in which the attempts of Klee, Miró or Kandinsky to pull archetypal forms out of the primordial soup have been replaced by shapes like children’s toys drifting through a Day-Glo ether. Like magic tricks, these paintings attract your gaze but do not hold it for long. My lingering feeling was that this was no longer a failure: the artist preferred, for reasons of temperament, to excite the eye rather than trouble the mind.Nothing wrong with this, of course: paintings can do all kinds of things. Yet three remarkable works are so at odds with the general bravado that no one seems sure they were finished (the artist died in 2024, and the wall text calls them “almost studies”). Sunset in Sinai is a grainy landscape of depressions and folds that might equally be the surface of Mars or the fabric of spacetime; Dunes, in gorgeous bright pastel tones, is embedded with trails of string (a characteristic technique) that pull the colour off a series of gentle ripples; Ocean is a marvellously delicate interplay of scintillating pinks and greens. These strangely melancholy close studies of the natural world strike me as far more transcendent than the aggressively cosmic scenes by which they are surrounded. Because they are so much less eager to impress, I found myself wanting to spend time with them. They made me wish that Khanna had more often resisted the urge to entertain.Balraj Khanna: Lines of Flightis at Ikon, Birmingham, until 21 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArtPaintingExhibitionsBirminghamreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A saving gesture’: the art exhibition spotlighting US prisoners’ creations | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: A trio of shows at Michigan’s Grand Rapids Art Museum humanizes people who are incarcerated and celebrates the resilience of creativity
Author: Veronica Esposito
Headline: A trio of shows at Michigan’s Grand Rapids Art Museum humanizes people who are incarcerated and celebrates the resilience of creativity
Content: Ray Materson. Sirens and Fishes, 1993. Sock threads. 3¼x5 inches.Photograph: Courtesy of Diana BowesView image in fullscreenRay Materson. Sirens and Fishes, 1993. Sock threads. 3¼x5 inches.Photograph: Courtesy of Diana BowesExhibitions‘A saving gesture’: the art exhibition spotlighting US prisoners’ creationsA trio of shows at Michigan’s Grand Rapids Art Museum humanizes people who are incarcerated and celebrates the resilience of creativityVeronica EspositoThu 1 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 15.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan.Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator atGrand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan, who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo showsfrom artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions.View image in fullscreenJulie Green, The Last Supper [Texas 22 May 2002], 2021. Paint on found ceramic plates. Diameter: 6in.Photograph: Courtesy of Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Bentonville, Arkansas. Gift of The Last Supper Irrevocable TrustIn centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all.Lesbian artists celebrated in three new California exhibitions: ‘long overdue’Read more“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments.Death row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned.View image in fullscreenGary Tyler, Fernanda’s Touch, 2025. Quilting fabric, thread and battling. 64in x 68.25in.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Grand Rapids Art MuseumAlthough Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it wasunconstitutionalto adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. When our patients passed, the quilt was passed into their family, and it was really moving for me.”View image in fullscreenGary Tyler in his studio.Photograph: Dorian Hill, courtesy of the artist and Library Street CollectiveAs Tyler continued making quilts for dying inmates, he developed a perspective that would later inform his transition to making textile art, and that would help him be able to tell his own story through the intricate quilts that he had made for years as an artist. “You realize that that could be you, and it will be you eventually, you’re just as human as the individual you’re taking care of,” he says. “Being a hospital volunteer was one of the greatest things in my life. I never would have thought that I had the creative gene in me.”Tyler’s quilts tend to be backgrounded by static colors shot through with rich texture and repeating motifs – flowers in one, abstract tear shapes in another. The scenes they depict are vivid and powerful: a bull smacking over a red table, a man literally struggling under the weight of the world, a child in shackles with their back turned to us.One work that stands out in Tyler’s mind depicts a moment from the trial, when he was being led away from the courthouse in handcuffs by an escort of police, while a crowd of supporters cheered for him. “I got this surge of energy,” he says. “I wanted to raise my hands in a fist, but I had handcuffs on, with deputies holding my arms, but I still managed to show defiance, that despite what happened I would continue to fight.”The Grand Rapids trio is rounded out by a comprehensive museum survey of Ray Materson, the outsider embroidery artist, who developed his signature technique of working with unraveled socks by necessity while serving seven years in prison due to drug addiction.View image in fullscreenRay Materson. Lords and Ladies, 1989. Sock threads. 2.75in x 2in.Photograph: Courtesy of Bob RennieWhile boxer shorts and bedsheets could supply Materson with plenty of white thread, socks were of special importance to him, as they gave him the colors that he required in order to create intricate scenes. He would spend hours and hours simply getting the dearly needed materials. “Ray said to me one time: ‘Your biggest enemy in prison is the clock,’” said Warren. “For him to be able to spend days and days in this meditative act was such a saving gesture.”Taryn Simon on her most ambitious exhibition yet: ‘It’s built almost like a novel’Read moreMaterson’s skills quickly became known to the other inmates, who soon began asking him to make embroidery of loved ones or items such as national flags with great symbolic meaning. These pieces gave Materson a purpose and allowed the men he created for to experience a sense of identity and selfhood in a profoundly dehumanizing environment.Life in prison has stuck with Materson, who to this day sources vintage socks like the ones he used while in jail in the 1980s. “Their nylon has the stretchability that he needs in order to work,” explained Warren. His work tends to depict intense scenes, often derived from the likes of Shakespeare, Ibsen and Chekhov, as well as royalty like Queen Victoria and Catherine the Great. While small, often measuring just 2in x 3in, the works are filled with pathos and are a wonder to behold.“This show brings a lot of shock at the facts of what’s the reality for a lot of people, but they also bring a lot of hope,” said Warren, sharing her hopes that the art on display can both humanize and inspire, as well as show audiences that artistic creation can be transformative for them too. “Ray was on a track of death through his addiction, but because of art his life turned around into something defined by creativity and giving.”Julie Green: The Last Supper; Gary Tyler: Rebirth and Ray Materson: Metamorphosis are all at Grand RapidsArtMuseum from 3 October 2026 until 24 October 2027 (Green) and 3 January 2027 (Tyler, Materson)Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsArtMuseumsPaintingUS prisonsDesignfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Heart-meltingly good: the best cooking chocolate to buy | Food | The Guardian
description: Those cookies and cakes will only be as tasty as the chocolate you use in their baking. Here are my favourites
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Those cookies and cakes will only be as tasty as the chocolate you use in their baking. Here are my favourites
Content: You cannot make Edd Kimber's double chocolate olive oil cookies with bad chocolate. Just don’t.Photograph: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.View image in fullscreenYou cannot make Edd Kimber's double chocolate olive oil cookies with bad chocolate. Just don’t.Photograph: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.The chocolate diariesFoodHeart-meltingly good: the best cooking chocolate to buyThose cookies and cakes will only be as tasty as the chocolate you use in their baking. Here are my favouritesAnnalisa BarbieriThu 1 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf course, you can bake with any sort of chocolate, and I do, but being Chocolate Correspondent means I have a lot of it spare, despite giving much away. I once made mychocolate rye cookiesand served them to a friend. She went away and made her own. “Mine were nice,” she said, “but not as nice as yours.” Mine had about £40’s worth of craft chocolate in them.Clearly this is madness and outside the remit of all but the privileged, but the quality of chocolate you use in baking really does make a difference. Although I can and do use chocolate bars chopped up post-testing, having specific cooking chocolate (which may have more cocoa butter in it for easier melting) makes life easier, because it often comes either in pastilles or little chocolate buttons, which are bliss for the lazy. The go-to for a lot of professional chefs isValrhona. I love the pastilles: for rich chocolate baking, the Ghana 80% is my favourite (I also love it as an eating chocolate), but theGuanaja 70%is more readily available. There are lots of variations in each cacao percentage, from 29%-85%, with different flavour profiles.
