For white-chocolate cooking, theDulcey, biscuity and caramelly, is hard to beat.Formy little breakfast briochesorItalian breakfast cake, and if you’re serious about baking (because it comes in 2kg bags), my go-to is Islands, which has micro chocolate buttons (in75% darkor55% milk) that are brilliant.View image in fullscreen‘Ideal as inclusions in cakes or cookies’: Pierre Marcolini cooking chocolate buttons.Photograph: Juan Vrijdag/Pierre MarcoliniPierre Marcolini recently launched anexcellent cooking chocolate rangefrom 45% cocoa to 82%. They come in small button shapes (but not as small as the Islands minis), which are ideal as inclusions in cakes or cookies, or for easy melting. They also make rather excellent munchies: I mix mine with salted popcorn for a relatively healthy snack.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe chocolate diariesChocolatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cheaper chips and melty mint slices: I try making five common ultra-processed foods from scratch – without the additives | Australian food and drink | The Guardian
description: UPFs are regarded as cheaper and faster than homemade dishes – but how much time and money will it cost to make alternatives?
Author: Jen Sherman
Headline: UPFs are regarded as cheaper and faster than homemade dishes – but how much time and money will it cost to make alternatives?
Content: Jen Sherman's homemade mint slice on the left, and an ultra-processed Mint Slice from the packet on the right.Composite: Guardian designView image in fullscreenJen Sherman's homemade mint slice on the left, and an ultra-processed Mint Slice from the packet on the right.Composite: Guardian designAustralian food and drinkCheaper chips and melty mint slices: I try making five common ultra-processed foods from scratch – without the additivesUPFs are regarded as cheaper and faster than homemade dishes – but how much time and money will it cost to make alternatives?Jen ShermanThu 1 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 20.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the past five years, I have been trying tocut down on the amount of ultra-processed foods my family consumes. There have beenvarious strategies we used tomanage this. One question comes up time and again: how much does this all cost? UPFs are often regarded as cheaper than preparing a from-scratch meal, and they’re a lot less time-consuming. Convenience is one of their selling points, after all.A nutritionist and public health researcher at Deakin Institute for Physical Activity and Nutrition, Dr Priscila Machado, describes UPFs as “branded, commercial formulations made from cheap ingredients extracted or derived from whole foods, combined with additives, and mostly containing little to no whole food”. She says looking at ingredient lists is a practical way to spot them: “If there are ingredients you don’t recognise or use at home, like protein isolates, emulsifiers, colour, flavours, and other additives, it’s probably ultra-processed.”Consuming these sorts of ingredients occasionally or in small quantities isn’t a problem. Additionally, there is no strong evidence supporting ranking the healthfulness of different types of UPF. Machado says the bigger concern is the role of UPFs in overall dietary patterns. “The evidence shows that the proportion of UPFs in our diets is what matters most; in Australia, UK and US almost half or more of the total energy consumption comes from UPFs. The issue is that UPFs can gradually crowd out foods and meals made from scratch ingredients, often without people really noticing that shift.”Three simple vegetarian spring pasta recipes from Julia Busuttil NishimuraRead moreMachado stresses that individuals aren’t to blame for high levels of UPF consumption, instead it is a reflection of the food system, which is “dominated by powerful UPF corporations that use those cheap ingredients and intensive marketing to make these products highly available, convenient and profitable”, she says.“We need to be careful not to put the responsibility back on individuals by telling people they should cook everything from scratch. People are making food choices within environments where UPFs are often cheaper, quicker and easier, particularly for families with limited time or money.”With that in mind, I set out to find out exactly how much time and money it costs to make non-UPF versions of five common UPF foods: chicken nuggets, muesli bars, almond milk, potato chips and Mint Slices. This experiment was not to say, “Look how easy it is to make these foods from scratch” but to ask, “Well, how muchdoesit cost to make these from scratch?”I used proportional cost allocation when calculating the price of homemade food items, so if I used 25% of a $10 bottle of oil, I costed this at $2.50.Chicken nuggetsI once made chicken nuggets from chicken mince. I followed a reputable recipe but no one in my family liked them. I have since had much better success making “nuggets” out of chicken thighs. To make them, I cut the thighs into nugget-sized pieces, then dip them in a mixture of egg, mayonnaise, garlic powder, salt, and pepper. They are then coated in bread crumbs (that have been sprayed with oil and baked briefly so they are golden brown), next I place the nuggets on a wire rack on a baking tray, spray them with oil, and bake until they are golden brown.For this attempt to find out the cost of a non-UPF nugget, I used store-bought bread crumbs containing only flour, yeast and salt, and made my own mayonnaise, because I couldn’t find store-bought mayonnaise without emulsifiers.View image in fullscreenChicken nuggets from scratch, made with chicken thigh, egg, oil and breadcrumbs.Photograph: Jen ShermanIn terms of time, the homemade mayo took about 20 minutes to make – I used a whisk and a bowl; it would have been quicker if I had used some kind of machine.Our kitchen set-up is temporary at the moment as we’re in the process of moving, so cooking takes longer than usual. In my previous home, without making the mayonnaise, this recipe typically took about 45 to 50 minutes.The non-UPF nuggets cost about double the UPF ones and are definitely more time-consuming but this is one UPF food I’m happy to make myself – it tastes significantly better. My eight-year-old’s verdict was two thumbs up and “this is better than restaurant nuggets”.Homemade cost:$21.74 for 800g ($2.72 per 100g)Packet cost:$5.50 for one 400g bag of frozen Ingham’s crumbed chicken breast nuggets ($1.38 per 100g)Homemade cook time:1 1/2 hoursPacket cook time:18 minutesMuesli barsMuesli bars are one of the easiest snacks for kids and I often think of them as one of those tricky foods that don’tseemunhealthy. But a glance at the ingredient list of the ones I’d been buying (Uncle Tobys chewy choc chip) reveals they are most definitely an ultra-processed food, as are other bars in the same aisle.View image in fullscreenMuesli bars from scratch, made with rolled oats, butter, honey and vanilla extract.Photograph: Jen ShermanThe muesli bar recipe I followed involved melting butter and honey, adding vanilla extract, then mixing it through the rolled oats. Next I pressed the mixture firmly into a slice tray lined with baking paper and baked. When done, the bars were chilled completely in the fridge before slicing. They tasted good but definitely fell apart more than store-bought muesli bars. That may have been user error.They are significantly cheaper than the ones I buy from the supermarket and weren’t particularly onerous to make – 10 minutes of prep, 20 minutes to bake, then chill time.My kids liked them fine but prefer the ones with chocolate chips. I’ve made them before with chocolate chips but for the purposes of this article I left the chips out, because I couldn’t find any without emulsifiers. I would make these again but next time I’d add the chocolate chips.Homemade cost:$3.25 for 14 muesli bars ($0.23 per unit)Packet cost:$5.50 for a box of six Uncle Toby’s chewy choc chip muesli bars at Woolworths ($0.92 per unit)Homemade cook time:30 minutes, plus at least one hour chill time.Packet cook time:InstantAlmond milkView image in fullscreenRaw almonds and water, ready to be blended to make almond milk.Photograph: Jen ShermanNon-dairy milk is a growing market, driven by dietary restrictions, environmental concerns and innovation in the non-dairy milk industry. Almond milk is a common non-bovine milk and one that I have bought in the past. The ingredient lists of four widely available brands of almond milk I looked at included various gums, stabilisers and emulsifiers, and almonds made up just 2.5% to 7% of the ingredients.I tried to make my own almond milk with just raw almonds and water. I soaked one cup of almonds overnight, then drained and rinsed them. I added them to a blender with two cups of water and blended on high for two minutes. I poured it out into a nut milk bag over a fine mesh strainer (cheesecloth will also work if you don’t have a nut milk bag), and squeezed. I had successfully milked almonds!I used one cup of raw almonds which yielded about two cups (500ml) of milk. My non-UPF version cost about double store-bought varieties and took longer than simply unscrewing a cap. While the active cooking time was only a few minutes, there was also soaking time and clean-up.View image in fullscreenAlmond milk made from scratch.Photograph: Jen ShermanI don’t reallylovestore-bought almond milk, so I was surprised when the almond milk I made tasted creamy and full, with a lovely depth of flavour. It turns out I do like almond milk – when it’s made with more almonds.Homemade cost: $2.90 for 500ml ($5.80 per litre)Packet cost:Between $1.85 and $3.40 per litreHomemade cook time:At least two hours of soaking, five minutes of active prep, plus clean-upPacket cook time:InstantPotato chipsIt is possible to buy crisps that are not ultra-processed, when the ingredient list simply reads “potatoes, oil, salt”. But if you want a flavour other than plain salt, such as barbecue or salt and vinegar, you run into ingredients that are markers of UPF including colourings and flavourings. I wanted to see if it was possible to recreate those chip flavours at home.I thinly sliced two potatoes, soaked them in water to remove the starch, then patted them dry and placed them on a baking tray in a single layer. I sprayed them with oil and sprinkled on some seasoning mixture before baking. I tried to make a barbecue flavour using smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, brown sugar, and salt. For salt and vinegar chips, I used vinegar powder and salt.View image in fullscreenPotato chips from scratch, made with potatoes oil and seasoning mixtures.Photograph: Jen ShermanFinancially, the non-UPF version cost a fraction of packet chips. But they took about three hours to make. This was because I used a small oven that could only hold two trays at a time, and when two potatoes have been sliced thinly and need to be baked in one layer, that is a lot of trays. It might also have been quicker to use an air fryer.View image in fullscreen‘Tasted, looked and felt like potato chips.’Photograph: Jen ShermanThe seasonings I made tasted great and I liked them more than store-bought barbecue flavoured chips. They were surprisingly crunchy, and actually tasted, looked and felt like potato chips. My husband and children also said they were better than chips from the shop. They were best eaten straight out of the oven – by the next day, the chips had lost their crunch. Though if I had stored them in a proper, airtight container that may have helped.Given how long it took to bake these, I think I will keep buying packet potato chips.Homemade cost:$5.70 for 670g ($0.85 per 100g)Packet cost:$6 for a 165g bag of Red Rock Deli sea salt and balsamic vinegar chips ($3.64 per 100g)Homemade cook time:Three hoursPacket cook time:InstantMint slicesI first made mint slices while living in the US. I wanted to eat a Mint Slice but couldn’t buy them. I found a recipe for a homemade version and followed it with great success. The challenge for this article was finding a chocolate for the coating that was not a UPF – almost all commercial chocolate has some kind of emulsifier. After much searching, I discovered that Lindt 70% dark chocolate has no emulsifiers (ingredients: cocoa mass, sugar, cocoa butter, vanilla). Mint Slices were a go.I made 19 biscuits and each was about 1.5 times the size of a Mint Slice made by Arnott’s.View image in fullscreenAdding peppermint cream to mint slices made from scratch.Photograph: Jen ShermanView image in fullscreenMint slices made from scratch using dark chocolate, flour, sugar, cocoa powder, butter, eggs, icing sugar, vanilla extract and peppermint essence.Photograph: Jen ShermanWe did a side-by-side taste test with homemade and packaged biscuits. The kids, my husband and I agreed: mine were more chocolatey and less minty than store-bought. Mine were also more melty. We also thought my Australian version tasted different to those I’d made before. In the US, I’d used peppermint oil (as opposed to essence), and 60% dark baking chocolate with emulsifiers. Those were mintier, the chocolate flavour wasn’t as strong, and they were also less melty, so closer to the Mint Slices from a packet. This makes sense – using ultra-processed ingredients get you closer to the taste of ultra-processed food.Homemade cost:$26.10 for 19 biscuits ($1.37 per unit)Packet cost:$5.50 for 200g packet with 13 biscuits ($0.42 per unit)Homemade cook time:Two hoursPacket cook time:InstantThe verdictAt the end of this process, I’ve learned it is cheaper to buy the ingredients for muesli bars and potato chips. Chicken nuggets, almond milk and mint slices all cost about twice the UPF price – but you do end up consuming more actual chicken, almonds and chocolate. It was no surprise that, in terms of time, it takes a lot longer to cook or bake from scratch than to open a packet.There are some items that – for me – are worth making from scratch. My goal is UPF reduction, not elimination. Machado says: “At an individual level, it also doesn’t have to be all or nothing. People don’t need to make their own bread or mayonnaise to improve their diet. The aim is to progressively shift the overall dietary pattern towards more minimally processed foods and meals prepared from scratch … in ways that are realistic for their time and budget.”In the spirit of the bookMake the Bread, Buy the Butter: make the nuggets, buy the chips.A detailed breakdown of the ingredient quantities and costs for this experiment can be found onJen Sherman’s SubstackExplore more on these topicsAustralian food and drinkUltra-processed foodsFoodHealth & wellbeingBakingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A perry respectable alternative to wine – in praise of pear cider  | Food | The Guardian
description: Beyond Babycham there is a whole cottage industry of small-batch fine perries that are surprisingly perfect for pairing with food
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Beyond Babycham there is a whole cottage industry of small-batch fine perries that are surprisingly perfect for pairing with food
Content: Wilding ciderproduces “November,” a limited-release sparkling perry made with late-season, hand-pressed pears.Photograph: Olivia Estebanez/The Fine Cider CompanyView image in fullscreenWilding ciderproduces “November,” a limited-release sparkling perry made with late-season, hand-pressed pears.Photograph: Olivia Estebanez/The Fine Cider CompanyFoodA perry respectable alternative to wine – in praise of pear ciderBeyond Babycham there is a whole cottage industry of small-batch fine perries that are surprisingly perfect for pairing with foodMina HollandThu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“They’re gorgeous little beasts,”Eddie Izzard said on the subject of pearsin her mid-1990s show Definite Article, “but they’re ripe for half an hour and you’re never there!” Little did she know that she was touching on one of the difficulties of making perry – the fermented juice of perry pears – a drink that remains, in comparison with cider, a relative cottage industry.There are some notable exceptions to that rule (anyone familiar withBabychamandLambriniwill have tried a commercial perry, albeit an industrially made one), but the perry I’m interested in is made from specific perry pears grown on vast trees in ancient, biodiverse orchards in the British West Country and northern France; it is made in small batches, because, as Izzard points out, pears are ripe for a notoriously short time; additionally, they begin to rot from the inside out and, such is the height of those gnarly branches, they can be difficult to pick, too. “Perry-making is hard to do well,” says Felix Nash ofthe Fine Cider Company, a retailer that specialises in craft drinks made from apples and pears.Nash holds that “fine perry”, a term he uses to distinguish his perries from the industrial kind, is a blank slate; unlike cider, it has no mass-market presence beyond the likes of Babycham, which is largely seen as a kitsch anachronism. The fine perries that Nash sells run the gamut from medium-dry and sparkling to sweet and still; aperitifs to pudding accompaniments. He lists vintage perries, single-varietals and blends of pears with names that make me want to take up wassailing: hendre huffcap, butt, green horse, thorn, gin … Perry-making dates back centuries in Gloucestershire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, and is said to have been one of Elizabeth I’s favoured tipples.Historic perry may be, but, as we head into 2026’s harvest season, it occurs to me that there is much to love about it for the modern drinker. It has a naturally low ABV (usually 5-6%) and pears contain sorbitol, a non-fermentable sugar alcohol that can leave even a technically dry perry with an impression of sweetness. It’s also surprisingly food-friendly; Nash cites the classic pairing with oysters or cheese, while I enjoyed a bottle of Tom Oliver’s sparkling medium-dry We Aren’t Stopping Now with chilli paneer; it would also be a doozy with most oily fish.Then there’s the price. The production of fine perry has all the elements of fine wine, Nash says, reflecting fruit varietal, terroir, vintage and skill (some of his perries are made using the champagne method, others have tannins with the grip of red wine): “It’s largely the little known nature of great perry that has helped keep the cost where it currently is.” Without wine’s prestige, and with relatively minimal transport costs and, at those ABVs, considerably lower UK alcohol duty than wine, some of the bottles in today’s picks are nothing short of a giveaway.Six perries - and what to pair with themOliver’s Fine Perry Wild Ferment Rolling Blend£3.50 (330ml) Secret Bottle Shop, 6.5% A great introduction to fine perry, this has notes of elderflower and is happy with everything from butter to spice.Ross On Wye Cider & Perry Company Red Longdon Perry 2025£12 (750ml) Fine Cider, 5.8%. Dry enough for an aperitif, grippy enough for a roast or a cheeseboard – extraordinary and moreish.Little Pomona FaussetPét Nat Perry2023£15 (750ml) Little Pomona, 6%. Juicy, aromatic and sparkling single-varietal perry. I drank it with mapo tofu.Wilding Cider Moorcroft 2022£25 (750ml) Fine Cider, 10.1%. Acid, structure, tannin and an unusually high ABV make this single-varietal perry an excellent stand-in for pudding wine.Eric Bordelet Poiré Authentique£16.50 (750ml) Gnarly Vines, 5%. A Norman perry made by a one-time sommelier, this is off-dry, biodynamic and bloody lovely.Oliver’s We Aren’t Stopping Now 2024£14 (750ml) Fine Cider, 5.5%. Struggling to find a wine pairing for your curry night? Look no further than this elegant, medium-dry perry made by a titan in British cider- and perry-making.Explore more on these topicsFoodCiderBritish food and drinkFrench food and drinkFruitfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballs | Food | The Guardian
description: A deep and ingredient-busy take on the classic, constructed with four layers of pasta and a little geometric thinking
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A deep and ingredient-busy take on the classic, constructed with four layers of pasta and a little geometric thinking
Content: Rachel Roddy’s lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballsA deep and ingredient-busy take on the classic, constructed with four layers of pasta and a little geometric thinkingRachel RoddyThu 1 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBearing in mind that lasagne is a construction, it pays to start with some easygoing geometry. That is, think about the size of the dish you want to fill in relation to the size of the sheets you are using and the number of layers you want the lasagne to have. For four to six servings, I use a particular ceramic dish, because its 20cm x 29cm proportions mean that, broadly speaking, two fresh sheets of shop-bought egg pasta or four dried ones make a single layer (homemade pasta can be rolled and cut with scissors to whatever size you like, so is less relevant here).Having calculated how many sheets are needed for each layer, the next question is: how high do you want your lasagne building to be? Height depends on the density of the filling, which, in the case of this week’s recipe, includes sausagemeat rolled (using wet hands and speed) into small, grape-sized meatballs that act like height-boosters in shoes. This elevation, along with tomato sauce and three cheeses, means that, even with just four layers, this lasagne has depth and cuts into satisfying squares. All this emphasis on the dish is also fitting because the word lasagne seems to derive from the Latinlasanum(cooking vessel), which in turn derives from the ancient Greek λάσανον, which signified either a cooking vessel or a tripod set over a fire.Back to 2026, though, and this busy, joyful lasagne borrows from both the Neapolitanlasagne di carnevale, with the inclusion of very small meatballs, tomato sauce and mozzarella, and a Sicilian lasagne in the use of ricotta loosened with a little milk (so it has a soft, spreadable texture) in place of bechamel. A four-layer lasagne is also convenient in that all the other components are split into quarters, then spread, splattered or arranged on each of the layers. I suggest using fresh pasta, but dried works, too, although that will need a more liquid tomato sauce to cook through. I also recommend a 30-second pre-boil, which starts to cook and firm the sheets, although please disagree and do otherwise.Leave the lasagne to rest for at least 30 minutes, so the flavours can settle and the whole thing firms up, before serving in geometric squares.Lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballsServes4-64 tbspolive oil1 smallgarlic clove, peeled and gently bashed so it’s broken but still intact250g sweet cherry tomatoes, chopped1400g tinplum tomatoes, crushed or passed through a food mill1 pinchred chilli flakesSalt1 small handfulbasil4 pork or vegetarian sausages250gricottaMilk, as required300g mozzarella, drained for at least 12 hours75-100g parmesan8-12 sheetsfreshlasagne, depending on the size of the sheets and your dishWorking in a deep frying pan or saucepan on a low heat, warm the olive oil and garlic for a minute or two. Add the fresh and tinned tomatoes and the chilli, stir, then raise the heat so the tomatoes simmer in a lively way for about 20 minutes, mashing them with the back of a spoon to break up any lumps. Once the sauce has lost any wateriness, add salt and a few basil leaves, then set aside.Squeeze the sausage meat from its casings, then, working with wet hands, form the meat into grape-sized balls. In another frying pan, heat two tablespoons of oil and fry the balls lightly, so they’re almost, but not quite, cooked through.Beat the ricotta with the milk and some salt to form a soft paste, thinly slice the drained mozzarella and grate the parmesan.If you are doing the pre-boil, bring a large pan of salted water to a boil; have a bowl of cold water ready and spread a tea towel alongside it. Working in batches, drop the pasta sheets into the boiling water for 30 seconds, lift into the cold water to cool, then lay them out on the tea towel.Construct the lasagne in a 20cm x 29cm (or similar sized) dish, bearing in mind that it has four layers, so divide all of the components by four, but the meatballs only by three, because they don’t go on top. Rub the dish with oil, then make a base layer of two (or more) pasta sheets. Spread with a quarter of the ricotta and the tomato sauce, dot with meatballs and mozzarella, some basil, and scatter over parmesan. Cover with a second layer of pasta and repeat until everything is used up. Finish with a scattering of parmesan.Bake at 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 for 25 minutes, until the top is golden and the sides are bubbling. Leave to rest for 30 minutes, then cut into squares and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkPastaMain courseStarterCheeseTomatoesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: From breakfast pancakes to dinner sides and pudding: Alissa Timoshkina’s apple recipes | Autumn food and drink | The Guardian
description: Fried in pancakes, braised with duck, pickled with a roast chicken or baked for pudding, apples are one of autumn’s star ingredients
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fried in pancakes, braised with duck, pickled with a roast chicken or baked for pudding, apples are one of autumn’s star ingredients
Content: Photograph: Laura Edwards / The Guardian/Photographer - Laura Edwards /The Guardian. Food Styling - Joss Herd. Prop Styling - Tabitha HawkinsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Laura Edwards / The Guardian/Photographer - Laura Edwards /The Guardian. Food Styling - Joss Herd. Prop Styling - Tabitha HawkinsAutumn food and drinkFrom breakfast pancakes to dinner sides and pudding: Alissa Timoshkina’s apple recipesFried in pancakes, braised with duck, pickled with a roast chicken or baked for pudding, apples are one of autumn’s star ingredientsAlissa TimoshkinaThu 1 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew ingredients are as familiar as apples, yet few carry such symbolic weight. Peaking just as the season’s begin to turn, they are the ultimate symbol of nature’s abundance, imbued with a sense of nostalgia for the retreating sunlight. The symbolism became unexpectedly tangible to me during a recent autumn apple-picking trip with my family: surrounded by branches heavy with fruit, I found myself seeing the humble apple with fresh awe. It looked nothing short of nature’s miracle. Native to the mountains of central Asia, near the modern Kazakhstan-China border, it has travelled further than perhaps any other fruit, becoming at home in cuisines from Normandy to New York, Caucasus to Kashmir. Sweet or savoury, everyday or celebratory, the apple is truly universal. Its versatility always reminds me of the simple joy of cooking with the seasons.Breakfast appleoladky(pictured top)Prep10 minCook25 minMakes24, to serve6200g plain flour,sifted1 shy tspbaking powder¼ tspbicarbonate of sodaA pinch of cinnamonA pinch of fine sea salt1 medium egg (50g)200ml whole milk50g unsalted butter,melted, plus extra for frying3 sweet apples,cored, then 1 grated and 2 thinly sliced on a mandoline2 tbsprunny honey, plus extra for servingNeutral oil,for fryingGreek yoghurt, for servingIn a bowl, mix all the dry ingredients together, then in a separate bowl whisk the wet ones, including the grated apple.Gently fold the wet and dry ingredients together with a silicone spatula – make sure you don’t over mix it. Leave to rest at room temperature for five minutes, or until you see bubbles appear.Heat a frying pan on a low-medium heat, and add enough oil to coat it evenly. Scoop up the batter (about 15-20g per oladky) and drop it into the pan – it should start sizzling straight away. Depending on the size of your pan, you should be able to cook around four oladky at the same time.Fry them on one side for 40 seconds, adding a few slices of apple on top halfway through cooking.Flip them over, adding a teaspoon of butter to help the apples soften and caramelise, and continue cooking undisturbed for 90 seconds to two minutes, until the pancakes have puffed up and the apples are caramelised.Repeat with the remaining batter and apple slices. Serve with Greek yoghurt and a drizzle of honey.Roast chicken salad with kale, fennel, pickled apples and tahini ‘mayo’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Photography: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.Prep20 minRest30 minCook15 minServes4For the salad150-200g kale,washed and stalks removed2 tbspextra-virgin olive oilFlaky sea salt andblack pepperJuice of ¼ lemon1grannysmith apple,thinly sliced on a mandolin2 celery sticks,sliced diagonally into long wedges1 small fennel bulb,trimmed and thinly sliced on a mandoline25gflat-leaf parsley,leaves picked, plus extra to garnish1 roast chicken breast(about 200g), or equivalent chicken meat leftover from a roast, shredded2 tbsptoasted sunflower seeds,to garnishFor the pickle4 tbspapple cider vinegarJuice of ½ lemon1 tbsprunny honeyA pinch of flaky sea salt1granny smith,finely dicedFor the tahini mayo150mltahini3 tbspextra-virgin olive oilJuice of ½ lemon1 tbsprunny honey1 tbspapple cider vinegarFlaky sea salt, to tastePickle brine(see above)1 ice cube,or 2 tsp of ice-cold waterStart by making the pickle. In a medium jar, mix two tablespoons of cold water, the vinegar, lemon juice, honey and salt. Add the diced apple and shake well to combine. Leave to rest in the fridge for about 30 minutes.Next, prep the kale. Massage the kale with the olive oil, salt and lemon juice in a large bowl until wilted. Set aside.To make the tahini mayo, add the first six ingredients into a mixing bowl, finishing with all the apple pickle brine. Start mixing slowly with a fork; if the paste gets too thick or splits, add an ice cube or ice-cold water and continue stirring gently, until you reach a silky consistency (you will!).Back to the salad. To the bowl with the kale, add the fresh and pickled apples, celery, fennel, parsley and chicken. Add a third of the tahini dressing and give everything a gentle toss.Transfer the salad to a large bowl or sharing platter, drizzle over the tahini sauce in wriggly lines, then scatter over the sunflower seeds and extra torn parsley leaves. Finish with an extra sprinkle of sea salt and a generous crack of black pepper. You will have some tahini dressing left over; serve this in the jar alongside.Duck legs with braised sauerkraut, apples and cranberriesView image in fullscreenPrep10 minCook2 hrServes41-2 tbspduck fat4 duck legs,at room temperatureSea salt and black pepper2 red onions,peeled and thinly sliced1 tsp caraway seeds1 tspdried thyme200ml red wine½ small red cabbage,shredded650g jarsauerkraut with brine3 red apples,sliced into chunky wedges (about 6-8 each)1 orange,zest and juice2 tbspdried cranberries1 tspsugar4 bay leaves400ml stock (vegetable or chicken)Melt a tablespoon of the duck fat in a heavy-based casserole. Pat the duck legs dry and salt on both sides, then place them in the casserole skin side down and sear on a medium-high heat for 10 minutes, to achieve a seductive crispy skin. Transfer the legs to a plate and set aside while you get on with the rest.Depending on how fatty the duck legs are, add another tablespoon of duck fat to the casserole. Lower the heat to medium, and fry the onion with a pinch of salt, the caraway and thyme for eight to 10 minutes.Deglaze the pan by adding the wine and scraping off any delicious bits of fat and onion that might be stuck to the pan. Cook with the lid off for a minute. Next, add the remaining ingredients, stir well to combine and bring to a gentle simmer.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the duck legs on top of the cabbage, skin side up, cover with a lid, and put in theoven for 90 minutes, or until tender.The dish goes down a treat as is (with a glass of red wine, of course), or add some creamy mash or roast potatoes for an extra comforting autumnal meal.Fermented apple salsaView image in fullscreenThis is a very versatile ferment: add it to salads or egg mayo (instead of capers), use it to top avocado or layer into a cheese toastie filling.Prep15 minCook15 minFerment3 days+Makes1 x 1.5L jarFor the apple salsa3 largegrannysmithapples,cored and diced2 spring onions,trimmed, white and green parts finely sliced100g white grapes,quartered2 celery sticks,diced1 jalapeño,seeds and pith removed, flesh finely diced10g fresh dill,stems and fronds finely chopped1 tspfennel seedsFor the brine7g fine, non-iodized sea salt(roughly 1½ level tsp)350ml filtered waterSterilise a 1.5L jar by running it through the dishwasher, then let it cool down before handling. Mix all the apple salsa ingredients in a bowl to make sure everything is well distributed. Make the brine by dissolving the salt in the water.Pack the jar tightly with the apple mix, and top with the brine, leaving about two fingers’ worth of space at the top (for the weight). Put a fermentation weight on top, close the lid and place in a small bowl to catch any leakages. Leave at room temperature and out of direct sunlight for three to six days, depending on how warm the room is.The salsa is ready when the brine becomes effervescent and the apples acquire a pleasant, piquant, sour quality. At this point, remove the weight, and transfer to the fridge. The salsa will keep in the fridge for up to three months.Ukrainian baked rice pudding with apples, cinnamon and raisinsView image in fullscreenPrep5 minCook1 hrServes4200glong-grain rice750mlwhole milkA pinch of salt50gunsalted butter,plus extra for greasing and dotting2 medium apples (gala,cox’s, braeburn, for example),cored and diced50graisinsZest of 1 medium orange1 tsp ground cinnamon,plus extra for dusting2 large eggs50gcastersugar1 tsp vanilla extractRinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear. Then, in a saucepan, combine the rice with the milk and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 18–20 minutes, until the rice is soft and creamy and most of the milk has been absorbed. It might feel like a lot of milk at first, but it will work.Meanwhile, melt the butter in a frying pan and saute the diced apples with the raisins, orange zest and cinnamon for five to seven minutes, until slightly softened. In a large bowl, beat the eggs with the sugar and vanilla extract.When the rice is cooked, let it cool slightly before stirring it into the egg mixture, followed by the sauteed apples, raisins and orange zest, until well combined.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/400F/gas 6 and grease a 20cm × 30cm ovenproof dish with butter. Pour the rice mixture into the dish, smoothing the top and dotting with small pieces of butter. Bake for 30–40 minutes, until the top is golden and set. Cool slightly before serving, dusted with extra cinnamon, if desired.Lozhka by Alissa Timoshkina is published in October by Quadrille at £28.
